0.why: An FDE lands on customer infrastructure you did not build: a bastion host, an air-gapped VM, a pod with no pip and no internet, where the only tooling guaranteed to exist is bash plus coreutils. The glue you write on-site during week one (data loads, migration runners, log triage, deploy hooks, cron jobs) becomes the customer's production overnight, and a script that exits 0 on partial failure silently corrupts their data and your credibility in the same afternoon. You also inherit the customer's own scripts and must read, debug and harden them live, in front of their engineers, without looking anything up.
prerequisites: Comfortable navigating a terminal: cd, ls, cat, less, man, pipes and redirection at a basic level
Knows what a process, PID, parent/child, stdin/stdout/stderr and an environment variable are (the later Track A topics on processes, signals and networking build on this)
Basic regular expressions (character classes, anchors, groups) as used by grep -E
git basics (clone, branch, commit, push) so the deliverable and proof-of-work can live in a repo with CI
bash 4+ installed locally (macOS ships 3.2; brew install bash) and a Linux VM or container to test portability
Understands what an HTTP API call with a bearer token is, since the research-script rewrite will call one

subtopics.name: Execution model and the exit-status contract
subtopics.learn: Trace how a line becomes a process: alias, then function, then builtin, then PATH lookup (`type -a cmd`, `command -v cmd`, `hash -r` after installing a binary), then fork+exec; understand why `cd` and `export` must be builtins and why `exec cmd` as the last line of an entrypoint replaces the shell so PID 1 receives signals directly. Know the exit-status contract cold: 0 success, 1-125 yours, 126 found but not executable, 127 not found, 128+N killed by signal N (130 SIGINT, 137 SIGKILL, 143 SIGTERM), and that `$?` is overwritten by every command including `[ ]`. Adopt sysexits conventions (64 usage, 65 bad input data, 69 service unavailable, 70 internal error, 75 temporary failure, retry) so cron, CI and other scripts can branch on your codes.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Exit Status

subtopics.name: Quoting, word splitting and the -- guard
subtopics.learn: Internalise the expansion order (brace, tilde, parameter, command substitution, arithmetic, word splitting on IFS, pathname expansion, quote removal) so you can predict what `$var`, `"$var"`, `$@`, `"$@"` and `$*` each produce when the value contains spaces, `*`, or a leading `-`. Rule: every expansion is double-quoted unless you can say why not; iterate lists with `"${arr[@]}"`, never `for f in $(ls)` or `$(find ...)`, and terminate option parsing with `--` before user-supplied paths (`rm -- "$f"`, `grep -e "$pat" -- "$file"`). Build a hostile fixture directory with `touch -- '-rf' 'a b' $'new\nline' '*'` and prove your script survives it; use `printf '%q'` when you must serialise a value back into a shell command line.

resource.label: ShellCheck wiki - SC2086 Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting

subtopics.name: Strict mode: what -e, -u and pipefail actually do, and where they lie
subtopics.learn: `set -e` exits on a failing simple command but is suppressed inside `if`/`while`/`until` conditions, on the left of `&&`/`||`, in every pipeline stage except the last (without pipefail), and inside `$(...)` in an assignment unless `shopt -s inherit_errexit`; a function invoked from a condition runs with -e disabled for its entire body. `set -u` makes an unset expansion fatal, so write `${VAR:-}` or `${VAR:?message}` deliberately, and know that `$1` with no args and `"${arr[@]}"` on an empty array (bash < 4.4) both trip it. `set -o pipefail` returns the rightmost non-zero status of a pipeline; combine as `set -Eeuo pipefail` (`-E` so ERR traps fire inside functions) and still write explicit `cmd || die 'msg'` on every step that matters, because -e is a safety net, not the design.

resource.label: Greg's Wiki BashFAQ/105 - Why doesn't set -e do what I expected?

subtopics.name: Traps: EXIT, ERR, INT/TERM and cleanup that always runs
subtopics.learn: Register `trap cleanup EXIT` immediately after creating anything that needs undoing (temp dirs, lock fds, background PIDs); EXIT fires on normal completion, `exit N`, and after a caught signal, but never on SIGKILL or a dead host, so cleanup must also be idempotent on the next start. Use `trap 'on_err $? $LINENO "$BASH_COMMAND"' ERR` with `set -E` to log the failing command and line, and `trap 'exit 130' INT` / `trap 'exit 143' TERM` so the EXIT trap still runs and the parent sees the conventional status; a trap that swallows a signal without exiting turns Ctrl-C into a hang. Save `$?` on the first line of the EXIT handler before anything clobbers it, inspect with `trap -p`, reset with `trap - INT`, and remember traps are not inherited by subshells or `$(...)`.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Bourne Shell Builtins (trap)

subtopics.name: getopts, usage() and CLI ergonomics
subtopics.learn: Parse flags with `while getopts ':hvo:n:' opt; do case $opt in o) out=$OPTARG;; :) die "-$OPTARG requires a value";; \\?) usage >&2; exit 64;; esac; done; shift $((OPTIND-1))` - the leading `:` in the optstring puts getopts in silent mode so you own the error text. Write `usage()` with a one-line synopsis, every flag with its default, honoured env vars and exit codes; `-h` prints to stdout and exits 0, errors print to stderr and exit 64, and required-argument checks happen after the loop (`[[ -n ${out:-} ]] || { usage >&2; exit 64; }`). Read secrets from env or a `--token-file`, never argv (visible in `ps` and trace logs); long options are not in getopts, so either add a `case "$1" in --output=*)` pre-loop or accept that a tool with many long flags is a Python argparse job.

resource.label: POSIX.1-2017 Shell & Utilities - getopts

subtopics.name: Parameter expansion instead of forking sed and basename
subtopics.learn: Use `${x:-default}`, `${x:=default}`, `${x:?error text}` and `${x:+alt}` for defaults and required-var checks; `${path##*/}` (basename), `${path%/*}` (dirname), `${f%.*}` / `${f##*.}` (strip or get extension), `${s//pat/rep}` for global replace, `${s^^}` / `${s,,}` for case (bash 4+), `${#s}` for length, `${s:off:len}` for slicing, `${@:2}` to drop the first positional. Know that `${x-d}` triggers only when unset while `${x:-d}` also triggers on empty, and that the patterns are globs, not regex. Every one of these in a loop body replaces a fork+exec of `sed`, `cut` or `basename`, which is the difference between 2 seconds and 2 minutes on a 100k-line file on an underpowered customer jump host.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Shell Parameter Expansion

subtopics.name: Arrays, mapfile and the read -r loop
subtopics.learn: Build lists with `arr=()`, `arr+=("$item")`, iterate `"${arr[@]}"`, count `${#arr[@]}`, list indices `${!arr[@]}`, and use `declare -A map` for associative lookups with `[[ -v map[$k] ]]` to test presence. Read files line by line with `while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do ...; done < "$file"` (`-r` stops backslash mangling, the `|| [[ -n ]]` catches a final line without a newline), slurp with `mapfile -t lines < <(cmd)`, and consume `find -print0` with `while IFS= read -r -d '' f`. `cmd | while read` runs the loop body in a subshell so counters and arrays set inside vanish afterwards - fix with `done < <(cmd)` process substitution or `shopt -s lastpipe`.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Arrays

subtopics.name: Conditionals: [[ ]], (( )), case and =~
subtopics.learn: Prefer `[[ ]]` over `[ ]` in bash scripts: no word splitting inside, `&&`/`||` work, unquoted right-hand `==` does glob matching (quote it for a literal compare), and `=~` does ERE with captures in `BASH_REMATCH[n]` (store the regex in a variable to sidestep quoting bugs). Know the file tests ops scripts actually need: `-e -f -d -L -r -w -x -s`, `-nt`/`-ot`, `-v var` (is set), `-z`/`-n`, and use `(( n > 0 ))` for integers because `[[ $n > 0 ]]` is a string comparison. Dispatch on strings and globs with `case` (`*.csv|*.tsv)`), and use `;;&` / `;&` fall-through only with a comment justifying it.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Bash Conditional Expressions

subtopics.name: Redirection, file descriptors and a real log() function
subtopics.learn: Master the ordering rule: `cmd >file 2>&1` sends both streams to the file, `cmd 2>&1 >file` does not; all diagnostics go to `>&2` so stdout stays a clean data channel for the next pipe stage. Open a dedicated descriptor for logs (`exec 3>>"$LOG"`) and write `log() { printf '%(%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z)T %-5s %s\n' -1 "$1" "${*:2}" >&3; }` (bash 4.2+ `%(...)T` avoids forking `date`), or mirror everything with `exec > >(tee -a "$LOG") 2>&1` at the top; add `exec </dev/null` in cron scripts so nothing blocks waiting on a TTY. Gate verbosity on `LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-info}`, ship to syslog/journald with `logger -t "$prog"` when you cannot copy files off a customer host, and redact tokens before they reach any log line.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Redirections

subtopics.name: Pipelines, process substitution and SIGPIPE (exit 141)
subtopics.learn: `$(...)` strips all trailing newlines and runs in a subshell; `<(cmd)` yields a path you can hand to programs that need two inputs (`diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`) and `>(cmd)` feeds output to a process with no temp file. Capture per-stage status with `status=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")` on the very next line (any command clobbers it). Understand exit 141: with pipefail, `producer | head -1` fails because `head` closes the pipe and the producer dies of SIGPIPE - handle by consuming fully, checking `${PIPESTATUS[0]} -eq 141`, or restructuring with `awk 'NR==1{print; exit}'` style consumers. Note that pipefail is what finally makes `cmd | tee log` report `cmd`'s failure instead of `tee`'s success.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Pipelines

subtopics.name: Temp files, atomic writes, flock and restartability
subtopics.learn: Create scratch space with `tmp=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/$prog.XXXXXX")` and remove it in the EXIT trap; never write output in place - write `"$out.tmp.$$"` on the same filesystem and `mv -f` onto the target so readers see the old file or the new one, never a truncated one. Prevent overlapping runs with `exec 9>"/var/lock/$prog.lock"; flock -n 9 || { log warn 'already running'; exit 75; }` - the kernel releases the lock when the process dies, unlike a PID file that goes stale after `kill -9`. Make batch work restartable with a checkpoint (a `last_id` file or a `done/<id>` marker per item) so a mid-run crash plus a rerun converges instead of double-inserting rows into the customer's table.

resource.label: man7.org - flock(1)

subtopics.name: Concurrency: background jobs, wait, xargs -P and timeouts
subtopics.learn: Fan out with `work "$item" & pids+=($!)` and collect each result with `for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || failed+=("$p"); done`; `wait -n` (bash 4.3+) lets you keep exactly N jobs in flight. For lists use `printf '%s\0' "${items[@]}" | xargs -0 -P 8 -n 1 -I{} bash -c 'work "$1"' _ {}` and know xargs exits 123 when any invocation failed. Wrap every network or DB call in `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=10 60 cmd` (exit 124 on timeout) and make the parent's INT/TERM trap `kill "${pids[@]}"` or `kill -- -$$` on the process group so children do not survive as orphans holding locks when Kubernetes or a human stops the job.

resource.label: man7.org - xargs(1)

subtopics.name: The text toolbox: grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq, cut, comm
subtopics.learn: Compose one-liners at typing speed: `grep -E -o -c -v -n -r -l`, `sed -E 's/(a)(b)/\\2\\1/'` and `sed -n '/start/,/end/p'`, `awk -F'\t' '$3 > 100 {sum+=$3} END {print sum}'`, `sort -t, -k2,2n -k1,1 | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`, `cut -d: -f1,3`, `tr -s ' ' '\n'`, `comm -23 <(sort a) <(sort b)` for set difference, `paste -sd,`, `column -t`. Know the sharp edges: `sed -i` differs between GNU (`-i`) and BSD/macOS (`-i ''`); `LC_ALL=C` makes sort and grep byte-wise and several times faster on large logs; `sort -u` dedupes on the sort key only; and the moment you need a variable or a second field, reach for awk before a bash `while read` loop.

resource.label: MIT Missing Semester - Data Wrangling

subtopics.name: curl + jq: hardened API calls from a script
subtopics.learn: Call APIs with `curl -sS --fail-with-body --retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 60 -H @headers.txt -o "$body" -w '%{http_code}'` so transient 5xx/429 are retried, non-2xx returns non-zero, and you keep the body for the error log; put the bearer token in the header file or a `-K` config, never argv. Parse with `jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .name] | @tsv'` into `while IFS=$'\t' read -r id name` loops, use `jq -e` so a null/false result exits non-zero, `--arg k "$v"` / `--argjson` to inject values safely, `-c` for one-object-per-line NDJSON, and drive pagination with `while cursor=$(jq -r '.next_cursor // empty' "$body"); [[ -n $cursor ]]`. Assert the response shape (`jq -e '.items | type == "array"' "$body"`) before anything is written downstream.

resource.label: jq Manual

subtopics.name: Debugging: bash -x, PS4, BASH_XTRACEFD and ERR context
subtopics.learn: Run `bash -n script` for a syntax check and `bash -x` for a trace, with `PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}(): '` so every traced line names file, line and function; send the trace to its own descriptor (`exec 5>trace.log; BASH_XTRACEFD=5; set -x`) so stdout data stays clean. Scope tracing to one block with `{ set -x; risky_step; set +x; } 2>/dev/null`, and keep `trap 'echo "ERR $? at ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' ERR` in production scripts. When the shell itself is not the problem, `strace -f -e trace=execve,openat -o st.log bash script` shows exactly which binaries and files were touched - usually the fastest route to a wrong PATH or missing config on a customer host.

resource.label: MIT Missing Semester - Debugging and Profiling

subtopics.name: ShellCheck as a merge gate
subtopics.learn: Run `shellcheck -S style -x -o all script.sh` locally and in CI and learn the codes you will hit weekly: SC2086 (unquoted expansion), SC2046 (unquoted `$(...)`), SC2155 (`local x=$(cmd)` masks the exit status), SC2164 (`cd` without `|| exit`), SC2115 (`rm -rf "$dir/"` when dir may be empty), SC2181 (testing `$?` instead of the command), SC2034 (unused variable, usually a typo). Silence a finding only with an inline `# shellcheck disable=SCxxxx` plus a reason on the same line, use `# shellcheck source=lib.sh` so sourced files are followed, and `# shellcheck shell=bash` when the shebang is `env`. Wire it into pre-commit and a GitHub Actions step so a customer-facing script cannot merge with warnings.

resource.label: ShellCheck wiki - checks index and directives

subtopics.name: Testing with BATS: fixtures, PATH shims and exit-code assertions
subtopics.learn: Write `@test 'fails with 64 on missing -o' { run ./tool -n 3; [ "$status" -eq 64 ]; [[ ${lines[0]} == Usage:* ]]; }` using bats-core's `run`, `$status`, `$output` and `${lines[@]}`, with `setup()`/`teardown()` building a fixture under `$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR` that includes the hostile filenames from the quoting subtopic. Stub external commands by prepending a shim directory to PATH containing fake `curl`, `psql` or `aws` scripts that assert their arguments and emit canned JSON, so the suite runs offline in CI; exercise the retry path by making the shim fail on the first N calls via a counter file. Run `bats -r tests/ --tap`, add `bats-assert` and `bats-support` for readable failures, and treat any script without a `.bats` file as unshippable.

resource.label: bats-core documentation

subtopics.name: Portability and style: bash 3.2, GNU vs BSD, sh vs dash
subtopics.learn: Ship with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and guard `((BASH_VERSINFO[0] >= 4)) || die 'bash 4+ required'` because macOS still ships 3.2 (no `mapfile`, `declare -A`, `${x,,}`, `wait -n`); on Debian/Ubuntu `#!/bin/sh` is dash, where `[[`, arrays and `local -n` do not exist, and Alpine containers run busybox ash. Keep a mental diff table for GNU vs BSD userland: `sed -i` vs `sed -i ''`, `date -d` vs `date -v`, `readlink -f` (absent on older macOS), `stat -c` vs `stat -f`, `xargs -r`, `grep -P`. Follow the Google Shell Style Guide (`main "$@"` last, `local` everything, `readonly` constants, `snake_case` functions, 2-space indent) including its rule that anything past ~100 lines or needing real data structures gets rewritten in Python.

resource.label: Google Shell Style Guide

subtopics.name: Interactive fluency: readline, history and dotfiles
subtopics.learn: Work at typing speed on any customer box: `Ctrl-R` incremental search, `Ctrl-A/E/W/U/K/Y`, `Alt-.` for the last argument, `!!`, `!$`, `!:2`, `^wrong^right`, `fc` to edit the previous command in `$EDITOR`, `cd -`, `pushd`/`popd`, `Ctrl-Z`/`fg`/`bg`/`jobs`. Set `HISTSIZE=100000 HISTFILESIZE=200000 HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth:erasedups`, `shopt -s histappend`, and `HISTTIMEFORMAT='%F %T '` so you have an audit trail of exactly what you ran during an incident. Know which file loads when - `.bash_profile` for login shells, `.bashrc` for interactive non-login, `BASH_ENV` for non-interactive - so aliases you defined for yourself never leak into a script's behaviour, and keep dotfiles in a repo you can bootstrap onto a fresh host with one command.

resource.label: GNU Bash Manual - Bash Startup Files

outcomes: You can write, closed-book in under 45 minutes, a 200-line bash CLI with set -Eeuo pipefail, EXIT/ERR/INT/TERM traps, getopts with usage(), leveled logging to stderr and a log file, and it passes `shellcheck -S style -o all` with zero disables.

You can read an unfamiliar script and mark every line where set -e will not fire (conditions, &&/||, non-final pipeline stages, $(...) in assignments, functions called from tests) and rewrite each with an explicit `|| die`.

You can take a script that uses `for f in $(ls)` and unquoted variables and make it pass a fixture directory containing filenames with spaces, newlines, globs and a leading dash, verified by a BATS test.

You can make a batch job idempotent and restartable - mktemp + atomic mv, flock so two cron runs cannot overlap, checkpoint file - and demonstrate it by `kill -9` mid-run and rerunning to a converged result.
You can fan out 200 API calls with xargs -P or background jobs + wait, enforce a per-call timeout and a total budget, collect per-item exit codes, and ensure Ctrl-C or SIGTERM kills every child.

You can write a BATS suite that stubs curl/psql via PATH shims and asserts exit code, stdout and stderr for the success, usage-error, upstream-failure and retry paths, running offline in GitHub Actions.
You can locate the failing line in a 300-line script on a host you have never seen using only PS4 with BASH_SOURCE/LINENO, BASH_XTRACEFD and an ERR trap, without polluting the script's stdout.
You can state, for any given script, whether it will run on macOS bash 3.2, Debian dash and Alpine busybox, name the constructs that break it, and either fix them or justify requiring bash 4+.
failureModes: The nightly loader has `set -e` but its critical step is `extract | tee extract.log`; without pipefail the pipeline exits 0 when extract fails, the empty file loads cleanly, and cron reports success for three weeks before the customer notices stale dashboards.

A cleanup trap runs `rm -rf "$WORKDIR/"` and WORKDIR is unset because the config file failed to source earlier; without `set -u` or `${WORKDIR:?}` the expansion becomes `/` and the script wipes the host it is running on.

A script developed against tidy test data uses `for f in $(find $dir -name '*.csv')`; the customer's export directory has filenames with spaces, so half the files are split into non-existent paths and skipped silently while the summary line still says 'processed N files'.

A 5-minute cron job has no flock and no timeout; one run stalls on a hung upstream API, the next twelve runs stack up, and the customer's database connection pool is exhausted by your script rather than their application.

A script written on a Mac uses `mapfile`, `declare -A` and `sed -i ''`; it fails with 'command not found' on the customer's RHEL bastion, or the reverse - `sed -i ''` on GNU sed treats the empty string as a filename and edits nothing.

The bearer token is passed as `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"` while `set -x` is on for debugging; the token lands in the trace log, which is shipped to the customer's central log store and read by everyone with Kibana access.

`psql ... | while read -r id; do count=$((count+1)); done` runs the loop in a subshell, so the final report says '0 rows migrated' and the on-call engineer rolls back a migration that actually succeeded.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what `set -euo pipefail` does, then give me three concrete cases where `set -e` will not stop the script. How would you structure a script so it is correct even if -e were removed?

Design: you need a nightly job on a customer's bastion that pulls 50k records from a paginated REST API, transforms them, and loads them into Postgres. Only bash, curl, jq and psql are available. How do you make it idempotent, restartable after a crash, observable, and safe if cron fires it twice concurrently?

Debug: a cron job's log says 'done' every night but the target table has not updated in three weeks. The script is 300 lines of bash written by someone who has left. Where do you look first, what tools do you use and in what order, and how do you avoid making it worse while you investigate?

A script has a `trap cleanup EXIT` and three background `curl` jobs. The user presses Ctrl-C. Which processes receive SIGINT, which do not, what does the EXIT trap see in `$?`, and how do you guarantee the children die with the parent?

When do you refuse to write something in bash and reach for Python? Name the specific signals in the requirements that trip that decision, and how you would explain the trade-off to a customer engineer who insists on 'just a shell script'.

How do you test a bash script that calls curl, psql and the aws CLI without touching real services? Describe the test structure, how you fake the external commands, how you exercise the retry and failure paths, and what runs in CI.

Your script works on your MacBook and fails on the customer's Ubuntu host - or the other way around. Explain the portability landscape (bash 3.2 vs 5, GNU vs BSD coreutils, sh as dash, busybox) and what policy you would set for scripts shipped to customers.
0.proofOfWork: A public repo `shell-hardening-kata` containing a deliberately broken 80-line 'legacy' script that exhibits the seven failure modes above, a fixture generator that reproduces each one (hostile filenames, unset config var, a `sleep`-based hung upstream, two concurrent invocations, a Mac-only construct), and a hardened rewrite in `bin/` that passes every reproduction. The repo runs `shellcheck -S style -o all` and a BATS suite with PATH-shimmed curl/psql in a GitHub Actions matrix across bash 3.2, bash 5 and dash (for the POSIX-only helper), plus a one-page BASH-HARDENING-CHECKLIST.md written for a customer's platform team. The README includes the closed-book timing: you wrote the 200-line template from memory, timed, and diffed it against the reference with the delta listed.

1.topic: Linux internals: processes, systemd, permissions, filesystems, packaging
1.why: An FDE is the person standing in the customer's VPC at 6pm when the model-serving box stops answering, and the fix is almost never in the Python. It is a systemd unit that hit its start-limit, a service account that cannot read the TLS key, a deleted log file still pinned open by a process, or an OOM kill nobody noticed because Restart=always hid it. Being able to read /proc, journald and the cgroup tree directly, and to explain the exact chain from power-on to a socket accepting traffic, is what lets you debug on a locked-down customer host with no APM, no root shell to the container runtime, and a nervous platform team watching.
prerequisites: Comfortable in a shell: pipes, redirection, exit codes, job control (Ctrl-Z, bg, fg, &), and reading man pages — topic 0 'Shell mastery and scripting'
Basic SSH usage with key-based auth, and a Hetzner (or any) VPS you can root and rebuild freely
Understanding of what a process, a file descriptor and a socket are at the C-API level (open/read/write/close, fork/exec) even if you have never written C
Python 3.11+ with venv and pip, and a small HTTP app (FastAPI/uvicorn or http.server) to use as the guinea-pig service
Enough of TCP/HTTP to know what 'listening on 0.0.0.0:8000' means; the deeper networking material is topic 2, so do not block on it

subtopics.name: Boot chain: firmware to PID 1 to your service
subtopics.learn: Trace the full path on your VPS: UEFI/BIOS loads GRUB from the ESP, GRUB loads vmlinuz plus initramfs and passes the kernel command line (read it with `cat /proc/cmdline`; note `root=UUID=...`, `ro`, `console=`), the initramfs mounts the real root and does switch_root, then the kernel execs /sbin/init which is systemd. Then systemd walks default.target -> multi-user.target -> your unit. Use `systemd-analyze`, `systemd-analyze blame`, `systemd-analyze critical-chain your.service`, and `journalctl -b -1 -p err` to see the previous boot's failures. Know why a wrong root= UUID or a missing virtio module in the initramfs drops you into emergency.target with no network.

resource.label: bootup(7) — systemd boot process man page

subtopics.name: systemd units, targets and the dependency graph
subtopics.learn: Understand unit search path precedence (/etc/systemd/system overrides /run/systemd/system overrides /usr/lib/systemd/system) and drop-in overrides in foo.service.d/*.conf via `systemctl edit`. Distinguish ordering (After=, Before=) from requirement (Wants=, Requires=, BindsTo=, PartOf=) and why After=network-online.target without Wants=network-online.target does nothing. Know WantedBy=multi-user.target in [Install], what `systemctl enable` actually does (creates a symlink in .wants/), and that `systemctl daemon-reload` is required after any unit edit. Inspect with `systemctl cat`, `systemctl show -p`, `systemctl list-dependencies --reverse`, `systemd-analyze verify unit.service`.

resource.label: systemd.unit(5) — unit file syntax, dependencies, search paths

subtopics.name: Writing a production service unit: Type=, Restart=, timeouts
subtopics.learn: Choose Type= correctly: simple (fires 'started' immediately), exec (waits for execve to succeed, so a bad ExecStart path fails loudly), notify (process calls sd_notify READY=1, the only way systemd knows you are actually serving), forking (legacy daemons, needs PIDFile=), oneshot (with RemainAfterExit=). Configure Restart=on-failure vs always, RestartSec=, and the start-rate limiter (StartLimitIntervalSec=, StartLimitBurst=) that produces the 'start request repeated too quickly' failure. Set TimeoutStartSec=, TimeoutStopSec=, KillMode=mixed vs control-group, KillSignal=, and ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID. Use ExecStartPre= for migrations and WatchdogSec= with periodic WATCHDOG=1 notifications for hang detection.

resource.label: systemd.service(5) — service unit options

subtopics.name: Sandboxing the service with systemd.exec directives
subtopics.learn: Run as a dedicated account with User=/Group= (or DynamicUser=yes for stateless services), and lock down with NoNewPrivileges=yes, ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=yes, PrivateTmp=yes, PrivateDevices=yes, ProtectKernelTunables=yes, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX, SystemCallFilter=@system-service, and CapabilityBoundingSet= with AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind :443 without root. Under ProtectSystem=strict the whole tree is read-only, so declare StateDirectory=, LogsDirectory=, RuntimeDirectory=, CacheDirectory= (systemd creates and chowns them) or ReadWritePaths=. Score your unit with `systemd-analyze security your.service` and get it below 3.0. Know that MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes breaks some JIT/ffi libraries and how to spot the EPERM in strace.

resource.label: systemd.exec(5) — execution environment and sandboxing options

subtopics.name: cgroups v2 resource control from systemd
subtopics.learn: Set MemoryMax= (hard, triggers cgroup OOM), MemoryHigh= (throttle first), CPUQuota=200%, CPUWeight=, TasksMax=, IOWeight= in the [Service] section and see them land in the unified hierarchy under /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/your.service/ (memory.max, cpu.max, pids.max). Read memory.current, memory.events (the oom_kill counter is your OOM evidence), cpu.stat (nr_throttled), and pids.current. Use `systemd-cgls` and `systemd-cgtop` to see the tree live, and `systemctl set-property --runtime` to change limits without restart. Know the default TasksMax (often 15% of pid_max, around 4915) silently kills thread-heavy Python workers with 'Resource temporarily unavailable'.

resource.label: systemd.resource-control(5) — cgroup settings on units

subtopics.name: journald: querying, persistence, rate limits
subtopics.learn: Master the query flags: `journalctl -u app -f`, `-b`, `-b -1`, `-p err..alert`, `--since '-15m'`, `-k` (kernel ring buffer), `_PID=`, `_SYSTEMD_UNIT=`, `-o json-pretty` for structured fields, `--disk-usage`, `--vacuum-size=1G`. Make the journal survive reboots with Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (or by creating /var/log/journal) and understand RateLimitIntervalSec=/RateLimitBurst= which silently drop bursty logs with a single 'Suppressed N messages' line. For Python set Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 or stdout is block-buffered and your logs arrive minutes late or not at all on crash; use SyslogIdentifier= to make -t filtering work.

resource.label: journalctl(1) — journal query and maintenance

subtopics.name: Process lifecycle: fork/exec, exit status, zombies, reaping
subtopics.learn: Walk fork -> execve -> _exit -> parent wait4 and how the 8-bit exit status is encoded (systemd shows 'status=1/FAILURE' vs 'signal=KILL'; a shell reports 128+signum). Understand a zombie is an exited child whose parent has not called wait(): it holds only a PID slot, cannot be killed, and accumulates until pid_max is exhausted. Orphans reparent to PID 1 or the nearest PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER. Read `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,wchan:20,etime,cmd` and the STAT letters (R S D Z T, plus s for session leader, l for multithreaded, + foreground). Use `pstree -p -s PID` to see ancestry. Know why a service that daemonises with a double fork loses systemd's main-PID tracking unless Type=forking and PIDFile= are set.

resource.label: wait(2) — wait for process state change; zombie semantics

subtopics.name: Signals and graceful shutdown under systemd
subtopics.learn: Know the default dispositions and meanings of SIGTERM, SIGKILL (uncatchable), SIGHUP (reload convention), SIGINT, SIGUSR1/2, SIGPIPE and SIGCHLD. Trace systemd's stop sequence: KillSignal (SIGTERM) to the control group, wait TimeoutStopSec (default 90s), then SIGKILL; FinalKillSignal and SendSIGHUP=. Implement a handler in Python (`signal.signal(SIGTERM, ...)` or `loop.add_signal_handler`) that stops accepting, drains in-flight requests and exits 0. Understand signal masks (SigBlk/SigIgn in /proc/PID/status) and the classic bug: `ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'python app.py'` means SIGTERM hits sh, which does not forward it; fix with `exec` or by removing the shell. Use `systemctl kill -s SIGUSR1 app` to poke a live process.

resource.label: signal(7) — overview of signals, dispositions, delivery

subtopics.name: Diagnosing a stuck process from /proc
subtopics.learn: Be able to triage a hung PID with nothing but /proc: /proc/PID/status (State, Threads, VmRSS, SigBlk, voluntary_ctxt_switches — if not changing, the process is not being scheduled), /proc/PID/wchan and /proc/PID/stack (root only; the kernel function it is sleeping in — an NFS or io_schedule frame means D state, uninterruptible, kill -9 will not work), /proc/PID/fd and fdinfo (what it is blocked on; compare count against /proc/PID/limits), /proc/PID/task/*/stat for per-thread state, /proc/PID/io (is it still doing I/O?), /proc/PID/cwd and /proc/PID/exe (a '(deleted)' suffix means the binary was replaced under it), /proc/PID/environ and /proc/PID/cgroup. Confirm with `strace -f -tt -p PID` (a blocked futex vs read vs connect tells you the layer) and `py-spy dump --pid PID` for the Python stack. Note /proc/loadavg counts D-state tasks, so 'high load, idle CPU' means I/O or NFS.

resource.label: proc(5) — the /proc filesystem, per-process files

subtopics.name: Memory accounting and the OOM killer
subtopics.learn: Read /proc/meminfo correctly: MemAvailable, not MemFree, is what matters, and page cache counted as 'used' is reclaimable. Distinguish VSZ, RSS and PSS (/proc/PID/smaps_rollup) and why RSS overcounts shared libraries across gunicorn workers. Understand vm.overcommit_memory (0 heuristic, 1 always, 2 strict with vm.overcommit_ratio) and vm.swappiness. Know the two OOM killers: the global one (evidence in `journalctl -k` as 'Out of memory: Killed process', victim chosen by oom_score which you shape with OOMScoreAdjust= or /proc/PID/oom_score_adj) and the cgroup one from MemoryMax= (evidence in memory.events oom_kill). Configure OOMPolicy= so one killed worker takes the whole unit down and gets a clean Restart= rather than limping.

resource.label: Kernel docs: /proc/sys/vm tunables (overcommit, swappiness, oom)

subtopics.name: Users, groups, sudo and service accounts
subtopics.learn: Read /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group; know the system UID range (<1000, from /etc/login.defs) and create a locked service account with `useradd --system --no-create-home --home-dir /var/lib/app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app`. Understand primary vs supplementary groups (`id`, `getent group`, `usermod -aG`, and why new group membership needs a re-login or `newgrp`). Write sudo rules in /etc/sudoers.d/ via `visudo -f`, scope NOPASSWD to exact commands (`deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart app.service`), and audit with `sudo -l -U user`. Know that membership in docker, disk or adm is root-equivalent, and that `PermitRootLogin no` plus `PasswordAuthentication no` in sshd_config is the first hardening step on any customer VPS.

resource.label: sudoers(5) — sudo policy syntax and defaults

subtopics.name: Permissions, special bits, umask, ACLs and capabilities
subtopics.learn: Go beyond rwx/octal: x on a directory means traverse, r means list; setgid on a directory (chmod 2775) makes new files inherit the group, sticky (1777 on /tmp) stops deleting others' files, setuid binaries are how passwd and sudo work (`find / -perm -4000`). Understand umask (022 vs 027, and UMask= in the unit, since systemd ignores the shell's). Use `stat`, `getfacl`, `setfacl -m u:app:r-- /etc/app/cert.pem`, default ACLs on directories (`setfacl -d`), and `chattr +i`/`lsattr` for immutable files. Know Linux capabilities as the alternative to root: `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep` on a binary versus AmbientCapabilities= in the unit, and why file capabilities are lost on copy and on Python interpreters (they are on the interpreter, not the script).

resource.label: capabilities(7) — Linux capability model and list

subtopics.name: Filesystem layout, block devices, mounts and fstab
subtopics.learn: Know the FHS well enough to place things correctly: /etc for config, /var/lib/app for state, /var/log for logs, /run (tmpfs) for PID files and sockets, /opt/app or /usr/local for your code, /srv for served data. Inspect storage with `lsblk -f`, `blkid`, `findmnt`, `df -hT`, `df -i`. Read and write fstab: UUID= or PARTUUID= (never /dev/sdX), fs type, options (defaults, noatime, nofail, x-systemd.automount, x-systemd.device-timeout=), dump and pass fields, and understand systemd-fstab-generator turns each line into a .mount unit. Practise attaching a Hetzner volume, `mkfs.ext4 -L data`, mounting it with nofail, and growing it online with `resize2fs` (or `xfs_growfs`). Know that a missing nofail on a detached volume drops the box into emergency mode at boot.

resource.label: fstab(5) — static filesystem table fields and options

subtopics.name: Inodes, links, deleted-but-open files, disk-full forensics
subtopics.learn: Understand that a filename is a directory entry pointing at an inode, so hard links share the inode (`ln`, `stat -c '%i %h'`), symlinks are separate inodes holding a path (`readlink -f`), and rm only decrements the link count — the blocks are freed when the last reference, including open file descriptors, goes away. This is why df says 100% while du says 60%: find the culprit with `find /proc/*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' 2>/dev/null` or `lsof +L1`, and free space by truncating (`: > /proc/PID/fd/N`) or restarting the process. Never rm a live log; truncate it or use logrotate with copytruncate. Check inode exhaustion with `df -i` (millions of session files or mail spool), reserved blocks with `tune2fs -l | grep Reserved`, and locate usage fast with `du -xsh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h`.

resource.label: inode(7) — file inode fields, link counts, timestamps

subtopics.name: Packaging: apt/dpkg, repositories, pinning, unattended upgrades
subtopics.learn: Separate the layers: dpkg installs .deb files and tracks state in /var/lib/dpkg/status (`dpkg -l`, `dpkg -L pkg`, `dpkg -S /path/to/file`, `dpkg -i`), apt resolves dependencies from indices (`apt update` refreshes indices only; `apt upgrade` vs `apt full-upgrade`; `apt-cache policy pkg` shows candidate and pin). Add third-party repos the modern way: deb822 files in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/*.sources with Signed-By: pointing at a keyring in /etc/apt/keyrings (apt-key is dead), and pin with /etc/apt/preferences.d/ so a vendor repo cannot replace libc. Hold with `apt-mark hold`, run non-interactively with `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold`, and configure unattended-upgrades for security-only with a reboot window. Know the dpkg lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend) and how a stuck unattended-upgrades run blocks your deploy.

resource.label: Debian Administrator's Handbook — Maintenance and Updates: The APT Tools

subtopics.name: Deploying the Python service: venv, lockfile, systemd, secrets
subtopics.learn: Never pip install into the system interpreter (PEP 668 'externally-managed-environment' exists for a reason; apt owns /usr/lib/python3). Build an isolated tree: `python3 -m venv /opt/app/venv`, install from a pinned requirements file (`pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`, or a uv/pip-tools lock), and point ExecStart at /opt/app/venv/bin/python -m app or venv/bin/uvicorn directly, with WorkingDirectory= and Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. Load config from EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/env owned root:app mode 0640, and pass real secrets with LoadCredential=api_key:/etc/credstore/api_key (read from $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, never visible in `systemctl show-environment` or /proc/PID/environ). Deploy atomically: install into a new release directory, flip a symlink, `systemctl restart`, because pip-upgrading in place under a running process produces ImportError mid-request.

resource.label: Python docs: venv — creation of virtual environments

subtopics.name: Dynamic linking, PATH and the 'works in my shell, dies under systemd' class
subtopics.learn: Understand that systemd starts services with a minimal environment (PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin, no HOME unless User= is set, no LANG), so anything that worked in your login shell because of ~/.bashrc will fail; compare with `systemctl show-environment` and `cat /proc/PID/environ | tr '\0' '\n'`. Debug shared-library failures with `ldd /opt/app/venv/bin/python`, `objdump -p binary | grep NEEDED`, /etc/ld.so.conf.d/ plus `ldconfig -p`, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH via Environment= (not exported in the unit's shell, because there is no shell). Know that Python wheels are tagged manylinux_2_28 etc. against a glibc version (`ldd --version`), which is why a wheel built on Ubuntu 24.04 will not load on a customer's RHEL 8 box ('GLIBC_2.34 not found').

resource.label: ld.so(8) — dynamic linker search order and environment

subtopics.name: Kernel tunables and per-process limits
subtopics.learn: Persist kernel parameters in /etc/sysctl.d/99-app.conf and apply with `sysctl --system`; know the ones that bite services: fs.file-max, fs.inotify.max_user_watches (uvicorn --reload, file watchers), net.core.somaxconn (accept backlog cap), net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, vm.max_map_count (Elasticsearch, some ML runtimes), kernel.pid_max. Separate these from per-process rlimits: /etc/security/limits.conf only applies to PAM logins, so for a systemd service you must set LimitNOFILE=65536, LimitNPROC=, LimitCORE= in the unit and verify with `cat /proc/PID/limits` or `prlimit --pid PID`. Recognise EMFILE ('Too many open files') and 'Cannot allocate memory' from RLIMIT_NPROC as limit failures, not bugs.

resource.label: sysctl.d(5) — persistent kernel parameter configuration

subtopics.name: systemd timers instead of cron
subtopics.learn: Pair a oneshot .service with a .timer using OnCalendar= (`systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:00'` to validate), Persistent=true so a missed run fires at next boot, RandomizedDelaySec= to avoid thundering herds, and OnBootSec=/OnUnitActiveSec= for monotonic schedules. Inspect with `systemctl list-timers --all` and see output in the journal with the same -u filter as any service, with the unit's User=, sandboxing and resource limits applied — none of which cron gives you. Use `systemd-run --on-active=30s --unit=oneoff /path/cmd` for ad-hoc scheduled jobs on a customer box you must not leave cron entries on.

resource.label: systemd.timer(5) — timer unit configuration

outcomes: You can narrate, without notes, the boot-to-traffic chain on your VPS from GRUB through initramfs, systemd targets and unit activation to the socket accept, and back each step with a command that shows it (`/proc/cmdline`, `systemd-analyze critical-chain`, `ss -ltnp`).

You can write a systemd unit for a Python HTTP service that scores under 3.0 on `systemd-analyze security`, runs as a non-root account, binds :443 via AmbientCapabilities, survives SIGTERM with a graceful drain, and restarts on failure without tripping the start-rate limiter.

Given only a PID on a host you have never seen, you can determine within five minutes whether it is CPU-bound, blocked on I/O in D state, waiting on a futex/socket, a zombie, or stopped, using /proc/PID/{status,wchan,stack,fd,task} and strace, and say which of those kill -9 will not fix.

You can prove an OOM kill happened, name the victim and the killer (global vs cgroup) from `journalctl -k` and memory.events, and explain which MemoryMax/OOMScoreAdjust/OOMPolicy change would have altered the outcome.
You can resolve a 'disk 100% full but du disagrees' incident by locating deleted-but-open files via /proc/*/fd and truncating through the fd, and explain to the customer why rm did not free space.

You can add a vendor apt repository with a deb822 .sources file, Signed-By keyring and a pin so it cannot upgrade core packages, and run the install non-interactively in a script that does not hang on a dpkg lock or a debconf prompt.

You can list at least six differences between the environment of a login shell and a systemd service (PATH, HOME, umask, rlimits, cgroup, capabilities) and diagnose 'works in my shell, fails under systemd' from `systemctl show-environment` and /proc/PID/environ.

You can move a stateful directory to a newly attached cloud volume with an fstab entry that uses UUID= and nofail, grow it online, and reboot with confidence that a detached volume will not block boot.
failureModes: A service is deployed with Restart=always and MemoryMax=; it OOMs every 40 seconds and restarts, so health checks flap green and nobody notices for a week until memory.events shows oom_kill in the thousands.

ExecStart wraps the app in `/bin/sh -c`, so on `systemctl stop` SIGTERM reaches sh and is never forwarded; after TimeoutStopSec the whole cgroup gets SIGKILL and in-flight customer requests are dropped on every deploy.

Logs are rotated with rm plus a new file; the process keeps the deleted inode open, /var fills to 100%, df and du disagree by 40 GB, and the on-call engineer expands the volume instead of truncating the fd.
A vendor repo (NVIDIA, Docker, a database) is added with no pin; `apt upgrade` pulls a newer libssl or systemd from it, and the customer's compliance-scanned baseline drifts with no change record.

The unit says After=network.target but not network-online.target, so on cold boot the app starts before DHCP finishes, fails DNS on its first outbound call, exits 1, and the start-rate limiter leaves it dead until someone runs `systemctl reset-failed`.

TLS key is 0600 root:root and the service runs as User=app; it worked in testing because the engineer ran it with sudo. On the first real reboot the service fails with EACCES and the cert path looks correct to everyone reading the config.

A process on a customer host is in D state on a hung NFS mount; the team spends two hours running kill -9 and restarting the service before checking /proc/PID/wchan, which would have pointed at the storage team in thirty seconds.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through everything that happens between the moment a Hetzner VM is powered on and the moment a systemd-managed Python service accepts its first TCP connection. Where in that chain would a missing initramfs driver, a bad fstab entry, and a wrong ExecStart path each fail, and how would the symptoms differ?

A customer says their inference service is 'hung'. You have SSH as a non-root user with sudo, no APM, and one PID. Show me, command by command, how you decide within five minutes whether it is deadlocked in userspace, blocked in the kernel, out of file descriptors, or being CPU-throttled by its cgroup.

Design the systemd unit for a FastAPI service that needs to bind port 443, write to /var/lib/app, read a secret API key, and restart on crashes but not mask a config error. Justify every directive, and tell me which ones you would remove on a customer host running an older systemd.

df reports the root filesystem at 100% but du of / sums to 60%. Explain the mechanism, find the culprit without rebooting, and free the space without losing the process. What would you change in the deployment so it does not recur?

Explain the difference between the kernel OOM killer and a cgroup memory.max kill, how you would prove which one fired from logs and sysfs, and how OOMScoreAdjust, MemoryHigh and OOMPolicy each change the outcome for a multi-worker gunicorn service.

A deploy script that works when run by hand hangs forever when run from CI over SSH on a customer box. List the most likely causes in the apt/dpkg layer and in the environment differences, and describe how you would make the script idempotent and non-interactive.

You need to hand a customer's platform team a service they can operate without you. What do you put in the unit file, the journal configuration, and the sudoers rules so that a junior engineer can restart, read logs, and roll back safely without being able to become root?
1.proofOfWork: A public repository containing a reproducible bring-up of the hardened VPS as a single idempotent shell script (or Ansible playbook) plus a 'break/fix' lab: five scripted faults you inject on the box (a D-state simulation via a FUSE or NFS hang, a deleted-but-open log filling the disk, a zombie storm from a broken subprocess handler, an OOM under MemoryMax with Restart=always masking it, and a start-rate-limit failure from an After= without Wants= ordering bug) each paired with a screencast-free written transcript of the exact commands you ran, the /proc, journalctl and cgroup evidence you collected, the root cause, and the one-line fix. The README ends with the unit file's `systemd-analyze security` output under 3.0 and a table of every systemd directive used and why it is there.

2.topic: Networking: TCP/IP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, load balancers, firewalls
2.why: An FDE ships into networks the customer owns: corporate forward proxies, TLS-intercepting appliances, private DNS, egress allowlists, and load balancers someone else configured years ago. The first week of almost every deployment produces a ticket that is really a network problem in disguise (the webhook never arrives, the cert chain is incomplete, a 60-second idle timeout kills a long model call) and the engagement stalls until someone can isolate the layer with dig, curl -v, ss and tcpdump and explain the evidence to the client's network team in their own vocabulary. That person has to be you, because you are the only engineer in the room who owns both the application and the delivery.
prerequisites: Shell fluency from 'Shell mastery and scripting' (topic 0): pipes, sudo, reading man pages, running multi-flag commands without hesitation
Linux internals from topic 1: systemd units, journalctl, /proc, and the capabilities model (tcpdump needs root or CAP_NET_RAW)
A Linux VPS you control with a public IPv4 and a domain whose DNS records you can edit (the Hetzner box from topic 1)
Python 3: bytes versus str, context managers, exceptions, and a first exposure to asyncio (async def / await)
Having written at least one HTTP endpoint (Flask/FastAPI) and called at least one third-party API with requests or httpx
Comfort reading hex and binary: you know what a byte, a port and an IPv4 address are and can convert 0x01BB to 443

subtopics.name: Latency, bandwidth and the hop-by-hop request trace
subtopics.learn: Know the four latency components (propagation, transmission, processing, queuing) and why round trips, not bandwidth, dominate small API calls: Mumbai to us-east-1 is roughly 200 ms RTT, so a TLS 1.2 connection burns about three RTTs before the first byte. Be able to draw the canonical trace for https://api.example.com from memory: stub resolver, recursive resolver, root/TLD/authoritative, TCP three-way handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP request, load balancer, backend, with an RTT count on every arrow. Measure it with curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n' https://... and attribute each delta to a layer; this one-liner is the first thing you run on any 'it is slow' ticket.

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking, ch. 1: Primer on Latency and Bandwidth

subtopics.name: Host-side name resolution: the path before any packet leaves
subtopics.learn: Trace the resolver path on a Linux host: the hosts: line in /etc/nsswitch.conf (files, dns, myhostname, resolve), /etc/hosts, and /etc/resolv.conf with nameserver, search, and options ndots:5 timeout:2 attempts:2. Recognise the systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53, which makes resolv.conf lie about the real upstream (resolvectl status shows it). Understand that getaddrinfo(3) returns AAAA and A and that ndots plus the search list in Kubernetes turns one lookup into five (the .svc.cluster.local suffix chain), and that getent ahosts host exercises the libc path the application uses while dig bypasses it entirely. 'dig works but the app fails' is therefore a real, diagnosable state, not a mystery; Go and Java may also ship their own resolvers that ignore parts of this chain.

resource.label: man7: resolv.conf(5)

subtopics.name: Recursive DNS with dig: delegation, record types, TTLs, failure codes
subtopics.learn: Run dig +trace example.com and name each delegation (root, .com, authoritative), then dig @1.1.1.1 example.com A +noall +answer +comments and read status (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED), flags (qr rd ra aa) and the TTL column counting down on cached answers. Know the record types you will actually touch and their rules: A/AAAA, CNAME (cannot sit at the zone apex or alongside other records), NS, SOA (its minimum field sets the negative-cache TTL per RFC 2308), MX, TXT (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification), SRV, CAA. Understand the 512-byte UDP limit, EDNS0 buffer size, the TC bit forcing a TCP retry, and that a resolver's cached NXDOMAIN outlives your fix by up to the SOA minimum. Always check propagation from more than one public resolver (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, the customer's) rather than trusting your laptop's view.

resource.label: BIND 9 documentation: manual pages (dig, delv, nslookup)

subtopics.name: IP routing, NAT and MTU from the host's point of view
subtopics.learn: Use ip -br addr, ip route and ip route get 8.8.8.8 to state exactly which interface and gateway a packet leaves through, and ip neigh to see the ARP/NDP cache that must resolve before the first frame moves. Know the RFC 1918 ranges, source NAT at a home router or cloud NAT gateway, why the server sees the NAT's address, and why an inbound webhook to a private IP is impossible without a public endpoint or a tunnel. Know MTU 1500 and the roughly 1460-byte MSS after headers, overlays (VXLAN, WireGuard, VPNs) that shrink it, PMTUD's dependence on ICMP type 3 code 4 not being filtered, net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing as the workaround, and the black-hole symptom: small requests succeed while large POST bodies hang with retransmissions. Read mtr -T -P 443 host and traceroute -T output and know that * * * at a middle hop usually means ICMP rate limiting, not a fault.

resource.label: man7: ip-route(8)

subtopics.name: TCP handshake, socket states, and what 'refused' versus 'timeout' proves
subtopics.learn: Draw the three-way handshake with initial sequence numbers and the SYN options (MSS, SACK-permitted, window scale, timestamps) exactly as tcpdump prints them: Flags [S], [S.], [.], [P.], [F.], [R]. Walk the state machine (LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1/2, CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT) and map each to ss -tan state <name>; a pile of CLOSE-WAIT means your application never called close(), and TIME-WAIT (60 s) on the active closer plus the ephemeral range in net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range is how outbound port exhaustion happens. Understand the accept backlog (listen(backlog), net.core.somaxconn, tcp_max_syn_backlog) and SYN cookies. Discriminate at the packet level: an RST in reply to a SYN is 'connection refused' (host reachable, no listener or a REJECT rule); no reply at all with SYN retransmits at 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds is 'timeout' (a DROP rule, routing, or a dead host).

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking, ch. 2: Building Blocks of TCP

subtopics.name: Flow control, congestion control, retransmission and keepalive, read from ss -ti
subtopics.learn: Separate rwnd (the receiver's advertised, scaled window) from cwnd (the sender's congestion window, starting at 10 segments), and know slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit on three duplicate ACKs, SACK, and RTO (200 ms minimum on Linux) with exponential backoff. Read ss -ti fields (rto, rtt:avg/var, cwnd, ssthresh, bytes_retrans, retrans:cur/total, unacked, lastsnd, lastrcv, delivery_rate) and decide whether a slow transfer is network loss (retrans climbing), receiver-bound (small rwnd, application not reading) or sender-idle (large lastsnd, unacked 0: the application is the bottleneck). Know the Nagle plus delayed-ACK interaction and when TCP_NODELAY matters (small request/response, token streaming), and the keepalive knobs TCP_KEEPIDLE / TCP_KEEPINTVL / TCP_KEEPCNT (default 7200 s idle, useless against a NAT or LB that drops idle mappings after 5 minutes). Check sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control and know the difference between cubic and bbr.

resource.label: man7: tcp(7) socket options and /proc/sys/net/ipv4 tunables

subtopics.name: UDP: datagrams, where they are the right tool, and how they fail
subtopics.learn: UDP gives you a port and a checksum and nothing else: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control, and a firewall or NAT tracks only a short-lived mapping. Know why DNS, QUIC/HTTP-3, syslog, StatsD and WireGuard chose it, and that a UDP protocol must define its own request/response matching and stay under roughly 1200 bytes to avoid fragmentation. In Python use socket.SOCK_DGRAM with recvfrom/sendto, and know that a missing listener yields ICMP port-unreachable that the sender may or may not surface as an error. Solve Protohackers problem 4 (Unusual Database Program) to feel the difference from the TCP problems.

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking, ch. 3: Building Blocks of UDP

subtopics.name: TLS 1.3 handshake message by message
subtopics.learn: Name each message and what it carries: ClientHello (supported_versions, server_name SNI, ALPN list such as h2,http/1.1, key_share, cipher suites like TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, signature_algorithms), ServerHello (chosen key_share), then the encrypted EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished; one RTT to application data versus two in TLS 1.2, and PSK resumption giving 0-RTT with replay risk. Understand that SNI is plaintext and is what lets one IP serve many certificates (and what corporate firewalls filter on), and that ALPN is where HTTP/2 is negotiated. Run openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -alpn h2 -tls1_3 -msg and identify each message in the output, then repeat with -tls1_2 and count the extra round trip; note the 'Verify return code' line, which is your fastest certificate check.

resource.label: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3), section 2: Protocol Overview

subtopics.name: Certificates, chains, trust stores and ACME
subtopics.learn: Read a certificate with openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text and check the fields clients actually validate: Subject Alternative Names (CN is ignored), notBefore/notAfter, issuer, and EKU serverAuth. Understand chain building leaf to intermediate to root, that the server must send the intermediate (serve fullchain.pem, not cert.pem), and that browsers hide a missing intermediate by fetching it via AIA while Python ssl, Java and Go do not, producing 'unable to get local issuer certificate' or CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED. Know where trust lives: /etc/ssl/certs plus update-ca-certificates on Debian, Python certifi versus SSL_CERT_FILE / REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, Node NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, and that slim or scratch images may ship no CA bundle at all. Know ACME HTTP-01 (port 80 must reach the box) versus DNS-01 (works behind firewalls, needs DNS API access), the 90-day expiry, and verify chains offline with openssl verify -CAfile chain.pem cert.pem and online with openssl s_client -showcerts. Use badssl.com to deliberately trigger expired, wrong-host, self-signed and incomplete-chain failures and memorise each error string.

resource.label: Let's Encrypt: How It Works (ACME, challenges, chains)

subtopics.name: Enterprise TLS: mTLS, forward proxies, interception, and where termination happens
subtopics.learn: Understand the three shapes an FDE meets on customer sites. (a) An explicit forward proxy: HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY environment variables, the HTTP CONNECT host:443 tunnel, and clients that ignore the env (Java wants -Dhttps.proxyHost, some SDKs need explicit proxy config). (b) A TLS-intercepting appliance (Zscaler, Netskope, Palo Alto) that re-signs every certificate with a private CA, so your container fails only inside their network until that CA is added to the trust store; verify=False is never the fix. (c) Mutual TLS, where the server sends CertificateRequest and the client presents a certificate; test with openssl s_client -cert client.pem -key client.key and be able to state the operational cost (issuing, rotating, revoking per-tenant client certs). Know where TLS terminates in each topology (at the LB with plaintext to the backend and X-Forwarded-Proto set, re-encrypted to the backend, or L4 passthrough with SNI-based routing and the backend holding the certificate) and what each means for observability and for who owns certificate renewal.

resource.label: OpenSSL docs: openssl-s_client(1) (-servername, -alpn, -cert/-key, -proxy, -showcerts)

subtopics.name: HTTP/1.1 on the wire, read through curl -v
subtopics.learn: Know the request line, mandatory Host, Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding: chunked (and why a message carrying both is a request-smuggling vector), Connection: keep-alive versus close, the six-connections-per-origin browser limit, and the head-of-line blocking HTTP/2 was built to remove. Know the status semantics that bite operationally: 301/308 preserve the method, 302/303 turn POST into GET, 307 preserves; 401 versus 403; 429 with Retry-After; 502/503/504 are emitted by proxies, not your app. Read curl -v line by line: * lines are connection and TLS chatter (resolved IP, ALPN chosen, certificate subject/issuer/expiry), > is the request, < is the response. Use --resolve host:443:IP to bypass DNS, -H and --data-binary @file for exact payloads, -k only to isolate a TLS fault, --http1.1 to force a version, --trace-ascii - for raw bytes, -w with timing variables, and --connect-timeout / --max-time to make failures deterministic instead of hanging.

resource.label: curl manual page (all options, with the -w variable list)

subtopics.name: HTTP/2 framing, multiplexing, the LB downgrade problem, and where HTTP/3 fits
subtopics.learn: One TCP connection carries many streams; know the frame types (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, GOAWAY, PING), HPACK header compression, and per-stream plus per-connection flow control (SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, typically 100 to 128). Negotiation happens via ALPN h2 or cleartext h2c (needed for gRPC without TLS). Understand that head-of-line blocking moves down to TCP, that gRPC requires h2 end to end, and that most L7 load balancers (ALB, default nginx proxy_pass) speak h2 to the client but HTTP/1.1 to the backend unless explicitly configured for grpc or h2 upstreams, so 'we use HTTP/2' often ends at the edge. Inspect with curl --http2 -v (watch for ALPN: server accepted h2) and nghttp -nv https://host. Know HTTP/3 as HTTP over QUIC over UDP 443, advertised with Alt-Svc, immune to TCP HOL blocking but blocked by enterprise firewalls that drop UDP 443 and falling back to h2. Know the 2023 Rapid Reset attack (CVE-2023-44487) as the reason your LB now rate-limits RST_STREAM.

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking, ch. 12: HTTP/2

subtopics.name: L4 versus L7 load balancing and preserving the real client IP
subtopics.learn: L4 balancers (NLB, IPVS, HAProxy in tcp mode) forward TCP flows: fast, protocol-agnostic, TLS passthrough possible, but the backend sees either the true client IP (if preserved) or the balancer's IP. L7 balancers (ALB, nginx, Envoy) terminate TLS and HTTP and can route on host, path or header, retry, and rewrite. Two mechanisms carry the client IP: X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto / X-Forwarded-Port (or RFC 7239 Forwarded) at L7, and PROXY protocol v1/v2 at L4, which prepends a header the backend must parse (nginx: listen 443 ssl proxy_protocol) or every request becomes a 400 with binary garbage in the access log. Trust only the hop you control: nginx set_real_ip_from <LB CIDR>; real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; real_ip_recursive on; and never take the leftmost XFF entry for rate limiting or allowlisting because the client wrote it. Know round-robin, least-connections and consistent hashing (cache locality), and treat sticky sessions as a design smell to be justified.

resource.label: nginx docs: ngx_http_realip_module (set_real_ip_from, real_ip_header, real_ip_recursive)

subtopics.name: Health checks, idle timeouts, draining, and what 502/503/504 mean at the edge
subtopics.learn: A health check is a contract (path, interval, timeout, healthy and unhealthy thresholds, expected codes); a deep check that touches the database turns a DB blip into a full outage while a shallow one hides broken dependencies, so choose deliberately and return 503 during shutdown so the balancer drains you. Know the idle-timeout race: the LB (ALB default 60 s) reuses a keep-alive connection to a backend whose own keepalive timeout is shorter (gunicorn --keep-alive defaults to 2 s, uvicorn --timeout-keep-alive to 5 s); the backend closed first, the LB writes a request into a dead socket, the client gets a 502 and nothing appears in application logs. The fix is backend keepalive strictly longer than the LB idle timeout. Know that a non-streaming request longer than the idle timeout returns 504 while the backend still finishes (and still bills the tokens). Understand deregistration delay / connection draining, and the vocabulary: 502 bad upstream response, 503 no healthy targets or overload, 504 upstream timed out. Configure proxy_read_timeout, proxy_next_upstream, proxy_buffering off for SSE, and keepalive N inside an nginx upstream block as the software equivalents.

resource.label: AWS docs: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups

subtopics.name: Host firewalls: netfilter hooks, conntrack, nftables, and the Docker bypass
subtopics.learn: Know the five netfilter hooks (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting) and the filter/nat/mangle tables so you can predict where a rule must live; inspect with nft list ruleset or iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers and iptables -t nat -L -n. Understand stateful filtering: ct state established,related accept is why return traffic needs no rule, conntrack -L shows the table, and hitting nf_conntrack_max logs 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet', which presents as intermittent new-connection timeouts while existing flows stay healthy. Know DROP versus REJECT (reject with tcp reset) and why REJECT gives the far side an immediate, debuggable 'connection refused' instead of a two-minute hang. Know that Docker inserts its own FORWARD and DOCKER chains and that -p 5432:5432 is reachable from the internet regardless of ufw unless you add rules to DOCKER-USER; prove it from outside with nc -vz host 5432. Write a minimal default-deny ruleset for your VPS (lo, ct established, ssh from your IP, 80/443, ICMP) and apply it with a scheduled rollback (at now + 10 min) so a mistake cannot lock you out.

resource.label: nftables wiki: Quick reference, nftables in 10 minutes

subtopics.name: Cloud firewalls: security groups versus NACLs, and the egress rules that eat webhooks
subtopics.learn: Security groups are stateful allow-lists attached to network interfaces: return traffic is implied, rules can reference other security groups, and there is no deny. NACLs are stateless, ordered, subnet-level, and need explicit ephemeral-port return rules (1024 to 65535) or everything half-works. Outbound is open by default in a security group but locked down at regulated customers, so your webhook sender or model API call fails silently on egress; ask for the egress allowlist (destination CIDRs or FQDNs and ports) before deploy day. Know the layered pattern: LB SG allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, app SG allows 8000 only from the LB SG, DB SG allows 5432 only from the app SG, and test each hop with nc -vz from inside the VPC. Know VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer as the cloud analogue of tcpdump when you cannot get a shell on the box.

resource.label: AWS VPC User Guide: Control traffic to your AWS resources using security groups

subtopics.name: Packet-level debugging: ss, tcpdump, nc, and a layer-isolation routine
subtopics.learn: Internalise the routine, in order, each step producing one line of evidence: dig +short host (DNS), nc -vz -w 3 host 443 (TCP), openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host (TLS), curl -v --resolve host:443:IP https://host/path (HTTP), then application logs. Know ss -tulpn for listeners (bound to 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0 is the classic container mistake), ss -tanp state established '( dport = :443 )', ss -ti for per-flow TCP statistics, and lsof -i :8000. Capture with sudo tcpdump -nn -i any -s0 -w /tmp/case.pcap 'host 1.2.3.4 and port 443' using BPF capture filters (host, net, port, tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0), read back with tcpdump -nn -r case.pcap -A or in Wireshark (tcp.analysis.retransmission, tcp.flags.reset==1, Follow TCP Stream), and know that -i any drops Ethernet headers and that for a container you capture from the host with nsenter -t <pid> -n tcpdump. Prove negatives: an empty capture on the receiver during a claimed send is evidence the packet never arrived, which moves the conversation to the sender or the path.

resource.label: tcpdump.org: pcap-filter(7) capture filter syntax

subtopics.name: Webhook failure post-mortem: classification, retries, signatures, idempotency
subtopics.learn: Classify the symptom first because each class has a different owner: never arrived, arrived and rejected (4xx from signature, TLS or auth), arrived late, arrived more than once. Know typical sender behaviour: HTTPS only with publicly trusted CAs (a private CA means permanent failure), a 5 to 30 s timeout, exponential retries for 24 to 72 hours, and therefore that a receiver must return 2xx well under the timeout by enqueueing and processing asynchronously. Verify HMAC signatures over the raw body (never over re-serialised JSON) with a timestamp tolerance, and deduplicate on the delivery or event id with an idempotency store because retries plus partitions guarantee duplicates. Build the post-mortem from evidence: the sender's delivery log (status, response body, latency), the receiver's access log, tcpdump on the receiver, dig from a public resolver, openssl s_client -showcerts against the receiver; then write timeline, root cause, contributing factors, and the single change that prevents recurrence, in language a client PM can forward.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Best practices for using webhooks (respond fast, verify, handle redelivery)

subtopics.name: TCP servers in Python for Protohackers: framing, partial reads, half-close, concurrency
subtopics.learn: Understand that recv(n) returns any number of bytes up to n and b'' on EOF, so every protocol needs explicit framing: newline-delimited (Prime Time: readline(), one JSON object per line, reject malformed input and keep serving), fixed-length binary (Means to an End: 9-byte messages via struct.unpack('!cii') and readexactly(9)), or length-prefixed. Use asyncio.start_server(handler, '0.0.0.0', port) with StreamReader/StreamWriter, await writer.drain() for backpressure, writer.close() then await writer.wait_closed(), and handle IncompleteReadError, ConnectionResetError and BrokenPipeError per client without taking the server down. Know SO_REUSEADDR so restarts do not fail on TIME-WAIT sockets, the listen backlog, and half-close semantics (shutdown(SHUT_WR)) that Smoke Test requires: echo until EOF, flush, then close. Deploy on your VPS, open the port with the firewall ruleset you just wrote, pass Protohackers 0, 1 and 2 against the official checker, and tcpdump your own traffic to see your framing on the wire.

resource.label: Python docs: asyncio Streams (start_server, StreamReader, StreamWriter)

outcomes: You can narrate, unprompted and without notes, every step from a URL to the first byte (stub resolver, recursive and authoritative DNS, TCP three-way handshake, TLS 1.3 one-RTT handshake with SNI and ALPN, HTTP/2 stream, load balancer to backend) and name the tool whose output proves each step happened.

You can take a failing HTTPS call and, in under ten minutes, classify it as DNS, TCP connect, TLS, HTTP or application using dig, nc -vz, openssl s_client and curl -v, quoting the specific output line that proves the classification.
You can read ss -ti output for a slow connection and state whether it is limited by loss (retrans), the receiver (rwnd), congestion control (cwnd) or the application (lastsnd high, unacked 0).

You can capture a webhook attempt with tcpdump -nn -i any -w, open it in Wireshark, and prove whether packets arrived, were reset, or never reached the host, then hand the pcap and a two-sentence conclusion to a client network team.

You can explain what an ALB does to a request (TLS termination, X-Forwarded-* headers, h2 to HTTP/1.1 downgrade, 60 s idle timeout) and predict the two configurations that produce 502s with no application log entry.

You can write a default-deny nftables ruleset or a set of security groups from a written requirement and explain why return traffic works without an explicit rule, and why a NACL needs the ephemeral range.
You can diagnose a certificate error from openssl s_client -showcerts output (missing intermediate, expired, SAN mismatch, private CA) and state the exact fix and on which side it belongs.

You can implement a newline-delimited and a fixed-length binary TCP protocol server in Python asyncio that survives partial reads, slow clients and abrupt disconnects, passing Protohackers 0, 1 and 2.
failureModes: Backend keepalive shorter than the load balancer idle timeout (gunicorn keep-alive 2 s behind an ALB at 60 s): the backend closes an idle connection, the LB reuses it, and customers see intermittent 502s that appear in no application log, so the team blames the network for a week.

A certificate renewal deploys cert.pem instead of fullchain.pem; browsers still work because they fetch the missing intermediate via AIA, but the webhook sender's Python or Java client fails with 'unable to get local issuer certificate' and deliveries silently stop until the retry window expires.

A 90-second non-streaming model call is cut at 60 s by the ALB idle timeout: the backend finishes, logs a 200 and bills the tokens while the client receives a 504 and retries, doubling cost and creating duplicate side effects.

The NAT gateway or Kubernetes node hits nf_conntrack_max under a traffic spike; dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet', new connections time out while established ones are fine, and it gets misdiagnosed as a flaky upstream API.

A DNS record is created after the first failed lookup, so the customer's resolver holds NXDOMAIN for the SOA negative-cache TTL; you cannot reproduce it from your laptop on a different resolver and 'DNS is fixed' is true everywhere except where it matters.

The customer's TLS-intercepting proxy re-signs every certificate with a private CA; your container image lacks it, requests fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED only inside their network, and someone ships verify=False to make the demo work.

A WireGuard or VXLAN overlay lowers the path MTU and ICMP fragmentation-needed is filtered: health checks and small requests pass, but any JSON payload over roughly 1400 bytes hangs forever with retransmissions visible only in tcpdump.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through everything that happens between a customer typing https://app.example.com and the first byte rendering. At each step, name the tool you would use to prove it happened and one way it fails in a corporate network.

A customer says our webhooks stopped arriving on Tuesday; nothing changed on their side and nothing changed on ours. Without access to their network, how do you isolate this, what exactly do you ask them to run, and what do you run yourself?

Design the ingress path for a multi-tenant API that serves streaming LLM responses lasting up to five minutes on AWS: which load balancer, which timeouts, HTTP/2 or not, where TLS terminates, and how you preserve the client IP for per-tenant rate limiting without trusting a spoofable header.

Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake versus TLS 1.2, and what SNI and ALPN are each for. Then: the customer's security team mandates mTLS for the webhook receiver. What changes on each side, and what is the operational cost over twelve months?

You see intermittent 502s at the load balancer with no corresponding error in application logs. Give me the three most likely causes and the specific evidence (command and output line) that confirms or rules out each.
Here is ss -ti output for a slow connection showing rto, rtt, cwnd, retrans, unacked and lastsnd. Tell me whether the bottleneck is the network, the sender or the receiver, and what you would change.

A security group allows inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and the subnet's NACL allows inbound 443 only; nothing works. Why, and what is the minimal fix? Follow-up: which of these is stateful, and what does that imply for connection tracking under load?
2.proofOfWork: A public repository, network-postmortem-kit, containing a reproducible fault lab and its diagnoses. Two Docker Compose stacks: a sender that fires HMAC-signed webhooks with realistic retries and timeouts, and a receiver behind nginx with TLS. A break.sh script injects one of six faults on demand: a missing intermediate certificate, an NXDOMAIN via a poisoned resolver, a DROP versus a REJECT firewall rule, a keepalive/idle-timeout mismatch, an MTU clamp on the receiver interface, and a wrong ALPN/h2c expectation. For each fault the repo holds the pcap you captured, the single tcpdump, ss, curl -v or openssl line that proves the cause, and a three-sentence client-facing explanation. It closes with a one-page sequence diagram of a real HTTPS request to your own VPS, annotated with the actual frame numbers from your capture next to every arrow. A reviewer should be able to run make fault=3, watch the webhook fail, and reproduce your diagnosis from your instructions alone.

3.topic: Performance and troubleshooting on a single box
3.why: An FDE is the person on the customer's VM, pod or on-prem box when their own team says 'it's slow' and there is no dashboard, no APM and often no root. You have to name the saturated resource in minutes using only what is already installed, do it while a customer engineer watches over your shoulder, and then explain the cause in one sentence they will repeat to their CTO. The systems you ship (Kaupex, DefenderMate) will be judged by their worst hour, and the worst hour is almost always a disk that filled, a core that pinned, a cgroup that throttled, or an OOM kill nobody read.
prerequisites: Shell fluency from 'Shell mastery and scripting' (topic 0): pipes, awk column extraction, watch, sudo, reading man pages fast
Linux internals from topic 1: process lifecycle and states, /proc layout, systemd units and journalctl -u/-k, file permissions and mounts
TCP basics from 'Networking' (topic 2): socket states, LISTEN backlog, what a retransmit is, ss and tcpdump at a beginner level
Virtual memory vocabulary: page, page cache, swap, RSS vs virtual size, page fault (major vs minor)
A Linux box you are allowed to break with sudo (the Hetzner VPS from topic 1 or a local VM) with sysstat, strace, linux-tools/perf, bcc-tools and py-spy installed
Enough Python to read a py-spy dump of your own uvicorn/gunicorn worker and recognise which frame is yours

subtopics.name: USE method and the three anti-methods
subtopics.learn: For every physical and logical resource (each CPU, memory, each disk, each NIC, the storage controller, mutexes, connection pools) check Utilization (fraction of the interval it was busy), Saturation (queue length or wait time beyond capacity) and Errors (counts), in the order errors, saturation, utilization because errors are cheap to check and often decisive. Understand why utilization hides bursts: 50% over one second can be 100% for 500 ms, which is why you sample at 1 s and trust saturation over utilization. Name the anti-methods you will be tempted into on a live customer call: streetlight (only looking where your favourite tool shines), random-change (restart it and see), blame-someone-else (it's the network).
