resource.label: ACM Queue: Brendan Gregg, 'Thinking Methodically about Performance' (the USE method and the anti-methods it replaces)

subtopics.name: USE checklist for Linux: resource to metric to command
subtopics.learn: Memorise the map so you never hunt for a tool under pressure: CPU utilization = vmstat us+sy, mpstat -P ALL; CPU saturation = vmstat r greater than nproc, /proc/pressure/cpu, runqlat; memory utilization = free -m 'available'; memory saturation = vmstat si/so, sar -B pgscan, /proc/pressure/memory; disk utilization = iostat -xz %util (with caveats); disk saturation = aqu-sz and await; NIC utilization = sar -n DEV rxkB/s against ethtool Speed; NIC errors and saturation = sar -n EDEV rxdrop/txdrop, nstat ListenOverflows. Know which checks need root (perf, /proc/PID/stack, bcc) and which you can run as an unprivileged customer account, because that is often what you will be given.

resource.label: Brendan Gregg: USE Method Linux Performance Checklist

subtopics.name: The 60-second triage sequence, run from memory
subtopics.learn: Run ten commands in a fixed order and read one field in each: uptime (three load averages, is it rising or falling), dmesg -T | tail (OOM kills, I/O errors, hung_task, conntrack table full), vmstat 1 (r, si/so, us sy id wa st; discard the first line because it is the since-boot average), mpstat -P ALL 1 (a single hot core), pidstat 1 (which PID, %usr vs %system), iostat -xz 1 (r/s w/s await aqu-sz), free -m (available), sar -n DEV 1 (rxkB/s vs link speed), sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 (active/s passive/s retrans/s), top (confirm). Have a fallback one-liner for boxes without sysstat: cat /proc/loadavg /proc/pressure/*; grep -E 'MemAvailable|SwapFree|Dirty' /proc/meminfo. Time yourself: the whole pass should take under two minutes including reading.

resource.label: Netflix Tech Blog: Linux Performance Analysis in 60,000 Milliseconds (the ten-command first-minute checklist, field by field)

subtopics.name: Load average and pressure stall information
subtopics.learn: Linux load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE, shown as D in ps) since a 1993 patch, exponentially damped over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. So load 40 on 4 cores with 5% CPU means disk, NFS, driver or lock waits, not CPU. Find them: ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:32,comm | awk '$2 ~ /D/' then cat /proc/PID/stack (root) to see the kernel function it is stuck in. On kernels 4.20 and later prefer /proc/pressure/cpu, /proc/pressure/memory and /proc/pressure/io: 'some avg10' is the percentage of the last 10 s in which at least one task stalled on that resource, 'full avg10' is when all non-idle tasks stalled; any sustained non-zero 'full' for memory or io is a saturation you can quote to the customer.

resource.label: Brendan Gregg: Linux Load Averages: Solving the Mystery

subtopics.name: CPU: top, mpstat -P ALL and pidstat columns
subtopics.learn: Read the top summary line as eight distinct signals: us user, sy kernel (high sy = syscall storm, spinning on locks, or memory reclaim), ni niced, id idle, wa iowait (idle CPU while I/O is outstanding, a disk signal not a CPU one), hi/si hard and soft IRQ (si high on one core = network packet processing on a single RX queue), st steal (the hypervisor took cycles: noisy neighbour or burstable-credit exhaustion on shared vCPUs). In top press 1 for per-core, H for threads, P and M to sort. mpstat -P ALL 1 exposes a single saturated core that the average hides: a GIL-bound Python worker, a single-threaded Node process, or an IRQ pinned to one core (check /proc/interrupts and /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity). pidstat -u 1 for per-process, pidstat -t for threads, pidstat -w for context switches per second. vmstat r at or above nproc sustained is CPU saturation regardless of what %idle says.

resource.label: man7.org: mpstat(1)

subtopics.name: vmstat 1 line by line
subtopics.learn: Know every column of vmstat 1 cold: procs r (runnable, compare to nproc) and b (blocked in uninterruptible sleep); memory swpd free buff cache; swap si so (KB/s swapped in and out, any sustained non-zero value is memory saturation and explains 'everything is slow'); io bi bo (blocks in/out per second); system in cs (interrupts and context switches, cs far above 100k/s on a small box points at lock contention or a futex storm); cpu us sy id wa st. Use vmstat -w for aligned wide output and vmstat -SM for megabytes, vmstat -s for lifetime counters, vmstat -d for per-disk. Pattern-match: r high plus us high = CPU bound; b high plus wa high = I/O bound; si/so plus high sy = swapping; cs and in both spiking with low us = interrupt or scheduler storm.

resource.label: man7.org: vmstat(8)

subtopics.name: Memory: what free, /proc/meminfo and smaps_rollup actually say
subtopics.learn: free -m 'used' is not what a customer thinks it is; 'buff/cache' is reclaimable page cache and 'available' (MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo, kernel 3.14 and later) is the only number that decides whether adding RAM helps: low free with high available is a healthy box. Per-process, VSZ is useless for leaks; use RSS from ps -o rss and, when shared libraries skew it, Pss and Pss_Anon from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup. Watch Dirty and Writeback in /proc/meminfo for write-back stalls, Slab and SReclaimable (slabtop) for dentry/inode caches blown up by millions of files, and Shmem for tmpfs (a /dev/shm or tmpfs /tmp full of files is RAM you are paying for). Track major faults with ps -o maj_flt or sar -B majflt/s; a rising rate with si/so non-zero is the box paging its working set.

resource.label: Kernel docs: The /proc Filesystem (meminfo, vmstat, PID entries)

subtopics.name: OOM killer: reading the report and steering the victim
subtopics.learn: Read the dmesg block top to bottom: the trigger ('X invoked oom-killer', or 'Memory cgroup out of memory' which means a container limit, not the host), the per-process table with rss and oom_score_adj, then 'Out of memory: Killed process PID (comm) total-vm, anon-rss, file-rss, shmem-rss'. The victim is the highest oom_badness, roughly rss plus oom_score_adj scaled by total pages, so a database with adj 0 loses to a leaking worker someone set to -500. Steer it with OOMScoreAdjust= in systemd units (-1000 exempts entirely, 1000 volunteers) or by writing /proc/PID/oom_score_adj. Know the sysctls that change who gets hurt: vm.overcommit_memory (0 heuristic, 1 always, 2 strict with vm.overcommit_ratio), vm.swappiness, vm.oom_kill_allocating_task, vm.panic_on_oom for hosts you would rather have rebooted than limping. In cgroups check memory.events oom_kill and memory.max before blaming the host.

resource.label: Kernel docs: Documentation for /proc/sys/vm/

subtopics.name: Disk I/O: iostat -xz, await vs aqu-sz, and why %util lies
subtopics.learn: Run iostat -xz 1 and ignore the first sample. r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s give the load; rareq-sz wareq-sz the I/O size (tiny writes with high count = fsync-heavy workload such as a Postgres WAL or SQLite); r_await w_await are milliseconds per completed I/O including queue time (baseline: HDD about 10 ms, SATA SSD under 1 ms, NVMe about 0.1 ms, EBS gp3 1 to 2 ms); aqu-sz is average outstanding requests, above 1 on a single HDD or far above queue depth on NVMe is saturation. %util is only the fraction of time any I/O was outstanding: SSD, NVMe and RAID can sit at 100% while serving far more, so never call saturation from %util alone. Find the process with pidstat -d 1 (kB_rd/s kB_wr/s iodelay) or iotop -oPa. Check dmesg for 'task X blocked for more than 120 seconds' (hung_task) and I/O error or reset lines; a D-state process plus these lines is a storage or NFS problem, not an application bug.

resource.label: man7.org: iostat(1)

subtopics.name: Disk full: space, inodes and deleted-but-open files
subtopics.learn: Three different 'no space left on device' causes, three commands: df -h (blocks), df -i (inodes, exhausted by millions of tiny session, cache or mail files while df -h shows 30%), and du -xsh --max-depth=1 / (-x stays on one filesystem). When df is far above du a deleted file is still held open: lsof +L1, or find /proc/[0-9]*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' -printf '%p -> %l\n' 2>/dev/null; reclaim it with : > /proc/PID/fd/N (truncate through the fd, do not kill the service). Other places space hides: files shadowed under a mount point (mount --bind / /mnt/root and look), ext4 5% reserved blocks (tune2fs -m), journald (journalctl --disk-usage, --vacuum-size=500M), Docker overlay2 and dangling images (docker system df), core dumps in /var/lib/systemd/coredump. Verify the fix with the same df line you started with.

resource.label: man7.org: lsof(8)

subtopics.name: Process states and the /proc/PID files that explain them
subtopics.learn: Read ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,wchan:30,etime,comm: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible (cannot be killed, almost always disk, NFS or a driver), Z zombie (parent has not called wait(); kill or restart the parent, not the zombie), T stopped (a tracer died or someone sent SIGSTOP), l multithreaded. Then go to /proc/PID: status (State, VmRSS, Threads, voluntary_ctxt_switches vs nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches where high nonvoluntary means CPU contention), stack (kernel stack, root), wchan, fd (ls | wc -l against the 'Max open files' line in limits), io (read_bytes, write_bytes), cgroup (which container or slice it belongs to), cwd and exe (a '(deleted)' exe means the binary was replaced under a running process, the classic 'we upgraded but nothing changed'), environ and cmdline (what config it actually started with).

resource.label: man7.org: proc(5)

subtopics.name: strace: attach, read, detach, and know the cost
subtopics.learn: Attach with strace -f -tt -T -p PID -o /tmp/st.txt (follow threads, wall-clock timestamps, per-syscall duration, write to file so your terminal does not slow the tracee). Narrow with -e trace=network,file or -e trace=%desc, decode fds to paths and socket endpoints with -yy, widen strings with -s 256, get a syscall count and time summary with -c, and a user stack per syscall with -k. Read the patterns: stuck in futex() is a lock or GIL; read(7, ...) blocked for seconds with fd 7 resolving to a socket is an upstream not answering; connect() EINPROGRESS then poll() timing out is a firewall or dead host; EAGAIN storms are a busy loop; openat() ENOENT loops are a library hunting for config or certificates. Understand the cost: ptrace stops the tracee on every syscall, 10x to 100x slowdown on syscall-heavy servers, so never leave it attached, never on the only database primary at peak, and know that a tracer killed with -9 can leave the tracee stopped. Lower-overhead alternatives are perf trace -p PID and bpftrace.

resource.label: man7.org: strace(1)

subtopics.name: perf and flame graphs, including Python via py-spy
subtopics.learn: perf top -p PID for live hottest symbols; perf stat -e task-clock,cycles,instructions,cache-misses,context-switches -p PID -- sleep 10 for IPC (below 1 the process is stalled on memory, above 2 it is genuinely computing; this is why 100% CPU does not mean 'needs more CPU'); perf record -F 99 -g -p PID -- sleep 30 then perf report --stdio --no-children, or perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > out.svg with the FlameGraph repo. Stacks break without frame pointers: use --call-graph dwarf for C, C++ and Rust binaries. For Python perf only shows _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault, so use py-spy dump --pid PID (a point-in-time stack of every thread, safe on a live uvicorn or gunicorn worker) and py-spy record -o prof.svg --pid PID --native for a flame graph with your own function names. perf needs kernel.perf_event_paranoid at 1 or lower or root, and inside containers CAP_PERFMON (or CAP_SYS_ADMIN on older kernels).

resource.label: brendangregg/FlameGraph on GitHub (perf record to flame graph: stackcollapse-perf.pl and flamegraph.pl, plus dwarf/frame-pointer caveats)

subtopics.name: Off-CPU analysis: slow but not busy
subtopics.learn: When a process shows 3% CPU and still misses its latency target, on-CPU profiling is the wrong tool; measure where it is blocked. Cheap first look: /proc/PID/wchan, /proc/PID/stack, and /proc/PID/schedstat (run time, time waiting on the run queue, timeslices; a large second number means CPU saturation or cgroup throttling, not I/O). perf sched record then perf sched latency shows run-queue delay per task. For the full picture offcputime-bpfcc -p PID 10 (bcc) collects stacks weighted by blocked time, which you render as an off-CPU flame graph. Classify what you find: futex (lock contention), sock_recvmsg or tcp_recvmsg (waiting on an upstream), io_schedule or blk_mq (disk), or plain run-queue wait (CPU).

resource.label: Brendan Gregg: Off-CPU Analysis

subtopics.name: Network as a single-box resource: ss, nstat, conntrack, softirq
subtopics.learn: ss -s for totals and the TIME-WAIT count; ss -tlnp where Recv-Q on a LISTEN socket is the current accept backlog and Send-Q the configured backlog (net.core.somaxconn), a Recv-Q at Send-Q means the app is not calling accept() fast enough; ss -tnp state established '( dport = :5432 )' | wc -l to count a pool's real connections; ss -tni for rto, retrans, cwnd per flow. nstat -az TcpRetransSegs TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtTCPSynRetrans (or netstat -s): ListenOverflows climbing is your process, retransmits are the path or the peer. dmesg 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' means intermittent connection failures under load (raise net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max or stop tracking that traffic). Ephemeral port exhaustion shows as TIME-WAIT approaching the width of net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range; fix client pooling and keep-alive, not tcp_tw_recycle. sar -n DEV 1 rxkB/s against ethtool eth0 Speed, sar -n EDEV 1 for rxdrop, /proc/net/softnet_stat third column for backlog drops, and top si pinned to one core means a single RX queue or IRQ.

resource.label: man7.org: ss(8)

subtopics.name: cgroups v2: the box inside the container
subtopics.learn: Inside a container top, free and nproc report the host; the limits that actually bind live in cgroup v2 under /sys/fs/cgroup (the container sees its own subtree as the root). cpu.max is 'quota period' (200000 100000 means two CPUs); cpu.stat nr_throttled and throttled_usec growing under load is CFS throttling, the reason a pod with limits equal to requests has 10x p99 while the node shows 80% idle. memory.max, memory.current, memory.stat (anon vs file, because page cache counts toward the limit and a file-heavy workload looks like a leak), memory.events oom_kill, io.stat, and per-cgroup PSI in cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, io.pressure. From the host find a pod's cgroup via /proc/PID/cgroup, systemd-cgls and systemd-cgtop. For systemd services the same knobs are CPUQuota=, MemoryMax=, TasksMax= (pids.max: a thread leak hits 'Resource temporarily unavailable' on fork long before the host runs out of anything).

resource.label: Kernel docs: Control Group v2

subtopics.name: bcc and bpftrace point tools: one question, near-zero overhead
subtopics.learn: Install bcc-tools (Ubuntu package names end in -bpfcc) and learn the eight that answer questions strace and top cannot: execsnoop (what is being exec'd: cron storms, shell-outs from your app, a health check forking curl 50 times a second), opensnoop -p PID (which files and configs it really reads, and the ENOENTs), biolatency (block I/O latency histogram; bimodal means cache hits vs misses), biosnoop (each I/O with PID and latency), tcpretrans and tcpconnect/tcpaccept (who is talking to whom and what is failing), runqlat (run-queue latency histogram, the direct evidence of CPU saturation or throttling), cachestat (page-cache hit ratio), ext4slower 10 (file operations slower than 10 ms with the process name). bpftrace one-liners cover the rest. These need root, a kernel with BTF for recent versions, and in Kubernetes a privileged debug pod on the node with the host PID namespace.

resource.label: iovisor/bcc on GitHub (tools/ directory and tutorial)

subtopics.name: Writing the diagnosis note and verifying the fix
subtopics.learn: For every scenario you solve, write one page: the symptom as the customer stated it; the timeline; the resource in USE terms and the single command output line that proved it (paste the line, not a screenshot); the root cause in one sentence a non-Linux engineer can repeat; the fix with the exact command; the verification (the same metric, after, with the number); and the prevention (an alert threshold, a ulimit, log rotation, a cgroup limit). Follow the SRE book loop of hypothesis, test, refine and record the hypotheses you rejected and why, because a note that shows what it ruled out is the one a customer's platform team trusts. Keep raw outputs in an appendix. This is the format for the SadServers notes in the deliverable and for every real incident after it.

resource.label: Google SRE Book: Effective Troubleshooting

outcomes: You can run the 60-second checklist (uptime, dmesg -T | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1, top) from memory on a box you have never seen and name the saturated resource in under two minutes.

Given load average 40 on a 4-core box with 5% CPU, you can list the D-state processes with their wchan and say whether the wait is disk, NFS or a lock, and show the /proc/PID/stack line that proves it.

You can read one line of iostat -xz 1 and state whether the device is saturated using await and aqu-sz against a stated baseline, and explain in one sentence why %util alone is not evidence on SSD or RAID.

You can attach strace -f -tt -T -yy to a hung worker, identify the blocking syscall and what its fd points at, detach cleanly, and state the overhead you imposed and why you would not do it on a database primary at peak.
You can produce a CPU flame graph of your own running Python service with py-spy (and of a C binary with perf record -g) and point at the hottest frame that is your code, not the interpreter.

You can read an OOM-killer dmesg block and state whether it was a host or cgroup OOM, which process was killed, why it was chosen from the rss and oom_score_adj table, and what OOMScoreAdjust or memory.max change prevents a repeat.
You can explain why a pod with a 500m CPU limit is slow while the node shows 80% idle, show nr_throttled and throttled_usec climbing in cpu.stat, and say what you would change in the limit and why.
You can write a one-page diagnosis note (symptom, evidence line, cause, fix, verification, prevention, rejected hypotheses) that a customer's platform team accepts without asking for a screenshot.
failureModes: A rotated log is deleted while a service still holds the fd: df reports 100%, du reports 40%, the API returns ENOSPC on every write and the on-call deletes unrelated files for an hour before anyone runs lsof +L1.
Inode exhaustion from millions of small session or cache files: df -h shows 30% used, writes fail with 'No space left on device', and the team resizes the disk twice before someone runs df -i.

Kubernetes CPU limits set equal to requests: the Python worker is CFS-throttled every 100 ms period, p99 latency goes 10x under a traffic bump, the node dashboard shows 70% idle, and the customer concludes the model is slow.

One core pinned at 100% by a GIL-bound worker or a single NIC RX queue while fifteen cores idle: top's summary line says 7% CPU, the team adds more replicas on the same box, and only mpstat -P ALL shows the hot core.

Memory pressure with no single culprit: MemAvailable near zero, si/so non-zero, major faults climbing, everything 'randomly slow', then the OOM killer takes Postgres instead of the leaking worker because nobody set OOMScoreAdjust.

strace left attached to a production process without -o, or attached without -f to a multi-threaded server so it shows nothing, or the tracer is killed with -9 and the worker stays in T state until someone notices it stopped serving.

nf_conntrack table full or ephemeral port exhaustion on a webhook-heavy box: intermittent connection failures only under load, retries make it worse, and the one line in dmesg that names the cause is never read.
interviewQuestions: Load average is 60 on an 8-vCPU customer host, CPU is 10% busy and iostat %util is 5%. Walk me through your first three minutes, the exact commands, and what you expect to find.

A customer's FastAPI pod has a 500m CPU limit and its p99 tripled after a traffic increase; node metrics show 70% idle. Diagnose it, show me the evidence you would collect, and explain why raising the limit is not the whole fix.
Explain what iostat -xz 1 tells you and what does not. Which fields let you say a device is saturated, and give me a case where %util is 100% and the disk is fine.
You need to look inside a stuck worker in production. When do you reach for strace, when for perf, when for py-spy, when for bcc, and what is the cost and blast radius of each?

A box has 200 MB free out of 64 GB and the customer wants to buy RAM. How do you decide whether there is a memory problem at all? Name the exact numbers you would read and the threshold that changes your answer.
The OOM killer just killed the database instead of the leaking Python worker. Explain how the victim is chosen and how you would prevent a recurrence without adding memory.

Design what you would leave behind on a single customer VM with no Kubernetes and no cloud metrics so that next time it slows down they can hand you a diagnosis instead of a complaint. What do you sample, at what cadence, where does it go, and what is the one alert you would set?
3.proofOfWork: A 15-minute recorded screencast in which you break your own Hetzner VPS three ways without telling your future self which is which (fill the disk through a deleted-but-open log, pin one core with stress-ng --cpu 1, and throttle the Kaupex worker with a systemd CPUQuota=20% drop-in), then diagnose each one blind from the 60-second checklist while narrating what every field means and stopping the moment you have the evidence line. Alongside it, a one-page 'single-box triage card' in markdown checked into the Dokeo repo's runbooks: the ten commands, the one field to read in each, the threshold that means saturated, and the follow-up tool for each resource (strace, perf, py-spy, bcc), formatted so a customer engineer with no Linux performance background can follow it on a call with you.

4.topic: Git at depth: rebase, bisect, reflog, hooks, monorepo hygiene
4.why: An FDE lands in a customer's repo on day one, often a multi-year monorepo with conventions nobody documented, and is expected to ship a clean, reviewable change the same week without breaking their history. When a customer says 'this worked last Tuesday', bisect and log archaeology turn a vague complaint into a single culprit commit in minutes, which is the difference between a credible engineer and a guest. And when a teammate force-pushes over your branch at 6pm before a demo, reflog recovery is what keeps the demo on schedule.
prerequisites: Shell fluency from 'Shell mastery and scripting' (topic 0): pipes, exit codes, writing a 10-line bash script that returns 0 or 1
Filesystem permissions and executable bits from 'Linux internals' (topic 1), since hooks are plain executables under .git/hooks
Basic Git: clone, branch, commit, push, pull, resolving a simple merge conflict in an editor
Knowing what a SHA-1/SHA-256 content hash is and why identical content hashes identically
A local project with a lint and test command you can run in under a minute (Dokeo is the target for the hook deliverable)

subtopics.name: Object model: blobs, trees, commits, refs
subtopics.learn: Understand that Git is a content-addressed store: `git hash-object -w file` writes a blob, `git cat-file -t <sha>` and `git cat-file -p <sha>` show type and contents, and a commit is a pointer to a tree plus parent SHAs plus author/committer metadata. Know that a branch is a 41-byte file under `.git/refs/heads/` (or a line in `.git/packed-refs`) and `HEAD` is a symref to it. Be able to explain why 'rewriting history' never mutates objects, it creates new ones and moves refs, which is exactly why reflog recovery works until `git gc` prunes unreachable objects.

resource.label: Pro Git 10.2: Git Internals - Git Objects

subtopics.name: The three trees: reset, restore, switch, checkout
subtopics.learn: Model every command as moving HEAD, the index, or the working tree. `git reset --soft <c>` moves only HEAD, `--mixed` (default) also resets the index, `--hard` also overwrites the working tree and is the only one that destroys uncommitted work. Use `git restore --staged <path>` to unstage, `git restore <path>` to discard, `git restore --source=<c> <path>` to pull one file from history, and `git switch -c` / `git switch --detach` instead of the overloaded `checkout`. Be able to predict the exact state of all three trees after each command without running it.

resource.label: Pro Git 7.7: Reset Demystified

subtopics.name: Revision syntax and log archaeology
subtopics.learn: Master the selectors you need to talk about history precisely: `HEAD~2` (second ancestor via first parent) vs `HEAD^2` (second parent of a merge), `A..B` (reachable from B not A) vs `A...B` (symmetric difference), `@{upstream}`, `main@{2.days.ago}`, `:/regex`. Then find things: `git log -S'string' --oneline` (pickaxe: commits that changed the count of a string), `-G'regex'` (commits whose diff matches), `-L :funcname:path` (history of one function), `--first-parent` on a merge-heavy main, `--follow` across renames, and `git blame -w -C -C -C` to see through whitespace and code movement. Know that `git log --all --oneline --graph --decorate` is the first command to run in an unfamiliar repo.

resource.label: git-scm.com: gitrevisions manual

subtopics.name: Interactive rebase: the full instruction set
subtopics.learn: Run `git rebase -i <base>` and use every verb with intent: pick, reword, edit (stop to split or amend), squash (merge messages), fixup (discard message), drop, `exec <cmd>` (run tests after every commit to guarantee each is green), `break`, and `label`/`reset`/`merge` under `--rebase-merges`. Adopt the fixup workflow: `git commit --fixup=<sha>` then `git rebase -i --autosquash <base>`, with `rebase.autosquash=true` and `rebase.autostash=true` in config. Use `--onto <newbase> <oldbase> <branch>` to transplant a range, and `--update-refs` (Git 2.38+) so stacked branches move together. Know `--continue`, `--skip`, `--abort`, and that `ORIG_HEAD` holds where you started.

resource.label: git-scm.com: git-rebase manual

subtopics.name: Conflict resolution mechanics, zdiff3, rerere
subtopics.learn: Set `merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3` so conflict hunks show the common ancestor, which is what makes a 3-way conflict legible. Know that `--ours`/`--theirs` flip meaning during a rebase (ours = the branch being rebased onto, theirs = your commit being replayed) and use `git checkout --ours <path>` / `--theirs <path>` only when you have reasoned about that. Enable `rerere.enabled=true` so Git records each hunk resolution and replays it automatically when the same conflict recurs across a long rebase or repeated integration merges; inspect with `git rerere status` and `git rerere diff`. Use `git diff --base` and `git log --merge` to see only the commits that touch the conflicted paths.

resource.label: Pro Git 7.8: Advanced Merging

subtopics.name: Force-pushing without destroying teammates' work
subtopics.learn: Never type `git push --force` on a shared remote. `--force-with-lease` refuses the push if the remote ref has moved since your last fetch, and `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected-sha>` pins the exact SHA you believe is there. Pair it with `--force-if-includes` (Git 2.30+) to close the hole where a background `git fetch` (IDE, prompt plugin) silently updated your tracking ref so the lease passes even though you never saw the new commits. On the server side know `receive.denyNonFastForwards` and `receive.denyDeletes`, and that branch protection is what enforces this for the whole team, not etiquette.

resource.label: git-scm.com: git-push manual (--force-with-lease, --force-if-includes)

subtopics.name: Reflog and data recovery
subtopics.learn: `git reflog` (alias for `git reflog show HEAD`) lists every position HEAD occupied; `git reflog show <branch>` does the same per branch, and `git reflog show --date=iso` puts real timestamps on it. Recover a deleted branch with `git branch restored HEAD@{n}` or a bad `reset --hard` with `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`. Know the expiry knobs: `gc.reflogExpire` (90 days) and `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` (30 days), and that a fresh clone has no reflog, so on a server or CI runner you reach for `git fsck --lost-found` or `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs` to list dangling commits and then `git show` them. Recover a dropped stash the same way, since stashes are commits with a two- or three-parent structure.

resource.label: Pro Git 10.7: Maintenance and Data Recovery

subtopics.name: Bisect: automated regression hunting
subtopics.learn: Start with `git bisect start <bad> <good>` (you can pass multiple good commits) and hand off to `git bisect run ./check.sh`; the script must exit 0 for good, 1-127 for bad, and exactly 125 to mark a commit untestable so bisect skips it (use this when the build fails for unrelated reasons). Use `--first-parent` on a merge-heavy main so you bisect merges, not every feature-branch commit, and `--term-old=fast --term-new=slow` when hunting a performance change rather than a bug. Write the check script to be hermetic: build from scratch, run one targeted test, never depend on files bisect will overwrite. Save `git bisect log > bisect.log` before `git bisect reset` so you can `git bisect replay` if you misjudged a step. Expect log2(N) iterations, so 4000 commits is 12 checks.

resource.label: git-scm.com: git-bisect manual

subtopics.name: Hook lifecycle: client-side and server-side
subtopics.learn: Know which hook fires when and what it receives: pre-commit (no args, exit non-zero aborts), prepare-commit-msg and commit-msg (path to message file), pre-push (remote name and URL as args, ref tuples `<local ref> <local sha> <remote ref> <remote sha>` on stdin), post-checkout and post-merge (for dependency re-install), and on the server pre-receive/update/post-receive. Hooks live in `.git/hooks/`, are not versioned, and must be executable, so a team ships them via `core.hooksPath=.githooks` set by a bootstrap script or via the pre-commit framework. Understand that `--no-verify` bypasses client hooks, so anything that must be enforced belongs in CI or a server-side hook, and that a hook slower than a few seconds will be bypassed by the whole team within a week.

resource.label: git-scm.com: githooks manual

subtopics.name: pre-commit framework for Dokeo
subtopics.learn: Author `.pre-commit-config.yaml` with `repos:` entries pinned by `rev:`, each with `hooks: - id:`; use `repo: local` with `language: system` and `entry: make lint` for project-native tools. Install with `pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type pre-push` so fast lint runs on staged files at commit time and the test suite runs at push time via `stages: [pre-push]`. Scope with `files:` and `exclude:` regexes and `types: [python]`, run everything once with `pre-commit run --all-files`, and bump pins with `pre-commit autoupdate`. Run the same `pre-commit run --all-files` in CI so the hook is a convenience and CI is the enforcement, never the reverse.

resource.label: pre-commit.com: framework documentation

subtopics.name: Atomic commits and reviewable series
subtopics.learn: Stage by hunk with `git add -p` (y/n/s to split/e to edit the hunk), so each commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own; use `rebase -i` with `exec make test` to prove it. Write messages as `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>` under 72 chars per Conventional Commits, with a body that explains why and what alternatives were rejected, since the diff already says what. Use `git commit --amend --no-edit` for the last commit and `--fixup` for older ones. Before re-requesting review on a rebased branch, run `git range-diff <old-base>..<old-tip> <new-base>..<new-tip>` and paste the summary so reviewers see only what changed between the two versions of the series.

resource.label: Conventional Commits v1.0.0 specification

subtopics.name: Commit signing with SSH keys
subtopics.learn: Configure `gpg.format=ssh`, `user.signingkey=~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, `commit.gpgsign=true`, and `tag.gpgsign=true` so every commit carries a signature without a GPG keyring. Verify locally with `git log --show-signature` or `git verify-commit <sha>`, which needs `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile` pointing at a file of `email ssh-ed25519 AAAA...` lines. Understand that signing proves the committer identity, not code safety, and that customer environments with branch protection requiring signed commits will reject an unsigned rebase, so this must be set up before the first push, not after. This feeds the provenance chain in topic 18 (CI/CD and supply chain).

resource.label: Pro Git 7.4: Signing Your Work

subtopics.name: Purging secrets and large files from history
subtopics.learn: Use `git filter-repo` (not the deprecated `filter-branch`): `git filter-repo --path config/prod.env --invert-paths` removes a file from every commit, `--replace-text expressions.txt` scrubs strings (one `literal:AKIA...==>REDACTED` per line), and `--strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M` drops accidentally committed binaries. Know that filter-repo requires a fresh clone, rewrites every SHA after the first touched commit, and that every collaborator must re-clone or hard-reset because their old refs will reintroduce the objects on the next push. Treat any leaked credential as compromised regardless: rotate it first, then rewrite history, because forks, CI caches, and reviewer clones still hold the blob.

resource.label: git-filter-repo official repository and README

subtopics.name: Working at monorepo scale: partial clone, sparse checkout, worktrees
subtopics.learn: Clone a 20 GB monorepo without the blobs using `git clone --filter=blob:none <url>` (blobs fetched lazily on checkout) or `--filter=tree:0` for CI that only needs one commit, and use `--depth 1` only when you will never need history. Then `git sparse-checkout init --cone && git sparse-checkout set services/billing libs/common` so the working tree holds only your directories; `--cone` mode is the fast path because it matches whole directories, not arbitrary patterns. Use `git worktree add ../hotfix main` to check out a second branch alongside your feature work without stashing, `git worktree list` and `git worktree prune` to manage them, and `git maintenance start` to schedule background `prefetch`, `commit-graph`, and `incremental-repack` so `git status` and `git log` stay fast.

resource.label: git-scm.com: git-sparse-checkout manual

subtopics.name: gitattributes and gitignore that survive a mixed OS team
subtopics.learn: Commit a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` so CRLF from Windows contributors never lands in the repo, `*.png binary`, `*.lock -diff` and `merge=ours` or `merge=union` for generated files and changelogs that conflict on every rebase, and `linguist-generated=true` so GitHub collapses generated diffs. Use `export-ignore` so `git archive` skips test fixtures, and `filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text` is what `git lfs track` writes for large binaries. For `.gitignore`, know the precedence chain (`.gitignore` per directory, `.git/info/exclude` for local-only, `core.excludesFile` for global) and use `git check-ignore -v <path>` to find which rule is hiding a file that a customer swears they added.

resource.label: git-scm.com: gitattributes manual

subtopics.name: Branch protection, CODEOWNERS, and merge queues
subtopics.learn: Configure protected branches to require pull request reviews, dismiss stale approvals on new pushes, require status checks to pass with `Require branches to be up to date`, require linear history (forces squash or rebase merges), require signed commits, and restrict who can push. Write a `CODEOWNERS` file in `.github/` (or repo root or `docs/`) with path patterns like `/services/billing/ @org/billing-team` where the last matching line wins, so reviews auto-route and `Require review from Code Owners` blocks merges without a domain owner. Understand why a merge queue exists: with required up-to-date branches, N concurrent PRs each trigger a rebase-and-retest storm, and the queue batches them into a single tested sequence.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: About code owners

subtopics.name: Submodules vs subtrees vs vendoring
subtopics.learn: A submodule is a gitlink entry in the parent tree pointing to a fixed SHA plus a `.gitmodules` URL mapping; `git clone --recurse-submodules` or `git submodule update --init --recursive` populates it, and `submodule.recurse=true` makes `pull` and `checkout` follow. Know the failure surface: the submodule sits in detached HEAD, a forgotten `--recursive` in CI yields an empty directory, and bumping the pinned SHA is a commit in the parent that reviewers routinely miss. Compare with `git subtree add --prefix=vendor/lib <url> main --squash`, which copies content into the parent history with no extra clone step, and with plain vendoring plus a `VENDORED_FROM` file; be able to recommend one given the customer's CI and update cadence.

resource.label: Pro Git 7.11: Submodules

outcomes: You can recover a branch deleted by `git branch -D` or a commit lost to `git reset --hard` within two minutes using reflog, and within five using `git fsck --lost-found` on a clone with no reflog.
You can take a 4000-commit repo with a known-good tag and a failing test and produce the exact culprit commit via `git bisect run` with a hermetic script, handling untestable commits with exit 125.

You can turn a 15-commit branch with WIP messages into a 4-commit series where every commit builds and passes tests, proven by `rebase -i` with `exec`, and show the reviewer a `range-diff` of what changed since their last review.
You can resolve a rebase conflict across multiple replayed commits using zdiff3 hunks and explain correctly which side `--ours` refers to during a rebase.
You can install a pre-commit and pre-push hook on Dokeo via `.pre-commit-config.yaml` that lints staged files in under 3 seconds and runs the test suite on push, with the same config run in CI.
You can remove a leaked credential from every commit of a repo with `git filter-repo`, write the collaborator re-clone instructions, and state why rotating the secret is still mandatory.
You can set up a sparse cone checkout of two directories from a partial clone of a monorepo and add a second worktree for a hotfix without disturbing the feature branch.
You can force-push a rebased branch with `--force-with-lease --force-if-includes` and explain the exact race each flag closes.
failureModes: A teammate runs `git push --force` on a shared feature branch after an IDE auto-fetched, silently dropping two days of a colleague's commits; nobody notices until the demo build lacks the feature.
The pre-commit hook grows to run the full 4-minute test suite, so the team commits with `--no-verify` by habit and the hook becomes theatre while CI stays red half the day.

A `.env` with production database credentials is committed and then 'deleted' in the next commit; six months later a contractor's clone is compromised and the still-valid credential in history is used.
A CI pipeline clones with `--depth 1`, then a release script runs `git describe --tags` and produces garbage versions because the tag is outside the shallow history.
Submodules pinned to a SHA that was force-pushed away on the upstream repo; `git submodule update` fails with 'fatal: reference is not a tree' on every fresh clone and blocks all deploys.
Windows contributors commit CRLF files with no `.gitattributes`, so every rebase touching those files shows the whole file as a conflict and a 3-line change becomes an unreadable 800-line diff.

Someone bisects on a merge-heavy main without `--first-parent`, lands on a mid-feature-branch commit that never built on its own, and reports a false culprit that sends the team investigating the wrong service for a day.
interviewQuestions: A customer's on-call engineer says a nightly job started failing 'sometime in the last three weeks' and there are about 900 commits on main. Walk me through exactly how you find the culprit, including how you handle commits that do not build.
Explain what `git reset --hard HEAD~3` actually does to HEAD, the index, and the working tree, and then tell me how you would recover if you ran it by mistake on a branch that was never pushed.
During a rebase you see a conflict hunk and decide to keep 'your' change. Which of `--ours` and `--theirs` do you use and why is that the opposite of what you would use during a merge?
Design the Git-side guardrails for a 40-engineer monorepo: what goes in client hooks, what goes in CI, what goes in branch protection, and how do you keep the hooks from being bypassed?
A production API key was committed to a repo with 30 forks and a 2-year history. What do you do in the first 10 minutes, what do you do in the first day, and what can you never fully undo?
Why does `--force-with-lease` still lose data in some setups, and what flag closes that gap? Describe the exact sequence of events that produces the data loss.
A customer's CI clones a 15 GB monorepo from scratch on every run and it takes 9 minutes before tests start. Which clone and checkout flags do you reach for, and what does each one trade away?
4.proofOfWork: A public repository named `git-forensics-lab` containing a scripted, reproducible incident set: (1) a `make break` target that generates a 500-commit synthetic history with a planted regression, a planted non-building range, and a leaked fake credential, and (2) a `RUNBOOK.md` plus `scripts/` that walk through recovering a deleted branch via reflog, locating the regression via `git bisect run` with a hermetic checker that returns 125 on the non-building range, scrubbing the credential via `git filter-repo --replace-text` with the collaborator re-clone notice, and demonstrating a `--force-with-lease` rejection versus a `--force-if-includes` rejection. Every step is asserted by a `make verify` target so a reviewer can clone the repo and watch the whole recovery pass in under five minutes; the README links the Dokeo `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and the CI job that runs the same hooks.

5.topic: Docker internals: namespaces, cgroups, layers, networking
5.why: FDEs ship into environments they do not control: a customer's hardened VM, an air-gapped Docker host, a security team that treats every container as root-on-the-node until proven otherwise. When the image 'works on my machine' but the customer's container exits 137 every few hours, cannot reach their on-prem Postgres after the VPN comes up, or is 3 GB because a secret was deleted in a later layer, the FDE is the person on the bridge call. Being able to explain from the kernel up what the customer is actually running, and to debug it with host tools when the container has no shell, is what earns the right to deploy into their production.
prerequisites: Linux process model from Topic 1 (Linux internals): fork/exec, what PID 1 is, SIGTERM vs SIGKILL, /proc, mount(2) and chroot; namespaces only make sense if you know what they are isolating.

Networking from Topic 2: CIDR notation, reading a routing table, what NAT and DNAT are, how /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/hosts drive resolution; you will read iptables rules and debug the 127.0.0.11 resolver.
Shell fluency from Topic 0: pipes, Go-template --format strings, jq, and comfortable reading ss, ip, tcpdump and dmesg output.
Troubleshooting habits from Topic 3: reading OOM-killer lines in dmesg, strace -f, knowing the difference between exit code 137 and 143.

A real Linux host with root (VM, Multipass, Lima or a cloud instance). Docker Desktop hides the Linux VM; most hands-on steps here need /sys/fs/cgroup, /var/lib/docker and iptables on the actual host.
Have written at least one Dockerfile and run docker compose up once. This topic assumes CLI familiarity and goes underneath it.

subtopics.name: A container is a process: clone() flags and the eight namespaces
subtopics.learn: Know the namespace types (mnt, pid, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time) and precisely what each isolates. Understand that docker run bottoms out in runc calling clone(2)/unshare(2) with CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWNS and friends, then execve() on the entrypoint. List a running container's namespaces with ls -l /proc/$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' c)/ns and lsns -p <pid>, and show the same process in host ps -ef under a different PID than it sees inside. Be able to state what is NOT isolated: the kernel and its modules, the clock unless a time namespace is used, sysctl values that are not namespaced, and the hardware.

resource.label: man7: namespaces(7)

subtopics.name: Build a container by hand: unshare, pivot_root, nsenter
subtopics.learn: Reproduce the core of docker run with no Docker involved: export a rootfs with docker export or debootstrap, then unshare --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid --fork --mount-proc, mount --make-rprivate / so mounts do not leak to the host, pivot_root into the rootfs (know why Docker uses pivot_root rather than chroot: chroot is escapable with CAP_SYS_CHROOT), mount a fresh /proc, set the hostname. Then use nsenter -t <pid> -n -m -p to enter a running container's namespaces selectively; this is how you run host tools (ip, ss, tcpdump, strace) against a distroless container that has no shell. Understand what --fork does for PID namespaces and why the first process inside becomes PID 1.

resource.label: man7: unshare(1)

subtopics.name: PID 1 semantics: signals, zombies, --init and stop timeouts
subtopics.learn: Inside a PID namespace the entrypoint is PID 1 and inherits init duties: it must reap orphaned children with waitpid, and the kernel installs no default SIGTERM handler for PID 1, so a naive process silently ignores docker stop. Know the stop sequence: SIGTERM (or the STOPSIGNAL instruction) then wait --stop-timeout / -t seconds (default 10) then SIGKILL, yielding exit 137; a clean SIGTERM exit is 143. Know why shell-form CMD python app.py wraps in /bin/sh -c so the signal hits sh and never reaches Python, when to use exec form, and when docker run --init (tini) is needed to reap zombies from a forking app. Verify with docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}', docker top, and ps -o pid,ppid,stat inside the container looking for Z state.

resource.label: man7: pid_namespaces(7)

subtopics.name: cgroups v2: the unified hierarchy and its controllers
subtopics.learn: On a cgroup v2 host find a container's cgroup under /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope (systemd driver) or /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/<id> (cgroupfs driver), and confirm which driver is in use with docker info | grep -i cgroup. Read the files that matter: memory.max, memory.high, memory.current, memory.events (the oom_kill counter), cpu.max (quota and period, e.g. 200000 100000 means two CPUs), cpu.weight, cpu.stat (nr_throttled), pids.max, io.max. Understand that cgroups limit and account but do not isolate: free, nproc and /proc/meminfo inside a container still show host totals, which is why the JVM, Go and Node need container-aware sizing. Confirm membership from inside with cat /proc/self/cgroup and from outside with docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.CgroupParent}}'.

resource.label: Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2

subtopics.name: Docker resource flags and the OOM-kill path
subtopics.learn: Map each flag to its cgroup file: --memory to memory.max, --memory-reservation to memory.high (soft), --memory-swap (set equal to --memory to disable swap entirely), --cpus 1.5 to cpu.max, --cpu-shares to cpu.weight, --pids-limit to pids.max, --cpuset-cpus to cpuset.cpus. Trace an OOM end to end: the kernel picks the largest-RSS process in the cgroup (not necessarily PID 1, so a worker can die while PID 1 keeps running), docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' flips to true, the exit code is 137, and dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' on the host names the victim. Know that --oom-kill-disable is a trap that turns OOM into a livelock, that CPU limits throttle rather than kill, and how to observe both live with docker stats --no-stream and cpu.stat.

resource.label: Docker docs: Resource constraints

subtopics.name: Capabilities, seccomp, no-new-privileges: what --privileged really grants
subtopics.learn: Know Docker's default capability set (CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD, AUDIT_WRITE, SETFCAP) and that SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE and NET_ADMIN are dropped. Apply --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE and verify with capsh --print or grep Cap /proc/1/status decoded via capsh --decode. Understand that --privileged means all capabilities plus every /dev device plus seccomp and AppArmor disabled plus writable /sys, which is root on the host in practice. Know the default seccomp profile blocks roughly 40 syscalls (mount, reboot, keyctl, ptrace on older kernels) and that --security-opt seccomp=unconfined is what people reach for when strace fails in a container. Establish a baseline of --security-opt no-new-privileges, --read-only with --tmpfs /tmp, and a non-root --user; know how userns-remap changes what uid 0 inside maps to on the host.

resource.label: Docker docs: Engine security

subtopics.name: OCI image anatomy: manifest, config, content-addressed layers
subtopics.learn: Pull an image apart: docker manifest inspect nginx:latest shows an image index with one manifest per platform; each manifest lists a config blob and an ordered list of layer blobs, all addressed by sha256 digest. Know the difference between the compressed layer digest (in the manifest, what the registry stores and what docker pull downloads) and the uncompressed diffID (in the config's rootfs.diff_ids, what docker inspect -f '{{.RootFS.Layers}}' prints). Understand that docker history shows one row per config history entry, including zero-byte rows for ENV, CMD, LABEL and WORKDIR that produce no filesystem layer. Pin by digest with image@sha256:... for reproducibility and know that a tag is a mutable pointer, so latest tells you nothing about what is running on the customer's host.

resource.label: OCI Image Format Specification (GitHub)

subtopics.name: OverlayFS: lowerdir, upperdir, copy-up and whiteouts
subtopics.learn: Read docker inspect -f '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}' to find LowerDir (colon-separated, one path per layer, deepest image layer last), UpperDir (the container's writable layer), WorkDir and MergedDir, then cat the same file at each level under /var/lib/docker/overlay2/ to see which layer wins. Understand copy-up: the first write to a file that lives in a lower layer copies the entire file into upperdir, so appending one byte to a 2 GB file copies 2 GB; deletions create whiteout entries (character device 0:0) or opaque directories (xattr trusted.overlay.opaque=y). Explain from this why RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists in a later layer does not shrink the image and why apt-get update && apt-get install && rm -rf must be one RUN. Know the kernel's 128 lower-layer limit and read docker system df -v to see shared versus unique layer bytes.

resource.label: Linux kernel docs: Overlay Filesystem

subtopics.name: Layer cache rules and BuildKit cache mounts
subtopics.learn: State the cache-hit rule per instruction: a step is reused only if its parent matched and the instruction is byte-identical; RUN is keyed on the command string alone (so RUN apt-get update never re-runs by itself and can pin you to a stale package index), COPY and ADD are keyed on a checksum of file contents and mode. One miss invalidates every step after it, hence the ordering: copy lockfiles, install dependencies, then copy source. Use RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip for a package cache that persists across builds without landing in the image, --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc so credentials never enter a layer, and COPY --link where it applies. Know --no-cache, --cache-from type=registry,ref=... and --cache-to type=registry,mode=max for CI runners with empty local caches, that a missing .dockerignore (stray .git, node_modules, .env) busts COPY on every build, and read --progress=plain output to see CACHED per step.

resource.label: Docker docs: Build cache

subtopics.name: Multi-stage builds through the layer lens
subtopics.learn: Understand that each FROM ... AS name starts an independent layer chain with its own cache and only the final stage's layers ship; COPY --from=build /app/dist /app produces one layer regardless of how many steps built it. Use docker build --target build to stop at an intermediate stage for a debug image, and know that BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel and skips stages the target does not depend on. Measure the effect with docker image ls and docker history when moving from python:3.12 (roughly 1 GB) to python:3.12-slim to a distroless runtime, and know the alpine trade-offs (musl DNS resolver behaviour, glibc wheels that will not install). Non-root USER, SBOM generation, scanning and signing are covered in Topic 6; here the goal is knowing exactly which bytes end up in the shipped image and why.

resource.label: Docker docs: Multi-stage builds

subtopics.name: Writable layer vs volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs
subtopics.learn: Know where writes go and what survives: the writable layer dies with docker rm and counts toward the Containers line in docker system df; named volumes live at /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, survive rm, and die on docker volume prune or compose down -v; bind mounts are a host path where uid and gid are raw numbers, so a host uid 1000 file is owned by whichever container user happens to be uid 1000; tmpfs is RAM and vanishes on stop. Understand that the VOLUME Dockerfile instruction creates anonymous volumes that accumulate silently, the --mount versus -v syntax, :ro, :z and :Z on SELinux hosts, and that a bind mount over a directory hides whatever the image had there (the empty node_modules problem). Prove persistence by running postgres with -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data, writing a row, docker rm -f, recreating, and reading the row back.

resource.label: Docker docs: Volumes

subtopics.name: Network namespaces, veth pairs and the docker0 bridge by hand
subtopics.learn: Rebuild Docker's bridge networking with iproute2: ip netns add c1, ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1, ip link set veth1 netns c1, ip link set veth0 master docker0, assign 172.17.0.x/16 inside, set the default route via 172.17.0.1, add a MASQUERADE rule, and ping 1.1.1.1 from inside the netns. Then compare with a real container: nsenter -t $(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' c1) -n ip addr (most containers lack ip), and on the host use bridge link show plus ethtool -S vethX | grep peer_ifindex to map which veth belongs to which container. Know that net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 and the br_netfilter module are required for outbound traffic and port publishing, that Docker sets them for you at daemon start, and therefore that a CIS hardening script resetting sysctls breaks every container's networking while docker ps still looks healthy.

resource.label: man7: ip-netns(8)

subtopics.name: Bridge driver, user-defined networks and the embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11
subtopics.learn: Know why the default bridge network has no name resolution between containers (only the legacy --link) while user-defined bridges do: Docker writes nameserver 127.0.0.11 into the container's /etc/resolv.conf and its embedded DNS answers container names, --network-alias entries and Compose service names, forwarding everything else to the host's resolvers or the --dns you set. Read docker network inspect <net> for the IPAM subnet, gateway and the Containers map; know com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false and --internal networks for egress-free tiers. Understand the classic client-site failure: Docker's default pool 172.17.0.0/16 and Compose's 172.18.0.0/16 onward collide with the customer's VPN or on-prem CIDR, so packets to their database are routed to the bridge; fix with default-address-pools in /etc/docker/daemon.json or ipam.config.subnet per network. Know that an MTU mismatch on VPN or overlay hosts (com.docker.network.driver.mtu) makes small requests succeed and large responses hang.

resource.label: Docker docs: Bridge network driver

subtopics.name: Port publishing: DNAT, the DOCKER and DOCKER-USER chains, docker-proxy
subtopics.learn: Trace -p 8080:80 to the rules it creates: iptables -t nat -S DOCKER shows a DNAT to <container-ip>:80, iptables -S DOCKER shows the ACCEPT in the filter table, and a MASQUERADE rule handles return traffic. Know that Docker's chains are evaluated before the host's own INPUT/FORWARD rules, which is why ufw deny 8080 does nothing for a published port; put your rules in the DOCKER-USER chain instead, or bind to loopback with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 so the service is only reachable through a reverse proxy. Understand that docker-proxy (the userland proxy) is the process ss -ltnp shows listening on the host port, not your app, and handles localhost and IPv6 edge cases. Know that --network host skips all of this (no NAT, no isolation, host port collisions), -P publishes every EXPOSEd port on an ephemeral host port, docker port <c> prints the mapping, and that the nftables backend or iptables: false in daemon.json changes what you will see.

resource.label: Docker docs: Packet filtering and firewalls

subtopics.name: Bridge network debugging playbook with netshoot
subtopics.learn: Run a fixed sequence when 'the container cannot reach X': (1) docker network inspect for both endpoints, same network and subnet? (2) inside the netns via nsenter -n or docker run --rm -it --network container:<c> nicolaka/netshoot: ss -ltnp to see whether the app is bound to 0.0.0.0 or only 127.0.0.1 (the number one cause of connection refused on a published port), ip route, dig @127.0.0.11 <service>, curl -v; (3) on the host: iptables -t nat -S DOCKER, sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward, lsmod | grep br_netfilter, tcpdump -ni docker0 port 5432 to see whether packets arrive and whether replies leave; (4) MTU with ping -M do -s 1400; (5) subnet overlap by comparing ip route on the host with the customer's CIDRs. Know the healthcheck trap: curl localhost inside the container succeeds while the published port fails because the process listens on loopback only. Practise on a stack you deliberately break four ways: loopback bind, wrong network, overlapping subnet, ip_forward=0.

resource.label: nicolaka/netshoot: network troubleshooting container (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Healthchecks, restart policies and Compose dependency ordering
subtopics.learn: Write HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=3s --start-period=30s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health || exit 1 (or the Compose healthcheck block, knowing CMD versus CMD-SHELL test forms) and read .State.Health.Status and .State.Health.Log from docker inspect. Know that plain Docker never restarts an unhealthy container: health only gates depends_on with condition: service_healthy in Compose and routing in Swarm, while restart policies (no, on-failure[:n], always, unless-stopped) react to exit codes, not health. Understand that depends_on without a condition orders start, not readiness, so the Postgres race still happens; use pg_isready -U <user> as the database healthcheck and give the app a start_period long enough for migrations. Know that failures during start_period do not count toward retries, and that a healthcheck which calls an external dependency makes your service flap whenever that dependency does.

resource.label: Compose file reference: services (healthcheck, depends_on)

subtopics.name: The runtime stack: dockerd, containerd, shim, runc and the OCI bundle
subtopics.learn: Draw the process tree: dockerd talks to containerd over gRPC, containerd starts one containerd-shim-runc-v2 per container, the shim invokes runc which creates the namespaces and cgroups then exits, and the shim keeps holding stdio and the exit status. Confirm with pstree -p $(pgrep -x containerd) and ctr -n moby containers ls. Generate an OCI runtime bundle with runc spec and read config.json to see how namespaces, the cgroupsPath, mounts, capabilities and the seccomp profile appear as fields; this is exactly what the Kubernetes CRI hands to containerd in Topic 7. Know that live-restore: true in daemon.json keeps containers running across a dockerd restart or upgrade and that its absence is why a routine apt upgrade docker-ce takes a customer's whole single-node stack down.

resource.label: OCI Runtime Specification (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Logging drivers, disk hygiene and the full /var/lib/docker failure
subtopics.learn: Know that the default json-file driver writes every stdout and stderr line to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log with no rotation unless log-opts max-size and max-file are set in daemon.json or via --log-opt; this is the single most common way a customer's single-node Docker host fills its disk and takes Postgres down with it. Know that docker logs only works with json-file, local and journald drivers, that local is the better default (compressed, rotated), the --since, --until and --tail flags, and that an app writing logs to a file inside the container hides them from all of this and from any log shipper. Use docker system df -v to attribute disk across images, container writable layers, volumes and build cache, and be able to say exactly what docker system prune -a --volumes will destroy before running it on a customer machine.

resource.label: Docker docs: Configure logging drivers

outcomes: You can explain to a non-engineer what a container is in under two minutes using only 'a process', 'namespaces', 'cgroups' and 'a tar of files', then prove it by showing the container's process in host ps with a different PID than it sees inside.
You can build a working isolated shell with unshare, pivot_root, a cgroup v2 memory limit and a veth pair to a bridge, with no Docker binary on the machine, in under 15 minutes from memory.

You can draw an image's layer stack from docker history and docker inspect, predict which steps print CACHED before rebuilding, and reorder a Dockerfile so a source-only change rebuilds in under 10 seconds.
You can explain why an image grew after a RUN rm step by naming the whiteout mechanism, and cut a 1.2 GB image by more than half using single-RUN cleanup, a slim base and a multi-stage build.

You can triage a container exiting 137 to either OOM (State.OOMKilled, dmesg) or a stop-timeout kill (signal handling, shell-form CMD) within five minutes and fix the root cause with the right flag or Dockerfile change.

You can debug a published port returning connection refused from the host, distinguishing loopback bind, missing DNAT rule, ip_forward=0, host firewall and subnet overlap using ss, iptables -t nat -S, nsenter and tcpdump.

You can write a Compose stack where the app waits on a real Postgres readiness healthcheck, logs rotate, memory is capped, and the app runs as non-root with capabilities dropped, and prove each property with a specific docker inspect field.
You can read a DOCKER-USER chain and state which container ports are reachable from which source CIDRs, and write the rules that restrict a database container to the app container only.
failureModes: A JVM or Node service is OOM-killed (exit 137) under a 2 GB --memory limit because the runtime sized its heap from the host's 64 GB visible in /proc/meminfo; the fix is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage or --max-old-space-size, not a bigger limit.

docker stop on the customer's app always takes the full 10 seconds and returns 137 because the entrypoint is sh -c 'python app.py', so SIGTERM stops the shell and never reaches Python; in-flight writes are killed mid-transaction on every deploy.
A single-node Docker host stops scheduling containers and Postgres crashes with 'No space left on device' because json-file logs for a chatty service grew to 200 GB with no max-size configured.

After the client VPN connects, the container can no longer reach the client's on-prem SQL Server at 172.18.4.20 because Compose created a 172.18.0.0/16 network and the host now routes that CIDR to the bridge.

A published port that works in dev returns connection refused at the customer site because the app binds to 127.0.0.1 when HOST is unset, and DNAT delivers packets to the container's eth0 where nothing is listening.

A nightly docker system prune -a --volumes cron deletes the customer's Postgres data because the image's VOLUME instruction created an anonymous volume instead of the named volume everyone assumed Compose had declared.

A CIS benchmark hardening script sets net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 on the customer host; containers start and docker ps looks healthy but nothing has outbound connectivity, and two hours go to DNS theories before anyone checks sysctl.
interviewQuestions: A customer CTO says 'containers are lightweight VMs, so our tenants are isolated from each other on the node.' Correct them precisely: what is shared, what is isolated, and what would you change in the run configuration before agreeing to run their untrusted plugin code in a container?

Walk me through everything that happens from docker run -p 8080:80 nginx to the first HTTP response arriving at a browser on the host. Name the processes, syscalls, filesystem mounts and iptables rules involved, in order.

This Dockerfile takes nine minutes to rebuild after a one-line code change: it copies the whole repo, then runs pip install, then sets CMD. Draw the layer stack, tell me exactly which layers are invalidated and why, then rewrite it so the rebuild takes under ten seconds and the final image is under 200 MB.

A container in the customer's environment exits with code 137 every few hours. Give me your diagnostic sequence, the two distinct root causes that produce 137, and how you would tell them apart from the host in under five minutes.

The app container can curl the Postgres container by service name in Compose on your laptop, but on the customer's VM it intermittently fails with 'could not translate host name'. What is 127.0.0.11, how does it forward queries, and what would you check on the host?

Two services must talk to each other over Docker networking on one host; the security team requires that neither is reachable from the host's public interface and that the database is reachable from nothing except the app. Design the networks, port bindings and DOCKER-USER rules, and show how you would prove the properties with iptables and ss.
You deleted a 400 MB dataset in a later RUN step and the image got larger. Explain what overlayfs did on disk, and how you would fix it both with and without a multi-stage build.
5.proofOfWork: A public repo named container-from-scratch containing three things. First, a roughly 150-line bash or Python script that, on a stock Ubuntu VM with no Docker installed, downloads an alpine rootfs, creates mount, pid, net, uts and ipc namespaces via unshare, pivot_roots into the rootfs, places the process in a cgroup v2 leaf with memory.max=64M and pids.max=50, wires a veth pair to a hand-made bridge with a MASQUERADE rule so wget works from inside, and drops to a shell; the README walks each step next to the equivalent docker run flag and shows the process in host ps. Second, a broken-network-lab directory with one Compose stack and four deliberately broken variants (loopback bind, wrong network, overlapping subnet, ip_forward=0) plus a debug.md with the exact commands and output that pinpoint each fault. Third, an asciinema recording of a Dockerfile rebuild after a code-only change, first at several minutes and then at under ten seconds after reordering and adding a pip cache mount, with the --progress=plain output annotated to show which steps hit CACHED. The CTO one-pager from the plan deliverable links to this repo as its evidence.

6.topic: Production images and supply chain: multi-stage, non-root, SBOM, scanning, signing
6.why: The container image is the unit an FDE actually hands to a customer, and it is the customer's security team, not yours, that decides whether it runs: their Wiz or Prisma scan, their admission controller, their procurement checklist asking for an SBOM. A PoC that took three weeks to build dies on go-live day when the image is 1.2 GB, runs as root, and shows 300 CVEs, and the FDE is the only person in the room who can fix it before the change window closes. Knowing how to make an image small, non-root, scannable, attested and signed is what lets you say 'yes, deploy it to prod' in a regulated bank or a FedRAMP boundary instead of 'let me get back to you'.
prerequisites: Layers, union filesystems, namespaces and cgroups from 'Docker internals' (topic 5): you should already know why deleting a file in a later RUN does not shrink the image
Linux users, UIDs/GIDs, file permission bits and capabilities from 'Linux internals' (topic 1), because non-root is mostly a permissions problem
Signals and PID 1 semantics (SIGTERM vs SIGKILL, zombie reaping) from 'Linux internals' (topic 1)
TLS certificates and what an OIDC identity token is, from 'Networking' (topic 2), since keyless signing is OIDC plus short-lived x509
A GitHub repository with a working CI job from 'Git at depth' (topic 4); Dokeo (Python) and DefenderMate (TypeScript/Next.js) are the two images you will harden
Comfort reading JSON with `jq` and a SHA-256 digest without flinching

subtopics.name: OCI image anatomy: manifest, config, layers, tag vs digest
subtopics.learn: Read a real manifest with `docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw <ref>` and identify the three parts: the config blob (`application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json`, holding `config.User`, `Env`, `Entrypoint`, `rootfs.diff_ids`, `history`), the ordered layer descriptors (`mediaType`, `digest`, `size`) and, for multi-arch, the image index that points at per-platform manifests. Understand that the image digest is the sha256 of the manifest bytes, so `repo@sha256:...` is immutable while `repo:tag` is a mutable pointer a registry can move under you. Be able to pull by digest, read `RepoDigests` from `docker image inspect`, and explain why a scanner result is only meaningful against a digest.

resource.label: OCI Image Spec: Image Manifest

subtopics.name: Layer cache mechanics and instruction ordering
subtopics.learn: Know exactly how BuildKit decides a cache hit: `RUN` is keyed on the instruction string plus parent layer, `COPY`/`ADD` on the checksum of the copied files, and any miss invalidates every later instruction. Order Dockerfiles so lockfiles (`uv.lock`, `package-lock.json`) are copied and dependencies installed before application source, keep `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in one RUN to avoid stale package indexes, and use `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv` (or `/root/.npm`) so package caches persist between builds without landing in a layer. In CI use `--cache-from type=registry,ref=...` with `--cache-to type=registry,mode=max` or `type=gha` so cold runners still hit cache.

resource.label: Docker Docs: Build cache

subtopics.name: Multi-stage builds: builder/runtime split, --target, COPY --from
subtopics.learn: Structure every production Dockerfile as at least two stages: a `builder` with compilers, headers (`gcc`, `libpq-dev`, `python3-dev`) and dev dependencies, and a `runtime` stage that starts from a slim base and receives only artifacts via `COPY --from=builder`. Use `docker build --target builder` to run tests inside the build, `COPY --link` so copied layers are cache-independent of the base, and name stages so `--from` references survive refactors. Verify the split worked by checking the runtime stage has no `gcc` or `pip` cache and that shared libraries the binary needs (`libpq5`, not `libpq-dev`) are still present with `ldd` or by simply starting the app; a runtime that lacks a `.so` fails at import time, not build time.

resource.label: Docker Docs: Multi-stage builds

subtopics.name: Base image choice: slim vs Alpine/musl vs distroless vs Wolfi
subtopics.learn: Compare the four real options on size, CVE count and debuggability: `python:3.12-slim-bookworm` (~150 MB, glibc, apt, dozens of 'will not fix' Debian CVEs), `python:3.12-alpine` (~50 MB, musl: wheels need `musllinux` tags or compile from source, different DNS resolver behaviour, slower malloc), `gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12` (no shell, no package manager, `:debug` tag adds busybox) and Chainguard/Wolfi `cgr.dev/chainguard/python` (glibc, apk, rebuilt nightly, near-zero CVEs, `-dev` variant for a shell). Understand that the CVE count on Debian stable is mostly unfixed-upstream noise and that distroless trades `kubectl exec` debugging for attack surface, which you recover with ephemeral debug containers. Pick per customer: a bank that mandates a specific approved base wins over your preference.

resource.label: GoogleContainerTools/distroless

subtopics.name: Python runtime slimming with uv (Dokeo)
subtopics.learn: Build Dokeo with `uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project` in the builder against a cache mount, then copy the finished `.venv` into a slim runtime and set `PATH=/app/.venv/bin:$PATH`. Set `UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1` and `UV_LINK_MODE=copy` in the builder, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` and `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` in the runtime so logs stream and no `__pycache__` is written to a read-only filesystem at run time. Know why the venv must be created with the same Python path in both stages (the venv's `pyvenv.cfg` and shebangs are absolute) and why `pip install --no-cache-dir` or a cache mount is mandatory if you fall back to pip.

resource.label: uv Docs: Using uv in Docker

subtopics.name: Node runtime slimming (DefenderMate)
subtopics.learn: For DefenderMate run `npm ci` with a `--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm` in the builder, build, then either `npm ci --omit=dev` into a clean stage or `npm prune --omit=dev`, and copy only `dist/`, production `node_modules` and `package.json` into `node:22-bookworm-slim` or `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12`. For the Next.js front end use `output: 'standalone'` in `next.config.js` and copy `.next/standalone` plus `.next/static` and `public`, which drops the image from ~1 GB to ~150 MB. Set `NODE_ENV=production`, use the existing `node` user (uid 1000) or your own high UID, and know that `npm start` is shell-form and breaks signal delivery (covered in the PID 1 subtopic).

resource.label: nodejs/docker-node: Docker and Node.js Best Practices

subtopics.name: Build context, .dockerignore and build-time secrets
subtopics.learn: Understand that everything in the build context is sent to the daemon and available to `COPY .`, so `.dockerignore` (next to the Dockerfile, or `<Dockerfile>.dockerignore`) must exclude `.git`, `.env*`, `node_modules`, `.venv`, `__pycache__`, test fixtures and local data; a 'Sending build context 2.1GB' line is a bug. Never pass credentials as `ARG` or `ENV`: ARG values are recorded in `docker history` and ENV is baked into the image config forever. Use `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc` with `--secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc` (or `env=NPM_TOKEN`) and `--mount=type=ssh` for private git, and know that 'deleting' a secret in a later RUN or using multi-stage does not help if it was ever written to a layer of the final stage.

resource.label: Docker Docs: Build secrets

subtopics.name: Non-root by construction: USER, numeric UID, --chown, writable paths
subtopics.learn: Create a dedicated user with a high, fixed UID (`useradd -u 10001 -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin app` or `addgroup`/`adduser` on Alpine) and set `USER 10001:10001` numerically, because Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot: true` cannot verify a named user and fails with 'cannot verify user is non-root'. Copy application files with `COPY --chown=10001:10001` and give the process exactly one writable directory (a mounted `emptyDir` at `/tmp` or `/app/data`) so the pod can run with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`. Bind to a port above 1024 (8080, not 80) so you do not need `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, and test locally with `docker run --read-only --user 10001 --cap-drop ALL --tmpfs /tmp` before the customer's Pod Security 'restricted' profile does it for you.

resource.label: Kubernetes Docs: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

subtopics.name: PID 1, signals and exec-form ENTRYPOINT
subtopics.learn: Know that shell-form `CMD npm start` or `CMD python app.py` makes `/bin/sh -c` PID 1, which does not forward SIGTERM, so `docker stop` and Kubernetes pod deletion wait the full grace period (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, default 30 s) and then SIGKILL in-flight requests. Always use exec form `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "uvicorn", ...]`, set `STOPSIGNAL` if the app expects something other than SIGTERM, and if your process spawns children (gunicorn, a shell wrapper, Playwright) add `tini` (`ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--", ...]`) or run with `--init` so zombies get reaped. Prove it: `docker stop` should return in under 2 seconds and the app log should show the graceful shutdown hook firing.

resource.label: krallin/tini: A tiny but valid init for containers

subtopics.name: Dockerfile linting: hadolint and docker build --check
subtopics.learn: Run `hadolint Dockerfile` and be able to fix the rules that matter in production: DL3006/DL3007 (unpinned or `latest` base), DL3008/DL3018 (unpinned apt/apk packages), DL3009 (apt lists not cleaned), DL3002 (final USER is root), DL3025 (shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT) and DL4006 (missing `set -o pipefail`). Run BuildKit's own linter with `docker build --check .` and add `# check=error=true` after the `# syntax=` line so checks like `JSONArgsRecommended`, `SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv`, `UndefinedVar` and `LegacyKeyValueFormat` fail the build rather than warn. Wire both into the pre-commit config you built for Dokeo in topic 4 so they run in under a second.

resource.label: Docker Docs: Build checks reference

subtopics.name: Image forensics: dive, docker history, wasted-space hunting
subtopics.learn: Use `dive <image>` to walk layers and see the efficiency score and 'wasted space' from files added then removed or overwritten; run it headless in CI with `CI=true dive --lowestEfficiency=0.95 --highestUserWastedPercent=0.05 <image>`. Cross-check with `docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}'` to find the one RUN that added 400 MB, and `docker image inspect --format '{{.Size}}'` for the total. The usual culprits you should recognise on sight: apt lists, pip or npm cache, dev dependencies, `.git`, test data copied by `COPY .`, and compilers left in the final stage.

resource.label: wagoodman/dive: explore layers and wasted space

subtopics.name: Trivy image scanning: flags, package types, exit codes
subtopics.learn: Run `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 --pkg-types os,library --scanners vuln,secret <image>@<digest>` and read the output by package type: `os` findings come from the base image's dpkg/apk database and are fixed by bumping the base, `library` findings come from `uv.lock`/`package-lock.json`-installed packages and are fixed by bumping your dependency.
