Understand the vulnerability DB is pulled from a registry on first run (`~/.cache/trivy`) and must be cached or mirrored (`TRIVY_DB_REPOSITORY`) in CI to avoid rate limiting, and that `--scanners misconfig` (or `trivy config .`) also lints the Dockerfile itself with checks such as running as root or a missing HEALTHCHECK. Know what `--ignore-unfixed` hides so you can defend it to a customer.

resource.label: Trivy Docs: Container Image target

subtopics.name: Vulnerability triage: severity, EPSS, unfixed, .trivyignore with expiry, VEX
subtopics.learn: Triage a CVE in this order: is a fixed version available (`FixedVersion` column), is the vulnerable code reachable in your process (a `curl` CVE in a distroless image with no curl is not), what is the EPSS exploitation probability versus the CVSS score, and is it in the customer's own scanner's list. Record every accepted finding in `.trivyignore` (or `.trivyignore.yaml` with `statement` and `expired_at`) with an expiry date so the suppression fails the build when it lapses, and for statements a customer must consume, emit an OpenVEX document and feed it with `trivy --vex`. Never suppress by severity alone and never use `--ignore-unfixed` on a language package, since 'unfixed' there almost always means 'you have not bumped it'.

resource.label: Trivy Docs: Filtering (severity, ignore file, VEX)

subtopics.name: SBOM: SPDX vs CycloneDX, generation, attestation, rescanning
subtopics.learn: Generate an SBOM three ways and know when each applies: `syft <image> -o spdx-json=sbom.spdx.json -o cyclonedx-json=sbom.cdx.json` for a standalone file a customer's GRC team asked for, `trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.cdx.json` when you want the same tool to scan it, and `docker buildx build --sbom=true --push` to attach an in-toto SBOM attestation to the image index (readable with `docker buildx imagetools inspect <ref> --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'`). Set `BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true` on the builder stage if the customer wants build-time dependencies listed too. Then prove the value: run `trivy sbom sbom.cdx.json` a week later without pulling the image, and diff two SBOMs to answer 'what changed between the version you approved and this one'.

resource.label: Docker Docs: SBOM attestations

subtopics.name: Provenance and SLSA levels
subtopics.learn: Understand what each SLSA Build level actually guarantees: L1 is provenance that exists, L2 is provenance signed by a hosted build platform, L3 adds an isolated, hardened build so the provenance cannot be forged by the repo's own workflow. Attach provenance with `docker buildx build --provenance=mode=max` (records Dockerfile, build args, source commit and materials as an in-toto statement of type `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1`) and use the `slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator` reusable workflow when a customer needs L3. Know the operational gotcha: provenance and SBOM attestations turn a single manifest into an image index with `unknown/unknown` platform entries, which confuses some registries and breaks AWS Lambda container deploys, so `--provenance=false` is sometimes the right call per target.

resource.label: SLSA v1.0: Build levels

subtopics.name: Signing with cosign keyless: Fulcio, Rekor, identity-bound verification
subtopics.learn: Trace the keyless flow end to end: the CI job's OIDC token (GitHub Actions needs `permissions: id-token: write`) is exchanged at Fulcio for a ~10-minute x509 certificate binding the workflow identity, the signature is made with an ephemeral key, the cert and signature are recorded in the Rekor transparency log, and the bundle is pushed to the registry as an OCI artifact tagged `sha256-<digest>.sig` next to the image. Always sign the digest, never the tag: `cosign sign --yes ${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}` using the digest output of the build step. Verify with `cosign verify --certificate-identity https://github.com/<org>/<repo>/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com <ref>@<digest>` and understand that omitting the identity check means 'signed by anyone with a GitHub account'. Know the key-based alternative (`cosign generate-key-pair --kms awskms://...`) for customers who cannot reach the public Sigstore instance.

resource.label: Sigstore Docs: Signing containers with cosign

subtopics.name: Enforcing at admission: digest pinning, imagePullPolicy, verifyImages
subtopics.learn: Turn signing into a control: deploy by digest (`image: repo@sha256:...`) or have the policy engine mutate tags to digests, and understand why `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` with a mutable tag means different nodes silently run different code. Install Kyverno in a kind cluster and write a `ClusterPolicy` with `verifyImages` that requires a keyless attestor with your workflow `subject` and the GitHub `issuer`, sets `mutateDigest: true` and `required: true`, then watch an unsigned image get rejected with the exact error message a customer's platform team would see. Know the equivalent in Sigstore `policy-controller` (`ClusterImagePolicy` plus the `policy.sigstore.dev/include: "true"` namespace label) and how Pod Security admission 'restricted' independently requires non-root, dropped capabilities and a `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile.

resource.label: Kyverno Docs: Verify Images

subtopics.name: The Trivy gate in GitHub Actions
subtopics.learn: Build the deliverable's CI job: `docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` for a pre-push scan (or scan the pushed digest from `steps.build.outputs.digest`), then `aquasecurity/trivy-action` with `image-ref`, `severity: HIGH,CRITICAL`, `ignore-unfixed: true`, `exit-code: '1'` and a second run with `format: sarif` uploaded via `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` so findings appear in the Security tab. Cache `~/.cache/trivy` with `actions/cache` or set `TRIVY_DB_REPOSITORY` to a mirror so the vulnerability DB download does not get rate-limited and take every pipeline down at once. Add a scheduled workflow that rescans the currently deployed digest nightly, because a green build on Monday says nothing about Thursday's CVE disclosure.

resource.label: aquasecurity/trivy-action

subtopics.name: Hardening the pipeline itself: permissions, OIDC, SHA-pinned actions
subtopics.learn: A signed image is only as trustworthy as the workflow that signed it. Set job-level `permissions:` to the minimum (`contents: read`, `packages: write`, `id-token: write`), pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA with a version comment (`uses: docker/build-push-action@<sha> # v6.x`) and let Dependabot bump them, and never interpolate untrusted event data such as `github.event.pull_request.title` into a `run:` script. Use OIDC federation to the cloud (ties to topic 15) instead of long-lived registry credentials in secrets, avoid `pull_request_target` with a checkout of the PR head, and understand that anyone who can edit the workflow file on the default branch can produce a validly signed image, which is exactly the gap SLSA L3 closes.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Secure use reference for GitHub Actions

subtopics.name: Reproducible and multi-platform builds
subtopics.learn: Pin the base image by digest (`FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:...`) and package versions so two builds from the same commit produce the same layers, set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` (BuildKit honours it) and add `rewrite-timestamp=true` to the image output so layer mtimes stop changing the digest on every build. Build for both architectures with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` on a `docker-container` driver (`docker buildx create --use`), and know that QEMU emulation via `docker/setup-qemu-action` is 5 to 20 times slower than native arm runners or cross-compiling with `--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM` and the `TARGETARCH` build arg. The result is an image index, so verify each platform manifest with `imagetools inspect` before telling a customer on Graviton it is supported.

resource.label: Docker Docs: Reproducible builds with GitHub Actions

outcomes: You can take Dokeo from a naive single-stage `python:3.12` image to a multi-stage image under 200 MB with a dive efficiency score above 0.95, and show the `docker history` line-by-line explanation of where the other 900 MB went.

You can run both Dokeo and DefenderMate under `docker run --read-only --user 10001 --cap-drop ALL --tmpfs /tmp` and under a Kubernetes Pod Security 'restricted' namespace with `runAsNonRoot: true` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` without CreateContainerConfigError or a PermissionError at startup.

You can produce a `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1` result of zero findings on both images, with every accepted CVE in `.trivyignore` carrying a written justification and an expiry date, and a CI job that goes red when a new HIGH appears.

You can attach SPDX and CycloneDX SBOMs plus SLSA provenance to an image at build time, read them back with `docker buildx imagetools inspect --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'`, and rescan the SBOM file a week later with `trivy sbom` without pulling the image.

You can sign an image keyless from GitHub Actions and verify it by digest with `cosign verify --certificate-identity ... --certificate-oidc-issuer ...`, then explain to a customer's security reviewer what Fulcio, Rekor and the `.sig` tag each contribute and what verification does not prove.

You can install Kyverno in a kind cluster, write a `verifyImages` policy bound to your workflow identity, and demonstrate the unsigned 'before' image being rejected while the signed 'after' image is admitted with its tag mutated to a digest.

You can diagnose a container that takes 30 seconds to stop, prove it is shell-form CMD swallowing SIGTERM with a `docker stop` timing and a `ps` of PID 1, and fix it so shutdown completes in under 2 seconds with the graceful hook logged.

You can receive a 300-item CVE export from a customer's Wiz or Prisma scan and, in 15 minutes, sort it into base-image fixes, dependency bumps, unreachable-in-this-image, and accepted-with-expiry, and write the one-page disposition their security team will actually sign.
failureModes: A team ships `FROM python:3.12` with gcc, perl and 1.1 GB of Debian, the customer's Wiz scan on go-live morning reports 400 CVEs, and the change window closes while everyone argues about which of them are real.

Switching to Alpine to 'fix' image size makes a Python wheel with no musllinux build compile from source for 18 minutes on every CI run, and later the musl resolver's handling of Kubernetes search domains produces intermittent NXDOMAIN under load that nobody connects to the base-image change.

The Dockerfile says `USER appuser` and the pod spec says `runAsNonRoot: true`; the pod sits in CreateContainerConfigError with 'cannot verify user is non-root' because the kubelet cannot resolve a named user without reading /etc/passwd from the image.

`CMD npm start` makes `sh` PID 1, SIGTERM is never delivered to Node, every pod takes the full 30-second grace period and then is SIGKILLed mid-request, so a 20-pod rolling deploy takes 10 minutes and drops traffic the whole time.

A private registry token is passed as `ARG NPM_TOKEN` and the image is pushed to a shared registry; six weeks later someone runs `docker history` on it and the still-valid token is in the layer metadata for everyone with pull access.

The Trivy gate runs with `--exit-code 1` and without `--ignore-unfixed` on a Debian base, goes red every other day on CVEs with no upstream fix, and within a month the job has `continue-on-error: true` and the gate is theatre.

Cosign signs the tag instead of the digest; a later build moves the tag, verification of `repo:v1.2` still passes because the signature was looked up by whatever digest the tag now points at, and the customer's audit trail no longer says what actually ran.
interviewQuestions: A customer's security team sends you a 312-row CVE export from their scanner and says nothing deploys until it is zero, and go-live is Thursday. Walk me through your first hour, what you would actually change in the image, what you would push back on, and what the document you hand them on Wednesday night looks like.

Explain exactly what happens between `cosign sign` starting in a GitHub Actions job and `cosign verify` succeeding on a customer's laptop: which services are contacted, what is stored where, and what would an attacker need to control to produce a signature that passes your verify command?

Design the image supply chain for a customer whose production cluster is air-gapped: how do images, SBOMs, signatures, the Trivy database and trust roots get across the boundary, how does the cluster verify without reaching public Sigstore, and where does your CI's SLSA level stop meaning anything?

A pod goes into CrashLoopBackOff right after you switch the image to non-root and enable `readOnlyRootFilesystem`; logs show `PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/app/.cache'`. List the possible causes, the fix you would pick for each, and how you would have caught this before it reached the customer's cluster.

Why is `--ignore-unfixed` both necessary and dangerous in a CI vulnerability gate? Describe a gate design that stays green for months without anyone adding `continue-on-error`, including how suppressions expire and how new disclosures on already-deployed digests get caught.

What is the difference between an SBOM, a SLSA provenance attestation and a cosign signature? For each, tell me which customer question it answers, how it is stored in the registry relative to the image, and one way each can be technically valid yet misleading.

Write, at the whiteboard, a multi-stage Dockerfile for a FastAPI service that depends on psycopg with C extensions, such that the runtime stage has no compiler and runs as a numeric non-root user. Then tell me how you would prove the runtime stage still has every shared library it needs before the first customer request hits it.
6.proofOfWork: A public repository, `hardened-images-lab`, containing the naive and hardened Dockerfiles for both Dokeo and DefenderMate side by side, with a `make compare` target that builds each pair and prints a table of image size, dive efficiency score, layer count, Trivy HIGH/CRITICAL count and `docker stop` latency, and a `make verify` target that a reviewer can run cold: it pulls the hardened images by digest, checks `cosign verify` with the pinned workflow identity and GitHub issuer, checks `cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx` and diffs the SBOM against the committed baseline, then spins up a kind cluster with Kyverno, applies the `verifyImages` ClusterPolicy and shows the naive image rejected and the hardened image admitted under a Pod Security 'restricted' namespace with `runAsNonRoot` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem`. The GitHub Actions workflow that produces the images is itself the reference: SHA-pinned actions, job-level least-privilege permissions, OIDC-only registry auth, multi-arch build with SBOM and provenance attestations, a Trivy gate with a `.trivyignore` whose every entry has a justification and an expiry, and a nightly rescan of the deployed digest. The README ends with a one-page 'Image Security Review' written for a customer security team, listing digest, base image and its rationale, signature identity, SBOM location and the CVE disposition table, in the exact shape you would attach to a change request.

7.topic: Kubernetes core: Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, namespaces
7.why: An FDE almost never gets a cluster; they get a namespace, an IngressClass name, a registry pull secret and a platform team that will say 'the cluster is fine, it is your app' the first time a customer sees a 503. Being able to draw exactly how a request travels DNS -> load balancer -> ingress controller -> EndpointSlice -> Pod, and exactly how a config value or credential reaches a process, is what lets you fix the deploy on the bridge call instead of filing a ticket with the platform team and losing a week of the engagement. It is also the vocabulary every customer architecture review is conducted in: if you cannot say 'the Service has no ready endpoints because the readiness probe hits your database', you cannot lead the conversation.
prerequisites: Docker internals from Topic 5: namespaces, cgroups, image layers, exit codes 137 vs 143, SIGTERM to PID 1. A Pod is a shared network namespace plus a pause process; nothing here makes sense without that.
Production images from Topic 6: a non-root, digest-pinned image of Dokeo pushed to a registry (GHCR or Docker Hub) that you can pull from a fresh machine with credentials.

Networking from Topic 2: DNAT and conntrack, reading iptables -t nat, /etc/resolv.conf search and ndots, the TLS handshake and SNI, what a reverse proxy does with the Host header, and HTTP status semantics for 404/502/503/504.
Linux internals from Topic 1: systemd units and journalctl -u (k3s is one unit), /proc/<pid>/environ, tmpfs, file modes, and how a process reads config at start versus on SIGHUP.
Shell from Topic 0: jq, yq, Go templates, reading and writing YAML by hand without an IDE, and sed -n '/Events/,$p' style extraction.

A Hetzner CX22-class VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB, public IPv4) with a DNS A record you control pointing at it, and the Hetzner Cloud Firewall allowing 22, 80, 443 and 6443 from your IP. The deliverable needs a real public IP for HTTP-01.

subtopics.name: Control plane anatomy and the reconcile loop
subtopics.learn: Name every component and what it owns: kube-apiserver (the only process that talks to etcd; every request passes authn -> authz -> mutating admission -> validation -> validating admission -> persist), etcd (source of truth; watch streams keyed by resourceVersion), kube-scheduler (finds Pending pods with no spec.nodeName and binds them), kube-controller-manager (Deployment, ReplicaSet, EndpointSlice, Namespace, ServiceAccount, garbage-collector controllers in one binary), kubelet (watches pods bound to its node and drives the CRI, containerd on k3s), kube-proxy (programs Service VIPs), CoreDNS. Internalise the controller pattern: level-triggered reconcile of spec against observed state via list/watch, no controller ever talks to another directly, everything flows through the API server. Prove the chain with kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -w in one terminal while you apply a Deployment in another: ScalingReplicaSet -> SuccessfulCreate -> Scheduled -> Pulling -> Created -> Started, each Event stamped with the component that emitted it. Check health with kubectl get --raw /readyz?verbose.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Kubernetes Components

subtopics.name: k3s anatomy: what you actually installed on the Hetzner box
subtopics.learn: k3s is upstream Kubernetes packaged as one binary and one systemd unit: apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet and kube-proxy in a single process, sqlite by default (embedded etcd with --cluster-init), bundled containerd, flannel VXLAN as the CNI, and addons shipped as manifests in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests: CoreDNS, Traefik (IngressClass traefik), ServiceLB (klipper-lb, which implements type: LoadBalancer with a DaemonSet of hostPort pods on every node, so on one node a LoadBalancer Service simply gets the node's public IP on 80/443), local-path-provisioner and metrics-server. Install with curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -s - --write-kubeconfig-mode 644, read the kubeconfig from /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml and copy it to your laptop with the server field pointed at the public IP (6443 must be open), know the --disable=traefik,servicelb flags for when you want to bring your own, /etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml for private registry mirrors and auth, and journalctl -u k3s -f as your control-plane log. Understand what is missing versus EKS: no cloud controller creating real load balancers, no IAM integration, one node means no scheduling, and Traefik instead of the ingress-nginx or ALB controller a customer probably runs.

resource.label: k3s docs: Quick-Start Guide

subtopics.name: The object model: metadata, spec, status, ownership, finalizers
subtopics.learn: Every object is apiVersion + kind + metadata + spec + status. Know what metadata carries and why each field matters operationally: uid (immutable identity; a deleted-and-recreated object with the same name is a different object), resourceVersion (etcd revision used for optimistic concurrency; a stale PUT returns 409 Conflict, which is how kubectl edit and controllers avoid lost updates), generation versus status.observedGeneration (has the controller seen my change yet), ownerReferences (garbage collection: deleting a Deployment cascades to its ReplicaSets and Pods unless --cascade=orphan), finalizers (the reason objects hang in Terminating), deletionTimestamp. Discover schema without leaving the terminal: kubectl api-resources (short names, NAMESPACED column, API group), kubectl api-versions, kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate and kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive, kubectl get deploy x -o yaml --show-managed-fields to see which manager owns which field. Understand that status is written only by controllers, and that the apiserver defaults unset spec fields, so a round-tripped -o yaml never equals the manifest you wrote; kubectl neat or yq del is how you get a clean copy.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Working with Kubernetes Objects

subtopics.name: Labels, selectors and annotations as the wiring layer
subtopics.learn: Labels are indexed key/value identity that selectors match on; annotations are unindexed metadata that tools read (kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration, deployment.kubernetes.io/revision, cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer, kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt). Master both selector grammars: equality (matchLabels; kubectl get pods -l app=dokeo,tier!=canary) and set-based (matchExpressions with In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist; -l 'env in (prod,staging)'). Adopt the recommended app.kubernetes.io/name, instance, version, component, part-of and managed-by labels from day one because Helm, ArgoCD, Grafana dashboards and cost tools key off them. Know which selectors are immutable after creation (Deployment.spec.selector, ReplicaSet, Job) and which are not (Service.spec.selector), and the debugging trick that follows: kubectl label pod dokeo-7d9f-abcde app- removes the pod from every Service and lets the ReplicaSet replace it while you keep the broken instance alive for kubectl exec and kubectl debug.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Labels and Selectors

subtopics.name: Namespaces: what they scope, what they do not, quotas and limits
subtopics.learn: Namespaces scope names and RBAC for namespaced kinds; kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false lists what they do not scope (Node, PersistentVolume, ClusterRole, IngressClass, StorageClass, Namespace itself, most CRDs' cluster-wide config). Know the built-ins (default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease) and that a namespace is not a network boundary: any pod can reach svc.otherns.svc.cluster.local until a NetworkPolicy says otherwise (Topic 8). Know the hard cross-namespace rules you will hit: a Pod cannot mount a ConfigMap or Secret from another namespace, an Ingress cannot route to a Service in another namespace (hence ExternalName workarounds), a RoleBinding can reference a ServiceAccount in another namespace. Attach a ResourceQuota (requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.memory, count/pods, count/services.loadbalancers) and a LimitRange (default request and limit injected into every container that omits them); once a CPU or memory quota exists, any Pod without requests is rejected at admission with 'must specify requests.cpu', which is the single most common reason a customer's new namespace refuses your manifests. Set your working namespace with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dokeo, and unstick a Terminating namespace by reading kubectl get ns x -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' for the resources whose finalizers are blocking it.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Namespaces

subtopics.name: Pod anatomy, phases, container states and the shutdown sequence
subtopics.learn: A Pod is one or more containers sharing a network namespace (one IP, localhost between containers, port collisions are real), an IPC namespace, optionally a PID namespace (shareProcessNamespace: true), held open by the pause container; volumes are pod-scoped and mounted per container. Know the spec fields you will set daily: containers[].ports (documentation only, not a firewall), env and envFrom, resources.requests and limits (requests drive scheduling and the QoS class Guaranteed / Burstable / BestEffort; a Pending pod whose Events say 'Insufficient cpu' is a requests problem), restartPolicy, terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), lifecycle.preStop, securityContext.runAsNonRoot, serviceAccountName, nodeSelector. Distinguish Pod phase (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown) from container state (Waiting with reason ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff or CreateContainerConfigError; Running; Terminated with exitCode and reason OOMKilled, Error, Completed). Memorise the shutdown sequence because rollouts depend on it: pod gets deletionTimestamp and is removed from EndpointSlices concurrently, preStop runs, SIGTERM to PID 1, grace period counts down, SIGKILL; a preStop of sleep 5 exists purely to let kube-proxy and the ingress controller observe the endpoint removal before the process stops accepting. Read state fast with kubectl get pod x -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState}' and kubectl describe pod x | sed -n '/Events/,$p'.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Pod Lifecycle

subtopics.name: Init containers, native sidecars and ephemeral debug containers
subtopics.learn: initContainers run to completion in order before app containers start and share the pod's volumes and network: use them for one-shot schema migrations per rollout, for waiting on dependencies (until nc -z postgres 5432; do sleep 2; done), and for rendering config into an emptyDir. Since Kubernetes 1.29 an init container with restartPolicy: Always is a native sidecar: started before the app containers, kept running beside them, terminated after them, which fixes the classic Job-never-completes and log-shipper-dies-before-final-flush problems that plagued sidecars declared as ordinary containers. Ephemeral containers via kubectl debug -it pod/dokeo-xyz --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app attach a shell to a distroless pod without restarting it (--target shares the PID namespace so ps, ss -tlnp and strace -p see the app process); kubectl debug pod/x --copy-to=x-debug --set-image='*=ubuntu' clones a crashing pod with a different image so you can inspect the filesystem; kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox gives a host shell with the node root at /host. Know that ephemeral containers cannot be removed or restarted and never appear in the manifest you applied.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Init Containers

subtopics.name: Images: pull policy, tags versus digests, private registries
subtopics.learn: imagePullPolicy defaults to Always when the tag is :latest or omitted and IfNotPresent otherwise; that is why a customer who re-pushes :v1 sees stale code on nodes that cached it, and why production manifests pin image@sha256:... and treat the tag as documentation. Decode pull failures from kubectl describe pod: ErrImagePull then ImagePullBackOff (backoff grows to 5 minutes) with the registry's message: 'manifest unknown' (wrong tag), 'unauthorized' (missing or wrong imagePullSecrets), 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority' (private CA not trusted by containerd on the node), 'toomanyrequests' (Docker Hub anonymous limit, common at customers where every node egresses through one NAT IP). Create credentials with kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username --docker-password, reference them in spec.imagePullSecrets or patch them onto the namespace's default ServiceAccount so every pod inherits them; on k3s you can instead configure /etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml for node-level mirrors and auth and restart k3s. Confirm what actually ran with kubectl get pod x -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}' and compare to the digest in your CI log.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Images

subtopics.name: Deployment and ReplicaSet: rollouts, hashes, rollback, immutable selector
subtopics.learn: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets; every distinct pod template gets its own ReplicaSet labelled pod-template-hash, and a rollout is the Deployment controller scaling the new RS up and the old one down within strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge and maxUnavailable (defaults 25% and 25%, absolute or percent; maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 is the zero-capacity-loss setting for small replica counts). minReadySeconds delays counting a pod as available so a fast-crashing container does not pass the gate, progressDeadlineSeconds (600) flips the Progressing condition to False so kubectl rollout status exits non-zero in CI, revisionHistoryLimit keeps old ReplicaSets for kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=N. Drive it end to end: kubectl set image deploy/dokeo app=ghcr.io/you/dokeo@sha256:..., kubectl rollout status, history, pause, resume, undo, and kubectl rollout restart (which only patches kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt into the template). Understand why spec.selector is immutable and must be a subset of template labels, why changing any template label triggers a rollout even if the selector is untouched, why two Deployments with overlapping selectors in one namespace fight over pods, and when strategy: Recreate is the only correct choice (single-writer volume, schema-incompatible releases). Watch kubectl get rs -w during a rollout and narrate every number.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Deployments

subtopics.name: Probes and how readiness gates the EndpointSlice
subtopics.learn: Three probes, three jobs: startupProbe holds the other two off until a slow app boots (failureThreshold x periodSeconds is your boot budget), readinessProbe controls whether the pod's IP is present in the EndpointSlice (fail means removed from the Service, no restart), livenessProbe makes the kubelet kill and restart the container (repeated failure shows as CrashLoopBackOff). Handlers are httpGet (path, port, httpHeaders, scheme), tcpSocket, exec and grpc; tune initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds (default 1 second, the silent killer under load), successThreshold and failureThreshold. Production rule: readiness may check a dependency only if you consciously want that dependency's outage to remove you from rotation; liveness must never touch a dependency and should be a cheap in-process check, otherwise a database blip becomes a restart storm. Watch the mechanism: make one pod's readiness fail (kubectl exec into it and move the health file, or pause the app) and observe the IP disappear from kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=dokeo -o yaml within one period, while kubectl get pods shows READY 0/1 and the Pod stays Running. Topic 8 tunes these for HPA and real workloads; here you need the mechanics cold.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

subtopics.name: Service: types, the port triple, EndpointSlices, headless
subtopics.learn: A Service is a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a label selector; the EndpointSlice controller watches Pods that match spec.selector and writes the Ready ones' IPs and ports into EndpointSlices labelled kubernetes.io/service-name, which kube-proxy and the ingress controller consume. Get the port triple right every time: port (what clients hit on the ClusterIP), targetPort (the container's listening port, as a number or as a named containerPort so the image can change ports without touching the Service), nodePort (30000-32767, only for NodePort and LoadBalancer). Types: ClusterIP (default, in-cluster only), NodePort (opens the port on every node's IPs), LoadBalancer (asks the cloud controller or k3s ServiceLB for an external address and still allocates a NodePort underneath), ExternalName (returns a CNAME, no proxying, no selector). Headless (clusterIP: None) skips the VIP and returns pod IPs directly in DNS, used by StatefulSets and client-side balancing for gRPC. Know externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client source IP at the cost of only routing to nodes that have a local pod, sessionAffinity: ClientIP, and a selector-less Service with a hand-written EndpointSlice to give an external database an in-cluster name. The first debugging move is always kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=x: empty means selector mismatch or nothing is Ready.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Service

subtopics.name: Virtual IPs: how kube-proxy makes a ClusterIP exist
subtopics.learn: The ClusterIP is configured on no interface anywhere; kube-proxy on every node watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the kernel to DNAT traffic for VIP:port to one Ready endpoint. In iptables mode read the actual chain on the k3s node: PREROUTING and OUTPUT jump to KUBE-SERVICES, which matches -d <clusterIP> --dport <port> and jumps to KUBE-SVC-<hash>, which holds one -m statistic --mode random --probability rule per endpoint, each jumping to a KUBE-SEP-<hash> that does the DNAT --to-destination podIP:targetPort, with KUBE-MARK-MASQ for hairpin and off-cluster sources; find yours with sudo iptables -t nat -S | grep -A3 'dokeo'. Draw the consequences: ping to a ClusterIP fails because there is no rule for ICMP; balancing is per new connection via conntrack, so a long-lived gRPC or HTTP/2 connection pins to one pod forever and never rebalances after scale-out; a removed endpoint's established connections are not drained by kube-proxy, only by the pod's own shutdown. Know the variants you will meet at customers: ipvs mode (hash tables, needed past a few thousand Services), nftables mode, and CNIs like Cilium that replace kube-proxy entirely with eBPF so none of these chains exist and your iptables grep returns nothing. On k3s kube-proxy runs inside the k3s process, so there is no kube-proxy DaemonSet or ConfigMap in kube-system to inspect.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

subtopics.name: Cluster DNS: CoreDNS, search paths and the ndots:5 tax
subtopics.learn: CoreDNS answers <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local A/AAAA records for ClusterIP Services, per-pod A records for headless Services (and <pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local for StatefulSets), and SRV records for named ports (_http._tcp.dokeo.dokeo.svc.cluster.local). The kubelet writes each pod's /etc/resolv.conf as nameserver <cluster DNS IP>, search <ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local, options ndots:5, which means any name with fewer than five dots (api.stripe.com has two) is tried against every search suffix first: five queries, four NXDOMAINs, then the real answer, on every lookup unless the client caches. Fix hot paths with a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.) or spec.dnsConfig.options ndots: 2. Know dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst (default), ClusterFirstWithHostNet (for hostNetwork pods that still want cluster names), Default (inherit the node's resolver, so cluster names stop working), None (bring your own dnsConfig). Debug from inside: kubectl run -it --rm dns --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup dokeo.dokeo.svc.cluster.local, cat /etc/resolv.conf from an app pod, read the Corefile in kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml, and temporarily add the log plugin to see every query CoreDNS receives when a customer swears 'DNS is fine'.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: DNS for Services and Pods

subtopics.name: The Ingress resource: class, hosts, pathType, TLS block
subtopics.learn: Ingress is a portable L7 routing spec that does nothing until a controller implements it. Fields you must get right: spec.ingressClassName (must name an existing IngressClass; omit it and you depend on an ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class annotation that many customer clusters do not set, so the Ingress silently gets no ADDRESS), rules[].host (exact or a single leading wildcard *.example.com, matched against the Host header and SNI), http.paths[] with pathType Exact, Prefix (element-wise on / boundaries: /api matches /api/x but not /apix) or ImplementationSpecific, backend.service.name plus port.number or port.name, defaultBackend for anything unmatched, and tls[] with hosts and secretName naming a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in the same namespace. Everything else (timeouts, body size, redirects, rewrites, sticky sessions, rate limits, CORS) is controller-specific annotation soup, which is exactly why Gateway API (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) exists as the typed successor; read the Gateway API concept page once so you recognise it when a customer runs it. Verify wiring with kubectl describe ingress dokeo: the Backends column shows resolved pod IP:port or '<error: endpoints not found>', and Events show the controller's sync result. Confirm the Ingress is actually claimed by checking ADDRESS in kubectl get ingress.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Ingress

subtopics.name: The ingress controller and the full request path, hop by hop
subtopics.learn: The controller is just a Deployment (Traefik on k3s; ingress-nginx, the AWS Load Balancer Controller or Istio at most customers) running a reverse proxy that watches Ingress, IngressClass, Service and EndpointSlice objects and rewrites its own routing table; it is exposed by a Service of type LoadBalancer (k3s ServiceLB binds hostPort 80 and 443 on each node) or by hostNetwork. Draw the hop sequence and be able to name the component at each: client resolves DNS -> node public IP -> klipper-lb hostPort -> DNAT into the Traefik pod -> Traefik matches Host and path -> Traefik connects directly to a Ready pod IP taken from the EndpointSlice (controllers bypass the ClusterIP, so kube-proxy is not in this data path) -> container port -> response. Map status codes to layers so triage is mechanical: 404 from the controller means no rule matched (wrong host, wrong ingressClassName, pathType mismatch); 503 means the rule matched but the Service has no Ready endpoints; 502 or 504 means an endpoint refused, reset or timed out (wrong targetPort, app crash, slow upstream). On k3s read Traefik's view with kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/traefik --tail=100, and enable its dashboard through a HelmChartConfig in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests when you need to see the routers and services it built. Isolate layers with kubectl port-forward svc/dokeo 8080:80 (tests Service and Pod without Ingress) and curl -H 'Host: dokeo.example.com' http://<nodeIP>/ (tests Ingress without DNS or TLS).

resource.label: Traefik docs: Kubernetes Ingress provider

subtopics.name: TLS with cert-manager: ACME HTTP-01 from Issuer to Secret
subtopics.learn: Install cert-manager (Helm with crds.enabled=true or the release manifest), then create a ClusterIssuer of type ACME with server https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory first, an email, privateKeySecretRef, and solvers[].http01.ingress with ingressClassName: traefik. Annotate the Ingress with cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-staging and set spec.tls[].secretName; the ingress-shim controller creates a Certificate, which creates a CertificateRequest -> Order -> Challenge; the HTTP-01 solver runs a temporary pod and temporary Ingress for /.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>, Let's Encrypt fetches it over plain port 80, and on success a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with tls.crt and tls.key is written and the ingress controller reloads. Debug strictly in order: kubectl describe certificate, certificaterequest, order, challenge; the Challenge's status.reason quotes the ACME error verbatim (DNS not pointing at this IP yet, port 80 blocked by the Hetzner firewall, a controller-level HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect swallowing the challenge path, propagation check failing because the node cannot resolve its own public name). Only switch the server to acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org after staging succeeds: production rate limits (5 duplicate certificates per week per exact name set) will lock you out mid-debugging. Confirm with openssl s_client -connect dokeo.example.com:443 -servername dokeo.example.com < /dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer and know that renewal starts at two-thirds of the 90-day lifetime.

resource.label: cert-manager docs: Securing Ingress Resources

subtopics.name: ConfigMap: three injection paths, three update semantics
subtopics.learn: A ConfigMap holds up to 1 MiB across data (string values) and binaryData (base64); keys must be valid filenames and, if used as env vars, valid identifiers. The three ways in have different update behaviour and you must be able to predict each: env valueFrom.configMapKeyRef and envFrom.configMapRef are read once at container start and never change until the pod restarts; a volume mounting the whole ConfigMap is updated in place by the kubelet on its sync period (roughly a minute plus cache TTL) using an atomic symlink swap of a ..data directory, so inotify-based reloaders and processes that re-read on SIGHUP pick it up; a volume mount with subPath is a bind mount of one file and is never updated, the most common 'the app ignores my config' ticket. Set optional: true when the map may not exist yet, immutable: true for maps you never mutate (the kubelet stops watching them, lower API load, and any change forces a new name). Roll pods on change deliberately: put a hash of the ConfigMap into the pod template as an annotation (Helm's checksum/config idiom) or use kustomize configMapGenerator, which suffixes the name with a hash so the Deployment template changes. Author declaratively: kubectl create configmap dokeo-config --from-file=config.yaml --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml. Test all three paths on Dokeo and record which one saw the edit without a restart.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: ConfigMaps

subtopics.name: Secret: why it is not secret, types, mounts, rotation
subtopics.learn: A Secret is a ConfigMap with a type and base64 encoding, and base64 is not encryption: anyone with get on secrets in the namespace reads it with kubectl get secret x -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d, and by default it sits unencrypted in etcd (sqlite on k3s) unless EncryptionConfiguration is enabled (k3s: --secrets-encryption). Types you will create: Opaque (generic), kubernetes.io/tls (tls.crt and tls.key, consumed by Ingress and written by cert-manager), kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (imagePullSecrets), kubernetes.io/basic-auth. Write stringData in manifests for readability; the apiserver merges it into data. Consume via env (secretKeyRef; the value is hidden in kubectl describe pod but visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, crash dumps, and any child process) or via a volume (tmpfs, defaultMode 0644 by default, so set 0400 and a matching runAsUser; projected volumes let one directory combine several Secrets and ConfigMaps). Never commit a Secret manifest: generate it with kubectl create secret generic --from-literal --dry-run=client -o yaml at apply time, or point at an external source (External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver syncing from Vault or AWS Secrets Manager), which is what a customer's security team will require. Rotation reality: env-injected secrets need kubectl rollout restart; volume-mounted ones update like ConfigMaps unless subPath is used; TLS Secrets rewritten by cert-manager are picked up by the ingress controller without a restart.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Secrets

subtopics.name: kubectl fluency and declarative apply: diff, jsonpath, events, server-side apply
subtopics.learn: Work declaratively: kubectl apply -f dir/ computes a three-way merge between your manifest, the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation and the live object, so a field you delete from the file is actually removed; kubectl create and replace do not do this, and kubectl edit mutates live state that silently drifts from git. Always preview with kubectl diff -f (exit code 1 means there are changes, usable as a CI gate); learn --server-side and --field-manager so managedFields records ownership and conflicts surface as errors instead of overwrites when two tools touch one object; use -k for a kustomization with namespace, images and configMapGenerator. Output surgery: -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}', -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,IP:.status.podIP,NODE:.spec.nodeName, -o yaml | yq, --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp, --field-selector status.phase!=Running, and kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=dokeo-xyz --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. Daily verbs: logs -f --previous --all-containers --since=10m, exec -it -- sh, port-forward, cp, top pod, rollout, scale, label, annotate, and kubectl -v=8 to see the raw REST calls so you can reproduce the same thing with a client library or curl against the API. Build a kubeconfig with two contexts (laptop -> k3s, laptop -> kind) and switch with kubectl config use-context so you stop nuking the wrong cluster.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: kubectl Quick Reference

subtopics.name: The unreachable-service runbook, bottom-up
subtopics.learn: Run the official Debug Services procedure until it is reflex, then write your own one-page version with exact commands. Does the Pod answer on its own IP (kubectl run -it --rm dbg --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- curl -sv http://<podIP>:<containerPort>/healthz)? Does the Service exist with the right port and targetPort (kubectl get svc -o wide; kubectl describe svc x shows Endpoints)? Are there endpoints (kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=x -o yaml); if none, do the pod labels exactly match the selector (kubectl get pods -l app=dokeo --show-labels) and are they Ready? Does DNS resolve from a pod (nslookup x.ns.svc.cluster.local)? Does the VIP work from a pod, then from the node (curl http://<clusterIP>:<port>)? Are the kube-proxy rules present (sudo iptables-save | grep -c KUBE-SVC; grep for the Service's ClusterIP)? Then move up the stack: kubectl describe ingress for backend resolution, controller logs for the actual upstream and status it saw, and tcpdump -i any port <targetPort> inside the app pod via kubectl debug --target to prove whether packets arrive at all. Practise by breaking Dokeo five ways (wrong targetPort, selector typo, missing ingressClassName, readiness failing, wrong Secret key) and timing yourself to root cause using only these commands.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Debug Services

outcomes: You can draw from memory, in under five minutes on a whiteboard, the graph Ingress -> Service -> EndpointSlice -> Pod <- ReplicaSet <- Deployment with ConfigMap and Secret edges, and annotate each edge with the component that reads it (ingress controller, EndpointSlice controller, kube-proxy, kubelet, CoreDNS, Deployment controller).

You can take curl -v https://dokeo.example.com returning 404, 502 or 503, name the layer and the three most likely causes within two minutes, then confirm the root cause with kubectl get ingress, get endpointslices and describe pod in under ten.

You can roll out a new digest-pinned image of Dokeo under a continuous curl or hey load with zero failed requests, explain the pod-template-hash of every ReplicaSet in kubectl get rs, state what maxSurge, maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds and the preStop sleep each contributed, then roll back with kubectl rollout undo and prove the old digest is running.

You can take a Pod stuck in Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff or CreateContainerConfigError to Running and state the root cause from kubectl describe Events and containerStatuses alone, without opening the application logs first.

You can inject the same ConfigMap key three ways (env, whole-map volume, subPath volume), predict in writing which running containers will observe an edit without restart, verify the prediction, and force a rollout on config change using a checksum annotation or a kustomize generated name.

You can obtain a Let's Encrypt certificate via cert-manager HTTP-01 on k3s, explain the Certificate -> CertificateRequest -> Order -> Challenge chain, and diagnose a failed Challenge from kubectl describe challenge to a specific network or DNS cause.

You can explain why ping to a ClusterIP fails and then show, on the node, the iptables KUBE-SVC and KUBE-SEP rules (or their ipvs equivalent) that implement a specific Service, and explain why a long-lived gRPC connection never rebalances.

You can write Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace, ResourceQuota and LimitRange manifests for Dokeo from a blank file with no copy-paste, kubectl diff them before applying, and have the whole stack Ready and serving TLS on a fresh k3s node in under 30 minutes.
failureModes: A ConfigMap is mounted with subPath so the customer's config edits never reach the running process; the team concludes the app ignores configuration and hand-edits the container, and the fix (drop subPath, or roll pods via a checksum annotation) is discovered weeks later.

Two Deployments in one namespace share the label app: api; the second ReplicaSet adopts the first one's pods, both controllers fight to reach their replica counts, and the platform team sees a rollout that never converges and pods being killed with no obvious owner.

The readiness probe calls an endpoint that queries the database; a 20-second database failover marks every pod NotReady, the Service has zero endpoints, and a transient dependency blip becomes a full outage, made worse by a liveness probe that also hits the database and triggers a restart storm.

targetPort is set to the Service port (80) instead of the container port (8080); endpoints exist and describe looks healthy, but the ingress controller returns 502 for every request to the new pods only, so the rollout looks fine in kubectl and broken to users.

A database password is rotated in the Secret but the app still uses the old one because it was injected as an env var; nobody runs kubectl rollout restart, the old credential is revoked on schedule, and the customer's first symptom is connection-refused at 3am.

An Ingress is applied without ingressClassName on a cluster that runs both the customer's ingress-nginx and k3s Traefik; neither controller claims it, kubectl get ingress shows an empty ADDRESS, and the deploy is 'done' while the URL returns nothing.

cert-manager's HTTP-01 challenge fails because a controller-level HTTPS redirect (or a Hetzner firewall rule blocking port 80) swallows /.well-known/acme-challenge, and repeated retries against the production ACME endpoint exhaust the duplicate-certificate rate limit so the real fix cannot be validated for a week.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through, component by component, everything that happens between kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml and the first HTTP 200 through an Ingress: which controllers act, in what order, what they write, and what you would check if the process stalled at each stage.

A customer reports 503s for about 30 seconds after every deploy and says the platform is fine. What do you look at first, what are the three most likely causes, and what changes to the Deployment and Pod spec would you make to eliminate them?

How does a ClusterIP work when no network interface has that address? Explain kube-proxy in iptables mode, why ICMP to a ClusterIP fails, what changes with IPVS, and what disappears entirely when the cluster runs Cilium with kube-proxy replacement.

Design the config and secrets story for a service that must pick up feature-flag changes without a redeploy but rotate database credentials with zero downtime. What do you mount how, what are the update semantics of each path, and where does it break?
A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, kubectl logs is empty and kubectl logs --previous prints nothing. Describe your next five commands and what each exit code (1, 127, 137, 139, 143) would tell you.

A security lead says 'Kubernetes Secrets are base64, so they are plaintext; we will not use them.' What is accurate in that statement, what would you tell them about etcd encryption at rest, RBAC exposure and env versus volume injection, and what would you actually deploy on their cluster?

Explain what happens when a pod in namespace dokeo resolves the name postgres, and then api.stripe.com: how many DNS queries does CoreDNS see for each, why, and how would you fix the second case for a latency-sensitive path? When would you choose a headless Service instead?
7.proofOfWork: A repository plus a 15-minute recorded screencast titled 'Dokeo cluster autopsy'. The repo contains the full hand-written manifests for Dokeo on k3s (Namespace with ResourceQuota and LimitRange, Deployment with preStop and all three probes, Service with named targetPort, Ingress with ingressClassName and TLS via cert-manager, ConfigMap injected three ways, Secret generated at apply time) and a Makefile with break-1 through break-5 targets that inject a specific fault (wrong targetPort, selector typo, missing ingressClassName, subPath ConfigMap, readiness probe pointed at the database) and fix-N targets that revert it. In the screencast you run each break target, then diagnose it live using only kubectl and node-level commands while narrating the object model on a hand-drawn diagram, timing each diagnosis. A one-page RUNBOOK.md maps each symptom (404, 502, 503, Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, empty ADDRESS) to the first three commands and the most likely causes, and the README links the live https URL with a valid Let's Encrypt certificate.

8.topic: Kubernetes production ops: probes, HPA, requests and limits, storage, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, debugging
8.why: An FDE rarely owns the cluster: you are handed a namespace, a kubeconfig with whatever RBAC the customer's platform team allows, a ResourceQuota you did not choose, and a go-live date. When the pilot's pods sit in Pending or CrashLoopBackOff at 5pm with the customer's VP watching, the person who can read describe/events/logs and name the root cause in ten minutes is the one who keeps the account; the one who says 'let me ask our infra team' is a guest. Requests, limits, probes and HPA decide whether the deployment survives the customer's first real traffic, and RBAC plus NetworkPolicy are the two artifacts their security team will demand to see before they sign the production change ticket.
prerequisites: Kubernetes core from 'Kubernetes core: Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, namespaces' (topic 7): write a Deployment + Service + ConfigMap from memory, understand label selectors and how a Service finds pods
Docker internals from 'Docker internals: namespaces, cgroups, layers, networking' (topic 5): cgroup v2 memory.max and cpu.max, PID 1 signal handling, why `exec` in an entrypoint matters for SIGTERM
Linux internals from topic 1: reading dmesg/journalctl, what the OOM killer does, systemd units (the kubelet is one), file ownership and fsGroup semantics
Networking from topic 2: L3/L4 versus L7, CIDR notation, how DNS search domains and ndots work, since NetworkPolicy is purely L3/L4 and cluster DNS is the first thing policies break
Single-box troubleshooting from topic 3: interpret CPU steal, RSS versus cache, and thread counts, so `kubectl top` and cAdvisor counters mean something

A cluster you can break: kind with the default CNI swapped for Calico or Cilium (kindnet does not enforce NetworkPolicy), metrics-server installed, and kubectl 1.28+ so `kubectl debug` and `kubectl create token` exist

subtopics.name: Pod phases, container states, exit codes, and reading describe top-down
subtopics.learn: Separate Pod phase (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown) from container state (Waiting, Running, Terminated) and know the Waiting reasons that actually show up: ContainerCreating, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff/ErrImagePull, CreateContainerConfigError, and the Terminated reasons OOMKilled, Error, Completed. Read `kubectl describe pod` in a fixed order: Status and Reason, the four Conditions (PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready), per-container Last State with Exit Code and Restart Count, then Events by age. Map exit codes without looking them up: 0 completed, 1 application error, 137 SIGKILL (OOM or grace period expired), 143 SIGTERM handled, 139 SIGSEGV, 126/127 entrypoint not executable or not found. Know CrashLoopBackOff doubles from 10s to a 5m cap and resets after the container runs cleanly for 10 minutes, which is why a flapping pod looks 'fine' every so often.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Pod Lifecycle

subtopics.name: Liveness, readiness and startup probes: three different contracts
subtopics.learn: Readiness controls membership in EndpointSlices and never restarts anything; liveness makes the kubelet kill and restart the container; startup disables both until it first succeeds, which is how you protect a slow JVM or a model-loading container without a huge initialDelaySeconds. Know every field and default: initialDelaySeconds 0, periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1 (the single most common misconfiguration on Python services), successThreshold (must be 1 for liveness and startup), failureThreshold 3, terminationGracePeriodSeconds override per probe. Know handler types: httpGet succeeds on 200-399, tcpSocket, exec (a fork per probe, expensive at scale), grpc. Rule you must be able to defend: liveness checks only the process itself, never a downstream dependency, otherwise a database blip restarts the whole fleet; readiness may check dependencies. Compute time-to-first-restart as initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold x periodSeconds and time-to-ready the same way.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

subtopics.name: Requests, limits and QoS: what the scheduler uses versus what the kubelet enforces
subtopics.learn: Requests are consumed by the scheduler against node Allocatable (Capacity minus kube-reserved, system-reserved and eviction threshold); limits are enforced by the kubelet through cgroups: a CPU limit becomes a cpu.max quota over a 100ms period and produces throttling, never a kill, while a memory limit becomes memory.max and produces an OOM kill. Derive QoS class by inspection: Guaranteed when every container has requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory, Burstable when any request is set, BestEffort when none; eviction order under node pressure is BestEffort, then Burstable pods exceeding their request, then Guaranteed. Use `kubectl describe node` Allocated resources and `kubectl top pod --containers` to size. Know the defensible production pattern: set memory limit equal to memory request, set a CPU request and either no CPU limit or a generous one, and set ephemeral-storage limits because exceeding them evicts the pod with no other warning.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

subtopics.name: OOMKilled, CFS throttling and node-pressure eviction: proving it from the node
subtopics.learn: OOMKilled appears as Last State Terminated, Reason OOMKilled, Exit Code 137; confirm from the node with `dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'` or `journalctl -k`, and from the container's cgroup with the oom_kill counter in memory.events and the high-water mark in memory.peak. Throttling leaves no event at all: compute container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total divided by container_cpu_cfs_periods_total from cAdvisor and treat anything above 20-25% as a too-low limit or a runtime spawning more threads than the limit (Go GOMAXPROCS, Java, uvicorn workers); fix by raising the limit or pinning GOMAXPROCS/UV workers from the downward API resourceFieldRef limits.cpu. Node-pressure eviction: the kubelet watches memory.available, nodefs.available, imagefs.available and pid.available against --eviction-hard and --eviction-soft; evicted pods show Reason Evicted with a message naming the resource. Distinguish this from API-initiated eviction (drain, PDB-respecting) and from scheduler preemption by PriorityClass.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Node-pressure Eviction

subtopics.name: LimitRange and ResourceQuota: the guardrails on a per-client namespace
subtopics.learn: A LimitRange of type Container injects default and defaultRequest into pods that omit them and rejects pods outside min/max or exceeding maxLimitRequestRatio at admission; a ResourceQuota caps the namespace aggregate of requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.cpu, limits.memory, pods, persistentvolumeclaims, requests.storage per StorageClass (e.g. gp3.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage) and object counts like count/deployments.apps. Know the trap you will hit in a customer cluster: once a ResourceQuota constrains cpu or memory, every pod that omits requests is rejected with 'must specify requests.cpu' unless a LimitRange supplies defaults, and the rejection surfaces only as a ReplicaSet FailedCreate event, not on any pod. Read `kubectl describe quota -n <ns>` Used versus Hard before every deploy, and know scopeSelector for quotas by PriorityClass.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Resource Quotas

subtopics.name: Pending forever: decoding FailedScheduling, taints, affinity and topology spread
subtopics.learn: Read the FailedScheduling event as a per-node tally and decode each clause: 'Insufficient cpu/memory' means requests exceed Allocatable on those nodes; 'untolerated taint' means a NoSchedule/NoExecute/PreferNoSchedule taint without a matching toleration (and NoExecute with tolerationSeconds evicts running pods after the timer); 'didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector' means nodeSelector or requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution; 'didn't match pod anti-affinity rules' points at podAntiAffinity with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname or topology.kubernetes.io/zone; 'didn't satisfy topology spread constraints' at maxSkew with whenUnsatisfiable DoNotSchedule. Also know the non-scheduler causes of Pending: an unbound PVC with WaitForFirstConsumer waiting on a zonal disk, a referenced PriorityClass that does not exist, and a ResourceQuota rejection that never produces a pod at all. Know that cluster-autoscaler only reacts to Pending pods whose reason is Insufficient, so a taint mistake will never scale a node group.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Taints and Tolerations

subtopics.name: HPA v2: metrics-server, the replica formula, and scaling behaviour
subtopics.learn: HPA needs metrics-server (verify with `kubectl top pod`) and per-container requests, because type Resource with averageUtilization is a percentage of the request, not the limit. Compute by hand: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue) with a 10% tolerance band; pods not yet Ready and pods missing metrics are treated conservatively on scale-up and ignored on scale-down. Tune behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds (default 300) and policies (Percent or Pods per periodSeconds) to stop flapping, and know scaleUp defaults to the larger of doubling or adding 4 pods every 15s. Know when to reach for type Pods, type Object and type External (queue depth via Prometheus Adapter or KEDA). Read `kubectl describe hpa` Conditions: ScalingActive False with FailedGetResourceMetric means missing requests or a dead metrics-server; ScalingLimited means you hit minReplicas/maxReplicas. Never let an HPA and a GitOps-managed spec.replicas fight; remove replicas from the manifest.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling

subtopics.name: PersistentVolumes, claims and StorageClasses: binding modes, access modes, reclaim
subtopics.learn: Know that a PVC binds to a PV by StorageClass, accessModes and capacity, and that ReadWriteOnce is per node not per pod (ReadWriteOncePod is the per-pod variant; ReadWriteMany needs NFS, EFS, CephFS or similar). Read a StorageClass: provisioner (ebs.csi.aws.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io), volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer (binds in the AZ of the scheduled pod, mandatory for zonal disks) versus Immediate (binds in a random AZ and strands the pod), reclaimPolicy Delete versus Retain, allowVolumeExpansion. Know the failure signatures: Pending with 'pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims'; FailedAttachVolume 'Multi-Attach error' when an RWO volume's old node has not detached; a PV stuck in Released that needs spec.claimRef cleared to rebind. Before any risky operation on a customer database, patch the PV to persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy Retain so deleting the PVC cannot delete the disk.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes

subtopics.name: StatefulSets for the client database: ordinals, volumeClaimTemplates, expansion
subtopics.learn: A StatefulSet gives stable names (db-0, db-1), per-pod DNS through a headless Service (db-0.db.<ns>.svc.cluster.local), ordered rollout and teardown under podManagementPolicy OrderedReady (or Parallel), and volumeClaimTemplates that create one PVC per ordinal which survives pod deletion; persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy whenDeleted/whenScaled controls whether the PVCs outlive the set. Use updateStrategy RollingUpdate with partition to canary a single ordinal. Know the immutability trap: volumeClaimTemplates cannot be edited, so to grow storage you edit each PVC's spec.resources.requests.storage directly (requires allowVolumeExpansion), then `kubectl delete sts db --cascade=orphan` and recreate with the new template so future ordinals match. Set securityContext.fsGroup so the database process owns the mounted volume, and know that a StatefulSet pod stuck Terminating on a dead node needs `kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0` only after you have confirmed the node is really gone.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: StatefulSets

subtopics.name: RBAC: Role versus ClusterRole, bindings, subresources and kubectl auth can-i
subtopics.learn: Role and RoleBinding are namespaced; ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide; a RoleBinding may reference a ClusterRole to grant it inside one namespace, which is how you reuse the built-in view, edit and admin roles. Write rules as apiGroups + resources + verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection) and know the subresources that matter for a read-only role: pods/log yes, pods/exec and pods/portforward no, deployments/scale no; use resourceNames to scope to specific objects. Subjects are User, Group, or ServiceAccount addressed as system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>. Prove behaviour rather than assert it: `kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n client-a --as system:serviceaccount:client-a:reader` and `kubectl auth can-i --list --as ...`. Know RBAC is deny-by-default and purely additive, there is no deny rule, so audit with `kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide` and grep for the subject; and know the escalation guard: you cannot grant verbs you do not hold unless you hold escalate or bind on roles.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization

subtopics.name: ServiceAccounts and tokens: projected tokens, automount, a kubeconfig for the customer
subtopics.learn: Every pod runs as a ServiceAccount (default unless set) and, unless automountServiceAccountToken is false on the pod or the SA, gets a projected token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token that is time-bound (expirationSeconds, default 1h, rotated by the kubelet) and audience-bound to the API server. Mint a human-usable short-lived token with `kubectl create token reader -n client-a --duration=1h`; know that long-lived Secret-backed tokens are legacy and only exist if you create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token by hand. Build the auditor kubeconfig with `kubectl config set-cluster`, `set-credentials --token`, `set-context --namespace` and hand it over with the expiry stated. Know the API server validates via TokenReview and the token's sub claim is system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>, which is what shows up in audit logs.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Configure Service Accounts for Pods

subtopics.name: NetworkPolicy: default-deny, selector semantics, DNS egress and CNI enforcement
subtopics.learn: NetworkPolicy is an additive allow-list at L3/L4 keyed on podSelector; a pod becomes isolated in a direction only when at least one policy selects it with that direction in policyTypes. Write the canonical default-deny (podSelector {} with policyTypes Ingress and Egress and no rules), then the allows: ingress to app=postgres on TCP 5432 from app=api only; egress from every pod to CoreDNS on UDP and TCP 53 using namespaceSelector kubernetes.io/metadata.name kube-system plus podSelector k8s-app=kube-dns; egress to the internet via ipBlock 0.0.0.0/0 with except for the RFC1918 ranges. Know the YAML gotcha that fails security reviews: two list items `- namespaceSelector` and `- podSelector` are OR, both keys in one item are AND. Enforcement is the CNI's job: Calico, Cilium and AWS VPC CNI with network policy enabled enforce; kindnet, flannel and default kubenet silently accept and ignore the object. Always prove it with `kubectl exec api -- nc -zv -w2 db 5432` and from an unlabeled pod before and after applying.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Network Policies

subtopics.name: The ten-minute debugging sequence: describe, events, logs --previous, kubectl debug
subtopics.learn: Run the same sequence every time so you never skip a step under pressure: `kubectl get pod -o wide` (phase, restarts, node, IP); `kubectl describe pod` (events, last state, exit code); `kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous` for the crashed instance, since the current one has nothing yet; `kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` for scheduler, ReplicaSet and quota events that never attach to a pod; then `kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox:1.36 --target=<container>` to add an ephemeral container sharing the PID namespace when the image is distroless, or `kubectl debug <pod> --copy-to=dbg --set-image='*=ubuntu' --share-processes -- sleep 1d` to replace a crashing entrypoint and inspect the filesystem. Know the CreateContainerConfigError causes by heart: a ConfigMap or Secret key that does not exist, a subPath on a missing key, runAsNonRoot against an image whose USER is root. Pull structured facts with `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState}'` when the customer wants the evidence in a ticket.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Debug Running Pods

subtopics.name: Debugging Services and cluster DNS: endpoints, selectors, ports, CoreDNS
subtopics.learn: A Service with zero endpoints (`kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>`) means its spec.selector matches no Ready pod: diff the selector against pod labels and check readiness before anything else. Second cause is a targetPort that does not match containerPort or a named port that does not exist. Test resolution from inside a pod: `nslookup <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`, then read /etc/resolv.conf for ndots:5 and the search list to understand why short names cost five lookups and why external names occasionally NXDOMAIN under load. Read CoreDNS logs with `kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns` and temporarily add the log plugin to the Corefile ConfigMap. Know which dataplane you are on (kube-proxy iptables, ipvs, or Cilium eBPF kube-proxy replacement) because the debugging commands differ, and remember that headless Services return pod IPs and ExternalName returns a CNAME that NetworkPolicy cannot see.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Debug Services

subtopics.name: Deployment rollouts: maxSurge, progress deadlines, history, undo, and what undo cannot fix
subtopics.learn: Know RollingUpdate with maxSurge and maxUnavailable as absolute counts or percentages, minReadySeconds as the gate before a new pod counts as available, and progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) flipping the Progressing condition to False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded when the rollout stalls. Drive it with `kubectl rollout status`, `rollout history`, `rollout undo --to-revision=N`, `rollout pause`/`resume` to batch several edits into one revision, and `kubectl set image` for an emergency pin; history is the retained ReplicaSets under revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) and CHANGE-CAUSE comes from the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation. Understand what undo reverts (the pod template only) and what it does not: a ConfigMap or Secret edited in place under the same name, a database migration, PVC contents, an Ingress change. Fix the first with immutable ConfigMaps under hashed names (Kustomize configMapGenerator, Helm checksum annotations). Rehearse the drill: push a bad tag, watch ProgressDeadlineExceeded, undo, confirm with `kubectl get rs` that the previous ReplicaSet scaled back up.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Deployments

subtopics.name: Graceful shutdown and PodDisruptionBudgets: SIGTERM, preStop, the endpoint race
subtopics.learn: On delete the API server marks the pod Terminating; the endpoints controller removes it from EndpointSlices and the kubelet runs preStop then sends SIGTERM in parallel, so for a few hundred milliseconds kube-proxy and the Ingress controller still route new connections to a process that is shutting down. Eliminate the resulting 502s with `preStop: exec: command: [sleep, '5']` and an application that handles SIGTERM by draining in-flight requests; make sure the entrypoint uses `exec` so PID 1 is your process and not a shell that swallows the signal. After terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) the kubelet sends SIGKILL and you see exit 137 that is not an OOM. PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable or maxUnavailable constrains voluntary disruptions only (drain, cluster-autoscaler, node upgrades), never node crashes; a single-replica Deployment with minAvailable 1 makes `kubectl drain` hang forever, which is the most common reason a managed cluster upgrade stalls. Check `kubectl get pdb` ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS before touching nodes.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Specifying a Disruption Budget for your Application

subtopics.name: Node-level debugging: kubectl debug node, kubelet journal, crictl, cordon and drain
subtopics.learn: When the pod view says the node is the problem (NotReady, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, PLEG is not healthy), start with `kubectl describe node` Conditions and Events, then `kubectl debug node/<name> -it --image=ubuntu` for a privileged pod with the host filesystem at /host; `chroot /host` and run `journalctl -u kubelet -n 300`, `crictl ps -a`, `crictl logs <id>`, `crictl inspect <id>` to find the cgroup path, and `df -h /var/lib/containerd` for the disk-pressure culprit (usually image layers or emptyDir). Know the kubelet flags a customer's platform team will quote at you: --max-pods, --kube-reserved, --system-reserved, --eviction-hard. Take a node out safely with `kubectl cordon` (no new scheduling) then `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data` (evicts respecting PDBs), and `kubectl uncordon` when done.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Troubleshooting Clusters

subtopics.name: Assembling the per-client namespace as the tenancy unit
subtopics.learn: Compose everything into one kustomization per client: a Namespace labelled with kubernetes.io/metadata.name and pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce restricted (deepened in topic 10), a ResourceQuota and LimitRange, the default-deny NetworkPolicy plus DNS and ingress allows, a client-reader Role bound to both a ServiceAccount and the customer's OIDC group, the API Deployment with tuned probes and resources, the Postgres StatefulSet with Retain, an HPA and a PDB. Know precisely where namespace tenancy stops: CRDs, nodes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles and the kernel are shared, a noisy neighbour on the same node still competes for CPU and network, and a compromised pod with a hostPath still owns the node, so hard isolation means dedicated node pools via taints and nodeSelector or separate clusters. Be able to explain this trade-off to a customer security lead in two minutes with the specific controls that mitigate each gap. This kustomization is the input to the Helm/ArgoCD work in topic 9.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Multi-tenancy

outcomes: You can take a pod in CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending or CreateContainerConfigError in an unfamiliar namespace and state the root cause with evidence within ten minutes using only get, describe, events, logs --previous and kubectl debug, then apply a one-line fix.

You can read `kubectl describe hpa`, explain each Condition, compute the desired replica count by hand from current utilisation and target, and set stabilizationWindowSeconds and scale policies so a bursty API does not flap.

You can set requests and limits for a Python API and a Postgres StatefulSet with a one-sentence rationale per number, name the resulting QoS class, and prove OOM or CFS throttling from cgroup counters rather than guessing.

You can write a read-only Role that includes pods/log but excludes pods/exec and secrets, bind it to a ServiceAccount, mint a one-hour token, produce a working kubeconfig, and demonstrate the boundaries with `kubectl auth can-i --list`.

You can write a default-deny NetworkPolicy set that still permits API-to-DB on 5432 and DNS for every pod, and prove enforcement with nc from an allowed and a denied pod on a CNI that actually enforces.

You can break a rollout with a bad image tag, watch ProgressDeadlineExceeded fire, roll back with `kubectl rollout undo`, verify via ReplicaSets, and list the classes of change that undo cannot revert.
You can rebind a Released PersistentVolume to a fresh claim after an accidental PVC deletion because you set Retain first and know how to clear claimRef.
You can drain a node for a customer's cluster upgrade without violating a PDB, or explain in one sentence exactly which PDB blocks it and what to change.
failureModes: A liveness probe on /health that also pings Postgres: a 30-second RDS failover restarts every API pod at once, and the reconnect storm turns a blip into a ten-minute outage that the customer blames on your product.

timeoutSeconds left at the default 1s on a Python service that pauses for GC under load: probes time out, the kubelet restarts healthy pods, restarts add load, and the fleet enters CrashLoopBackOff while the customer reports that Kubernetes keeps killing the app.

A CPU limit set equal to a low request on a Go or Java service: CFS throttling adds 100-300ms of tail latency with zero errors and a calm `kubectl top`; only container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total reveals it, weeks later.

HPA scales the API to 40 replicas during the customer's load test, each opening a 20-connection pool, exhausting Postgres max_connections at 100 and taking down the very database the autoscaler was meant to protect.

The platform team adds a ResourceQuota to the client namespace; the next CronJob without requests fails admission at 02:00 as a ReplicaSet FailedCreate event nobody watches, and the nightly report silently stops for a week.

A NetworkPolicy is signed off in the security review on a cluster whose CNI does not enforce policy (kindnet in staging, AWS VPC CNI without network policy enabled in prod); a pentest six months later finds the DB reachable from every pod.
