A managed cluster upgrade hangs for hours because a single-replica Deployment has a PDB with minAvailable 1; the drain never completes, someone force-deletes the pod, and in-flight requests are lost during the customer's business hours.

An RWO EBS volume's pod is rescheduled to a different AZ after a node failure and sits Pending on a zone mismatch or Multi-Attach error while the customer's database is down, because the StorageClass used Immediate binding.
interviewQuestions: A customer pages you: the new version will not start and pods keep restarting. You have kubectl and ten minutes. Walk me through exactly what you run, in what order, and what each output rules in or out.

Explain how requests and limits flow from the manifest through the scheduler and the kubelet into cgroups. Now a service shows p99 latency doubling under load with no errors and CPU at 60% in kubectl top; what do you check and why?

Design the probes, resources, HPA and PDB for a FastAPI service with a Postgres backend on a customer's EKS cluster where the platform team enforces ResourceQuota and Pod Security restricted. Give actual numbers and defend each one.

A NetworkPolicy is applied and `kubectl get netpol` shows it, but the API can still reach a database it should not. Give three distinct root causes and how you would distinguish them in under five minutes.

Your `kubectl rollout undo` succeeded and every pod is Ready, but the application is still broken. What kinds of change does undo not revert, and how do you structure deploys so a rollback is actually atomic?

The customer's security team wants read-only access for their auditors. Describe the Role, the binding, the token lifetime and how you prove to them what the identity can and cannot do, including Secrets and pods/exec.

Walk through everything that happens between `kubectl delete pod` and the container exiting, including the race that produces 502s during a rolling update and how you eliminate it without slowing deploys.
8.proofOfWork: A public repository named k8s-client-tenancy-lab containing a kind cluster config with Calico installed so NetworkPolicy is enforced, a Kustomize base per client namespace (Namespace with PSA labels, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, default-deny plus DNS and API-to-DB NetworkPolicies, client-reader Role and ServiceAccount), a sample API Deployment with tuned probes and resources, a Postgres StatefulSet with Retain, an HPA and a PDB. A `make chaos` target injects one failure at a time (bad image tag, missing ConfigMap key, memory limit below RSS, probe timeout at 1s under load, NoSchedule taint on every node, PVC deleted under the StatefulSet) and RUNBOOK.md pairs each with an asciinema recording of the diagnosis finishing under ten minutes, ending with the rollout undo drill and the `kubectl auth can-i --list` output for the reader identity. A `make verify` target asserts with nc that an unlabeled pod is refused on 5432 while the API pod connects, that the reader token cannot read Secrets, and that the HPA reports ScalingActive True, so a reviewer can clone and watch every claim pass.

9.why: An FDE ships into a cluster the customer owns: their platform team holds the kubeconfig, their change-control process wants a reviewable diff and a rollback story, and you will not be on call after you leave. A Helm chart plus an Argo CD Application manifest is the deliverable that gets through that gate, because it turns your deployment into a pull request their team can read, approve and revert without you. Argo CD is also what you will meet on-site at most Palantir, Databricks and Anthropic enterprise customers, so you need to be able to debug their Argo (perpetual OutOfSync, hooks that never run, a rollback that disabled auto-sync) as fluently as your own.
prerequisites: Topic 7 (Kubernetes core): can write Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap and Secret manifests by hand and use kubectl apply, get, describe, diff and rollout status

Topic 8 (Kubernetes production ops): readiness and liveness probes, rolling update strategy (maxSurge, maxUnavailable), resource requests and limits, HPA, and basic RBAC, because Argo CD's health assessment and sync waves depend on probes and status
Topic 6 (production images): the Dokeo image is already built non-root, tagged and pushed to a registry such as ghcr.io, since the CI to CD handoff promotes image tags and digests
Topic 4 (Git at depth): git revert, tags, protected branches, PR review flow and webhooks, because in GitOps a rollback is a Git operation
A local cluster (kind or k3d) with about 4 GB RAM free plus kubectl, helm 3.x and the argocd CLI installed and on PATH
Read the Go text/template syntax page once and understand YAML block scalars, indentation semantics and why two-space drift silently changes meaning

subtopics.name: GitOps operating model and the reconciliation loop
subtopics.learn: State the four OpenGitOps principles (declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled) and what each one rules out in practice: kubectl apply from CI (push model, cluster credential leaves the cluster), kubectl edit hotfixes, floating image tags like latest. Trace the loop Argo CD runs: fetch desired state from Git, render it (helm template or kustomize build), compare to live state through the Kubernetes API, report Synced or OutOfSync, optionally apply. Be able to explain why the agent lives inside the cluster (outbound-only, works through customer firewalls, no kubeconfig in CI secrets) and why 'Git is the audit log' only holds when branch protection, required reviews and signed commits are enforced. Draw the whole thing on a whiteboard in two minutes and mark where CI ends and CD begins.

resource.label: OpenGitOps - the GitOps principles (CNCF GitOps Working Group)

subtopics.name: Chart anatomy and where Helm stores release state
subtopics.learn: Know every file `helm create` emits and which to delete: Chart.yaml (apiVersion: v2; `version` is the chart SemVer, `appVersion` is the packaged app; `type: application|library`; `kubeVersion` constraint), values.yaml, templates/, templates/_helpers.tpl, templates/NOTES.txt, templates/tests/, charts/, crds/, .helmignore. Understand that Helm 3 stores each release revision as a Secret of type `helm.sh/release.v1` named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<N>` in the release namespace (gzipped, base64-encoded protobuf), so `helm list`, `helm history`, and `helm get manifest|values|notes -n ns rel --revision N` all read from those Secrets and deleting them orphans the release. Know that crds/ is installed on first install and never upgraded or deleted by Helm, and what that means when a customer runs an operator chart for two years.

resource.label: Helm docs - Charts (file structure, Chart.yaml, CRDs)

subtopics.name: Template engine: builtin objects, Sprig functions, pipelines
subtopics.learn: Use .Values, .Release.{Name,Namespace,IsUpgrade,IsInstall,Revision}, .Chart.{Name,Version,AppVersion}, .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "autoscaling/v2", .Capabilities.KubeVersion.Version, .Files.Get|Glob|AsConfig|AsSecrets and .Template.Name. Chain Sprig functions in pipelines: `default`, `required "image.tag is required" .Values.image.tag`, `quote`, `toYaml | nindent 8`, `tpl` for values that themselves contain templates, `trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-"` for DNS-1123 names, `sha256sum` of a rendered ConfigMap as a pod-template annotation so config changes restart pods, and `lookup "v1" "Secret" .Release.Namespace "name"` to read existing objects, knowing it returns empty under `helm template` and inside Argo CD's repo-server so correctness can never depend on it. Whitespace control: `{{-` eats to the left, `-}}` to the right; the classic bug is `indent` where `nindent` was needed, producing YAML that lints clean but nests under the wrong key.

resource.label: Helm Chart Template Guide - Template Functions and Pipelines

subtopics.name: Control flow, scope and named templates
subtopics.learn: Use if/else if/with/range and understand that `with` and `range` rebind `.`, so inside them you reach the root through `$` (`$.Release.Name`) or a captured `{{- $root := . }}`. Range over maps with `{{- range $k, $v := .Values.env }}` and rely on Go sorting map keys so output is stable and diffs are quiet. Define helpers in _helpers.tpl with `{{ define "dokeo.fullname" }}` and call them with `include` (returns a string you can pipe to nindent), not `template` (cannot be piped); prefix every define with the chart name because defines are global across parent and subcharts and the last loaded wins. Build `dokeo.labels` (app.kubernetes.io/name, instance, version, managed-by, helm.sh/chart) and a separate `dokeo.selectorLabels` without version or chart, because Deployment `spec.selector` is immutable and a chart bump would otherwise break every upgrade.

resource.label: Helm Chart Template Guide - Named Templates

subtopics.name: Values design, precedence and values.schema.json
subtopics.learn: Know the precedence: chart values.yaml < parent-chart values for a subchart < `-f a.yaml -f b.yaml` (last wins; maps deep-merge, lists replace) < `--set`, `--set-string`, `--set-file`, `--set-json` (last wins). Know the `--set` coercion traps: `--set port=8080` becomes an int, `--set image.tag=1.10` becomes the float 1.1, `--set list[0]=x` replaces the whole list; use `--set-string` for tags. Write values.schema.json (JSON Schema draft 7) with `required`, `enum`, a `pattern` for image tags and `additionalProperties: false` at the top level; it is enforced by helm install, upgrade, lint and template, which turns a typo in a customer's values file into a hard failure before anything reaches the cluster. Follow the conventions: camelCase keys, flat over nested, every key commented, `image.repository` / `image.tag` / `image.digest` kept separate, `resources: {}` so the deployer must choose, and no environment names baked into the chart.

resource.label: Helm Chart Best Practices - Values

subtopics.name: Dependencies, subcharts and global values
subtopics.learn: Declare `dependencies:` in Chart.yaml with name, version (a SemVer range such as `~15.2.0`), repository (`https://`, `oci://` or `file://../local`), `condition: redis.enabled`, `alias`, `tags` and `import-values`. Run `helm dependency update` (writes Chart.lock and charts/*.tgz) and `helm dependency build` (from the lock); commit Chart.lock and decide explicitly whether to commit charts/*.tgz, because Argo CD's repo-server must be able to fetch them at render time (vendor them, or give repo-server registry access and accept the render latency). Values reach a subchart only under its name key (`redis:`) or under `global:`; a subchart can never see parent values. Know when to wrap an upstream Bitnami or vendor chart as a dependency behind a thin parent versus fork it: fork only when a template must change, and record the upstream version and the diff in the repo.

resource.label: Helm Chart Template Guide - Subcharts and Global Values

subtopics.name: Chart verification: lint, template, kubeconform, unittest, helm test
subtopics.learn: Build a pre-commit and CI gate: `helm lint --strict -f ci/prod-values.yaml`; `helm template rel . -f values.yaml --debug` (renders even invalid YAML so you can see it); `helm template ... | kubeconform -strict -kubernetes-version 1.29.0 -schema-location default` plus a CRD schema location for cert-manager or ESO kinds; `helm install --dry-run=server` (needs a cluster; catches admission webhooks and unknown fields); the helm-unittest plugin asserting rendered paths such as `spec.template.spec.containers[0].image`; chart-testing `ct lint` and `ct install` across `ci/*-values.yaml`; and `helm test` running pods in templates/tests annotated `helm.sh/hook: test`. Add `helm template ... | kubectl diff -f -` to see what a change does to a real cluster. Decode the three classic errors on sight: `nil pointer evaluating interface` (missing values key, fix with default or schema), `error converting YAML to JSON: mapping values are not allowed` (indent bug), and `unable to recognize` (apiVersion not served by this cluster).

resource.label: Helm Chart Template Guide - Debugging Templates

subtopics.name: Upgrade mechanics, hooks, three-way merge and immutable fields
subtopics.learn: Run `helm upgrade --install rel . -n ns --create-namespace --atomic --wait --wait-for-jobs --timeout 5m --cleanup-on-fail --history-max 10` and know what each flag buys: --atomic rolls back on failure, --wait blocks until Deployments hit minimum ready and PVCs bind. Helm 3 performs a three-way merge (previous manifest, new manifest, live object), so manual edits to fields the chart never set survive an upgrade while fields the chart used to set and then dropped are reverted. Hooks: `helm.sh/hook: pre-install,pre-upgrade`, `helm.sh/hook-weight: "-5"` (string, ascending), `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded`; hook resources are not part of the release and a failed hook aborts the upgrade. Know the immutable-field failures cold: Deployment spec.selector, StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates, Job spec.template, Service spec.clusterIP; the only fixes are `--force` (delete and recreate, with downtime) or a rename. `helm rollback rel N` reapplies a stored manifest; `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` protects PVCs on uninstall; `helm uninstall --keep-history` keeps forensics.

resource.label: Helm docs - Chart Hooks

subtopics.name: Packaging and publishing charts to an OCI registry
subtopics.learn: `helm package . --version 1.4.0 --app-version 2.3.1` produces dokeo-1.4.0.tgz; `helm registry login ghcr.io -u $USER --password-stdin`; `helm push dokeo-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/org/charts`; consumers run `helm install rel oci://ghcr.io/org/charts/dokeo --version 1.4.0` and `helm show values oci://...`. The OCI tag is the chart version, so SemVer `+build` metadata is rewritten to `_`. OCI charts have no index.yaml, so `helm repo add` does not apply; Argo CD references them with `repoURL: ghcr.io/org/charts`, `chart: dokeo`, `targetRevision: 1.4.0` and needs a repository credential of type helm with `enableOCI: "true"`. Sign with `helm package --sign --key ... --keyring ...` or cosign the OCI artifact so the customer's admission policy can verify provenance. Bump chart `version` on any template change and `appVersion` on any image change; never overwrite a published version.

resource.label: Helm docs - Use OCI-based registries

subtopics.name: Argo CD architecture and how it actually renders Helm
subtopics.learn: Name each component and what breaks when it is down: argocd-server (API, UI, CLI; stateless), argocd-repo-server (clones repos, runs helm template or kustomize build, caches rendered manifests in Redis; CPU-bound; `--parallelismlimit`), argocd-application-controller (reconciles every Application on `timeout.reconciliation`, default 180s, or on webhook; compares live to target; runs the sync), redis (cache only, safe to lose), dex (SSO), applicationset-controller, notifications-controller. The crucial fact: Argo CD never runs helm install. It runs `helm template` with your values and applies the output, so there are no sh.helm.release.v1 Secrets, `helm list` is empty, `.Release.IsUpgrade` is always false, `lookup` returns nothing, and Helm hooks are mapped to Argo hooks (pre-install and pre-upgrade become PreSync, post-* become PostSync, crd-install and test hooks are ignored). Know the two resource-tracking methods (default label app.kubernetes.io/instance, or annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id` via `application.resourceTrackingMethod: annotation` in argocd-cm) and why the label default collides with Helm's own instance label when several apps share a namespace.

resource.label: Argo CD Operator Manual - Architectural Overview

subtopics.name: The Application CRD end to end
subtopics.learn: Write an argoproj.io/v1alpha1 Application from memory: `metadata.namespace: argocd`, `finalizers: [resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io]` (so deleting the Application cascades to its resources; without it they are orphaned), `spec.project`, `spec.source.{repoURL,path,targetRevision}`, `spec.destination.{server: https://kubernetes.default.svc | name, namespace}`, `spec.syncPolicy.automated.{prune: true, selfHeal: true, allowEmpty: false}`, `syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true, PruneLast=true, ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true, ServerSideApply=true, RespectIgnoreDifferences=true, PrunePropagationPolicy=foreground]`, `retry.{limit: 5, backoff.{duration: 5s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 3m}}`, `revisionHistoryLimit`, `ignoreDifferences`, `info`. Read `status.sync.status` (Synced/OutOfSync), `status.health.status`, `status.operationState.phase` and `status.history[].id` (what rollback consumes). Drive it with `argocd app create|get|sync|diff|history|wait --health --timeout 300|delete --cascade`, and know that `kubectl apply -f app.yaml` of the Application itself is how you bootstrap without the CLI or UI.

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Application Specification Reference

subtopics.name: Helm source settings inside an Application
subtopics.learn: Under `spec.source.helm`: `releaseName` (defaults to the Application name; changing it changes the instance label and re-creates every resource), `valueFiles: [values.yaml, values-prod.yaml]` (relative to path), `values: |` as an inline string and `valuesObject:` as structured YAML, `parameters: [{name: image.tag, value: abc123, forceString: true}]`, `fileParameters`, `skipCrds`, `passCredentials`, `ignoreMissingValueFiles: true` for optional per-environment overrides, and `kubeVersion` / `apiVersions` overrides so `.Capabilities` resolves correctly when repo-server cannot reach the target cluster's discovery API. Use multiple sources to pull the chart from an OCI registry and values from your Git repo: a source with `ref: values` and `helm.valueFiles: [$values/envs/prod/values.yaml]`. Precedence: valueFiles < values/valuesObject < parameters. Know that parameters edited in the UI are written back into the Application spec, so unless they also live in Git the app-of-apps will revert them on its next sync.

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Helm

subtopics.name: Sync phases, waves, resource hooks and the sync engine
subtopics.learn: Argo orders a sync by phase (PreSync, Sync, PostSync, SyncFail, PostDelete), then wave (`argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"`, default 0, ascending), then kind (Namespace, CRDs, ServiceAccount, ConfigMap, Secret before workloads), then name, and waits for every resource in a wave to be Healthy before starting the next (with a delay set by ARGOCD_SYNC_WAVE_DELAY, default 2s), so a Job in wave 0 with no completion blocks the whole app. Hooks: `argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync` plus `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation|HookSucceeded|HookFailed`; a hook Job needs `generateName` or BeforeHookCreation to run again next sync. Use this to run the Dokeo DB migration as a PreSync Job with `backoffLimit: 1` so a failed migration fails the sync and leaves the old Deployment serving. Distinguish selfHeal (reverts live drift; debounce `--self-heal-timeout-seconds`, default 5s) from prune (deletes resources removed from Git) and the per-resource escape hatches `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false` and `Replace=true` (for objects over the 256 KB last-applied annotation limit or with immutable fields).

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Sync Phases and Waves

subtopics.name: Health assessment, diffing and ignoreDifferences
subtopics.learn: Health rolls up from resources: a Deployment is Healthy when updatedReplicas, replicas and availableReplicas agree and observedGeneration matches; a Job on completion; an Ingress once status.loadBalancer is populated; a PVC once Bound; custom resources default to Healthy unless a Lua check exists in argocd-cm under `resource.customizations.health.<group>_<kind>`. Write a Lua health check for a CRD such as cert-manager Certificate or ESO ExternalSecret that returns Progressing or Degraded so waves gate correctly. Diffing: Argo compares desired to live minus system-managed fields, so perpetual OutOfSync almost always comes from mutating admission (sidecar injection, defaulted resources), HPA-managed spec.replicas, cert-manager-injected caBundle, or API-server defaulting. Fix with `ignoreDifferences: [{group: apps, kind: Deployment, jsonPointers: [/spec/replicas]}]`, `jqPathExpressions` for list elements (`.spec.template.spec.containers[] | select(.name == "istio-proxy")`), or `managedFieldsManagers: [kube-controller-manager]`, and add `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` so the sync stops overwriting what you ignore. Preview with `argocd app diff --local ./chart` and inspect with `argocd app manifests --source live|git`.

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Diffing Customization

subtopics.name: Rollback: Git revert first, argocd app rollback second
subtopics.learn: The GitOps rollback is `git revert <sha> && git push` (or moving a tag), which keeps Git and cluster in agreement and preserves history; measure push-to-Healthy time with a webhook (seconds) versus polling (up to 180s plus sync duration). `argocd app rollback <app> <history-id>` redeploys a revision from status.history but refuses while syncPolicy.automated is set, so the emergency sequence is `argocd app set <app> --sync-policy none`, `argocd app rollback`, then fix Git and re-enable automated sync, and you must record that the cluster is temporarily ahead of Git. Pin `targetRevision` to a tag or SHA for prod and use HEAD only for dev; know the meanings of HEAD, branch, tag, SHA and SemVer ranges for chart sources. Know what no rollback undoes: PreSync migration Jobs (you need down-migrations), PVC contents, resources marked Prune=false, and Secrets rotated out of band. Drill it: break the readiness probe path, push, watch Degraded, revert, confirm Healthy, and write the timeline into the repo.

resource.label: Argo CD CLI reference - argocd app rollback

subtopics.name: App-of-apps and ApplicationSet
subtopics.learn: Bootstrap a cluster with a root Application whose `path: bootstrap/apps` contains other Application manifests (app-of-apps), so `kubectl apply -f root.yaml` is the only imperative step; know that child apps sync in parallel unless you put sync-wave annotations on the Applications themselves, and that deleting the root with the finalizer cascades everything beneath it. ApplicationSet replaces copy-pasted Applications: generators `list`, `clusters` (with `selector.matchLabels` on cluster Secrets), `git` `directories` (one app per envs/* folder) and `files` (a config.json per environment), `matrix`, `merge`, `pullRequest` (preview environments per PR) and `scmProvider`; `goTemplate: true` with `goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]`; template fields such as `{{.path.basename}}` and `{{.name}}`. While learning, set `syncPolicy.preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true` and `applicationsSync: create-update` so a bad template cannot delete prod, then turn on `strategy.type: RollingSync` to gate prod behind staging health.

resource.label: Argo CD Operator Manual - ApplicationSet controller

subtopics.name: Projects, RBAC and multi-tenant guardrails
subtopics.learn: An AppProject bounds what an Application may do: `sourceRepos: ['https://github.com/org/*']`, `destinations: [{server, namespace: 'team-a-*'}]`, `clusterResourceWhitelist` (empty means no cluster-scoped resources, which is why CreateNamespace=true fails silently in a tenant project), `namespaceResourceBlacklist: [ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy]`, `sourceNamespaces` for Applications outside the argocd namespace, `syncWindows` (`kind: deny, schedule: '0 22 * * *', duration: 8h, applications: ['*-prod'], manualSync: true`) and `orphanedResources.warn: true`. Project roles: `roles: [{name: ci, policies: ['p, proj:team-a:ci, applications, sync, team-a/*, allow']}]` with `argocd proj role create-token team-a ci --expires-in 720h` for CI. Global RBAC in argocd-rbac-cm policy.csv: `g, org:team-a, role:team-a-dev`, `policy.default: role:readonly`, groups mapped from OIDC claims via Dex. Design for a customer: one project per team, humans get sync in dev, prod is automated-only with humans able to read, diff and rollback.

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Projects

subtopics.name: Secrets in a GitOps repository
subtopics.learn: Rule: nothing decryptable sits in Git. Compare the three patterns you will meet at customers. Sealed Secrets: `kubeseal --controller-namespace kube-system --scope namespace-wide < secret.yaml > sealed.yaml`, cluster-private key, re-seal on rotation, unrecoverable if the controller key is lost, so back it up. External Secrets Operator: a SecretStore or ClusterSecretStore pointing at AWS Secrets Manager or Vault plus an ExternalSecret with `refreshInterval` and `dataFrom`; the Secret is materialised in-cluster and Argo tracks only the ExternalSecret. SOPS with age or KMS via a Config Management Plugin or helm-secrets, where decryption happens in repo-server, which then holds the KMS credential. Argo redacts Secret data in the UI and in `argocd app diff` (shown as ++++++++), but repo-server logs and the rendered-manifest cache do not, so treat repo-server as a secret-bearing component. Argo's own credentials are Secrets labelled `argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: repository` or `cluster`, and argocd-secret holds webhook and OIDC secrets.

resource.label: Argo CD Operator Manual - Secret Management

subtopics.name: CI to CD handoff and environment promotion
subtopics.learn: Separate the app repo (code, Dockerfile, CI) from the config repo (chart values per environment, Application manifests) so a code change and a deploy are distinct commits with distinct reviewers. CI: build, push the image and capture its digest, then `yq -i '.image.tag = strenv(TAG)' envs/dev/values.yaml` and commit with [skip ci], or open a PR for staging and prod. Configure the Git webhook to `https://argocd.example.com/api/webhook` with the shared secret stored in argocd-secret under `webhook.github.secret`, which removes the three-minute polling latency. Alternative: Argo CD Image Updater watching the registry and writing back to Git. Promote dev to staging to prod through directories on one branch, never branch-per-environment (merges drift, hotfixes get lost). Make the deploy a test: `argocd app wait <app> --sync --health --timeout 600` as the CI gate, and `argocd app diff` or `argocd app sync --dry-run` in PR checks. Give CI a project-scoped token, never the admin password.

resource.label: Argo CD User Guide - Automation from CI Pipelines

subtopics.name: Operating Argo CD: notifications, metrics, tuning, disaster recovery
subtopics.learn: Notifications: argocd-notifications-cm triggers (on-sync-failed, on-health-degraded, on-deployed) and templates to Slack or a webhook, subscribed per Application with the annotation `notifications.argoproj.io/subscribe.on-sync-failed.slack: deploys`. Metrics: scrape argocd-metrics:8082 and argocd-repo-server:8084; alert on `argocd_app_info{sync_status="OutOfSync"}` persisting more than 15 minutes, `argocd_app_info{health_status="Degraded"}`, the rate of `argocd_app_sync_total{phase="Failed"}`, growth in `argocd_app_reconcile` p95, and `argocd_git_request_duration_seconds`. Tuning that bites on large charts: repo-server ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT (default 90s; `helm template` on umbrella charts can exceed it), `reposerver.parallelism.limit`, `controller.status.processors` and `controller.operation.processors`, `timeout.reconciliation`, and sharding the controller across clusters with ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS. Disaster recovery: workloads are already in Git; Argo's own state (projects, repo and cluster credentials, settings) is captured with `argocd admin export > backup.yaml` and restored with `argocd admin import`, so rebuild is install, import, apply root app. Upgrade one minor version at a time and read the version-specific upgrade notes first.

resource.label: Argo CD Operator Manual - Metrics

outcomes: You can author, from an empty directory in under 60 minutes, a Helm chart for Dokeo with Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, HPA, ServiceAccount, checksum-triggered restarts, values.schema.json and NOTES.txt, and it passes `helm lint --strict`, kubeconform and helm-unittest with zero warnings.

You can install Argo CD on a kind cluster, register the repo, apply an Application with automated sync, prune and selfHeal, and show a values change pushed to main reaching Healthy in the cluster within three minutes with no kubectl apply.

You can break a deploy (bad image tag or probe path), watch it go Degraded, `git revert` and demonstrate recovery to Healthy, then repeat the recovery with `argocd app rollback` after disabling automated sync, and state exactly what Git and the cluster contain after each path.

You can diagnose a perpetually OutOfSync Application in under ten minutes with `argocd app diff` and `argocd app manifests --source live`, name the controller mutating the object, and fix it with the narrowest ignoreDifferences rule plus RespectIgnoreDifferences=true.

You can run a database migration as a PreSync hook Job with correct hook-delete-policy and backoffLimit, gated ahead of the Deployment by sync waves, and show that a failing migration fails the sync while the previous version keeps serving.

You can collapse three copy-pasted per-environment Applications into one ApplicationSet with a git directory generator, and explain what preserveResourcesOnDeletion and applicationsSync: create-update each protect against.

You can write an AppProject that lets a customer team sync only into their own namespaces from their own repos with a scoped, expiring CI token, and prove with `argocd app sync` under that role that cross-namespace and cluster-scoped resources are denied.

You can explain to a customer's platform lead in five minutes, without notes, why Argo's helm template model leaves `helm list` empty, what happens to Helm hooks and lookup, and which of their Helm runbooks must change.
failureModes: The chart puts the helm.sh/chart version label inside Deployment spec.selector.matchLabels; a routine chart bump changes the selector, Argo reports 'field is immutable', the sync fails, and prod stays on the old version until someone applies Replace=true and takes an unplanned outage.

The app-of-apps root has prune: true; an engineer moves an Application file to a new directory in one PR, the root prunes the old Application first, the finalizer cascades and deletes the workload namespace including PVCs seconds before the new file is picked up.

A chart relies on lookup to reuse a previously generated admin password; repo-server has no cluster access so lookup renders empty on every sync, Argo writes a fresh random Secret, pods restart and sessions invalidate every three minutes, and selfHeal keeps the loop going until someone reads the Secret's history.

The HPA scales the Deployment to six replicas while the chart says replicas: 2 and selfHeal is on; Argo and the HPA fight, pods churn on every reconciliation, and p99 latency doubles during the customer's peak until /spec/replicas is added to ignoreDifferences.

Someone hot-fixes prod with argocd app rollback, which disables automated sync, and never reverts Git; three weeks later an unrelated commit through the app-of-apps re-enables sync and silently redeploys the broken revision at 2am.

An umbrella chart with eight subcharts takes 110 seconds to render; repo-server hits the 90-second ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT, every app sharing that repo-server flaps between Unknown and Synced, and on-call spends an hour chasing a phantom network problem.

CI promotes with `--set image.tag=1.10`, Helm coerces it to the float 1.1, the registry has no 1.1 tag, and because one pipeline template feeds all three environments, dev, staging and prod all ImagePullBackOff within the same minute.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through everything that happens between a git push to the config repo and a pod running the new image. Name each Argo CD component involved, where the latency comes from, and what you would change to make it both faster and safer.

Argo CD renders Helm with helm template instead of helm install. What are the concrete consequences for hooks, lookup, release Secrets, .Release.IsUpgrade and CRDs, and how would you adapt a customer's existing chart that depends on each of those?

Design a GitOps repository layout for a customer with dev, staging and prod clusters, five teams, and a compliance rule that every prod change is reviewed by two people. Directories or branches? App-of-apps or ApplicationSet? Where do secrets live? How does a hotfix reach prod in ten minutes without breaking the rule?

Debug: an Application is permanently OutOfSync with selfHeal enabled, pods restart every three minutes, and the diff shows an annotation that keeps changing. Walk me through your investigation and the fix, including which fields you would ignore and the risk of ignoring them.

A deploy went Degraded at 3am. Compare git revert and argocd app rollback as recovery paths: what each does, which you run first and why, what state Git and the cluster are in afterwards, and what neither of them will undo.

You must run a schema migration before the new Deployment rolls, and the customer's DBA insists that a failed migration blocks the release. Show me the manifests: hook annotations, sync waves, delete policy, backoffLimit, and how health assessment gates the Deployment.

A customer's platform team says GitOps is too slow and wants CI to kubectl apply directly. Make the case for pull-based delivery in terms they care about (audit trail, credential exposure, drift, rollback), and tell me where you would concede.
9.proofOfWork: A public repo `dokeo-gitops` split into `chart/` (the Dokeo Helm chart with values.schema.json, helm-unittest tests, a PreSync migration Job, and checksum-restart annotations) and `envs/{dev,staging,prod}/` consumed by a single ApplicationSet with a git directory generator, plus `bootstrap/root-app.yaml` so a fresh kind cluster is fully populated by one kubectl apply. GitHub Actions on the chart runs lint, kubeconform and unittest, then publishes the chart to oci://ghcr.io/<you>/charts with a cosign signature; a second workflow on the app repo bumps the dev image tag by digest with yq and commits. The README contains a recorded rollback drill with timestamps: push a broken readiness path, `argocd app get` showing Degraded, git revert, time to Healthy, then a second run using `argocd app rollback` with the exact commands to disable and re-enable automated sync. Include `docs/ARGO-FOR-HELM-USERS.md`, a one-page note written for a customer platform team explaining the helm template model, what changes for their runbooks, and the ignoreDifferences rules they will need for their HPA and sidecar injector.

10.topic: Kubernetes security: Pod Security, RBAC, secrets, image policy, runtime
10.why: An FDE deploying into a customer's cluster is, from the customer's security team's point of view, a new attack surface arriving with a Helm chart — and the review that gates your go-live is a person asking why your pod wants hostPath, cluster-admin, and a long-lived secret in an env var. Being able to ship a workload that passes `restricted` Pod Security, a namespace-scoped Role, a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and a signed image on the first pass turns a three-week security review into a one-hour call. When the customer's own cluster is the thing that is broken — an over-permissive ServiceAccount, an unencrypted etcd, a pod reading the node's IMDS credentials — you are the person in the room who can name the finding, show the exploit, and hand over the fix.
prerequisites: Kubernetes core objects from 'Kubernetes core' (topic 7): Pod, Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, ConfigMap, Secret, namespaces, and reading a full `kubectl get -o yaml`
Production ops from 'Kubernetes production ops' (topic 8): you have already written a NetworkPolicy and a basic Role/RoleBinding and debugged a CrashLoopBackOff
Linux namespaces, cgroups, and capabilities from 'Docker internals' (topic 5) — specifically what CAP_SYS_ADMIN, PID namespace sharing, and a bind mount of /proc actually grant
Image supply chain from topic 6: multi-stage builds, non-root USER, distroless bases, SBOM generation, and what a cosign signature is
Comfort with TLS, x509 client certs, and JWT structure from 'Networking' (topic 2) — the API server authenticates you with one of these on every request
A working local cluster you can wreck: kind or minikube with at least 4 GB and the ability to run a privileged pod

subtopics.name: The cluster threat model: what an attacker gets from one RCE
subtopics.learn: Write out the actual kill chain rather than a list of CVEs: app RCE inside a container -> read the projected ServiceAccount token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token -> query the API server -> list Secrets or create a privileged pod -> mount the host filesystem -> read every kubelet credential on the node -> lateral to other tenants. Map each hop to the control that breaks it (PSA restricted, namespaced RBAC, NetworkPolicy egress, IMDSv2 hop limit, node isolation). Be able to state, for any customer cluster, which of those hops is currently unguarded and what the blast radius is.

resource.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Containers matrix — tactics and techniques targeting Kubernetes

subtopics.name: How the API server decides who you are
subtopics.learn: Know the authentication chain: client x509 certs (CN becomes the username, O becomes groups — and there is no revocation, which is why cert-based human access is a liability), bootstrap tokens, ServiceAccount JWTs, OIDC id_tokens (`--oidc-issuer-url`, `--oidc-username-claim`, `--oidc-groups-claim`), and webhook token authn. Understand that Kubernetes has no User object — usernames come from the authenticator, so you cannot 'delete a user', you revoke the credential or the binding. Read your own identity with `kubectl auth whoami` and decode a SA token with a JWT decoder to see `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and the `kubernetes.io` claims binding it to a specific pod and node.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Authenticating

subtopics.name: RBAC mechanics: verbs, resources, subresources, aggregation
subtopics.learn: Internalise that RBAC is purely additive (no deny rules), that Role/RoleBinding are namespaced while ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide, and that a RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole grants that ClusterRole's rules *only within the binding's namespace* — the single most useful pattern for tenant isolation. Know the verb set (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection, plus non-standard ones like `use` on PSPs and `impersonate`), that `list` and `watch` return full object bodies so `list secrets` equals `read every secret`, and that subresources are separate rule entries: `pods/exec`, `pods/portforward`, `pods/log`, `pods/attach`, `deployments/scale`, `*/status`. Understand `resourceNames` scoping and its limitation (it cannot restrict `list`/`watch`), `nonResourceURLs` for /healthz and /metrics, and ClusterRole aggregation via `aggregationRule.clusterRoleSelectors`.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization

subtopics.name: RBAC privilege-escalation paths you must be able to name
subtopics.learn: Learn the escalation primitives an auditor will ask you about: `create pods` in any namespace is effectively 'run as any ServiceAccount in that namespace' (mount its token) and often 'root on the node' (hostPath /); `escalate` on ClusterRoles bypasses the built-in privilege-escalation prevention; `bind` lets you grant permissions you do not hold; `impersonate` on users/groups/serviceaccounts is a full identity swap (`kubectl --as`, `--as-group`); `create serviceaccounts/token` mints tokens for other SAs; `get/list secrets` harvests credentials; `patch nodes` or `update pods/status` can subvert scheduling; `create` on `certificatesigningrequests/approval` mints client certs. Also know that write access to a validating/mutating webhook config, a CRD, or a controller's SA is equivalent to cluster-admin by proxy.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: RBAC Good Practices

subtopics.name: Auditing effective permissions in a cluster you did not build
subtopics.learn: Be fast at answering 'what can this identity do?'. Use `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:name` for a full matrix, `kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=... -n ns` for a single check, and `--as-group` for group-derived access. Grep for the dangerous bindings: every ClusterRoleBinding to `cluster-admin`, any subject of `system:masters` (which bypasses RBAC entirely and is unauditable in RBAC terms), any rule with `resources: ['*']` and `verbs: ['*']`, and any binding to the `system:anonymous` user or `system:unauthenticated` group. Install `kubectl-who-can` to answer the inverse query ('who can create pods in kube-system'). Produce this inventory as a table — it is the first page of the hardening report you hand a client.

resource.label: kubectl-who-can (aquasecurity)

subtopics.name: ServiceAccounts, projected tokens, and turning off automount
subtopics.learn: Understand that since 1.24 Secret-based SA tokens are no longer auto-created and pods get a *bound, audience-scoped, time-limited* token via the TokenRequest API, projected by the kubelet and rotated at ~80% of its lifetime — so a stolen token expires, unlike a legacy `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount (defaults for everything using it) or on the PodSpec (per-pod override) for any workload that never calls the API server, which is most of them. Know how to mint a short-lived token deliberately with `kubectl create token <sa> --duration=10m --audience=...`, and why binding a token to a non-default audience stops it being replayed against the API server.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Service Accounts

subtopics.name: Pod Security Standards: privileged, baseline, restricted
subtopics.learn: Learn the three profiles as concrete field lists, not vibes. `baseline` blocks hostNetwork/hostPID/hostIPC, hostPath volumes, privileged, host ports, adding capabilities beyond a small set, and unconfined seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux overrides. `restricted` adds: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, `capabilities.drop: ['ALL']` (only NET_BIND_SERVICE may be added back), `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` or Localhost, and volume-type restrictions to a safe list (configMap, secret, emptyDir, projected, downwardAPI, PVC, ephemeral). Be able to look at any PodSpec and say, without running it, which profile it violates and on which exact field.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Pod Security Standards

subtopics.name: Pod Security Admission: rolling it out without breaking the customer
subtopics.learn: PSA is a built-in admission controller driven by three namespace labels per mode: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/{enforce,audit,warn}` plus optional `-version` pins (`v1.30` rather than `latest`, so a cluster upgrade cannot silently tighten policy). Know the rollout order that does not cause an outage: label with `warn` and `audit` first, watch the API server warnings and audit annotations for a full deploy cycle, fix workloads, then set `enforce`. Know the hard limits: enforce is checked only on pod create/update, so *existing* pods and higher-level controllers keep running while Deployments silently fail to create ReplicaSet pods — you must check `kubectl get events` / ReplicaSet conditions, not just `kubectl get deploy`. Know cluster-wide defaults via the AdmissionConfiguration `PodSecurity` plugin with `exemptions.usernames/runtimeClasses/namespaces` for kube-system and CNI DaemonSets.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Pod Security Admission

subtopics.name: securityContext: the fields that actually change the kernel
subtopics.learn: Write the securityContext block from memory and know what each field does at the syscall level. Pod-level: `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup`/`fsGroup` (and `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` to avoid a 20-minute chown on a large PVC), `supplementalGroups`, `seccompProfile`, `seLinuxOptions`. Container-level: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` (sets PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, killing setuid binaries and file capabilities), `capabilities: {drop: ['ALL'], add: ['NET_BIND_SERVICE']}`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` paired with emptyDir mounts for /tmp and any cache dir, `privileged: false`. Know that `runAsNonRoot: true` fails the pod at *runtime* with CreateContainerConfigError if the image's USER is numeric-unset, which is why you also pin `runAsUser`.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

subtopics.name: Container escape primitives: what a dangerous PodSpec really grants
subtopics.learn: Be able to demo, not just describe, each escape: `hostPath: /` + chroot = full node filesystem including /var/lib/kubelet/pods and every mounted Secret on that node; `hostPID: true` + `nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p` = a root shell in the host's namespaces; `privileged: true` = all capabilities plus unmasked /dev and the ability to mount the host block device; a mounted `/var/run/docker.sock` or containerd socket = create any container on the node; CAP_SYS_ADMIN alone is enough via cgroup release_agent or /proc writes on older kernels; hostNetwork bypasses every NetworkPolicy and exposes localhost-bound node services. Run each one in your kind cluster once so the client demo is muscle memory.

resource.label: EKS Best Practices Guide: Pod Security

subtopics.name: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
subtopics.learn: Know that a Secret is a plain object in etcd, base64-encoded only, readable by anyone with `get secrets` in that namespace, by anything that can read etcd, and by any pod on the node whose kubelet mounted it. Enable encryption at rest with an `EncryptionConfiguration` file passed via `--encryption-provider-config`: understand provider ordering (the first provider encrypts, all listed providers can decrypt), why `identity` first means plaintext, and why you must run `kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -` to rewrite existing objects after enabling it. Prefer a KMS v2 provider (envelope encryption with a remote KEK, DEK caching, key-rotation without re-encrypting everything) over `aescbc`, and verify by reading the raw etcd value with `etcdctl get /registry/secrets/...`.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest

subtopics.name: Secret delivery patterns and their trade-offs
subtopics.learn: Know four patterns and when each is the right recommendation. External Secrets Operator: syncs from Vault/AWS Secrets Manager/GCP SM into a native Secret — easy, but the plaintext still lands in etcd. Secrets Store CSI Driver: mounts secrets as a tmpfs volume, optionally without creating a Secret object at all, with rotation via `--enable-secret-rotation`. Sealed Secrets: asymmetric encryption so the ciphertext is safe in Git, but the controller's private key becomes a crown jewel and disaster recovery depends on backing it up. SOPS + age/KMS: file-level encryption that works with any GitOps tool. Independently, always prefer mounting secrets as files over `env` — env vars leak into crash dumps, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, child processes, and every debug endpoint that prints the environment.

resource.label: External Secrets Operator docs: Overview — SecretStore/ExternalSecret sync model

subtopics.name: NetworkPolicy as blast-radius containment
subtopics.learn: Understand that policies are additive allow-lists and a pod is unrestricted until *some* policy selects it, so the first thing you install in a tenant namespace is a default-deny for both directions (`podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]`). Then know the gotchas that break clusters: an egress default-deny kills DNS unless you explicitly allow UDP/TCP 53 to the kube-dns pods (namespaceSelector on kube-system + podSelector k8s-app=kube-dns); `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` in the *same* `from` element are an AND while separate list elements are an OR; `ipBlock` cannot select pods and is the tool for blocking the cloud metadata IP 169.254.169.254; policies do not apply to hostNetwork pods; and the API is a no-op unless the CNI enforces it (Calico/Cilium yes, plain kubenet no). Know that a client asking for L7 or FQDN egress rules needs CiliumNetworkPolicy or a service mesh, not core NetworkPolicy.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Network Policies

subtopics.name: The cloud identity boundary: IMDS, IRSA, and node roles
subtopics.learn: The most common real-world cluster-to-cloud escape is a pod curling `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and getting the *node's* IAM role, which usually has ECR pull, EBS, and sometimes far more. Fix it two ways and know both: enforce IMDSv2 with `HttpTokens: required` and `HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 1` so containers (one hop away) cannot reach it at all, and/or block 169.254.169.254 via NetworkPolicy egress `ipBlock.except`. Then give workloads their own identity: IRSA (an OIDC provider on the cluster, an IAM role trust policy on `system:serviceaccount:ns:sa`, and the `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` annotation) or EKS Pod Identity. Be able to explain to a client why the node role must be the minimum needed to join and pull, never the app's role.

resource.label: EKS Best Practices Guide: Identity and Access Management

subtopics.name: Image provenance: registry allow-lists, digests, and signature verification
subtopics.learn: Enforce that only images from approved registries run, that tags are resolved to immutable digests (`image: registry/app@sha256:...` — a mutable `:latest` means the thing you scanned is not the thing that runs), and that `imagePullPolicy` is understood (`Always` on a mutable tag is a supply-chain hole *and* a pull-rate-limit outage; `IfNotPresent` on a digest is correct). Then add cryptographic verification: sign with `cosign sign --key ...` or keyless OIDC, attach an SBOM/attestation, and enforce at admission with sigstore policy-controller or a Kyverno `verifyImages` rule that also mutates the tag to the verified digest. Know that the legacy built-in `ImagePolicyWebhook` admission plugin exists but that policy engines are what customers actually run.

resource.label: sigstore/cosign — container signing and verification

subtopics.name: Policy engines: Kyverno, Gatekeeper, and built-in CEL policies
subtopics.learn: Know the three options and pick correctly for a customer. ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA, built-in, CEL expressions, no external webhook so no availability risk) handles most 'reject this field' rules and should be the default answer for simple constraints. Kyverno writes policies as Kubernetes YAML and can validate, *mutate* (inject securityContext defaults, sidecars, imagePullSecrets), generate (auto-create a default-deny NetworkPolicy per new namespace), and verify image signatures — usually the fastest path to a working policy set. Gatekeeper uses OPA/Rego with ConstraintTemplates and audits existing resources against constraints. Critically: understand `failurePolicy: Fail` vs `Ignore`, `namespaceSelector`/`objectSelector` exemptions for kube-system, webhook timeouts, and that a Fail-closed webhook whose pods are down will brick the entire cluster's ability to create pods — including the webhook's own pods.

resource.label: Kyverno documentation

subtopics.name: Runtime detection and the audit log
subtopics.learn: Admission stops bad specs; runtime tooling catches bad behaviour from a spec that looked fine. Learn Falco's model (eBPF or kernel-module syscall capture, rules matching on syscall + container metadata + k8s labels) and the handful of default rules that actually matter — `Terminal shell in container`, `Write below etc`, `Contact K8S API Server From Container`, `Read sensitive file untrusted` — and how to tune out the noise that makes teams disable it. Separately, configure the API server audit log with a Policy that records `RequestResponse` for secrets and RBAC objects, `Metadata` for everything else, and `None` for the read-only noise; know the audit stages (RequestReceived, ResponseStarted, ResponseComplete, Panic) and that PSA writes its `audit` violations as annotations on these events. Know that without an audit log you cannot answer 'what did the attacker do' after an incident.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Auditing — audit policy, levels, and stages

subtopics.name: Sandboxing and node-level hardening
subtopics.learn: Know the layers beneath the pod. `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` blocks roughly 40+ dangerous syscalls at near-zero cost and should be on every workload; a Localhost profile is for when you have measured the syscall set. AppArmor via `securityContext.appArmorProfile` and RuntimeClass with gVisor or Kata gives you a real kernel boundary for untrusted or customer-supplied code. User namespaces (`hostUsers: false`) remap in-container root to an unprivileged host UID so a container escape lands as nobody. On the node itself: the kubelet must run with `--authorization-mode=Webhook` and `--anonymous-auth=false` (the read-only port 10255 and an open 10250 are classic findings), and Node authorization plus the NodeRestriction admission plugin must be on so a compromised kubelet cannot read Secrets for pods it does not run.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

subtopics.name: Continuous assessment: CIS benchmarks and in-cluster scanning
subtopics.learn: Run `kube-bench` against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark as a Job and read the output critically — many control-plane checks are Not Applicable on managed clusters (EKS/GKE), and telling a client that 40 findings are 'informational because AWS owns the control plane' is exactly the kind of judgement they are paying for. Add `trivy-operator` for continuous VulnerabilityReports, ConfigAuditReports, and RbacAssessmentReports as CRDs you can query with kubectl, and know that image CVE counts must be triaged by reachability and fix availability, not shipped raw. Use `kubescape` for NSA/CISA and MITRE ATT&CK framework mappings when a customer asks for a named framework. Turn the union of these into a prioritised list, not a 300-row dump.

resource.label: kube-bench (CIS Kubernetes Benchmark checks)

subtopics.name: Kubernetes Goat: exploit, then map every finding to a control
subtopics.learn: Work the Goat scenarios end to end — sensitive keys in code, DIND exploitation, SSRF, container escape to the host, docker.sock exposure, kubectl in a container, hidden-in-layers secrets, RBAC least-privilege misconfiguration, KubeAudit, Falco, Kyverno, Gatekeeper, cloud metadata SSRF, hostPath mount escape. For each one write three lines: the exploit command you ran, the single manifest field or RBAC rule that made it possible, and the exact control that closes it (PSA profile, securityContext field, NetworkPolicy, admission policy, or IMDS setting). That three-column table is the hardening checklist deliverable and the script for explaining findings to a non-security stakeholder.

resource.label: Kubernetes Goat scenarios documentation

outcomes: You can take an arbitrary Deployment manifest and, without a cluster, list every field that violates the `restricted` Pod Security Standard and rewrite it so it admits — including the emptyDir mounts needed to make `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` work.

You can roll Pod Security Admission onto a live namespace using warn/audit first, collect the violations from API server warnings and ReplicaSet events, and cut over to `enforce` with a version-pinned label and a documented exemption list.

You can audit an unfamiliar cluster's RBAC in under 30 minutes and produce a table of every subject with cluster-admin, every wildcard rule, every SA with `get/list secrets` or `create pods` outside its own namespace, and every binding to `system:unauthenticated`, using `kubectl auth can-i --list --as` and kubectl-who-can.
You can demonstrate a container escape in your own kind cluster three different ways (hostPath, hostPID + nsenter, privileged) and then show the exact PSA/securityContext change that blocks each.
You can prove a Secret is stored unencrypted in etcd, enable a KMS v2 EncryptionConfiguration, re-encrypt existing objects, and show the ciphertext in the same raw etcd read.

You can write a default-deny NetworkPolicy pair for a tenant namespace that still allows DNS, intra-namespace traffic, and egress to one external CIDR, while blocking 169.254.169.254 — and explain why hostNetwork pods bypass it.

You can enforce signed-image-only deployment with a Kyverno verifyImages policy or sigstore policy-controller, show a rejected unsigned image, and explain the failurePolicy blast radius if the webhook goes down.
You can complete every Kubernetes Goat scenario and explain each finding to a non-security stakeholder in two sentences: what an attacker gets, and the one-line manifest change that stops it.
failureModes: A team labels namespaces with `enforce: restricted` in one PR; existing pods keep running so dashboards stay green, but every subsequent Deployment rollout silently fails at the ReplicaSet level and nobody notices until an unrelated deploy needs to scale during an incident.

A default-deny egress NetworkPolicy ships without a DNS allow rule, so every service resolves nothing, connection errors look like a database outage, and the team spends two hours on the wrong system before someone checks the CNI.

A validating webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` and no kube-system exemption is deployed, its own pods get evicted during a node rotation, and the cluster can no longer admit any pod — including the webhook's replacement — requiring manual webhook-config deletion via a break-glass credential.

An application pod with no IAM role of its own quietly uses the node instance role via IMDS to read an S3 bucket; it works fine for a year, and the finding only surfaces in an audit after the same path is used to reach a bucket the workload was never meant to see.

Secrets are injected as env vars, the app's unhandled-exception handler ships the full environment to an error-tracking SaaS, and a production database password ends up in a third-party system with a different retention policy and access list.

A Helm chart from an internal platform team ships `automountServiceAccountToken: true` with a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin 'temporarily for the migration', and it is still there eighteen months later on every install of that chart.
Falco is installed, generates 4,000 alerts a day from a noisy CI namespace, gets muted in Slack within a week, and is therefore silent on the night an actual `Terminal shell in container` fires.
interviewQuestions: A customer's security team says your workload cannot ship because it needs to write to disk and bind port 80. Walk me through exactly how you make it pass a `restricted` Pod Security Standard without asking for an exemption.

An attacker gets RCE in a pod running as non-root with the default ServiceAccount. Walk me through, hop by hop, everything they can reach in a default-configured EKS cluster, and tell me which single control cuts the most of it.

Design the RBAC model for a multi-tenant platform where each customer team can fully manage their own namespace but must never read another tenant's Secrets or run privileged pods. Which objects do you create, and where does namespace-level RBAC stop being sufficient?

Deployments in one namespace stopped creating pods after a policy change, but `kubectl get deploy` shows no error and there are no pod events. How do you debug this, and what are the three most likely causes?
A client asks whether Kubernetes Secrets are 'encrypted'. Answer them precisely, then describe what you would actually implement and how you would prove to their auditor that it works.

Compare enforcing 'no privileged containers' with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno, and Gatekeeper. Which do you recommend for a 400-node regulated-industry cluster, and what is the failure mode of your choice?

You are told a workload must reach one external SaaS endpoint but the cluster has default-deny egress and a CNI with no FQDN support. What options do you present, and what is the operational cost of each?
10.proofOfWork: Build a public repo called `k8s-hardening-kit` that turns the Kubernetes Goat run into a reusable client artifact. It contains: (1) a findings table with one row per Goat scenario — exploit command, the specific manifest field or RBAC rule that enabled it, the control that closes it, and a severity with a one-line business impact statement a non-engineer can read; (2) a `policies/` directory with the actual working controls, applied to a kind cluster in CI — a namespace-labelling script for PSA warn/audit/enforce, a default-deny plus DNS-allow NetworkPolicy pair, a Kyverno policy set (require restricted securityContext, block hostPath and hostNetwork, require digest-pinned images from an allow-listed registry, verifyImages against a cosign key, auto-generate a default-deny NetworkPolicy on namespace creation), an EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider, and a namespaced Role/RoleBinding template for a tenant; (3) a `verify/` directory with a script that deploys a deliberately-vulnerable pod and asserts each policy *rejects* it, so the repo proves its own controls work rather than just asserting them; and (4) a two-page `CHECKLIST.md` written for a customer platform lead, ordered by blast-radius reduction per hour of work, with an explicit 'what we are consciously not doing and why' section. Wire the whole thing into a GitHub Actions workflow that spins up kind, applies the policies, runs the negative tests and kube-bench, and fails the build if any control regresses.

11.topic: Serving models on Kubernetes and GPUs
11.why: A large share of FDE engagements at Anthropic, Palantir and Databricks-style shops end with a customer saying 'we cannot send this data to an API, run it on our GPUs.' The FDE is then the person who has to turn a bare g6e node or an on-prem A100 box into a working, measured OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the customer's Kubernetes, and who has to defend, with numbers, why it costs what it costs and how many users it can hold before p95 latency falls over. Nobody on the customer side knows the driver/CUDA/device-plugin stack, so if you cannot debug 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' or a CUDA OOM at 11pm the whole pilot slips; if you cannot size KV cache you will either buy four H100s for a 7B model or promise 50 users to a card that holds 20.
prerequisites: Kubernetes core from Topic 7: you can write a Deployment, Service and Ingress from memory, read kubectl describe pod Events, and know what an extended resource and a taint are.
Kubernetes production ops from Topic 8: startup vs readiness vs liveness probes, requests vs limits and QoS classes, HPA mechanics, PVC access modes, and kubectl debug / ephemeral containers.
Docker internals from Topic 5: what a runtime hook is, how /dev nodes and host libraries get bind-mounted into a container, what /dev/shm is and why the default 64 MB matters.

Networking from Topic 2: HTTP keep-alive, SSE streaming, proxy read timeouts and idle timeouts on L7 load balancers (ALB 60 s default, nginx 60 s default) since token streams are long-lived responses.
Troubleshooting habits from Topic 3: reading dmesg, exit codes, and top/nvidia-smi side by side; comfortable computing bytes from parameter counts (7B x 2 bytes = 14 GB).

Accounts and budget: a Hugging Face account with Llama gated-model access approved (takes hours, request it on day one), an HF token, and roughly USD 25-40 of GPU-hours on RunPod or a cloud account with a non-zero G/VT On-Demand vCPU quota (new AWS accounts default to 0 and the quota request takes a day or two).

subtopics.name: The GPU stack from silicon to Pod: driver, CUDA, toolkit, device plugin
subtopics.learn: Draw the four layers and who owns each: the kernel module (nvidia.ko) plus libcuda.so live on the node and are the 'driver'; the CUDA toolkit/runtime (libcudart, cuBLAS) lives inside the image; the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is an OCI runtime hook that bind-mounts /dev/nvidia*, libcuda.so and nvidia-smi into the container at create time; the k8s-device-plugin DaemonSet talks to kubelet's device plugin gRPC socket to advertise nvidia.com/gpu as an extended resource and, on allocation, sets NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for the container. Be able to state which layer produced each of these: 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version' (image CUDA newer than node driver), 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' (device plugin or scheduling), 'Failed to initialize NVML: Unknown Error' (toolkit/cgroup device access).

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Schedule GPUs (device plugins, node labels, NFD)

subtopics.name: Driver and CUDA compatibility: read nvidia-smi before you pull an image
subtopics.learn: The 'CUDA Version' in the top-right of nvidia-smi is the maximum CUDA runtime the installed driver supports, not what is installed; a driver is backward compatible with older runtimes, and forward compatibility (running a newer runtime on an older driver via the cuda-compat package) exists only for datacenter GPUs. Check the image with python -c 'import torch; print(torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())' and compare to the node. Know the practical failure: a vLLM wheel built against CUDA 12.8 on a node with a 535 driver fails at import, and the fix is either upgrading the node driver (GPU Operator can do it) or pulling an image built for an older CUDA. Understand why a kernel upgrade on the node can silently break a DKMS-built driver until reboot plus rebuild.

resource.label: NVIDIA docs: CUDA Compatibility

subtopics.name: NVIDIA Container Toolkit on a raw node: nvidia-ctk runtime configure
subtopics.learn: On a bare GPU VM (RunPod secure-cloud or a g5 instance) install nvidia-container-toolkit, run sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd (or --runtime=docker), restart the engine and verify /etc/containerd/config.toml gained the nvidia runtime under plugins.'io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri'.containerd.runtimes. Prove it with docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi. Understand the two env vars the hook reads: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (all, none, 0,1, or GPU-UUID) and NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES (compute,utility is the minimum for CUDA plus nvidia-smi). In Kubernetes, know when you need a RuntimeClass named nvidia (toolkit installed but not set as default runtime) and what the symptom is when you forget it: the pod runs, nvidia.com/gpu is allocated, but the container sees no /dev/nvidia0.

resource.label: NVIDIA Container Toolkit: Installing the NVIDIA Container Toolkit

subtopics.name: GPU Operator: what the Helm chart deploys and when to turn pieces off
subtopics.learn: helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --create-namespace deploys, via a ClusterPolicy CR, a driver DaemonSet, the container-toolkit DaemonSet, the device plugin, DCGM exporter, GPU Feature Discovery (GFD), Node Feature Discovery, MIG manager and a validator pod per node. Learn the two most common overrides: --set driver.enabled=false when the node image already ships drivers (EKS accelerated AMI, GKE, RunPod), and --set toolkit.enabled=false when the toolkit is baked in. Verify with kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator (every nvidia-operator-validator must be Completed) and kubectl get node <n> -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}'. Know what breaks when the driver DaemonSet is enabled on a node that already has a driver: the container driver fails to load and every GPU pod on that node goes Pending.

resource.label: NVIDIA GPU Operator: Installing the NVIDIA GPU Operator

subtopics.name: Scheduling onto GPUs: extended resources, taints, GFD labels
subtopics.learn: nvidia.com/gpu is requested under resources.limits only (requests, if given, must equal limits), is an integer, cannot be overcommitted, and is not shared between containers in a pod. Taint GPU nodes (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) so CPU workloads never land on a USD 4/hour node, and add the matching toleration to the vLLM pod. Pin GPU type with a nodeSelector on the GFD labels nvidia.com/gpu.product (e.g. NVIDIA-A10G, NVIDIA-L40S) or nvidia.com/gpu.memory, and read them with kubectl get nodes -L nvidia.com/gpu.product,nvidia.com/gpu.count. When a pod sits Pending with '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu', walk the checklist: is the device plugin pod Running on the target node, does Allocatable show the GPU, is another pod already holding it, does the pod tolerate the taint.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Taints and Tolerations

subtopics.name: Managed GPU node groups and scale-from-zero: EKS accelerated AMI, Karpenter
subtopics.learn: Know the cloud GPU menu you will actually be offered: g5 (A10G 24 GB), g6 (L4 24 GB), g6e (L40S 48 GB), p4d (8x A100 40 GB), p5 (8x H100 80 GB); the EKS accelerated AL2023 AMI ships driver and toolkit so you disable them in the operator. Write a Karpenter NodePool whose requirements select karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name In [l40s] and karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-count In [1], carries the nvidia.com/gpu taint, and has a long consolidateAfter so a 5-minute lull does not delete a node that took 4 minutes to boot. Understand the cold-start chain when scaling from zero: instance launch (2-3 min) plus 10-15 GB image pull plus weight load, so the first user waits 5-8 minutes; mitigate with a warm minimum of one replica and a pre-pull DaemonSet. Check the account's 'Running On-Demand G and VT instances' quota before the customer call; it is often 0.

resource.label: Karpenter docs: NodePools

subtopics.name: vLLM in a container: the vllm serve flags an operator must own
subtopics.learn: Use the official vllm/vllm-openai image and know the flags that change capacity or safety: --model and --served-model-name (what clients put in 'model'), --dtype auto (bf16 on Ampere+), --max-model-len (caps context and therefore per-request KV; do not leave it at the model's 128k default on a 24 GB card), --gpu-memory-utilization (fraction reserved for weights plus KV, default 0.9), --max-num-seqs (hard cap on sequences in one batch, i.e. concurrency), --tensor-parallel-size, --enable-prefix-caching, --kv-cache-dtype fp8, --quantization, --api-key, --port 8000, --download-dir, --trust-remote-code. Know --enforce-eager is for debugging only (disables CUDA graphs, costs throughput). Understand why tensor parallel needs a big /dev/shm and IPC (NCCL uses shared memory) and how that maps to an emptyDir medium Memory in Kubernetes instead of Docker's --ipc=host.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Engine Arguments

subtopics.name: Model weights: getting 16 GB into the cluster without downloading on every restart
subtopics.learn: An 8B bf16 checkpoint is roughly 16 GB in safetensors shards; pulling that from the Hub on every pod start turns a 30-second restart into a 5-10 minute outage and can hit rate limits. Compare the four patterns and pick per customer: a PVC pre-filled by a Job running hf download <repo> --local-dir /models (ReadWriteMany or one pod per PV), a hostPath cache on dedicated GPU nodes, an object-store mount (S3 Mountpoint or GCS FUSE), and baking weights into the image (avoid: 16 GB layers, slow pulls, registry limits). Set HF_HOME or --download-dir to the mount, HF_TOKEN from a Secret for gated Llama models, and HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 in air-gapped sites so vLLM never tries the network. For corporate proxies, know that allowlisting huggingface.co alone is not enough because files are served from cdn-lfs and xethub hostnames.

resource.label: Hugging Face Hub docs: Downloading models (CLI, proxies, allowlist hosts)

subtopics.name: The Deployment manifest: GPU limits, /dev/shm, probes, memory, update strategy
subtopics.learn: Write the vLLM Deployment from scratch and justify every field: resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 1 plus a memory request at least the size of the weights (vLLM stages tensors through host RAM while loading; too low and you get OOMKilled during startup, exit 137); an emptyDir with medium: Memory and sizeLimit mounted at /dev/shm; a startupProbe on GET /health with periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold high enough to cover download plus load (60 = 10 minutes) so the liveness probe never kills a still-loading engine; readinessProbe and livenessProbe on /health with timeoutSeconds 5; terminationGracePeriodSeconds at least as long as your longest generation so in-flight streams finish. Set strategy to Recreate or rollingUpdate with maxSurge 0 when you own exactly one GPU, because the default 25% surge schedules a second pod that can never get a GPU and the rollout hangs forever. Know that zero-downtime rollouts cost an N+1 GPU.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Deployment - Using Kubernetes

subtopics.name: Exposing it: Service, Ingress or Gateway, API key, and streaming timeouts
subtopics.learn: Front the pod with a ClusterIP Service and your Ingress or HTTPRoute from Topics 7 and 8, then exercise the OpenAI-compatible surface: GET /v1/models, POST /v1/chat/completions with stream: true, GET /health, GET /metrics. Streaming responses are long-lived SSE, so raise the proxy read timeout (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: '600') and disable response buffering (proxy-buffering: 'off'); an ALB with the default 60 s idle timeout will cut off any generation longer than a minute with no error in vLLM's logs. Decide where auth lives: --api-key on vLLM is a single shared secret, so put real per-tenant auth on the gateway and keep the vLLM Service unreachable from outside the namespace with a NetworkPolicy. Verify from a laptop with the openai Python client pointed at base_url and from inside the cluster to separate ingress latency from model latency.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Online Serving (OpenAI-compatible server and endpoints)

subtopics.name: Inference-aware routing: why round-robin is the wrong load balancer for LLM replicas
subtopics.learn: A Service spreads requests round-robin and knows nothing about which replica has 40 sequences queued or which one already holds the KV cache for this conversation's prefix. Understand what the Gateway API Inference Extension adds: an InferencePool pointing at the vLLM pods, an endpoint picker (Envoy ext_proc) that reads each replica's queue depth and kv_cache_usage from /metrics and routes to the least-loaded or prefix-affine one, and per-model criticality. Know when it matters (two or more replicas, mixed long and short prompts) and what the cheap substitute is with plain ingress (consistent-hash on a session header for prefix locality, accepting hot spots). Be able to explain to a customer's platform team why their existing LB health check on /health does not protect them from one saturated replica.

resource.label: Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension: Introduction

subtopics.name: Metrics: vLLM /metrics, DCGM exporter, and the six panels that predict an outage
subtopics.learn: Scrape vLLM's Prometheus endpoint (PodMonitor on port 8000, path /metrics) and know the names: vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting (queue; the earliest saturation signal), vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:num_preemptions_total (any growth means KV cache is too small for the load), vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds (or time_per_output_token_seconds), vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds, vllm:prompt_tokens_total and vllm:generation_tokens_total for cost accounting. From the GPU Operator's DCGM exporter use DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP, DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE and DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS. Understand why GPU_UTIL at 100% does not mean saturated (it means a kernel was resident, not that SMs were busy) and why waiting-queue depth plus TTFT p95 is the pair you alert on.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Design - Metrics

subtopics.name: Capacity math: weights plus KV cache decides how many concurrent users fit
subtopics.learn: Do the arithmetic from config.json, not from vibes. Weights = params x bytes per param (Llama-3.1-8B bf16 = 16 GB). KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x num_hidden_layers x num_key_value_heads x head_dim x bytes per element; for Llama-3.1-8B that is 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes, i.e. 128 KiB per token thanks to GQA. KV budget = GPU memory x gpu-memory-utilization minus weights minus roughly 1-2 GB of activations and CUDA graphs. On a 24 GB A10G that leaves about 4-5 GB, roughly 35k tokens, so 50 users each holding a 2k-token conversation (100k tokens, 12.8 GB) do not fit at bf16; on a 48 GB L40S they do with headroom. Confirm against the two lines vLLM logs at startup, 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' and 'Maximum concurrency for X tokens per request: Y', and against kv_cache_usage_perc under load. Levers: lower --max-model-len, --kv-cache-dtype fp8, weight quantization (deferred to Topic 56), or a bigger card. Distinguish 50 named users from 50 in-flight sequences: with think time, 50 users is often 10-20 concurrent requests.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Conserving Memory

subtopics.name: Throughput vs latency knobs: max-num-seqs, max-num-batched-tokens, chunked prefill, preemption
subtopics.learn: Continuous batching means every decode step advances all running sequences by one token; more sequences in the batch raise aggregate tokens per second and raise per-user inter-token latency, while TTFT is governed by prefill work and queue time. Chunked prefill (default in V1) slices long prompts and mixes them with decode steps; --max-num-batched-tokens is the budget per step, where a smaller value protects ITL and a larger one improves TTFT and throughput. When KV blocks run out the scheduler preempts a sequence and recomputes it later, which shows up as num_preemptions_total climbing and e2e latency p99 spiking; the fix is more KV (memory, shorter max-model-len) or a lower --max-num-seqs, never a bigger batch. Write down the SLO you will size against before benchmarking: for a chat UI, TTFT p95 under 1 s and ITL p95 under 50 ms (about 20 tokens per second per user) is a defensible default.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Optimization and Tuning

subtopics.name: Benchmark it properly: vllm bench serve, closed vs open loop, reading the table
subtopics.learn: Run the load generator from a pod inside the cluster so ingress is out of the picture: vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://vllm:8000 --model <served-name> --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts 500 --max-concurrency N (closed loop, N users hammering) and separately --request-rate R (open loop, Poisson arrivals). Sweep N over 1, 8, 16, 32, 50, 64 and record request throughput, output token throughput, and mean, median and p99 TTFT, TPOT and ITL; the knee where p99 TTFT jumps while throughput flattens is your capacity. Warm up first (CUDA graphs, prefix cache), run each point twice, and use --save-result so the JSON lands in the repo. Also try --dataset-name sharegpt for realistic length distributions and note how much the answer changes versus fixed random lengths.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Benchmark CLI (vllm bench serve)

subtopics.name: Sharing and splitting GPUs: time-slicing vs MIG vs tensor parallel
