subtopics.learn: Time-slicing (device plugin ConfigMap with sharing.timeSlicing.resources[].replicas: N) makes one card advertise N nvidia.com/gpu units with no memory isolation: one tenant's CUDA OOM kills the others, so it is for dev clusters, never for a customer's shared production card. MIG on A100 and H100 (nvidia-smi mig -cgi, operator mig.strategy single or mixed, profiles like 1g.10gb through 7g.80gb) gives hard memory and compute partitions and shows up as nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb resources; A10G, L4 and L40S do not support MIG. Tensor parallel (--tensor-parallel-size 2) goes the other way and splits one model across GPUs in the same pod (must divide the attention head count; NVLink versus PCIe changes the result a lot), and multi-node uses pipeline parallel with LeaderWorkerSet. For 50 users on one 8B model the answer is one GPU, one model, no sharing; know how to say that.

resource.label: NVIDIA GPU Operator: Time-Slicing GPUs in Kubernetes

subtopics.name: Autoscaling GPU replicas: HPA cannot see the queue, KEDA plus Prometheus can
subtopics.learn: CPU-based HPA is useless here because a saturated vLLM pod shows low CPU. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting or vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc via a KEDA ScaledObject with a prometheus trigger (serverAddress, query such as sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{app='vllm'}), threshold like '5'), or via HPA plus prometheus-adapter. Set stabilization and cooldown windows in minutes, not seconds, because a scale-up takes 4-8 minutes (node, image, weights) and a flapping scaler will thrash. Keep minReplicaCount at 1 unless the customer accepts multi-minute cold starts, add a PodDisruptionBudget so node upgrades do not take the only replica, and pre-pull the image with a DaemonSet on GPU nodes. Understand that scaling out also multiplies cost linearly with no discount, so present it next to the capacity plan.

resource.label: KEDA docs: Prometheus scaler

subtopics.name: Debugging the GPU node: nvidia-smi, Xid errors, stuck Pending pods, CUDA OOM, NCCL
subtopics.learn: Build the triage sequence you can run in five minutes. Pod Pending: describe it, then check device plugin and validator pods on the target node and node Allocatable. CrashLoopBackOff with torch.OutOfMemoryError or 'No available memory for the cache blocks': lower --gpu-memory-utilization or --max-model-len, or check nvidia-smi for a zombie process from a previous pod still holding memory. 'NCCL error' or hangs with tensor parallel: /dev/shm too small or IPC missing, set NCCL_DEBUG=INFO. Slow or wrong: VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG and confirm the attention backend and dtype in the startup log. Hardware: kubectl exec nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,ECC and dmesg | grep -i xid on the node; Xid 79 (fallen off the bus) and Xid 48 (double-bit ECC) mean cordon, drain and replace the node, not restart the pod; Xid 31 and 43 usually point at the application. Know what a 'Failed to initialize NVML' after a driver upgrade means for every pod on the node.

resource.label: vLLM docs: Troubleshooting

subtopics.name: Cost and the capacity plan: from USD per GPU-hour to USD per million tokens
subtopics.learn: Turn the benchmark into the two numbers a customer buys on. Take output tokens per second at the highest concurrency that still meets the SLO, then USD per 1M output tokens = hourly GPU price / (tok/s x 3600 / 1e6); an L40S at about USD 1.8-2.0 per hour producing 1,500 tok/s is roughly USD 0.35 per million tokens at full utilization, and 5x that at 20% utilization, which is the honest number for a 50-user internal tool. Put the plan in one table: model and dtype, GPU type, replicas (N+1 if zero-downtime deploys are required), max in-flight sequences, expected named users given think time, SLO targets, KV headroom, monthly cost at expected and at peak utilization, and the same workload priced on a hosted API for comparison. State the quota, lead time and spot-interruption assumptions explicitly, because those, not tok/s, are what usually slips the pilot.

resource.label: AWS EC2 instance types (accelerated computing: G5, G6, G6e, P4, P5 specs)

outcomes: You can take a fresh Ubuntu GPU VM with nothing but the driver installed and, in under 20 minutes, have containerd running GPU containers via nvidia-ctk and a single-node cluster reporting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in Allocatable.

You can write a vLLM Deployment, Service and Ingress from memory with correct GPU limit, memory request, /dev/shm emptyDir, startup/readiness/liveness probes and Recreate strategy, and explain each field to a customer's platform engineer without looking anything up.

You can compute, from a model's config.json and a GPU's memory, the KV cache budget and maximum concurrent 2k-token conversations within 15% of what vLLM prints at startup, and show your working on a whiteboard in under five minutes.
You can run a vllm bench serve concurrency sweep, produce a table of throughput and p50/p99 TTFT and ITL per concurrency level, identify the knee, and state the supported concurrency at a given SLO.

You can triage a GPU pod stuck Pending or CrashLooping to one of: driver/toolkit mismatch, device plugin absent, taint, held GPU, CUDA OOM, shm/NCCL, or hardware Xid, using kubectl describe, nvidia-smi and dmesg, in under ten minutes.
You can configure a Prometheus scrape of vLLM and DCGM metrics and name the two signals you alert on for impending saturation, with the PromQL for each.
You can explain and demonstrate why a streaming completion longer than 60 seconds dies behind a default ALB or nginx ingress, and fix it with the exact annotation or attribute.
You can present a one-page capacity and cost plan for 50 users that a CFO and a platform lead both accept, including USD per million tokens at expected utilization and the hosted-API comparison.
failureModes: The customer's platform team upgrades the node kernel during a patch window; the DKMS driver no longer loads, nvidia-smi says 'NVML: Driver/library version mismatch', the device plugin reports 0 GPUs, and the vLLM pod sits Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' until someone reboots and rebuilds the module.

A rolling update of the vLLM Deployment with default maxSurge schedules a second pod on a cluster with one GPU; the new pod is Pending forever, the old one keeps serving the previous model, and the release 'succeeded' in ArgoCD because the Deployment never reported failure.

--max-model-len was left at the model's 131k default on a 24 GB card; vLLM reserved almost nothing for KV cache, num_preemptions_total climbed under 12 concurrent users, and p99 latency went from 2 s to 40 s while GPU utilization looked fine on the dashboard.

Long RAG answers were truncated mid-stream at exactly 60 seconds in production but not in staging; the difference was an AWS ALB with the default idle timeout in front of production, and vLLM logged nothing because the client, not the server, was disconnected.

The liveness probe used the same 30-second initial delay as a web service; on a cold node the 16 GB weight load took four minutes, kubelet killed the container at 30 seconds every time, and the pod CrashLooped for an hour before anyone read the events.

Time-slicing was enabled to 'share' one A10G between the dev and staging vLLM instances; a staging load test drove CUDA OOM, which also killed the dev replica mid-demo, and nobody could explain to the customer why two isolated namespaces went down together.

The pilot was sized at 50 users against a benchmark run with 128-token prompts and 128-token outputs; real prompts averaged 3k tokens of pasted documents, TTFT p95 was 9 seconds on day one, and the fix required a bigger GPU that had a two-week quota lead time.
interviewQuestions: A customer hands you an EKS cluster with one g6e.xlarge node and asks for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for Llama-3.1-8B for 50 internal users by Friday. Walk me through everything from node to first token: what has to be installed, every field in the manifest you would write, how you would expose it, and how you would know it is actually ready for 50 people.

Show me how you would compute the maximum number of concurrent 2,000-token conversations a 48 GB L40S can hold for an 8B GQA model at bf16, then tell me what changes if the customer insists on 32k context. Which two flags would you touch first and what does each cost?

A vLLM pod is stuck Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' on a node where nvidia-smi on the host shows the card. Give me your ordered diagnostic sequence, the commands, and the three most likely root causes with how you would tell them apart.

GPU utilization is 95% on the DCGM dashboard, but users complain the model is slow and p99 TTFT is 8 seconds. Explain why the utilization number is misleading, which vLLM metrics you would look at instead, and what the likely configuration fix is.

Design the autoscaling for this service. Why is CPU-based HPA wrong, what metric would you scale on, what threshold and cooldown, and how do you handle a 6-minute scale-up latency when a marketing team launches an internal announcement that triples traffic at 9 am?

The security team asks you to run three teams' models on one shared A100 with strong isolation, and the platform team suggests time-slicing. Compare time-slicing, MIG and separate nodes on isolation, utilization and operational risk, and tell me what you would recommend and how you would demonstrate the isolation property.

Streaming responses die at exactly one minute in production only. Debug it out loud: where in the path could a 60-second limit live, how do you prove which hop it is without customer downtime, and what is the fix at each candidate layer?
11.proofOfWork: A public repository named vllm-on-k8s containing a Kustomize or Helm deployment of vLLM (Deployment with GPU limit, shm emptyDir, staged probes, Recreate strategy, Secret-fed HF_TOKEN, PVC weight cache with a fill Job, Service, Ingress with streaming timeouts, PodMonitor, KEDA ScaledObject) that a reviewer can apply to any cluster with an NVIDIA GPU Operator; a capacity.py script that reads a Hugging Face config.json plus GPU memory, dtype, max-model-len and gpu-memory-utilization and prints KV bytes per token, KV budget, max in-flight sequences at a given conversation length, and USD per million output tokens from a supplied hourly price, with a test asserting its prediction is within 15% of the 'GPU KV cache size' line captured from a real vLLM startup log checked into the repo; a bench/ directory with the raw --save-result JSON from a vllm bench serve sweep at concurrency 1, 8, 16, 32, 50 and 64 on one GPU type, a script that renders them into a markdown table and a throughput-versus-p99-TTFT plot with the knee marked; and a runbook.md with five incident drills (Pending after kernel upgrade, CUDA OOM, stuck rollout, 60-second stream cutoff, Xid 79) each with the exact commands and the expected output that confirms the diagnosis. The plan deliverable's benchmark table and capacity plan link to this repo as their evidence.

13.topic: Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI
13.why: An FDE stands up the customer's environment on week one and hands it to their two-person platform team on week twelve; if the VPC, IAM roles and cluster were built by clicking, nobody can reproduce it in the second region, nobody can audit who changed the security group, and the hand-over is a screenshot deck. Terraform with remote state and plan-on-PR is how you turn 'trust me, it is configured' into a reviewable diff the customer's security team can sign, and how you avoid the two career-ending moments: applying dev code to their production account, and a plan that quietly says 'forces replacement' on the database. Senior FDE loops at Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks ask about state corruption, drift and blast radius because those are the incidents that actually happen at customer sites.
prerequisites: AWS vocabulary at console level: VPC, subnet, route table, internet and NAT gateway, security group, EC2, IAM role; the full depth arrives in 'AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda' (topic 13), which you should run in parallel with this one

IAM assume-role mechanics: what a trust policy is, what `aws sts get-caller-identity` and `aws sts assume-role` return, and why a role with an OIDC trust beats an access key; deepened in 'IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys' (topic 15)

Shell and Git from topics 0 and 4: `jq` over JSON, exit codes in `if` and `set -e`, environment variable precedence, Git tags versus branches, protected branches and required status checks, because plan-on-PR is a Git workflow first
A sandbox AWS account with a billing alarm at 20 USD, AWS CLI v2 configured with an SSO profile or named profile, and the account ID memorised so you recognise it in `allowed_account_ids` and ARNs
Terraform 1.10 or newer installed through tfenv or mise (so `use_lockfile`, ephemeral values, import and removed blocks all exist), plus tflint, trivy, conftest and jq on PATH
Comfort reading a directed acyclic graph and a JSON document a few thousand lines long; state files and plan JSON are both

subtopics.name: init, providers, the dependency lock file, and the graph plan builds
subtopics.learn: `terraform init` resolves `required_providers` constraints (`~> 5.0` means >= 5.0, < 6.0), downloads provider binaries into `.terraform/providers/`, and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl` with `h1:` and `zh:` hashes per platform; commit the lock file, and run `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` so a lock generated on a Mac does not fail with a checksum error in Linux CI. Set `required_version` in a `terraform {}` block so a colleague on 1.5 cannot apply a config using 1.10 features. Plan builds a DAG from references (`aws_subnet.a.vpc_id` implies an edge) and explicit `depends_on`; render it with `terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > g.svg` and know the default `-parallelism=10` walks that graph concurrently. Understand 'known after apply': any attribute the provider only returns after creation is unknown at plan, and anything computed from it becomes unknown too.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Dependency Lock File

subtopics.name: Reading a plan like a reviewer: symbols, forces replacement, saved plans, exit codes
subtopics.learn: Know the six change markers cold: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create, `+/-` create then destroy (create_before_destroy), `<=` read data source during apply. Every `-/+` line has a `# forces replacement` comment on the attribute responsible; that comment is the single most important line in any review. Use `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform show -json tfplan | jq '[.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete"))] | length'` to fail CI on any destroy; a saved plan is a binary bound to the exact config, state serial and provider versions, and it contains sensitive values in plaintext. `-detailed-exitcode` returns 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes, which is what drift jobs key on. `-refresh=false` speeds a plan on a large state; `-target=module.network` is an emergency tool that leaves the rest of the graph unplanned and should never appear in CI; `-replace=aws_instance.bastion` is the modern `taint`.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: plan command

subtopics.name: State internals: what is in terraform.tfstate and why it exists
subtopics.learn: Open a real state file: `version: 4`, `terraform_version`, `serial` (monotonic counter, bumped on every write), `lineage` (UUID assigned at creation; a mismatch means two unrelated states), and `resources[]` each with `mode` (managed or data), `type`, `name`, `module`, `provider`, and `instances[]` carrying `schema_version`, `index_key`, `attributes`, `dependencies` and `sensitive_attributes`. State is the map from Terraform address to real-world ID plus a cache of last-known attributes; without it Terraform cannot tell 'create' from 'update'. Everything a provider returns lands in `attributes` in plaintext, including `random_password.result` and RDS master passwords. Practise `terraform state pull > backup.json` before any surgery and `terraform state push -force` only for a deliberate lineage or serial override. Hand-editing state is a last resort and requires bumping `serial`.

resource.label: Terraform docs: State purpose and structure

subtopics.name: S3 remote backend: locking, encryption, partial config and the bootstrap problem
subtopics.learn: Write `backend "s3" { bucket, key = "network/prod.tfstate", region, encrypt = true, kms_key_id, use_lockfile = true }` (1.10+ native S3 conditional-write locking creating `key.tflock`) or the older `dynamodb_table` with a `LockID` string hash key; `assume_role { role_arn }` inside the backend lets state live in a separate audit account. Backend blocks cannot reference variables, so use partial configuration: `terraform init -backend-config=envs/prod.s3.tfbackend`, and know `-migrate-state` (copy local to remote) versus `-reconfigure` (forget the old backend). The chicken-and-egg: the bucket must exist before the first init, so keep a tiny `bootstrap/` root with local state that creates the bucket with versioning (your only undo for a bad push), Block Public Access, SSE-KMS and a bucket policy denying `aws:SecureTransport = false`, then either import it or accept that one root is local. IAM for the CI role: `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket, `s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject` on the state prefix, `kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey` on the key, and for DynamoDB `GetItem/PutItem/DeleteItem` on the lock table. 'Error acquiring the state lock' means a run is active or died; `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only after confirming no apply is in flight.

resource.label: Terraform docs: S3 backend

subtopics.name: State surgery: state mv/rm/list/show, import blocks, moved and removed blocks
subtopics.learn: `terraform state list`, `terraform state show aws_vpc.main`, `terraform state mv 'module.old.aws_subnet.x[0]' 'module.net.aws_subnet.x["a"]'` (single-quote addresses so the shell leaves brackets alone), and `terraform state rm` to stop managing something without destroying it. Prefer declarative equivalents that go through code review: `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = module.compute.aws_instance.web }` for zero-downtime refactors across module boundaries, `removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs  lifecycle { destroy = false } }` (1.7+), and `import { to = aws_vpc.main  id = "vpc-0abc123" }` (1.5+) combined with `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` to write the HCL for you. Import IDs are provider-specific and documented in the Import section of every resource page: an `aws_security_group_rule` ID is a composite string, an `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` is `role-name/policy-arn`. The exit criterion for adoption is a plan that says 'No changes' with no `-target` and no `ignore_changes` hiding real differences.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: state subcommands

subtopics.name: Module design: structure, inputs as an API, pinned sources, no provider blocks inside
subtopics.learn: Standard layout: `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `versions.tf`, `README.md`, `examples/complete/`. Sources: registry `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"  version = "~> 5.0"`, Git `source = "git::https://github.com/org/modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.4.0"` pinned to a tag or SHA and never a branch, local `./modules/x` for the same repo. A child module declares `required_providers` but never a `provider` block; the root passes providers with `providers = { aws = aws.us_west_2 }` and the child lists `configuration_aliases` when it needs more than one. Outputs are the module's contract: export IDs, ARNs and CIDRs, not whole resource objects, because whole objects leak schema changes to every consumer. Keep modules cohesive (one network, one cluster), refuse 80-variable 'wrapper' modules, and add `validation {}` blocks and `optional()` attributes with defaults so callers get an error at plan rather than an AWS API error at apply.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Creating Modules

subtopics.name: for_each versus count, dynamic blocks, and the index-shift trap
subtopics.learn: `count` produces list-indexed instances (`aws_subnet.private[0]`), so removing or reordering an element shifts every later index and the plan destroys and recreates them; `for_each` over a `map` or `set(string)` yields stable keys (`aws_subnet.private["eu-west-1a"]`). Build maps with `for_each = { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }` and reference `each.key` and `each.value`. Keys must be known at plan time: `toset(aws_subnet.x[*].id)` fails with 'keys derived from resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply', so key on static names, not IDs. Convert `count` to `for_each` with one `moved` block per instance (`from = aws_subnet.private[0]  to = aws_subnet.private["a"]`) or the plan will be all destroys. `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules  content { from_port = ingress.value.port ... } }` generates nested blocks; keep `try()`, `lookup()`, `one()` and `coalesce()` in reach for optional structure.

resource.label: Terraform docs: for_each meta-argument

subtopics.name: lifecycle meta-arguments and controlling replacement
subtopics.learn: `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` flips `-/+` to `+/-` so a replacement never leaves a gap, but it propagates to dependents and collides with fixed `name` values, so pair it with `name_prefix`. `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the resource error out, including a full `terraform destroy`, and does nothing if the resource block itself is deleted from config. `ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"], desired_capacity]` is the fix for attributes owned by another controller (cluster autoscaler, a Lambda deploy pipeline, a security scanner adding tags). `replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.revision]` recreates a resource when something unrelated changes; `terraform_data` is the built-in replacement for `null_resource`. `precondition` and `postcondition` blocks turn assumptions ('the AMI is x86_64', 'the subnet has an IPv4 CIDR') into plan-time errors with a readable message.

resource.label: Terraform docs: lifecycle meta-argument

subtopics.name: Variables, locals, outputs: precedence, type constraints, sensitive and ephemeral
subtopics.learn: Assignment precedence, lowest to highest: `TF_VAR_name` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars` in lexical order, then `-var` and `-var-file` in command-line order. Write real types: `object({ cidr = string, azs = optional(list(string), []), nat = optional(bool, true) })` so callers get a type error rather than a silent default, and `validation { condition = can(cidrnetmask(var.cidr))  error_message = "cidr must be IPv4 CIDR" }`. `sensitive = true` redacts plan output and forces `sensitive = true` on any output that carries it, but the value is still in state; `ephemeral = true` (1.10+) is the flag that keeps a value out of state and plan files entirely. `terraform output -raw kubeconfig > ~/.kube/config` and `terraform output -json` are the CI-facing forms. Use `locals` for `merge(var.tags, { ManagedBy = "terraform", Env = var.env })` and provider `default_tags` so every resource is tagged without touching each block.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Input Variables

subtopics.name: Environment strategy: CLI workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt
subtopics.learn: CLI workspaces (`terraform workspace new prod`, `terraform.workspace` in expressions) store state under `env:/prod/<key>` in the same bucket with the same backend credentials and the same provider config; that means one IAM role can touch every environment and a forgotten `workspace select` applies dev values to prod. Directory-per-environment (`envs/dev`, `envs/prod`, each with its own `.s3.tfbackend`, its own `assume_role` target and `allowed_account_ids`) gives real credential and state separation at the cost of duplicated root boilerplate; Terragrunt removes that duplication with `generate` blocks and `run-all`. The FDE default for a customer with separate accounts: one state per (account, region, layer), layers split into network, data and compute so plan time stays under a few minutes and a broken compute plan cannot lock the network state; pass IDs between layers with `terraform_remote_state` or SSM parameters, never by copy-paste.

resource.label: Terraform CLI: Workspaces

subtopics.name: Drift: refresh-only, reconciling click-ops, and the things refresh cannot see
subtopics.learn: Drift is real infrastructure differing from state. `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows exactly what changed outside Terraform without proposing config changes; `terraform apply -refresh-only` accepts reality into state. A normal plan refreshes first and then diffs config against the refreshed state, so a manual security group rule shows up as a `~` update reverting it. Schedule `plan -detailed-exitcode -lock-timeout=2m` nightly; exit 2 means drift, page or open an issue. Triage each diff into one of three actions: revert (someone opened 0.0.0.0/0 on 22), adopt (import the resource they created in the console), or ignore (`ignore_changes` for an attribute owned by an autoscaler or a deploy pipeline). Refresh only inspects addresses already in state, so resources created outside Terraform are invisible to it; that gap needs AWS Config rules or a tag-based sweep (`aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources` filtered on missing `ManagedBy`). A resource deleted manually shows as `+ create`; a resource removed from state but not AWS becomes an orphan billing you forever.

resource.label: Terraform tutorial: Manage resource drift

subtopics.name: Plan on PR, apply on merge: the GitHub Actions pipeline
subtopics.learn: On `pull_request`: `terraform fmt -check -recursive`, `init -input=false -backend-config=...`, `validate`, tflint, trivy config, then `plan -out=tfplan -no-color -input=false -lock-timeout=5m` with `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1` and `TF_INPUT=0`; post the plan as a PR comment (GitHub truncates at 65,536 characters, so summarise counts and attach the full plan as an artifact) and upload `tfplan` with a short retention because it contains secrets. On `push` to `main`: either apply the exact saved plan from the merged PR or re-plan and `apply -auto-approve`, inside `concurrency: { group: terraform-prod, cancel-in-progress: false }` so applies serialise, and inside a GitHub Environment with required reviewers for prod. Use `hashicorp/setup-terraform` with `terraform_wrapper: false` when you need real exit codes. The plan job executes provider code and data sources, so it must never receive apply credentials and must never run for forks with secrets (`pull_request_target` is the classic mistake). Separate plan and apply roles; the plan role needs read on AWS plus write on the state lock only.

resource.label: Terraform tutorial: Running Terraform in automation

subtopics.name: OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS: no long-lived keys
subtopics.learn: Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the job and call `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume` and `aws-region`; the action exchanges GitHub's OIDC token for STS credentials via `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`. In AWS, create the `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` identity provider once, then a role whose trust policy checks `aud` = `sts.amazonaws.com` and `sub` with `StringLike` on `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` for the apply role and `repo:org/repo:pull_request` for the plan role; a wildcard `repo:org/*` lets any repo in the org assume your prod role. Set `role-duration-seconds` to the minimum that covers your longest apply. Verify with `aws sts get-caller-identity` as the first step of every job so the account ID is in the log. This is the pattern you will be asked to reproduce at every customer that still has `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in repository secrets.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services

subtopics.name: Static checks and policy: tflint, trivy/checkov, conftest on plan JSON, terraform test
subtopics.learn: `terraform validate` is schema-only and never calls AWS, so it will pass an invalid instance type; tflint with the AWS ruleset (`.tflint.hcl` with `plugin "aws" { enabled = true  version = "..."  source = "github.com/terraform-linters/tflint-ruleset-aws" }`) catches that plus deprecated syntax and unused declarations. `trivy config .` or `checkov -d .` flag misconfiguration classes: unencrypted S3, security groups open to the world on 22 or 3389, IAM wildcards. Policy on the plan is stronger than policy on the source because it sees resolved values: `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json` then `conftest test plan.json -p policy/` with Rego rules that deny any `resource_changes[_]` where `change.actions` contains `delete` for `aws_db_instance` or where `tags.Owner` is missing. `terraform test` (1.6+) runs `.tftest.hcl` files with `run` blocks, `command = plan` and `assert` conditions so module contracts are tested without creating resources. Order in CI: fmt, validate, tflint, scanner, plan, policy, comment.

resource.label: tflint official repository

subtopics.name: Provider configuration for multi-account, multi-region: aliases, assume_role, allowed_account_ids
subtopics.learn: `provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-1"  assume_role { role_arn = var.deploy_role_arn  session_name = "terraform"  external_id = var.external_id }  default_tags { tags = local.tags }  allowed_account_ids = [var.account_id] }`. `allowed_account_ids` makes the provider refuse to run if `AWS_PROFILE` points at the wrong account, and it is the cheapest guard you will ever add against applying a sandbox config to a customer's production. A second `provider "aws" { alias = "dr"  region = "us-west-2" }` is used with `provider = aws.dr` on a resource or `providers = { aws = aws.dr }` on a module. Never put credentials in HCL; understand the credential chain the provider walks (env vars, shared config profile with SSO, ECS or EC2 instance metadata, IRSA web identity) so you can explain which identity a given plan ran as. `data "aws_caller_identity" "current"` and `data "aws_region" "current"` belong in every root so ARNs are never hard-coded.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Provider Configuration

subtopics.name: Debugging and recovery: TF_LOG, partial applies, errored.tfstate, lock and hash errors
subtopics.learn: `TF_LOG=DEBUG TF_LOG_PATH=./tf.log terraform apply` (levels TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` split them) shows the exact AWS API call and response behind an opaque error. A failed apply is normal and partial: every resource that completed is already in state, so the recovery is to read the error, fix, and plan again, never to delete state. If Terraform cannot write state to the backend after applying, it drops `errored.tfstate` in the working directory and tells you; recover with `terraform state push errored.tfstate` before anyone else runs. 'Provider produced inconsistent final plan' is almost always a provider bug or an unknown value that changed between plan and apply; 'Cycle:' errors come from `depends_on` or mutual references and `terraform graph` shows the loop. Set resource `timeouts { create = "30m" }` for EKS and RDS, use `-parallelism=5` when the AWS API throttles, and fix 'checksum mismatch' in the lock file with `providers lock -platform=...` rather than deleting `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Debugging Terraform

subtopics.name: Building the deliverable: VPC, subnets, NAT and EC2 with the community VPC module, ready for EKS
subtopics.learn: Consume `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` with `cidr`, `azs = slice(data.aws_availability_zones.available.names, 0, 3)`, `private_subnets` and `public_subnets` computed with `cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, i)`, `enable_nat_gateway = true`, `single_nat_gateway = true` for dev (one gateway, roughly 32 USD a month plus data) versus `one_nat_gateway_per_az = true` for prod HA, and `enable_dns_hostnames = true`. Tag subnets now so the EKS topic (16) works later: `public_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/elb" = 1 }` and `private_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb" = 1 }`. Add VPC endpoints for S3 (gateway) and ECR (interface) so image pulls do not pay NAT egress. Launch EC2 from `data "aws_ami"` filtered on `al2023-ami-*` with `most_recent = true` and `owners = ["amazon"]`, an instance profile with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` so there is no SSH key and no port 22, and a security group with no inbound rules. Output `vpc_id`, `private_subnet_ids`, `public_subnet_ids`. Finish every session with `terraform destroy` or a nightly destroy job in the sandbox.

resource.label: terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc official repository

subtopics.name: Secrets in state and what never to put in Terraform
subtopics.learn: State stores every returned attribute in plaintext: `random_password.db.result`, `aws_db_instance.password`, `aws_iam_access_key.secret`, `tls_private_key.private_key_pem`. Mitigate in layers: SSE-KMS on the bucket with a key policy that only the CI roles and a break-glass group can decrypt, bucket policy scoped to those principals, S3 access logging on. Remove the secret from state where the provider allows it: `manage_master_user_password = true` on `aws_db_instance` puts the password in Secrets Manager and leaves only an ARN in state; write-only arguments (1.11+, suffixed `_wo`) and ephemeral resources (1.10+) let you pass a secret at apply without persisting it. Remember `sensitive = true` hides values from CLI output only; `terraform show -json` and the plan artifact reveal them, so lock down CI logs and artifact retention. Do not template kubeconfigs or tokens into local files with `local_file`, and do not manage things that change hourly (feature flags, Lambda code) in the same state as the network.

resource.label: Terraform docs: Sensitive Data in State

outcomes: You can bootstrap an S3 remote backend with versioning, SSE-KMS and locking (use_lockfile or DynamoDB), migrate an existing local state into it with `init -migrate-state`, and name every IAM permission the CI role needs and why.

You can read any plan and, before approving, list which resources will be replaced and which attribute forces it, then rewrite the change so the plan is non-destructive using moved blocks, state mv, ignore_changes, or create_before_destroy as appropriate.

You can adopt an existing click-ops VPC, its subnets and security groups into a module using import blocks and -generate-config-out, and end with `terraform plan` reporting 'No changes' without -target or hidden ignore_changes.

You can write a module with typed object inputs using optional() defaults and validation blocks, no provider block inside, a pinned Git or registry source, and consume it from two environment roots with separate backends, assume_role targets and allowed_account_ids.

You can build a GitHub Actions pipeline that plans on PR under a read-only OIDC role, posts the plan and uploads the artifact, and applies on merge under a separate role inside a concurrency group and a protected environment, with zero AWS access keys anywhere.
You can run a drift review: execute plan -refresh-only, classify every diff as revert, adopt or ignore with a one-line justification, and explain why resources created outside Terraform never appear.

You can recover from a stale lock (force-unlock with a verified lock ID), an errored.tfstate after a backend write failure, and a lock-file checksum mismatch between macOS and Linux CI, each in under ten minutes.

You can argue for an environment isolation strategy (workspaces, directories, Terragrunt) for a customer with three AWS accounts in terms of blast radius, credential separation and plan time, and state what would make you change it.
failureModes: A subnet list built with count gets a new AZ inserted at position 1; the plan replaces two subnets, the apply destroys the ones the customer's RDS subnet group depends on, RDS refuses the change, and state is left half-applied on a Friday evening.

Two engineers apply from laptops against the same S3 backend configured without locking; the second write overwrites the first's state, and the next plan proposes creating 40 resources that already exist, each failing with AlreadyExists.
A workflow uses pull_request_target so plan runs on forks with the apply role; a contributor's PR adds an `external` data source that curls the OIDC token and STS credentials to their server.

The RDS master password and an IAM user's secret key sit in plaintext in state, the state bucket grants s3:GetObject to an engineering-wide role, and the customer's SOC 2 auditor lists it as a finding against your delivery.

A module source pins `ref=main` instead of a tag; a colleague pushes an unrelated change, and the next prod PR's plan shows a NAT gateway replacement nobody asked for, approved by a reviewer who only read the PR description.
Nobody set ignore_changes on the EKS managed node group scaling_config.desired_size; every apply after the cluster autoscaler scales up resets the node count to 2 and evicts customer workloads.

An engineer with AWS_PROFILE pointing at the customer's production account applies the sandbox root because the code is identical and allowed_account_ids was never set; the plan output scrolled past and the prod NAT gateway is gone.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through exactly what happens between `terraform plan` and `terraform apply`: what the lock protects against, what 'known after apply' means, why a plan can succeed and the apply fail, and what state looks like after a failed apply.

A customer has a hand-built VPC with six subnets, twelve security groups and an ALB and wants it under Terraform with zero downtime. Design the adoption: how you import, how you prove the plan is clean, what you do about resources whose config cannot be made to match, and what the first production PR contains.

Your PR plan shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (forces replacement)` because someone renamed the identifier. The customer cannot take downtime. Give me your options in order of preference and what each does to state.

Design Terraform CI/CD across dev, staging and prod in three AWS accounts. Where do credentials come from, how do you stop a fork PR from exfiltrating them, how do you stop two applies racing on the same state, and where exactly does a human approve?

A nightly drift job started returning exit code 2 every night on an aws_autoscaling_group and nobody changed anything. What is happening, what are three ways to fix it, and which would you choose for a customer whose platform team will own this in six months?

Workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt: pick one for a customer deployment you will hand over, defend it in terms of blast radius and credentials, and tell me what would make you change your mind.

An engineer ran `terraform state push` with a week-old file and now the plan wants to create everything. What do you do in the first fifteen minutes, and what structural change stops it from happening again?
13.proofOfWork: A public repository, tf-aws-foundation, laid out as modules/network and modules/compute plus envs/dev and envs/prod roots, each root with its own .s3.tfbackend, assume_role target and allowed_account_ids, and a bootstrap/ root that creates the versioned SSE-KMS state bucket and OIDC provider. GitHub Actions plan on PR under a read-only role and apply on merge under a separate role behind a protected environment and a concurrency group; conftest policies that deny untagged resources and any delete on aws_db_instance or aws_s3_bucket; tflint and trivy in the same pipeline. A recorded terminal session (asciinema or pasted output in the README) demonstrates three things end to end: (1) a VPC created by hand with the AWS CLI is adopted with import blocks and -generate-config-out until plan says No changes; (2) a count-based subnet set is migrated to for_each with moved blocks and the plan shows zero destroys; (3) a security group rule added in the console is caught by the nightly plan -detailed-exitcode job and reverted by the next apply. A one-page ADR in the repo explains the choice of directory-per-environment over workspaces and the network/data/compute state layering, in language a customer platform lead could sign off on.

14.topic: AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda
14.why: FDEs almost never get a greenfield account: you deploy into a customer's VPC, get handed two private subnet IDs and a security-group naming convention, and are asked where your load balancer goes and why your app needs egress. The customer's network and security teams will review every rule before they sign the production change, and when the pilot cannot reach RDS or the model API at 4pm on go-live day, the FDE who can read a route table and a flow log in minutes keeps the account while the one who files a ticket with the customer's platform team loses a week. This topic is the mechanics behind every 'it works in our account but not in theirs' escalation.
prerequisites: Networking from 'Networking: TCP/IP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, load balancers, firewalls' (topic 2): CIDR arithmetic by hand, the three-way handshake and what a SYN with no SYN-ACK looks like, ephemeral port ranges, TLS termination, L4 versus L7 balancing, stateful versus stateless filtering

Terraform from 'Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI' (topic 12): providers, `for_each`, `cidrsubnet()`, data sources, remote state, and a clean `terraform destroy` habit, since the deliverable is written in it
Linux from topics 1 and 3: systemd units, cloud-init, and reading `ss -tlnp`, `ip route`, `tcpdump -i eth0 port 8080` and `curl -v` on an instance to distinguish a listening app from a blocked path

Enough IAM to attach an instance profile and a Lambda execution role and read a resource-based policy; 'IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys' (topic 15) goes deep afterwards

An AWS account with a budget alarm at 20 USD, AWS CLI v2 configured through IAM Identity Center or short-lived credentials (`aws sts get-caller-identity` works), and a DNS zone you control for ACM validation
Docker basics from topic 5 so you can run the sample app on the instance and know why 172.17.0.0/16 matters when you pick a VPC CIDR

subtopics.name: Regions, AZs, and what is zonal versus regional
subtopics.learn: Know that an AZ name (us-east-1a) is randomised per account while the AZ ID (use1-az1) is stable, so two accounts in one customer agreeing on 'zone a' may be talking about different data centres; run `aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]'` and record the mapping on the diagram. Classify every resource you will create as zonal (subnet, EC2 instance, EBS volume, NAT gateway, ENI, each ALB node) or regional (VPC, route table, security group, NACL, IGW, the ALB as a whole, Lambda function, ACM certificate), because that classification is exactly what tells you which pieces must be duplicated for AZ resilience. A single-AZ event is the failure unit AWS designs for, and anything with one NAT gateway or one subnet has silently opted out of that protection.

resource.label: EC2 User Guide: Regions and Availability Zones

subtopics.name: VPC CIDR planning against a customer's address space
subtopics.learn: Choose a VPC CIDR between /16 and /28 from RFC 1918 space that does not overlap the customer's on-prem ranges, their other VPCs, or the 172.17.0.0/16 Docker default that bites the moment a container talks to an instance; ask for the corporate IP plan before you pick. Every subnet loses five addresses (network, VPC router at +1, Route 53 Resolver at +2, reserved +3, broadcast), so a /28 has 11 usable IPs and an ALB refuses any subnet smaller than /27 or with fewer than 8 free addresses. Be able to add a secondary CIDR with `aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block` when the first fills up, and know the restrictions (no overlap, at most 5 IPv4 blocks by default). Use `cidrsubnet()` arithmetic to carve a /16 into one block per tier per AZ and write the plan down before touching Terraform.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: VPC CIDR blocks

subtopics.name: Subnets and route tables: public, private and isolated are just routes
subtopics.learn: A subnet is public only because its route table has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at an igw; private means 0.0.0.0/0 points at a nat; isolated means only the implicit `local` route for the VPC CIDR exists. Every subnet is associated with exactly one route table and falls back to the main route table if you forget the association, which is how a 'private' subnet becomes public when someone edits main. Routes use longest-prefix match, the local route cannot be deleted, and targets can be igw, nat, eni, pcx (peering), tgw, vgw, a gateway-endpoint prefix list (pl-xxx), or a blackhole once the target is deleted. Draw the route table for every subnet on your diagram and be able to reproduce it from `aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-xxx`.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Route tables

subtopics.name: Internet gateway, public IPs, and one NAT gateway per AZ
subtopics.learn: The IGW performs 1:1 NAT between an ENI's private IP and its public or Elastic IP; the instance never sees its public address, which is why `ip addr` shows only 10.x and why `curl 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/public-ipv4` exists. A public subnet still yields an instance with no public IP unless `map_public_ip_on_launch` is true or you attach an EIP. NAT gateways are zonal: one NAT in AZ-a serving private subnets in AZ-b means an AZ-a outage kills egress for both and you pay cross-AZ data charges on every byte, so the pattern is one NAT per AZ with one private route table per AZ. Know the limits that bite in production: 55,000 simultaneous connections to a single destination IP:port, surfaced as the `ErrorPortAllocation` metric and fixed by attaching secondary EIPs; 5 Gbps baseline scaling to 100 Gbps; and roughly 0.045 USD per hour plus 0.045 USD per GB processed, the line item that shocks customers when a pipeline pulls from S3 through NAT instead of a gateway endpoint. Use an egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 outbound.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: NAT gateways

subtopics.name: Security groups: stateful, ENI-scoped, reference by ID
subtopics.learn: Security groups attach to ENIs, not subnets; they are allow-lists only (no deny), stateful via connection tracking, and default to allow-all egress and deny-all ingress. The single most important habit is referencing other groups instead of CIDRs: the app SG allows tcp/8080 from the ALB's SG ID, the database SG allows tcp/5432 from the app SG ID, so scaling or IP churn never breaks a rule and the diagram reads as a graph of trust. Know the quotas: 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules per group, 5 groups per ENI by default (rules times groups must stay under 1000), and the tracking exception where flows allowed by 0.0.0.0/0 in both directions are untracked and so escape the conntrack table that otherwise shows up as `conntrack_allowance_exceeded` in `ethtool -S eth0`. Read rules with IDs and descriptions via `aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules --filters Name=group-id,Values=sg-xxx`, and in Terraform use `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` resources rather than inline blocks so two groups can reference each other without a dependency cycle.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Security groups

subtopics.name: Network ACLs: stateless, ordered, and the ephemeral-port trap
subtopics.learn: NACLs attach to subnets, are stateless, and evaluate rules from the lowest number upward until one matches, ending in the implicit `*` deny. The default NACL allows everything; a custom NACL denies everything until you add rules, and because there is no connection tracking you must explicitly allow return traffic on ephemeral ports: 1024-65535 for NAT gateways and load balancers, 32768-60999 for modern Linux clients, 49152-65535 for Windows. Know when a NACL is the right tool (blocking a specific abusive CIDR, a compliance requirement for subnet-level deny, a second layer in front of the database tier) and when it is just a source of asymmetric-return bugs. Diagnose a NACL problem from flow logs by the signature ACCEPT inbound then REJECT outbound on the same flow, and remember the 20-rule default quota per NACL.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Network ACLs

subtopics.name: DNS inside the VPC: the +2 resolver, private hosted zones, hybrid resolution
subtopics.learn: Every VPC gets a Route 53 Resolver at CIDR base +2 (also 169.254.169.253) that answers public names, VPC-internal hostnames such as ip-10-0-1-23.ec2.internal, private hosted zones associated with the VPC, and interface-endpoint private DNS. Both `enableDnsSupport` and `enableDnsHostnames` must be true for endpoint private DNS and public hostnames to work, and `enableDnsHostnames` is false by default on API-created VPCs, which is the first thing to check when a customer's new VPC cannot resolve `sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` to a private IP. The resolver accepts 1024 packets per second per ENI, so a chatty service without a local DNS cache hits SERVFAIL under load. For hybrid setups understand inbound and outbound Resolver endpoints plus forwarding rules so `corp.example.com` resolves from inside the VPC and the customer's on-prem resolvers can see your private zone.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: DNS attributes for your VPC

subtopics.name: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface, and why NAT bills drop
subtopics.learn: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, cost nothing, and work by injecting a prefix-list route (pl-xxx to vpce-xxx) into selected route tables so traffic to those services never touches NAT or the IGW; an endpoint policy can restrict which buckets are reachable. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) place an ENI with a private IP into each chosen subnet, are protected by a security group that must allow tcp/443 from your workloads, and with private DNS enabled make the normal service hostname resolve to that ENI so SDKs need no configuration; they cost about 0.01 USD per AZ-hour plus 0.01 USD per GB. Know which endpoints an isolated subnet needs to run a typical FDE workload with no internet at all: ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages for Session Manager, ecr.api, ecr.dkr and the S3 gateway for image pulls, logs for CloudWatch, sts for role assumption, secretsmanager, and bedrock-runtime if the customer insists model calls stay on the AWS backbone.

resource.label: AWS PrivateLink Guide: What is AWS PrivateLink

subtopics.name: Connecting VPCs: peering, Transit Gateway, and reaching the customer's network
subtopics.learn: VPC peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link: CIDRs must not overlap, you add routes on both sides pointing at pcx-xxx, and within a region you can reference the peer's security group ID in your rules; DNS resolution across the peer is a separate flag on each side. Transit Gateway is a regional hub where each VPC is an attachment with its own TGW route table, so a customer with 40 VPCs and a Direct Connect gateway gives you one attachment and a CIDR allocation rather than 40 peerings. Understand enough about Site-to-Site VPN (two tunnels, BGP or static routes) and Direct Connect to hold a conversation with the customer's network team about how on-prem clients will reach your internal ALB, and know that whichever they choose, the return route from your subnet back to their CIDR still has to exist in your route table.

resource.label: VPC Peering Guide: What is VPC peering

subtopics.name: ALB architecture: nodes per AZ, subnets, addressing, cross-zone
subtopics.learn: An ALB is a regional resource that materialises as one or more nodes (ENIs) in each subnet you enable; you must give it at least two subnets in different AZs, each /27 or larger with 8 free IPs, and the node IPs change as it scales, so clients and firewalls must use the DNS name, never a resolved address. Choose internet-facing (nodes get public IPs, subnets need an IGW route) or internal (private IPs only, the right choice when the customer fronts it with their own edge or VPN). Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB, so a node in AZ-a will send requests to healthy targets in AZ-b; know the connection idle timeout (60 s default, 1-4000 s) and the client keepalive setting, and that the ALB has its own security group which should be the only source allowed to reach the target SG. Set `enable_deletion_protection` in production and understand that the ALB is billed per hour plus LCU-hours across new connections, active connections, processed bytes and rule evaluations.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: What is an Application Load Balancer

subtopics.name: Listeners, rules and TLS termination
subtopics.learn: A listener is protocol plus port; a production ALB has an HTTP:80 listener whose only default action is `redirect` to HTTPS with status 301, and an HTTPS:443 listener carrying an ACM certificate, a security policy (`ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06` unless the customer's compliance team says otherwise) and additional certificates served via SNI. Rules are evaluated by priority (1 to 50000, lowest first, default rule last) and match on host-header, path-pattern, http-header, http-request-method, query-string or source-ip, then take an action: forward (optionally to several target groups with weights for canaries), redirect, fixed-response, or authenticate-oidc and authenticate-cognito to push login to the edge before traffic reaches your app. TLS terminates at the ALB, so the target sees plain HTTP plus `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Port`. ACM public certificates are free but must be issued in the ALB's region and validated by a DNS record in the customer's zone, which is a ticket you open on day one.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Create an HTTPS listener

subtopics.name: Target groups, health checks and traffic shaping
subtopics.learn: Target groups have a target type (instance, ip, lambda, or alb) that cannot change after creation; instance targets register by ID and receive the client IP in X-Forwarded-For, while ip targets are how you point at ECS tasks, on-prem servers over Direct Connect, or a peered VPC. Health checks default to HTTP GET on `/` every 30 s with a 5 s timeout, 5 healthy and 2 unhealthy threshold, matcher 200; set the path to a real readiness endpoint, keep the interval short enough that a bad deploy is pulled within a minute, and know that when every target in a group is unhealthy the ALB fails open and routes to all of them. Tune `deregistration_delay` (300 s default) down to your longest request so rolling deploys are fast, enable `slow_start` for JVM or model-loading targets, pick `least_outstanding_requests` over round robin when request cost varies, and use `lb_cookie` stickiness (the AWSALB cookie) only when the app truly holds session state, because it defeats even distribution across AZs.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Health checks for target groups

subtopics.name: Debugging through the ALB: status codes, metrics and access logs
subtopics.learn: Separate `HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count` (the balancer generated it) from `HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count` (your app did), and read the ELB-generated codes literally: 502 means the target closed the connection, sent a malformed response or the Lambda errored; 503 means no registered or no healthy targets; 504 means the target did not answer before the idle timeout or the TCP connect failed; 460 means the client gave up before the ALB idle timeout, common when a customer's proxy timeout is shorter than yours. Enable access logs to S3 and learn the field order well enough to `awk` them: `elb_status_code`, `target_status_code`, `request_processing_time`, `target_processing_time`, `response_processing_time`, where -1 in a processing time means no target was ever selected. Alarm on `UnHealthyHostCount`, `RejectedConnectionCount`, `TargetConnectionErrorCount` and p99 `TargetResponseTime`, and use `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` to join an access-log line to the application log on the instance.

resource.label: ALB User Guide: Troubleshoot your Application Load Balancer

subtopics.name: EC2 as an FDE runs it: instance choice, IMDSv2, user data, no SSH
subtopics.learn: Pick the family by what the workload is bound by (m general, c compute, r memory, g or p GPU, t burstable) and understand the t-family CPU credit model, including that T3 launches in unlimited mode and will quietly bill for sustained CPU. Resolve the AMI at plan time from the SSM public parameter `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` rather than hardcoding an ID that differs per region. Enforce IMDSv2 with `HttpTokens=required`, understand the token dance (`PUT /latest/api/token` with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds`, then GET with the token header) and the `HttpPutResponseHopLimit` of 1 that breaks the SDK inside a container until you raise it to 2. Bootstrap with user data through cloud-init, debug it in `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`, attach an instance profile instead of keys, and reach the box with Systems Manager Session Manager (SSM agent, `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`, outbound 443 to ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages) so the security group has no port 22 at all. Know that bandwidth advertised as `Up to 5 Gbps` is a burst figure and that `ethtool -S` exposes `bw_in_allowance_exceeded` and `pps_allowance_exceeded` when you hit the real ceiling.

resource.label: EC2 User Guide: Configure the Instance Metadata Service options

subtopics.name: Auto Scaling groups across AZs behind the ALB
subtopics.learn: An ASG built from a launch template with `vpc_zone_identifier` set to one private subnet per AZ and `target_group_arns` pointing at the ALB target group is the minimum unit of an AZ-resilient compute tier; min_size 2 with the ASG's automatic AZ balancing means one instance per AZ. Set `health_check_type = ELB` so a failed target-group health check replaces the instance instead of leaving a running-but-broken box in service, and set `health_check_grace_period` longer than boot plus warmup or the ASG will kill instances mid-startup in a loop. Use instance refresh with `min_healthy_percentage` to roll a new launch-template version, understand lifecycle hooks for draining, and know the ASG rebalances across AZs by launching in the under-served AZ before terminating in the over-served one. Confirm behaviour by terminating one instance and watching the target group go unhealthy, the ASG launch a replacement, and the access logs show zero ELB-generated 5XX.

resource.label: EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide: Use Elastic Load Balancing to distribute traffic

subtopics.name: Lambda execution model: init, invoke, concurrency and throttles
subtopics.learn: An execution environment goes through Init (runtime plus your module-level code, 10 s limit), Invoke (the handler, up to 900 s), and Shutdown; environments are reused, so anything at module scope (SDK clients, connection pools, model weights) is a cold-start cost paid once and a warm-path win thereafter, and `/tmp` (512 MB up to 10 GB) survives between invocations in the same environment. Memory is the only performance dial: 128 MB to 10,240 MB with CPU scaling linearly and a full vCPU at about 1,769 MB. Account concurrency defaults to 1,000 per region shared across all functions; each function can scale by 1,000 concurrent executions every 10 s; exceeding limits returns 429 `TooManyRequestsException` on synchronous calls and silently retries twice on asynchronous ones, so configure a destination or DLQ. Use reserved concurrency to cap a function that talks to a fragile customer system and provisioned concurrency or SnapStart when cold starts break an SLA; sync payloads cap at 6 MB and async at 256 KB.

resource.label: Lambda Developer Guide: Lambda execution environment

subtopics.name: Lambda inside the VPC and as an ALB target
subtopics.learn: Attaching a function to a VPC creates Hyperplane ENIs per unique subnet-plus-security-group combination, so the execution role needs `ec2:CreateNetworkInterface` and friends (`AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole`), the function never has a public IP, and it reaches the internet only through a NAT gateway in the private subnets you chose; pick subnets in at least two AZs. The function's security group is the source you reference in the RDS or ElastiCache SG. Behind an ALB, register the function in a target group of type lambda, grant `lambda:InvokeFunction` to `elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com` in the function's resource policy, return an object with statusCode, headers or multiValueHeaders, body and isBase64Encoded, and stay under the 1 MB response limit; the ALB health check, if enabled, is a real invocation you pay for. For a quick webhook receiver without an ALB, a function URL with `AuthType AWS_IAM` or `NONE` plus CORS is the right tool, and knowing which to choose is a common FDE trade-off with a customer's security team.

resource.label: Lambda Developer Guide: Giving Lambda functions access to resources in a VPC

subtopics.name: Seeing the packets: VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer
subtopics.learn: Turn on flow logs at the VPC level to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and read the default record (version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status), then add the custom fields `tcp-flags`, `flow-direction`, `traffic-path`, `pkt-srcaddr` and `pkt-dstaddr` so you can tell a SYN that was REJECTed by a security group from a flow that was ACCEPTed in and then REJECTed on the way out by a NACL. Know what flow logs do not show: DNS to the VPC resolver, IMDS traffic to 169.254.169.254, DHCP, and anything inside the 60 s or 600 s aggregation window that has not flushed, which is why a fresh reproduction takes a minute to appear. Use Reachability Analyzer to prove a path between two ENIs or an ENI and an IGW; it evaluates route tables, SGs, NACLs and endpoints statically and names the exact component that blocks, which is the artifact to paste into the customer ticket instead of an opinion.

resource.label: VPC User Guide: Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs

subtopics.name: Building the reference VPC and ALB tier in Terraform
subtopics.learn: Compose the whole diagram as code: `data.aws_availability_zones` (state available) feeding a `for_each` over two AZs, `aws_vpc`, `aws_subnet` per tier using `cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, index)`, `aws_internet_gateway`, one `aws_eip` and `aws_nat_gateway` per AZ, a public route table plus one private route table per AZ with their `aws_route_table_association`s, `aws_security_group` shells with separate `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` and `aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule` resources using `referenced_security_group_id`, `aws_lb` (application, public subnets), `aws_lb_target_group` with a `health_check` block, `aws_lb_listener` for the 80 redirect and the 443 forward with `certificate_arn`, `aws_launch_template` with `metadata_options` setting http_tokens to required and an `iam_instance_profile`, and `aws_autoscaling_group` with `vpc_zone_identifier` and `target_group_arns`. Read the terraform-aws-modules/vpc module source to see how per-AZ NAT is handled, then decide deliberately whether to consume the module or own the resources. Run `terraform plan` until the diff is zero, `terraform destroy` at the end of every session, and keep a cost line in the README.

resource.label: Terraform Registry: AWS provider documentation

outcomes: You can draw a two-AZ VPC (public, private and isolated tiers, per-AZ NAT, IGW, endpoints) from memory and, for every arrow and every SG or NACL rule, state which resource it protects, which direction is stateful, and what breaks if it is removed.

You can stand up an internet-facing ALB in front of an ASG of two EC2 instances in two AZs with Terraform, TLS via ACM, an 80 to 443 redirect and a real readiness health check, and reach a zero-diff `terraform plan` in under an hour from an empty account.

You can take a 'the app is unreachable' report and, within fifteen minutes using only describe-route-tables, describe-security-group-rules, flow logs and Reachability Analyzer, name whether the block is routing, SG, NACL, health check or DNS, with the log line that proves it.

You can read an ALB access log and CloudWatch metrics and distinguish 502, 503, 504 and 460 by cause, tell whether the balancer or the target produced a 5XX, and correlate one request to the instance log via X-Amzn-Trace-Id.

You can explain to a customer's network team, without notes, why they need one NAT gateway per AZ, which VPC endpoints let your workload run with no internet route at all, and roughly what each costs per month.

You can deploy a Lambda function into private subnets, wire it to RDS through a security-group reference, put it behind the same ALB on a path rule, and explain its cold-start, concurrency and 429 behaviour under a burst of 2,000 requests.

You can lock down EC2 the way a security reviewer expects: IMDSv2 required, no port 22, instance profile instead of keys, Session Manager for access, and show the SSM session working from an isolated subnet through interface endpoints.

You can list the quotas that will bite this architecture first (SG rules per ENI, NAT ports per destination, ALB rules per listener, Lambda account concurrency, resolver packets per second) and name the CloudWatch metric or alarm that would tell you.
failureModes: A single NAT gateway in AZ-a serves private subnets in both AZs: AZ-a degrades, every instance in AZ-b loses egress to the model API and package repos, and the 'multi-AZ' pilot goes down with one zone while the customer's dashboard still shows healthy EC2.

The app security group allows tcp/8080 from the ALB subnet CIDRs instead of the ALB's SG ID; a later subnet re-carve or a second ALB in the same subnets silently widens access, and the customer's pen test flags the app port reachable from a jump host.

A custom NACL on the database subnet allows inbound 5432 but the return rule only covers 32768-60999; ALB health checks and NAT-sourced connections using ports below 32768 fail intermittently, half the targets flap unhealthy, and on-call chases a phantom application bug for a day.

The health check path is left at `/` returning 200 from an nginx placeholder while the real app crashed on boot; the target group is green, the ALB happily forwards, and users get 502 from the balancer while every dashboard is healthy.

A Lambda function is attached to the VPC but placed in a subnet whose route table has no NAT route: calls to the Anthropic API hang until the 30 s timeout, the async invocations retry twice with no destination configured, and the customer sees three duplicated webhook side effects hours later.

A data-ingest job reads 20 TB from S3 through the NAT gateway because nobody added the S3 gateway endpoint; the month-end bill has a 900 USD NAT data-processing line, and the customer's FinOps lead asks why your design doc did not mention it.

Someone resolved the ALB DNS name once and put the two IPs into the customer's on-prem firewall allowlist; the ALB scaled and rotated its nodes overnight and the integration went dark, with nothing in your logs because the packets never arrived.
interviewQuestions: Draw a two-AZ VPC for a web tier, an app tier and Postgres that a bank's security team will accept. For every security group and NACL rule you write, tell me exactly what would happen if I deleted it.

A customer says the app behind your ALB returns 502 intermittently, about 3 percent of requests, only during deploys. Walk me through the investigation from ALB metrics to access logs to target-group settings, and name the two configuration values you expect to change.

Explain what happens at each hop when a browser requests https://app.customer.com served by an internet-facing ALB in front of instances in private subnets: DNS, TLS, the ALB node, the target, and the response path. Where does NAT happen and where does it not?

The customer wants zero internet access from the VPC. List the endpoints you need for an EC2 fleet pulling from ECR, logging to CloudWatch, reached over Session Manager and calling Bedrock. What changes if they also need to call an external SaaS API?

Flow logs show ACCEPT on ingress and REJECT on egress for the same 5-tuple. What is the cause, why does a security group never produce that pattern, and how would you confirm without touching production?

When would you put a Lambda function in a VPC and when would you refuse to? Cover cold starts, ENIs, NAT cost, concurrency, and the failure modes of async invocation against a customer system that is not idempotent.

Our Terraform created an ALB in two subnets, but one AZ shows UnHealthyHostCount equal to HealthyHostCount and the other is fine. Give me three plausible root causes in order of likelihood and the single command or console view that rules each one in or out.
14.proofOfWork: A public repository `aws-two-az-breakfix-lab` that extends the plan's Terraform with a `faults/` directory of six deliberately broken variants selected via `terraform apply -var fault=<name>`: missing NAT route in one AZ, NACL ephemeral-port block on the app subnet, app SG allowing from a CIDR rather than the ALB SG, health check on a placeholder path, Lambda in a subnet without egress, and a single-AZ NAT. For each fault the README records the exact evidence that identifies it (the flow-log line with tcp-flags, the Reachability Analyzer blocking component, the ALB access-log fields, or the CloudWatch metric) and the one-line fix, plus a `cost.md` estimating the monthly bill for the reference architecture with and without endpoints. Finish with a ten-minute recorded walkthrough in which you terminate every instance in one AZ while running a load generator against the ALB and show the access logs registering zero ELB-generated 5XX during recovery.

15.topic: AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB
15.why: Almost every FDE engagement ends with the customer's data living in one of these four services, on the customer's AWS account, under the customer's compliance rules. The FDE is the person on the call when the CFO asks whether the deleted orders table from Tuesday can come back, when the app team says the cache 'lost data' after a failover, or when the AWS bill for a pilot triples because a lifecycle rule pushed ten million tiny objects into Glacier. Being able to restore a database within a measured RTO, lock down a bucket so the security review passes first time, and say with evidence whether a workload belongs in DynamoDB or Postgres is what lets you be trusted with production in week one instead of month three.
prerequisites: Topic 12 (Terraform): providers, state, plan/apply, lifecycle blocks, import, and why ForceNew attributes destroy resources; every hands-on step here is done through Terraform.

Topic 13 (AWS networking and compute): VPC, private vs public subnets, security groups referencing other security groups, route tables (for gateway endpoints), and the AWS CLI configured with a profile.
Working Postgres: psql, roles, CREATE EXTENSION, pg_stat_statements, what WAL is and why replication lag exists; Topic 29 goes deeper, but the basics are assumed now.

IAM policy reading ability: Effect/Action/Resource/Condition, the difference between an identity policy and a resource policy, and that an explicit Deny wins; Topic 15 formalises this, so at minimum read the IAM policy evaluation logic page first.
Shell and jq fluency from Topic 0 so that aws ... --query and --output json become a scripting substrate rather than something you click through in the console.
An AWS account you can spend roughly 15-25 USD in for a week of db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ time, snapshots and a few GB of S3; set a billing alarm at 30 USD before starting.

subtopics.name: RDS anatomy: instance classes, gp3 vs io2, subnet groups, security groups
subtopics.learn: Know what an RDS instance actually is: an EC2-class VM (db.t4g burstable with CPU credits, db.m memory-balanced, db.r memory-optimised; the g suffix means Graviton) plus an EBS volume you cannot see. For gp3 on PostgreSQL the baseline is 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s under 400 GiB and 12,000 IOPS / 500 MiB/s at 400 GiB and above, so a 100 GiB volume that needs 10,000 IOPS must be resized or moved to io2. Understand storage autoscaling (max_allocated_storage triggers when free space is under 10% for five minutes, then grows by the larger of 10% or 5 GiB with a six-hour cooldown) and the storage-full status that makes the instance unavailable. Place the instance with a DB subnet group spanning at least two AZs of private subnets, a security group that allows 5432 only from the application security group, and publicly_accessible=false; confirm the endpoint resolves to a private IP with dig.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: DB instance storage

subtopics.name: Multi-AZ instance vs Multi-AZ DB cluster vs read replicas, and a forced failover
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the three: a Multi-AZ instance has one synchronous standby that never serves reads and fails over in roughly 60-120 seconds by swapping the CNAME behind the same endpoint hostname; a Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer plus two semi-synchronous readable standbys, a separate reader endpoint and typically sub-35-second failover; a read replica is asynchronous streaming replication (watch ReplicaLag) that you can promote but that does not fail over automatically. Run aws rds reboot-db-instance --force-failover on your test instance while a psql loop with \watch 1 is running, and time how long connections fail. Then explain why the endpoint's CNAME TTL is only a few seconds and why a JVM with a cached DNS answer (networkaddress.cache.ttl) or a pooled connection with no keepalive keeps failing long after AWS says the failover finished. Know that Multi-AZ replication traffic is not billed but cross-AZ traffic from your app to the DB is.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Multi-AZ deployments

subtopics.name: Backups: automated backups, 5-minute log shipping, snapshots, sharing and copying
subtopics.learn: Understand that automated backups are a daily storage-level snapshot taken in the backup window plus transaction logs uploaded to S3 every five minutes, which is why the RPO of a point-in-time restore is up to five minutes; check the exact number with aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[0].LatestRestorableTime'. Retention is 0-35 days and setting it to 0 deletes all existing automated backups immediately, a change that has been made 'to save money' in real accounts. Manual snapshots persist until deleted and are incremental after the first; backup storage is free up to 100% of the provisioned storage in the region and billed per GB-month beyond that. Know the KMS constraint: a snapshot encrypted with the AWS-managed aws/rds key cannot be shared with another account, so cross-account DR requires a customer-managed key from day one, and cross-region copies re-encrypt with a key in the destination region.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Introduction to backups

subtopics.name: The restore drill: point-in-time restore, repoint, measure RTO and RPO
subtopics.learn: Run the whole drill from the CLI and time every step. Seed the instance with pgbench -i -s 300 (about 4.5 GB), insert a marker row with now(), then drop pgbench_accounts and record the wall-clock time. Restore with aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier X --target-db-instance-identifier X-pitr --restore-time <30 s before the drop>, passing --db-subnet-group-name, --vpc-security-group-ids and --db-parameter-group-name explicitly because a restore otherwise lands in the default parameter group and default security group, which is the classic reason the app cannot connect to the 'successful' restore. Time aws rds wait db-instance-available, then time the first SELECT count(*): restored EBS volumes lazy-load blocks from S3, so the first pass is slow and pg_prewarm or a full-table read is part of RTO. Finish by renaming: aws rds modify-db-instance --new-db-instance-identifier on the old instance first, then on the restored one, so the original endpoint hostname is preserved and the app needs no config change. Write down RTO (drop to app healthy) and RPO (marker row present or not) and what dominated each.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Restoring a DB instance to a specified time

subtopics.name: Postgres on RDS: rds_superuser, parameter groups, extensions and logs
subtopics.learn: Know what you lose without real superuser: rds_superuser cannot read pg_hba.conf, cannot install unlisted extensions, and cannot write to the filesystem, so shared_preload_libraries (pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, pg_cron) is set in a custom parameter group rather than postgresql.conf. Understand static versus dynamic parameters: static ones show as pending-reboot in describe-db-parameters and only take effect after aws rds reboot-db-instance, and a modified parameter group attached to an instance is not applied until that reboot. Set log_min_duration_statement, log_connections and log_lock_waits, then ship logs with --cloudwatch-logs-export-configuration '{"EnableLogTypes":["postgresql","upgrade"]}' and read them with aws logs tail. Know rds.force_ssl=1 is the default on PostgreSQL 15+, rds.logical_replication=1 is required for Debezium or DMS and needs a reboot, and that rds.allowed_extensions and rds.restrict_password_commands exist for locked-down customers.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Working with parameters on RDS for PostgreSQL

subtopics.name: Connections: max_connections, RDS Proxy pinning, IAM auth tokens, Secrets Manager
subtopics.learn: Compute the default max_connections from LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392},5000): a 1 GiB db.t4g.micro gets about 112, a 4 GiB db.t4g.medium about 450, and 30 Kubernetes pods with a pool of 20 each will exhaust that. Know when RDS Proxy is the answer (Lambda, serverless bursts, many short-lived clients) and what defeats its multiplexing: SET session variables, temp tables, advisory locks, LISTEN and some prepared-statement flows pin the client to a backend connection, visible in the DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned metric. For IAM database authentication, GRANT rds_iam TO app_user, generate a token with aws rds generate-db-auth-token, understand it is valid for 15 minutes and that the service caps roughly 200 new IAM-auth connections per second, so it belongs behind a pool or proxy. Prefer manage_master_user_password (Secrets Manager) over a password in state, and read the secret with aws secretsmanager get-secret-value to see the JSON shape the app must parse.

resource.label: RDS User Guide: Amazon RDS Proxy

subtopics.name: RDS observability: Database Insights wait events, Enhanced Monitoring, the alarms that matter
subtopics.learn: Use Performance Insights (now surfaced as CloudWatch Database Insights) to read DB load in average active sessions, split by wait event: IO:DataFileRead means you are disk-bound, Lock:transactionid means row lock contention, LWLock:buffer_content or CPU means a query problem; the top-SQL view maps load back to statements, and seven days of retention is free.
