failureModes: Every pipeline in the org turns red on Monday morning with TOOMANYREQUESTS pulling the Trivy vulnerability DB from ghcr.io, and the team responds by setting `exit-code: 0`, which quietly disables the CVE gate for months.

A `paths` filter or a renamed job means the required 'test' check either reports skipped (treated as passing, so an untested change merges) or never reports at all (so every PR sits pending and someone adds a bypass rule).

A Deployment references a mutable `latest` tag; Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy while two of three pods run last week's image because `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` kept the cached layer, and the customer sees inconsistent behaviour per request.

An ECR lifecycle rule with `tagStatus: any` or an aggressive count expires the digest the live Deployment points at, or deletes cosign's `sha256-*.sig` tags; nothing happens until a node is replaced at 3am, then pods fail ImagePullBackOff or are rejected by Kyverno.

A workflow uses `pull_request_target` and checks out the PR head to 'run the PR's tests with secrets'; a fork PR modifies `conftest.py` to print `$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` or the ECR token, and the customer's registry is writeable by a stranger.

`argocd app sync` returns success and the pipeline goes green, but the new pods crash-loop; Deployment health stays Progressing for the full 600s `progressDeadlineSeconds`, longer than anyone watched, and prod is on the old version while the release notes say otherwise.

The GitOps bump is committed with a departed engineer's PAT; the day their account is deactivated, deploys stop with a 403 in the least-read job of the pipeline, and the on-call spends two hours before finding it.
interviewQuestions: Design the path from `git push` to a pod running in a customer's EKS cluster such that their security team can verify the image was built from a reviewed commit, tested and scanned. Where does each gate live, what identity is carried between stages, and what is enforced at admission rather than in CI?

The pipeline is green but the customer says the fix is not live. Walk me through your debugging in order: which digest was pushed, what the GitOps repo contains, what Argo CD reports, and what `imageID` the pods actually run. Where are the places 'green' can lie?
Why deploy by digest rather than tag? Describe two concrete production failures that mutable tags cause, and how you make the registry itself refuse the mistake.

Your Trivy gate blocks on a HIGH CVE in glibc with no fix available in the base image. The customer wants the release today. What do you do, what do you write down, and how do you prevent the exception becoming permanent?

The customer's policy is no long-lived credentials anywhere. Explain exactly how a GitHub Actions job obtains permission to push to their ECR, what the OIDC `sub` claim looks like, and how you ensure only merges to main in the prod environment can assume the prod role.
All CI runs started failing this morning with a rate-limit error pulling the vulnerability database. What is happening, what is the fix in the next 30 minutes, and what is the durable fix?

A bad release went out through GitOps ten minutes ago. Give me the rollback sequence, the expected time to recovery, what makes it safe to do under pressure, and how you would turn it into a one-click job.
19.proofOfWork: A recorded red-to-green walkthrough plus a written chain-of-custody sheet. Open three pull requests against Dokeo: one that breaks a test, one that pins a dependency or base image with a known HIGH CVE, and one clean change. Show the first two stopped at the test and scan jobs respectively with the merge button disabled, and the third flowing through push, signing, GitOps commit and `argocd app wait` to Healthy. Then produce a one-page document for that third change listing commit SHA, run URL, image digest, `cosign verify` output with the certificate identity, `gh attestation verify` output, the GitOps commit SHA, the Argo CD revision, and the `imageID` from the running pod, with a short paragraph on what would need to be compromised to break the chain. Finish by extracting the pipeline into a reusable workflow and onboarding DefenderMate with a caller of under 25 lines, showing both repositories' runs side by side.

20.why: An FDE quotes numbers that end up in a customer's budget: the pilot price, the 'what does this cost at 20 sites' question in the steering committee, and the run-rate that decides whether the deployment renews. When you deploy into the customer's own AWS account their invoice is your architecture made visible, and the platform team, procurement and eventually the CFO read it line by line; the FDE who can explain NAT processing and log ingestion in plain English, attribute cost per tenant, and name three levers with a dollar figure keeps trust that the design alone never earns. Cost is also the quietest way to lose an account: nobody files an incident for a bill that doubled, they just do not expand.
prerequisites: AWS networking and compute from 'AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda' (topic 13): every line on the bill maps to a resource you built there, and you need to know which are zonal, which bill per hour and which bill per GB

AWS data from 'AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB' (topic 14): RDS instance classes and the Multi-AZ flag, gp2 versus gp3, S3 storage classes, ElastiCache node types, DynamoDB on-demand versus provisioned
EKS from topic 16 and 'Kubernetes production ops' from topic 8: control plane versus node cost, managed node groups, Karpenter, and what requests and limits mean for bin packing
Terraform from topic 12: a provider block you can add `default_tags` to, remote state, and a CI plan step that Infracost can hook into

Working knowledge of the DefenderMate build so far: which components exist (Next.js front end, webhook ingestion, Redis idempotency store, Postgres with RLS, LLM classifier, S3 exports, weekly email) and a rough count of events, tokens and GB per tenant per month

An AWS account with Cost Explorer enabled at least 24 hours before you start, IAM permission for `ce:*`, `budgets:*` and `compute-optimizer:*`, and spreadsheet fluency (SUMPRODUCT, scenario columns, break-even)

subtopics.name: FinOps vocabulary: the Inform, Optimize, Operate loop and the capabilities you will actually touch
subtopics.learn: Learn the three phases as a loop, not a ladder: Inform is allocation and visibility, Optimize is rate and usage levers, Operate is the cadence and guardrails that stop savings regressing. Memorise the principles because they settle arguments with a customer platform team, in particular 'decisions are driven by the business value of cloud' (never cut a cost that costs revenue) and 'everyone takes ownership for their cloud usage' (the FDE owns the pilot's bill, not the customer's FinOps team). Map the capabilities you use this week: Allocation, Reporting and Analytics, Anomaly Management, Rate Optimization, Workload Optimization, Unit Economics, Budgeting and Forecasting. Know that FOCUS is the vendor-neutral billing schema (BilledCost, EffectiveCost, ListCost, ChargeCategory) that AWS Data Exports, GCP and Azure can all emit, which is what lets a multi-cloud customer compare your GCP variant from topic 17 like for like.

resource.label: FinOps Foundation: FinOps Principles

subtopics.name: Reading the bill: Cost Explorer, the three cost metrics and `aws ce get-cost-and-usage`
subtopics.learn: Enable Cost Explorer on day one: it needs about 24 hours before data appears and only backfills about 13 months. Know the three cost metrics and when each is right: UnblendedCost is what the invoice line says (a Savings Plan purchase lands as a lump on the day you buy it), AmortizedCost spreads commitments across the hours they cover (use this for run-rate and unit economics), NetAmortizedCost also applies credits and negotiated discounts (use this for what the customer actually pays). Pull numbers with the CLI so they land in a sheet, not a screenshot: `aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-08-01,End=2026-09-01 --granularity DAILY --metrics AmortizedCost UsageQuantity --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE`, then regroup by `Key=USAGE_TYPE` with a `--filter` on the EC2 service to discover that 'EC2-Other' is NAT gateways, EBS and data transfer, not instances. Each Cost Explorer API call costs 0.01 USD. When the console's grouping hides the answer, the CUR or Data Exports Parquet in S3 (`line_item_usage_type`, `line_item_line_item_type`, `line_item_unblended_cost`, `pricing_public_on_demand_cost`, `resource_tags`) is the source of truth you query with Athena or the DuckDB you use in topic 36.

resource.label: AWS Cost Management User Guide: What is AWS Cost Explorer

subtopics.name: Cost allocation tags and attributing shared cost to tenants
subtopics.learn: Put `tenant`, `env`, `service` and `owner` on every resource through a `default_tags` block in the Terraform `aws` provider so nothing is created untagged, then activate them as user-defined cost allocation tags in the Billing console; activation takes up to 24 hours and is never retroactive, so an untagged first month is lost for good. Enforce the keys with an Organizations tag policy plus an SCP that denies `ec2:RunInstances` and `rds:CreateDBInstance` when `aws:RequestTag/tenant` is null. Learn what cannot carry a tenant tag: NAT processing, cross-AZ transfer, the EKS control plane, a shared RDS instance pooled behind RLS (topic 30), and every LLM token. For those, build a driver table per tenant per month (webhook events received, items classified, rows stored, tokens by `metadata.user_id`) and split the shared lines proportionally; that split, not the tag report, is what a customer's chargeback team will actually consume, so document the driver for every shared line.

resource.label: AWS Billing User Guide: Using cost allocation tags

subtopics.name: Rate levers: Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot and Graviton
subtopics.learn: A Savings Plan is a commitment to spend N USD per hour for one or three years, applied automatically to the most expensive eligible usage first: a Compute SP (up to about 66 percent off) covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda in any region or family, an EC2 Instance SP (up to about 72 percent) locks a family in one region, and the payment option (No, Partial, All Upfront) trades cash for a few more points. RDS and ElastiCache have no Savings Plans, only Reserved Instances, keyed to instance class and Multi-AZ flag and size-flexible only within a family, so a move from db.t4g to db.r7g strands the reservation. Spot is a different lever: up to 90 percent off for capacity AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning on the `spot/instance-action` metadata path and an EventBridge event, right for stateless classifier workers and the k6 load generator, wrong for RDS and the Redis idempotency store. Graviton (arm64) is roughly 20 percent cheaper per vCPU and needs the multi-arch image from topic 6 plus a check that every native Node dependency ships an arm64 build. Rule for the cost sheet: commit only to the twelve-month floor you can prove from Cost Explorer; at one client that floor is small and the honest lever is rightsizing, at twenty it is a Compute SP.

resource.label: Savings Plans User Guide: What are Savings Plans

subtopics.name: Rightsizing: Compute Optimizer, Kubernetes requests versus usage, RDS class
subtopics.learn: Run `aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations` and read the finding (Underprovisioned, Overprovisioned, Optimized) and projected utilisation; it looks back 14 days and cannot see memory unless the CloudWatch agent publishes `mem_used_percent`, so an instance at 5 percent CPU and 90 percent memory looks safe to shrink and is not. On EKS the bill follows requests, not usage: compare `kubectl top pods` against `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns` of `.spec.containers[*].resources.requests`, run the VPA recommender in `updateMode: Off` for a week and copy its targets, then let Karpenter consolidate with `consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized` so emptied nodes actually leave. For RDS the signals are `CPUUtilization`, `FreeableMemory`, `DatabaseConnections` and `ReadIOPS` over a week; a db.t4g.medium is right for one client, and remember the T family burns CPU credits, so a steadily falling `CPUCreditBalance` is a hidden cost cliff (surplus credit charges) before it is a performance one.

resource.label: AWS Compute Optimizer User Guide: What is Compute Optimizer

subtopics.name: The network tax: NAT gateways, cross-AZ, egress, endpoints and public IPv4
subtopics.learn: Price the two per-AZ NAT gateways from topic 13 honestly: roughly 0.045 USD per hour each plus 0.045 USD per GB processed, so a classifier that pulls 300 GB a month of webhooks and model responses through NAT pays more for processing than for the gateways, and every byte to S3 or DynamoDB via NAT is waste when a gateway endpoint is free. An interface endpoint costs about 0.01 USD per AZ-hour plus 0.01 USD per GB, so across two AZs it beats NAT processing only above roughly 400 GB a month for that one service; do the arithmetic per service rather than adding endpoints reflexively. Cross-AZ traffic is about 0.01 USD per GB in each direction, which is why Multi-AZ RDS and a Redis replica are worth it but a chatty cross-zone service graph is not; where pods and ALB targets are zonal, use `service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`. Internet egress is about 0.09 USD per GB after the first 100 GB, which is what SSE streaming to twenty customers' browsers and weekly export downloads turn into. Since 2024 every public IPv4 address costs 0.005 USD per hour whether attached or not, so count ALB nodes, NATs and forgotten EIPs on the sheet.

resource.label: Amazon VPC pricing (NAT gateway, data transfer, IPv4)

subtopics.name: Storage: RDS gp3 and backups, S3 lifecycle rules, orphaned EBS
subtopics.learn: Use gp3 for RDS storage: on RDS it is the same per-GB price as gp2 but includes 3000 IOPS and 125 MB/s below 400 GB (12000 and 500 above) with IOPS provisionable separately, so you stop buying capacity to get IOPS. Multi-AZ doubles both instance and storage cost, and automated backups are free only up to 100 percent of allocated storage, after which a long `backup_retention_period` and manual snapshots bill per GB-month. Put S3 exports under a lifecycle configuration: `Transition` to STANDARD_IA after 30 days (128 KB minimum billable size and 30-day minimum duration, so tiny objects get dearer, not cheaper), `Expiration` at the contractual retention, and `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` at 7 days; Intelligent-Tiering adds a per-object monitoring fee and ignores objects under 128 KB, so it is wrong for millions of small JSON events. Sweep EBS volumes in `available` state and snapshots of volumes that no longer exist; both bill until deleted.

resource.label: Amazon S3 User Guide: Managing the lifecycle of objects

subtopics.name: Observability cost: CloudWatch Logs ingestion, retention, log classes and metrics
subtopics.learn: The line that surprises everyone is CloudWatch Logs at roughly 0.50 USD per ingested GB plus storage: a pod left at debug level logging 20 GB a day costs more than the node it runs on. Set `aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name <group> --retention-in-days 30` on every group (the default is never expire), drop health-check and readiness lines in Fluent Bit before they leave the node, log at INFO with sampling for hot paths, and use the Infrequent Access log class (about half the ingest price, but no metric filters, subscription filters or Live Tail) for audit trails you must keep but rarely read. Custom metrics bill per metric per month, so a `tenant` dimension on ten metrics across twenty tenants is two hundred metrics; Container Insights bills per metric too. Self-hosting Prometheus and Grafana as in topic 21 moves the cost to nodes and EBS rather than removing it, so put both options on the sheet. ALB access logs to S3, by contrast, are nearly free and answer most of the same questions.

resource.label: Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide: Log classes

subtopics.name: LLM tokens as a bill line: caching, batch, routing and per-tenant attribution
subtopics.learn: Model the classifier as tokens per event times price per million, input and output separately, and read the current per-model table rather than remembering numbers. The three ratios that matter are stable: prompt caching charges 1.25x for a cache write and about 0.1x for a cache read on the prefix marked with `cache_control` (5-minute TTL refreshed on each hit, so a steady webhook stream keeps the system prompt and few-shot examples hot and cuts input cost by up to 90 percent), the Message Batches API halves the price for anything that can wait up to 24 hours (weekly email, backfills, not the live SSE path), and routing the easy 80 percent to a small model with a large model only on low-confidence cases changes the blended rate more than any infrastructure lever. Cap `max_tokens`, log `usage.input_tokens`, `usage.output_tokens`, `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` and `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` with the tenant id on every request so the driver table has real numbers, and keep a per-tenant token budget with a kill switch so one customer's misconfigured webhook cannot burn the month's margin. Topic 59 goes deep on the engineering; here you need the arithmetic and the attribution.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform: Pricing

subtopics.name: Fixed versus variable: the 1-client and 20-client model and unit economics
subtopics.learn: Split every line into a fixed floor that exists at zero tenants and a variable slope per tenant. For DefenderMate the floor is the EKS control plane (about 73 USD a month), two NAT gateways, the ALB, two minimum nodes across AZs, the Multi-AZ RDS instance, the Redis node, Route 53 zones and baseline logs, roughly 400 to 500 USD a month before the first customer; the slope is tokens, S3, egress and log volume, plus the step functions where a third node or a larger RDS class becomes necessary. Build the sheet with a tenants column, total = floor + tenants x slope + steps, and derive cost per tenant per month, gross margin against price per tenant, and break-even tenant count; at one client cost per tenant is dominated by the floor and no rate lever helps, at twenty it is dominated by tokens and NAT processing. Learn the SaaS Lens vocabulary the customer's architects will use: pooled (shared RDS with RLS, cheapest, noisy-neighbour risk), siloed (a full stack per tenant, twenty times the floor, what regulated customers ask for) and bridge, and be able to say in dollars what siloing one tenant costs.

resource.label: FinOps Framework: Unit Economics capability

subtopics.name: Pricing Calculator drill: estimate the stack, then reconcile against actuals
subtopics.learn: Build the estimate service by service with the real configuration from your Terraform, not defaults: region, 730 hours a month, EKS cluster, two m7g.large or t4g nodes, two NAT gateways with GB processed, ALB with LCUs derived from requests and new connections per second, RDS db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ with gp3 GB and backup GB, ElastiCache node, S3 GB plus PUT and GET counts, CloudWatch GB ingested, data transfer out in GB. Use the utilisation fields (percent of month) for non-prod, save the estimate to a share link and export the CSV so the CFO sheet cites it. Then reconcile after a week of actuals: `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` grouped by USAGE_TYPE against the calculator lines. The variance is always in the usage-based lines (NAT GB, log GB, LCUs, tokens) because those were guesses, and the reconciliation is what turns a quote into a forecast you can defend in a steering meeting.

resource.label: AWS Pricing Calculator User Guide

subtopics.name: Guardrails: Budgets with actions, Cost Anomaly Detection, and cost in the pull request
subtopics.learn: Create a cost budget with alerts at 50, 80 and 100 percent of actual and at 100 percent of forecasted spend, plus a Savings Plans utilisation budget once you commit so an idle commitment is visible. Attach a budget action on the non-prod account that applies a deny IAM policy or stops tagged EC2 and RDS instances when the threshold trips; alerts get read the next morning, actions fire at 3am. Enable Cost Anomaly Detection with one monitor per AWS service and one per `tenant` cost allocation tag, delivering to an SNS topic wired to Slack; it is free, baselines on recent history and catches the NAT or logs spike a monthly budget would only report at invoice time. Put cost in the review loop with Infracost: `infracost breakdown --path infra/ --usage-file infracost-usage.yml` locally and the GitHub Action posting `infracost diff` on every Terraform PR, so a reviewer sees that a Multi-AZ flag or an instance class change is 95 USD a month before it merges.

resource.label: AWS Cost Management User Guide: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets

subtopics.name: Non-production hygiene: schedules, stop and destroy, orphan sweeps
subtopics.learn: Non-prod runs 168 hours a week but is used about 50, so a schedule is worth 60 to 70 percent of its cost: stop RDS with `aws rds stop-db-instance` (it auto-starts after seven days, storage and backups still bill, and it cannot be stopped while a read replica exists), scale EKS node groups to zero or let Karpenter drain to zero at night, and use the Instance Scheduler on AWS solution or a scheduled Lambda keyed on a `Schedule` tag for EC2. Give every preview environment a `ttl` tag and a nightly job that runs `terraform destroy` on anything past it. Run a weekly orphan sweep: `aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available`, `aws ec2 describe-addresses` entries with no `AssociationId`, load balancers with zero healthy targets, snapshots older than the retention policy, and NAT gateways in VPCs with nothing left in them. Each orphan is small; a hundred of them is the mystery 15 percent on the invoice.

resource.label: Amazon RDS User Guide: Stopping a DB instance temporarily

subtopics.name: The CFO page: translating levers into margin, payback and risk
subtopics.learn: Write one page in the CFO's units, not yours: monthly run-rate today, cost per tenant, gross margin per tenant at the current price, and the three levers as a table with saving per month, one-off effort in engineer-days, payback period, and the risk you are accepting (Spot interruption, a one-year commitment if the client churns, cache staleness, a smaller model's accuracy). State on-demand versus committed exposure, name the step costs coming (a third node at roughly 12 tenants, a bigger RDS class at 25), and separate COGS (per-tenant infrastructure and tokens) from opex (non-prod, tooling) because finance books them differently. End with the decision you are asking for and a date; a cost memo without a decision is a status report. Rehearse saying the three levers aloud in under a minute, the way you would in a steering call, and have the reconciliation from the calculator subtopic ready as the appendix nobody reads but everyone trusts.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Framework: Cost Optimization Pillar

outcomes: You can produce, from Cost Explorer or a CUR query, a monthly breakdown of the DefenderMate stack by service and by `tenant` tag, and explain every line above 5 percent of the total in one sentence each, including exactly what 'EC2-Other' contains.

You can build a spreadsheet model with a fixed floor, a per-tenant slope and step costs that outputs total cost, cost per tenant and break-even tenant count at 1, 5, 20 and 100 tenants, and it reconciles within 15 percent of a Pricing Calculator estimate and within 10 percent of actuals after one billing month.
You can name three savings levers for the stack with a dollar saving, effort, payback and risk for each, and defend why rightsizing beats a Savings Plan at one client and the reverse at twenty.
You can compute the token cost per classified event with and without prompt caching and batch from real `usage` fields in your logs, and attribute it per tenant.
You can tag every Terraform-managed resource through `default_tags`, activate the cost allocation tags, and show a Cost Explorer report grouped by `tenant` in the following billing cycle.
You can configure a budget with a stop-instances action, an anomaly monitor per tag with SNS delivery, and Infracost on PRs, and demonstrate each one firing.
You can explain to a non-engineer, in under two minutes and without jargon, what a NAT gateway is and why its line went up when traffic to the model API doubled.
You can do the interface-endpoint break-even and the Multi-AZ RDS cost delta on a whiteboard, with the per-hour and per-GB rates written down.
failureModes: Cost allocation tags are activated in month two, so the pilot's first invoice cannot be split by tenant; the customer's chargeback team books the whole bill to the sponsoring department and the expansion conversation stalls on 'we do not know what this costs per team'.

Debug logging left on in one pod pushes CloudWatch Logs ingestion to 25 GB a day; logs quietly become the largest line on the invoice, larger than the EKS nodes, and nobody notices until invoice time because the budget was set on total spend rather than per service.

All traffic to S3 and the model API leaves through NAT; at 20 tenants NAT data processing exceeds the gateways and the compute combined, and a free S3 gateway endpoint would have removed a third of it on day one.

A three-year all-upfront RDS Reserved Instance is bought on a db.r6g.large; six months later the workload moves to a different family, the reservation is stranded, and 'unused commitment' appears in every quarterly review with your name on it.

Spot is used for webhook ingestion pods to save 70 percent; a capacity reclaim lands during a customer's bulk import, nodes disappear faster than the two-minute warning is handled, events are duplicated because the idempotency TTL was shorter than the retry window, and the saving is smaller than the one incident's service credit.

A preview environment per pull request is created with Terraform and never destroyed; forty stacks each with a NAT gateway, an ALB and a small RDS run for three months and the 'dev' account spends more than production.

The cost sheet is built in on-demand unblended cost while the customer's finance team reads net amortized in their own Cost Explorer; the two disagree by the Savings Plan and credits, and the FDE is accused of underquoting by 30 percent.
interviewQuestions: Here is a Cost Explorer view for a small multi-tenant SaaS: EC2-Other is the second largest line and has grown four times while EC2 instance cost is flat. What is in it, how do you find out, and what are the first two changes you would make?

Cost a small multi-tenant LLM product on EKS plus Multi-AZ RDS at 1, 20 and 500 customers. Which lines scale with tenants, which are steps, where does your model break down, and at what tenant count does a Compute Savings Plan start making sense?

A customer's CFO asks why the pilot costs 900 USD a month when they were told 'a few hundred'. Walk me through the investigation and what you would say in the meeting, including what you would refuse to promise.

Design per-tenant cost attribution for a pooled architecture where tenants share a database, a Kubernetes cluster and one LLM API key. What can you tag, what must you estimate, and how do you make the estimate defensible to a chargeback team?

You are asked to cut infrastructure cost 30 percent without touching reliability on a two-AZ EKS plus Multi-AZ RDS stack. Rank the levers you would consider, and tell me which ones you would refuse and why.
Explain prompt caching and batch pricing to a finance person, then tell me how you decide which traffic goes down each path and how you prove the saving after the fact.
A Savings Plan you recommended shows 60 percent utilisation three months in. What happened, how do you find out, and what do you do about it this quarter?
20.proofOfWork: A public repository `defendermate-cost-model` containing the reproducible model behind the CFO sheet: a `model.csv` (or a short Python script with the same rows) listing every line item with its unit, unit price, fixed-or-per-tenant classification and step thresholds, which prints total cost, cost per tenant and gross margin at 1, 5, 20 and 100 tenants; an `infracost-usage.yml` plus a GitHub Actions workflow that posts `infracost diff` on every Terraform PR in the plan's infra repo, with one merged PR showing a real cost comment; Terraform for the guardrails (a `tenant`/`env`/`service` `default_tags` block, an AWS Budget with a stop-instances action on the non-prod account, and a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor per tag delivering to an SNS topic); a `reconcile.sh` that pulls thirty days of `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` by USAGE_TYPE and by `tenant` tag and diffs it against the model with a variance column; and a one-page `VARIANCE.md` written after the first full billing month explaining every line that missed by more than 10 percent and what changed in the model as a result. A reviewer should be able to change the tenant count or one unit price in a single cell and watch the three recommended levers re-rank.

21.topic: SRE fundamentals: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil, on-call
21.why: An FDE is the person the customer asks 'how reliable is this, and what happens when it breaks' before they sign off the production rollout, and the person whose phone rings at 02:00 when the answer turns out to be wrong. SLIs, SLOs and an error budget turn that conversation from adjectives into one number both sides can measure, gate releases against, and write into a contract; toil accounting and on-call design are what let a one- or two-person deployed team run a customer's system for a year without burning out or handing the customer a pager they cannot hold. Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks deployed teams all inherit this vocabulary from Google SRE, so fluency is checked in the loop and expected on day one of the engagement.
prerequisites: PromQL basics: `rate()`, `sum by (...)`, label matchers and dividing two series; this topic teaches the SLO-specific queries, and 'Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, logs, traces, metrics' (topic 21) goes deep on instrumentation afterwards

Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes, rollouts and `kubectl rollout undo` from 'Kubernetes production ops' (topic 8), so you know why health-check traffic pollutes an SLI and how a page actually gets mitigated

Single-box troubleshooting from 'Performance and troubleshooting on a single box' (topic 3): saturation, OOM kills, full disks, so a runbook step such as 'check event-loop lag and Postgres connection count' is something you can do under pressure

DefenderMate running locally via Docker Compose (the hardened image from topic 6) with a `/metrics` endpoint from prom-client that exposes an `http_request_duration_seconds` histogram labelled by route and status code
A Grafana Cloud free-tier account or a local Prometheus + Alertmanager + Grafana stack in Docker Compose, plus a 40-line Python or k6 script that generates traffic with a controllable error rate
Percentiles versus means, and why a p50 of 80 ms can coexist with a p99 of 4 s; you should be able to read a cumulative histogram
Git and CI habits from 'Git at depth' (topic 4) so rules, dashboards and documents live in one repository with `promtool` checks on every pull request

subtopics.name: Why 100% is the wrong target: the cost of the next nine
subtopics.learn: Read Embracing Risk and be able to state, for DefenderMate, what the marginal nine costs (a second region, a queue in front of the classifier, a warm standby Postgres) and what it buys (about 39 extra minutes per month going from 99.9 to 99.99). Know the two availability formulas, time-based (uptime / total time) and aggregate (good requests / total requests), and why Google and every cloud SLA use the request-based form: a 30-second blip at 03:00 and a 30-second blip during the customer's Monday triage are identical in uptime terms and wildly different in the request form. Be ready to explain to a customer that the target is set by user tolerance and by what their alternatives offer, not by engineering pride, and that an error budget that is never spent is a signal you are shipping too slowly.

resource.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 3: Embracing Risk

subtopics.name: The SLI menu and the good-events / valid-events ratio
subtopics.learn: Every SLI in this plan is written as good events / valid events x 100, so the first job for each user journey is to define 'valid' (exclude /healthz, exclude 4xx caused by the caller, exclude synthetic traffic) and 'good' (2xx or 3xx, and under the latency threshold). Use the Workbook's SLI menu by service type: request/response gets availability, latency and quality; data processing gets freshness, correctness, coverage and throughput; storage gets durability. Map DefenderMate's journeys onto it: dashboard page loads and API calls are request/response; inbound alert webhooks are request/response with an acceptance-latency SLI; the LLM classification pipeline is freshness plus correctness; the weekly digest email is a count-based freshness SLI. Write each as a one-line SLI specification before touching any query, for example 'proportion of /api/* requests served in under 500 ms, measured at the ingress controller'.

resource.label: SRE Workbook, ch. 2: Implementing SLOs

subtopics.name: Where you measure changes what you see
subtopics.learn: For each SLI pick a measurement point and write down its blind spots. Server-side application metrics (prom-client's histogram) miss every request the app never saw, so during a crashloop they report 100% availability while the ingress returns 503. Load-balancer or ingress-controller metrics (`nginx_ingress_controller_requests`, ALB `HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count`) see failures the app missed but not app-internal correctness. Blackbox probes (`probe_success` from blackbox_exporter) see the whole path including DNS and TLS but only for the paths you probe and at low volume. Client-side telemetry sees the truth including the customer's flaky Wi-Fi. Choose ingress metrics for API availability and latency, a probe for 'is the dashboard up at all', and app-side counters only for internal pipeline steps. Know the PromQL defence against silence, `absent(up{job="dm-api"})` or a probe, because a missing series is not a good series.

resource.label: Prometheus guide: Understanding and using the multi-target exporter pattern (blackbox probing)

subtopics.name: Availability SLI in PromQL, including the 'valid' filter
subtopics.learn: Write the ratio with `rate()` over a window and identical label sets on both sides: `sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="defendermate",status!~"5..",path!="/healthz"}[5m])) / sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="defendermate",path!="/healthz"}[5m]))`. Understand why `rate()` needs at least two samples inside the range (so `[5m]` at a 30 s scrape interval is fine and `[1m]` at 60 s is not), why `increase()` is `rate()` times the range and is the primitive for 'errors in the last 30 days', and why dividing two series with different label sets without `sum by (...)` on both sides yields an empty result and a panel that silently shows nothing. Decide explicitly whether 429 and 499 count as bad: for the webhook endpoint a 429 you returned under load is your failure, a 400 on malformed JSON is the caller's. Record the result as `slo:sli_error:ratio_rate5m` with a recording rule so panels and alerts share one definition.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Querying basics

subtopics.name: Latency SLI from histograms: threshold form, not quantile form
subtopics.learn: Instrument DefenderMate's Node API with prom-client's `Histogram` for `http_request_duration_seconds` and choose buckets so every SLO threshold is exactly a bucket boundary (0.5 and 2 for the dashboard SLO); `histogram_quantile()` interpolates inside a bucket, so a 'p95 under 500 ms' computed from buckets [0.25, 1] is a guess, and quantiles cannot be averaged across instances or windows. The SLO-compatible form counts good events directly: `sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5",route=~"/api/.*"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{route=~"/api/.*"}[5m]))`; because `_bucket` is cumulative, the `le="0.5"` series already includes everything faster. Know that `le` is a string label ('0.5', never '.5' or '0.50'), that the `+Inf` bucket equals `_count`, and that Prometheus native histograms with `histogram_fraction(0, 0.5, ...)` remove the boundary problem when the customer's stack has them enabled. Keep the quantile panel for humans; alert and budget on the fraction.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Histograms and summaries (best practices)

subtopics.name: Pipeline SLIs for ingestion and the weekly digest: freshness, correctness, coverage
subtopics.learn: DefenderMate's value is asynchronous: a webhook lands, an LLM classifies it, the dashboard and weekly email reflect it, so request SLIs alone say nothing about whether the customer's analyst sees the right alert in time. Define freshness as the proportion of events classified within 300 s of receipt: emit a histogram of `classified_at - received_at` with a 300 bucket and use the threshold form, or for a batch job export `job_last_success_timestamp_seconds` and alert on `time() - max(job_last_success_timestamp_seconds) > 900`. Define correctness as the proportion of a golden sample (a fixed set of known alerts replayed hourly) classified to the expected label, which is the bridge to 'Evals as infrastructure' (topic 53). Define coverage as events processed / events accepted at the webhook over the window, which is how you catch a queue silently dropping messages. For the weekly digest treat each scheduled send as one event and set a count-based objective over a quarter ('at most one late digest per thirteen'), because a 99.9% ratio over four weekly events is meaningless.

resource.label: SRE Workbook, ch. 13: Data Processing Pipelines

subtopics.name: Picking targets and windows; SLO versus SLA and the dependency ceiling
subtopics.learn: Choose a rolling 28- or 30-day window for engineering decisions (a rolling window keeps the budget continuously meaningful; a calendar month resets it and invites end-of-month risk-taking) and know that the customer's SLA is almost always calendar-month, so you will report both. Do the arithmetic cold: 30 days is 43,200 minutes, so 99.9% leaves 43.2 minutes of full outage, 99.95% leaves 21.6, 99.5% leaves 3 h 36 m, 99% leaves 7.2 h; over 28 days 99.9% is 40.3 minutes. Set the internal SLO tighter than any contractual SLA so you are paged before you owe credits, and never set an SLO above the availability of a serial dependency: if classification calls one LLM provider with a 99.9% published SLA and Postgres at 99.95%, the naive ceiling is 0.999 x 0.9995, about 99.85%, so a 99.9% classification SLO requires a retry queue or a degraded rules-based fallback, and that trade-off belongs in the SLO document's rationale. Start from measured history (run the SLI query over the last four weeks before committing) but do not simply codify current performance.

resource.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 4: Service Level Objectives (Choosing Targets)

subtopics.name: Writing the SLO document (Workbook Appendix A shape)
subtopics.learn: Produce one document per service with the sections the Workbook's example uses: service overview and owner; for each SLI the specification (plain English) and the implementation (the exact query and measurement point), the target and window, and the rationale (why 99.9 and not 99.5, what the customer said, what history showed); an error budget section linking the policy; clarifications and caveats (traffic excluded, known measurement gaps such as ingress-level blindness to DNS failures); and a review schedule with a next-review date. The document is a contract between you, the customer's ops lead and their product owner, so every query is paired with a sentence a non-engineer can read. Store it in the repository next to the rules and version it; a customer will ask 'what did the SLO say in March' during a dispute. Have a colleague read the SLI implementation and reproduce the number in Grafana without asking you anything; if they cannot, the document is not finished.

resource.label: SRE Workbook, Appendix A: Example SLO Document

subtopics.name: The error budget policy: thresholds, consequences, signatures
subtopics.learn: Write the policy from the Workbook's example: what happens when the 30-day budget is below 100% but above zero (normal operation), when a single incident burns more than 20% (mandatory postmortem within five working days), when the budget is exhausted (feature freeze on the affected service until the trailing window recovers, engineers redirected to reliability items, exceptions only by a named executive), and when the budget is untouched for two consecutive windows (loosen the SLO or ship faster). Name who has authority to override and where the decision is recorded. Rehearse the FDE version of the hard conversation: the customer's product owner wants a Friday release with the budget at zero, and you point at the policy they signed rather than argue in the moment. Define how customer-caused outages (their firewall change, their identity-tenant misconfiguration) are handled: excluded from the SLA, counted in the SLO unless the document's caveats say otherwise, always postmortemed.

resource.label: SRE Workbook, Appendix B: Example Error Budget Policy

subtopics.name: Burn-rate alerting math: deriving 14.4, 6 and 1
subtopics.learn: Burn rate is observed error ratio / (1 - SLO); burn rate 1 spends exactly the budget over the whole window. Over a 30-day window an alert on burn rate B over a lookback of L hours fires when B x L / 720 of the budget is gone, so 2% in 1 h needs B = 14.4, 5% in 6 h needs B = 6, 10% in 3 days needs B = 1. Convert to thresholds for a 99.9% SLO: 1.44%, 0.6% and 0.1% error ratio. Understand the reset problem (a 1 h window keeps firing for up to an hour after the outage ends) and the Workbook's fix of also requiring a short window (one twelfth: 5 m, 30 m, 6 h) to exceed the threshold so the alert clears within minutes. The 14.4x/1 h and 6x/6 h pairs page; the 1x/3 d pair opens a ticket. Know the failure of the naive alert this replaces ('error rate above 0.1% for 10 m'): it either pages on noise or misses slow burns. For low-traffic services (under roughly one request per second) know the options: longer windows, synthetic traffic to raise the denominator, or a minimum event count before the alert may fire.

resource.label: SRE Workbook, ch. 5: Alerting on SLOs

subtopics.name: Implementing the alerts as Prometheus recording and alerting rules
subtopics.learn: Create recording rules for the error ratio at every window you need, `slo:sli_error:ratio_rate5m`, `ratio_rate30m`, `ratio_rate1h`, `ratio_rate6h`, `ratio_rate3d`, so the alert expression is cheap, then write the page rule as `(ratio_rate1h > 14.4 * 0.001 and ratio_rate5m > 14.4 * 0.001) or (ratio_rate6h > 6 * 0.001 and ratio_rate30m > 6 * 0.001)` with `for: 2m`, `labels: {severity: page, slo: api-availability}` and `annotations: {summary, runbook_url}`; the ticket rule uses the 3 d / 6 h pair at burn rate 1. Validate with `promtool check rules rules.yaml` and, crucially, write a `promtool test rules` file whose `input_series` ramps error counts and whose `alert_rule_test` entries assert the page fires at `eval_time: 1h` for a 1.5% error ramp and does not fire for 0.05%. Understand `for:` semantics (pending until continuously true), that rule groups evaluate every `evaluation_interval` so a 3 d recording rule at 15 s is wasteful (put long windows in a group with `interval: 1m`), and that a rule's output inherits the labels of the expression's result, so `sum` without `by` erases the `service` and `slo` labels your routing depends on.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Alerting rules

subtopics.name: Generating SLOs from a spec: Sloth and OpenSLO
subtopics.learn: Hand-writing fifteen recording rules per SLO is toil, so declare each SLO once and generate. With Sloth write a `prometheus/v1` spec with `service`, per-SLO `objective: 99.9`, `sli.events.error_query` and `total_query` using the `{{.window}}` placeholder, and `alerting.page_alert` / `ticket_alert` labels; run `sloth validate -i slo.yaml` then `sloth generate -i slo.yaml -o rules.yaml` and read what it produces: the multiwindow error-ratio recording rules, metadata series such as `slo:objective:ratio`, `slo:error_budget:ratio`, `slo:period_error_budget_remaining:ratio` and `slo:current_burn_rate:ratio`, and two alert rules with the Workbook's windows already wired. Understand the trade-off: generated names are stable and one dashboard becomes reusable across every customer engagement, at the cost of learning the tool's naming scheme. Know that OpenSLO is a vendor-neutral YAML schema so an SLO written for one customer on Prometheus can be re-expressed for another on Datadog or Cloud Monitoring, and that Pyrra is the Kubernetes-CRD alternative when the customer runs kube-prometheus.

resource.label: Sloth: Prometheus SLO generator (GitHub)

subtopics.name: The Grafana SLO dashboard: four panels that answer four questions
subtopics.learn: Build one dashboard per service with `service` and `slo` variables and exactly these panels: (1) SLI over the window as a time series with a constant line at the objective; (2) remaining error budget as a Stat panel with thresholds green above 50%, amber 20-50%, red below 20%, fed by a recording rule such as `slo:period_error_budget_remaining:ratio` rather than a 30 d `increase()` in the panel, because range queries over 30 days of raw counters time out on a busy Prometheus and show 'No data' exactly when an executive is looking; (3) current burn rate as a time series with threshold lines at 1, 6 and 14.4 so a page is visually explained; (4) a budget-consumption timeline that shows when budget was spent, which is the panel that makes an incident review honest. Use `$__rate_interval` instead of a hard-coded `[5m]` so zooming does not break rates, set units to percent (0.0-1.0) correctly, and provision the dashboard as JSON through the provisioning directory or the HTTP API so it lives in git. On Grafana Cloud compare your hand-built dashboard with the native SLO feature under Alerts & IRM, which generates the same views from a query and an objective, and note what it hides.

resource.label: Grafana Cloud docs: SLO (Alerts & IRM)

subtopics.name: Page on symptoms, not causes: the four golden signals
subtopics.learn: From Monitoring Distributed Systems: a page must be urgent, actionable and about a user-visible symptom; a cause-based alert (CPU above 80%, pod restarted, queue depth high) belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket unless it predicts imminent SLO breach. The four golden signals, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, are the front page of every service dashboard, with saturation (connection-pool usage, Postgres connections against `max_connections`, Node event-loop lag, queue age) as the leading indicator. Audit DefenderMate's existing alerts and delete or downgrade every one not tied to an SLO or an imminent-saturation prediction; the target is that every page has a runbook and a person who would be upset to be woken by it. Record the reason for every page for a month in a sheet and count how many changed anyone's behaviour; that count is your alert-quality metric.

resource.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems

subtopics.name: Alertmanager routing: severity to pager, everything else to a channel
subtopics.learn: Configure `route` with `group_by: ['alertname', 'service', 'slo']`, `group_wait: 30s`, `group_interval: 5m`, `repeat_interval: 4h`, and child `routes` matching `severity="page"` to the PagerDuty or Opsgenie receiver and `severity="ticket"` to Slack or the issue tracker; add an `inhibit_rules` entry so the ticket alert for the same `service` and `slo` is suppressed while the page is firing, and a `mute_time_intervals` entry for the customer's agreed maintenance window. Learn `amtool check-config alertmanager.yml`, `amtool alert query`, and `amtool silence add alertname=... --duration=2h --comment="INC-123"` so every silence carries an owner and an expiry, because a silence without an expiry is how a customer outage goes unpaged three months later. Know that Grafana Alerting has the same concepts (notification policies, mute timings, silences) under different names when the customer runs Grafana-managed rules.

resource.label: Prometheus Alertmanager docs: Configuration

subtopics.name: Toil: measuring it and removing it on a customer engagement
subtopics.learn: Toil is work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without enduring value, and that grows linearly with the service; the SRE book caps it at 50% of an engineer's time, and FDE engagements drift far above that because customers ask for 'quick' manual actions. Keep a toil log for two weeks on DefenderMate, every rerun of a failed classification batch, every manual tenant onboarding, every certificate or API-key rotation, every 'can you pull me the numbers', with minutes spent and frequency; sort by minutes x frequency and automate the top item with a script that is checked in, tested and runnable by the customer's ops team without you. Distinguish toil from overhead (meetings, planning) and from engineering (a fix that removes the class of work). Bring the inventory to the engagement steering meeting as a number, 'we spend 11 hours a week on manual reruns; two days of engineering removes it', which is the argument that funds reliability work.

resource.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 5: Eliminating Toil

subtopics.name: On-call design for a shared FDE and customer team
subtopics.learn: From Being On-Call: a sustainable rotation keeps on-call under 25% of anyone's time (the book's floor is roughly eight engineers for a single-site 24/7 rotation, or six per site when two sites split the day), allows at most two incidents per 12-hour shift, and compensates in time off or money. Design DefenderMate's arrangement explicitly: business-hours primary is the customer's ops team with you as escalation; out-of-hours pages route only for the two SLOs that matter overnight (webhook acceptance and ingestion freshness); dashboard latency is a ticket until 08:00; the escalation matrix names people and response times (acknowledge within 5 minutes, escalate at 15). Write the handoff checklist (open incidents, active silences and their expiry, degraded dependencies, upcoming changes) and insist on a shadowing period before anyone takes a solo shift. Know the cognitive-load argument: responders under stress make worse decisions, so clear pages and runbooks are an engineering deliverable, not documentation polish.

resource.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 11: Being On-Call

subtopics.name: Runbooks, runbook_url and the first five minutes of a page
subtopics.learn: Every paging rule carries a `runbook_url` annotation to a page that fits on one screen: what the alert means in user terms, the dashboard link, the three most likely causes each with the exact command or query that confirms it (`kubectl -n defendermate get pods`, a `pg_stat_activity` count, the LLM provider's status endpoint), the mitigation for each (`kubectl rollout undo`, scale out, fail over to rules-based classification), and when to escalate. Use PagerDuty's open incident response guide for the roles and vocabulary (incident commander, communications lead, severity levels) you will formalise in 'Incident response and postmortems' (topic 23), and adopt its rule that the person paged owns the incident until it is handed off explicitly. Test each runbook by having someone who did not write it follow it during a game day; the steps that fail are your backlog. Keep runbooks in the same repository as the rules so a rule change and its runbook change are one pull request.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: During an Incident (roles and first-response steps)

outcomes: You can write a complete SLO document for DefenderMate with at least four SLIs (API availability, dashboard latency, webhook acceptance, classification freshness), each with a plain-English specification, the exact PromQL implementation and measurement point, a target, a window and a rationale, such that a colleague can reproduce every number in Grafana from the document alone.

You can do the budget arithmetic cold: state the minutes of downtime allowed by 99, 99.5, 99.9 and 99.95 percent over 28 and 30 days, derive the 14.4, 6 and 1 burn rates from the 2%/1 h, 5%/6 h and 10%/3 d budget-consumption targets, and convert them into error-ratio thresholds for any objective.

You can implement multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerts as Prometheus recording and alerting rules, pass `promtool check rules` and a `promtool test rules` suite, and demonstrate live that a 1.5% injected 5xx rate pages within five minutes while 0.05% stays silent and the page clears within minutes of the injection stopping.

You can build and provision a Grafana dashboard with SLI, remaining-budget, burn-rate and budget-timeline panels backed by recording rules that loads in under three seconds over a 30-day range, and explain the query behind every panel.

You can take a 'dashboard shows 100% but the customer saw an outage' report and, within fifteen minutes, name the measurement-point blind spot or query error responsible and propose the corrected SLI.

You can write an error budget policy with numeric thresholds, named consequences and named decision owners, and walk a customer's product owner through what it means for their Friday release when the budget is at zero.

You can design an on-call rotation and escalation matrix for a shared FDE and customer team that respects the two-incidents-per-shift and 25% ceilings, with a handoff checklist and a runbook behind every page.
You can quantify a fortnight of toil on an engagement in hours per week per category and present a costed automation proposal for the top item.
failureModes: The availability SLI is computed from the application's own request counters; during a 40-minute crashloop the pods emit nothing, the ratio has no data, the panel shows 100%, and meanwhile the ingress returned 503 to every request and the customer's SOC missed real alerts.

The latency SLO is 'p95 under 500 ms' but the histogram buckets are 0.1, 0.25, 1 and 2.5 seconds; `histogram_quantile` interpolates between 0.25 and 1 and reports 480 ms while real users see 900 ms, and nobody notices until a customer sends a screen recording.

Kubernetes readiness probes and a synthetic checker make up 35% of requests to the API; they are counted as valid and always succeed, so a 3% real-user error rate shows as 2% and the burn-rate page never reaches its threshold.

A single-window alert of 'error ratio above 0.1% for 10 minutes' fires 30 times a week on normal noise, the team routes it to a muted Slack channel, and a genuine six-hour slow burn that spends 40% of the budget is discovered from a customer email.

Every Grafana panel runs `increase(...[30d])` against raw counters; the dashboard takes 90 seconds to load and shows 'No data' during the very incident review where the customer's director asks how much budget is left.

The error budget policy exists as a document but was never signed by the customer's product owner; when the budget hits zero the release train continues, the number stops meaning anything, and the FDE has no leverage in the next reliability argument.

Weekend traffic drops to ten requests an hour; one failed request is a 10% error ratio, the 5-minute short window trips instantly, and the on-call FDE is paged at 03:00 for a single 500 that the caller retried successfully.
interviewQuestions: A customer's CISO says the DefenderMate alert dashboard must be 'five nines'. Walk me through the conversation: how you find the number they actually need, what 99.999 would cost on the current architecture, and what you propose instead.

Design the SLIs for an asynchronous pipeline that ingests webhooks, classifies them with a third-party LLM, and updates a dashboard. Where is each measured, what counts as a valid event, and what does an error budget mean when the biggest dependency is a provider you do not control?

Derive burn-rate alerting from first principles: why 14.4, why two windows, what the short window buys you, and what you lose if you only keep the long one. Then tell me how it breaks at ten requests an hour.
Our SLO dashboard shows 100% availability for the past week; the customer reports three outages. Give me every plausible explanation and the specific check that confirms or rules out each one.

The error budget is exhausted ten days into the window and the customer's product owner wants to ship a feature on Friday. What happens, who decides, what does the policy say, and how do you handle it if they overrule you?

A p99 latency alert fires every night at 02:00 and the team has learned to ignore it. Diagnose the alerting-design failure, fix it, and tell me what you would say in the retrospective about why it lasted so long.

You are the only engineer on a customer engagement with a two-person customer ops team. Design an on-call arrangement that is sustainable for a year and explain how you would measure and reduce toil over the first quarter.
21.proofOfWork: A public repository, `defendermate-slo`, that a reviewer can run cold with `make up && make burn`. It contains a Sloth spec (`slo/defendermate.yaml`) declaring four SLOs (API availability 99.9, dashboard latency 99.5 under 500 ms, webhook acceptance 99.95, classification freshness 99 within 300 s), the generated recording and alerting rules committed alongside it, and a `promtool test rules` suite that ramps synthetic error series and asserts the page alert fires at 14.4x and stays silent at 1x. A Docker Compose file brings up Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana and a small traffic generator with an `--error-rate` flag; `make burn` injects 1.5% 5xx for ten minutes and captures screenshots of the remaining-budget stat dropping, the burn-rate panel crossing the 14.4 line, and the page arriving in Alertmanager, then shows the alert clearing after injection stops. The repo also holds the signed SLO document and error budget policy as Markdown, a runbook per paging alert linked via `runbook_url`, and a `report.py` that queries `/api/v1/query` to produce a calendar-month attainment report alongside the rolling-window dashboard, with a README paragraph explaining why the two numbers legitimately differ.

22.topic: Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, logs, traces, metrics
22.why: When DefenderMate misclassifies a lead or a HubSpot write silently fails at a customer, the first question on the call is 'what happened to webhook 8813 at 14:02', and the FDE who can open one Grafana tab and walk from the latency spike to the exact trace to the log line holding the HubSpot 429 body owns that conversation; the one who says 'let me add some prints and redeploy' has already lost the week. FDEs inherit the customer's stack rather than choosing it, so you must speak Prometheus, OpenTelemetry and Grafana natively because that is what their platform team runs and what their security review will ask you to integrate with instead of replace. The SLOs you wrote in topic 20 are fiction until the metrics behind them exist, are labelled without cardinality bombs, and alert on burn rate, and that instrumentation is yours to ship, not the customer's.
prerequisites: SRE fundamentals from 'SRE fundamentals: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil, on-call' (topic 20): DefenderMate's SLIs and SLOs already written down, because every metric, bucket boundary and alert in this topic exists to measure one of them

Enough of 'FastAPI in production' (topic 26) to run DefenderMate locally as an API process plus a separate worker process consuming a queue, since the whole point is instrumenting a real webhook -> queue -> classifier -> HubSpot path, not a hello-world
Networking from topic 2: HTTP headers and how proxies treat unknown ones, HTTP/1.1 vs gRPC (HTTP/2) framing, ports; propagation is literally two headers and OTLP is gRPC on 4317 or HTTP on 4318

Docker from topic 5 and Kubernetes core from topic 7: docker compose for the local Collector/Tempo/Prometheus/Loki/Grafana stack, and a kind cluster for the DaemonSet, ServiceMonitor and Operator half
Python at depth: contextvars and how asyncio.create_task copies context, the logging module's LogRecord/Formatter/Handler chain, context managers and decorators, how gunicorn/uvicorn fork workers
Single-box troubleshooting from topic 3: what RSS, CFS throttling, file descriptors and run-queue length are, so the saturation panel is not decoration

subtopics.name: Three signals, one question each, and where cardinality is allowed to live
subtopics.learn: Metrics are pre-aggregated numbers with a bounded label set and answer 'is something wrong and how much'; traces are the per-request causal tree and answer 'where in this request did the time or the error go'; logs are arbitrary events with unbounded context and answer 'what exactly happened here'. Internalise the cardinality rule: a Prometheus time series costs memory per unique label set and the OTel SDK keeps one aggregator per attribute set, so hubspot_contact_id or tenant email can never be a metric label but is fine as a span attribute or log field. Map the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) and RED (rate, errors, duration) onto DefenderMate: webhook receipt, classifier call and HubSpot write each get a span; classification outcome and HubSpot status class become counters; classifier latency becomes a histogram; the webhook payload id and HubSpot response body go to logs only. Write this allocation down before touching code; it is the design artifact a customer's SRE will review.

resource.label: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems (four golden signals)

subtopics.name: The span data model: the fields you will actually set
subtopics.learn: A span carries a name, a SpanContext (16-byte trace_id, 8-byte span_id, trace_flags whose 01 bit means sampled, trace_state), a parent span id, a SpanKind, start and end timestamps, typed attributes (default cap 128 via OTEL_SPAN_ATTRIBUTE_COUNT_LIMIT, values must be str/bool/int/float or homogeneous lists; dicts are dropped with a warning), timestamped events (record_exception writes an 'exception' event with exception.type, exception.message, exception.stacktrace), links to spans in other traces, and a Status of UNSET, OK or ERROR. Know the SpanKind contract cold: SERVER/CLIENT pairs are how backends build service graphs and compute network time; PRODUCER/CONSUMER is what the webhook -> queue -> worker hop must use; INTERNAL is for the classifier logic. Resource attributes (service.name, service.version, deployment.environment) describe the emitting process and are set once at provider creation. Span names must be low-cardinality templates ('POST /webhooks/{source}', 'classify_lead', 'hubspot.contacts.update'), never contain ids, because every backend groups and searches on them.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Traces (spans, context, kinds, status)

subtopics.name: W3C traceparent, tracestate and baggage: the headers that make it one trace
subtopics.learn: traceparent is 'version-traceid-parentid-flags', e.g. '00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01'; the last byte's 01 bit is the sampled flag that lets downstream services honour the root's sampling decision. tracestate carries vendor key=value pairs and is opaque to you. baggage is a separate header carrying arbitrary key/values (tenant_id, webhook_source) across hops, and it is not copied onto spans automatically: if you want it queryable you write a SpanProcessor whose on_start copies chosen baggage entries into span attributes. Know what happens at the edge: a HubSpot webhook arrives with no traceparent so your SERVER span becomes the root, which is correct; a request arriving with a foreign traceparent makes you a child of someone else's trace, which is sometimes what you want (customer's API gateway) and sometimes a bug (a test harness reusing a fixed id). Default OTEL_PROPAGATORS=tracecontext,baggage; add b3multi only for Zipkin-era neighbours. A load balancer or WAF that strips unknown headers breaks propagation silently, so check the header actually arrives with a request dump before blaming the SDK.

resource.label: W3C Recommendation: Trace Context

subtopics.name: Python SDK bootstrap: providers, processors, exporters, env vars, shutdown
subtopics.learn: Install opentelemetry-sdk and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc (or -proto-http). Wire Resource.create({'service.name': ..., 'service.version': ..., 'deployment.environment': ...}) into TracerProvider(resource=..., sampler=...), attach BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint='http://otel-collector:4317', insecure=True)) and trace.set_tracer_provider(provider). Never use SimpleSpanProcessor outside tests: it exports synchronously inside the request path. Know BatchSpanProcessor's knobs and defaults: max_queue_size 2048, schedule_delay_millis 5000, max_export_batch_size 512, export_timeout_millis 30000; when the queue is full spans are dropped with a single warning you will not see. Prefer environment over code so the same image runs everywhere: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT (gRPC 4317; for HTTP 4318 the SDK appends /v1/traces), OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER, OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug when nothing arrives. Call provider.shutdown() (or provider.force_flush()) on process exit, in a FastAPI lifespan teardown and in the worker's SIGTERM handler, otherwise the final batch is lost and the last spans before a crash never appear. Metrics mirror this: MeterProvider with PeriodicExportingMetricReader(OTLPMetricExporter) and OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL (60000 ms default).

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Python

subtopics.name: Zero-code instrumentation: FastAPI, httpx, psycopg, redis under opentelemetry-instrument
subtopics.learn: Run 'opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install' to detect installed libraries and install the matching opentelemetry-instrumentation-* packages, then launch with 'opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn app:app'. Know what each instrumentor gives you: FastAPI/ASGI creates a SERVER span per request named by route template with http.request.method, http.route, http.response.status_code, url.scheme and server.address; httpx and requests create CLIENT spans and inject traceparent on every outgoing call, which is what makes the HubSpot API call a child of your worker span; psycopg adds db.system and a sanitised db.statement; redis adds db.operation and db.statement. Know the forking gotchas: gunicorn --preload or uvicorn --workers creates the exporter before fork and the export thread dies in the children, so instrument in gunicorn's post_fork hook or per-worker startup; uvicorn --reload spawns an uninstrumented child. Set OTEL_PYTHON_EXCLUDED_URLS='health,ready,metrics' (and the FastAPI-specific OTEL_PYTHON_FASTAPI_EXCLUDED_URLS) so probes and scrapes do not become 70 percent of your spans. When zero-code fights your process model, call FastAPIInstrumentor().instrument_app(app), HTTPXClientInstrumentor().instrument() and friends explicitly at startup instead.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Python zero-code instrumentation

subtopics.name: Manual spans and gen_ai semantic conventions around the classifier
subtopics.learn: Get a named tracer once per module: tracer = trace.get_tracer('defendermate.classifier', version). Wrap the LLM call with 'with tracer.start_as_current_span("classify_lead", kind=SpanKind.INTERNAL) as span:' and set the gen_ai semantic-convention attributes so any backend understands it: gen_ai.system ('anthropic'), gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.request.max_tokens, gen_ai.request.temperature, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens. Keep prompt and completion text off the span by default: it is PII and size; gate capture behind an explicit env flag and document it. Add your own namespaced attributes for what the business asks about: defendermate.classification (bounded enum), defendermate.confidence, defendermate.webhook.source. On failure call span.record_exception(exc), span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(exc))) and re-raise; never swallow, and never set OK manually unless you have checked the result. Emit span.add_event('retry', {'attempt': n, 'backoff_ms': ms}) inside retry loops so the trace shows why 3 s became 20 s. Use span links when one classifier batch serves many webhooks. Verify in Tempo that the classifier span's duration matches the provider-side latency you see in the API response headers.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions: Generative AI

subtopics.name: Context across async boundaries: webhook -> queue -> worker without breaking the trace
subtopics.learn: The webhook handler must return 200 in milliseconds, so the classifier runs later in a worker and the trace breaks at the queue unless you carry context by hand. Producer side: carrier = {}; propagate.inject(carrier); store carrier next to the job (Redis Stream field, Kafka record header, Temporal header, a JSONB column). Consumer side: ctx = propagate.extract(carrier); with tracer.start_as_current_span('process_webhook', context=ctx, kind=SpanKind.CONSUMER). Decide parent versus link deliberately: a job processed once is a child span; a job retried many times or drained in batches gets a new trace per attempt with a Link back to the PRODUCER span, so one poison message cannot create a 10,000-span trace that no UI renders. Know Python's context rules: asyncio.create_task copies contextvars at creation so spans flow into tasks, but ThreadPoolExecutor and run_in_executor do not, so wrap with contextvars.copy_context().run or install opentelemetry-instrumentation-threading. A span must end in the same execution that started it; a span started in the request and ended in the worker is a bug that shows as spans with absurd durations. Prove the whole thing with a single trace id visible in the API log, the queue payload, the worker log and the HubSpot CLIENT span.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Python manual instrumentation (context, propagation)

subtopics.name: The Collector: receivers, processors, exporters, connectors, pipelines
subtopics.learn: The Collector config has receivers, processors, exporters, connectors, extensions and service.pipelines.{traces,metrics,logs} that wire them together; a component that is defined but not referenced in a pipeline does nothing, which is the first thing to check when nothing arrives. Production processor order: memory_limiter first (check_interval 1s, limit_mib, spike_limit_mib; it refuses data instead of letting the process OOM), then resourcedetection or k8sattributes, then attributes/transform for redaction (action: delete on http.request.header.authorization, hash on user.email), then batch last (send_batch_size, timeout). Exporters you will use: otlp to Tempo or Jaeger on 4317, prometheusremotewrite or prometheus (exposes a /metrics endpoint for scraping), loki or otlphttp for logs, and debug with verbosity: detailed while developing. Connectors join pipelines: spanmetrics turns spans into RED metrics, servicegraph builds the service map. Run 'otelcol validate --config=config.yaml' before every deploy. Know that tail_sampling, k8sattributes, transform and loki live in the contrib distribution, not core. Enable the health_check extension on 13133 for liveness and zpages on 55679 to inspect live pipelines.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Collector configuration

subtopics.name: Sampling: head, parent-based, tail, and the scaling constraint
subtopics.learn: Head sampling decides at the root: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio with OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 keeps 10 percent of roots and every child honours the parent's flag, so traces stay complete; always_on for dev. Head sampling cannot 'keep all the errors' because the decision precedes the error. Tail sampling in the Collector's tail_sampling processor buffers each trace for decision_wait (10-30 s) then applies policies: status_code ERROR keep, latency threshold_ms above your SLO keep, string_attribute on tenant for a VIP customer keep, probabilistic 5 percent for the rest; compose them with and/composite policies. The cost: every span of a trace must reach the same Collector instance, so with more than one replica you put the loadbalancing exporter (routing_key: traceID) in a first tier in front of the samplers. Metrics derived from traces are wrong after sampling, so run the spanmetrics connector before tail_sampling or compute RED from the SDK instead. Be able to answer 'why is there no trace for my successful fast request' and 'why is the error trace missing' in one sentence each.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry docs: Sampling

subtopics.name: Prometheus data model, metric types, naming and finding cardinality offenders
subtopics.learn: A time series is a metric name plus a label set; a sample is (timestamp, float64). Counter is monotonic and only ever read through rate() or increase(); Gauge is a point-in-time value read with avg_over_time or max_over_time; Histogram exposes cumulative _bucket series with an le label plus _sum and _count and aggregates correctly across instances; Summary computes quantiles client-side and cannot be aggregated, so avoid it. Naming: defendermate_classifier_requests_total, defendermate_hubspot_write_duration_seconds; base units (seconds, bytes), _total suffix for counters, no label value baked into the name. Label values must be bounded enumerations: outcome in {qualified, disqualified, error}, status_class in {2xx, 4xx, 5xx}; tenant is acceptable only while tenants number in the tens. Python client: Counter(...).labels(outcome='qualified').inc(), Histogram(..., buckets=[...]).observe(seconds); under gunicorn set PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR because each worker holds its own registry and the parent must aggregate. Find offenders on a customer's server with topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~'.+'})) and the /api/v1/status/tsdb endpoint's seriesCountByMetricName. Pick one path per service: prometheus_client scraped directly, or OTel Meter.create_counter/create_histogram exported through the Collector; never both for the same numbers.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Metric types

subtopics.name: Scrape configuration, service discovery, relabeling and the /metrics contract
subtopics.learn: prometheus.yml scrape_configs: job_name, scrape_interval (15 s default; every rate() window and alert 'for' depends on it), scrape_timeout below the interval, static_configs for compose, kubernetes_sd_configs (role: pod or endpoints) for clusters, relabel_configs to keep only pods annotated prometheus.io/scrape=true and to rewrite the instance and job labels into something a human recognises. The exposition format is plain text with '# HELP' and '# TYPE' lines then samples; a /metrics endpoint that computes on demand and takes seconds will stall scrapes, so precompute in a background task. The synthetic 'up' metric is 1 when the scrape succeeded, and 'up == 0' is your first alert. With Prometheus Operator, ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor CRDs are selected by label; a missing 'release' label matching the Prometheus CR's serviceMonitorSelector is the single most common reason a customer's Prometheus ignores your service. Verify at /targets and /service-discovery, reload with SIGHUP or POST /-/reload (requires --web.enable-lifecycle).

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Configuration (scrape_configs, relabel_configs)

subtopics.name: PromQL for RED: the six queries you paste into every dashboard
subtopics.learn: rate(x_total[5m]) is the per-second average over the window and the window must be at least four times scrape_interval or you get gaps; increase() gives the count in the window; irate() is for spike hunting only, never alerts. Aggregate with sum by (route, status_class) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])). Error ratio: sum(rate(x_total{status_class='5xx'}[5m])) / sum(rate(x_total[5m])). Latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(x_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) and the le label must survive the aggregation or the result is garbage. Saturation: queue depth gauges, process_resident_memory_bytes, container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total, process_open_fds. Know why histogram_quantile returns NaN (no samples), why it can report a value above your largest finite bucket (+Inf interpolation) and why coarse buckets make p99 a lie. Recording rules with the level:metric:operations convention (job:http_requests:rate5m) for anything a dashboard or alert evaluates more than once a minute. Learn absent(), offset, topk(), label_replace() and the 'on'/'ignoring' vector-matching keywords because each one will save you an afternoon at a customer once.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Querying basics (PromQL)

subtopics.name: Histograms done right: bucket edges at SLO thresholds, exemplars, native histograms
subtopics.learn: The Python client's default buckets (.005 to 10 s) are wrong for an LLM call that takes 2-30 s; choose buckets that bracket your SLO thresholds, for example 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 60 for classifier latency, because histogram_quantile interpolates linearly inside a bucket and the only exact measurement is 'fraction under a bucket edge' via x_bucket{le='5'} / x_count. Every extra bucket is one more series per label set: 12 buckets x 10 routes x 3 status classes is 360 series for one metric. Exemplars attach a trace_id to an observation (observe(value, {'trace_id': hex}) in the client, exposed only in the OpenMetrics format, stored by Prometheus with --enable-feature=exemplar-storage) so a Grafana latency panel shows dots that click through to the exact slow trace; this is the concrete link between metrics and traces. Know native histograms and OTel exponential histograms as the fix for bucket choice (bucket boundaries chosen automatically, aggregatable across differently configured services) and their current feature-flag status so you can tell a customer when to adopt them.

resource.label: Prometheus docs: Histograms and summaries (best practices)

subtopics.name: Structured logs that carry trace_id and span_id
subtopics.learn: The target is that every log line emitted while a request is in flight carries trace_id and span_id so a click on a span lands on exactly its lines. Two ways in Python: OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_CORRELATION=true with the logging instrumentation injects otelTraceID, otelSpanID and otelServiceName into every LogRecord; or in your own JSON formatter read trace.get_current_span().get_span_context() and format trace_id as a 32-character lowercase hex (format(ctx.trace_id, '032x')) because Tempo and Loki expect hex, not the integer. Emit exactly one JSON object per line on stdout; never multi-line tracebacks in production since each line becomes a separate log entry, put the traceback in an 'exc_info' field.
