28.topic: FastAPI in production: DI, settings, lifespan, background tasks, workers, deployment
28.why: An FDE ships the service into the customer's cluster and is the person standing next to their platform team when it returns 502s on every deploy or freezes at 09:00 when one tenant sends a slow prompt; the HTTP layer's worker model, timeouts, shutdown sequence and health semantics are exactly where a working demo dies on contact with a real load balancer and real traffic. FastAPI is the default Python service layer for LLM-backed systems on Palantir, Anthropic and Databricks deployed teams, so the interview loop probes whether you know its DI, lifespan and threadpool mechanics at the level of flags and syscalls, not tutorials. Getting this right is what turns Kaupex from a prototype into something a customer SRE will accept a pager for.
prerequisites: The service, repository and domain layers from 'Production Python architecture: domain models, repositories, DI, packaging' (topic 25); this topic wires them into routers and dependencies without letting FastAPI leak into them

asyncio fundamentals: the event loop, `await`, `asyncio.gather`, `asyncio.timeout()`, `CancelledError`, and the ability to name what does and does not block a loop (`time.sleep`, `requests`, sync `psycopg2` all do)
Docker exec-form `CMD`, PID 1 signal handling, non-root images and multi-stage builds from 'Docker internals' (topic 5) and 'Production images and supply chain' (topic 6)
Kubernetes probes, requests and limits, HPA and rolling updates from 'Kubernetes production ops' (topic 8), because this topic defines the endpoints and shutdown behaviour those mechanisms depend on
HTTP keep-alive, load-balancer idle timeouts and `X-Forwarded-*` headers from 'Networking' (topic 2), and enough k6 from 'Load testing and chaos' (topic 22) to run a ramping-arrival-rate script

Kaupex running locally under Docker Compose: a FastAPI service with Postgres via SQLAlchemy asyncio + asyncpg, an outbound LLM call through httpx, and a Temporal client, on a box where you can read `ps`, `ss` and `pg_stat_activity`

subtopics.name: def vs async def: which thread your handler actually runs on
subtopics.learn: FastAPI runs `async def` path operations on the event-loop thread and plain `def` ones in a worker thread via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`; the same rule applies to dependencies. Any blocking call inside `async def` (`requests.get`, `time.sleep`, a sync SQLAlchemy session, the sync OpenAI client) freezes every request in that process until it returns. Prove it: an `async def` endpoint calling `time.sleep(2)` hit by 10 concurrent curls takes 20 s; switch to `def` or `await asyncio.sleep(2)` and it takes 2 s. Rule for Kaupex: `async def` with async clients (httpx.AsyncClient, SQLAlchemy asyncio, temporalio) everywhere, `def` only for legacy sync libraries; when a worker stalls, `py-spy dump --pid <pid>` shows which frame is holding the loop.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Concurrency and async / await

subtopics.name: The 40-token anyio threadpool and CPU-bound work
subtopics.learn: All sync endpoints and sync dependencies in a process share one anyio thread limiter with 40 tokens; the 41st concurrent sync call queues, which presents as rising latency with idle CPU. Raise it in lifespan with `anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter().total_tokens = N`, and know that it does not govern `loop.run_in_executor(None, ...)`, which uses asyncio's own default ThreadPoolExecutor. Threads do not help CPU-bound work under the GIL (PDF parsing, tokenising a 2 MB prompt, a pandas transform in the compile step): move it to `loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, fn, arg)` with a `ProcessPoolExecutor` created in lifespan, or off the request path into a Temporal activity. Compare `time.process_time()` against wall clock on a slow request to tell the two cases apart.

resource.label: AnyIO docs: Working with threads (default thread limiter)

subtopics.name: Depends() mechanics: sub-dependencies, per-request cache, router-level guards
subtopics.learn: A dependency is any callable; FastAPI resolves the graph once per request, and the same callable appearing twice in that graph runs once unless declared `Depends(fn, use_cache=False)`. Use `Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_session)]` type aliases so signatures stay one line, classes as dependencies for parametrised ones (`class Pagination: def __init__(self, limit: int = 50, offset: int = 0)`), and `dependencies=[Depends(verify_tenant)]` on `APIRouter` or `include_router` for side-effect-only guards every route under a prefix must pass. Know what belongs in DI (request-scoped: session, current user, tenant id, idempotency key) versus lifespan and `app.state` (process-scoped clients), and that `app.dependency_overrides` is the seam tests use, so anything constructed inline in a handler is untestable.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Dependencies tutorial (sub-dependencies, classes, caching)

subtopics.name: Dependencies with yield: sessions, commit/rollback and Depends(scope=...)
subtopics.learn: `async def get_session(): async with SessionLocal() as s: yield s` gives a request-scoped session whose exit code runs after the response has been sent by default (`scope="request"`), so a `commit()` placed after the yield can fail after the client already saw 200. Where the client must see the failure, commit inside the handler or declare `Depends(get_session, scope="function")` so the exit block runs before the response; a `"request"`-scoped dependency may only depend on other `"request"`-scoped ones, while `"function"` may depend on either. Wrap the yield in `try/except/finally` so `rollback()` runs on exceptions and re-raise, because swallowing the exception in the dependency turns a 500 into a silent 200. Verify with a test that asserts the row is absent after a handler raises.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Dependencies with yield (scope, exceptions after yield)

subtopics.name: Typed settings with pydantic-settings and a cached get_settings() dependency
subtopics.learn: Define `class Settings(BaseSettings)` with `model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="KAUPEX_", env_file=".env", env_nested_delimiter="__", extra="forbid")`, typed fields (`database_url: PostgresDsn`, `llm_api_key: SecretStr`, `request_timeout_s: float = 30`), and expose it through `@lru_cache def get_settings() -> Settings` used as `Depends(get_settings)`; the cache means one parse per process and tests swap it with `app.dependency_overrides[get_settings]`. Instantiate settings once at import of `main.py` so a missing or malformed variable crashes the process at start with a `ValidationError` naming the field, instead of at the first request. Know the precedence: constructor args, then environment, then `.env`, then a secrets directory (`_secrets_dir="/run/secrets"`, one file per field, which is how Docker and Kubernetes secret mounts arrive), then defaults. Never log a settings object without `SecretStr` on every credential, because `repr()` ends up in the customer's log aggregator.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Settings and Environment Variables

subtopics.name: Lifespan: build process-scoped clients once, tear down in reverse
subtopics.learn: `@asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI)` replaces the deprecated `@app.on_event`; before `yield` build the SQLAlchemy async engine, the `httpx.AsyncClient`, the Temporal client and any `ProcessPoolExecutor`, put them on `app.state` (or yield a dict that lands on `request.state`), and after `yield` close them in reverse (`await client.aclose()`, `await engine.dispose()`, `pool.shutdown()`). Lifespan runs once per worker process, so `--workers 4` means four pools of everything; an exception before `yield` sends ASGI `lifespan.startup.failed` and uvicorn exits non-zero, which is what you want when the DB URL is wrong. Do not put slow warmups (model download, a 30 s migration) in lifespan on Kubernetes unless the startup probe's `failureThreshold * periodSeconds` covers the worst case.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Lifespan Events

subtopics.name: Connection-pool arithmetic: engine pools x workers x replicas vs Postgres max_connections
subtopics.learn: `create_async_engine(url, pool_size=5, max_overflow=10, pool_timeout=30, pool_recycle=1800, pool_pre_ping=True)` allows up to 15 connections per process; the fleet total is (pool_size + max_overflow) x workers per pod x replicas, and it must stay under Postgres `max_connections` (default 100) minus `superuser_reserved_connections` and whatever Temporal workers, migrations and the dashboard also hold. Know the two symptoms apart: `QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out` in the app means this process exhausted its pool (a leaked session or a slow query), while `FATAL: too many connections` from Postgres means the fleet is oversubscribed. When replicas x workers grows, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front and drop per-process pools to 2 or 3; `pool_pre_ping` costs one round trip per checkout but survives an RDS failover without a restart.

resource.label: SQLAlchemy 2.0 docs: Connection Pooling

subtopics.name: Outbound httpx: one shared AsyncClient, explicit Timeout and Limits
subtopics.learn: Never build `httpx.AsyncClient()` per request; it defeats keep-alive and leaks sockets under load. Create one in lifespan with `timeout=httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=3.0, read=60.0, pool=5.0)` and `limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=100, max_keepalive_connections=20)`; the `pool` timeout fires when every connection is busy and is usually the first visible sign an upstream slowed down. For LLM calls the `read` timeout must exceed the provider's worst-case generation time, and the whole call still has to fit inside the load balancer's idle timeout, otherwise stream tokens instead of waiting. Wrap upstream calls in `asyncio.timeout()` at the handler level so a hung dependency cannot pin a request forever, and map `httpx.TimeoutException` to a 504 carrying the request id rather than a 500 with a traceback.

resource.label: HTTPX docs: Timeouts

subtopics.name: BackgroundTasks: the exact guarantee, and when to hand off to Temporal instead
subtopics.learn: `background_tasks.add_task(fn, *args)` runs after the response is sent, in the same process and on the same event loop (sync functions go to the threadpool); there is no retry, no persistence, no visibility from other workers, and a SIGTERM or OOM kill between response and completion loses it silently. Use it only for work whose loss is acceptable: audit-log fan-out, cache warm, a metrics push. Anything a customer would notice missing (billing event, callback webhook to their system, the compile job itself) goes to Temporal or a Redis stream with the enqueue inside the request's DB transaction (outbox pattern) so the 200 and the job are atomic. A background task that raises after the response is sent appears only in logs, so give it its own exception wrapper and a counter.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Background Tasks

subtopics.name: Bigger-applications layout with APIRouter and the service layer from topic 25
subtopics.learn: Split Kaupex into `app/main.py` (an app factory `create_app()` with lifespan, middleware and `include_router` calls), `app/api/v1/{tasks,compile,health}.py` (thin routers built as `APIRouter(prefix="/tasks", tags=["tasks"], dependencies=[...])`), `app/core/{settings,deps,logging}.py`, and `app/services/` plus `app/repositories/` from topic 25 that never import FastAPI. Routers obtain services through `Depends`, so the domain code stays importable in a plain pytest run with no ASGI app. Declare `responses={404: {"model": Problem}}` on routers so OpenAPI stays honest for the customer's client generator, and run the factory with `uvicorn 'app.main:create_app' --factory` so tests can build one app per settings object without import-time side effects.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Bigger Applications - Multiple Files

subtopics.name: Error handlers and middleware: problem responses, request ids, pure ASGI
subtopics.learn: Register `@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)` to return your `Problem` shape (422 with `detail` and `X-Request-ID`), `@app.exception_handler(Exception)` to return a 500 carrying the id but never the traceback, and map domain exceptions to 4xx in one place. Write middleware as pure ASGI (`async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send)`) rather than `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, which buffers responses, breaks streaming and background tasks in some version combinations, and hides exceptions from your handlers; middleware order is last-added-outermost. Build a request-id middleware that reads `X-Request-ID` or mints a UUID, stores it in a `ContextVar` for log records, and echoes it on the response; know that uvicorn's `--reset-contextvars` exists because contextvars can otherwise leak between requests on a keep-alive connection.

resource.label: Starlette docs: Middleware (BaseHTTPMiddleware limitations, pure ASGI middleware)

subtopics.name: Health endpoints that mean something: /healthz, /readyz, /startupz
subtopics.learn: `/healthz` (liveness) must only prove the process serves HTTP, with no DB or upstream checks, because a flaky Postgres would otherwise get every pod restarted in rotation. `/readyz` runs `SELECT 1` through the pool under a 1 s timeout, confirms the Temporal client is connected, and returns 503 with a JSON body naming the failing check; it also flips to 503 the moment SIGTERM arrives so the load balancer drains. `/startupz` covers migrations or model load, paired with a startup probe whose `failureThreshold * periodSeconds` exceeds the worst-case start. Exclude all three from access logs, metrics and SLIs (topic 20), mount them on a router with no auth, and know the probe knobs: `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds` (default 1 s, easily tripped under load), `failureThreshold`.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

subtopics.name: Process model and worker sizing: uvicorn --workers, gunicorn, or one process per pod
subtopics.learn: `uvicorn app.main:app --workers 4` (or `fastapi run --workers 4`) forks a supervisor plus N processes, each with its own event loop, pools and memory; gunicorn with `-k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker` adds `--max-requests`, `--graceful-timeout` and hot restart, but the FastAPI docs now steer you to uvicorn's own manager. On Kubernetes run one worker per container and scale with replicas, because requests and limits, HPA and readiness all reason per pod; use `--workers` on a single VM such as Kaupex on Hetzner under Compose. For async apps start at workers = cores, not the `2n+1` gunicorn folklore that assumes blocking workers, then measure RSS per worker (`ps -o pid,rss,cmd`) so N x RSS plus pools fits the container limit with headroom for LLM response buffers. `--limit-max-requests` with `--limit-max-requests-jitter` is the honest answer to slow memory growth you have not found yet.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Server Workers

subtopics.name: Uvicorn flags that decide production behaviour
subtopics.learn: Set these deliberately and keep them in version control: `--timeout-keep-alive` (default 5 s; must exceed the load balancer's idle timeout or the LB reuses a connection uvicorn just closed and the customer sees intermittent 502s), `--timeout-graceful-shutdown` (unset means wait indefinitely for in-flight requests), `--limit-concurrency` (returns 503 instead of queueing once connections plus tasks exceed N, your first load-shedding knob), `--backlog` (default 2048, the kernel accept queue), `--limit-max-requests` with jitter, `--proxy-headers` plus `--forwarded-allow-ips` (default trusts only 127.0.0.1, so behind an ingress `request.client.host` is wrong until you widen it), `--root-path`, `--loop uvloop --http httptools` for a real throughput gain, `--no-access-log` when the ingress already logs, `--log-config` pointing at your dictConfig, and `--timeout-worker-healthcheck` for the supervisor. Put them in the Dockerfile `CMD` so they are code-reviewed, not remembered.

resource.label: Uvicorn docs: Settings (official repo)

subtopics.name: Graceful shutdown end to end: SIGTERM, drain, in-flight, lifespan, grace period
subtopics.learn: On SIGTERM uvicorn stops accepting, closes idle keep-alive connections, waits for in-flight requests up to `--timeout-graceful-shutdown`, then runs lifespan shutdown. On Kubernetes the pod is removed from Endpoints concurrently with SIGTERM, so add `lifecycle.preStop: exec sleep 5` (or flip `/readyz` to 503 and sleep) so traffic stops arriving before the server stops accepting, and make `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30) exceed preStop + graceful timeout + lifespan teardown, otherwise SIGKILL cuts the longest LLM request mid-stream. Test it: start a 20 s request, `kubectl delete pod`, confirm the request completes and the ingress logs no 502; repeat with a 40 s request and watch it die so you know the ceiling. Gunicorn semantics differ (SIGTERM graceful, SIGINT and SIGQUIT quick), which matters when a customer runbook mixes them.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs: Pod Lifecycle (termination of Pods)

subtopics.name: Production Dockerfile for FastAPI: multi-stage uv, non-root, exec-form CMD and PID 1
subtopics.learn: Build with `uv` in a builder stage (`uv sync --frozen --no-dev` into `/app/.venv`), copy only the venv and source into `python:3.12-slim`, run as a non-root `USER` with a fixed UID, set `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` so shutdown logs are not lost in a stdout buffer, and finish with exec-form `CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", ...]`. Shell-form `CMD uvicorn ...` runs under `/bin/sh -c`, which does not forward SIGTERM, so every stop waits the full grace period and SIGKILLs a healthy server; if an entrypoint script must run migrations first it must end in `exec "$@"`, and use `--init` or `tini` when a `ProcessPoolExecutor` could leave zombies. Verify with `time docker stop <id>`: a correct image exits in under a second when idle, ten seconds means SIGTERM never reached uvicorn. The FastAPI docs now deprecate the old `uvicorn-gunicorn-fastapi` base image; write the Dockerfile yourself and be able to explain every line to a customer's platform team. Ties to topic 6 for SBOM, scanning and signing.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: FastAPI in Containers - Docker

subtopics.name: Behind a proxy or load balancer: root_path, forwarded headers, timeout alignment
subtopics.learn: When the customer mounts Kaupex under `/api/kaupex` at their ingress, `--root-path /api/kaupex` (or `FastAPI(root_path=...)`) makes the OpenAPI `servers` entry and `url_for` correct without touching routes; `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-For` are honoured only when `--proxy-headers` is on and the proxy's IP is in `--forwarded-allow-ips`, otherwise redirects go to `http://` and every log line shows the proxy's address. Align the timeouts along the path: LB idle (ALB 60 s, nginx `proxy_read_timeout` 60 s) must be shorter than uvicorn `--timeout-keep-alive` for connection reuse to be safe, and longer than your slowest handler or you stream. Reproduce the classic intermittent 502 locally with nginx `keepalive_timeout 10s` in front of uvicorn's 5 s keep-alive under k6 load, then fix it, so you recognise the pattern in a customer's environment on day one.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Behind a Proxy

subtopics.name: Testing the wiring: dependency_overrides, ASGITransport, lifespan in tests
subtopics.learn: Replace external edges with `app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(database_url=test_url, llm_api_key="x")` and an override of `get_session` that yields a session inside a transaction rolled back after each test. Use `httpx.AsyncClient(transport=ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test")` under pytest-anyio for async tests, and `with TestClient(app) as c:` when a test needs lifespan to have run, because a bare `TestClient(app)` outside the context manager skips startup and `app.state` is empty. Write one test asserting `/readyz` returns 503 when the DB override raises, one asserting the request-id header is echoed, and one asserting a handler exception leaves no row committed; these three catch most wiring regressions before a customer does.

resource.label: FastAPI docs: Testing Dependencies with Overrides

subtopics.name: Load-test the worker matrix with k6 and commit the decision
subtopics.learn: Write a k6 script using the `ramping-arrival-rate` executor against two endpoints (an IO-bound call to an LLM stub that sleeps 300 ms, and the CPU-bound compile step) with thresholds `http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500']` and `http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01']`. Run the matrix `--workers 1,2,4` x `--limit-concurrency 64,256,unset` on a 2 vCPU box, capturing p50, p95, p99, RPS, 503 count and per-worker RSS. Expect the IO-bound endpoint to scale with concurrency rather than workers, the CPU-bound one to scale with workers up to the core count, and an unset concurrency limit to turn saturation into timeouts instead of fast 503s. Record the winning configuration and the evidence table in `DEPLOY.md` beside the Dockerfile, and keep the script running in CI as a smoke threshold; topic 22 goes deeper on load and chaos.

resource.label: Grafana k6 docs

subtopics.name: Metrics across worker processes
subtopics.learn: With `--workers 4`, `prometheus_client`'s default registry is per process, so each scrape hits whichever worker accepted the connection and counters appear to move backwards. Either run one worker per pod (the Kubernetes default from the worker-sizing subtopic) or enable multiprocess mode: set `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR`, serve `/metrics` from a fresh `CollectorRegistry()` with `multiprocess.MultiProcessCollector(registry)`, and call `multiprocess.mark_process_dead(pid)` on worker exit. Gauges are the trap in this mode; pick `multiprocess_mode="livesum"` or `"max"` deliberately per gauge. With OpenTelemetry instead, `FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app, excluded_urls="healthz,readyz,metrics")` keeps probe noise out of traces and the `http.server.duration` histogram that topic 21 builds dashboards on.

outcomes: You can demonstrate, with 10 concurrent curls and a `py-spy dump`, why a blocking call inside an `async def` handler stalls every request in the process, and fix it three ways (async client, `def`, `run_in_executor` with a process pool), choosing correctly between IO-bound and CPU-bound work.

You can start Kaupex with `KAUPEX_DATABASE_URL` unset and have it exit non-zero within one second with a `ValidationError` naming the field, and show that every credential in the settings `repr()` prints as `**********`.

You can write the connection budget for a deployment as (pool_size + max_overflow) x workers x replicas against Postgres `max_connections` and prove it by running the fleet at full pool while reading `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity`.

You can `kubectl delete pod` (or `docker stop`) during a 20 s in-flight request and show that the request completes with 200, the pod leaves Endpoints before uvicorn stops accepting, and shutdown finishes inside the grace period, with the ordering visible in timestamped logs.

You can produce a k6 results table for workers {1,2,4} x `--limit-concurrency` {64,256,unset} on a 2 vCPU host with p95, RPS, 503 rate and RSS per worker for an IO-bound and a CPU-bound endpoint, and defend the chosen configuration in writing.

You can implement `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/startupz` such that a Postgres outage flips readiness to 503 within 2 s without a single liveness restart, with all three excluded from access logs, metrics and SLIs.

You can write a pure-ASGI request-id middleware and problem-shaped exception handlers so every 4xx and 5xx from Kaupex carries `X-Request-ID` and no response ever contains a traceback, verified by tests using `dependency_overrides` and `ASGITransport`.

You can explain to a customer's platform team in under five minutes why the same image runs one uvicorn process per pod on their cluster but `--workers 4` on the Hetzner VM, and what changes in memory, metrics scraping and probe behaviour if they choose the other.
failureModes: An `async def` handler calls the sync OpenAI client for a 20 s completion; one slow prompt from one tenant freezes the worker's event loop, readiness probes time out at their 1 s default, kubelet restarts pods in rotation, and the customer reports that 'the API dies every morning at nine'.

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is left at 30 while `--timeout-graceful-shutdown` is unset and compile requests take 45 s; every rolling deploy SIGKILLs in-flight compilations, clients see connection resets, and their retries double the load on the freshly started pods.

uvicorn's default `--timeout-keep-alive 5` sits behind an ALB with a 60 s idle timeout; the ALB reuses a connection uvicorn closed a millisecond earlier and roughly 0.1% of requests return 502 with nothing in the application logs, which takes a week to attribute.

`pool_size=5, max_overflow=10` with `--workers 4` across six replicas plus Temporal workers exceeds RDS `max_connections` on a db.t3.medium; Postgres refuses with `FATAL: too many connections`, and because readiness checks the DB, every pod leaves service at the same moment.

A yield dependency commits after the response is sent under the default `scope="request"`; the commit fails on a unique-constraint violation, the client already received 201, and the 'created' task never exists, surfacing weeks later as a phantom-ID support ticket.

Shell-form `CMD uvicorn ...` in the Dockerfile means SIGTERM reaches `/bin/sh`, not uvicorn; every stop waits the full grace period then SIGKILLs, lifespan teardown never runs, and httpx connections and PgBouncer server slots leak until `server_idle_timeout` reaps them.

`BackgroundTasks` is used to send the customer's job-complete webhook; an OOM kill between the 200 and the task loses the callback, their system waits forever, and there is no queue to inspect because the work only ever existed in one process's memory.
interviewQuestions: Kaupex p99 latency triples every weekday at 09:00 while CPU sits at 15% and the database is idle. Walk me through diagnosis on a running pod with only `kubectl exec`, `py-spy` and the uvicorn logs: what are your top three hypotheses, and how does each one show up?

Design settings and secrets handling for a FastAPI service a customer will run in three places: a developer laptop, a staging namespace, and an air-gapped production cluster where secrets arrive as mounted files. What is the precedence order, how does a wrong value fail, and how do tests override it?

We are moving from 3 replicas with `--workers 4` to 12 replicas with one worker each on the customer's EKS cluster. What changes for connection pools, metrics scraping, probes, memory and graceful shutdown, and what would you set differently in each place?

A rolling deploy produces about eight seconds of 502s at the ingress each time a pod terminates, yet the application logs show every request completed with 200. Explain the race, the two fixes, and how you would prove which one closed it.

When would you reach for `BackgroundTasks`, a Temporal workflow, or a Redis stream for work that happens after the request returns? Give a concrete example of each and the failure the wrong choice produces in production.

Compare `--limit-concurrency`, the anyio thread limiter, the SQLAlchemy pool size and the load balancer's connection limit as load-shedding points. Under sustained overload, which one do you want to trip first, and why?

A customer's security team insists on `BaseHTTPMiddleware` to audit every request and response body. Explain what that does to streaming LLM responses and background tasks, and propose a pure-ASGI design that still satisfies the audit requirement.
28.proofOfWork: A public repository, `kaupex-api-prod`, that a reviewer can run cold with `make up && make load && make chaos`. `make up` starts the FastAPI service, Postgres and an LLM stub under Compose and includes a recorded three-second clip of the service exiting non-zero with a `ValidationError` when `KAUPEX_DATABASE_URL` is removed. `make load` runs the k6 matrix (workers 1/2/4 x `--limit-concurrency` 64/256/unset) against the IO-bound and CPU-bound endpoints on a 2 vCPU host and writes `LOAD_REPORT.md` with p50/p95/p99, RPS, 503 rate and RSS per worker, ending in a one-paragraph decision that is reflected verbatim in the Dockerfile `CMD`. `make chaos` starts a 20 s in-flight request, sends SIGTERM, and a pytest asserts that the request returned 200, `/readyz` flipped to 503 before accepting stopped, lifespan teardown logged `engine disposed`, and total shutdown fit inside a 30 s budget; it then rebuilds with a shell-form `CMD` to demonstrate the ten-second hang and SIGKILL. Alongside sits a `k8s/` folder with a Deployment carrying all three probes, `preStop`, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, requests and limits, plus a one-page `RUNBOOK.md` a customer SRE could follow to size workers and pools for their node type and Postgres `max_connections`.

29.topic: Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims
29.why: The first two questions a customer's security team asks before a pilot may touch real data are 'how do our people log in with our IdP' and 'prove tenant A can never see tenant B', and the FDE is the person who answers both on the call and then makes them true in code that week. You do not get to choose the IdP (it will be Entra ID, Okta, Ping or a SAML-only ADFS), so you need a model of OAuth2 and OIDC precise enough to wire any of them in a day, explain PKCE and cookie attributes to a reviewer without hand-waving, and diagnose an `iss` mismatch from a token pasted into a ticket. Authorization bugs are the ones that end contracts: a cross-tenant read is a breach notification and a renewal conversation, not a bug ticket.
prerequisites: HTTP redirects, the `Authorization` header, cookies and TLS termination with `X-Forwarded-Proto`/`X-Forwarded-Host` from 'Networking' (topic 2): OIDC is a choreography of 302s, and the issuer URL changes the moment a proxy sits in front of the IdP.
FastAPI `Depends`, settings and lifespan from 'FastAPI in production' (topic 26): the verifier is a dependency and the JWKS client is lifespan state built exactly once.
Repository and domain layering from 'Production Python architecture' (topic 25): `tenant_id` becomes a mandatory argument on every repository method, sourced from the verified principal.
Docker Compose from 'Docker internals' (topic 5) to run Keycloak plus Postgres locally, and a working DefenderMate dashboard with at least one page and one API route to put behind login.

Cryptography at the level of 'private key signs, public key verifies', SHA-256, and base64url versus base64; you do not implement RSA here, you need to know why HS256 is wrong when the IdP is a third party.
Postgres transactions and `SET LOCAL` (row-level security is previewed here and deepened in 'PostgreSQL at depth', topic 29, and 'Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems', topic 30).

subtopics.name: Authorization code grant, parameter by parameter
subtopics.learn: Trace the front channel and the back channel separately: the browser is sent to `GET {authorization_endpoint}?response_type=code&client_id=&redirect_uri=&scope=openid%20profile&state=&nonce=&code_challenge=&code_challenge_method=S256`, comes back to `redirect_uri?code=&state=`, and only then does your server (never the browser) `POST {token_endpoint}` with `grant_type=authorization_code&code=&redirect_uri=&code_verifier=` plus client authentication (`client_secret_basic` header or `private_key_jwt`). Know the invariants the AS enforces and you rely on: the code is single-use and short-lived (the spec recommends at most 10 minutes; Keycloak's client login timeout defaults to one minute), `redirect_uri` must exactly string-match a registered value, and `state` must round-trip unchanged or the callback is treated as a CSRF attempt. Be able to say what each of the four roles (resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server) maps to in DefenderMate: the analyst, the BFF, Keycloak, the API.

resource.label: RFC 6749 section 4.1 - Authorization Code Grant

subtopics.name: PKCE: what it computes and which attacks it stops
subtopics.learn: Generate a `code_verifier` of 43-128 characters from the unreserved set `[A-Za-z0-9-._~]`, derive `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier)))` with `code_challenge_method=S256` (never `plain`), send the challenge on the authorize request and the verifier on the token request; the AS stores the challenge with the code and refuses the exchange if the hash of the verifier does not match. Understand the two attacks it kills: authorization-code interception on public clients (a malicious mobile app registering the same custom URI scheme receives the code but not the verifier) and authorization-code injection on any client (attacker swaps their code into your session), which is why RFC 9700 and OAuth 2.1 require PKCE even for confidential clients that already hold a secret. Practise the 90-second version for a customer's security reviewer: 'we prove at exchange time that the same party that started the login is finishing it, using a one-time secret that never left our server'.

resource.label: RFC 7636 - Proof Key for Code Exchange

subtopics.name: The grant zoo and what OAuth 2.1 removed
subtopics.learn: Map every grant to a legitimate use and know which are dead: authorization code plus PKCE for anything with a human; `grant_type=client_credentials` for service-to-service with no user; device authorization (RFC 8628: `device_code`, `user_code`, poll with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`) for CLIs and kiosks; `grant_type=refresh_token` to extend sessions. Explain why implicit (`response_type=token`, token in the URL fragment, no client authentication, leaks through history and Referer) and resource-owner password (`grant_type=password`, teaches users to type IdP passwords into apps, breaks MFA and federation) were removed from OAuth 2.1, and that Keycloak's 'Direct access grants' checkbox is the password grant and must stay off on production clients. Be ready to push back when a customer's legacy integration insists on the password grant: offer client credentials or device flow instead.

resource.label: oauth.net - OAuth 2.1

subtopics.name: OIDC on top of OAuth: ID token, nonce, discovery, sub
subtopics.learn: Adding `scope=openid` turns an OAuth delegation into an authentication event: the token response gains an `id_token` (a JWT whose `aud` is your client_id, asserting who authenticated and when via `auth_time`, `acr`, `amr`) while the `access_token` remains the credential for the API and may be opaque. Fetch `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` and read `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `jwks_uri`, `end_session_endpoint`, `userinfo_endpoint`, `code_challenge_methods_supported` and `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`; for Keycloak the issuer is `https://<host>/realms/<realm>` and `iss` must match byte-for-byte, including scheme and no trailing slash. Generate a `nonce` per login, store it in the pre-login session, and reject an ID token whose `nonce` claim differs (replay defence). Key the local user row on (`iss`, `sub`) because `sub` is the only claim guaranteed stable and unique per issuer; `email` can change, be unverified (`email_verified=false`) or be reassigned, and `preferred_username` is display text.

resource.label: OpenID Connect Core 1.0

subtopics.name: JWT structure and the non-negotiable validation checklist
subtopics.learn: Read a JWS compact token as `BASE64URL(header).BASE64URL(payload).BASE64URL(signature)`; the header carries `alg`, `typ`, `kid`; the payload carries the registered claims `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti`. Implement validation in this order and be able to justify each step: pin the allowed algorithms server-side (`algorithms=['RS256']` or ES256; never let the token's `alg` decide, which kills `alg=none` and the RS256-to-HS256 key-confusion attack where the public key is used as an HMAC secret), resolve the key by `kid` from a trusted JWKS (ignore `jku`, `x5u` and embedded `jwk` headers), verify the signature, then `iss` exact, `aud` contains your API's identifier, `exp` and `nbf` with a leeway of at most 30-60 seconds, and require `sub`, `exp`, `iat` to be present. Know that JWS is signed-not-encrypted (anyone can read the payload, so no secrets in claims), JWE is encrypted and rare for access tokens, and that base64url differs from base64 (`-_` not `+/`, no padding), which is why a naive `base64 -d` fails on tokens.

resource.label: RFC 8725 - JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

subtopics.name: JWKS fetching, kid-based caching and key rotation
subtopics.learn: The IdP publishes public keys at `jwks_uri` as `{"keys":[{"kty":"RSA","kid":"...","use":"sig","alg":"RS256","n":"...","e":"AQAB"}]}` (Keycloak: `/realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/certs`); your verifier must cache keys by `kid`, refetch once on an unknown `kid` (rate-limited, no more than about once a minute) so scheduled rotation causes zero 401s, and keep serving cached keys if the IdP is unreachable rather than failing the read path closed. Use `jwt.PyJWKClient(jwks_uri, cache_keys=True, lifespan=300)` with `get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)` in Python, or `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(jwks_uri), {cooldownDuration, cacheMaxAge})` with `jwtVerify` from `jose` in Node; construct the client once at startup (FastAPI lifespan, topic 26), never per request. Rehearse a rotation in Keycloak: Realm settings -> Keys -> add a new `rsa-generated` provider with a higher priority, watch the JWKS document list both keys, confirm new tokens carry the new `kid`, then remove the old provider only after the longest token lifetime has elapsed.

resource.label: PyJWT usage docs - retrieving signing keys from a JWKS endpoint

subtopics.name: Token lifetimes, refresh rotation, revocation and introspection
subtopics.learn: Set the access-token lifetime to 5-15 minutes and accept that a stateless JWT cannot be recalled before `exp`; everything longer-lived is a refresh token that is exchanged with `grant_type=refresh_token` and rotated on every use (Keycloak: Realm settings -> Tokens -> 'Revoke Refresh Token' ON with 'Refresh Token Max Reuse' 0), so a replayed refresh token is detected and the whole token family is revoked. Use RFC 7009 `POST {revocation_endpoint}` with `token` and `token_type_hint=refresh_token` on logout, and RFC 7662 `POST {introspection_endpoint}` (authenticated as the resource server) to get `{"active":true,"scope":...,"exp":...}` for the few operations where 'revoked 30 seconds ago' must be honoured (tenant deletion, API-key rotation) instead of stretching every token to a day. Know that `offline_access` produces offline tokens in Keycloak for background jobs with their own idle rules, and that SSO Session Idle/Max and Client Session Idle/Max cap what any refresh can extend.

resource.label: RFC 7009 - OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation

subtopics.name: Browser clients: the BFF pattern, cookie attributes and CSRF
subtopics.learn: Decide where tokens live before writing a line of frontend: a SPA holding tokens in `localStorage` hands them to any XSS payload, holding them in memory still exposes them to same-origin script, so the browser-based-apps BCP recommends the backend-for-frontend pattern: the server does the code exchange, stores access and refresh tokens server-side (Redis, topic 31) keyed by an opaque session id, and the browser holds only `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<random>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`. Know exactly what each attribute does: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from `document.cookie`, `Secure` restricts it to TLS, the `__Host-` prefix forbids `Domain=` and forces `Path=/`, and `SameSite=Lax` blocks cross-site POST cookies but still sends on top-level GET navigations, so state-changing routes must also check `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`, or use a double-submit token. Remember the 4096-byte cookie cap: never put a Keycloak access token carrying roles and group paths into a cookie; store the token server-side and give the browser only the session id.

resource.label: IETF draft - OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications

subtopics.name: Standing up Keycloak: realm, clients, scopes, roles, export and import
subtopics.learn: Run `docker run -p 8080:8080 -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=... quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.x start-dev`, create realm `defendermate`, a confidential OIDC client `defendermate-bff` (Client authentication ON, Standard flow ON, Direct access grants OFF, exact Valid redirect URIs, Web origins set, PKCE method S256 under Advanced) and a second client `defendermate-api` that exists so it can appear in `aud`. Distinguish realm roles from client roles (`realm_access.roles` vs `resource_access.<client>.roles` in the token), composite roles, groups with role mappings, and client scopes (default vs optional: `roles`, `profile`, `email`, `offline_access`). Make it reproducible: `kc.sh export --dir /opt/keycloak/data/export --realm defendermate --users realm_file`, commit the JSON, and start with `--import-realm` reading `/opt/keycloak/data/import/` in Compose so a fresh checkout logs in with no clicking. For production run `start` not `start-dev`: `KC_DB=postgres`, `KC_DB_URL`, `KC_HOSTNAME`, `KC_PROXY_HEADERS=xforwarded`, and `KC_HTTP_ENABLED=true` only behind a TLS-terminating proxy.

resource.label: Keycloak - Getting started with Docker

subtopics.name: Putting tenant and audience claims into the token
subtopics.learn: By default a Keycloak access token's `aud` is `account`, not your API, so add an 'Audience' protocol mapper (Included Client Audience = `defendermate-api`, Add to access token ON) or your `aud` check fails the day you enable it. Model the tenant one of four ways and be able to argue the trade-off: a `tenant_id` user attribute surfaced by a 'User Attribute' mapper (simplest; one tenant per user), groups as tenants via a 'Group Membership' mapper (`/tenants/acme`, full path ON), Keycloak Organizations (26+) exposing an `organization` claim through the `organization` client scope for many-to-many membership, or one realm per tenant (hardest isolation, N discovery URLs, N admin surfaces). For users in several tenants prefer a token bound to one tenant at a time (a tenant picker that re-authorizes) over a `tenants: [...]` array plus an `X-Tenant-Id` header; if you must use the header, the API intersects it with the claim and never trusts it alone. Keep tokens small: turn 'Full scope allowed' OFF on the client, map only the roles the API needs, and never map every group path, or a 50-group admin gets a 6 KB token.

resource.label: Keycloak Server Administration Guide (protocol mappers, roles, groups, organizations)

subtopics.name: Bearer token usage and the JWT access-token profile
subtopics.learn: Accept tokens only in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (RFC 6750); never from a query string (leaks into access logs, Referer and browser history) and never from a cookie on a pure API. Return `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="defendermate", error="invalid_token", error_description="..."` for missing, malformed, expired or badly-signed tokens, and `403` with `error="insufficient_scope", scope="alerts:write"` when the token is valid but lacks scope; the distinction matters because well-behaved clients refresh and retry on 401 and must not retry on 403. Read RFC 9068 so you recognise a well-formed JWT access token: header `typ: at+jwt`, required `iss`, `exp`, `aud`, `sub`, `client_id`, `iat`, `jti`; checking `typ` is a cheap way to refuse an ID token presented to the API, the single most common frontend mistake.

resource.label: RFC 6750 - OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Usage

subtopics.name: The FastAPI verifier dependency and the Principal object
subtopics.learn: Build one dependency and put nothing auth-related anywhere else: `HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)` extracts the header, `jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)` resolves the key, `jwt.decode(token, key.key, algorithms=['RS256'], audience='defendermate-api', issuer=settings.issuer, leeway=30, options={'require': ['exp', 'iat', 'sub']})` validates, and the claims are mapped into a frozen `Principal(sub, tenant_id, roles, scopes, sid)` dataclass. Catch `jwt.ExpiredSignatureError`, `jwt.InvalidAudienceError`, `jwt.InvalidIssuerError` and `jwt.PyJWKClientError` separately and turn each into a 401 with the matching `error_description`, so field debugging is one log line rather than a stack trace. Layer authorization as further dependencies (`require_role('tenant_admin')`, `require_scope('alerts:write')`) that take `Principal` via `Depends` and raise 403; pass `Principal` to handlers and repositories as a parameter, never through a global or a thread-local. Same shape in Node for the DefenderMate API: `jose.jwtVerify(token, remoteJwks, {issuer, audience, algorithms: ['RS256']})` in a middleware that attaches `req.principal`.

resource.label: FastAPI tutorial - Security

subtopics.name: RBAC design: roles in the token, permissions in the API
subtopics.learn: Keep the IdP's vocabulary coarse (`tenant_admin`, `analyst`, `viewer`, `integration`) and map roles to fine permissions (`alerts:read`, `alerts:reclassify`, `hubspot:write`, `tenant:manage`) inside the API in one table or module, so adding a permission is a deploy, not an IdP change plus a token reissue. Separate the three questions a request must answer: authentication (who: `sub`), delegation (what the client was allowed to ask for: `scope`) and authorization (what this user may do here: roles -> permissions), and check scope and permission both when the caller is a third-party client. Make every role tenant-relative: `tenant_admin` means admin of the tenant in the token, never of all tenants; a platform-operator role for your own staff must be a distinct realm role the API handles explicitly and audits loudly. Deny by default, centralise decisions in `require(perm)` so there is no `if 'admin' in roles` scattered through handlers, and know where RBAC stops working: per-object sharing and delegation ('let this contractor see only alerts from source X'), which is ABAC or relationship-based (Zanzibar-style OpenFGA/SpiceDB) territory.

resource.label: OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet

subtopics.name: Tenant enforcement in the API and the data layer (BOLA)
subtopics.learn: Broken object-level authorization is the number one API risk because it is the default outcome of writing `SELECT * FROM alerts WHERE id = :id`: every repository method takes `tenant_id` as a mandatory first argument sourced from `Principal`, every query carries `AND tenant_id = :tenant_id`, and any tenant identifier in the URL or body is compared against the token and rejected on mismatch. Decide and document 404 vs 403 on mismatch: 404 hides existence and defeats ID enumeration, 403 is more debuggable; pick one per API and test it. Add Postgres row-level security as the second lock: `ALTER TABLE alerts ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE alerts FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON alerts USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);` with the API running `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = :tenant_id` inside each transaction as a database role that is not the table owner (owners bypass RLS unless FORCE is set; superusers and `BYPASSRLS` roles always bypass). Carry `tenant_id` explicitly into background work (Temporal activity inputs, Kafka message keys) because there is no request principal there. Write the authorization-matrix test first: two tenants x every role x every route asserting the exact status code, plus URL-swap and header-spoof cases.

resource.label: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 - API1 Broken Object Level Authorization

subtopics.name: Machine identities: client credentials, private_key_jwt, token exchange
subtopics.learn: Service-to-service calls use `grant_type=client_credentials` and the token's `sub` is the service account (Keycloak: `service-account-<client-id>`, after enabling 'Service accounts roles' on the client); prefer `private_key_jwt` client authentication (RFC 7523, `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, the client signs a short-lived JWT with its own key) or mTLS (RFC 8705) over a shared `client_secret` that ends up in a `.env` file. When a worker must act for a user after the user's token has expired, do not stash the user's access token in a queue: use RFC 8693 token exchange (`grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, `subject_token`, `audience`, `requested_token_type`) at the boundary, or store only (`sub`, `tenant_id`) and run the job under the service identity with the tenant passed explicitly and the authorization decision re-evaluated at execution time. Give each integration its own client so revocation is per-integration, keep secrets in the secret manager (topics 15 and 62), and rotate by creating the new credential before deleting the old one.

resource.label: RFC 8693 - OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange

subtopics.name: Logout, sessions and back-channel invalidation
subtopics.learn: There are three sessions to end: the IdP's SSO session (Keycloak cookies `KEYCLOAK_IDENTITY` and `KEYCLOAK_SESSION`), your BFF session, and any outstanding tokens. RP-initiated logout redirects to `{end_session_endpoint}?id_token_hint=<id_token>&post_logout_redirect_uri=<uri>&client_id=<id>`, and Keycloak requires that URI to be listed under 'Valid post logout redirect URIs'. Register a 'Backchannel logout URL' on the client: when the IdP ends a session (admin kills it, or the user logs out of another app) Keycloak POSTs a logout token (a JWT whose `events` claim contains `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, plus `sid` and `sub`), which you verify like any JWT and use to delete every BFF session with that `sid`, so store the ID token's `sid` next to the session when you create it. Know that front-channel logout (iframes) breaks under third-party cookie blocking, that deleting your own cookie leaves the SSO session alive so the next visit silently re-logs the user in, and that already-issued access tokens keep working until `exp` unless the API consults a `sid` denylist or introspects.

resource.label: OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0

subtopics.name: Threat model: what RFC 9700 requires and the attack behind each rule
subtopics.learn: Read the OAuth Security BCP as a checklist and map each item to a config line you can point at: exact-string `redirect_uri` matching (no wildcards, no prefix match, no `*` in Keycloak's Valid redirect URIs); PKCE on every code flow; `state` bound to the browser session; `iss` in the authorization response (RFC 9207) to stop mix-up attacks when a client trusts more than one AS; audience-restricted access tokens (`aud`, or the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter) so a token issued for the wiki cannot be replayed at DefenderMate; refresh tokens rotated or sender-constrained (DPoP, RFC 9449, or mTLS); no tokens in URLs; no open redirectors on your own domain that an attacker can chain into a registered `redirect_uri`. Add the JWT-layer items from your verifier: pinned `alg`, `kid` treated as an opaque lookup key (never interpolated into a path or SQL), `jku`/`x5u` ignored, `typ` checked. For each control be able to state the concrete attack it stops in one sentence, because that is exactly the question the customer's AppSec team asks.

resource.label: RFC 9700 - Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

subtopics.name: Enterprise IdPs in the field: Entra ID, Okta, Google, and brokering
subtopics.learn: You will not choose the IdP; the customer has Entra ID, Okta, Ping or Google Workspace, and sometimes a SAML-only ADFS. Decide between trusting their issuer directly (their `iss`, their JWKS, their claim names in your verifier) and brokering through Keycloak as an identity provider (Keycloak federates to their OIDC or SAML IdP, maps attributes with Identity Provider Mappers, and your API trusts exactly one issuer regardless of customer). Learn the Entra specifics that break integrations: `tid` is their directory id (not your app tenant), `oid` is the stable user id while `sub` is pairwise per app, v1.0 and v2.0 tokens have different `iss` (`https://sts.windows.net/{tid}/` vs `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0`) and `aud` formats (`api://<app-id>` vs the client id), app roles arrive in `roles` only after assignment in the enterprise application, and a user in more than 200 groups gets an overage indicator (`_claim_names`/`_claim_sources`) instead of `groups`. Okta gotchas: the org authorization server issues access tokens you cannot validate locally (use a custom authorization server), and `groups` needs a claim filter. Provision users just-in-time on first login keyed on (`iss`, `sub`), never on email, and ask for SCIM or a nightly directory sync for deprovisioning.

resource.label: Microsoft Entra - Access token claims reference

subtopics.name: Debugging auth in a customer environment
subtopics.learn: Start with `curl -s $ISSUER/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .` to confirm the issuer the IdP believes it is, then decode without verifying (`python3 -c 'import jwt, sys; print(jwt.decode(sys.argv[1], options={"verify_signature": False}))' "$TOKEN"`) and compare `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `typ` and `kid` against what the API expects; never paste a production token into a web decoder. Know the canonical messages and their fixes: `invalid_redirect_uri` (scheme, host, port, trailing slash, `localhost` vs `127.0.0.1` differing from the registered value); `invalid_grant` at the token endpoint (code reused, older than the client login timeout, `redirect_uri` differs from the authorize request, PKCE verifier mismatch, refresh token already rotated); 'Invalid audience' (missing Audience mapper); `iss` mismatch (Keycloak behind a proxy issuing `http://keycloak:8080/...` because `KC_HOSTNAME` and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS` are unset); 'token used before issued' or instant expiry (clock skew on the customer VM: check `chronyc tracking`, then add `leeway`); CORS failure on `/token` from a SPA (Web origins); `unauthorized_client` (grant type disabled on the client). Turn on Keycloak's login and admin event logging (Realm settings -> Events -> Save events) to read the server-side reason instead of guessing from the client's generic error.

outcomes: You can stand up Keycloak with Docker Compose, create the realm, the confidential BFF client and the audience-restricted API client, export the realm JSON, and have a fresh checkout log in end to end via `--import-realm` in under 15 minutes without opening the admin console.

You can draw the authorization code + PKCE + BFF sequence from memory with every parameter (`response_type`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, `code`, `code_verifier`) and, for each, name the attack it defeats in one sentence.

You can write the FastAPI verifier dependency (pinned `RS256`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` with leeway of at most 30 seconds, required claims, RFC 6750 `WWW-Authenticate` errors) and show a test suite in which `alg=none`, HS256 key confusion, wrong `aud`, wrong `iss`, expired, future `nbf`, tampered payload and an ID token presented as an access token are each rejected with the expected `error` value.

You can pass an authorization-matrix test (2 tenants x 3 roles x every route) with zero cross-tenant reads, including URL tenant swaps and `X-Tenant-Id` header spoofing, then delete the application-level `WHERE tenant_id` filter and show Postgres RLS still returns zero foreign rows.

You can explain to a non-engineer security reviewer in under three minutes why the browser holds only an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` session cookie, why PKCE is on for a confidential client, and what is and is not revocable before `exp`, and have them repeat it back correctly.

You can rotate Keycloak's realm signing key under load and show a flat 401 line in Grafana because the verifier refetches JWKS on an unknown `kid`, then state the safe ordering (publish new key, wait the longest token lifetime, remove old key).

You can take an Entra ID or Okta token a customer pastes into a ticket and, within a minute, name why the API rejects it (v1 vs v2 `iss`, `api://` vs client-id `aud`, unassigned app roles, groups overage, opaque org-server token) and the exact setting that fixes it.

You can implement refresh-token rotation and back-channel logout so that replaying a used refresh token revokes the family and an admin-initiated Keycloak logout kills the BFF session on the next request, and demonstrate both with curl.
failureModes: Keycloak behind the customer's ALB mints tokens with `iss` = `http://keycloak:8080/realms/prod` because `KC_HOSTNAME` and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS` were never set; every token fails the API's issuer check after the go-live DNS cutover, and the on-call 'fix' is to remove `issuer=` from `jwt.decode`, which stays in production for a year.

The API validates signature and `exp` but not `aud` because Keycloak's default token says `aud: account` and nobody added the Audience mapper; a token minted for the customer's internal wiki client in the same realm is accepted by DefenderMate's API and a contractor with wiki access lists alert data.

`tenant_id` is read from an `X-Tenant-Id` header 'because the frontend already sends it' and the token claim is never compared; the customer's pentest changes the header and reads another tenant's HubSpot write history, which is a breach notification and a renewal conversation, not a bug.

The IdP rotates its signing key on the first Sunday of the quarter; the API fetched JWKS once at startup with no refetch on unknown `kid`, so every pod returns 401 at 03:00 until someone restarts the deployment, and the incident is misdiagnosed as an IdP outage for 40 minutes.

A Temporal workflow stores the analyst's access token in its input so an activity can call the API 40 minutes later; it is expired, so the realm's Access Token Lifespan is bumped to 24 hours to make the demo work, and every leaked token is now a day-long credential.

The local user table is keyed on email; the customer's Okta admin changes an employee's address during a domain migration, JIT provisioning creates a second account, the old one keeps `tenant_admin`, and the audit trail for a disputed reclassification is split across two identities nobody can reconcile.

Full group paths and every client role are mapped into the access token and the BFF stores the whole token in the session cookie; for the customer's IT director, who is in 60 groups, the cookie exceeds 4096 bytes, the browser drops it, and only that one person is stuck in a login loop, on demo day.
interviewQuestions: A customer's security reviewer asks why your confidential backend uses PKCE when it already authenticates with a client secret. Explain the authorization-code injection attack, what `state` and `nonce` already cover, and what PKCE adds on top.

DefenderMate will be sold to 30 customers, each with their own IdP: Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace and one on-prem ADFS that only speaks SAML. Design login and tenant-claim handling. Compare trusting 30 issuers directly with brokering through your own IdP on `sub` stability, key rotation, JIT provisioning, offboarding, and blast radius when one customer's IdP is compromised.

After a Keycloak upgrade, about 3 percent of API calls return 401 for ten minutes every six hours and then recover on their own. Walk me through the diagnosis: what you look at in the token, in the API logs and in the IdP, and what the fix is.

Your API is stateless and validates JWTs locally. The customer's compliance team requires that a terminated employee loses access within 60 seconds. What do you change, what does each change cost in latency and operational complexity, and where do you refuse to go?

A user belongs to three tenants. Design the claim shape and the API contract for choosing the active tenant so that no client can escalate into a tenant it is not a member of. Where does the check live, what do you return on mismatch (403 or 404) and why, and how does this survive into background jobs?

A frontend developer is sending the ID token to your API 'because it has the user's email in it' and it works in dev. Explain what is wrong, what breaks first in production, and the fix on both the Keycloak side and the client side.

A pentest report says 'JWT accepted with alg=HS256 signed with the server's public key'. Explain the vulnerability class, how a verifier ends up vulnerable, and the exact code and configuration that make it impossible; then name the other two JWT header fields you also refuse to honour.
29.proofOfWork: A public `auth-kit` directory in the DefenderMate repository that a customer's security reviewer could read in fifteen minutes and a new engineer could run in five. It contains: (1) a `docker-compose.yml` bringing up Keycloak, Postgres, the API and the BFF with a committed `realm-export.json` that reproduces two tenants (acme, globex), three roles, the Audience mapper and the `tenant_id` mapper, imported automatically with `--import-realm`; (2) a `SECURITY-REVIEW.md` written for a non-vendor reviewer with a sequence diagram of authorization code + PKCE + BFF, token lifetimes, cookie attributes, logout behaviour, key-rotation handling and an explicit list of what is and is not revocable before `exp`, where every claim in the document links to the test that proves it; (3) an authorization-matrix suite (`pytest -m authz`) that mints real tokens from Keycloak for 2 tenants x 3 roles and asserts the status code of every route, plus negative tests for `alg=none`, HS256 key confusion, wrong `aud`, wrong `iss`, expired, future `nbf`, tampered payload, an ID token used as an access token, `X-Tenant-Id` spoofing and URL tenant swaps, and an RLS test that drops the application filter and proves zero foreign rows; (4) a recorded key-rotation drill in which realm keys are rotated while `k6` traffic runs, with the Grafana panel showing a flat 401 line and the verifier's JWKS refetch visible in logs; and (5) a five-minute recording in which you explain PKCE and the BFF cookie model to a non-engineer using only the diagram, followed by them repeating it back.

30.why: Customer platform teams, internal tools, agent tooling and nearly every vendor SDK (including the MCP reference SDK) are TypeScript-first, so a Python-first FDE who cannot read a tsconfig, diagnose an ESM import error or explain why a Node service stalls loses the platform team's trust in week one. The fastest way to build an integration or demo UI over a customer's API that survives their next backend deploy is a client whose types are generated from their OpenAPI document and whose boundaries are validated at runtime. This topic gets you to the point where you ship a small, tested Node service and a typed MCP client without asking the customer's frontend lead for help.

subtopics.name: Event loop phases and what actually blocks it
subtopics.learn: Trace one tick: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check (`setImmediate`), close; the microtask queue drains between every macrotask and `process.nextTick` runs before promise microtasks, which is why a recursive `nextTick` starves I/O. Know the sync calls that freeze every concurrent request on the single thread: `JSON.parse` of a multi-MB body, `fs.readFileSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`, catastrophic regex backtracking, and a tight `for` over a large array. Measure with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` p99 and `node --cpu-prof`; offload to `worker_threads` or a child process. The libuv threadpool (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, default 4) covers only fs, `dns.lookup`, zlib and crypto, so `dns.lookup` under load serialises behind slow file reads.

resource.label: Node.js Learn - The Node.js Event Loop, Timers, and process.nextTick()

subtopics.name: A tsconfig that catches real bugs
subtopics.learn: Start from `strict: true` and add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (indexing returns `T | undefined`, which kills a whole class of customer-data crashes), `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `noImplicitOverride`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`. For a Node service choose `module: "NodeNext"` and `moduleResolution: "NodeNext"` (forces explicit `.js` extensions in relative imports), `target: "ES2022"`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` so type-only imports are `import type` and cannot leak into runtime, `isolatedModules` for esbuild/tsx compatibility, `sourceMap` plus `node --enable-source-maps` for readable production stack traces, and `declaration` + `declarationMap` only for libraries. Understand `skipLibCheck` as a speed trade you accept knowingly, and that `tsc --noEmit` is the CI type gate while emit is a separate concern.

resource.label: TypeScript TSConfig Reference - strict (the strict-mode family of checks)

subtopics.name: ESM vs CommonJS and the exports map
subtopics.learn: `"type": "module"` in package.json makes `.js` files ESM; `.mjs`/`.cjs` override per file. ESM has no `__dirname`, `__filename` or `require`: use `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` and `createRequire(import.meta.url)`. Diagnose `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` (CJS requiring an ESM-only package; Node 22 lifts this for synchronous ESM graphs), `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (missing `.js` extension or a deep import the package does not export), and `Cannot use import statement outside a module`. Read an `exports` map with `import`/`require`/`types`/`default` conditions and understand that `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` resolves only because the SDK exports that subpath; use the `imports` field (`#internal/*`) for in-package aliases instead of tsconfig `paths`. Know the dual-package hazard: two copies of a module, two `instanceof` identities.

resource.label: Node.js API - Modules: Packages (type, exports, imports, conditions)

subtopics.name: Narrowing, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness
subtopics.learn: TypeScript is structural, so `unknown` (not `any`) is the type of anything crossing a boundary, and you narrow it with `typeof`, `in`, `instanceof`, equality and truthiness checks. Model MCP `content` items as a discriminated union on the `type` literal (`text` | `image` | `audio` | `resource_link` | `resource`) and `switch` on it with `default: assertNever(item)` returning `never`, so a new variant fails compilation instead of silently falling through. Write type predicates `(x): x is ToolResult` and assertion functions `asserts x is Config`; use `satisfies` to check a literal against a type without widening it and `as const` to keep literal types. Know where narrowing does not survive: inside callbacks, across `await`, and on `obj[dynamicKey]`.

resource.label: TypeScript Handbook - Narrowing

subtopics.name: Generics, mapped and conditional types you will actually use
subtopics.learn: Generic functions with constraints (`<T extends { id: string }>`), default type parameters, and when inference from arguments beats an explicit type argument. Build the four tools you need daily: `keyof` and indexed access `T[K]`; mapped types `{ [K in keyof T]-?: ... }` with `readonly`/`?` modifiers and `as` key remapping; conditional types with `infer` (this is how `Awaited`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters` are defined) and their distribution over unions; template literal types for event and route names. Derive `ToolName = keyof Tools` and `ToolInput<N extends ToolName> = z.infer<Tools[N]["input"]>` so adding a tool is one line. Recognise a type that has become a liability: `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` instantiation counts and `--generateTrace` when the editor slows down.

resource.label: TypeScript Handbook - Creating Types from Types

subtopics.name: Runtime validation with Zod at every boundary
subtopics.learn: Types are erased at compile time, so every value from `JSON.parse`, `process.env`, HTTP bodies, stdin and tool results must be parsed, not cast. Use `z.object` with the default strip behaviour understood (unknown keys are silently dropped), `.strict()` when drift must be loud, `.passthrough()` when you forward opaque data; `z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])` for tagged payloads; `z.coerce.number()` for env vars; `.transform` to normalise at the edge. Prefer `.safeParse` returning `{ success, data | error }` in request paths so validation never throws; surface `error.issues[].path` and `message` as customer-readable text. `z.infer<typeof Schema>` is the single source of truth, never a hand-written interface next to the schema. Validate at boundaries only; interior code trusts its types.

resource.label: Zod - Defining schemas (z.object strict/passthrough, discriminatedUnion, coerce, transform)

subtopics.name: Generating TypeScript from FastAPI's OpenAPI document
subtopics.learn: FastAPI serves `/openapi.json`; set `generate_unique_id_function` so `operationId` becomes `{tag}-{name}` instead of `read_items_items__get`, because every generator turns operationId into a method name. Run `npx openapi-typescript http://localhost:8000/openapi.json -o src/api/schema.d.ts` and read the output: a `paths` interface keyed by route and method with `parameters`, `requestBody` and `responses` by status code, and `components["schemas"]` for Pydantic models. Know the mapping rules: `Optional[str]` with a default is optional and nullable, `str | None` without default is required and nullable, `Literal` becomes a union of literals, `dict` becomes `Record<string, unknown>`. Commit the generated file and add a CI step that regenerates and runs `git diff --exit-code` so backend drift fails the build.

resource.label: FastAPI - Generate Clients (OpenAPI, operationId, client generation)

subtopics.name: A typed HTTP client with openapi-fetch
subtopics.learn: `createClient<paths>({ baseUrl })` gives you `client.GET("/items/{id}", { params: { path: { id } } })` where path, query, headers and body are all typed from the generated schema and a typo in a route is a compile error. The response is `{ data, error, response }` discriminated by status, so a 2xx `data` and 4xx `error` have different types and you cannot forget the failure branch. Add middleware with `onRequest` for `Authorization` and `X-Request-Id` headers and `onResponse` for retry-on-429 with `Retry-After`; pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` on every call. Understand why this beats heavyweight codegen (orval, openapi-generator) for an FDE: zero runtime schema, a few kB, and regeneration is one command. Wrap it in a domain module so callers never see raw paths.

resource.label: openapi-fetch API reference - createClient, fetch options, middleware

subtopics.name: Promises, cancellation and timeouts done right
subtopics.learn: `Promise.all` rejects on the first failure and leaves the rest running; `allSettled` for fan-out where partial results matter; `Promise.race` for timeouts leaks the loser, so use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, timeoutSignal])` and pass the signal into `fetch`, `setTimeout` from `timers/promises`, `events.once(emitter, "x", { signal })` and your own loops via `signal.throwIfAborted()`. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process (`--unhandled-rejections=strict|warn|none`), so a `.then` without `.catch` or an un-awaited async call in an event handler is a latent outage. Bound concurrency with a semaphore or `p-limit` instead of `Promise.all` over ten thousand items; consume async iterables with `for await`.

resource.label: MDN - AbortController and AbortSignal

subtopics.name: Streams, backpressure and newline-delimited JSON
subtopics.learn: Node streams: `Readable`, `Writable`, `Transform`, `highWaterMark` (16 KiB in bytes, 16 items in `objectMode`), `write()` returning `false` and waiting for `drain`. Never chain `.pipe()` in production; use `pipeline()` from `stream/promises`, which propagates errors and destroys every stream on failure. `fetch().body` is a Web `ReadableStream`, not a Node stream; bridge with `Readable.fromWeb` and `Readable.toWeb`, decode with `TextDecoderStream`. For the MCP stdio transport, read `process.stdin` line by line with `readline.createInterface({ input })` and `for await (const line of rl)`, parse each line as one JSON-RPC message, and write responses with `process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(msg) + "\n")`; logs go to stderr because any stray byte on stdout corrupts the protocol stream.

resource.label: Node.js API - Stream (pipeline, backpressure, Web Streams interop)

subtopics.name: HTTP servers, keep-alive and graceful shutdown
subtopics.learn: `http.createServer` timeouts you must set consciously: `server.keepAliveTimeout` (default 5 s; must exceed the load balancer idle timeout, typically 60 s on an ALB, or the LB reuses a socket Node already closed and the customer sees 502s), `server.headersTimeout`, `server.requestTimeout`, `maxHeadersCount`. Graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM`: stop accepting with `server.close()`, call `server.closeIdleConnections()`, give in-flight requests a deadline, then `process.exit(0)`; the Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` must exceed that deadline and readiness must flip first. Global `fetch` is undici: configure an `Agent` with `connections`, `keepAliveTimeout`, `headersTimeout` and `bodyTimeout` rather than trusting defaults. Trust `X-Forwarded-For` only behind a proxy you control.

resource.label: Node.js API - HTTP (server timeouts, close, closeIdleConnections)

subtopics.name: Errors: unknown catch, cause chains and system codes
subtopics.learn: With `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `catch (e)` is `unknown`; narrow with `instanceof Error` and wrap anything else. Chain context with `new Error(msg, { cause: e })` and define `class ToolCallError extends Error` with a `code` and `toolName`, setting `this.name` so logs and `instanceof` work. Node system errors carry `code` (`ECONNRESET`, `ECONNREFUSED`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `ENOTFOUND`, `EPIPE`, `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`), so branch on `code`, never on message text. `process.on("uncaughtException")` and `"unhandledRejection"` exist to log and exit, not to keep running in a corrupted state. Use a result type `{ ok: true, value } | { ok: false, error }` for expected failures (validation, not found) and throw only for bugs and infrastructure faults. `--enable-source-maps` and `Error.stackTraceLimit` for usable traces from `dist/`.

resource.label: Node.js API - Errors (system error codes, cause, captureStackTrace)

subtopics.name: MCP wire protocol: JSON-RPC, lifecycle and transports
subtopics.learn: Every MCP message is JSON-RPC 2.0: requests carry `jsonrpc`, `id`, `method`, `params`; responses carry `result` or `error` with `code` and `message`; notifications have no `id`. Lifecycle: client sends `initialize` with `protocolVersion`, `capabilities` and `clientInfo`; server replies with its `capabilities` (`tools`, `resources`, `prompts`, `logging`, each optionally with `listChanged`) and `serverInfo`; client sends `notifications/initialized`; only then may it call `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/read`, `prompts/get`. stdio transport is one message per line on stdout with stderr free for logs. Streamable HTTP uses a single endpoint, POST for client messages, optional `text/event-stream` responses, `Mcp-Session-Id` for session affinity and `Last-Event-ID` for resumption. Standard error codes -32700 to -32603, server range -32000 to -32099; a tool result with `isError: true` is a tool-level failure, not a protocol error.

resource.label: Model Context Protocol Specification - Lifecycle (2025-06-18)

subtopics.name: Building the DefenderMate client on the TypeScript SDK
subtopics.learn: Import `Client` from `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` and a transport: `StdioClientTransport({ command, args, env })` spawns the server as a child process; `StreamableHTTPClientTransport(new URL(endpoint), { requestInit: { headers } })` for a remote server. `await client.connect(transport)` performs the handshake; then `client.listTools()`, `client.callTool({ name, arguments })`, `client.listResources()`, `client.readResource({ uri })`, `client.getServerCapabilities()`. Pass per-request `RequestOptions` with `timeout` and `resetTimeoutOnProgress` for long tools; subscribe to `notifications/tools/list_changed` and re-list. Always `await client.close()` in `finally` so the child process does not orphan. Wrap all of this in a `DefenderMateClient` class exposing one typed method per tool so consumers never touch raw JSON-RPC.

resource.label: Model Context Protocol - TypeScript SDK (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Typing tool inputs and outputs end to end
subtopics.learn: MCP `inputSchema` and optional `outputSchema` are JSON Schema, so author one Zod schema per DefenderMate tool and emit JSON Schema with Zod 4's `z.toJSONSchema(schema)`; write a test that fetches `tools/list` from the running server and asserts each emitted schema deep-equals the server's `inputSchema`, which turns silent contract drift into a red test. Validate every `callTool` result: `content` as a discriminated union on `type`, `isError`, and `structuredContent` parsed with the tool's output schema. Implement `callTyped<N extends ToolName>(name: N, args: ToolInput<N>): Promise<ToolOutput<N>>` on top of the SDK so the compiler rejects a wrong argument shape and the runtime rejects a wrong response shape. Know the conversion edges: Zod `.optional()` vs `.nullable()`, `z.record`, `z.enum` to `enum`, and unrepresentable types like `z.date()` and transforms.

resource.label: Zod - JSON Schema conversion (z.toJSONSchema)

subtopics.name: Testing with Vitest: transport mocks, fake timers, type tests
subtopics.learn: `vitest.config.ts` with `test.include`, `coverage.provider: "v8"` and thresholds; `describe`/`it`/`expect`, `vi.fn()`, `vi.spyOn`, and `vi.mock("module", factory)` with its hoisting rules. Mock the transport, not the network: implement the SDK `Transport` interface with an in-memory fake that returns canned JSON-RPC responses so `Client` runs the real handshake against your fixtures. Use `vi.useFakeTimers()` and `await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(ms)` to test exponential backoff and `AbortSignal.timeout` paths in milliseconds of wall time. Add type-level tests with `expectTypeOf<ToolInput<"scan">>().toEqualTypeOf<{ target: string }>()` and run `vitest --typecheck` so a regenerated schema that changes a type fails a test. A contract test in `globalSetup` starts the FastAPI server and hits it through the generated client; `--reporter=junit` for CI.

resource.label: Vitest Guide - Mocking (vi.mock hoisting, spies, fake timers)

subtopics.name: Dev loop, build and run: tsx, tsc, native type stripping
subtopics.learn: Development: `tsx --watch src/main.ts` (esbuild under the hood, no type checking, so keep `tsc --noEmit --watch` running beside it). Node 22.6+ runs `.ts` directly with `--experimental-strip-types`, and Node 23.6+ strips by default; only erasable syntax is allowed (no `enum`, `namespace`, parameter properties) unless you pass `--experimental-transform-types`, and the `erasableSyntaxOnly` tsconfig flag enforces this at compile time. Production: `tsc -p tsconfig.build.json` to `dist/` and `node --enable-source-maps dist/main.js`, or bundle with `esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --platform=node --format=esm --outfile=dist/main.js` (externalise native modules) to sidestep the `.js` extension problem and ship one file.
