For a CLI, `bin` in package.json plus `#!/usr/bin/env node`. Know `NODE_OPTIONS` and `--max-old-space-size` when a container OOMs at 2 GB while the heap default is lower.

resource.label: Node.js API - Modules: TypeScript (type stripping, transform types)

subtopics.name: Dependency hygiene and npm supply chain
subtopics.learn: `npm ci` installs exactly the lockfile, deletes `node_modules` first and fails if `package.json` and lock disagree; `npm install` re-resolves and mutates the lock, so CI and Dockerfiles use `ci`. Commit `package-lock.json` (lockfile v3) and pin the runtime with `engines` plus `.nvmrc` or `.node-version`. `npm audit --omit=dev` for what ships; `overrides` to force a patched transitive version; `npm ls <pkg>` to find who pulls a dependency; `--ignore-scripts` to defuse install-time payloads in untrusted environments. Pin the MCP SDK to an exact version while the protocol is moving and upgrade deliberately with a changelog read. Verify publisher provenance with `npm view <pkg> dist.integrity` and prefer packages published with `--provenance`. pnpm's strict `node_modules` layout is the cheap way to kill phantom imports.

resource.label: npm Docs - npm ci

subtopics.name: Type-aware ESLint rules that prevent outages
subtopics.learn: Flat config `eslint.config.js` using `tseslint.config(...tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked)` with `languageOptions.parserOptions.projectService: true` so rules can see types. The rules that pay for themselves on day one: `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` (an un-awaited promise is a swallowed error and a future crash), `no-misused-promises` (an async function passed where a void callback is expected, e.g. `server.on("request", async ...)` or an Express handler), `switch-exhaustiveness-check`, `no-unnecessary-condition`, `consistent-type-imports`, `no-unsafe-argument`. Run `eslint . --max-warnings 0` in CI and let Prettier own formatting only. Know how to introduce these on a legacy codebase: enable as `warn`, fix the hottest paths, flip to `error` per directory.

resource.label: typescript-eslint - no-floating-promises rule

subtopics.name: Config, structured logging and debugging a live Node process
subtopics.learn: Parse `process.env` once at boot with `z.object({ DEFENDERMATE_URL: z.string().url(), TIMEOUT_MS: z.coerce.number().default(30000), ... }).parse(process.env)` into a frozen typed `config`, so a missing variable fails fast with a list of every issue rather than `undefined` three calls deep. Log JSON lines to stdout with pino: `pino({ level, redact: ["req.headers.authorization", "*.apiKey"] })`, child loggers carrying `requestId` and `toolName`, `pino-pretty` only in development. Debug a running service with `node --inspect` and `chrome://inspect`, `--inspect-brk` for start-up bugs, `--cpu-prof` and `--heap-prof` for profiles written to cwd, `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` trended over an hour for leaks, `NODE_DEBUG=http,net` when a connection mysteriously hangs.

resource.label: Node.js Learn - Debugging Node.js

outcomes: You can take a customer's FastAPI `/openapi.json`, generate `paths` and `components` types with openapi-typescript, and produce an openapi-fetch client where a backend field rename fails `tsc` in CI instead of failing a demo.

You can write a `DefenderMateClient` that connects over stdio or Streamable HTTP, completes the `initialize` handshake, lists tools, calls a tool with Zod-validated arguments and results, and closes cleanly in `finally` without orphaning the child process.

You can diagnose `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`, `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and `Cannot use import statement outside a module` in under five minutes by reading `package.json` `type` and `exports` and the tsconfig `module` and `moduleResolution` settings.

You can prove a Node service is blocking its event loop with `monitorEventLoopDelay` or `--cpu-prof`, name the offending synchronous call, and move it to a worker thread or a stream with a measured before/after p99.

You can write a Vitest suite that mocks the MCP transport rather than the network, uses fake timers to test retry and backoff, asserts generated types with `expectTypeOf`, and enforces coverage thresholds in CI.

You can enable `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `no-floating-promises` on an existing codebase and explain to the customer's team which category of production bug each newly surfaced error represents.

You can shut a Node HTTP server down on SIGTERM behind an ALB with zero 502s, with `keepAliveTimeout`, load balancer idle timeout, drain deadline and Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` correctly ordered and verified under load.
You can explain to a Python team, in their vocabulary, that Zod is Pydantic, `tsc --noEmit` is mypy, `npm ci` is a locked `pip install -r`, Vitest is pytest, and precisely where each analogy breaks.
failureModes: The service passes every type check but crashes nightly with `ERR_UNHANDLED_REJECTION` because one `client.callTool()` inside an event handler was never awaited; `no-floating-promises` would have flagged it on the first commit.

An MCP server prints a `console.log` startup banner to stdout; the client's JSON-RPC parser hits `Starting DefenderMate...` as its first line, throws, and every tool call fails with an opaque parse error while the server process looks perfectly healthy.

The TypeScript client was generated from `/openapi.json` once in March; the backend made `tenant_id` required in June, the client kept sending `undefined`, and the resulting 422s were swallowed by a `catch (e) { console.error(e) }` for six weeks.

Behind an ALB with a 60 s idle timeout, `server.keepAliveTimeout` is left at Node's 5 s default, so the ALB reuses sockets Node has already closed and the customer sees intermittent 502s that never reproduce in a load test against the pod directly.

`JSON.parse` on a 40 MB tool result blocks the event loop for 800 ms, every concurrent SSE stream stalls, the liveness probe times out, and Kubernetes restarts the pod in the middle of the executive demo.

Results are validated with Zod's default strip mode, so the server's new `warnings` field is silently dropped and nobody notices for a month that the model is no longer being told when a scan returned degraded data.

CI runs `npm install` instead of `npm ci`, resolves a fresh transitive MCP SDK version with a protocol bump, and the handshake fails only in staging because every developer machine still has the old lockfile-resolved tree.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through everything that happens between `node dist/main.js` and the first `tools/call` response of an MCP client: module resolution, the initialize handshake, transport framing, and where each class of failure would surface and how you would recognise it.

A customer's Node service handles 200 requests per second comfortably, then p99 jumps to three seconds whenever one specific report endpoint is hit, with nothing in the logs. How do you find the cause, what are the three most likely culprits, and what is the fix for each?

Design the type layer for a client that calls twelve MCP tools whose schemas are owned by another team. Where do types come from, where exactly do you validate at runtime, and what fails in CI on the day they change a schema without telling you?

Explain the difference between `Promise.race` against a timeout promise and `AbortSignal.timeout` passed into `fetch`. What leaks in the first approach, and how would you cancel a chain of three dependent async calls when the user closes the tab?

We have a mixed codebase with `require` in some files and `import` in others, and the build intermittently fails with `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`. What are the realistic options, and what would you recommend for a team that publishes a library consumed by both CommonJS and ESM customers?

You are handed a TypeScript service with `strict: false` and roughly four hundred `any`s, and the customer wants it hardened in two weeks without pausing feature work. What sequence of compiler flags and lint rules do you introduce, in what order, and how do you keep the team from reverting them?

How would you drain a Node HTTP server in Kubernetes behind an ALB so a rolling deploy produces zero 502s? Name every timeout that has to be ordered, the order, and how you would verify it before telling the customer it is safe.
30.proofOfWork: A public repository `defendermate-ts-client` containing: (1) `src/api/schema.d.ts` generated from DefenderMate's `/openapi.json` with a `npm run gen && git diff --exit-code` CI step that fails on drift; (2) a `DefenderMateClient` class wrapping the MCP TypeScript SDK with a generic `callTyped<N>()` whose argument and return types derive from per-tool Zod schemas, plus a test asserting that each `z.toJSONSchema` output deep-equals the server's `tools/list` `inputSchema`; (3) a Vitest suite at or above 85 percent coverage that mocks the transport, uses fake timers to verify exponential backoff on `-32000` errors and `AbortSignal.timeout` paths, and includes `expectTypeOf` type tests run under `vitest --typecheck`; (4) `docs/EVENT_LOOP.md` with a captured `--cpu-prof` profile showing a deliberately introduced `JSON.parse` stall, its fix via a worker thread, and before/after `monitorEventLoopDelay` p99 numbers; and (5) a Dockerfile plus a SIGTERM drain test proving zero failed requests during a rolling restart under k6, with `keepAliveTimeout`, drain deadline and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` documented in one table. The README explains every design choice in terms a Python-first team can map to Pydantic, mypy, pip lockfiles and pytest.

31.topic: PostgreSQL at depth: planner, indexes, EXPLAIN, locks, transactions, window functions
31.why: On almost every engagement the customer's Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL, or a VM their DBA guards) is the shared dependency your feature lands on, and the new access patterns you introduce (per-tenant filters, JSONB metadata, event tables, job queues, embeddings side tables) are what turns 'the AI thing is slow' into a P1 with your name on it. You will be asked to read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a screen-share in front of their DBA and propose an index they will accept, and to ship a schema change to a multi-billion-row table with no maintenance window. Knowing the planner, MVCC and the lock table cold is what lets you say 'this will take 40 seconds and block nothing' and be right.
prerequisites: SQL fluency: joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, basic DDL and DML; the pgexercises Basic and Joins sets should feel like warm-up, not learning

A running Dokeo with real tables from topics 25 and 26 (Production Python architecture; FastAPI in production), plus the ability to generate 5-10M rows of skewed seed data with generate_series so plans actually change
Topic 14 (AWS data: RDS Postgres) for parameter groups, shared_preload_libraries on managed Postgres, Performance Insights and where slow-query logs land
Topic 3 (Performance and troubleshooting on a single box) so 'random_page_cost', 'page cache' and 'spilled to disk' map to iostat, vmstat and real hardware
Docker: run postgres:16 with a named volume and custom postgresql.conf flags (-c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements,auto_explain), psql with \timing, \x and \watch
Topic 21 (Observability) is helpful, not required, for wiring pg_stat_statements and lock waits into Grafana

subtopics.name: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE line by line
subtopics.learn: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, SETTINGS, WAL, FORMAT TEXT|JSON) and read a plan tree bottom-up and inner-to-outer: cost=startup..total, rows and width are estimates; actual time=first..last, rows and loops are measured, and a child's actual rows must be multiplied by loops to get the true row count. Hunt for the first node where estimated rows diverges from actual by more than 10x, for Filter and Rows Removed by Filter (rows fetched then thrown away), for Buffers: shared hit vs read vs dirtied and temp read/written (a Sort or Hash that spilled), and for Planning Time vs Execution Time. Know that EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement, so wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, that TIMING adds overhead on high-node-count plans (use TIMING OFF for a fair measurement), and that BUFFERS is only on by default from PostgreSQL 18. Paste the same plan into explain.depesz.com or explain.dalibo.com when it is more than a screen long, but be able to read raw text when the customer's laptop has no internet.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Using EXPLAIN

subtopics.name: The cost model and the planner knobs that actually matter
subtopics.learn: Understand the arbitrary-unit cost model: seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0 (drop to 1.1 on SSD/EBS gp3 or the planner will avoid index scans on big tables), cpu_tuple_cost 0.01, cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005, cpu_operator_cost 0.0025, and effective_cache_size (a hint about OS cache, default 4GB, set to ~50-75% of RAM) which makes index scans look cheaper without allocating anything. Know work_mem (per sort/hash node, per query, default 4MB; set per session with SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB' for a known-heavy report rather than globally) and hash_mem_multiplier, and when JIT (jit_above_cost 100000) adds seconds of compile time to a plan that would have run in milliseconds. Use enable_seqscan/enable_nestloop/enable_hashjoin = off only as a diagnostic to see the plan the optimizer rejected and what it costed it at, never in production, and read the SETTINGS block in EXPLAIN to see which non-default knobs were in play on the customer's box.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Query Planning configuration (runtime-config-query)

subtopics.name: Statistics, ANALYZE and the anatomy of a misestimate
subtopics.learn: Read pg_stats for a column: null_frac, n_distinct (negative means a fraction of rows), most_common_vals/most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds and correlation (near 1 or -1 means index range scans are cheap sequential IO). Know that default_statistics_target 100 samples 30000 rows and gives 100 MCVs/histogram buckets, that a skewed tenant_id column with 5000 distinct values needs ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN tenant_id SET STATISTICS 1000 followed by ANALYZE, and that autovacuum only re-analyzes after autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor (10%) of the table changes, so a freshly bulk-loaded table is planned on empty-table stats until you run ANALYZE yourself. Fix correlated-column misestimates (city implies country, status implies is_closed) with CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON a, b FROM t, and recognise the unfixable ones: functions on columns, JSONB path expressions and inequality on parameters all default to fixed selectivity guesses (0.005, 0.333) regardless of data.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Statistics Used by the Planner

subtopics.name: B-tree anatomy and the column-order rule
subtopics.learn: Picture the B-tree: a balanced tree of 8kB pages whose leaf level is a doubly linked list of sorted (key, ctid) entries, so every lookup is O(log n) page reads to a leaf followed by a sequential walk along leaves, and every row visit from the leaf is a random heap read. Internalise the concatenated-index rule: the index is sorted by column 1, then column 2 within equal column 1, so equality predicates go first and the single range or ORDER BY column goes last; (tenant_id, created_at) serves WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at with one range walk, while (created_at, tenant_id) has to scan every tenant's rows in the date range and filter. Distinguish Index Cond (used to navigate the tree) from Filter (evaluated on each row fetched) in the plan, and know why a leading column not in the WHERE clause makes the index unusable except for the rarely-chosen skip-scan-like full index scan.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - Concatenated Indexes (column order)

subtopics.name: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap scans and when each fires
subtopics.learn: Predict the scan type from selectivity and correlation: Seq Scan for anything past roughly 5-10% of a large table (and always for tiny tables), Index Scan for a handful of rows, Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan for the middle ground where the planner sorts matching ctids by page to turn random IO into sequential IO (look for Recheck Cond and Heap Blocks: exact=N lossy=M; lossy means the bitmap exceeded work_mem and whole pages were rechecked). Understand Index Only Scan needs every referenced column in the index (add non-key columns with INCLUDE) and a visibility map bit set for each page, otherwise it reports Heap Fetches: N and costs the same as an Index Scan; freshly loaded or heavily updated tables have unset VM bits until VACUUM runs, which is why the same index is fast on Monday and slow on Friday. Know how BitmapAnd/BitmapOr combine two single-column indexes, and why a composite index still beats them for a hot query.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes

subtopics.name: Partial, expression, covering and ordered indexes
subtopics.learn: Build each shape and prove it is used: a partial index CREATE INDEX ... ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' is tiny and stays hot, but the planner only picks it when it can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate, so a parameterised status = $1 executed as a generic plan will skip it; an expression index ON users (lower(email)) is required when the ORM emits WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) (a plain index on email is useless there, see Use The Index Luke's 'obfuscation' chapter); INCLUDE (payload_size) turns an Index Scan plus heap fetch into an Index Only Scan for a read-heavy path without widening the key. Match index order to ORDER BY: a B-tree can be walked backwards, so (tenant_id, created_at) serves ORDER BY created_at DESC, but ORDER BY created_at DESC, id ASC needs (created_at DESC, id ASC) explicitly, and NULLS FIRST/LAST must match too. Check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan before dropping an index the customer swears is used.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Partial Indexes

subtopics.name: GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash: indexing JSONB, text search, arrays and time series
subtopics.learn: Choose the non-B-tree index by operator: GIN on a jsonb column with the default jsonb_ops supports @>, ?, ?|, ?& and key-existence, while jsonb_path_ops is roughly 3x smaller and faster but only supports @>; a B-tree on an extracted path ((metadata->>'customer_id')) beats both for equality on one known key. Use GIN with pg_trgm's gin_trgm_ops for LIKE '%term%' and ILIKE (the only way those get an index) and GIN on a stored tsvector generated column for full-text search; know GIN's fastupdate pending list (gin_pending_list_limit, 4MB) makes inserts cheap but the first query after a burst pays to merge it. Use BRIN (pages_per_range 128) on append-only, physically ordered columns like created_at on an events table: a few kB instead of GBs, but useless once updates and deletes scramble physical order. GiST is for ranges, geometry and EXCLUDE constraints (no overlapping bookings); hash indexes are equality-only and rarely worth it over B-tree.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Index Types

subtopics.name: Join algorithms: Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join and how misestimates pick the wrong one
subtopics.learn: Know the three algorithms and their sweet spots: Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan is ideal when the outer side is small (a handful of rows) and catastrophic when the planner estimated rows=1 but got 50000, because the inner scan runs 50000 times (loops=50000 in the plan); Hash Join builds an in-memory hash on the smaller input (Batches: 1 is good, Batches: 16 means it spilled to disk because the build side exceeded work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier); Merge Join needs both inputs sorted and wins when indexes already provide the order or both sides are huge. Read Hash Cond, Merge Cond and Join Filter, and know the planner only considers all join orders up to join_collapse_limit/from_collapse_limit (8) and switches to the genetic optimizer above geqo_threshold (12) tables, so a 14-table ORM join is planned heuristically. Recognise parallel plans (Gather, Parallel Seq Scan, Parallel Hash Join; max_parallel_workers_per_gather default 2) and why a query that ran in parallel on your laptop runs serially on a 2-vCPU RDS instance.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - The Join Operation

subtopics.name: Sorting, LIMIT, top-N and keyset pagination
subtopics.learn: Read Sort Method: quicksort Memory: NkB (fine), external merge Disk: NkB (spilled: raise work_mem for the session or provide the order via an index), and top-N heapsort (a LIMIT let the sort keep only N rows). Know that an index whose order matches ORDER BY lets a LIMIT 20 stop after 20 index entries (Index Scan with no Sort node at all), that Incremental Sort (PG13+) can exploit a partial prefix match (Presorted Key), and that OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 must produce and discard 100000 rows every page so admin exports and infinite scroll get slower per page until they time out. Replace it with keyset pagination: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 with WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) using row-value comparison, which walks the (created_at DESC, id DESC) index directly and is stable under concurrent inserts.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - Fetching the next page (keyset pagination)

subtopics.name: Finding the slow queries: pg_stat_statements, auto_explain and the slow log
subtopics.learn: Enable shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain' (a restart; on RDS via the parameter group) and CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements, then rank by total_exec_time (what burns the box), by mean_exec_time (what users feel) and by calls (N+1 candidates), reading shared_blks_read, temp_blks_written and wal_bytes per statement; normalised queryid lets you join to auto_explain output and to pg_stat_activity.query_id when compute_query_id = auto. Configure auto_explain.log_min_duration = '250ms', log_analyze = on, log_buffers = on, log_timing = off (timing on every node is expensive), log_nested_statements = on for functions, log_format = json and sample_rate < 1 on busy systems, so the plan that was slow in production is captured with the parameter values that made it slow, which is exactly what you cannot reproduce by hand. Set log_min_duration_statement, log_lock_waits = on and log_temp_files = 0 as the baseline on every customer database you touch, and call pg_stat_statements_reset() at the start of a measurement window rather than reading lifetime averages.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - pg_stat_statements

subtopics.name: MVCC: tuple versions, snapshots, dead tuples and HOT updates
subtopics.learn: Understand that every row version carries xmin (creating transaction), xmax (deleting or updating transaction) and ctid, that a snapshot decides visibility per transaction, and that UPDATE never modifies in place: it writes a new version and marks the old one dead, so an update-heavy table is a delete-heavy table. Know the HOT (heap-only tuple) optimisation: when no indexed column changes and the page has free space (leave room with ALTER TABLE t SET (fillfactor = 90)), the new version is chained inside the page and no index entries are written; watch n_tup_hot_upd vs n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables to see whether an 'updated_at' index is silently defeating it. Understand why a transaction left open for hours (state = 'idle in transaction' in pg_stat_activity, backend_xmin far behind) pins every dead tuple since it began across the entire database, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and know the 2^31 transaction-ID wraparound story well enough to explain autovacuum_freeze_max_age and why 'database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound' is the outage you never want to be on-site for.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Concurrency Control: Introduction (MVCC)

subtopics.name: VACUUM, autovacuum tuning and diagnosing bloat
subtopics.learn: Know the trigger math: autovacuum vacuums a table when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) times reltuples, so a 500M-row table waits for 100M dead rows; fix it per table with ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50000) and, for append-only tables, autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor so the visibility map gets set. Understand that autovacuum is throttled by autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2ms) and cost_limit (200), that three workers (autovacuum_max_workers) can be starved by one huge table, and that cancelled autovacuums (log line 'canceling autovacuum task') come from DDL and lock conflicts. Measure bloat with pgstattuple (dead_tuple_percent, free_percent) or the pg_stat_user_tables n_dead_tup/n_live_tup ratio, watch pg_stat_progress_vacuum during a long run, and know your repair options ranked by lock cost: plain VACUUM (no exclusive lock, does not return space to the OS), REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY for index bloat, pg_repack for online table rewrite, VACUUM FULL only with an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and a maintenance window.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Routine Vacuuming

subtopics.name: Isolation levels, lost updates, write skew and the 40001 retry contract
subtopics.learn: Demonstrate each level in two psql sessions: READ COMMITTED (the default) takes a fresh snapshot per statement, so a read-modify-write in application code (SELECT balance; compute; UPDATE) loses updates, while a single UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 is safe because UPDATE re-reads the latest committed version of the row; REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot per transaction and aborts a writer that touches a row modified since with SQLSTATE 40001; SERIALIZABLE adds SSI predicate locks (SIReadLock in pg_locks) and detects write skew such as two on-call doctors both reading 'two on call' and both leaving. Know the retry contract: any code that uses REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE must catch 40001 and rerun the whole transaction with backoff, and be able to choose between the pessimistic tools (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE, and how FK checks take FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row) and optimistic ones (a version column with UPDATE ... WHERE version = $1, or SERIALIZABLE) based on contention and transaction length.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Transaction Isolation

subtopics.name: Lock modes, the lock queue, deadlocks and reading pg_locks
subtopics.learn: Memorise the table-level lock ladder and which statement takes which: SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE take ROW EXCLUSIVE, VACUUM and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, plain CREATE INDEX takes SHARE (blocks writes), and most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE which conflicts with everything including SELECT. Understand the killer property: lock requests queue FIFO, so an ALTER TABLE waiting behind one long SELECT blocks every subsequent SELECT on that table too, which is why every migration session must SET lock_timeout = '3s' and retry rather than wait. Diagnose live with pg_stat_activity (wait_event_type = 'Lock', wait_event relation/transactionid/tuple), pg_blocking_pids(pid) to find the head of the chain, pg_locks joined on pid and granted = false, and pg_cancel_backend/pg_terminate_backend to break it; reproduce a deadlock (two sessions updating rows in opposite order) and read the deadlock_timeout (1s) detector's error, which names both queries. Implement a job queue correctly with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 and know when NOWAIT or advisory locks (pg_try_advisory_xact_lock) are the better tool.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Explicit Locking

subtopics.name: Zero-downtime schema changes on live tables
subtopics.learn: Build a checklist of what rewrites, what scans and what is metadata-only: ADD COLUMN with a constant DEFAULT (even NOT NULL) is instant since PG11 (attmissingval), a volatile default such as clock_timestamp() rewrites the table; adding NOT NULL to an existing column scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so instead ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT c (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, concurrent writes allowed), then SET NOT NULL which PG12+ skips the scan for because a valid CHECK exists; ADD FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE follows the same pattern; varchar(n) to text is metadata-only, int to bigint is a rewrite you do with a new column, a trigger or batched backfill, and a swap. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (two table scans, waits for every transaction that could see the table, cannot run inside a transaction block, so your migration tool must run it outside BEGIN), check pg_index.indisvalid afterwards because a failed or cancelled build leaves an INVALID index that writes still maintain and the planner ignores, and drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Wrap every DDL in SET lock_timeout = '3s' with an exponential-backoff retry loop, and create primary keys on big tables as CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY followed by ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - ALTER TABLE (Notes section on locking and rewrites)

subtopics.name: Window functions: frames, ranking, lag/lead and latest-per-key
subtopics.learn: Write OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o frame) fluently and know the default frame trap: with ORDER BY and no frame clause the frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes peer rows with equal ORDER BY values, so a running sum over dates with ties jumps in steps; use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for true row-by-row totals, ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-row moving average, GROUPS (PG11+) for peer groups, and EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW where needed. Use row_number(), rank(), dense_rank(), ntile(), lag(x, 1, default)/lead() for gap and change detection, first_value() and last_value() (last_value needs a frame ending at UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or it returns the current row), FILTER (WHERE ...) on aggregates, and a named WINDOW w AS (...) clause to avoid repetition. Know that window results cannot be referenced in WHERE (wrap in a subquery or CTE), that a WindowAgg node requires a Sort unless an index on (p, o) provides the order, and compare row_number() = 1 against DISTINCT ON (device_id) ... ORDER BY device_id, ts DESC and LATERAL for the latest-per-key problem you will write on every telemetry engagement.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Window Functions tutorial

subtopics.name: CTEs, materialization fences, recursive queries and LATERAL rewrites
subtopics.learn: Know that since PG12 a non-recursive CTE referenced once is inlined into the parent query and optimised with it, that WITH x AS MATERIALIZED forces the old optimisation fence (useful to pin a good plan or to force a filter to happen first), that NOT MATERIALIZED inlines even a multiply-referenced CTE, and that CTEs containing INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... RETURNING are always materialised and run exactly once. Write WITH RECURSIVE for org charts and dependency trees, understand UNION vs UNION ALL cycle behaviour and the PG14+ CYCLE and SEARCH DEPTH FIRST clauses, and cap depth defensively. Master the rewrites that fix real slow queries: LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE d.device_id = x.id ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1) for top-N per group hitting an index once per outer row; NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN (NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a single NULL, and cannot become an anti-join); WHERE a = $1 OR b = $1 split into UNION ALL when the planner will not use BitmapOr; and col = ANY($1::int[]) instead of a 2000-item IN list.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)

subtopics.name: Declarative partitioning and partition pruning
subtopics.learn: Partition when a table is large and queries carry the partition key: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) monthly for events and audit logs, LIST (tenant_id) for a few huge tenants, HASH when you only need to spread. Verify pruning in EXPLAIN (only the matching partitions appear; Subplans Removed: N shows execution-time pruning for parameters and nested loops; enable_partition_pruning must be on) and know the constraints: the partition key must be part of every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint, indexes created on the parent cascade to partitions, ATTACH PARTITION scans the new table unless it already carries a matching CHECK constraint, and DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY (PG14+) avoids the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Understand the operational win (DROP or DETACH an old partition instead of a DELETE that creates months of bloat and vacuum work, use pg_partman or a cron to pre-create partitions) and the cost: planning time grows with partition count, thousands of partitions hurt every query, and partition-wise joins and aggregates are off by default (enable_partitionwise_join).

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Table Partitioning

subtopics.name: Connections, PgBouncer transaction mode and the prepared-statement plan cache
subtopics.learn: Understand that every connection is a forked backend process (several MB of memory plus lock-table and snapshot overhead), that max_connections = 500 on a 4-vCPU RDS instance is a cry for help, and that PgBouncer in pool_mode = transaction is the standard fix but breaks anything session-scoped: SET (use SET LOCAL), server-side prepared statements (until PgBouncer 1.21's max_prepared_statements, or disable the driver cache with asyncpg statement_cache_size=0 / psycopg prepare_threshold=None), LISTEN/NOTIFY, session advisory locks, temp tables and WITH HOLD cursors; size default_pool_size to roughly (2 x cores) + spindles on the server side and let clients queue. Know the plan_cache_mode behaviour for prepared statements: five custom plans, then a generic plan if it is not costlier on average, which is how a skewed tenant_id gets the small-tenant plan forever (force_custom_plan fixes it at the cost of re-planning). Round out the write path: synchronous_commit = off per transaction for non-critical writes (risk: lose the last ~600ms on crash, never corruption), INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE/DO NOTHING for idempotent ingestion, and COPY FROM STDIN rather than batched INSERTs for bulk loads.

resource.label: PgBouncer docs - Configuration (pool_mode, prepared statements)

outcomes: You can take an unfamiliar EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output for a five-table join and, within three minutes and without tooling, point at the node where estimated rows diverges from actual rows by more than 10x, name the cause (stale statistics, correlated columns, function on a column, generic plan, missing extended statistics) and state the change that fixes it.

You can, for WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 on a 10M-row table, write the single index (column order, partial predicate, INCLUDE columns, direction) that yields an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with no Sort node and Heap Fetches: 0, and prove it with the before and after plans.

You can generate 5-10M rows of Zipf-skewed multi-tenant seed data with generate_series, take three real Dokeo queries from seconds to under 5 ms, and explain every line of each before/after plan including Buffers and Sort Method.

You can add a NOT NULL column, a foreign key and a unique index to a 10M-row table while pgbench -c 16 writes to it, with zero failed client transactions and no lock wait above one second, using CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID/VALIDATE, and a lock_timeout retry wrapper, and read the lock modes each step took from pg_locks while it runs.

You can reproduce a deadlock, a lock-queue pile-up behind an ALTER TABLE, and an INVALID index in two or three psql sessions, then diagnose each from pg_stat_activity, pg_blocking_pids() and pg_locks alone and state what every session holds and waits on.

You can write a lost-update demonstration in READ COMMITTED, show it becomes a 40001 under REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, implement the retry loop, and justify which of atomic UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, a version column, or SERIALIZABLE is right for a given contention profile.

You can write latest-row-per-key, 7-day moving average, gap detection and top-N-per-group three ways each (window function, DISTINCT ON, LATERAL) and say which one the planner executes without a Sort given a specific index.

You can read pg_stat_statements on a customer database, rank by total_exec_time and by mean_exec_time x calls with shared_blks_read, defend the choice of the three statements worth fixing in a 10-minute conversation with their DBA, and configure auto_explain so the next slow plan is captured with its real parameters.
failureModes: A 500M-row events table keeps the default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor of 0.2 while a nightly analytics job holds a transaction open for six hours; vacuum cannot clear anything behind that backend_xmin, the table reaches 3x bloat, every Index Only Scan reports thousands of Heap Fetches, p99 climbs weekly and the customer's response is to buy a larger instance.

The ORM emits WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) against a table with a plain B-tree on email; the plan is a 20M-row Seq Scan with Rows Removed by Filter, login p95 hits four seconds, and the fix nobody found for a month is a single expression index on lower(email).

A deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ... without lock_timeout; it queues for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a 20-minute report SELECT, every subsequent SELECT on orders queues behind the ALTER, the connection pool saturates and the entire application freezes until someone finds the head of the chain with pg_blocking_pids() and terminates it.

A migration script runs CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction on a 200M-row table, holding a SHARE lock that blocks all writes for 40 minutes; the follow-up attempt with CONCURRENTLY is cancelled by a timeout and leaves an INVALID index that is maintained on every write and used by nothing, silently taxing the table for the next year.

PgBouncer in transaction mode sits in front of a FastAPI service whose driver caches prepared statements; the app throws intermittent 'prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_12__" does not exist' errors only under load, the team blames the database, and the fix is statement_cache_size=0 or PgBouncer 1.21 with max_prepared_statements.

A job queue uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE LIMIT 1 without SKIP LOCKED, so twenty workers serialise on the first locked row and throughput equals one worker; when someone adds SKIP LOCKED but keeps a composite index ordered (created_at, tenant_id) the queue is fast for small tenants and scans the whole index range for the largest one because the equality column is not leading.

A prepared statement with a tenant_id parameter switches to the generic plan after five executions; the plan chosen for typical 2000-row tenants is a Nested Loop that runs 600000 times for the tenant holding 60% of the data, that one customer times out every hour, and no one connects it to plan_cache_mode because the query is fast every time they run it by hand with a literal.
interviewQuestions: Here is an EXPLAIN ANALYZE: a Nested Loop whose outer Seq Scan was estimated at rows=1 and produced rows=48000, with an inner Index Scan showing loops=48000. Explain why the planner chose this, what you would check in pg_stats, and give three fixes ranked from least to most invasive with the risk of each.

A customer's multi-tenant SaaS has three tenants holding 70% of the rows and two thousand small ones; the same endpoint is 20 ms for small tenants and times out for the big three. Walk me through your diagnosis, covering plan caching and generic plans, statistics targets, partial indexes and partitioning, and tell me what you would actually ship this week and what you would defer.

Design the migration that adds a NOT NULL column with a default, a foreign key to accounts, and a unique index on (tenant_id, external_id) to a two-billion-row table on RDS with no maintenance window. For each step name the lock mode, whether it scans or rewrites, where it can fail, and how your migration runner recovers.

Explain MVCC as Postgres implements it: what an UPDATE physically does, what a HOT update is and what defeats it, how a forgotten idle-in-transaction connection or a replica with hot_standby_feedback causes bloat, and the four numbers you would put on a dashboard to catch it early.

Twenty workers pull jobs from a jobs table. Write the dequeue SQL that is correct under concurrency, explain the lock semantics that make it correct, and then describe what changes if each job triggers a non-idempotent external API call and the process can die between the call and the commit.

When would you choose SERIALIZABLE over explicit row locks, and when the reverse? Describe SSI briefly, the 40001 retry contract that the application must honour, the throughput cost, and give one concrete case for each choice from a system you have built.

A query on a customer database got 100x slower overnight with no deploy and no schema change. Give the first five catalog queries you would run, what each one would tell you, and the three most likely root causes in order of probability.
31.proofOfWork: A public repository, pg-autopsy, that anyone can clone and run with docker compose up: a postgres:16 container preloaded with pg_stat_statements and auto_explain, a seed.sql that builds a realistic multi-tenant schema (tenants, users, documents, events, jobs) with 10M rows and Zipf-skewed tenant sizes, and a queries/ directory holding ten slow queries drawn from Dokeo patterns, each with its before.explain and after.explain (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) captured verbatim, the DDL that changed the plan, and a paragraph naming the exact node and mechanism that was wrong. A locks/ lab contains two-session scripts that reproduce a deadlock, an ALTER TABLE lock-queue freeze and an INVALID index, with the pg_locks and pg_blocking_pids() queries that diagnose each. A migrations/ lab runs a NOT NULL column, a foreign key and a unique index onto the 10M-row table while pgbench -c 16 -T 120 writes to it, using a lock_timeout retry wrapper, and commits the pgbench summary showing zero failed transactions. A 12-minute recorded screencast shows you reading three of the plans cold and narrating the fix, and a one-page INDEX-DECISION-CARD.md distils the column-order rule, when to go partial, expression, INCLUDE, GIN or BRIN, and the lock mode of every DDL statement you are likely to run on a customer's database.

32.topic: Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems: RLS, PII, encryption, audit trails
32.why: An FDE is usually the person who puts a customer's data into an AI system for the first time, and the customer's security team will not let a pilot touch production data until someone shows them, table by table, how tenant A cannot read tenant B, where PII lives, how it is encrypted and who can prove what was accessed. Application-layer `WHERE tenant_id = ?` filters fail the moment an engineer forgets one, an LLM-generated query bypasses the ORM, or a background job runs as the wrong principal; Postgres row-level security, pgcrypto and an append-only audit log move those guarantees into the database where a reviewer can actually verify them. The schema you design in week one is the schema that survives the handover, so getting isolation, PII handling and auditability right before the first customer row lands is the cheapest security work you will ever do.
prerequisites: PostgreSQL fundamentals from 'PostgreSQL at depth' (topic 29): EXPLAIN ANALYZE, B-tree and composite indexes, transactions and isolation levels, `SET ROLE`, and reading `pg_catalog` views

Auth model from 'Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims' (topic 27): where `tenant_id` and `sub` come from in a verified JWT and why the database must never trust a tenant id the client supplied in a body or query string

FastAPI dependency injection and request lifecycle from topic 26 (or the Next.js route-handler and server-action equivalent for DefenderMate) so you can set per-request session state at the exact point the connection is checked out

IAM and KMS basics from topic 15: what a KMS key policy is, `kms:Decrypt` versus `kms:GenerateDataKey`, and why the application role must never hold both the ciphertext store and unrestricted key access
Docker Compose with a local Postgres 16 container and psql, plus a pytest (or Vitest) harness that can open two connections as different roles inside one test
A written list of every table in DefenderMate today, which columns hold customer-supplied free text, and who (human or service) reads each one

subtopics.name: Choosing the tenancy model: shared schema, schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant
subtopics.learn: Lay out the three isolation models with their real costs: pooled (one schema, `tenant_id` on every row, RLS enforces isolation), bridge (schema-per-tenant with `search_path` switching and N copies of every migration), and silo (database or cluster per tenant, hard isolation, N connection pools and N backups). Know the questions that decide it: does the customer's security policy require physical separation or a dedicated encryption key per tenant, how many tenants will exist in 18 months, does any tenant need a different region for residency, and can you afford per-tenant migrations at 3 a.m. Be able to defend pooled-with-RLS as the default for an AI product with hundreds of small tenants, and name the two triggers (a regulated customer demanding a dedicated key or region; one tenant at 100x the load of the rest) that move a specific tenant to a silo while the others stay pooled.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens (tenant isolation and data partitioning)

subtopics.name: Tenant key discipline: tenant_id on every row and composite foreign keys
subtopics.learn: Every tenant-owned table gets `tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id)` and a `UNIQUE (tenant_id, id)` constraint, and every child table references its parent with a composite `FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, parent_id) REFERENCES parent (tenant_id, id)` so a row cannot point at another tenant's parent even when application code is wrong. Put `tenant_id` first in every index so RLS predicates and tenant-scoped queries show up as `Index Cond` rather than `Filter` in EXPLAIN. Write a catalog query against `information_schema.columns` that lists tables in the `public` schema lacking a `tenant_id` column and run it in CI; the exceptions list (lookup tables, the `tenants` table itself) should be explicit, short and reviewed.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (composite unique and foreign keys)

subtopics.name: RLS mechanics: ENABLE, FORCE, USING vs WITH CHECK, PERMISSIVE vs RESTRICTIVE
subtopics.learn: Understand exactly what `ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` does (default-deny for every role that is not the owner, a superuser or BYPASSRLS) and why you always also run `ALTER TABLE t FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` so the owner is bound too. Write `CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON t FOR ALL TO app_user USING (tenant_id = current_tenant_id()) WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_tenant_id())` and know the asymmetry: `USING` filters rows visible to SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, `WITH CHECK` validates rows produced by INSERT and UPDATE, and a policy with only `USING` lets an UPDATE move a row into another tenant. Know that multiple PERMISSIVE policies are ORed while `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies are ANDed on top, so a second permissive policy added for a 'support can read everything' feature silently widens access to every row; use RESTRICTIVE for hard constraints such as `deleted_at IS NULL` or region pinning.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Row Security Policies

subtopics.name: Getting the tenant into the session: set_config, current_setting and pooled connections
subtopics.learn: Carry the verified tenant id from the JWT into Postgres with `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)` at the start of every transaction and read it inside policies as `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`; the second argument to `current_setting` is `missing_ok`, which turns an unset variable into NULL (the policy evaluates to NULL, so zero rows) instead of raising. The third argument of `set_config` (`is_local = true`, the equivalent of `SET LOCAL`) scopes the value to the current transaction; with PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode a session-level `SET` leaks the previous tenant to whichever request gets that connection next, which is the single most common cross-tenant bug in pooled RLS deployments. Wrap `set_config` and the business query in one explicit transaction in the repository layer, and add a test that checks out two connections from the pool in sequence and proves the second one sees no tenant.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Configuration Settings Functions (set_config, current_setting)

subtopics.name: Role model: app role without BYPASSRLS, migrator as owner, SECURITY DEFINER escape hatches
subtopics.learn: Create three roles: `app_migrator` owns every object and runs migrations, `app_user` (NOLOGIN, NOBYPASSRLS) is granted to the login role the API uses, and `app_readonly` for analytics gets SELECT on masked views only. Never connect the application as the owner or a superuser; verify with `SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles` in a CI check. When a cross-tenant operation is genuinely required (a system job aggregating usage across tenants), implement it as a `SECURITY DEFINER` function owned by a dedicated role with `SET search_path = pg_catalog, public` in the definition to block search_path hijacking, `REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM PUBLIC`, and a narrow signature that cannot be turned into a generic query runner.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE ROLE (BYPASSRLS, NOLOGIN, INHERIT)

subtopics.name: RLS performance: InitPlan wrapping, LEAKPROOF, and reading EXPLAIN as the app role
subtopics.learn: A policy expression is appended to every query as a predicate, so `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` is evaluated per row unless you write it as `(SELECT current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)`, which the planner turns into a single InitPlan. Understand the leakproof rule: the planner will not push a user-defined or non-`LEAKPROOF` function below the RLS filter (an error message could leak a row), so a `WHERE my_func(col)` that used an index without RLS becomes a sequential scan with it; check `proleakproof` in `pg_proc` and mark trusted immutable functions `LEAKPROOF` only as superuser and only when they cannot throw on any input. Always benchmark with `SET ROLE app_user; SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = ...; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` because the owner or a BYPASSRLS role gets a different plan, and confirm the composite index led by `tenant_id` is the one used.

resource.label: Supabase docs: Row Level Security (RLS performance recommendations)

subtopics.name: The RLS test matrix: positive, negative and privilege-escalation cases per table
subtopics.learn: For every RLS-protected table write at least five tests as the application role: tenant A sees exactly A's rows; tenant B sees zero of A's rows; INSERT with a foreign `tenant_id` fails with `new row violates row-level security policy for table`; UPDATE that changes `tenant_id` to another tenant fails on `WITH CHECK`; DELETE of another tenant's row affects 0 rows and raises no error (silent filtering is RLS behaviour you must document for the client). Add the bypass checks: with no `app.tenant_id` set the count is 0 not an exception; the owner is also filtered because of `FORCE`; and `SET ROLE app_user` cannot then `SET ROLE app_migrator`. Generate the matrix from the catalog (loop over `pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'public'`) so a new table without a policy fails the suite instead of being forgotten, and run it against a real Postgres container in CI, never SQLite or a mock.

resource.label: pgTAP documentation (throws_ok, results_eq, policies_are)

subtopics.name: Catalog invariants in CI: pg_policies, relrowsecurity, relforcerowsecurity, event triggers
subtopics.learn: Encode the security posture as queries the pipeline runs after migrations: every table in `public` has `relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity` true in `pg_class` (joined to `pg_namespace`), every such table has at least one row in `pg_policies` for the app role, no role other than the migrator owns any object, and no function referenced from a policy is `SECURITY DEFINER` unless allow-listed. Print the offending table names as the failure message so the reviewer does not have to dig. Optionally add an event trigger `ON ddl_command_end` that inspects `pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands()` and runs `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` on any newly created table in `public`, so an engineer who forgets RLS creates an inaccessible table (a loud failure) rather than an open one.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: pg_policies system view

subtopics.name: PII inventory and classification per column
subtopics.learn: Classify every column as: direct identifier (email, phone, full name, national id), quasi-identifier (postcode, birth date, IP address, device id), special category (health, biometrics, ethnicity, union membership, sexual orientation under GDPR Art. 9), secret (password hash, API key, refresh token), or free text that may contain any of the above (support tickets, chat transcripts, the prompt and completion columns of your AI system). Record the classification, lawful basis, retention period and encryption treatment in one place the security team can read: a `data_inventory` table, or `COMMENT ON COLUMN customers.email IS 'pii:direct;retain:account+30d;enc:column'` parsed by a script into the model doc. The rule for AI systems is that any column an LLM writes to is free text and inherits the highest classification of its inputs.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet: User Privacy Protection

subtopics.name: Encryption layers and pgcrypto: what each layer actually protects against
subtopics.learn: Separate the three layers and the threat each defeats: volume encryption (RDS/EBS with a KMS key) stops a stolen disk or snapshot and nothing else; column encryption with pgcrypto (`pgp_sym_encrypt(text, key)` / `pgp_sym_decrypt(bytea, key)`, or `encrypt(data, key, 'aes-cbc/pad:pkcs')` when you manage IVs yourself) stops a DBA or a leaked `pg_dump` from reading plaintext, but the key is visible in `pg_stat_statements` and server logs if it is passed as a literal; application-layer encryption before the row reaches Postgres stops even the database host from seeing plaintext at the cost of losing SQL search and indexing on that column. Know the pgcrypto footguns: `pgp_sym_encrypt` output is non-deterministic (good for confidentiality, means no equality index), the column type is `bytea`, and keys must travel as bound parameters with `SET LOCAL log_statement = 'none'` for that transaction or they end up in the log.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: pgcrypto module

subtopics.name: Envelope encryption, per-tenant data keys and crypto-shredding
subtopics.learn: Implement the KMS hierarchy: one customer-managed KEK in KMS with a key policy granting the application role `kms:GenerateDataKey` and `kms:Decrypt` only; per tenant, call `GenerateDataKey` once, store the encrypted DEK in `tenants.dek_ciphertext`, cache the plaintext DEK in process memory with a short TTL, and encrypt PII columns with the tenant's DEK using AES-256-GCM with `tenant_id` and the column name as additional authenticated data so a ciphertext copied between rows or tenants fails to decrypt. Rotation is re-wrapping DEKs under the new KEK version, not re-encrypting rows. Crypto-shredding is the payoff: deleting a tenant's DEK (and every copy of it) renders every PII row, backup and replica unreadable, which is how you honour an erasure request without rewriting PITR history; document this as the deletion mechanism in the model doc.

resource.label: AWS KMS Developer Guide: Concepts (envelope encryption, data keys, key policies)

subtopics.name: Searchable PII: HMAC blind indexes, last-four columns, and password hashing
subtopics.learn: You cannot index or filter on a non-deterministic ciphertext, so for each PII column that needs exact lookup (email for login, phone for dedupe) add a sibling `email_hmac bytea` computed as `hmac(lower(trim(email)), :blind_index_key, 'sha256')` with a key different from the encryption key, index that column, and query by HMAC. Understand why a plain `digest(email, 'sha256')` is unacceptable (offline dictionary attack on a low-entropy space like emails) and why per-row salts defeat the purpose (you could no longer look anything up). Store display fragments (`card_last4`, `phone_last2`) as separate plaintext columns rather than decrypting for every list view. For passwords use `crypt(password, gen_salt('bf', 12))` or, better, application-side argon2id; never `pgp_sym_encrypt` a password.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet: Cryptographic Storage

subtopics.name: Masked views, column-level GRANT and security_invoker
subtopics.learn: Give analysts, dashboards and the eval pipeline a redacted surface instead of base tables: `CREATE VIEW customers_masked WITH (security_invoker = true) AS SELECT id, tenant_id, left(email, 1) || '***@' || split_part(email, '@', 2) AS email, ...` so RLS on the base table is evaluated as the querying role (without `security_invoker`, a view runs with the owner's privileges and bypasses RLS). Add `security_barrier = true` when the view filters rows, so a malicious function in the caller's WHERE clause cannot execute before the view's predicate and leak rows through error messages. Use column-level privileges for the reverse case: `GRANT SELECT (id, tenant_id, created_at) ON customers TO app_readonly` lets a role read a table without its PII columns, and `SELECT *` from that role fails loudly with a permission error.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE VIEW (security_barrier, security_invoker)

subtopics.name: Trigger-based audit log: who, what, when, why on every tenant table
subtopics.learn: Design `audit_log (id bigint generated always as identity, tenant_id uuid, occurred_at timestamptz default clock_timestamp(), actor_id uuid, actor_role text, session_user_name text default session_user, application_name text, request_id text, table_name text, row_pk text, op text, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, changed_cols text[])` and one generic PL/pgSQL function attached with `CREATE TRIGGER audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON t FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_row()` that reads `TG_OP`, `TG_TABLE_NAME`, `to_jsonb(OLD)`, `to_jsonb(NEW)`, and the actor from `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)` and `current_setting('app.request_id', true)`. Strip or encrypt PII columns in `old_row`/`new_row` using the inventory from the classification step so the audit log does not become the least protected copy of the data. Use `AFTER` not `BEFORE` so a rolled-back statement leaves no audit row, and compute `changed_cols` from a jsonb diff so reviewers can filter for changes to sensitive fields.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: PL/pgSQL Trigger Functions (TG_OP, OLD, NEW)

subtopics.name: Making the audit trail append-only and tamper-evident; pgaudit for DDL and roles
subtopics.learn: Append-only means four things: `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE ON audit_log FROM PUBLIC, app_user` plus a `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE OR TRUNCATE` trigger that raises `EXCEPTION 'audit_log is append-only'` to cover the owner as well; RLS on `audit_log` so tenants read only their own entries; a `prev_hash bytea` chain (`digest(prev_hash || canonical_row_json, 'sha256')`) that lets an auditor detect a deleted or edited row; and periodic export of closed partitions to object storage with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. Application triggers cannot see `ALTER ROLE`, `GRANT`, `DROP TRIGGER` or a DBA at a psql prompt; enable the `pgaudit` extension with `pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role'` (and `read, write` on sensitive schemas via `pgaudit.role`) so those events land in the server log shipped to the SIEM, and document which events live in which log.

resource.label: pgaudit: PostgreSQL Audit Extension (GitHub, configuration reference)

subtopics.name: Retention, erasure and partitions: deleting without breaking the audit trail
subtopics.learn: Partition high-volume tables (`audit_log`, `llm_calls`, `messages`) by month with `PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at)` so retention is `DROP TABLE audit_log_2025_03` (instant, no bloat) rather than a `DELETE` that vacuums for hours; pre-create partitions from a scheduled job and test the 'no partition for this month' failure before it happens on a Sunday. Separate three deletion semantics and put each in the model doc: soft delete (`deleted_at` plus a RESTRICTIVE policy `deleted_at IS NULL` so hidden rows stay hidden from every query path), hard delete (row gone, audit rows remain but the PII inside them is pseudonymised by rewriting `actor_id` to a tombstone via a privileged job), and crypto-shred for tenant offboarding. State plainly that PITR backups retain data for the backup window and that any erasure SLA must include that window.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Table Partitioning (declarative range partitioning, detaching)

subtopics.name: Modelling AI-specific tables: conversations, llm_calls, tool_calls and embeddings under RLS
subtopics.learn: Design `conversations`, `messages`, `llm_calls` (model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, latency_ms, cost_usd, provider_request_id, `prompt_ref` pointing at redacted storage), `tool_calls` (name, arguments jsonb, result jsonb, approved_by) and `embeddings` (pgvector `vector(1536)` plus `source_table`, `source_id`, `tenant_id`) all carrying `tenant_id` and the same RLS policy; the vector table is the one people forget, and a `<->` nearest-neighbour query without tenant scoping returns another tenant's document chunks as context. Treat embeddings as derived PII (inversion attacks recover text) and tool `arguments`/`result` as free text with the highest classification of their inputs. Store raw prompts and completions in a short-TTL partition or as a hash plus a redacted copy, add `training_opt_out boolean` and `data_region text` on `tenants`, and make sure the LLM observability exporter (topic 54) reads from the masked view, never the base table.

resource.label: pgvector (GitHub README: indexing, filtering with WHERE, iterative scans)

subtopics.name: Writing the data model doc a client security team signs off
subtopics.learn: Structure the document the way reviewers read it: one data-flow diagram with trust boundaries (browser, API, worker, Postgres, KMS, LLM provider, object storage), a table of every store with its tenancy model and encryption layer, a threat list with the control that answers each one (IDOR across tenants -> RLS + composite FKs + test matrix; SQL injection -> parameterised queries + RLS as defence in depth; snapshot theft -> KMS volume + column encryption; insider DBA -> pgaudit + column encryption + no superuser app role; log leakage -> masked views + `log_statement` policy; backup retention -> stated PITR window + crypto-shred), and an evidence section linking to the CI output for the RLS matrix and catalog invariants. Map controls to the frameworks the client will cite (SOC 2 CC6.1 and CC6.7, ISO 27001 Annex A.8, GDPR Art. 32 and Art. 17) without claiming compliance, and end with the residual risks you are asking them to accept, because a doc with no residual risks is the one they do not believe.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet: Threat Modeling

outcomes: You can stand up DefenderMate's schema in a fresh Postgres 16 container and run an RLS test matrix (positive, negative, cross-tenant INSERT and UPDATE, unset tenant, owner-with-FORCE) generated from the catalog across every table in `public`, passing in CI in under 60 seconds; deliberately dropping one policy makes the suite fail naming that table.

You can explain, with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output captured as `app_user`, why a policy written as `(SELECT current_setting(...))` produces an InitPlan and why a non-LEAKPROOF function in the query turned an index scan into a sequential scan, then fix it without weakening the policy.

You can reproduce the PgBouncer transaction-pooling leak (session-level `SET app.tenant_id` visible on the next checkout) in an automated test, and show the `set_config(..., true)` fix turning it green.

You can encrypt a PII column with a per-tenant data key wrapped by a KEK, look rows up by HMAC blind index, rotate the KEK without touching rows, and crypto-shred one tenant so its rows fail to decrypt while every other tenant is unaffected.

You can show an `audit_log` where UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE fail for every role including the owner, each row carries actor, request id, `TG_OP` and a redacted jsonb diff, and a hash-chain verification query pinpoints a manually deleted row.
You can run one catalog query that lists any table missing `tenant_id`, RLS, FORCE or a policy, and the CI job fails with that list when a new migration forgets any of them.

You can walk a security reviewer through the model doc in 20 minutes and answer 'what stops your support engineer reading tenant B's chat logs' and 'what happens to my data in your backups after I churn' with the specific control, its limits and a link to the evidence.
failureModes: A support tool needed read-all-tenants access, so an engineer added a second PERMISSIVE policy `USING (true) TO app_user` instead of a separate role; because permissive policies are ORed, every API request could read every tenant, and it was found by a customer who saw another company's name in an autocomplete dropdown.

RLS was enabled but never FORCED, and the API connected as the table owner because the Terraform module reused the migration credentials; RLS applied to nobody for eight months and the first indication was a penetration tester swapping a UUID in a URL.

Session-level `SET app.tenant_id` behind PgBouncer in transaction mode: under load, connections were reused mid-request and roughly one in 400 requests ran as the previous request's tenant, surfacing as 'random' data-corruption tickets nobody could reproduce in staging, which had no pooler.

The pgvector table for RAG had no `tenant_id` column because it was created from a notebook, so nearest-neighbour retrieval pulled another tenant's contract clauses into a prompt; the model summarised them fluently and the leak was only visible in the LLM trace store weeks later.

pgcrypto keys were interpolated as string literals by the ORM, so every encryption key sat in `pg_stat_statements`, the slow-query log and the APM tool's query capture, meaning the column encryption protected against nothing the volume encryption did not already cover.

The audit trigger logged `to_jsonb(NEW)` for the users table including plaintext PII columns, so the audit log became the largest unencrypted copy of customer data in the system and was excluded from the encryption review because 'it's just logs'.

A GDPR erasure request was fulfilled with `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ...` while the audit log, the embeddings table and 35 days of PITR backups still held the data; the DPO found out when the same person's name appeared in a support search a month later.
interviewQuestions: A regulated customer wants to run our multi-tenant AI product but their security team says shared tables are unacceptable. Walk me through how you decide between arguing for pooled tables with RLS, moving them to a dedicated schema or database, and what evidence you bring to the meeting to change their mind or to concede gracefully.

Explain how a Postgres row-level security policy is actually evaluated inside a query, what USING versus WITH CHECK protect, how permissive and restrictive policies combine, and give me a concrete case where a correct-looking policy still leaks data.

We run the API behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode and set the tenant with `SET app.tenant_id` at the start of each request. Production shows occasional cross-tenant reads that never reproduce in staging. Debug it out loud, then tell me the fix and the test that proves the fix.

Design the encryption story for PII in a system where customers must be able to search by email, we must honour erasure requests within 30 days, and we keep 35 days of backups. Which layer encrypts what, where do the keys live, how does lookup work, and what exactly happens on an erasure request?

After enabling RLS, a dashboard query went from 40 ms to 6 seconds. The policy is `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` and the query filters on a user-defined function. What is happening in the planner, and how do you fix it without weakening the policy?

Design an append-only audit trail for a multi-tenant system that a SOC 2 auditor will accept. How do you make it immutable when the table owner can always drop a trigger, what do you deliberately keep out of it, and how would you prove to the auditor that nothing was deleted last quarter?

Our RAG pipeline stores document chunks and embeddings in pgvector. A customer asks whether another tenant could ever see their documents in a model answer. Give me the complete answer: the retrieval query, the storage model, the tests, and the residual risk you would disclose.
32.proofOfWork: A public repository containing DefenderMate's multi-tenant schema as versioned migrations (tenants, users, conversations, messages, llm_calls, tool_calls, embeddings, audit_log) with RLS enabled and forced on every table, composite tenant foreign keys, pgcrypto-encrypted PII columns with HMAC blind indexes, an envelope-encryption module with per-tenant data keys (a local KEK stub for CI, KMS in production), and a generic audit trigger with hash chaining and an append-only guard. The CI workflow spins up Postgres 16 behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, runs the catalog-generated RLS test matrix across every table, runs the catalog invariant queries, demonstrates the pooled-connection tenant leak failing before the `set_config` fix and passing after, and crypto-shreds one tenant while asserting the others still decrypt. Alongside the code sits a six-page security review document with a data-flow diagram, threat-to-control table, framework mapping, evidence links to the green CI run and a residual-risk section, written so a client CISO could sign it without a call.

33.topic: Redis: caching, rate limiting, idempotency, streams
33.why: Every customer integration an FDE ships sits between a flaky upstream (webhooks that retry, LLM providers that 429 you, browsers that double-submit) and a database the customer cannot afford to overload, and Redis is the component you put in that gap: a cache so the demo stays fast on their real data, a limiter so one tenant cannot starve the others, an idempotency store so a retried webhook does not create two invoices, and a stream so the work survives a pod restart. The customer usually already runs ElastiCache or a Redis in a corner of the cluster, so you inherit its eviction policy, persistence settings and single-threaded limits rather than choosing them, and you need to know which of your guarantees silently disappear when that instance is configured as a cache. Take-home reviewers at Anthropic, Databricks and Palantir specifically look for whether your rate limiter is atomic, whether your idempotency layer survives a crash between claim and completion, and whether you can say what happens to each of them on failover.
prerequisites: HTTP semantics at the level of topic 2 (status codes, `Retry-After`, `X-Forwarded-For` behind an ALB, what a client library does on 429 vs 503) and FastAPI middleware, dependencies and `lifespan` from topic 26, because the limiter and idempotency layer are wired in as middleware/dependencies sharing one connection pool

PostgreSQL transactions and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` / unique indexes from topic 29, because in this design Postgres is the source of truth and Redis is the fast path; you must be able to say which one catches a duplicate when the other fails

Docker Compose from topic 5 to run `redis:7` locally with a mounted `redis.conf`, and the ElastiCache basics from topic 14 (cluster mode on/off, reader endpoint, Multi-AZ failover) so the production section maps onto something you have already provisioned
Python asyncio fluency (`async with`, task groups, `asyncio.gather`) and the ability to read redis-py source, since every code sample uses `redis.asyncio`
Enough Lua to read a 30-line script: `local`, tables, `tonumber`, `math.min`, `redis.call` vs `redis.pcall`; 30 minutes with the EVAL introduction page covers it

Access to the DefenderMate webhook receiver code and a week of real numbers (events per minute per provider, p99 handler time, duplicate rate seen in Postgres) so limits and TTLs are sized from data rather than guessed

subtopics.name: Single-threaded command loop: what blocks Redis and how to see it
subtopics.learn: Redis executes commands on one main thread (`io-threads` in 6+ only parallelise socket read/write), so any O(N) command stalls every client: `KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS`/`HGETALL` on a million-element key, `DEL` of a huge key (use `UNLINK` and `lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes`), `FLUSHALL`, or a Lua script that loops. Find the culprits with `SLOWLOG GET 25` (threshold `slowlog-log-slower-than`, default 10000 microseconds), `LATENCY DOCTOR` after setting `latency-monitor-threshold 100`, `INFO commandstats` for per-command usec, `redis-cli --latency` from an app pod, and `redis-cli --bigkeys` / `--memkeys` to find the keys that cause them. Replace `KEYS pattern` with a `SCAN cursor MATCH pattern COUNT 1000` loop and accept that SCAN may return duplicates and misses keys created during the scan. Be able to explain why a 200 ms `HGETALL` on one tenant's key shows up as a p99 spike on every other tenant's API.

resource.label: Redis docs: Diagnosing latency issues

subtopics.name: Key naming, hash tags and TTL semantics (SET EX/PX/NX/XX/KEEPTTL, GETEX, expiry mechanics)
subtopics.learn: Adopt one key grammar for the engagement, `{tenant}:domain:id` (e.g. `{t_42}:idem:7f3a...`), where the `{...}` hash tag pins every key for a tenant to the same Cluster slot so multi-key commands and Lua scripts still work when the customer moves to cluster mode. Know the SET options cold: `SET k v EX 300 NX` is the atomic set-if-absent-with-TTL that replaced `SETNX` + `EXPIRE`, `PX` for milliseconds, `XX` for update-only, `KEEPTTL` to overwrite a value without resetting its expiry, and `GET` to return the old value; `GETEX k EX 60` refreshes TTL on read, `GETDEL` reads-and-removes, `EXPIRE k 60 NX|XX|GT|LT` (7.0+) sets expiry conditionally, `TTL` returns -1 for no expiry and -2 for missing. Expiry is passive on access plus an active sampler (20 keys per cycle, `hz` cycles per second), so expired keys linger in memory and in `DBSIZE` under load. Jitter TTLs by plus or minus 10% so ten thousand keys written by the same batch job do not expire and refill in the same second.

resource.label: Redis command reference: SET (options and patterns)

subtopics.name: Cache-aside done properly: negative caching, stampede control, versioned invalidation
subtopics.learn: Implement cache-aside (read key, on miss load from Postgres, `SET k v EX ttl`) and know its race: a reader misses and reads the old row, a writer updates the row and `DEL`s the key, then the reader `SET`s the stale value which now lives for a full TTL; mitigate with short TTLs, a delayed second delete, or versioned keys (`v3:` prefix bumped by the writer) rather than pretending it cannot happen. Negative-cache 'not found' with a sentinel value and a 30 second TTL so a scraper hitting missing IDs does not turn into a full-table-scan storm on the customer's database. Stop stampedes on a hot key expiring three ways and be able to choose: a per-key mutex `SET lock:k token NX PX 5000` where losers serve stale or wait; probabilistic early recomputation (recompute when `now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry`); or a soft TTL stored inside the value with a hard Redis TTL so one worker refreshes while others serve stale. Pick serialisation deliberately (JSON for debuggability, msgpack for size, never unpickle anything a tenant could influence) and measure hit ratio from `INFO stats` `keyspace_hits` / (`keyspace_hits` + `keyspace_misses`) before claiming the cache helps.

resource.label: AWS whitepaper: Database Caching Strategies Using Redis

subtopics.name: Fixed and sliding window counters with INCR/EXPIRE and sorted sets
subtopics.learn: Build the naive fixed-window limiter, key `rl:{tenant}:route:<floor(now/window)>`, `INCR` then `EXPIRE` when the result is 1, and then break it: a crash or timeout between the two commands leaves a key with no TTL that blocks that tenant forever, and two requests racing on a fresh key can both see 1. Fix it with `SET k 0 EX window NX` followed by `INCR`, or a MULTI block, and note fixed windows still admit 2x the limit across a boundary. Build the sliding-window log with a sorted set in one MULTI/EXEC: `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE k -inf (now-window)`, `ZADD k now <now:uuid>` (unique member or two requests in the same millisecond collapse), `ZCARD k`, `EXPIRE k window`; it is exact but costs O(limit) memory per key, fine for 100/min and wrong for 100k/min. Know the sliding-window counter approximation (`prev_count * (1 - elapsed/window) + curr_count`) as the cheap middle ground. The INCR command page documents the canonical versions of these patterns and their pitfalls.

resource.label: Redis command reference: INCR (rate limiter patterns)

subtopics.name: Token bucket in Lua: EVAL, KEYS/ARGV, EVALSHA and NOSCRIPT, Redis Functions
subtopics.learn: Write the token bucket as one Lua script so refill, check and debit are atomic: state is a hash with `tokens` and `ts`, refill is `min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate_per_ms)`, debit `cost` if enough, return `{allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms}`, and `PEXPIRE` the key to `ceil(capacity / rate)` so idle buckets clean themselves. Pass the key in `KEYS[1]` and rate/capacity/now/cost in `ARGV` (declaring keys correctly is what lets Cluster route the script); pass `now` from the client and clamp `elapsed = max(0, now - ts)` so clock skew between app pods cannot drive tokens backwards. Load once with `SCRIPT LOAD` and call `EVALSHA sha 1 key ...`; handle the `NOSCRIPT` error after a restart or failover by falling back to `EVAL` (redis-py's `Script` object does this for you). Know the Redis 7 alternative, `FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=ratelimit ..."` with `redis.register_function` and `FCALL ratelimit_take 1 key ...`, which is persisted and replicated so there is no NOSCRIPT after failover. Verify atomicity with 20 concurrent workers hammering one key and asserting total admitted equals capacity plus rate times elapsed, plus or minus one.

resource.label: Redis docs: Scripting with Lua (EVAL introduction)

subtopics.name: The 429 contract: Retry-After, RateLimit headers, limit dimensions, fail-open vs fail-closed
subtopics.learn: Return 429 for a client exceeding its quota and 503 for server-side load shedding, always with `Retry-After` in whole seconds derived from the limiter's `retry_after_ms`. Emit the IETF draft headers (`RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` structured fields in the current draft; older drafts and most vendors still use `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset` or `X-RateLimit-*`) so the customer's SDK and your own retry code can back off precisely.
