Choose dimensions explicitly and layer them: per API key or tenant for fairness, per route for expensive endpoints, per source IP only from the first trusted hop of `X-Forwarded-For`, and a burst bucket (10/s) stacked on a sustained bucket (5000/h). Decide and document what happens when Redis is unreachable (`ConnectionError`, `TimeoutError`): a public unauthenticated endpoint fails closed or falls back to an in-process limiter, an internal paid API fails open and pages someone; a limiter that silently fails open is how a customer discovers their bill.

resource.label: IETF httpapi draft: RateLimit header fields for HTTP

subtopics.name: Idempotency keys for mutating APIs: claim, fingerprint, replay, conflict
subtopics.learn: Implement the Stripe-style contract: the client sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid4>` on POST/PATCH, the server scopes it to (tenant, key), and fingerprints the request as SHA-256 over method, path and canonicalised body. Claim with `SET idem:{tenant}:key '{state:in_progress, fp}' NX PX 60000`; if NX fails, `GET` it and branch: `in_progress` returns 409 (a retry is racing the original), `completed` with a matching fingerprint replays the stored status, headers and body byte-for-byte, and a mismatched fingerprint returns 422 (Stripe returns a 400 `idempotency_error`), because the same key with a different payload is a client bug you must not paper over. On completion, `SET ... '{state:completed, status, body}' PX 86400000 XX` (24 hour retention like Stripe), and decide whether to store 5xx results (Stripe does; for your own service prefer not to, so the client's retry can succeed). The 60 second in-progress lease is the crash recovery mechanism: if the pod dies between claim and completion, the retry re-claims after the lease expires, so the handler itself must be safe to run twice, which means a unique index on `idempotency_key` in Postgres is the real guarantee and Redis is the fast path in front of it. Cap stored bodies and store a pointer for anything large.

resource.label: Stripe API reference: Idempotent requests

subtopics.name: Webhook dedup and at-least-once processing for the DefenderMate receiver
subtopics.learn: Providers (Stripe, GitHub, Slack, Twilio) deliver at least once and retry on any non-2xx or slow response, so the receiver must verify the HMAC signature (`Stripe-Signature` with timestamp tolerance, `X-Hub-Signature-256`) before touching Redis, then dedup on the provider's event id with `SET wh:{provider}:event_id <pod> NX EX 259200` (three days, longer than any provider's retry horizon); on NX failure return 200 immediately. Hand the event off with `XADD webhooks:{provider} MAXLEN ~ 100000 * ...` and return 200 within a second; never do the work inline. Find the crash window between the `SET NX` and the `XADD` (event marked seen, never enqueued) and close it by putting both in a MULTI or a single Lua script, or by enqueueing first and deduping in the consumer. Dedup again at the consumer with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (provider, event_id) DO NOTHING`, because Redis can lose the dedup key on failover. Handle out-of-order delivery by fetching current resource state from the provider API rather than trusting event sequence. Export `duplicates_dropped_total`, `signature_failures_total` and ack latency; the same draft standard tells you how DefenderMate's own outbound webhooks should let receivers dedup you.

resource.label: IETF httpapi draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP header field

subtopics.name: MULTI/EXEC, WATCH and pipelines: which atomicity you actually get
subtopics.learn: MULTI/EXEC queues commands and runs them without interleaving, but there is no rollback: a command that fails at runtime (`WRONGTYPE`) fails alone while the others commit, and only a queue-time error aborts the whole EXEC. You cannot read a value and branch inside MULTI, which is exactly why the limiter and lock release are Lua. `WATCH k` then MULTI/EXEC gives optimistic compare-and-set: EXEC returns nil if any watched key changed, and you retry in a bounded loop. Pipelining (redis-py `pipeline(transaction=False)`) batches N commands into one round trip and turns 10k SETs from 10k RTTs into a handful, but the replies buffer server-side against `client-output-buffer-limit`, so chunk to about a thousand; redis-py's `pipeline()` defaults to `transaction=True`, which silently wraps your batch in MULTI. In Cluster every key in a MULTI, pipeline or script must hash to one slot or you get `CROSSSLOT`. Rule of thumb: MULTI for grouping, WATCH for rare contention, Lua for read-then-decide, and all three hold the single thread for their whole duration.

resource.label: Redis docs: Transactions (MULTI, EXEC, WATCH)

subtopics.name: Distributed locks: SET NX PX with a token, compare-and-delete release, fencing
subtopics.learn: Acquire with `SET lock:resource <random-token> NX PX 30000` and release only through a Lua compare-and-delete (`if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end`), because a plain `DEL` after your lease expired releases the next holder's lock. The lease must exceed the work or you extend it on a heartbeat (`PEXPIRE` guarded by the same token check); if a GC pause or slow disk pushes work past the lease, two workers run concurrently, so the protected operation must be idempotent or carry a fencing token (`INCR lock:fence`, stored with the lock, rejected by the resource if stale). Know the Redlock argument (N/2+1 of independent masters) and Kleppmann's critique (unsafe without fencing under clock jumps and pauses), and be ready to say when you would instead use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or `pg_advisory_xact_lock` from topic 29, or a Temporal workflow from topic 34. redis-py ships `redis.lock.Lock` with `blocking_timeout`, `extend()` and `thread_local`; read it before writing your own.

resource.label: Redis docs: Distributed Locks with Redis

subtopics.name: Streams as an append-only log: XADD, entry IDs, MAXLEN/MINID trimming vs Pub/Sub vs Lists
subtopics.learn: A stream is an append-only log whose entries have IDs `<unix-ms>-<seq>`; write with `XADD key MAXLEN ~ 100000 * field value ...` (the `~` makes trimming O(1) amortised; exact trimming is expensive), trim by time with `MINID`, use `NOMKSTREAM` when the stream must pre-exist, read ranges with `XRANGE key - + COUNT 10` / `XREVRANGE`, block on new entries with `XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS key $`. Pick the right primitive: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no persistence and drops slow subscribers at `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub` (right for cache-invalidation broadcasts, wrong for jobs); a List with `LPUSH` and `BLMOVE src processing RIGHT LEFT 0` gives a reliable queue with one consumer per item and no replay or fan-out; Streams give replay, fan-out via groups and per-consumer acknowledgement. Everything lives in RAM under `maxmemory`, so an untrimmed stream is the single most common Redis OOM in production; every `XADD` in your code carries `MAXLEN` or `MINID`, and `XINFO STREAM` length is a dashboard panel. Say clearly what Streams are not: no partitions (shard across N streams by key yourself), no disk retention, no Kafka-style consumer offsets.

resource.label: Redis docs: Redis Streams data type

subtopics.name: Consumer groups: XREADGROUP, XACK, XPENDING, XAUTOCLAIM and a dead-letter policy
subtopics.learn: Create with `XGROUP CREATE key grp $ MKSTREAM` (`$` = only new entries, `0` = from the beginning). Consume with `XREADGROUP GROUP grp consumer-a COUNT 10 BLOCK 2000 STREAMS key >`; delivered entries enter the group's pending entries list until `XACK key grp id`. On restart, read with ID `0` instead of `>` to recover your own unacked entries first. `XPENDING key grp - + 10` shows idle time and delivery count per entry; `XAUTOCLAIM key grp consumer-b 60000 0-0 COUNT 100` (6.2+) atomically steals entries idle over 60 seconds from dead consumers and returns them, replacing the old XPENDING plus XCLAIM loop, and in 7.0 also reports IDs whose data was already trimmed. Define the poison-message rule up front: when delivery count exceeds five, `XADD key:dlq` the entry and `XACK` the original, and alert on DLQ length. Monitor `lag` and `pending` from `XINFO GROUPS key` (7.0+). Use stable consumer names (the pod name) so restarts reclaim their own work, run a reclaimer loop in every consumer, and never `MAXLEN`-trim below the oldest pending ID unless you accept losing in-flight work. This is at-least-once delivery; the consumer's handler is idempotent by construction (subtopic 8) or it is wrong.

resource.label: Redis command reference: XAUTOCLAIM

subtopics.name: maxmemory and eviction policies; memory accounting and fragmentation
subtopics.learn: The default `maxmemory 0` means unlimited on 64-bit, so an unbounded cache grows until the kernel OOM-kills the process; always set it (and to at most 50 to 60 percent of RAM when RDB or AOF rewrite is on, for fork copy-on-write headroom). Know each `maxmemory-policy` and which data it is safe for: `noeviction` makes writes fail with `OOM command not allowed` and is the correct setting for limiter buckets, idempotency keys and streams; `allkeys-lru` and `allkeys-lfu` (tune `lfu-log-factor`, `lfu-decay-time`) for pure caches with skewed access; the `volatile-*` policies only evict keys that have a TTL, so a store with no TTLs under `volatile-lru` behaves like `noeviction` and surprises everyone. LRU and LFU are approximate, sampling `maxmemory-samples` keys (default 5; 10 is close to true LRU). Hard rule for engagements: cache data and state data never share an instance with an `allkeys-*` policy, because one hot cache day evicts your dedup keys and the duplicates appear a week later in the customer's ledger. Read `INFO memory`: `used_memory` vs `used_memory_rss`, `mem_fragmentation_ratio` above 1.5 means turn on `activedefrag yes`, below 1.0 means you are swapping; `MEMORY USAGE key SAMPLES 5` and `redis-cli --memkeys` find the offenders; `evicted_keys` in `INFO stats` must stay at zero on a state instance.

resource.label: Redis docs: Key eviction (maxmemory and policies)

subtopics.name: Persistence and durability: RDB fork/COW, AOF appendfsync, WAIT and async replication
subtopics.learn: RDB snapshots (`save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000`, or `BGSAVE`) fork a child that writes a point-in-time file using copy-on-write, so a write-heavy workload during a snapshot can double resident memory and a `vm.overcommit_memory=0` host can refuse the fork; the loss window is everything since the last snapshot. AOF (`appendonly yes`) logs every write, with `appendfsync everysec` (default, about one second of loss) versus `always` (fsync per write, slow) versus `no`; rewrites are triggered by `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100` and `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb`, and Redis 7 stores a multi-part AOF (RDB base plus incremental files under `appenddirname`). Replication is asynchronous: `WAIT numreplicas timeout` blocks until replicas acknowledge receipt (not fsync; `WAITAOF` in 7.2 covers fsync), and a failover can promote a replica missing the last writes. Map each of your four uses onto this: a cache gets `save ""` and no AOF and reboots cold; a limiter tolerates losing buckets (limits reset once); idempotency keys and streams get AOF everysec plus a replica, and the critical path still relies on the Postgres unique index because none of this is a durable database.

resource.label: Redis docs: Persistence (RDB and AOF)

subtopics.name: HA topologies and managed Redis: Sentinel vs Cluster slots, ElastiCache, TLS and ACLs
subtopics.learn: Sentinel is one master with replicas plus at least three sentinels agreeing a quorum to fail over; clients must be Sentinel-aware (`redis.sentinel.Sentinel(...).master_for('mymaster')`) and the dataset is bounded by one box. Cluster shards 16384 hash slots across at least three masters each with a replica; `CLUSTER KEYSLOT k` shows where a key lives, cluster-aware clients (`redis.cluster.RedisCluster`) follow `MOVED` and `ASK` redirects, multi-key commands, MULTI and Lua require every key in one slot (hence the `{tenant}` hash tags from subtopic 2), and there is no `SELECT db`. On ElastiCache, cluster mode disabled gives one shard with a primary endpoint and a reader endpoint, cluster mode enabled gives a configuration endpoint, and Multi-AZ auto-failover flips DNS so clients see `ReadOnlyError` or `ConnectionError` for some seconds; leave `reserved-memory-percent 25` for fork overhead and pin the engine version. Lock it down the way the customer's security review expects: ACL users instead of a shared `requirepass` (`ACL SETUSER app on >pw ~{app}:* +@read +@write -@dangerous` blocks FLUSHALL, KEYS, CONFIG and DEBUG), TLS in transit (`rediss://`), encryption at rest, VPC-only with no public endpoint. Know the licensing story in one sentence for the customer's lawyer: Redis 7.4 moved to RSAL/SSPL, 8.0 added AGPL, and ElastiCache now defaults to the Valkey fork, which is command-compatible for everything in this topic.

resource.label: Amazon ElastiCache docs: Best practices and caching strategies

subtopics.name: redis-py in production: pool sizing, timeouts, retries, failover errors, circuit breaking
subtopics.learn: Build one `redis.asyncio.Redis` on a shared `ConnectionPool(max_connections=50)` in the FastAPI lifespan and inject it; a `Redis()` per request exhausts the pool and leaves the box in TIME_WAIT. Set `socket_connect_timeout=1`, `socket_timeout=0.5` (never leave it None on a request path), `health_check_interval=30`, and `retry=Retry(ExponentialBackoff(cap=0.5, base=0.01), 3)` with `retry_on_error=[ConnectionError, TimeoutError, BusyLoadingError]`; know that `ReadOnlyError` during a failover means you are talking to the demoted node and must reconnect, which redis-py handles for Cluster but you must handle for a single endpoint. Do the latency arithmetic: 0.5 s timeout times three retries inside a 1 s API budget is broken by construction, so align timeouts with the latency budget from topic 43. Wrap the cache path in a circuit breaker that bypasses Redis to Postgres for N seconds after a failure so a Redis outage does not become a database outage through multiplied timeouts. Call `CLIENT SETNAME <service>-<pod>` so `CLIENT LIST` shows who owns each connection when the customer asks why there are 900 of them.

resource.label: Redis docs: redis-py production usage guide

subtopics.name: Observability and test harness: INFO metrics, redis_exporter, fakeredis vs testcontainers, chaos
subtopics.learn: Run oliver006's redis_exporter next to the instance and graph `redis_keyspace_hits_total` / `redis_keyspace_misses_total` (hit ratio), `redis_evicted_keys_total`, `redis_memory_used_bytes` against `redis_memory_max_bytes`, `redis_connected_clients`, `redis_blocked_clients`, `redis_rejected_connections_total`, `redis_commands_duration_seconds_total`, and with `--check-streams` the per-group pending and lag; alert on hit ratio under 0.8 for a cache instance, any eviction on a state instance, memory over 80 percent, and `master_link_down`. Match each metric to its `INFO` field so you can debug without Grafana. Unit-test limiter and idempotency logic with `fakeredis[lua]` (it runs your EVAL scripts in-process), integration-test with a testcontainers `RedisContainer` for real expiry timing and real `NOSCRIPT` behaviour, and run one chaos test in CI: `docker pause` the Redis container mid-request and assert the fail-open or fail-closed behaviour you documented in subtopic 6. Never leave `MONITOR` running in production; it roughly halves throughput.

resource.label: redis_exporter GitHub repository (Prometheus exporter for Redis)

outcomes: You can implement a token-bucket limiter as a single Lua script (or Redis Function) with per-tenant and per-route dimensions, prove under 20 concurrent workers that admitted requests never exceed capacity plus refill, and return 429 with correct `Retry-After` and RateLimit headers.

You can implement an idempotency layer that claims with `SET NX PX`, fingerprints the request, replays completed responses byte-for-byte, rejects mismatched payloads, and demonstrate by killing the process between claim and completion that the retry recovers and Postgres still holds exactly one row.
You can make a webhook receiver dedup at-least-once deliveries from Stripe or GitHub, ack within one second, and show in a test that replaying the same event id 50 times produces one side effect.

You can build a Streams consumer group that survives a consumer crash, reclaims idle work with XAUTOCLAIM, routes entries past five deliveries to a dead-letter stream, and exposes lag and pending counts as metrics.

You can read `INFO memory`, `INFO stats` and `SLOWLOG` on an unfamiliar customer instance and, within ten minutes, state its eviction policy, whether it has ever evicted, its fragmentation ratio, and which commands are stalling it.

You can state, for each of cache, limiter, idempotency store and stream, exactly what is lost on process crash, on RDB-only restart, on AOF everysec restart, and on async failover, and which Postgres constraint backstops each loss.

You can configure an ElastiCache or self-hosted instance for a state workload (noeviction, AOF everysec, replica, ACL user with `-@dangerous`, TLS, no public endpoint) and explain to a customer security reviewer why each setting is there.
You can size and defend redis-py timeouts, retries and pool size against an API latency budget, and show a circuit breaker that keeps a Redis outage from cascading into the database.
failureModes: A limiter written as `INCR` then `EXPIRE` times out between the two commands during a Redis blip; the counter key has no TTL, and one tenant is rate-limited to zero until someone runs `TTL` on the key three days later.

Cache and idempotency keys share one ElastiCache node with `allkeys-lru`; a marketing campaign fills the cache, dedup keys are evicted, Stripe retries a payment webhook, and the customer's ledger shows duplicate invoices that nobody connects to Redis.

A webhook stream is written with `XADD key *` and no `MAXLEN`; three weeks later the instance hits `maxmemory` with `noeviction`, every `SET` in the API returns `OOM command not allowed`, and the whole product goes down because a log was never trimmed.

A consumer group is deployed with random consumer names per pod restart and no XAUTOCLAIM loop; after a rolling deploy, thousands of entries sit in the pending list owned by consumers that no longer exist and are never processed.

An idempotency layer relies on Redis alone; Multi-AZ failover promotes a replica missing the last two seconds of writes, the client's retry re-executes, and two payouts are created because there was no unique index in Postgres behind the fast path.

A lock is released with a plain `DEL` after a slow LLM call ran past the 30 second lease; the DEL removes the next worker's lock, three workers process the same batch concurrently, and the bug reproduces only under load.

redis-py is constructed with default `socket_timeout=None` and three retries; when the instance stalls on a `BGSAVE` fork under memory pressure, every API worker blocks on Redis, the connection pool drains, and a 400 ms cache hiccup becomes a five minute total outage of the customer's API.
interviewQuestions: Design a rate limiter for a multi-tenant LLM gateway where tenants have both a requests-per-second burst limit and a tokens-per-day budget. Where does the state live, how do you keep the check atomic, what happens on Redis failover, and what do you return to the client?

A customer says their idempotency layer 'works' because they check Redis for the key before processing. Walk me through three ways it still produces duplicates and how you would fix each without a rewrite.

We see p99 latency spikes across all tenants every few minutes on an otherwise healthy Redis. Take me through your diagnosis: which commands you run, what you expect to see, and the three most likely root causes.

Compare Redis Streams with consumer groups to Kafka for a webhook ingestion pipeline handling 2,000 events per second with strict no-loss requirements. When would you accept Streams, and what specifically would you configure and monitor to make it safe?

Explain what happens to the data when a Redis node with `appendfsync everysec` and one async replica loses power. Now the same for RDB only. Which of your four workloads (cache, limiter, idempotency, stream) is acceptable under each, and why?

A Lua token-bucket script is running fine in one environment and returning `NOSCRIPT` intermittently in another. What is going on, what are two fixes, and which one would you ship to a customer on ElastiCache?

You inherit a customer's ElastiCache cluster running `volatile-lru` with `maxmemory` at 90 percent of RAM and a mix of cache and session data. What is wrong, what breaks first, and how do you migrate to a safe configuration with zero downtime?
33.proofOfWork: A public repository `redis-edge-kit` containing a FastAPI service with three middleware components (token-bucket limiter, idempotency layer, webhook receiver with Streams hand-off) and a `docker compose` file that runs the service, Redis 7 with a committed `redis.conf`, Postgres, redis_exporter and Prometheus. The README shows, with pasted terminal output, five experiments you ran: (1) 20 concurrent workers against one bucket with the admitted count matching capacity plus refill; (2) `kill -9` of the API between idempotency claim and completion followed by a retry, with Postgres showing one row; (3) the same Stripe event replayed 50 times through the receiver producing one Stream entry and one DB row; (4) `docker kill` of one consumer mid-batch with XAUTOCLAIM recovery visible in `XPENDING` before and after; (5) `docker pause redis` during traffic showing the documented fail-closed 503 on the public route and fail-open on the internal route, then recovery. A one-page `DURABILITY.md` table lists each of the four stores against crash, RDB restart, AOF restart and async failover, with what is lost and which Postgres constraint catches it. This is what you walk a reviewer through in a take-home defence.

34.topic: Real-time transports: SSE, WebSockets, streaming at scale
34.why: Every LLM feature an FDE ships at a customer site is judged on time-to-first-token and on whether a 40-second answer survives a flaky corporate VPN, a proxy that buffers, and a rolling deploy mid-stream. You will be the person in the customer's war room when their Nginx or ALB silently kills the stream at 60 seconds, when 3 uvicorn workers each hold a different third of a session, or when one slow browser tab makes the whole pod OOM. Choosing SSE vs WebSocket, making delivery resumable, and proving the numbers with a load test are the difference between a demo and a production integration the customer's platform team will sign off on.
prerequisites: HTTP/1.1 request/response lifecycle, headers, and chunked transfer encoding (Track E HTTP and API design topic)
TCP basics: send/receive buffers, keepalive, half-open connections, and what a proxy in the middle does to them (HPBN ch. 2 from the networking topic)
Python asyncio: coroutines, tasks, asyncio.Queue, asyncio.gather, cancellation semantics (Track E async Python topic)
FastAPI/Starlette request handling and dependency injection, since DefenderMate's API is built on it
Redis fundamentals: connection, key types, TTLs (Track E caching topic) - Streams and Pub/Sub are introduced here
Claude Messages API non-streaming calls and the tool_use content block shape (Track F Claude API topic)

subtopics.name: Transport decision matrix: SSE vs WebSocket vs long-poll vs plain HTTP streaming
subtopics.learn: Be able to pick a transport from the actual constraints, not habit: direction (server-to-client only favours SSE; true bidirectional or binary favours WebSocket), proxy/CDN friendliness (SSE is plain HTTP so WAFs, ALBs, service meshes and corporate proxies pass it; WebSocket needs Upgrade support end-to-end), reconnection (EventSource reconnects and resumes for free, WebSocket makes you write it), and auth (EventSource cannot set headers). Know the HTTP/1.1 six-connections-per-origin browser limit that makes multiple SSE tabs stall, and why HTTP/2 removes it. Write the one-paragraph justification you would put in a customer design doc for streaming LLM tokens: SSE for the token stream, a normal POST for user input, WebSocket only when you need client-to-server messages mid-generation (cancel, voice, cursor sync).

resource.label: HPBN ch. 16 - Server-Sent Events (SSE)

subtopics.name: HTTP streaming plumbing: chunked encoding, HTTP/2 streams, and where bytes get stuck
subtopics.learn: Understand what actually goes on the wire when you stream: HTTP/1.1 `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` with hex-length-prefixed chunks and a terminating `0\r\n\r\n`, versus HTTP/2 DATA frames on a single multiplexed connection with per-stream flow-control windows (WINDOW_UPDATE) and `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`. Know that any hop - TLS terminator, reverse proxy, Python WSGI server, gzip middleware - can buffer your chunks until a threshold and destroy time-to-first-token; `Content-Encoding: gzip` in particular must be disabled for `text/event-stream` or flushes never reach the client. Confirm with `curl -N` (no buffering) and `--http2` to see chunks arrive individually.

resource.label: HPBN ch. 12 - HTTP/2 (streams, multiplexing, flow control)

subtopics.name: SSE wire format: event, data, id, retry, and comment lines

resource.label: MDN - Using server-sent events (event stream format)

subtopics.name: EventSource client semantics and its hard limits
subtopics.learn: Know exactly what the browser does for you and what it will not: `new EventSource(url, {withCredentials})` auto-reconnects on network error and on server close, sends `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect, exposes `readyState` (CONNECTING 0, OPEN 1, CLOSED 2), and stops permanently only on HTTP 204 or a non-`text/event-stream` content type. It cannot set custom headers (so no `Authorization: Bearer`), only GET, and treats a 401/500 as fatal without retry. Be able to explain the reconnection algorithm from the spec: on error, wait `retry` ms, reconnect with `Last-Event-ID`, and why your server must therefore be idempotent on replay. Decide per project whether EventSource's convenience beats a fetch-based reader that can send headers.

resource.label: MDN - EventSource interface

subtopics.name: Claude streaming event schema and relaying it faithfully
subtopics.learn: Know the Messages API stream event sequence cold: `message_start` (usage.input_tokens), one or more `content_block_start` / `content_block_delta` / `content_block_stop` groups indexed by `index`, `message_delta` (stop_reason, usage.output_tokens), `message_stop`, plus `ping` events and an `error` event (`overloaded_error`) that can arrive mid-stream and must be surfaced, not swallowed. Deltas are typed: `text_delta` for prose, `input_json_delta` for tool_use arguments which arrive as partial JSON fragments you accumulate and parse only at `content_block_stop`, and `thinking_delta` when extended thinking is on. Build the relay so your SSE `event:` names mirror Anthropic's and you forward `usage` so the customer can meter cost per session; use the SDK's `client.messages.stream()` context manager and `stream.text_stream` / `get_final_message()`.

resource.label: Claude API docs - Streaming Messages

subtopics.name: FastAPI StreamingResponse: async generators, disconnect detection, and the headers that matter
subtopics.learn: Implement the endpoint as `StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream", headers={...})` where `gen` is an `async def` generator that yields encoded frames. Set `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform`, `X-Accel-Buffering: no` (Nginx), and `Connection: keep-alive`; never wrap it in GZipMiddleware. Detect client departure with `await request.is_disconnected()` between yields or catch `asyncio.CancelledError` in the generator's `finally` so you cancel the upstream Anthropic call and release the Redis handle rather than generating tokens nobody will read. Understand that Starlette runs the generator on the event loop, so a blocking `requests` call or `time.sleep` inside it freezes every other stream on the worker.

resource.label: FastAPI - Custom Response (StreamingResponse)

subtopics.name: Resumable delivery: Redis Streams as the replay buffer behind Last-Event-ID
subtopics.learn: Design resume properly: the generation task writes each delta to a per-session Redis Stream with `XADD stream:{session_id} MAXLEN ~ 1000 * data ...`, getting back a monotonic `ms-seq` ID that you emit as the SSE `id:`. The HTTP handler is now a pure reader: on connect it does `XRANGE stream:{sid} (last_event_id +` to replay what was missed, then `XREAD BLOCK 15000 STREAMS stream:{sid} $` (or the last replayed ID) to tail live. Set an `EXPIRE` on the stream keyed to your retention policy, write a terminal `done` entry so a late reconnect knows the generation finished, and handle the case where the ID in `Last-Event-ID` predates `MAXLEN` trimming by sending a `event: reset` so the client refetches. This decoupling is also what lets any worker serve any reconnect.

resource.label: Redis docs - Streams (XADD, XRANGE, XREAD, MAXLEN)

subtopics.name: Reverse proxies and load balancers: buffering, idle timeouts, and Upgrade handling
subtopics.learn: Know the exact knobs that break streams at each hop and their fixes. Nginx: `proxy_buffering off;` (or honour `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), `proxy_read_timeout` above your longest generation (default 60s kills long answers), `proxy_http_version 1.1;` plus `proxy_set_header Connection "";` for keepalive, and for WebSocket `proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";`. AWS ALB: idle timeout default 60s applies to both SSE and WS - raise it or heartbeat under it; classic ELB does not speak WebSocket on HTTP listeners. Cloudflare and many corporate proxies cap at 100s of inactivity. Add `proxy_cache off` and verify with `curl -N` through the proxy, not just against uvicorn, before telling a customer it works.

resource.label: Nginx - ngx_http_proxy_module (proxy_buffering, proxy_read_timeout)

subtopics.name: Heartbeats, retry hints, and detecting half-open connections
subtopics.learn: A silent TCP connection through NAT or a load balancer will be dropped without either end knowing; the server keeps writing into a dead socket until the kernel buffer fills. Send an SSE comment line (`: keepalive\n\n`) every 15s (under every timeout in the path), and for WebSocket rely on protocol-level ping/pong frames with a pong deadline. Use the `retry:` field to steer client reconnect backoff (for example 1000ms normally, larger when you are shedding load) and understand the spec's reconnection state machine so you know a `retry:` sent during a stream persists for future reconnects. On the server, treat a write that raises `ConnectionResetError`/`BrokenPipeError` as the client leaving and tear down the upstream call immediately.

resource.label: WHATWG HTML Living Standard - Server-sent events (reconnection, retry)

subtopics.name: WebSocket protocol: handshake, frames, control opcodes, and close codes
subtopics.learn: Read the RFC once so you can debug from a packet capture: HTTP/1.1 GET with `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, and the `101 Switching Protocols` response whose `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` is base64(SHA-1(key + GUID)). Frames carry FIN and opcode (0x1 text, 0x2 binary, 0x8 close, 0x9 ping, 0xA pong), client-to-server frames are masked, and large messages fragment across continuation frames. Know the close codes you will actually see: 1000 normal, 1001 going away (tab closed / server shutdown), 1006 abnormal closure (no close frame - the network died), 1008 policy violation, 1009 message too big, 1011 internal error, 1012 service restart, 1013 try again later. Be able to say why 1006 in your client logs points at a proxy or idle timeout rather than your code.

resource.label: RFC 6455 - The WebSocket Protocol (section 7.4.1 status codes)

subtopics.name: FastAPI WebSocket endpoints: bidirectional concurrency without deadlocks
subtopics.learn: Write `@app.websocket("/ws")` handlers that `await websocket.accept()`, then run a receive loop and a send loop concurrently with `asyncio.gather` or a TaskGroup so an inbound `cancel` message can stop an in-flight generation; a single sequential `receive_text()` then `send_text()` loop cannot do this. Catch `WebSocketDisconnect` (it carries `.code`), close deliberately with `await websocket.close(code=1011, reason=...)`, and never `send` after the socket has closed. Use `receive_json`/`send_json` for a typed envelope `{type, id, payload}` and enforce a max message size (uvicorn `--ws-max-size`, default 16 MiB) to stop a client from allocating your memory. Know that dependencies work in WebSocket routes but HTTP exception handlers do not - you must map errors to close codes yourself.

resource.label: FastAPI - WebSockets (accept, receive, WebSocketDisconnect)

subtopics.name: Backpressure: where the buffers are and what to do when a consumer is slow
subtopics.learn: Trace the chain of buffers a token passes through: your asyncio.Queue, the transport write buffer (`transport.get_write_buffer_size()`, limits via `set_write_buffer_limits(high, low)`), the kernel socket send buffer, the proxy, the client's TCP receive window, and on the browser side `WebSocket.bufferedAmount`. Producers that ignore these grow memory without bound; one slow mobile client on a fan-out channel can take down the pod. Apply the three legitimate responses: block the producer (`await writer.drain()` / a bounded `asyncio.Queue(maxsize=)` that makes `put` await), coalesce (merge pending text deltas into one frame when the queue is deep - safe for LLM tokens because order is preserved), or drop/disconnect with a documented close code when the queue exceeds a hard limit. Measure queue depth as a metric before you choose.

resource.label: Python docs - asyncio Streams (StreamWriter.drain, write buffer limits)

subtopics.name: Multi-worker fan-out: sticky sessions vs Redis Pub/Sub vs Streams consumer groups
subtopics.learn: With `uvicorn --workers 4` or 10 pods, the client's reconnect lands on a different process than the one generating tokens; in-memory dicts of sessions silently break. Compare the three fixes: sticky sessions at the LB (cookie or IP hash - fragile on deploys and uneven), Redis Pub/Sub (`PUBLISH`/`SUBSCRIBE` per session channel - fire-and-forget, a subscriber that is not connected at publish time loses the message, so it cannot resume), and Redis Streams with `XREAD` from a known ID (durable, resumable, one stream per session, readable by any worker). Understand `XGROUP CREATE` / `XREADGROUP` / `XACK` consumer groups for the different problem of distributing work across workers, and why a broadcast to many viewers of one session uses plain `XREAD` on the same stream rather than groups. Benchmark Pub/Sub message latency so you can quote it.

resource.label: Redis docs - Pub/Sub (PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, delivery semantics)

subtopics.name: Security: Origin checks, cross-site WebSocket hijacking, and authenticating EventSource
subtopics.learn: WebSocket handshakes are not subject to CORS; the browser sends cookies and the server must validate the `Origin` header itself against an allowlist or any site can open an authenticated socket to your API (CSWSH). EventSource sends cookies with `withCredentials` but cannot send `Authorization`, so pick one of: a short-lived (60s) single-use stream token minted by an authenticated POST and passed as a query parameter, a cookie scoped to the streaming path, or a fetch-based reader that can set headers. Never put a long-lived bearer token in a URL - it lands in proxy and LB access logs at the customer. Rate-limit connection establishment per user (not just messages) and cap concurrent streams per account to stop connection-exhaustion attacks.

resource.label: OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet (WebSockets section)

subtopics.name: Client-side: fetch + ReadableStream SSE parser with headers, abort, and partial lines
subtopics.learn: Build the client you will actually ship when EventSource is too limited: `fetch(url, {method: 'POST', headers: {Authorization}, signal: controller.signal})`, then `response.body.getReader()` with a `TextDecoder('utf-8', {stream: true})` so multi-byte characters split across chunks decode correctly. Buffer incoming text, split on `\n\n`, keep the trailing partial frame for the next read, and parse `id:`/`event:`/`data:` lines yourself. Implement the reconnect loop EventSource gave you for free: on error, wait, re-POST with a `Last-Event-ID` header, and de-duplicate by ID. Use `AbortController.abort()` on unmount or user cancel so the server sees the disconnect and stops the upstream generation.

subtopics.name: Load testing streams with k6: WebSocket scenarios, custom Trend metrics, and SSE caveats
subtopics.learn: Use `import ws from 'k6/ws'` with `ws.connect(url, params, socket => {...})`, registering `socket.on('open'|'message'|'close'|'error')`, `socket.setTimeout` to bound the session, and `socket.ping()` to exercise keepalive. Standard `http_req_duration` is meaningless for streams, so record what matters with `new Trend('ttft_ms')` (time from send to first token), `new Trend('tokens_per_sec')`, and `new Counter('reconnects')`, and gate the run with `thresholds: {ttft_ms: ['p(95)<800']}`. Model load with a `ramping-vus` executor to find the connection count where p95 TTFT degrades and where the server starts closing with 1013. Know that k6's core `http` module buffers the whole response, so SSE needs the `xk6-sse` extension or a WebSocket-equivalent path for load testing; state this limitation in the report.

resource.label: Grafana k6 docs - k6/ws module

subtopics.name: Server capacity and rolling deploys: uvicorn limits, file descriptors, graceful drain
subtopics.learn: Each open stream is a socket, a task, and buffers; tune `ulimit -n` (and the container's `nofile` limit) above your target concurrency, and set uvicorn `--limit-concurrency` so excess connections get a fast 503 instead of degrading everyone, `--timeout-keep-alive`, `--ws-ping-interval` / `--ws-ping-timeout` (defaults 20s/20s) and `--timeout-graceful-shutdown`. On SIGTERM uvicorn stops accepting and waits for in-flight requests - long streams exceed that window, so on shutdown proactively send an SSE `retry:` then close (or WS close 1012) so clients reconnect to the new pod and resume from `Last-Event-ID` via the Redis Stream. Align Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and a `preStop` sleep with LB deregistration delay so no connection is routed to a dying pod.

subtopics.name: Observability for streams: the five metrics and how to instrument them
subtopics.learn: Ordinary request metrics hide stream problems because a 40s stream and a 40s hang look identical. Export a Gauge `open_streams{transport}` (inc on connect, dec in `finally`), a Histogram `ttft_seconds`, a Histogram `stream_duration_seconds` labelled by termination reason (`completed`, `client_disconnect`, `upstream_error`, `shutdown`), a Counter `resume_total{outcome=replayed|reset}` and a Gauge `send_queue_depth`. Correlate with the upstream Anthropic `request-id` logged at `message_start`. Alert on `open_streams` flatlining at your `--limit-concurrency` and on `client_disconnect` share rising, which is the early signal of a proxy timeout in the customer's environment.

You can implement a FastAPI SSE endpoint that relays Claude's stream with matching event names, forwards usage, stops the upstream call within one second of client disconnect, and passes `curl -N` through an Nginx proxy with `proxy_buffering off`.
You can kill the server mid-generation and show the browser reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID`, receiving only the missed deltas from a Redis Stream, with no duplicated or lost text.
You can run the endpoint under `uvicorn --workers 4`, connect, reconnect onto a different worker, and still resume - and explain why Pub/Sub alone could not do that.

You can demonstrate backpressure by throttling a client to 1 KB/s and showing server memory stay flat because the producer blocks on a bounded queue or coalesces deltas, with `send_queue_depth` visible in metrics.
You can read a WebSocket close code from client logs (1006 vs 1011 vs 1012) and correctly attribute it to network/proxy, server bug, or deploy without looking at server logs.
You can produce a k6 report with p50/p95 TTFT and tokens/sec at 50, 200, and 500 concurrent streams, identify the knee, and name the limiting resource (FDs, event loop, upstream rate limit).
You can list the four hops that commonly buffer or time out a stream at a customer (gzip middleware, Nginx, ALB idle timeout, corporate proxy) and the exact config change for each.

Generation kept running after the user closed the tab because the handler never checked `is_disconnected()`; the customer's Anthropic bill showed 30 percent of output tokens were never delivered to anyone.
Session state lived in a module-level dict; after scaling to 3 pods, one in three reconnects returned 'unknown session' and support blamed the browser.
A dashboard that broadcast one agent run to 40 viewers used an unbounded per-viewer list; one viewer on a hotel Wi-Fi made the pod OOM and took down the other 39.

A rolling deploy sent SIGTERM with a 30s grace period while streams ran for 90s; clients received an abrupt close with no `retry:` or resume, and the resulting duplicate requests doubled load on the new pods.

35.why: Every customer above a certain size already runs Kafka in some form (MSK, Confluent Cloud, Redpanda, Event Hubs) and expects your product to consume from their topics and publish back onto them under their schema registry, ACLs and retention rules; the FDE is the person who reads their topic contract, sizes the consumer group, and explains on a Friday night why the pilot dropped or duplicated events.
