subtopics.name: Log, queue or webhook: the decision
subtopics.learn: Place the three on a table by what the receiver controls: a webhook is sender-push (receiver must be up, sender owns retries, no replay, ordering unspecified, each new consumer means another endpoint to register); a queue such as SQS or a Postgres table drained with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` is competing consumers with per-message ack and delete (visibility timeout, no fan-out without an extra layer, nothing to replay after ack); a Kafka topic is a durable, replayable log that any number of consumer groups read at their own pace with per-key ordering. Reach for a topic when at least two of these hold: more than one independent consumer needs the same events, you need replay or reprocessing from history, per-key ordering matters, or sustained throughput is thousands per second rather than hundreds per day. Be able to say out loud what Kafka costs you: no per-message ack or delete, no built-in delayed delivery or priority, and the operational weight of brokers, a schema registry and consumer-group hygiene.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Use Cases

subtopics.name: Partitions, offsets, segments and retention
subtopics.learn: A topic is N independent append-only logs; each record has a partition and a monotonic offset, and ordering exists only inside one partition. On disk a partition is a directory of segments (`segment.bytes`, `segment.ms`) with `.index` and `.timeindex` files; retention is enforced per closed segment by `retention.ms`/`retention.bytes` under `cleanup.policy=delete`, so a one-hour retention with a 1 GB active segment still keeps hours of data, or by compaction under `cleanup.policy=compact`. Partition count is a one-way door: you can add partitions (`kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions`, `rpk topic add-partitions`) but never remove them, and adding them changes the key-to-partition mapping for every keyed producer. Size it as max(target MB/s divided by per-partition MB/s, the most consumer instances you will ever run) and know that each partition costs file handles, replication traffic and leader-election time on failover.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Topic-Level Configs

subtopics.name: Keys, partitioners and what 'ordered' really means
subtopics.learn: The default partitioner is `murmur2(key) mod numPartitions`; null keys use the sticky partitioner (KIP-480, strictly uniform since KIP-794), which fills one batch to a single partition then moves on, so null-keyed records have no ordering at all. Ordering holds only for records with the same key in one partition from one producer, and only when `enable.idempotence=true` or `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1` stops a retried batch leapfrogging a later one. Choose keys deliberately for DefenderMate: `document_id` orders one document's lifecycle, `tenant_id` orders everything for a tenant but pins a large tenant to one partition (hot key). Detect skew with per-partition end offsets from `rpk topic describe -p` or `kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic documents.v1`.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: The Producer

subtopics.name: Producer path: acks, idempotence, batching, timeouts
subtopics.learn: Trace `send()` through the record accumulator: `batch.size` and `linger.ms` decide when a batch flushes, `compression.type=lz4|zstd` compresses per batch, and a full `buffer.memory` blocks for `max.block.ms` then throws. `acks=0` is fire-and-forget, `acks=1` is leader-only (lost on leader failover), `acks=all` waits for the in-sync replicas. `enable.idempotence=true` (default since 3.0) assigns a producer id plus per-partition sequence numbers so the broker dedupes retries, and forces `acks=all`, `retries=MAX_INT` and in-flight at most 5; it does not survive a producer restart. `delivery.timeout.ms` (default 120 s) is the total budget including retries and must exceed `linger.ms + request.timeout.ms`. The delivery callback, not the return value of `send()`, is where you learn a record was lost, so in confluent-kafka-python always pass `on_delivery=` and call `flush()` on shutdown.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Producer Configs

subtopics.name: Replication, ISR and the durability equation
subtopics.learn: Each partition has one leader and N-1 followers; the in-sync replica set (ISR) is the followers within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` of the leader, and the high watermark is the last offset replicated to the whole ISR, which is as far as consumers can read. `acks=all` waits for the ISR, and `min.insync.replicas` sets how small the ISR may shrink before writes fail with `NotEnoughReplicas` instead of quietly losing durability. RF=3 with `min.insync.replicas=2` and `acks=all` survives one broker; losing two makes the topic unwritable, which is the correct trade. `unclean.leader.election.enable=false` (default) chooses unavailability over electing an out-of-sync replica that truncates committed records. Spread replicas with `broker.rack`. Since 3.3 the controller quorum runs on KRaft (KIP-500) instead of ZooKeeper; Redpanda runs Raft per partition and has no separate controller tier.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: Replication

subtopics.name: Consumer group protocol and rebalances
subtopics.learn: A group coordinator broker owns each group: members send JoinGroup and SyncGroup (classic protocol) and one member, the leader, runs the `partition.assignment.strategy` (Range, RoundRobin, StickyAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor). Eager strategies revoke every partition from every member on any change (stop-the-world); cooperative (KIP-429) revokes only the partitions that move, across two rounds. KIP-848 (`group.protocol=consumer`, GA in 4.0) moves assignment into the broker so rebalances are incremental and driven by per-member heartbeats. Know the triggers: member join or leave, `session.timeout.ms` expiring on missed heartbeats, `max.poll.interval.ms` expiring, a partition-count change, or subscription change. More consumers than partitions leaves consumers idle; `group.instance.id` (static membership) lets a restarted pod reclaim its partitions without a rebalance if it returns within `session.timeout.ms`.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Consumer Rebalance Protocol (KIP-848)

subtopics.name: The poll loop: heartbeats, max.poll.interval.ms and backpressure
subtopics.learn: Heartbeats run on a background thread every `heartbeat.interval.ms`, but `poll()` itself is the liveness signal for processing: fail to call it within `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 300 s) and the consumer leaves the group and its partitions are reassigned while you are still working, guaranteeing duplicates. Bound work per poll with `max.poll.records` (Java) or one-message-at-a-time in librdkafka, and for slow per-record work such as an LLM call per chunk use `pause()`/`resume()` on the partitions while a bounded worker pool drains, so `poll()` keeps being called. `fetch.min.bytes` and `fetch.max.wait.ms` trade latency for batch efficiency; `max.partition.fetch.bytes` must exceed your largest record or the consumer stalls on it forever. Implement `on_revoke` to commit or flush in-flight work before partitions move.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Consumer Configs

subtopics.name: Offsets: commit ordering, auto.offset.reset, expiry and lag
subtopics.learn: Committed offsets live in `__consumer_offsets` keyed by (group, topic, partition) and mean 'next offset to read'. `enable.auto.commit=true` commits the offsets returned by the previous `poll()` on the next `poll()` every `auto.commit.interval.ms`, so any handler that has not finished can be committed past; explicit commit-after-process gives at-least-once and commit-before-process gives at-most-once. `auto.offset.reset` applies only when the group has no committed offset or it is out of range: `latest` (default) silently skips all history for a brand-new group, `earliest` replays everything, `none` throws. Offsets for an empty group expire after `offsets.retention.minutes` (7 days), so a service down for eight days restarts as if new. Operate with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group X` (CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET, LAG), `--reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000 --execute` while the group is inactive, or `rpk group seek`. Lag per partition, not the total, is the SLI.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Basic Operations: Managing Consumer Groups

subtopics.name: Delivery semantics: what 'exactly-once' actually claims
subtopics.learn: Decompose the guarantee into three hops: producer to broker (the idempotent producer removes duplicates caused by retries), consumer position (commit placement decides duplicate versus loss), and the side effect (whatever your consumer does to the outside world). Kafka's exactly-once semantics cover only consume-transform-produce where inputs, outputs and offset commits are all inside Kafka and committed atomically in one transaction, read by consumers with `isolation.level=read_committed`. The moment a consumer writes to Postgres, calls an HTTP API or invokes a model, EOS ends and you need an idempotent consumer or a transactional outbox; practise saying that in one sentence to an architect who has read a vendor slide. Know that `read_committed` consumers cannot read past the last stable offset (LSO), so a hung transaction blocks the partition until `transaction.timeout.ms` expires.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: Message Delivery Semantics

subtopics.name: Transactions internals: transactional.id, epochs and zombie fencing
subtopics.learn: A transactional producer sets `transactional.id` and calls `init_transactions()`, which registers with the transaction coordinator (owner of a `__transaction_state` partition) and bumps the producer epoch, fencing any older instance with the same id so its next send fails with `ProducerFenced`. Then `begin_transaction()`, `produce()` to any partitions, `send_offsets_to_transaction(offsets, consumer_group_metadata)` to fold the consumer commit into the same transaction, and `commit_transaction()`, which writes control markers into every involved partition. The `transactional.id` must be stable per input partition set (Kafka Streams uses one per task) or fencing protects nothing, and thousands of ids load the coordinator. Cost: extra round trips per commit, end-to-end latency bounded by commit interval, and `transaction.timeout.ms` must stay below the broker's `transaction.max.timeout.ms` (15 min default).

resource.label: KIP-98 - Exactly Once Delivery and Transactional Messaging

subtopics.name: Idempotent consumers: dedupe keys and the processed-events table
subtopics.learn: Make every handler safe to run twice: derive an idempotency key from the event (an `event_id` header, or `topic-partition-offset` as a fallback), and in the same Postgres transaction as the business write run `INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, skipping the work when zero rows were inserted; commit the Kafka offset only after that transaction commits. For state updates prefer natural idempotence, an upsert such as `ON CONFLICT (document_id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE EXCLUDED.version > documents.version`, over a dedupe table. For side effects you do not own (a customer's REST API, email) pass the key through as an `Idempotency-Key` header and persist the response. A Redis `SET NX EX` check (topic 31) is faster but not atomic with the database write; know when that gap is acceptable and when it is not.

resource.label: microservices.io - Pattern: Idempotent Consumer

subtopics.name: Transactional outbox and CDC with Debezium
subtopics.learn: Dual writes (commit the row, then produce) lose or orphan an event whenever the process dies between the two; the fix is an `outbox` table written in the same transaction as the business row and relayed to Kafka by a separate process. Relay options: a poller (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, delete after the delivery callback; simple, but adds polling latency and load) or change data capture, where Debezium reads the Postgres WAL through a logical replication slot (`wal_level=logical`, `pgoutput` plugin, `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` if you need old values on updates) and the outbox event router SMT turns each row into a record on a topic derived from `aggregatetype`, keyed by `aggregateid`. Understand slot risk: an idle slot pins WAL forever and fills the disk, so alert on `pg_replication_slots` lag. CDC is at-least-once, so the consumer side still needs the idempotency work from the previous subtopic.

resource.label: Debezium Documentation - Outbox Event Router

subtopics.name: Schemas: registry, wire format and compatibility modes
subtopics.learn: Serialise with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema through a schema registry; the Confluent wire format prefixes each payload with a magic byte and a 4-byte schema id, so consumers fetch the writer schema by id and resolve it against their reader schema. Set subject compatibility deliberately: BACKWARD (default; new schema reads old data, so consumers upgrade first, and you may only delete fields or add fields with defaults), FORWARD (producers upgrade first), FULL, and the `_TRANSITIVE` variants that check against every prior version rather than only the latest. Subject naming (`TopicNameStrategy` default versus `RecordNameStrategy` when many event types share one topic) decides what 'compatible' is checked against. JSON without a registry is a promise, not a contract, and renaming a field is always two releases: add the new field with a default, remove the old one later.

resource.label: Confluent Platform Documentation - Schema Registry

subtopics.name: Event design: notification vs state transfer, envelopes and PII
subtopics.learn: Decide per event type whether it is a thin notification (`document.uploaded {document_id}`; consumers call back for state and are coupled to your API's availability) or event-carried state transfer (the full document metadata rides along; consumers are decoupled but you have now published PII onto a retained log). Standardise the envelope on CloudEvents attributes (`id`, `source`, `type`, `time`, `subject`, `datacontenttype`), carried as Kafka headers in binary mode or as the JSON body in structured mode, and version the type name (`defendermate.document.uploaded.v1`). Never put PII in keys or headers: they survive compaction and show up in every console. For regulated customers pair state transfer with crypto-shredding, encrypting payload fields with a per-tenant key so erasure means deleting a key rather than rewriting an immutable log.

resource.label: CloudEvents Specification (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Log compaction and tombstones for state topics
subtopics.learn: `cleanup.policy=compact` keeps the latest record per key rather than a time window, turning a topic into a durable changelog that a new consumer can bootstrap from with `auto.offset.reset=earliest` and end up holding current state for every key. Deletes are tombstones, a record with the key and a null value, retained for `delete.retention.ms` (24 h default) so lagging consumers see the delete before it is compacted away. Compaction runs only on closed segments and is governed by `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio`, `min.compaction.lag.ms` and `max.compaction.lag.ms`; the active head is never compacted, so 'one record per key' is a guarantee only after the cleaner catches up. Use `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` when you want both a key snapshot and an age bound.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Design: Log Compaction

subtopics.name: Failure handling: retries, dead-letter topics, poison pills
subtopics.learn: Separate transient from permanent failures in the handler: retry transient ones in-process with bounded exponential backoff while keeping `poll()` alive (pause the partition), and route permanent ones (deserialisation error, schema violation, business-rule rejection) to `<topic>.dlq` carrying the original bytes plus headers for exception class, message, source topic/partition/offset and attempt count, then commit and move on. A record the deserialiser throws on will otherwise crash-loop the consumer at the same offset indefinitely, so deserialise inside a try or use an error-handling deserialiser wrapper. Retry topics (`<topic>.retry.1m`, `<topic>.retry.10m`) trade per-key ordering for throughput; say so explicitly when you choose them. Kafka Connect exposes the same knobs as `errors.tolerance=all`, `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name` and `errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true`. Build the replay path out of the DLQ before you need it.

resource.label: Confluent Developer - Event Streaming Patterns: Dead Letter Stream

subtopics.name: Observability: lag, broker health and trace propagation
subtopics.learn: Alert on consumer lag per partition and on its derivative (lag rising while produce rate is flat means a stuck consumer, not a busy one), exported by kafka-lag-exporter or Burrow, and on broker signals `UnderReplicatedPartitions`, `OfflinePartitionsCount`, `ActiveControllerCount != 1`, `RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent` and disk headroom. Propagate W3C `traceparent` through record headers so a trace spans producer, broker hop and consumer; follow the OpenTelemetry messaging semantic conventions (`messaging.system=kafka`, `messaging.destination.name`, `messaging.kafka.message.key`, `messaging.kafka.offset`, `messaging.consumer.group.name`) and model consumption as a `receive` span plus a `process` span per record with span links, because one poll can carry records from many producer traces. Log (topic, partition, offset, key) on every handler error so support can replay one record instead of a day.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions - Kafka messaging

subtopics.name: Security and multi-tenant isolation on a shared cluster
subtopics.learn: Authenticate clients with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 or mTLS on a TLS listener (`security.protocol=SASL_SSL`, `sasl.mechanism=SCRAM-SHA-512`) and authorise with ACLs: `kafka-acls.sh --add --allow-principal User:ingest --operation Write --topic documents.v1`, `--operation Read --group ingest-workers` for the consumer group, and `--resource-pattern-type prefixed` to cover `tenant-a.*`. Once `authorizer.class.name` is set, a resource with no ACL is denied unless `allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true`, which you should never ship. Protect tenants from each other with quotas (`producer_byte_rate`, `consumer_byte_rate`, `request_percentage` per user or client id via `kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config`) so one tenant's replay cannot starve the rest. Decide topic-per-tenant (hard, ACL-enforceable isolation; partitions and metadata scale linearly with tenants) versus a shared topic keyed by tenant (efficient; isolation exists only in your application code) and write the reasoning down.

resource.label: Apache Kafka Documentation - Operations: Multi-Tenancy (naming, quotas, ACLs)

subtopics.name: Lab: rebuild DefenderMate ingestion on a local Redpanda cluster
subtopics.learn: Run a three-broker Redpanda cluster with Docker Compose (`redpanda start --smp 1 --memory 1G --advertise-kafka-addr <node>:9092` per node) plus its built-in schema registry and console, create topics with `rpk topic create documents.v1 -p 6 -r 3 -c min.insync.replicas=2`, and rebuild the ingestion path as `document.uploaded` to chunker to `chunk.created` to embedder to `embedding.ready` using confluent-kafka-python with `acks=all`, `enable.idempotence=true`, manual commits after the Postgres write and the processed-events dedupe. Then break it on purpose: `docker kill` one broker mid-produce and compare lost-record counts under `acks=1` versus `acks=all`; SIGKILL the consumer between database commit and offset commit and count duplicates with and without the dedupe table; inject a malformed record and watch it land in the DLQ; watch lag with `rpk group describe`. Every assertion is a number printed by a script, not a screenshot.

resource.label: Redpanda Docs - Redpanda Quickstart (Docker)

outcomes: You can bring up a three-broker Redpanda cluster from Compose, create a topic with RF=3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, produce 100k keyed records with `acks=all` and idempotence on, kill one broker mid-run and show zero loss and zero reordering per key; kill a second and show writes fail with `NotEnoughReplicas` rather than silently degrading.

You can demonstrate all three commit-placement outcomes (loss, duplicates, correct) by moving `commit()` before or after processing and SIGKILLing the consumer between them, then explain each outcome from the numbers in `rpk group describe` or `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`.

You can run a consumer whose handler takes 90 seconds per record without it being evicted from the group, by pausing partitions and bounding work per poll, and show the rebalance log lines before and after the fix.

You can state in one sentence what Kafka's exactly-once semantics do and do not cover, then show a consume-transform-produce transaction where a `read_committed` consumer never sees the aborted records and a `read_uncommitted` one does.

You can implement outbox plus Debezium CDC into Redpanda and prove atomicity: kill the API between the Postgres commit and any produce call, and show the event still arrives and is processed exactly once downstream thanks to the processed-events table.

You can register an Avro schema, attempt a breaking change (removing a field without a default under BACKWARD compatibility), have the registry reject it with an HTTP 409, and show an old consumer still reading records written by a compatible new producer.

You can size a topic from a throughput target and consumer parallelism ceiling, explain why the count cannot shrink, and demonstrate what breaks for a keyed, stateful consumer when partitions are added.

You can hand a customer a one-page 'when not to Kafka' memo with a decision matrix across webhook, SQS, Postgres queue, Redis Streams and Kafka, each row backed by a concrete number (events/day, consumers, replay window, ordering need, ops headcount).
failureModes: A new consumer service shipped with the default `auto.offset.reset=latest`; because the group had no committed offset it skipped the entire backlog produced before its first deploy, and nobody noticed until a monthly reconciliation found 40,000 documents that were never embedded.

Each record triggered an LLM call with client-side retries, so a batch took longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`; the consumer was evicted, its partitions moved to a peer that reprocessed the same batch and was also evicted, producing a rebalance storm where lag climbed for hours while CPU sat near zero.

One malformed message from an upstream team made the deserialiser throw before `poll()` returned; the consumer crash-looped on the same offset for six hours and the fix (catch, publish to a DLQ with the offset in headers, commit) took ten minutes once someone looked at the offset in the logs.

Someone added partitions to a keyed topic to 'increase throughput'; murmur2 now mapped the same `document_id` to a different partition, the stateful downstream consumer saw updates out of order, and its last-write-wins logic reverted several documents to stale versions before anyone connected the two events.

A team turned on transactions and told the customer the pipeline was exactly-once, but the consumer also POSTed purchase orders to the customer's ERP; a rebalance re-delivered a batch and the ERP received duplicate orders, because Kafka transactions never covered the HTTP side effect.

A consumer group was offline for eight days during a migration, longer than `offsets.retention.minutes`; on restart the expired offsets fell back to `earliest`, replaying a week of events through a non-idempotent notification forwarder that sent every customer duplicate emails.

`advertised.listeners` was left pointing at `localhost:9092` inside Compose, so clients could connect for metadata but were redirected to an unreachable address; the producer hung and eventually failed with 'Local: Message timed out' and half a day was lost before anyone compared bind address to advertised address.
interviewQuestions: A customer's architect insists on Kafka for a pilot that ingests about 5,000 documents a day from a SaaS webhook into our product. Walk me through how you decide, what you propose instead if you disagree, how you make that case without losing the room, and what facts would change your mind.

Define exactly-once in Kafka precisely: which components participate, which configs enable it, and where the boundary of the guarantee sits. Then our consumer writes to Postgres and calls a third-party REST API for every event; design effectively-once end to end and name what is still not guaranteed.

Debug this: lag on a single partition grows without bound while other partitions are healthy, consumer CPU is low, and the logs show repeated 'Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing'. Talk me through your hypotheses, what you check in what order, and the fix.

Design multi-tenant event ingestion for an AI product where tenants differ 100x in volume, per-document ordering matters, and one tenant's replay must never starve another. Topics per tenant or a shared topic keyed by tenant? Partition count, quotas, ACLs, and how the answer changes at 10 tenants versus 2,000.

A service writes an order row to Postgres and then publishes to Kafka. Sometimes there is a row and no event, sometimes an event and no row. Fix it, then compare the two relay implementations for the outbox (polling versus WAL-based CDC) on latency, load, failure modes and what happens when the relay is down for a day.

We need to add a field now and rename another field next quarter in an event schema consumed by four teams we do not control. Which compatibility mode do you set, what is the rollout order for producers and consumers, and what exactly breaks if you get the order wrong?

Configure a topic for durability at a customer who cannot lose a single event: replication factor, `min.insync.replicas`, `acks`, unclean leader election, rack placement. For each single- and double-broker failure, tell me precisely what the customer experiences and what, if anything, they lose.
35.proofOfWork: A public repository with a `make prove` target that runs six named, self-asserting chaos scenarios against a three-broker Redpanda cluster, Postgres 16 with `wal_level=logical`, Debezium Connect and the rebuilt DefenderMate ingestion consumers: (1) broker kill under `acks=1` versus `acks=all` with idempotence, printing lost and reordered record counts per key; (2) consumer SIGKILL between database commit and offset commit, printing duplicate counts with and without the processed-events table; (3) a 90-second handler under default versus tuned poll settings, printing whether the member was evicted; (4) a poison-pill record, asserting it lands in the DLQ with source topic, partition, offset and exception headers while the group keeps moving; (5) outbox atomicity, killing the API between commit and any produce call and asserting the event still arrives exactly once downstream; (6) a breaking Avro change rejected by the schema registry with a 409 while an old consumer keeps reading new records. Each scenario ends with PASS or FAIL against a numeric assertion, the run writes a results table into the README, and a Grafana dashboard JSON in the repo shows per-partition lag, under-replicated partitions and end-to-end trace latency during the run. Alongside it sits a two-page 'consuming from the customer's Kafka' runbook covering credentials, ACL requests, schema registry access, offset reset procedure and the questions to ask before the first connection.

36.topic: Temporal at depth: signals, queries, versioning, sagas, worker tuning
36.why: Kaupex-style engagements live or die on long-running, side-effecting orchestration: an LLM compile step, a CRM write, a Postgres commit, a webhook back to the customer, each of which fails independently and none of which can be blindly re-run. Temporal is what lets you promise a customer 'nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated' after a node reboot, but only if you can change workflow code while thousands of their executions are mid-flight, unwind a half-finished business transaction without a human reconciling spreadsheets, and size workers so the backlog drains inside the SLO you signed. FDE loops at Temporal-heavy shops probe exactly these three things, because the FDE is the person who will be standing in the customer's cluster when a deploy strands 2,000 workflows.
prerequisites: Temporal basics from 'Load testing and chaos' (topic 22): start a workflow, run a Python worker on the `kaupex` task queue, read `temporal workflow show`, and the timeout/retry/heartbeat behaviour you measured when killing a worker mid-activity

asyncio fluency: tasks, `await`, `asyncio.gather`, `asyncio.shield`, `CancelledError`, `asyncio.Lock`; Temporal's Python workflows run on a custom deterministic event loop and everything below assumes you can reason about interleaving at await points

The layered Kaupex Task Compiler from 'Production Python architecture' (topic 25): activities become ten-line adapters over service functions and idempotency lives in the repository, not in the workflow
Postgres transactions and unique constraints from topic 29, because idempotency keys land as `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on a `(workflow_id, activity_id)` unique index
Kubernetes pod lifecycle (SIGTERM, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, `preStop`) from topic 8 and Prometheus/Grafana from topic 21, so worker SDK metrics land on the existing Kaupex dashboard
A local `temporal server start-dev --db-filename ./dev.db`, the Kaupex k3s deployment reachable, Python SDK `temporalio` >= 1.11 and server >= 1.29.1 (Worker Versioning needs both)

subtopics.name: Event history, commands and deterministic replay
subtopics.learn: Read a history end to end with `temporal workflow show -w <id> --detailed` and name what each event means: `WorkflowTaskScheduled/Started/Completed` brackets one run of your Python code, `ActivityTaskScheduled` is the `ScheduleActivityTask` command your code emitted, `MarkerRecorded` is a patch or local-activity marker, `TimerStarted` is an `asyncio.sleep`. The worker rebuilds state by re-running `@workflow.run` from the top against the recorded events and checking each command it produces against the next event; any divergence (a new activity call, a different activity type name, a missing timer, reordered `asyncio.gather` branches) is a non-determinism error that fails the workflow *task*, not the workflow, so the execution sits in Running with `WorkflowTaskFailed` events retrying on backoff until the code is fixed. Know the Python sources of non-determinism and their replacements: `datetime.now()` -> `workflow.now()`, `random`/`uuid.uuid4` -> `workflow.random()`/`workflow.uuid4()`, threads and I/O -> activities, iterating an unordered `set` -> sort first. Know the ceilings: warning at 10,240 events, termination at 51,200 events, 10,000 signals or 2,000 updates per execution.

resource.label: Temporal docs: Workflow Execution - Events and Event History

subtopics.name: Failure taxonomy: workflow task failure vs execution failure vs activity failure
subtopics.learn: An arbitrary exception escaping `@workflow.run` fails the workflow task (retried, execution stays Running, fix-and-redeploy heals it), while `temporalio.exceptions.ApplicationError` fails the execution (terminal `WorkflowExecutionFailed`); promote specific types with `Worker(workflow_failure_exception_types=[...])` or `@workflow.defn(failure_exception_types=[...])`. Activities are the inverse: every exception is retried per `RetryPolicy(initial_interval, backoff_coefficient, maximum_interval, maximum_attempts, non_retryable_error_types)` until `schedule_to_close_timeout` expires, unless raised as `ApplicationError(..., non_retryable=True)` or its type is listed in `non_retryable_error_types`; the workflow sees an `ActivityError` whose `.cause` is that `ApplicationError` or a `TimeoutError` whose `.type` says START_TO_CLOSE or HEARTBEAT. Map Kaupex's domain exceptions from topic 25 onto this: `InvalidTaskSpec` non-retryable, `HubSpotRateLimited` retryable with a long `maximum_interval`, a `psycopg` `OperationalError` retryable but bounded. Be able to compute from a policy exactly how many attempts fit inside a given `schedule_to_close_timeout`.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Failure detection (timeouts, retry policies, heartbeats)

subtopics.name: Signals and queries: async writes, sync reads, signal-with-start
subtopics.learn: Define `@workflow.signal async def approve(self, who: str)` handlers that only mutate state and set flags, and have the main coroutine block on `await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approved, timeout=timedelta(days=3))`; signals are `WorkflowExecutionSignaled` events, delivered even if they arrive before the first workflow task or while every worker is down, and fire-and-forget from the client (`await handle.signal(MyWorkflow.approve, 'ops')`). Use `client.start_workflow(..., id=f'task-{uuid}', start_signal='approve', start_signal_args=[...])` so a retried webhook either starts or signals but never duplicates. `@workflow.query` methods must be synchronous, read-only and command-free (no `execute_activity`, no `asyncio.sleep`); a query against an execution evicted from the sticky cache forces a full replay on some worker, which is why polling queries against large histories hurt, and the built-in `__stack_trace` query is what the Web UI's Stack Trace tab uses to show where a stuck workflow is blocked. Drive Kaupex with `temporal workflow query -w <id> --type status` and `temporal workflow signal -w <id> --name approve --input '"ops"'`.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Message passing (signals, queries, updates)

subtopics.name: Updates: validated, synchronous, tracked writes
subtopics.learn: Use `@workflow.update` when the caller needs a result or a rejection: the paired `@my_update.validator` runs before anything is recorded and raising in it rejects the update with no history written, while the handler body runs as a workflow coroutine that can await activities and return a value. From the client `await handle.execute_update(MyWorkflow.add_step, step)` waits for completion; `await handle.start_update(..., wait_for_stage=WorkflowUpdateStage.ACCEPTED)` returns once the validator passes and lets you fetch the result later by update id. Update-with-Start (server 1.28+) lets one round trip create-or-address a workflow and get a synchronous answer, which is the right primitive for a FastAPI endpoint that must return 201 with the compiled plan id. Know the ceiling of 2,000 updates per execution and that entity workflows must Continue-As-New long before it.

resource.label: Temporal Encyclopedia: Workflow message passing (signals, queries, updates)

subtopics.name: Handler concurrency, all_handlers_finished and safe message handlers
subtopics.learn: Handlers interleave with the main coroutine at every `await`, so two `add_step` updates can both read `len(self.steps) < limit`, both pass and both append; guard multi-step handlers with an `asyncio.Lock` created in `__init__` and held across the awaited activity. Before returning or calling `continue_as_new`, `await workflow.wait_condition(workflow.all_handlers_finished)` so an in-flight handler is not killed with the run; the SDK logs a warning per unfinished handler unless the handler sets `unfinished_policy=HandlerUnfinishedPolicy.ABANDON` because it is genuinely fire-and-forget. Make signal handlers idempotent on a caller-supplied id (`if req.id in self.seen: return`) because a client that timed out will send the same signal twice and both land in history. Port the lock-and-wait shape from the `safe_message_handlers` sample into the Kaupex compile workflow.

resource.label: temporalio/samples-python: message_passing/safe_message_handlers

subtopics.name: Durable timers, wait_condition timeouts and Continue-As-New
subtopics.learn: `await asyncio.sleep(timedelta(hours=6).total_seconds())` inside a workflow is a server-side timer (`TimerStarted`/`TimerFired`) that survives worker restarts; `workflow.wait_condition(pred, timeout=...)` raises `asyncio.TimeoutError` and is how you implement 'wait for approval or escalate after 48 h'. For entity-style workflows (one long-lived execution per Kaupex project receiving signals for months) check `workflow.info().is_continue_as_new_suggested()` and `workflow.info().get_current_history_length()` at the top of each loop iteration, drain handlers with `all_handlers_finished`, then `workflow.continue_as_new(State(...))` to carry state into a fresh run with the same workflow id and a new run id; signals the old run has not processed are carried over by the server. Design the state dataclass so every field is serialisable by the default converter and versionable (optional fields with defaults) because the new run may be picked up by a newer worker build. Test it with a `max_history_length` hook rather than waiting for 10k events.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Continue-As-New

subtopics.name: Patch-based versioning: patched(), deprecate_patch(), and when the old branch can go
subtopics.learn: Wrap any change that alters the command sequence (new or removed activity, changed timer, reordered calls, renamed activity type) in `if workflow.patched('compile-v2'):`; new executions record a `MarkerRecorded` for the patch and take the new branch, old executions replay without the marker and take the old branch, so one worker build serves both. Changing only an activity's implementation, retry policy or timeouts needs no patch; changing the arguments passed to an activity does not fail replay but changes behaviour, so patch it if old runs must keep old semantics. Lifecycle: ship `patched()` with both branches; once `temporal workflow list --query 'WorkflowType="CompileTask" AND ExecutionStatus="Running" AND StartTime < "<deploy time>"'` returns nothing, replace the conditional with a bare `workflow.deprecate_patch('compile-v2')` plus only the new code; once every execution that contains the deprecated marker is past retention (they can still be queried or reset until then), delete the call. Patch ids are per workflow type and must be evaluated at the same logical point on every code path; a `patched()` inside a branch only some runs reach is a classic replay failure. Do it live on Kaupex: deploy the patched worker while ten compile workflows are mid-activity and prove none fail.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Versioning (patching and Worker Versioning)

subtopics.name: Replay testing against production histories in CI
subtopics.learn: Before any worker image ships, replay real histories through the new code: `temporal workflow show -w <id> -o json > histories/<id>.json`, then `await Replayer(workflows=[CompileTask]).replay_workflow(WorkflowHistory.from_json('<id>', json_text))`; for breadth, iterate `client.list_workflows('WorkflowType="CompileTask" AND CloseTime > "<7 days ago>"')`, feed each `client.get_workflow_handle(wf.id, run_id=wf.run_id).fetch_history()` into `replay_workflows`, and fail CI on the first `NondeterminismError`. Keep a curated corpus in the repo (one history per patch state, one with a cancellation, one with a signal burst) so the check runs offline in seconds, and refresh it from production weekly. This gate is what makes step three of the patch lifecycle safe: deleting a deprecated branch is only allowed when the replay job over all Running histories passes.

resource.label: temporalio/samples-python: replay (fetch and replay histories)

subtopics.name: Worker Versioning: deployment versions, pinned vs auto-upgrade, ramp and rollback
subtopics.learn: Worker Versioning (server >= 1.29.1, Python SDK >= 1.11) replaces most patching for services shipped as immutable builds, and Temporal now recommends it over patching where you can run versioned deployments: start the worker with `Worker(..., deployment_config=WorkerDeploymentConfig(version=WorkerDeploymentVersion(deployment_name='kaupex-worker', build_id=GIT_SHA), use_worker_versioning=True))` and give each workflow type a `versioning_behavior`: `VersioningBehavior.PINNED` (an execution finishes on the build it started on, so no patches) or `AUTO_UPGRADE` (moves to the current version, so patch discipline still applies). Roll out with `temporal worker deployment set-ramping-version --percentage 10`, verify, then `set-current-version`, or roll back instantly; old pinned builds must keep running until `temporal worker deployment describe` shows no executions on them, then sunset and `delete-version`. Know the trade: pinning means N versions of the worker alive in k3s, each costing pods and Postgres connections; patching means one build and more code. Decide per Kaupex workflow type and write the decision down.

resource.label: Temporal docs: Worker Versioning (worker deployments)

subtopics.name: Saga: compensation stack, reverse-order rollback, cancellation shielding
subtopics.learn: Implement the Kaupex compile-and-publish path as a saga: after each side-effecting activity succeeds, push its compensation (`self.compensations.append((undo_hubspot_record, record_id))`); on an `ActivityError` whose cause is non-retryable, or on a business rejection, walk the list in reverse and `await workflow.execute_activity(undo, arg, start_to_close_timeout=..., retry_policy=RetryPolicy(maximum_attempts=0))` for each, catching per-step failures so one stuck compensation does not skip the others, and finish with `ApplicationError('compensated', non_retryable=True)` or a `wait_condition` for a human `resolve` signal when a compensation is exhausted. Separate what to compensate (HubSpot record created, customer notified, credits deducted) from what simply did not happen (the Postgres write inside the activity that failed). Cancellation arrives as `asyncio.CancelledError` at the current await; catch it, run the compensation loop under `asyncio.shield(...)` so the cleanup activities are not themselves cancelled, then re-raise so the execution ends Cancelled rather than Completed. Compensations must be idempotent and must tolerate the forward action never having happened (a HubSpot 404 on delete is success).

resource.label: Temporal Design Patterns: Saga Pattern

subtopics.name: Activity contracts for sagas: idempotency keys, heartbeat details, timeout budgets
subtopics.learn: Every side-effecting Kaupex activity derives its idempotency key from `activity.info().workflow_id` plus `activity.info().activity_id` (stable across retries, unique per scheduled activity) and sends it as the partner API's idempotency header or as the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` key in Postgres, so a retry after a worker crash post-commit is a no-op. Long activities call `activity.heartbeat(progress)` at least every `heartbeat_timeout / 3`; on retry, read `activity.info().heartbeat_details` to resume from `progress` instead of restarting (a 500-record batch resumes at record 312). Set timeouts as a budget: `start_to_close_timeout` = worst honest single attempt, `heartbeat_timeout` = how fast a dead worker must be detected (topic 22 measured the gap), `schedule_to_close_timeout` = the total the business tolerates, and leave `schedule_to_start_timeout` unset on normal activities because a slow worker pool would then fail healthy work. Log `activity.info().attempt` on every attempt so the customer's log search shows retries explicitly.

resource.label: Temporal Encyclopedia: Detecting Activity failures (timeouts, heartbeats, retries)

subtopics.name: Child workflows, parent close policy and cancellation propagation
subtopics.learn: Reach for `workflow.execute_child_workflow(PublishTask.run, arg, id=f'publish-{task_id}', parent_close_policy=ParentClosePolicy.REQUEST_CANCEL)` when a sub-process needs its own history (size), its own id for signals and visibility, or a different task queue; otherwise an activity or a plain function is simpler and cheaper. Know the three `ParentClosePolicy` values and their production consequences: TERMINATE (default) kills children when the parent closes, ABANDON detaches them (fan-out where the parent is only a launcher), REQUEST_CANCEL sends a cooperative cancel so the child's saga can compensate. Cancelling a parent cancels the awaited child future; cancelling an activity only takes effect when the activity heartbeats (`activity.is_cancelled()` or `CancelledError` at the next heartbeat), and the `cancellation_type` (`ActivityCancellationType`) on the activity call decides whether the workflow waits for the activity to acknowledge or proceeds immediately. `id_reuse_policy` on child start decides whether a retried parent collides with a previous child of the same id; `WorkflowIDReusePolicy.ALLOW_DUPLICATE_FAILED_ONLY` is the usual choice for publish steps.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Child Workflows

subtopics.name: Sync vs async activities, the activity executor and the workflow sandbox
subtopics.learn: An `async def` activity runs on the worker's event loop, so one blocking call inside it (synchronous `requests`, `psycopg2`, a 30 s pandas transform) stalls every other activity, every heartbeat and every workflow task on that worker; either make it truly async (`httpx.AsyncClient`, asyncpg) or declare it `def` and pass `Worker(activity_executor=ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N))` with N >= `max_concurrent_activities`, or for CPU-bound work a `ProcessPoolExecutor` plus `shared_state_manager=SharedStateManager.create_from_multiprocessing(multiprocessing.Manager())` so heartbeats and cancellation cross the process boundary. Workflow code runs in a sandbox that re-imports your module per run and blocks non-deterministic calls (`datetime.date.today`, `random`, file I/O); wrap heavy or stateful imports (pydantic models, SQLAlchemy models, the Kaupex domain package) in `with workflow.unsafe.imports_passed_through():` to avoid re-import cost and false positives, and reserve `workflow.unsafe.sandbox_unrestricted()` or `SandboxRestrictions.default.with_passthrough_modules(...)` for cases you can justify in a comment. Measure `temporal_workflow_task_replay_latency` before and after passing imports through.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Python SDK sandbox

subtopics.name: Local activities: when the shortcut pays and when it bites
subtopics.learn: `workflow.execute_local_activity(fn, arg, start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=2))` runs the function inside the workflow worker and records only a `MarkerRecorded`, saving the schedule/start/complete round trips and three history events per call; use it for sub-second, idempotent lookups (feature flag, tenant config) executed thousands of times per workflow. Understand the costs: no heartbeats, in-worker retries until the workflow task timeout (10 s default) forces a workflow-task heartbeat that adds events and blocks signal processing, durability only when the enclosing workflow task completes, and a crash between the side effect and task completion re-runs it. Never put a non-idempotent write or a call that can stall behind a rate limit in a local activity; watch `local_activity_total` and marker counts in histories.

resource.label: Temporal docs: Local Activity

subtopics.name: Worker tuning: slots, pollers, sticky cache and the metric that drives each knob
subtopics.learn: Tune from SDK metrics scraped by Prometheus from `Runtime(telemetry=TelemetryConfig(metrics=PrometheusConfig(bind_address='0.0.0.0:9000')))`: `temporal_activity_schedule_to_start_latency` and `temporal_workflow_task_schedule_to_start_latency` (tasks waiting for a worker), `temporal_worker_task_slots_available{worker_type=...}` (zero means saturated), `temporal_sticky_cache_size` and `temporal_sticky_cache_total_forced_eviction` with `temporal_workflow_task_replay_latency` (evictions force full replays), plus `temporal_num_pollers`. Rules: high schedule-to-start with slots at zero -> raise `max_concurrent_activities` or add pods; high schedule-to-start with slots free -> too few pollers, raise `max_concurrent_activity_task_polls` or switch to `PollerBehaviorAutoscaling`; rising replay latency with forced evictions -> raise `max_cached_workflows` (memory per cached workflow is the price) and keep `sticky_queue_schedule_to_start_timeout` short so a dead worker's stickiness expires fast. Prefer `WorkerTuner.create_resource_based(target_memory_usage=0.8, target_cpu_usage=0.9)` in containers where the mix varies, and never combine a tuner with the `max_concurrent_*` kwargs (startup error). Load Kaupex with the k6 script from topic 22 and record the before/after of one knob change per run.

resource.label: Temporal docs: Worker performance (metrics, slots, pollers, cache tuning)

subtopics.name: Task queue topology, downstream rate limits and graceful shutdown on k3s
subtopics.learn: Split Kaupex into a workflow worker and activity workers on distinct task queues (`kaupex-wf`, `kaupex-llm`, `kaupex-crm`) so an LLM stall cannot starve compile-plan decisions, routing with `execute_activity(..., task_queue='kaupex-crm')`. Enforce a partner API's limit at the queue, not in code: `Worker(max_task_queue_activities_per_second=8.0)` is a server-side rate shared across every worker polling that queue, while `max_activities_per_second` caps one process; use the former for HubSpot's per-account limit. Use a worker-specific task queue (`samples-python/worker_specific_task_queues`) when consecutive activities need the same host (a downloaded file, a warmed model). On SIGTERM the pod must `await worker.shutdown()`, which stops polling, waits `graceful_shutdown_timeout` for running activities (which can observe `activity.is_worker_shutdown()` or `await activity.wait_for_worker_shutdown()` to checkpoint via heartbeat), then cancels the rest; set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` above that timeout plus the `preStop` sleep from topic 8, and confirm with `temporal task-queue describe -t kaupex-crm` that the old worker identity stops appearing as a poller.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK API reference: temporalio.worker.Worker (all worker options)

subtopics.name: Visibility, search attributes, batch operations and reset as the recovery tool
subtopics.learn: Register custom search attributes once per namespace (`temporal operator search-attribute create --name TenantId --type Keyword`, again for `Stage`), set them at start (`search_attributes=TypedSearchAttributes([...])`) and update them from the workflow with `workflow.upsert_search_attributes([TENANT.value_set(tid)])` so operators can answer 'which of Acme's compiles are stuck in publish' with `temporal workflow list --query 'TenantId="acme" AND Stage="publish" AND ExecutionStatus="Running"'`. Batch operations take the same query: `temporal workflow signal --query ... --name pause`, `temporal workflow cancel --query ...`, and `temporal batch describe --job-id` / `temporal batch terminate` to watch or stop a job. Reset is how you recover from a bad deploy without losing progress: `temporal workflow reset -w <id> --event-id <WorkflowTaskCompleted id>` or `--type LastWorkflowTask` creates a new run that replays history to that point and then executes the corrected code; batch resets over a query are limited to `FirstWorkflowTask`, `LastWorkflowTask` or `BuildId`. Rehearse on Kaupex: bad worker image -> `WorkflowTaskFailed` with a non-determinism cause -> roll back the image (workflows heal by themselves) or, if the old code is gone, reset to the last workflow task.

resource.label: Temporal CLI reference: temporal workflow (list, query, signal, reset, show)

subtopics.name: Testing workflows: time skipping, mocked activities and saga assertions
subtopics.learn: Use `async with await WorkflowEnvironment.start_time_skipping() as env:` so a workflow with a 48-hour escalation timer completes in milliseconds; time advances only when every coroutine is blocked, which also exposes accidental busy-waits. Register fakes with the real activity's name (`@activity.defn(name='publish_to_hubspot') async def fake_publish(...)`) on a `Worker(env.client, task_queue=..., workflows=[CompileTask], activities=[fake_publish, ...])` created inside the test, and have a fake raise `ApplicationError('boom', non_retryable=True)` on the third call to assert the compensations ran in reverse order and the result is the `compensated` failure. Test signals and updates by starting the workflow, calling `handle.signal` or `handle.execute_update`, then awaiting `handle.result()`. Unit-test activities alone with `ActivityEnvironment().run(fn, arg)` to check heartbeat details and idempotency-key derivation. Use `WorkflowEnvironment.start_local()` (a real dev server) for tests that need search attributes or replay of downloaded histories.

resource.label: Temporal Python SDK docs: Testing suite (time skipping, mocking activities, replay)

subtopics.name: Observability: replay-safe logging, OpenTelemetry interceptors and context propagation
subtopics.learn: Use `workflow.logger` and `activity.logger` rather than `logging.getLogger` inside Temporal code: they attach workflow id, run id, type and attempt, and the workflow logger suppresses output during replay so a redeploy does not triple every log line. Add `TracingInterceptor()` from `temporalio.contrib.opentelemetry` to `Client.connect(interceptors=[...])` (the Worker built on that client inherits it) so a Kaupex API request, its workflow tasks and each activity attempt share one trace on the backend from topic 21, and use a header-propagating interceptor (`samples-python/context_propagation`) to carry `tenant_id` and `X-Request-ID` from the FastAPI request into every activity's `contextvars` for the logging filter from topic 25. Be able to correlate the three views a customer SRE will ask for: the trace, the workflow history in the Web UI, and the SDK metrics dashboard.

outcomes: You can deploy a patched Kaupex worker (`workflow.patched('compile-v2')`) while at least ten compile workflows are mid-activity, show with `temporal workflow show` that old runs finish on the old branch and new runs record the patch marker, and later remove the old branch only after a query for pre-deploy Running executions returns zero.

You can run a replay job in CI that pulls the last seven days of `CompileTask` histories, replays them through the candidate image, and fails the pipeline on the first `NondeterminismError`; you can demonstrate it catching a deliberately reordered activity.

You can force a non-retryable failure in the third step of the Kaupex publish saga and show the compensations execute in reverse order with idempotent retries, the execution ends Failed with `compensated`, and repeating the failure with a worker kill mid-compensation produces no duplicate HubSpot records.

You can cancel a running saga from the CLI and prove the shielded cleanup activities still ran, the execution ended Cancelled, and the history shows `WorkflowExecutionCancelRequested` followed by the compensation `ActivityTaskCompleted` events.

Given a Grafana panel of `temporal_activity_schedule_to_start_latency` climbing with `temporal_worker_task_slots_available` at zero, you name the knob (`max_concurrent_activities` or replica count) before touching anything, change it, and show p95 fall under the topic 22 k6 load; given the same latency with slots free, you name pollers instead.

You can drive a Kaupex workflow entirely through messages: signal-with-start from a retried webhook with no duplicate, a validated update that rejects a bad step with nothing written to history, a query for progress, and a Continue-As-New that carries state after `is_continue_as_new_suggested()` flips.

You can demonstrate on a live execution the difference between a workflow task failure and a workflow execution failure, and recover a stuck execution either by rolling back the worker image or with `temporal workflow reset --type LastWorkflowTask`.
You can enforce a downstream API's 8 req/s limit with `max_task_queue_activities_per_second` across three worker pods and show in the metrics that the aggregate rate holds while the backlog drains.
failureModes: An engineer inserted a new `send_notification` activity ahead of an existing one without a patch; every in-flight execution hit a non-determinism error on its next workflow task, sat Running with `WorkflowTaskFailed` retrying all weekend, and the on-call terminated 2,000 workflows by hand because nobody knew that rolling back the worker image would have healed them.

A saga compensation deleted the CRM record by the id stored in Postgres, but the forward activity had crashed after HubSpot committed and before the id was stored; the compensation found nothing to delete, returned success, and the orphan records surfaced when the customer's sales team started calling leads twice.

The compile activity was `async def` and called a synchronous vendor SDK; one slow LLM response blocked the worker's event loop, heartbeats stopped, the server timed out twelve unrelated activities, and their retries on other workers doubled the load on the API that was already slow.

Query handlers were used as a polling API by a dashboard hitting 5,000 executions every two seconds; each evicted execution forced a full replay, `temporal_workflow_task_replay_latency` went to seconds, the sticky cache thrashed, and real workflow progress slowed to a crawl while the customer stared at a dashboard that said everything was fine.

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` stayed at the default 30 s while `graceful_shutdown_timeout` was five minutes; every rolling deploy SIGKILLed workers mid-activity, the activities were only retried after their ten-minute start-to-close timeout, and the customer logged each deploy as a ten-minute outage.

An entity workflow per tenant received one signal per event with no Continue-As-New; the busiest tenant crossed the 51,200-event ceiling after five months, the server terminated the execution, and the tenant's accumulated state existed only inside that history.

A patch was deprecated and deleted after checking for Running executions but not for closed executions still inside retention; during an incident a week later, `temporal workflow reset` replayed a history containing the marker against code with no `deprecate_patch` and the reset the customer needed failed.
interviewQuestions: You need to insert a new approval step into a workflow with 30,000 executions in flight, some of which will run for another six weeks. Walk through the options (patching, Worker Versioning with pinning, a new workflow type on a new task queue), what each costs operationally, how you verify safety before deploying, and how you know when the old code path can be deleted.

Design the compensation strategy for a workflow that charges a card, reserves inventory in a partner system with a 60 s p99, and emails the customer. Which steps are compensated, which are idempotent by construction, what happens when a compensation itself fails permanently, and what does the history look like when the workflow is cancelled halfway through?

A customer reports 400 workflows have been Running for two days with no progress. Using only the CLI and Prometheus, how do you determine whether this is a non-determinism error, a starved task queue, no worker polling, or an activity retrying against a dead dependency, and what is the remediation for each?

Explain what a worker does when it receives a workflow task for an execution that is not in its sticky cache, why that makes queries against large histories expensive, and how slots, pollers, cache size and sticky timeout interact under a burst of 10,000 new workflows.

A signal handler and the main workflow coroutine both mutate the same list, and in production the list occasionally has duplicates. Explain the interleaving that causes it, how you fix it while staying deterministic, and how you write a test that reproduces the race reliably.

Why does Temporal retry a workflow task forever on an unexpected exception but fail the execution on `ApplicationError`? Give a case where the default is wrong for a customer, show how you change it, and describe the blast radius if you get it backwards.

A partner API allows 10 requests per second per account across your entire fleet and you run six worker pods. Where do you enforce the limit, what breaks if you do it inside the activity, and how do you prove the aggregate rate to the partner from your own metrics?
36.proofOfWork: A public repository plus a fifteen-minute recorded walkthrough titled 'Change Kaupex while it runs'. The repo holds the Kaupex compile-and-publish saga (forward activities with idempotency keys derived from `workflow_id` and `activity_id`, a heartbeat-resumable batch step, reverse-order compensation with shielded cleanup under cancellation), a `histories/` corpus of real histories covering every patch state, a cancellation and a signal burst, and a CI pipeline with three gates: pytest under `start_time_skipping()` asserting compensation order and idempotency, a replay job that replays the corpus plus the last seven days of live `CompileTask` executions through the candidate image, and a load stage that runs the topic 22 k6 script against a kind cluster and asserts `temporal_activity_schedule_to_start_latency` p95 under a threshold. The recording shows, on the live k3s deployment: ten compile workflows started; a patched worker image rolled out mid-flight with old and new runs finishing on their respective branches; a deliberately non-deterministic image rolled out, the resulting `WorkflowTaskFailed` events, and the heal on rollback; one execution recovered with `temporal workflow reset --type LastWorkflowTask`; a saga forced to fail at step three with its compensations visible in history; and one worker-tuning change chosen from the Grafana panels with the before/after p95. A one-page `VERSIONING_POLICY.md` records, per workflow type, whether Kaupex uses patching or pinned Worker Versioning and the exact conditions under which a patch may be deprecated and then deleted.

39.topic: Testing and contracts: pytest, property tests, OpenAPI contract tests
39.why: An FDE ships an API into a customer's environment and then leaves; the customer's integration team keeps building against it for years, and the only thing that protects them from your successor's refactor is a machine-checked contract that fails the build. Customer data is the adversary: unicode task names, empty lists, 10 MB payloads, and out-of-order state transitions arrive on day one of production, and property-based tests are the cheapest way to meet them in CI first. A published coverage number and a green contract job are also what a customer's procurement and security review actually ask for in the vendor questionnaire, so the test suite is part of the sales artefact, not just engineering hygiene.
prerequisites: Production Python architecture (topic 25): the Kaupex Task Compiler's domain/repository split, Protocol-typed ports and the KaupexError hierarchy (InvalidTransition, NotFound, Conflict) that tests will assert on
FastAPI in production (topic 26): Depends, dependency_overrides, lifespan, settings via pydantic-settings, and the problem+json error handlers
PostgreSQL at depth (topic 29): SQLAlchemy 2.0 async engine and sessions, Alembic migrations, transactions and SAVEPOINT semantics
Docker running locally (topics 5-6) so testcontainers can start a Postgres container; understands ports, volumes and image tags
CI/CD (topic 18): can read and edit a GitHub Actions workflow with jobs, services, artifacts and required status checks
JSON Schema vocabulary as emitted by pydantic v2: type, required, properties, additionalProperties, enum, format, minLength/maxLength, anyOf

subtopics.name: Test layers for a FastAPI + Postgres + Temporal service
subtopics.learn: Lay out tests/unit (pure domain, no IO, milliseconds), tests/integration (repositories against a real Postgres), tests/api (handlers through the ASGI app) and tests/contract (Schemathesis against the OpenAPI document), each behind a registered marker so `pytest -m unit` runs in under five seconds and the full suite runs in CI. Use the src layout with `--import-mode=importlib` so test files need no `__init__.py` and can share basenames, set `testpaths = ["tests"]`, and put shared fixtures in a root conftest.py with layer-specific conftest.py files below it. Decide what each layer is allowed to touch: unit tests may not import sqlalchemy or httpx; integration tests may not mock the database; API tests may override dependencies but not monkeypatch internals. Be able to argue why a bug should be caught at a given layer and why moving a test down a layer makes it faster and more precise.

resource.label: pytest docs - Good Integration Practices (test layout, src layout, import modes)

subtopics.name: pytest configuration as a hard gate
subtopics.learn: Configure `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` so the suite fails on anything ambiguous: `addopts = "-ra --strict-markers --strict-config --import-mode=importlib"`, `filterwarnings = ["error", ...]` with narrow `ignore::DeprecationWarning:third_party.*` exceptions, `xfail_strict = true` so an xfail that starts passing fails the build, `faulthandler_timeout = 60`, `minversion`, `required_plugins` and `markers = [...]` for every custom marker. Know the debugging flags cold: `-x`/`--maxfail=3`, `--lf`, `--ff`, `--sw` (stepwise), `--pdb`, `-k "transition and not cancel"`, `--durations=10 --durations-min=0.5`, `--co -q` to check collection, `-p no:randomly` to pin ordering. Know the exit codes: 0 all passed, 1 failures, 2 interrupted, 3 internal error, 4 usage error, 5 no tests collected; a `-k` expression matching nothing returns 5 and must not be treated as success by a wrapper script.

resource.label: pytest docs - API Reference (ini options and command-line flags)

subtopics.name: Fixtures: scope, teardown order, conftest layering, factories
subtopics.learn: Understand fixture scopes (function, class, module, package, session), that a higher-scoped fixture cannot request a lower-scoped one (ScopeMismatch), and that yield fixtures tear down in reverse dependency order, so a session-scoped Postgres container outlives the function-scoped session that borrows a connection from it. Use `request.addfinalizer` when teardown must run even if setup partially failed, `autouse=True` only for cross-cutting invariants (reset `app.dependency_overrides`, clear a Redis test DB), and fixture overriding in a nested conftest.py to swap a real adapter for a fake in one directory. Prefer factory fixtures (`make_task(**overrides)` returning a domain object with sane defaults) over dozens of near-identical fixtures; inspect what is active with `pytest --fixtures`, `--fixtures-per-test` and `--setup-show`. Know that `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch` and `caplog` are function-scoped and that `tmp_path_factory` is the session-scoped alternative.

resource.label: pytest docs - How to use fixtures

subtopics.name: Parametrize as a state-transition matrix
subtopics.learn: Encode the Kaupex Task state machine as a table: `@pytest.mark.parametrize("state,event,expected", CASES, ids=...)` where CASES covers every (state, event) pair and `expected` is either the next state or `InvalidTransition`, so the test file is the executable specification of allowed transitions. Use `pytest.param(..., marks=pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, reason="..."))` for known gaps instead of deleting rows, stack two parametrize decorators for a cartesian product, `indirect=True` to route a parameter through a fixture (build the task in the requested state against the real DB), and `pytest_generate_tests` when the matrix must be computed from the enum at collection time so a new state cannot be added without a test row. Readable ids (`ids=lambda c: f"{c.state}-{c.event}"`) make `-k "queued-cancel"` selection and CI failure output usable.

resource.label: pytest docs - How to parametrize fixtures and test functions

subtopics.name: Test doubles at the boundary: monkeypatch, autospec, respx, in-memory fakes
subtopics.learn: Use `monkeypatch.setattr/setenv/delenv/setitem/chdir` for process-level state and `unittest.mock.patch("kaupex.adapters.llm.AsyncAnthropic", autospec=True)` with `spec_set=True` so a renamed or misspelled method raises AttributeError instead of silently returning a Mock; use `AsyncMock` for coroutines and `assert_awaited_once_with`. Patch where the name is looked up (the importing module), not where it is defined. For HTTP boundaries prefer `respx.mock` routers (`respx.post(url).mock(return_value=httpx.Response(429, headers={"retry-after": "1"}))`, `assert_all_called=True`) so retry and backoff paths are exercised against realistic responses. For the persistence boundary prefer an in-memory fake that implements the same `TaskRepository` Protocol, run the same test module against both fake and real repository (parametrised fixture), and never mock a SQLAlchemy Session: the mock will pass while the query is wrong.

resource.label: Python docs - unittest.mock (patch, autospec, spec_set, AsyncMock)

subtopics.name: Async API tests through ASGITransport with dependency overrides
subtopics.learn: Configure pytest-asyncio with `asyncio_mode = "auto"` and `asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope = "session"` so a session-scoped async engine and the test share one event loop; otherwise asyncpg raises 'attached to a different loop' on the second test. Build the client as `httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test")`; know that ASGITransport does not run lifespan, so wrap with `asgi_lifespan.LifespanManager(app)` when startup wiring (pool creation, Temporal client) matters. Override `get_session` and `get_current_user` via `app.dependency_overrides[...]` inside a fixture and call `app.dependency_overrides.clear()` in teardown; keep one test that uses a real signed JWT so the auth path is not permanently bypassed. Assert status code, full JSON body, `content-type: application/problem+json` on errors and the `X-Request-ID` header, and rely on server exceptions propagating into the test rather than being turned into a 500 you then miss.

resource.label: FastAPI docs - Async Tests (httpx ASGITransport)

subtopics.name: Real Postgres in tests: testcontainers, migrations, rollback isolation, xdist
subtopics.learn: Start `PostgresContainer("postgres:16-alpine")` once per session, take `get_connection_url()`, and run `alembic.command.upgrade(cfg, "head")` against it so every CI run also proves the migration chain applies from empty. Isolate tests with the SQLAlchemy 'join an external transaction' recipe: open a connection, `begin()`, bind the session, `begin_nested()` for a SAVEPOINT, roll back at teardown; fall back to `TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE` for tests that must observe a real commit (advisory locks, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` workers). For RLS-protected tables (topic 30) the test session must `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id` exactly as the app does or every query returns zero rows. Under pytest-xdist derive the database from `PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER` (`kaupex_test_gw0`) with `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE kaupex_test` so workers never share rows, and know the CI fallbacks when Docker is unavailable: a GitHub Actions `services:` container or `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true` in restricted runners.

resource.label: testcontainers-python docs - Postgres module

subtopics.name: Property-based testing with Hypothesis: strategies, shrinking, properties worth writing
subtopics.learn: Write `@given(st.text(), st.integers(min_value=0))` tests and understand that Hypothesis searches then shrinks to a minimal counterexample, which is why a failure reads like `text=''` rather than a 300-character string. Build strategies for domain types with `st.builds(TaskCreate, name=st.text(min_size=1, max_size=120))`, `st.from_type(...)` for simple pydantic models (constrained fields need explicit strategies), `st.sampled_from(TaskState)`, `st.lists(..., unique_by=...)`, `st.one_of`, `.map/.filter/.flatmap`, `@st.composite`, `assume()` for cheap preconditions and `@example(...)` to pin past regressions. Know the property families and pick the right one: round-trip (`Task.model_validate_json(t.model_dump_json()) == t`), invariant (compiled task DAG is acyclic), idempotence (normalise twice equals once), oracle (naive implementation equals optimised), and metamorphic (adding a step never shortens the plan). Read health checks (`too_slow`, `filter_too_much`, `data_too_large`) as strategy bugs to fix, not warnings to suppress.

resource.label: Hypothesis docs - Quick start guide

subtopics.name: Deterministic Hypothesis in CI: settings profiles, example database, reproduce_failure
subtopics.learn: Register profiles in conftest.py: `settings.register_profile("ci", max_examples=500, deadline=None, derandomize=True, print_blob=True)` and `"dev"` with `max_examples=50`, then `settings.load_profile(os.getenv("HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE", "dev"))`; select with `--hypothesis-profile` and pin with `--hypothesis-seed`. Understand the `.hypothesis/examples` DirectoryBasedExampleDatabase (gitignored, cached between CI runs with actions/cache or replaced by `GitHubArtifactDatabase` so a failure found on main is replayed on every branch), and paste the `@reproduce_failure(version, blob)` line from a `print_blob=True` report into the test to pin a specific counterexample. Know that the 200 ms default `deadline` is flaky on loaded CI runners and why `deadline=None` is the honest fix, and that a Hypothesis `Flaky` error means the test failed then passed on replay: the code under test is nondeterministic (time, dict order, uncontrolled randomness), not the framework.

resource.label: Hypothesis docs - API reference (settings, database, reproduce_failure)

subtopics.name: Stateful testing of the Task lifecycle with RuleBasedStateMachine
subtopics.learn: Model the Task service as a `RuleBasedStateMachine`: `tasks = Bundle("tasks")`, `@initialize()` to create a tenant, `@rule(target=tasks, payload=st.builds(...))` that calls create and returns the id, `@rule(task=tasks, event=st.sampled_from(Event))` that applies a transition and mirrors it in a plain-dict model, `consumes(tasks)` on delete, `@precondition(lambda self: self.model)` to gate rules, and `@invariant()` that after every step asserts each real task equals the model and every terminal task has `completed_at` set. Export with `TestTaskMachine = TaskMachine.TestCase` and `TestTaskMachine.settings = settings(max_examples=200, stateful_step_count=30)`. When it fails, Hypothesis prints the minimal `state.create(...)`, `state.transition(...)` sequence; paste it into a regression test. This is how you find the cancel-after-complete and double-retry bugs that a parametrised matrix cannot express because they depend on history.

resource.label: Hypothesis docs - Stateful testing

subtopics.name: OpenAPI as the contract: making FastAPI's generated schema complete and strict
subtopics.learn: Every route must declare what it can actually return: `response_model=`, `status_code=201`, and `responses={404: {"model": Problem}, 409: {"model": Problem}, 422: {"model": Problem}}` with `content` keyed by `application/problem+json`, otherwise Schemathesis `status_code_conformance` and `content_type_conformance` fail on the first real error. Set stable operation ids with `generate_unique_id_function=lambda r: f"{r.tags[0]}_{r.name}"` (or `operation_id=`) because generated clients and OpenAPI links key on them. Make request models `ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` so the schema emits `additionalProperties: false` and `negative_data_rejection` has teeth; push `Field(min_length, max_length, pattern, ge, le)` constraints into the schema so generated data hits real boundaries; document response headers under `responses[200]["headers"]`; hide `/healthz` and `/readyz` with `include_in_schema=False`; use `openapi_extra` for anything FastAPI cannot express, such as `links`.

resource.label: FastAPI docs - Additional Responses in OpenAPI

subtopics.name: Committed schema snapshot and breaking-change detection with oasdiff
subtopics.learn: Commit `openapi.json` and add a test `assert app.openapi() == json.loads(Path("openapi.json").read_text())` with a `make openapi` target to regenerate, so any schema change appears as a reviewable diff in the PR rather than a surprise to the customer's client generator. In CI fetch the base with `git show origin/main:openapi.json > base.json` and run `oasdiff breaking base.json openapi.json --fail-on ERR`; know the classes it flags: removed path or method, new required request property, removed or renamed response property, type narrowing, enum value removed from a request or added to a response, `required` added to a response schema, and know which of those are ERR versus WARN and why an added optional response field is not breaking. Use `oasdiff changelog` output as the PR comment and the customer-facing release note. Define the policy: a breaking diff requires a `/v2` path or a major version bump plus a deprecation window, and the CI job enforces it rather than a reviewer's memory.

resource.label: oasdiff - OpenAPI diff and breaking-change detection (GitHub)

subtopics.name: Schemathesis CLI: phases, checks, and reading a failure
subtopics.learn: Run `schemathesis run http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --max-examples 100 --seed 42 --max-failures 10 --wait-for-schema 30 --report junit` (or a file schema plus `--url`) and understand the four phases: examples (schema `example`/`examples` values), coverage (boundary values, `maxLength+1`, missing required fields, wrong types), fuzzing (Hypothesis-generated data) and stateful (OpenAPI links). Know each default check and what a failure means for Kaupex: `not_a_server_error` (unhandled exception), `status_code_conformance` (undocumented 403), `content_type_conformance`, `response_headers_conformance`, `response_schema_conformance` (nullable field not marked), `negative_data_rejection` (invalid body accepted), `positive_data_acceptance` (valid body rejected), `missing_required_header`, `unsupported_method`, `use_after_free`, `ensure_resource_availability`, `ignored_auth` (endpoint answers without a token). Tune with `--exclude-checks`, `--include-path-regex '^/v1/tasks'`, `--max-response-time 1.5`, `--phases`, and `schemathesis.toml` sections such as `[checks.negative_data_rejection] expected-statuses = ["400", "422"]`; reproduce a failure from the printed curl command and `--report-vcr-path`.

resource.label: Schemathesis docs - Checks reference

subtopics.name: Schemathesis inside pytest: from_asgi, parametrize, OpenAPI links, stateful
subtopics.learn: Load the schema straight from the app with `schema = schemathesis.openapi.from_asgi("/openapi.json", app)`, or from a fixture via `schemathesis.pytest.from_fixture("api_schema")` so the app under test carries the same `dependency_overrides` (test DB, fixed clock) as the rest of the suite; write `@schema.parametrize() def test_api(case): case.call_and_validate(headers=auth)` and scope with `schema.include(operation_id=...)` / `schema.exclude(path_regex=...)`.
