subtopics.learn: Accept that an LLM tier has a hard concurrency ceiling and design the queue in front of it on purpose: a bounded in-flight semaphore sized to the provider concurrency you actually have, a bounded wait queue, and a rejection when the queue is full. Learn why an unbounded queue is the worst option: under overload it grows until every request in it has already exceeded the client's timeout, so the server does 100% of the work and delivers 0% of the value. Apply the fixes from the SRE playbook: drop requests whose deadline has already passed before dispatching them, prefer LIFO over FIFO under sustained overload so at least the newest requests are still wanted, shed by criticality (interactive chat before batch enrichment), and return 503 with `Retry-After` for capacity versus 429 for policy. Use Little's Law (L = lambda x W) to size the queue: at 20 rps with a 2 s service time you need 40 concurrent slots, and a queue deeper than a few seconds of service time is a latency bomb, not a buffer.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Handling overload

subtopics.name: Fallback paths that actually hold: the degradation ladder and its rehearsal
subtopics.learn: Write the ladder explicitly, most to least preferred: retry same provider, switch to a secondary provider or region behind the same interface, drop to a smaller/faster model with a shortened prompt, serve a cached or template answer clearly labelled as degraded, queue the request for async completion with a notification, and finally fail with an honest error. For each rung state the trigger, the user-visible difference, and who is told. Then internalise the hard lesson from the Builders' Library: untested fallback code is the most likely thing to fail, because it only runs during an outage and it fails at exactly the moment load is highest; a fallback that requires a cold connection pool, an unwarmed cache, or a different auth path will not work when you need it. The fix is to exercise the fallback continuously (route 1% of traffic through it always) and to add a kill switch the on-call can flip without a deploy, backed by a feature flag the customer's ops team also understands.

resource.label: Amazon Builders' Library - Avoiding fallback in distributed systems

subtopics.name: Moving from sync to async: when the request/response model stops working
subtopics.learn: Recognise the tripwires that force a job model: work exceeding a hop timeout (multi-step agents, long extractions, anything over ~60 s), work that must survive a deploy or pod eviction, and work with side effects on the customer's systems. Design the async contract properly: POST returns 202 with a job id and a poll URL or webhook registration; state lives in Postgres and the orchestration in Temporal so retries, heartbeats and `start_to_close_timeout` are declarative rather than hand-rolled; the LLM call is an activity with its own timeout and retry policy separate from the workflow's. Get the semantics right at each hop: visibility timeout must exceed worst-case processing or the message is redelivered while still running, a DLQ with `maxReceiveCount` catches poison inputs, and the consumer must be idempotent on `custom_id` or `job_id` because at-least-once delivery is the only guarantee you get. State plainly what the user sees during each of the five crash points between their POST and the stored result.

resource.label: Azure Architecture Center - Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern

subtopics.name: Autoscaling an LLM workload: why CPU% is the wrong signal
subtopics.learn: Understand that an LLM-calling service is IO-bound waiting on a provider, so a pod at 8% CPU can be completely saturated on in-flight requests; scaling on `resource: cpu` will never fire and the HPA will sit idle while p95 triples. Scale on the signal that reflects saturation: in-flight requests per pod, queue depth, or provider concurrency utilisation, exposed as a Prometheus custom metric and consumed via the `external`/`pods` metric types or KEDA's Prometheus scaler. Tune the behaviour block: `scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0` with a fast policy so a burst is absorbed, `scaleDown` at 300 s so a lull does not flap, plus `minReplicas` sized for the cold-start floor. Know the limits of horizontal scaling here: adding pods does not add provider quota, so past a point you are only redistributing 429s, and for self-hosted GPU serving the scaling unit is a node with a multi-minute image pull and model load, which means you pre-warm or you shed.

resource.label: KEDA docs - event-driven autoscaling for Kubernetes

subtopics.name: Observability and cost attribution: OTel GenAI semantics, per-tenant dashboards, the alerts you actually set
subtopics.learn: Emit one span per model call using the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (`gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons`) plus your own `tenant.id`, `prompt.version`, `cache.hit` and `retry.attempt`, so a trace answers 'why was this request slow and what did it cost' in one view. Build two dashboards and ship them with the deployment: an ops board (TTFT and completion p50/p95/p99, error rate split 429/529/5xx, in-flight and queue depth, provider quota headroom) and a cost board (spend per tenant per feature per day, cache hit ratio, tokens per request trend). Set the four alerts that earn their pager: cache hit ratio dropping more than 20 points day-over-day, 429 rate above threshold for 5 minutes, p95 TTFT breaching the published budget, and daily spend on pace to exceed the agreed ceiling. Anything else is a dashboard, not an alert.

resource.label: OpenTelemetry - Semantic conventions for generative AI spans

subtopics.name: The write-up: Kaupex under Black Friday, with numbers and a rehearsed failure story
subtopics.learn: Turn the whole topic into the artefact a customer signs off on. Fix the scenario: Kaupex normally compiles 2k tasks/hour, Black Friday week is 15x with a two-hour spike at 40x, and the customer's SLA says a task is acknowledged in under 2 s and compiled within 5 minutes. Produce (1) an assumptions table where every number is derived, not asserted; (2) a per-hop latency budget for the interactive path and a throughput budget for the compile path; (3) cost per task and cost for the peak day, with the prompt-caching hit ratio as an explicit sensitivity row; (4) the capacity plan against the provider quota, showing the arithmetic for how many concurrent calls the quota permits and therefore where you queue; (5) the degradation ladder with triggers and kill switches; and (6) a failure story with a timeline: what breaks first, at what number, what the customer sees, and what the runbook says. Close with the one sentence the architect will repeat to their CTO. Then rehearse it aloud in 20 minutes and cut anything you cannot defend with a number.

resource.label: Eugene Yan - Patterns for building LLM-based systems and products

outcomes: You can write a per-hop latency budget for an LLM feature that sums to a stated p95, set every hop timeout from it, propagate a deadline down the chain, and show the `histogram_quantile()` query that proves the budget is being met in Grafana.

You can state cost per request as a formula with named token terms, name the four multipliers that inflate it (retries, agent loops, tool round-trips, judge models), and produce a per-tenant per-feature monthly cost number from a `llm_calls` table you designed.

You can restructure a prompt so the stable prefix is cacheable, place `cache_control` correctly, and demonstrate a measured cache hit ratio with `cache_read_input_tokens` before and after, including the cost break-even point where caching starts paying.

You can design a per-tenant admission controller over one shared provider quota (Redis Lua token bucket debiting estimated tokens and reconciling from `usage`) with a stated fairness policy and a correct 429 contract including `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-*` headers.

You can write a retry and circuit-breaker policy that provably cannot amplify an outage beyond ~1.1x (full jitter, single retrying layer, 10% retry budget, breaker thresholds) and explain which LLM operations are unsafe to retry and what idempotency key makes them safe.

You can draw the degradation ladder for a given feature with a trigger, user-visible effect and owner per rung, and show the always-on traffic slice and kill switch that keep the fallback from being dead code.
You can choose sync vs streaming vs async-job vs batch-API for a stated workload and defend it with the latency SLA, the cost delta and the crash-safety requirement rather than with preference.

You can run a 45-minute LLM system design end to end (requirements, numbers, diagram, two deep dives, failure story) and finish with 'the thing that saturates first is X at Y rps, and here is what the customer sees'.
failureModes: A prompt template rendered the current timestamp in the system block, so every prompt-cache lookup missed silently, and the customer's bill quadrupled over a weekend with no latency or error signal to catch it.

Retries were configured in the SDK, the internal gateway and the customer's frontend simultaneously; a 90-second provider degradation turned into 27x load, exhausted the org token quota, and kept the system down for twenty minutes after the provider had recovered.

An unbounded asyncio queue in front of the model tier absorbed a burst until every queued request had already exceeded the client's 30-second timeout, so the service spent an hour generating tokens for connections that were long closed while users saw only errors.

The provider outage fallback to a secondary region had never run in production; when it finally fired, its connection pool was cold, its API key had expired six weeks earlier, and the fallback path failed faster than the primary it was replacing.

Latency was tuned by shrinking the prompt from 6k to 3k tokens with no measurable effect, because p95 was dominated by a `max_tokens: 4096` default and a model that habitually wrote 1,200-token answers.
The semantic cache used a cosine threshold of 0.85 with no tenant prefix in the key, and one customer's support agent was served another customer's cached answer containing their account details.
The HPA was configured on CPU utilisation for an IO-bound LLM service; pods sat at 7% CPU while p95 tripled, no scaling event ever fired, and the postmortem blamed the model provider.
interviewQuestions: Design the LLM layer of an order-triage system that normally handles 2,000 requests an hour and hits 40x during a two-hour Black Friday spike, with a 2-second acknowledgement SLA and a 5-minute completion SLA. Give me the latency budget, the cost per request, where you queue, and the first thing that saturates, with numbers.

Your p95 latency is 9 seconds against a 4-second target. Walk me through diagnosis: what do you measure first, how do you tell queueing from generation, and what are the three levers you would pull in order of effect per unit of risk?

You have one organisation-level token-per-minute quota shared by 200 tenants, and one of them starts a bulk import. Design the admission control: what do you meter, where does the state live, what does a throttled tenant see, and how do you keep interactive traffic alive without hard-capping everyone?

The model provider is returning 529s for 40% of calls. Walk me through exactly what your system does in the first 60 seconds and the next 30 minutes, and tell me what the customer's users see at each stage. Then tell me how you tested that path before it happened.

When is it correct to retry an LLM call, and when does a retry corrupt state? Give me a concrete example from a system that writes to a customer's CRM, and show me the idempotency design that makes the retry safe.

A customer wants sub-second responses and refuses to accept streaming as an answer because their UI is a batch report. What options do you actually have, what does each cost, and which would you recommend for a 3,000-token summarisation task?

Prompt caching gives you a 10x read discount but costs more to write. Derive the break-even and tell me for which of these three workloads it pays: a single-turn classifier, a 20-turn support conversation, and a nightly fan-out of 50,000 documents against the same 8k-token policy prompt.
47.proofOfWork: A public `llm-load-lab` repository that turns the two written designs into something a reviewer can run. It contains a docker-compose stack with the Kaupex API in front of a deliberately hostile fake provider: a small FastAPI service that emulates a model endpoint with configurable TTFT and per-token delay, a token-bucket RPM/TPM quota that returns real 429s with `retry-after` and `anthropic-ratelimit-*`-style headers, a 529 injection rate, and a mid-stream error mode. Against it run four k6 `ramping-arrival-rate` scenarios that each reproduce one failure and then its fix, with before/after Grafana panels committed as PNGs: (1) a layered-retry storm showing 27x amplification collapsing to ~1.1x once full jitter, a single retry layer and a 10% retry budget are enabled; (2) an unbounded queue showing every request completing after its client deadline, fixed by a bounded semaphore plus deadline-aware LIFO shedding; (3) a prompt-cache regression where a timestamp in the system block drops the hit ratio to zero and doubles cost per request, caught by a hit-ratio alert rule checked into the repo; (4) an HPA-on-CPU non-event replaced by a KEDA Prometheus scaler on in-flight requests. Alongside the code sit the two design documents themselves, each with an assumptions table, a per-hop budget, a cost model with a prompt-caching sensitivity row, a degradation ladder with kill switches, and a dated failure timeline. The README opens with a one-paragraph summary written for a customer architect, and `make demo` reproduces every chart from scratch in under ten minutes.

48.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
48.why: An FDE does system design live and unprepared: in a customer's conference room, in front of their principal architect, with requirements that arrive as complaints rather than specs, and with a hard stop when the VP has to leave. The system design round in a Palantir, Anthropic or Databricks FDE loop is a compressed version of that meeting, and both reward the same muscle: turn a vague ask into numbers, draw something a stranger can follow, name the two things that will actually break, choose between options out loud, and stay coherent when someone pushes back. Topics 39 to 43 gave you the material; this topic trains delivery under a clock, and the recording is what lets you see the gap between what you know and what you can show in 45 minutes.
prerequisites: The component playbook from 'System design playbook' (topic 42): you should already be able to explain consistent hashing, cache-aside versus write-through, fan-out on write versus read, Kafka partitioning, token buckets and Snowflake IDs without notes; the mocks test whether you can reach for them under time pressure, not learn them.

The consistency vocabulary from 'DDIA' (topic 39) and 'MIT 6.824 selected lectures' (topic 40): linearizable versus eventual, leader-based replication and its failover, quorums, and why 'exactly once' means at-least-once plus idempotency.

The LLM serving constraints from 'LLM-era system design' (topic 43): token-based rate limits, p99 latency in seconds not milliseconds, and queue-plus-worker rather than synchronous model calls, so the one LLM-flavoured mock does not derail.

SLIs and SLOs from topic 20 and the four golden signals from topic 21, because the non-functional requirements you write in the first five minutes are SLOs and the operability close in the last five minutes is a monitoring design.

A working recording rig: OBS or QuickTime capturing screen plus microphone, Excalidraw open with a saved template, a visible countdown timer, and a private folder or repo to store six 45-minute recordings.

One peer (Exponent match or a friend who has run design interviews) who agrees to two sessions as interviewer and to score with your rubric, plus a written set of interviewer cards so solo mocks still get interrupted.

subtopics.name: The 45-minute time budget and phase transitions
subtopics.learn: Fix a budget and rehearse the transitions until they are reflexive: 0-5 requirements (three core functional requirements, explicit 'below the line' list, non-functional requirements with numbers), 5-8 estimation (only the numbers that change a decision), 8-12 API and data model, 12-22 high-level design that satisfies every functional requirement end to end, 22-40 two or three deep dives on the parts you named as hardest, 40-45 failure modes, operability and what you would build first. Know the two universal failure patterns: spending 15 minutes on requirements and never reaching a deep dive, and drawing a 'perfect' architecture before checking it against the functional requirements. Practise saying the transition sentence out loud ('I have the core flow working, let me name the two things that will break at this scale and go deep on them') because the interviewer is scoring whether you drive or wait to be driven.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Delivery Framework

subtopics.name: Writing the rubric: what 4/5 means on each dimension
subtopics.learn: Adapt the Hello Interview evaluation dimensions (problem navigation, high-level design, technical excellence, communication and collaboration) into a 1-5 rubric where every level is an observable behaviour you can timestamp in a recording. Define 4 concretely: problem navigation 4 = you named the hardest two components unprompted and spent at least 15 minutes on them; high-level design 4 = every box traces to a stated requirement and the diagram satisfies all core functional requirements before any deep dive; technical excellence 4 = each deep dive presents two options, a quantified reason for the choice, and its failure mode; communication 4 = you talked while drawing, checked in at each phase, and changed course on pushback without defending a bad choice. Write 5 as 'taught the interviewer something' and 2 as 'needed a hint to proceed'. This is the document a peer scores against, so it must be legible to someone who did not watch you prepare.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Introduction (how you are evaluated)

subtopics.name: Choosing six problems that cover six archetypes
subtopics.learn: Pick one problem per archetype so the six mocks exercise different bottlenecks rather than the same one six times: read-heavy fan-out (news feed or timeline), write-heavy ingestion (metrics or log pipeline at millions of events per second), real-time bidirectional (chat with presence and ordering), geospatial matching (ride dispatch or nearby search), contended inventory with money (ticket booking or payments with idempotency and holds), and the FDE-flavoured one: a multi-tenant document ingestion and LLM classification platform where one tenant must run inside their own VPC. Use the primer's solved questions to sanity-check that each archetype has a known 'hard part' and write that hard part on the interviewer card before you start, so afterwards you can check whether you found it unprompted. Do not pick a problem you have already watched a full walkthrough of; the mock measures reasoning, not recall.

resource.label: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer (interview questions with solutions)

subtopics.name: Recording rig and whiteboard template
subtopics.learn: Set up OBS with a display-capture source and your microphone, confirm audio levels and that the cursor is visible, and record a two-minute test before mock one so a broken recording never wastes a session. Build an Excalidraw template you reuse every time: a legend (solid arrow = synchronous call, dashed = asynchronous, cylinder = store, numbered circles for the core flow steps), a requirements box top-left, an estimation box below it, and a timer window pinned on top. Name recordings `mock-NN-problem-YYYY-MM-DD.mp4` and export the `.excalidraw` file alongside; the diagram file is what a reviewer will actually open. Never pause the timer or the recording; running out of time on camera is the data you are collecting.

resource.label: OBS Studio Knowledge Base - Quick Start Guide (display capture source, audio setup, first recording)

subtopics.name: Requirements in five minutes: functional scope and NFRs as SLOs
subtopics.learn: Drive the first five minutes with questions that change the design, not a checklist: who are the users and how many, what are the three operations that must work, what is explicitly out of scope, and for each core operation what consistency it needs (booking a seat is linearizable, viewing a seat map is eventual). Write non-functional requirements as numbers you can be held to: availability target and the consistency cost of the higher one (99.9 versus 99.99), p99 latency per operation, peak QPS with a stated peak-to-average ratio, retention, durability, and any compliance constraint (PII residency, audit). Phrase them as SLOs from topic 20 ('99.9 percent of reads under 200 ms over 30 days') because that is exactly how a customer architect will later ask you to commit. State 'I am designing for 10x today's numbers' and move on; a candidate still gathering requirements at minute ten has already lost the design phase.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: Estimation that changes decisions, not estimation for show
subtopics.learn: Memorise the handful of numbers you will use every time: 1 day is about 1e5 seconds, so 1M DAU doing 10 actions each is about 100 QPS average and roughly 1,000 at peak; a single well-tuned Postgres handles on the order of 10k simple reads per second and low thousands of writes; one Redis node does about 100k ops per second; a Kafka partition sustains tens of MB per second; memory access is about 100 ns, SSD random read about 100 us, same-region RPC about 1 ms, cross-region round trip about 100 ms. Compute only what decides something: does the hot dataset fit in memory on one node, do writes exceed one primary, does storage over the retention period force tiering, does fan-out multiply writes past what one partition can take. Round to powers of ten, write the number on the board next to the component it justifies, and say the decision it drives ('200 GB fits on one Postgres primary with replicas, so I will not shard yet').

resource.label: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know (jboner gist)

subtopics.name: API design in four minutes: resources, idempotency, pagination, async
subtopics.learn: Sketch the three or four endpoints that map to your core functional requirements as resources and verbs (`POST /v1/bookings`, `GET /v1/events/{id}/seats`), and state the non-obvious decisions rather than reading fields aloud: an `Idempotency-Key` header on every mutating call with server-side deduplication keyed by (tenant, key), cursor pagination with an opaque token instead of `offset` because deep offsets scan the table, `202 Accepted` plus a status resource for anything that takes longer than a request timeout, tenant and user identity taken from the token and never from the body, and a consistent error shape with a retryable flag. Mention versioning and rate-limit headers only if the problem is a public API. Be ready to defend REST versus gRPC versus WebSocket per endpoint in one sentence each, then move to the data model.

resource.label: GitHub - microsoft/api-guidelines (REST API guidelines)

subtopics.name: Data model and store selection from access patterns
subtopics.learn: List the entities and the top three access patterns first, then pick the store, and say the sentence that shows judgement: 'relational, a few hundred GB, needs transactions across seats and payments, so Postgres with an index on (event_id, status) and a partial index on held seats; I shard by tenant_id only when a primary can no longer absorb writes'. Know when a key-value or wide-column store is the right answer (single-row access by key at very high write rates, time-series with TTL) and what it costs you (no joins, secondary indexes that double writes, hot partitions). For any partitioned store, state the partition key and check it against cardinality, distribution and access locality; a tenant_id key with one tenant at 60 percent of traffic is a hot partition you must call out before the interviewer does. Name the write-amplification of every secondary index you add and whether the store gives you conditional writes for the contended path.

resource.label: AWS DynamoDB Developer Guide - Best practices for designing and using partition keys effectively

subtopics.name: High-level design: C4 container level, numbered flows, narrated
subtopics.learn: Draw at the C4 'container' level (deployable units and stores, not classes and not cloud icons) left to right: clients, edge (CDN, load balancer, API gateway with auth and rate limiting), stateless services, stores, and the asynchronous spine (queue, workers, schedulers) below. Number the arrows for the primary flow and walk each core functional requirement through the diagram out loud before any deep dive, ticking them off; a box you cannot trace to a requirement gets deleted on camera. Start boring (one service, Postgres, Redis, one queue) and add components only where a number from estimation forces it; the interviewer is scoring whether each box is justified, not how many there are. Talk while drawing; more than 30 seconds of silent drawing is a communication deduction in your own rubric.

resource.label: C4 model - software architecture diagrams (container level)

subtopics.name: Deep dive pattern: the read path (caching, replicas, stampedes, hot keys)
subtopics.learn: For a read-heavy bottleneck present the options and choose with a number: cache-aside with TTL versus write-through with event-driven invalidation, and the staleness each allows against the NFR you wrote. Name the failure modes and their fixes as a unit: stampede on expiry (lock or lease, request coalescing, jittered or probabilistic early expiration), hot keys (local in-process cache, key replication across cache nodes), replica lag breaking read-your-writes (route the writer's next read to the primary, or carry a version token), and consistent hashing so a cache node loss does not flush everything. Say where the CDN ends and the application cache begins. Close the deep dive with the metric you would watch (hit ratio, origin QPS, replica lag seconds) so it connects to the operability close.

resource.label: AWS ElastiCache Developer Guide - Caching strategies

subtopics.name: Deep dive pattern: the write path (queues, ordering, idempotent consumers, outbox)
subtopics.learn: For a write-heavy or asynchronous bottleneck, decouple with a log or queue and immediately state the three questions that follow: partition key for ordering (per entity, never global), delivery semantics (at-least-once plus a consumer dedupe table keyed by event id, because exactly-once at the application level is idempotency, not a broker feature), and backpressure (bounded consumer lag alerts, producer-side shedding, dead-letter topic with replay). Use the transactional outbox for the 'write to DB and publish an event' atomicity problem and say why dual writes fail. Quantify the partition count from throughput per partition and the retention from replay needs, and name the hot-partition risk of your chosen key. Know when a queue is the wrong answer: a synchronous confirmation the user is waiting for cannot hide behind eventual processing.

resource.label: Microservices.io - Pattern: Transactional outbox (atomic database write plus event publish, why dual writes fail)

subtopics.name: Deep dive pattern: consistency, replication and failover
subtopics.learn: Decide consistency per operation, not per system, and say it in Jepsen's vocabulary: the seat decrement is linearizable (single leader per shard with a conditional update or row lock), the seat map is eventual (replicas), the payment-to-booking relationship is a saga with compensations, not a distributed transaction. Explain what synchronous versus asynchronous replication buys and costs in RPO and write latency, how leader failover works and why unfenced failover produces split brain, and why a distributed lock without a fencing token is a bug rather than a design. When the interviewer asks for active-active across regions, know the honest answer: either partition the data so each key has one home region, or accept conflicts and define the merge; there is no third option that keeps linearizability. Quantify the availability you give up for the consistency you need and tie it back to the NFR line.

resource.label: Jepsen - Consistency Models

subtopics.name: Handling curveballs: 10x traffic, region loss, hot tenant, slow dependency
subtopics.learn: Rehearse a fixed response shape for any mid-design change: restate the change, point at the diagram component it stresses, quantify the new load against the number you already wrote, offer two options, choose one and name its cost, all inside three minutes. Prepare the standard set on interviewer cards: traffic grows 10x, one region is lost, one tenant becomes half the traffic, a downstream API caps you at 100 requests per second, the product adds a feature that changes the access pattern, the interviewer asks 'why not just use X'. For the dependency-failure card, reach for the cascading-failure toolkit by name: timeouts with deadline propagation, retries with exponential backoff and jitter capped by a budget, circuit breakers, load shedding by priority, graceful degradation, and a queue as a buffer during the outage. The score is for locating and quantifying the bottleneck, not for having anticipated the specific card.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Addressing Cascading Failures

subtopics.name: The operability close: golden signals, rollout, phasing
subtopics.learn: Spend the last five minutes proving you have run systems, not just drawn them: name the four golden signals for each service tier (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), map the NFRs from minute two onto SLO alerts, and say how the system rolls out (canary by tenant or percentage, feature flags, expand-and-contract migrations, backfills that can be paused). Give an order-of-magnitude cost and a phased plan ('phase one is the monolith plus Postgres plus one queue and ships in six weeks; sharding and the second region are phase three when the numbers demand them'). Finish with the two failure modes you are least comfortable with and how you would detect each; interviewers rate candour about weaknesses above a design that claims to have none.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Monitoring Distributed Systems (four golden signals)

subtopics.name: The FDE twist: designing inside the customer's constraints
subtopics.learn: In at least two of the six mocks, add the constraints an FDE actually faces and practise adapting the design out loud: deploy inside the customer's VPC or on-premises (so every managed service becomes a swap table: DynamoDB to Postgres, SQS to Redis Streams or Kafka, Lambda to a worker deployment), data residency that forces per-region shards and per-region key management, integration with systems you do not control (a CRM with a 100 requests-per-second limit, a nightly SFTP drop, an IdP you must federate with), change windows and a security review that will ask about every arrow on the diagram. Practise the migration story as part of the design: dual-write, backfill, verify, cut over, roll back. Use the Well-Architected pillars as the checklist a customer architect will use on you, and be able to say which pillar you consciously traded down in phase one and why.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Framework - Overview and pillars

subtopics.name: When the problem contains an LLM step
subtopics.learn: Treat a model call as an external dependency with unusual numbers and say them: p50 in seconds, p99 in tens of seconds, rate limits expressed in requests and tokens per minute (RPM, TPM, ITPM) per organisation rather than per user, 429 responses that carry a `retry-after` header, and cost per call that makes 'call it for every request' a budget conversation. Put it behind a queue and workers instead of in the request path, add a semantic or exact-match cache keyed by prompt hash, define a fallback (smaller model, rules, or 'pending' state) for rate-limit and outage cases, and make the output idempotent so a retried classification does not double-write to the customer's CRM. Say explicitly that evals and observability for the model step exist and that you will treat them as a separate design (topics 53 and 54), so the interviewer sees scope control rather than avoidance.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform docs - Rate limits

subtopics.name: Mocks 1 and 2: solo, timed, recorded, interviewer cards
subtopics.learn: Run the news-feed and metrics-ingestion problems alone under the full 45-minute clock with the recording running, using a shuffled deck of interviewer cards you draw at minutes 12, 25 and 35 to force interruptions you did not pick. Play both roles honestly: read the card aloud, respond, do not skip it because it is inconvenient. Expect these two to score around 3 and to overrun the requirements phase; the purpose is a baseline and a working rig, not a good score. Within 24 hours run the self-review protocol and write the three fixes for mock three before you forget what it felt like.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Core Concepts

subtopics.name: Mocks 3 and 4: peer sessions on Exponent, both chairs
subtopics.learn: Book two peer practice sessions and take the chat and ride-dispatch problems as candidate, sending your rubric to the peer beforehand so their score is on your scale. Sit in the interviewer chair for an equal number of sessions; running someone else's design interview teaches you what silence, unjustified boxes and unquantified claims look like from the other side faster than any amount of candidate practice. Give feedback with timestamps and rubric dimensions, ask for the same, and record your own sessions (with consent) so the peer score can be compared against your self-score. A gap of more than one point on any dimension between your score and theirs is the most important finding of the week.

resource.label: US Office of Personnel Management - Structured Interviews (developing, conducting and rating with a fixed scale)

subtopics.name: Mocks 5 and 6: contended inventory and the FDE tenant platform, under pushback
subtopics.learn: Run the ticket-booking problem and the multi-tenant ingestion and classification platform with the peer instructed to push back at least once every five minutes ('why not Kafka for everything', 'the customer will not allow a managed database', 'a tenant with 40 percent of traffic just signed'). These are the two archetypes whose hard parts (linearizable decrement under contention; a design that must survive being redeployed into a customer VPC) most resemble what an FDE loop asks. Your target is the third consecutive 4/5 across all rubric dimensions; if either falls short, the seventh mock is the same problem again with the same peer, not a new problem. Keep the `.excalidraw` from mock six, it becomes the design doc in the proof of work.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Common Patterns

subtopics.name: Self-review protocol and the pattern ledger
subtopics.learn: Within 24 hours of each mock, watch the recording at 1.5x with the rubric open and log: the timestamp of each phase transition against the budget, the number of design-changing questions asked in the first five minutes, boxes drawn without a stated requirement, statements that included a number versus statements that did not, seconds of silent drawing, and every moment you defended a choice after the interviewer gave you a reason to change it. Score each dimension with at least one timestamp as evidence and record it in a running table alongside the peer's score. Maintain a pattern ledger with two columns, 'reached for' and 'should have reached for', per mock; the second column across six mocks is your revision list for topic 42, and a pattern appearing there twice means a targeted 30-minute drill before the next mock. Write exactly three fixes for the next session and re-read them five minutes before it starts.

resource.label: Hello Interview - System Design in a Hurry: Key Technologies (checklist for the 'should have reached for' column)

outcomes: You can run a 45-minute design mock in which the recording shows each phase transition (requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, close) within two minutes of the planned budget, with no phase skipped.

You can, for any of the six archetypes, state three core functional requirements, an explicit out-of-scope list, and non-functional requirements with numbers (availability, p99 latency, peak QPS, retention, consistency per operation) inside five minutes without prompting.
You can derive QPS, storage and bandwidth in powers of ten in under three minutes and, for each number, say which design decision it changes (shard or not, in-memory or not, one primary or many).

You can draw a container-level diagram with numbered flows and a sync/async legend, walk every core requirement through it before deep diving, and delete or justify on camera any box that does not trace to a requirement.

You can name the two hardest components unprompted and deep dive each with two options, a quantified reason for the choice, its failure mode and the metric you would watch, spending at least 15 of the 45 minutes there.

You can respond to any of eight rehearsed curveballs (10x traffic, region loss, hot tenant, capped dependency, on-prem only, new access pattern, 'why not X', active-active demand) by locating it on the diagram, quantifying it and choosing, in three minutes or less.
You can score your own recording against the rubric with timestamped evidence and land within half a point of a peer's independent score on at least three of four dimensions.
You can show three consecutive peer-scored mocks at 4/5 or better on every rubric dimension, with the score table, recordings and diagrams as evidence.
failureModes: A design that scored well in the mock assumed DynamoDB, SQS and Lambda; the customer's security team requires everything inside their VPC with no managed services, and the FDE has to redesign the write path on site in a week because the swap table (Postgres, Kafka or Redis Streams, worker deployments) was never practised.

The read path uses cache-aside with a ten-minute TTL and no invalidation events, so after a customer changes a tenant's entitlements their users keep seeing the old plan for ten minutes and the customer files it as a security incident rather than a staleness bug.

The feed was designed fan-out-on-write because it demoed cleanly; a tenant with five million followers onboards, one post produces five million timeline writes, the queue backs up for hours and every other tenant's feed goes stale until someone adds the hybrid pull path for high-follower accounts.

Estimation used average traffic; the customer's users all log in at 09:00 Monday with a peak-to-average ratio above ten, the connection pool saturates, retries without jitter triple the load and the primary falls over exactly when the customer's leadership is watching.

The queue consumer was described as exactly-once in the interview but shipped as at-least-once with no dedupe table; a broker rebalance replays a batch and the classifier writes duplicate contacts into the customer's HubSpot, which the customer's sales team notices before your monitoring does.

Sharding by tenant_id was chosen because it sounded natural; one tenant is 60 percent of all writes, that shard's primary runs hot while the others idle, and rebalancing a live shard becomes a multi-week project that was avoidable by discussing key skew in the design review.

Offset pagination shipped because the API sketch used `?page=`; a customer's export job pages through 80 million rows, each deeper page scans further, p99 climbs past the gateway timeout on page 4,000 and the export never completes.
interviewQuestions: Design a document ingestion and LLM classification platform for 30 enterprise tenants where one tenant requires the whole thing to run inside their own VPC with no managed services. Walk me through the shared design first, then tell me exactly which components change for that tenant, what you lose, and how you keep one codebase.

You designed a news feed with fan-out on write. A customer account with five million followers is about to onboard. What breaks first, how would you have detected it before the customer did, and how do you evolve the design to a hybrid without downtime or a re-backfill of every timeline?

For a ticket-booking system, how do you guarantee no seat is sold twice? Tell me which operation needs linearizability, how you get it on a single shard, what happens at leader failover, and what you say when the customer insists on active-active across two regions.

A customer reports that users see stale data for several minutes after an update. Walk me through diagnosing it on your diagram: cache TTL versus missing invalidation versus replica lag versus CDN, what evidence distinguishes each, and what you tell the customer at each step before you know the cause.

Your pipeline needs to write into a CRM API that allows 100 requests per second for the whole customer account while your system produces bursts of 5,000 events per second. Design the shaping layer: where the buffer lives, how you prioritise, what you drop or delay, how the customer sees progress, and what your on-call alert is.

I am going to push back on your choice of Postgres plus an outbox instead of Kafka as the source of truth. Defend it with numbers, tell me the point at which you would switch, and tell me what the migration from one to the other looks like for a live customer.

You had 45 minutes and chose to deep dive on two components. Which did you skip, why was that the right call given the requirements, and what would you have said if I had told you at minute 30 that the skipped component was the one the customer cares about?
48.proofOfWork: A public `system-design-mocks` repository (or a section of the FDE dashboard) that a hiring manager can read in ten minutes and a peer can reuse in one. It contains: (1) `rubric.md` with the 1-5 definitions per dimension written as observable behaviours, plus the score table for all six mocks showing self-score, peer score and the gap per dimension, with the three consecutive 4/5 sessions highlighted; (2) six `.excalidraw` files and PNG exports, each with the requirements and estimation boxes filled in on the canvas, and a `scorecard-NN.md` per mock listing phase-transition timestamps against budget, the curveball cards drawn and the three fixes carried into the next session; (3) `interviewer-cards.md`, the deck of twelve curveballs with the 'hard part' for each of the six archetypes, usable by anyone running a mock for you or for themselves; (4) `pattern-ledger.md` with the 'reached for' and 'should have reached for' columns across all six mocks and the drills that resulted; and (5) a two-page `design-doc-tenant-platform.md` written from the mock-six diagram in the form a customer architect would review: requirements as SLOs, container diagram, the two deep dives, the managed-to-self-hosted swap table for the VPC tenant, a phased delivery plan with what ships in six weeks, and the failure modes you are least comfortable with and how each is detected.

49.topic: LLM fundamentals: tokens, attention, pretraining, RLHF, scaling, limits
49.why: An FDE is the person a customer's VP of Ops corners after the demo and asks "why did it make that up, and can you guarantee it won't?" — and the answer has to be mechanistic, honest, and scoped, not a shrug or a sales line. Everything else in this track (prompting, tool use, RAG, evals, fine-tuning) is a set of levers whose behaviour only makes sense once you can say which part of the stack each lever touches: tokenizer, attention, pretraining distribution, or post-training preference model. Getting this wrong in front of a customer costs you the engagement — you either overpromise a determinism the architecture cannot deliver, or you kill a viable use case because you could not explain that the failure was retrieval, not the model.
prerequisites: The LLM serving mental model from 'LLM-era system design' (topic 43): tokens-per-second rate limits, seconds-not-milliseconds p99, streaming responses, and queue-plus-worker rather than synchronous calls — this topic explains *why* those constraints exist.

Working Python and the ability to run a script against a hosted API (topic 25): you will call a tokenizer, count tokens, sweep temperature, and read logprobs, so `uv`/`venv`, `pip install tiktoken transformers`, and an API key in an env var must be non-events.

Basic linear algebra vocabulary: matrix multiply, dot product, vector norm, softmax. You do not need to derive backprop, but you must be able to read `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V` and say what each symbol is and what shape it has.

Napkin-maths fluency from topic 42's estimation drills: powers of two, GB/s versus GFLOP/s, and the habit of writing the number down before arguing about the architecture — scaling laws and KV-cache sizing are pure napkin maths.

Enough statistics to distinguish a sampled distribution from a point estimate: what a probability distribution over 100k+ classes means, what sampling from it does, and why a single benchmark score without a confidence interval is close to meaningless.

The writing discipline from topic 69 in draft form: this topic's deliverable is a client-facing one-pager, so you need to be able to compress a mechanism into two sentences a non-engineer can repeat to their boss.

subtopics.name: Tokenization: BPE merges, byte-level fallback, and the bugs they cause
subtopics.learn: Understand byte-pair encoding end to end: start from a byte-level alphabet, count adjacent pair frequencies in the training corpus, greedily merge the most frequent pair, repeat until you hit vocab size, and store the ordered merge list. Know that encoding at inference replays those merges in order, which is why the tokenizer is frozen with the model and why a fine-tune cannot add a token without resizing the embedding matrix. Learn the concrete consequences: leading whitespace makes ' the' and 'the' different tokens; digits split unpredictably so arithmetic and ID matching are brittle; non-Latin scripts and code inflate token counts 2-4x; a trailing space before a completion boundary silently degrades quality. Be able to run a tokenizer on a customer's actual document and show which fields fragment badly.

resource.label: Hugging Face LLM Course - Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization

subtopics.name: Token accounting: measuring, not guessing, before you quote a price
subtopics.learn: Get hands-on with at least two tokenizers and prove to yourself that '4 characters per token' is a Latin-prose-only heuristic. Use `tiktoken.encoding_for_model()` or `tiktoken.get_encoding('cl100k_base')` / `o200k_base` to count, and the provider's own token-counting endpoint for the model you will actually bill against, because vocabularies differ and a cross-vendor estimate can be 30% off. Measure the same 10 KB of the customer's real content in English prose, JSON, SQL, Japanese, and a base64 blob, and record the tokens-per-KB for each. Know that images and tool schemas also consume input tokens, and that a system prompt plus tool definitions is a fixed per-call tax you pay on every request.

resource.label: tiktoken (official OpenAI BPE tokenizer repository)

subtopics.name: Embeddings and position: why order is not free
subtopics.learn: Understand that the token ID indexes a row of an embedding matrix of shape [vocab_size, d_model], and that attention itself is permutation-equivariant — without position information, 'A caused B' and 'B caused A' are the same input. Learn the three families you will see in model configs: learned absolute positions (GPT-2), sinusoidal, and rotary (RoPE), which rotates Q and K by an angle proportional to position so attention scores depend on relative distance. Know that RoPE's `theta`/`rope_scaling` config is what vendors change to extend context, and that a naively extended context degrades before it breaks. Separately, do not confuse these internal token embeddings with the sentence-embedding models you will use in topic 49 for retrieval — different objective, different output.

resource.label: Hugging Face LLM Course - How do Transformers work?

subtopics.name: Self-attention: Q, K, V and the causal mask, at the level where you can draw it
subtopics.learn: Be able to derive and draw scaled dot-product attention: project each token into query, key and value vectors; score every query against every key with a dot product; divide by sqrt(d_k) to keep the softmax out of saturation; softmax over the key axis to get weights that sum to 1; take the weighted sum of values. Understand multi-head attention as running h of these in parallel on d_model/h dimensions and concatenating, so different heads can track different relations. Know the causal mask concretely: positions j > i are set to -inf before the softmax so a decoder-only model can be trained on every position of a sequence in one pass. From this, derive two things you will use constantly: attention is O(n^2) in sequence length, and every output token attends to every prior token, which is why the whole prompt is re-read (from cache) at each step.

resource.label: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (arXiv)

subtopics.name: The decoder-only stack and parameter arithmetic
subtopics.learn: Assemble the block: pre-norm (RMSNorm or LayerNorm) -> multi-head attention -> residual add -> norm -> MLP (usually SwiGLU, ~4x or 8/3x d_model wide) -> residual add, repeated n_layer times, then a final norm and an unembedding projection to vocab logits. Read `nanoGPT`'s `model.py` until you can point at each of those lines. Then do the arithmetic yourself: for a model with n_layer, d_model and vocab V, estimate parameters as roughly 12 * n_layer * d_model^2 plus V * d_model, and memory at bf16 as 2 bytes per parameter — so a 70B model needs ~140 GB of weights before any activations or KV cache. This one calculation lets you answer 'can we self-host this in our VPC on the GPUs we already own?' in a meeting, which is a question FDEs get constantly.

resource.label: karpathy/nanoGPT (reference decoder-only implementation)

subtopics.name: Decoding and sampling: temperature, top_p, top_k, stop, seed, logprobs
subtopics.learn: Understand generation as a loop: logits -> optional repetition/frequency penalty -> divide by temperature -> softmax -> truncate with top_k and/or top_p (nucleus) -> sample -> append -> repeat until an EOS or stop sequence or max_tokens. Know exactly what each knob does: temperature < 1 sharpens the distribution (T -> 0 approaches greedy), top_p=0.9 keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds 0.9, top_k caps the candidate count, and `stop`/`stop_sequences` truncate without consuming budget. Know that greedy decoding is not 'more accurate', it is lower-variance and more repetitive, and that beam search is wrong for open-ended generation. Learn to request logprobs and use the top-token probability as a cheap, real confidence signal for routing to human review.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - Generation strategies

subtopics.name: KV cache, prefill vs decode, and why TTFT and throughput are different problems
subtopics.learn: Know that without a cache, generating token n would recompute attention over all n-1 previous tokens; the KV cache stores per-layer key and value tensors so each new token does O(n) work instead of O(n^2). Split inference into prefill (the whole prompt processed in one compute-bound, highly parallel pass -> time to first token) and decode (one token at a time, memory-bandwidth-bound -> tokens per second). Size the cache: roughly 2 (K and V) * n_layer * n_kv_heads * head_dim * 2 bytes * sequence_length per request, which is why long contexts and high concurrency blow up GPU memory long before FLOPs run out, and why GQA/MQA exist. Understand that provider prompt caching is this cache persisted across calls, which is why a stable prefix is worth engineering for.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - Cache strategies (KV cache)

subtopics.name: Context windows: advertised length vs effective length
subtopics.learn: Learn that the advertised window is a hard architectural cap on input plus output tokens (and that `max_tokens` is carved out of it), while the *effective* window — where accuracy stays flat — is usually much shorter. Internalise the 'lost in the middle' result: retrieval accuracy is U-shaped in position, best at the start and end of the context, materially worse in the middle, so stuffing 80 documents in and hoping is a design error. Know what overflow actually does: a hard API error, not silent truncation, on most providers — so your app needs explicit budgeting and a truncation policy. Be able to compute a context budget for a real engagement: system prompt + tool schemas + retrieved chunks + conversation history + reserved output, with a named policy for what gets dropped first.

resource.label: Claude Platform Docs - Context windows

subtopics.name: Pretraining: the objective, the corpus, and what perplexity measures
subtopics.learn: Understand that pretraining is one objective — predict the next token, cross-entropy loss over the vocabulary — run over trillions of tokens of web crawl, code, books and curated data, with deduplication and quality filtering doing more for final quality than most architecture tweaks. Learn perplexity as exp(mean negative log-likelihood) and be able to say precisely what it does and does not tell you: it measures fit to a held-out distribution, is not comparable across tokenizers, and correlates only loosely with usefulness on a customer's task. Know that the corpus distribution is the single best predictor of where the model is strong: it is excellent at Python and Wikipedia-shaped facts, weak at your customer's internal jargon and their 2024 pricing table, and that no prompt fixes a knowledge gap that grounding should fix.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - Perplexity of fixed-length models

subtopics.name: Scaling laws: Kaplan vs Chinchilla, and compute-optimal vs inference-optimal
subtopics.learn: Know the shape of the result: test loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, with no discontinuity — which is why capability forecasts are possible at all. Know the correction Chinchilla made to Kaplan: for a fixed training-compute budget, parameters and training tokens should scale roughly in proportion (~20 tokens per parameter), so the earlier generation of models was badly undertrained rather than too small. Then know the practical twist that matters to your customer: nobody trains compute-optimal any more, because inference cost dominates over a model's lifetime, so vendors deliberately overtrain small models. That is the mechanism behind 'the 8B model this year beats last year's 70B' — and it is the honest argument for a cascade or router design instead of always calling the frontier model.

resource.label: Hoffmann et al., "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Chinchilla, arXiv)

subtopics.name: Post-training I: SFT and instruction tuning
subtopics.learn: Understand that a base model is a document completer, not an assistant: prompted with a question it may continue with more questions. Supervised fine-tuning on tens of thousands of (instruction, response) pairs, formatted with a chat template that inserts role markers and special tokens, is what creates the turn-taking behaviour you take for granted. Know that the chat template is part of the contract — using the wrong template on a self-hosted model produces quietly worse output with no error — and that loss is masked so only response tokens contribute. Know that SFT teaches format and style far more than it teaches facts, which is the core of the argument you will make again in topic 50 about when fine-tuning is the wrong tool.

resource.label: Hugging Face LLM Course - Supervised Fine-Tuning

subtopics.name: Post-training II: RLHF, DPO, and RLAIF/Constitutional AI
subtopics.learn: Walk the classic InstructGPT pipeline: SFT, then collect human rankings over sampled completions, then train a reward model to score responses, then optimise the policy with PPO against that reward plus a KL penalty to keep it near the SFT model. Understand what this buys (helpfulness, instruction-following, refusals) and what it costs: reward hacking, sycophancy — agreeing with a confidently wrong user because agreement was rewarded — verbosity bias, and an 'alignment tax' on some raw capabilities. Know DPO as the simpler alternative that skips the explicit reward model and optimises a closed-form preference loss directly, and RLAIF/Constitutional AI as replacing most human labels with model critiques against a written principle set. This is the layer that explains why models sound confident when they are wrong: confident, fluent answers were preferred by labellers.

resource.label: Ouyang et al., "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (InstructGPT, arXiv)

subtopics.name: Why models hallucinate: five distinct mechanisms, named separately
subtopics.learn: Stop treating hallucination as one phenomenon and learn to diagnose which of these you are looking at, because each has a different fix. (1) Objective mismatch: the model is trained to produce a likely continuation, and there is no term in the loss for 'I don't know'. (2) Parametric recall failure: facts are lossily compressed into weights, so rare entities, exact numbers, dates, citations and URLs get plausibly reconstructed rather than recalled. (3) Preference-tuning pressure: hedging was scored lower than a confident answer, so calibration was trained out. (4) Context failure: the right evidence is absent, buried mid-context, or contradicted by the model's prior — and the model splits the difference. (5) Tokenizer and format artefacts: character counting, digit arithmetic and exact-string echoing fail for reasons that have nothing to do with reasoning. Practise labelling 20 real failures from your own transcripts with one of these five.

resource.label: Prompt Engineering Guide - Factuality (risks)

subtopics.name: What actually reduces hallucination, ranked by effect size
subtopics.learn: Build the ranked list you will defend in front of a customer, with the mechanism for each. Highest leverage: ground the answer in retrieved source text and require verbatim citations that a system can check against the source (provider citation features return character/page spans you can validate programmatically — a fabricated span fails the check). Next: constrain the output space with JSON schema / structured outputs so the model cannot free-associate a field. Next: give an explicit abstention path ('answer only from the provided documents; if the answer is not there, return {"answer": null}') and reward it in your evals. Then: decompose and verify — a second pass that checks each claim against the source, or self-consistency across n samples. Know what does *not* work: 'do not hallucinate' in the system prompt, temperature 0 alone, and a bigger model. Know the honest ceiling: you reduce the rate and make failures detectable; you do not reach zero.

resource.label: Claude Platform Docs - Citations

subtopics.name: Reasoning models and inference-time compute
subtopics.learn: Understand the newer axis: rather than scaling training, spend more tokens at inference on an internal reasoning trace, trained with RL against verifiable outcomes (maths, code, tests). Know the operational consequences that hit your architecture: thinking tokens are billed and count against the context window, latency goes from seconds to tens of seconds, streaming semantics change, and a thinking budget becomes a tuning parameter you set per task. Know the honest scoping rule for a customer: reasoning models help on multi-step derivation, planning and code where a verifier exists; they do not help on extraction, classification, or anything where the bottleneck is missing information rather than missing computation — spending 8k thinking tokens on 'what is this invoice number' is pure waste.

resource.label: Claude Platform Docs - Extended thinking

subtopics.name: Reading a model card critically
subtopics.learn: Learn the intended anatomy of a model card — intended use, out-of-scope use, training data, evaluation, ethical considerations, caveats — then read three real cards (a frontier vendor card, an open-weights card such as Llama or Qwen, and a small fine-tune on the Hub) and grade each against it. Build a fixed checklist of questions you ask every time: what is the exact knowledge cutoff and does it match the marketing page; which context length is supported versus tested; are evals reported at 0-shot or few-shot, with or without CoT, and with what decoding parameters; is there a contamination analysis; what is the licence and does it permit your customer's use; what safety evaluations were run and on which languages. The senior move is naming what the card *omits*: an eval table with no error bars and no per-domain breakdown is a marketing asset, not evidence.

resource.label: Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting" (arXiv)

subtopics.name: Benchmarks and contamination: why a leaderboard number does not transfer
subtopics.learn: Learn how public evals are actually scored so you can read a claim precisely: multiple-choice with log-likelihood ranking (MMLU) versus generative exact-match versus pass@k with an executed test suite (HumanEval, SWE-bench). Know that the same model scores several points differently depending on prompt format, few-shot count and normalisation, which is why harness-reported numbers and vendor-reported numbers diverge legitimately. Know contamination: benchmark test sets leak into web-scale pretraining corpora, so a high score can be memorisation, and n-gram overlap analyses are the standard (partial) defence. Run at least one task with `lm-evaluation-harness` to see the machinery. The takeaway you sell to a customer: public benchmarks pick a shortlist, a 50-example eval on their own data picks the model (topic 53).

resource.label: EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness (official repo)

subtopics.name: Hard limits: determinism, arithmetic, self-knowledge, cutoffs
subtopics.learn: Be able to state each limit with its mechanism, because customers ask for guarantees you cannot give. Determinism: even with temperature=0 and a fixed seed, hosted inference is not bit-reproducible — batching changes floating-point reduction order, MoE routing depends on batch composition, and the served model version changes under you; so your contract language is 'stable behaviour under eval', never 'identical output'. Arithmetic and counting: digits are tokens, there is no ALU, so exact computation belongs in a tool call. Self-knowledge: a model cannot reliably report its own confidence, training data, or version — ask the API, not the model. Knowledge cutoff: fixed at pretraining, so anything after it must be retrieved. Also know sensitivity to prompt order and formatting, and that these are properties of the architecture, not bugs a vendor will patch.

resource.label: Hugging Face Transformers - GenerationConfig / text generation parameters

subtopics.name: Model-level safety: refusals, jailbreaks, and why injection is architectural
subtopics.learn: Understand that refusal behaviour is a post-training artefact, not a filter bolted on top, which explains both over-refusal on benign customer content (medical, security, legal, financial domains are common false positives) and the fact that jailbreaks work by shifting the input distribution away from where refusals were trained. Understand prompt injection at the fundamentals level: the model sees one flat token sequence, so 'instructions' and 'data' are a convention enforced by training, not a boundary enforced by the architecture — which is why retrieved documents, tool outputs and user files are all executable-by-accident. Read the OWASP LLM Top 10 categories so you have shared vocabulary with a customer's security team; the hands-on defences come in topic 51.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

subtopics.name: Translating all of this into client language, with sources
subtopics.learn: Convert each mechanism above into one claim a non-technical stakeholder can repeat, paired with a citable source and an explicit scope. Practise the four sentences you will use most: what an LLM is (a next-token predictor over a frozen corpus, tuned by human preference), why it invents citations (lossy parametric recall plus a preference for confident answers), what grounding actually changes (moves facts from weights into checkable context), and what you can and cannot guarantee (a measured error rate on their eval set, not zero errors and not identical outputs). Write the can/cannot table with a third column — 'what we would need to build to change this' — so the document opens scope rather than closing doors. Every claim gets a link; no claim gets an adjective.

resource.label: Hugging Face Hub - Model Cards (structure and metadata for sourcing claims)

outcomes: You can take a customer's real document, tokenize it with two different tokenizers, and state tokens-per-KB and the resulting per-1000-document cost within 10% of the actual billed amount.

You can draw scaled dot-product attention on a whiteboard from memory — Q/K/V projections, sqrt(d_k), softmax over keys, causal mask — and derive from the drawing why context is O(n^2) and why a KV cache exists.

You can size a self-hosted deployment on the spot: given parameter count, precision, concurrency and context length, you produce weight memory and KV-cache memory and say whether it fits the customer's GPUs.

You can take 20 logged failures from a running system and classify each into objective mismatch, parametric recall failure, preference-tuning pressure, context failure, or tokenizer artefact — and name the different fix for each class.
You can explain why temperature=0 does not give reproducible output, and write contract or SLA language that promises stable eval-measured behaviour instead of identical strings.

You can read a model card in ten minutes and produce a written list of what it omits — missing error bars, untested context length, unstated few-shot setting, no contamination analysis — and say which omissions block the customer's use case.

You can defend a ranked list of hallucination mitigations with a mechanism for each, and explicitly tell a customer that 'do not hallucinate' in the system prompt and a bigger model are not on the list.
You can explain Chinchilla scaling and the inference-cost twist well enough to justify a small-model-plus-router architecture to an economic buyer who was expecting 'use the biggest model'.
failureModes: Quoting a project cost from a '4 characters per token' estimate when the customer's corpus is Japanese contracts, JSON payloads or scanned-PDF text, then discovering the real bill is 2-3x the number in the SOW.
Promising deterministic output because the config sets temperature=0, then having a customer's QA team open a defect when two identical requests return different strings on a batched endpoint.
Diagnosing a retrieval failure as a model failure and burning three weeks on prompt tuning or a fine-tune, when the correct chunk was never in the context window in the first place.
Stuffing 60 retrieved chunks into a long context and reporting the system as working because spot checks passed, while accuracy on evidence placed in the middle of the context has quietly collapsed.

Shipping a model whose refusal behaviour over-triggers on the customer's actual domain — clinical notes, security incident reports, credit decisions — so the pilot looks broken to the exact users who matter.

Selecting a model from public leaderboard scores, then finding it loses to a cheaper model on the customer's own 50-example eval because the benchmark was contaminated or measured a different task shape.
Letting a model's own self-report — its claimed version, cutoff, or confidence — into a status update or a client email, and being contradicted later by the API's actual model metadata.
interviewQuestions: A customer says the assistant invented a policy number that looks exactly like their real format. Walk me through your diagnosis: what are the candidate mechanisms, what would you log or measure to distinguish them, and what do you change first?

Explain the KV cache to a customer's platform architect who is deciding whether to buy 8xA100 or 8xH100. Derive the memory arithmetic and tell them which of context length, concurrency, or model size hurts them most.

Your customer's legal team wants a contractual guarantee of reproducible outputs for an audit trail. What can you actually commit to, what can you not, and what would you build to satisfy the underlying audit requirement?

Chinchilla says compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter. Vendors deliberately violate that. Explain why, and then use the reasoning to argue for or against a cascaded small-model architecture for a 10M-document-per-month classification pipeline.
Here is a model card for an open-weights model a customer wants to self-host in their VPC. Read it and tell me the three things you would refuse to sign off on until you had run your own tests.

Rank the interventions that reduce hallucination on a document-QA product from highest to lowest effect, give the mechanism for each, and name two commonly-suggested interventions you would refuse to spend the customer's money on.

A security reviewer asks why you cannot just tell the model to ignore instructions inside uploaded documents. Answer at the level of the architecture, not the product, and then say what you would build instead.
49.proofOfWork: Build a small public repo, `llm-mechanics-lab`, that turns each claim in your client one-pager into a reproducible experiment with committed outputs. It should contain: (1) a tokenizer study that runs tiktoken and a SentencePiece/HF tokenizer over five content types (English prose, JSON, SQL, Japanese, base64) and emits a tokens-per-KB table plus a cost projection at current published prices; (2) a KV-cache and weight-memory calculator that takes n_layer, n_kv_heads, head_dim, precision, context length and concurrency and prints the GPU memory envelope, validated against one real open-weights config.json; (3) a determinism harness that fires the same request 50 times at temperature 0 against a hosted endpoint and reports the exact-match rate, the first divergent token position, and the distribution of top-token logprobs; (4) a hallucination taxonomy notebook that runs a closed-book vs grounded vs grounded-with-citations vs grounded-with-abstention comparison over 30 questions where you know the ground truth, reporting error rate and, critically, detected-error rate per condition; and (5) a `MODEL_CARD_REVIEW.md` applying your checklist to three real model cards with a written list of omissions. The README should state each finding as a one-line claim with a link to the script that produced it, so the client one-pager can cite your own measurements rather than vendor marketing.

50.topic: Prompt engineering as code: versioning, regression sets, structured outputs
50.why: An FDE ships prompts into a customer's production path - a classifier that writes into their CRM, an extractor that feeds their claims queue - and then changes them weekly as the customer discovers edge cases; without version control, a pinned model snapshot and a regression set that runs before merge, every improvement is an uncontrolled experiment on the customer's data. The failure you are preventing has no stack trace: a prompt edit that fixes the one document the customer complained about and silently degrades the other nine hundred, discovered a fortnight later in their monthly report. Treating prompts as code - files in Git, a changelog, typed outputs behind schemas, and a CI gate with a committed baseline - is what lets you say 'this change moved recall from 0.91 to 0.94 across 240 labelled cases, here is the diff and here is what it cost' instead of 'it seems better now'.
prerequisites: Production Python structure from 'Production Python architecture' (topic 25) and the pytest muscle from 'Testing and contracts' (topic 35): fixtures, conftest.py, parametrize, markers, and the habit of asserting on typed objects rather than strings.

LLM mechanics from 'LLM fundamentals' (topic 45): tokenisation and why token counts drive cost, sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k), context windows, and why the same input at temperature 0 can still produce different output.

Git at depth from topic 4: reading a diff properly, git log -p on a path, git bisect, and branch/PR review discipline - you will bisect a prompt regression across a dozen commits and it only works if prompts are files.
CI/CD from topic 18: GitHub Actions workflow syntax, path filters, repository secrets, required status checks, artifacts and job-level concurrency.

Working API access to at least Anthropic (and ideally OpenAI for contrast), the SDK installed, and the rate-limit behaviour from 'LLM-era system design' (topic 43): RPM/ITPM/OTPM buckets, 429 with retry-after, exponential backoff with jitter.

An inventory of DefenderMate's current LLM call sites: every prompt that exists today, what each is supposed to return, and which table or field consumes it (the multi-tenant schema from topic 30 - llm_calls, tool_calls, audit_log).

subtopics.name: Prompt files as versioned artifacts, not string literals
subtopics.learn: Move every prompt out of application source into prompts/<id>/v<N>.md with YAML front-matter carrying id, version, model snapshot, max_tokens, temperature, declared variables, output schema reference and owner. The loader resolves by (id, version), renders, and computes a SHA-256 of the rendered text; that hash - not the text - is what you log on every call. Choose a version bump rule and write it down: MAJOR when the output contract changes (a field removed, renamed or retyped), MINOR when behaviour changes but the contract holds, PATCH for wording. Never edit a released version in place - add v(N+1) - because traces, baselines and the customer's audit log all reference a version that must stay resolvable forever.

resource.label: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 specification

subtopics.name: Templating: strict rendering and the data/instruction boundary
subtopics.learn: Render with Jinja2 using Environment(undefined=StrictUndefined) so a missing or misspelled variable raises at render time instead of silently producing an empty slot - that silent empty slot is the single most common cause of 'the model suddenly got confused'. Never use str.format or f-strings on text that contains JSON braces or the customer's own curly braces. Wrap every injected value in explicit delimiters (<document>...</document>, <tenant_taxonomy>...</tenant_taxonomy>) and strip or escape the closing delimiter out of the value so customer content cannot close your tag and start issuing instructions. Snapshot-test the rendered result: a golden file per (prompt version, fixture) so a one-line template change shows up in review as a rendered-text diff, which is what reviewers can actually reason about.

resource.label: Claude docs - Use XML tags to structure your prompts

subtopics.name: Messages API anatomy: system, turns, prefill, stop_reason
subtopics.learn: Know the request surface cold: POST /v1/messages with model, max_tokens (required, and a truncation risk not a safety net), system as a top-level parameter (string or list of content blocks - there is no role: system message), messages strictly alternating user and assistant, plus temperature, top_p, stop_sequences and metadata.user_id. Force output shape by prefilling: make the final message role assistant with partial content such as '{' or '<analysis>'; the prefill must not end in trailing whitespace or the API rejects it. Branch on stop_reason every single time - end_turn, max_tokens (truncated, never hand it to json.loads), stop_sequence, tool_use, refusal - and persist usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens with the trace, because cost regressions are as real as accuracy regressions.

resource.label: Claude API reference - Messages

subtopics.name: Structured output by forced tool use
subtopics.learn: Define exactly one tool whose input_schema is your output contract and set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_finding"} so the model must emit it; then read the tool_use content block's input dict rather than parsing prose or stripping markdown fences. Understand why this beats 'reply with JSON only': the schema travels in the request, decoding is steered toward it, and there is no preamble to strip. Understand the costs too - tool definitions are input tokens on every call, forcing a tool removes the model's ability to abstain, so add an explicit no_finding branch or nullable fields rather than letting it fabricate, and forced tool choice interacts badly with extended thinking. Generate input_schema from your Pydantic model so the schema and the parser can never drift apart. Agentic multi-tool orchestration and MCP are topic 47; here the tool is only a typing mechanism.

resource.label: GitHub - anthropics/anthropic-cookbook (tool use and structured extraction recipes)

subtopics.name: Strict JSON Schema modes and the subset they actually enforce
subtopics.learn: With OpenAI's response_format {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": ..., "schema": ..., "strict": true}}, constrained decoding guarantees the output parses and matches the shape - but only over a subset of JSON Schema: every object needs "additionalProperties": false, every property must appear in required (optionality is expressed as a ["string", "null"] type union, not by omission), and most value constraints (minimum, maxLength, pattern, format) are not enforced by the decoder. Anthropic's strict output-schema mode carries the same class of restriction. The operating rule: the schema guarantees shape, your validator guarantees meaning. Enum values outside a tenant's taxonomy, dates in the wrong century and confidence scores of 1.7 all still arrive as perfectly valid JSON.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform docs - Structured Outputs

subtopics.name: Writing schemas the model reliably obeys
subtopics.learn: Field order is causal: JSON is generated left to right, so {"reasoning": ..., "label": ...} gives you chain-of-thought before the decision while the reverse commits to a label and then rationalises it. Prefer enums over free strings, flat over deeply nested, and avoid anyOf/oneOf unions and recursive definitions, which degrade both adherence and decoder support.
