Tracing from topic 54: you need trace and observation ids in your production path already, because prompt-version lineage is attached to generations, not to log lines.
Git at depth from topic 4: tags, reflog, revert vs reset, and why an immutable content-addressed history is the right mental model for a prompt registry.
Audit-trail and multi-tenant modelling from topic 30: who-changed-what-when tables, and per-tenant scoping, since prompt labels are frequently tenant-scoped in real deployments.

subtopics.name: Source of truth: Git only, registry only, or both (the two-writer problem)
subtopics.learn: Decide explicitly, in writing, which system is authoritative for prompt text, because the common failure is that both are and neither is. Git-only gives you review, blame and atomic rollback with the code, but couples every wording fix to a deploy and locks out the domain expert who actually knows the wording. Registry-only gives non-engineers a UI and decouples rollout from deploy, but ships with no review, no diff in the PR, and a SaaS dependency on the request path. Learn the pragmatic split most teams land on: the registry is the deployment source of truth, and a webhook mirrors every version into Git for review tooling and disaster recovery - the mirror is a read model, never a writer. Write the decision into the engagement's ADR with the escape hatch named.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Prompt management, get started

subtopics.name: Immutable versions, mutable labels: the pointer indirection
subtopics.learn: Internalise the one structural idea the whole topic rests on: versions are immutable and monotonically numbered, and what production reads is a mutable named pointer at a version. In Langfuse those pointers are labels - `production` is the default label served when you pass none, `latest` auto-tracks the newest version, and custom labels carry environments (`staging`), tenants (`tenant-acme`) or experiment arms (`prod-a`, `prod-b`). Fetch deliberately with `langfuse.get_prompt("finding-summary", label="production")` for the serving path and `version=7` for a reproduction, and never let application code compute a version number. The consequence to state out loud: promotion and rollback become label moves, which are O(1), auditable, and require no artefact rebuild.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Prompt version control (labels, protected labels, rollback)

subtopics.name: MLflow prompt registry mechanics end to end
subtopics.learn: Do the same shape in the other ecosystem so you can walk into either customer. `mlflow.genai.register_prompt(name=..., template=..., commit_message=..., tags={...}, response_format=PydanticModel)` creates version N+1 - it never mutates version N; the template uses `{{double_brace}}` variables and both plain strings and chat-style message lists are accepted. Aliases are the pointer layer: `mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias("finding-summary", alias="production", version=2)`, loaded as `mlflow.genai.load_prompt("prompts:/finding-summary@production")`, with `prompts:/finding-summary/2` for a pinned version and the reserved `@latest` alias for newest. Know `prompt.format(**vars)` and `prompt.to_single_brace_format()` for LangChain/LlamaIndex interop, and that a prompt version can carry a JSON response schema and a model configuration block so decoding params version together with the text.

resource.label: MLflow docs - Create and edit prompts (prompt registry)

subtopics.name: The fetch path in production: caching, staleness, fallback, cold start
subtopics.learn: A registry on the request path is a new dependency in your p99 and your availability budget, so learn its cache semantics exactly. Langfuse caches per process with `cache_ttl_seconds` (default 60; `0` disables) and serves stale-while-revalidate - an expired entry is returned immediately while a background refresh runs, which is why a label move is not instantaneous across a fleet. Always pass `fallback=` with the last-known-good template compiled into the image so a registry outage degrades to a slightly old prompt instead of a 500. Prefetch at startup rather than lazily on first request, and never call `get_prompt` at module import time in a long-lived worker - that pins the version for the process lifetime and quietly defeats every rollout mechanism you are about to build.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Prompt caching (cache_ttl_seconds, fallbacks)

subtopics.name: What exactly is 'a run': the fingerprint you must record
subtopics.learn: Define a run as a tuple and record every element as a param or tag, because any unrecorded element makes the number unattributable: prompt name and version, dated model snapshot, decoding params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, seed if supported), dataset name and content hash, judge prompt version and judge model snapshot, eval-harness version, git SHA, and the run's total USD and token counts. In MLflow that is `mlflow.start_run()` plus `log_param` for the fingerprint, `log_metric(key, value, step=)` for scores over time, `set_tag` for the git SHA and environment, and `log_artifact` for the per-case results file; use nested runs so a sweep over five prompt versions is one parent with five children. The test of whether you got this right: given only a run id, can you rebuild the exact call that produced it six months later without asking anyone a question.

resource.label: MLflow docs - Tracking API (runs, params, metrics, tags, artifacts)

subtopics.name: Lineage both directions: attaching prompt versions to production generations
subtopics.learn: An offline run history is half the value; the other half is being able to slice live traffic by prompt version. Pass the fetched prompt object through to the observation - Python `update_current_generation(prompt=prompt)`, `start_as_current_observation(..., prompt=prompt)`, or `propagate_attributes(prompt=prompt)` when several generations share it; JS `generation.update({ prompt })`. Once linked you get median latency, input/output tokens, cost, generation count and median score per prompt version for free, which is the chart you put in front of the customer when they ask whether last week's change helped. Also emit the version as a span attribute in your own OpenTelemetry pipeline so the same slice exists in Grafana and does not depend on one vendor.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Link prompts to traces (per-version metrics)

subtopics.name: Versioning the model and the decoding config with the prompt
subtopics.learn: A prompt version that does not carry its model and parameters is only two thirds of a configuration, and the missing third is where silent regressions live. Put the model id, temperature, max_tokens and any tool set into the prompt version's `config` object (Langfuse) or model-configuration block (MLflow) so a label move swaps text and settings atomically. Pin dated snapshots, never floating aliases, in anything a customer touches - a vendor rotating an alias underneath you produces a score change with no commit, and you will spend two days looking for a code cause that does not exist. Record the resolved model id returned in the API response next to the requested one, so you can prove after the fact which weights answered.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Prompt config (model and params on the version)

subtopics.name: The longitudinal ledger: append-only history you can chart for a year
subtopics.learn: Treat run results as an append-only ledger, not a dashboard's cache: one immutable row per (run_id, case_id) with the full fingerprint denormalised onto it, written to object storage or a warehouse table you own, mirrored into whatever tool renders it. Content-hash datasets and archive rather than delete old versions, because a chart of score-over-time is meaningless the moment the measuring instrument changes without a marker - so plot vertical annotations for dataset version bumps, judge changes and model snapshot changes on the same axis. Guard against the classic silent break: a metric renamed from `recall` to `recall_macro` splits the series in two and the old half quietly stops updating, so assert metric-key stability in CI. Six months of this ledger is the single most persuasive artefact in a renewal conversation.

resource.label: MLflow docs - GenAI version tracking

subtopics.name: The experiment script as a first-class CI artefact
subtopics.learn: Learn the `langfuse/experiment-action` script contract precisely because it is a good general shape: export a function `experiment(context: RunnerContext)`, call `context.run_experiment(name=..., task=..., evaluators=[...], run_evaluators=[...])`, pull the aggregate you gate on out of `result.run_evaluations` by name, and `raise RegressionError(result=result)` when it breaches the threshold. The distinction the action encodes is the one that matters operationally: a `RegressionError` (the system got worse) and a script crash (your harness is broken) are different failures with different owners, controlled by `should_fail_on_regression` and `should_fail_on_script_error`. Keep the script thin - dataset selection, task, evaluators, threshold, raise - and put everything reusable in a package that also runs from the CLI, so a red build is reproducible on a laptop with one command.

resource.label: GitHub - langfuse/experiment-action (script contract, inputs, outputs)

subtopics.name: Wiring the gate into the workflow: triggers, permissions, outputs
subtopics.learn: Build the workflow deliberately: `on: pull_request` with path filters so unrelated PRs do not burn tokens, `permissions:` narrowed to `contents: read`, `pull-requests: write` (needed to post the result comment) and `actions: read` (so the comment links the specific job and matrix legs are distinguishable), and third-party actions pinned to a release commit SHA rather than a tag so a moved tag cannot execute new code against your customer's keys. Pass `experiment_path`, `dataset_name` and `dataset_version` explicitly - pinning the dataset version is what stops a dataset edit from masquerading as a prompt improvement - and forward `experiment_metadata` with your prompt version and model snapshot so the run is findable later. Capture `steps.<id>.outputs.result_json` and `outputs.failed`, write the JSON to an artifact with `actions/upload-artifact`, and make the smoke tier finish in under two minutes so nobody has a reason to bypass it.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Events that trigger workflows

subtopics.name: Choosing the baseline: production label, not main HEAD
subtopics.learn: The gate must compare the candidate against the version currently serving the customer - the run recorded for whatever `production` points at - not against the previous commit, or you get boiling-frog drift where three PRs each lose two points, each passes, and the system is six points worse with no red build in the history. Record `baseline_run_id` in the candidate run's tags so the comparison is auditable rather than recomputed and forgotten. Apply the paired-comparison discipline from topic 53 (same cases, McNemar or paired bootstrap, interval on the delta) rather than comparing two aggregate numbers, and set the failure threshold from a measured noise budget - run the unchanged system five times, take the spread, gate at roughly two sigma below the per-class floor. Gate the non-accuracy budgets in the same job: p95 latency, tokens per case and USD per thousand cases are regressions too.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Experiments via SDK (including testing in CI)

subtopics.name: Secrets, forks, cost and flakiness: keeping the gate cheap and safe
subtopics.learn: Know why the experiment step fails with an empty key on an external contributor's PR - `pull_request` runs from forks get no repository secrets - and know why the obvious fix is dangerous: `pull_request_target` runs in the base repo's context with secrets available, so checking out and executing PR code under it hands the customer's registry keys to an arbitrary contributor. Prefer a labelled or manually dispatched job for fork PRs. Control spend with `concurrency: { group: ..., cancel-in-progress: true }` so force-pushes do not stack full eval runs, a hard USD ceiling inside the harness that aborts rather than warns, response caching keyed on model plus rendered prompt plus params, and a small stratified smoke tier on PRs with the full set on `schedule`. Treat a re-run that passes as a signal, not a resolution: track flake rate per gate, because a gate that flakes twice gets demoted from required and then it is just a document.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Using secrets in GitHub Actions

subtopics.name: Closing the loop from the UI: prompt-version webhook to repository_dispatch
subtopics.learn: A registry UI edit bypasses your PR gate entirely, so close that hole with an event path: Langfuse emits prompt-version events to an HTTPS endpoint with an HMAC signature; a small receiver verifies the signature (constant-time compare, reject on clock skew, dedupe on event id because delivery is at-least-once) and calls the GitHub REST `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/dispatches` with an `event_type` and a `client_payload` carrying the prompt name and version. The workflow triggers on `repository_dispatch`, runs the same experiment script against the new version, and writes the result back as a comment or a status - so an edit made in a customer workshop is measured within minutes without anyone opening an editor. Make the receiver idempotent and rate-limited: someone iterating in the playground will fire twenty version events in ten minutes.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Webhooks and Slack integrations for prompt events

subtopics.name: Promotion and approval: who may move the pointer
subtopics.learn: Separate the right to create a version from the right to promote one - the whole safety property collapses if anyone who can edit text can also point `production` at it. Use protected labels where the platform offers them (Langfuse restricts modifying a protected label to admins and owners) and mirror the same control on the Git side with a GitHub environment carrying required reviewers and a wait timer on the promotion job, so promotion is a reviewed deployment with a record rather than a click. Emit a structured audit event for every pointer move - actor, prompt, from_version, to_version, run_id of the passing eval, timestamp, ticket - into the audit table from topic 30, because 'who approved this change' is a question that arrives in writing during the customer's first security review, not during the pilot.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Using environments for deployment (required reviewers)

subtopics.name: Rollback as a rehearsed drill, and why it is never instant
subtopics.learn: Rollback is one operation - repoint `production` at the previous version (`update_prompt(name=..., version=N-1, new_labels=["production"])` or `set_prompt_alias(..., alias="production", version=N-1)`) - but treat the claim 'rolled back' as unproven until you can measure convergence. The tail is real: cache TTL on every process, stale-while-revalidate serving one more request per worker, in-flight requests, warm autoscaled pods that fetched at startup, and any CDN or gateway layer in front. Write the runbook with the actual numbers: trigger condition, the exact command, the verification query (count generations by prompt version over the last five minutes until the old version is zero), the expected convergence time from your TTL, and who to tell. Then rehearse it against staging with a stopwatch and put the measured number in the runbook - a rollback path first executed during an incident is a hypothesis, and drift-driven auto-rollback policy is topic 57's problem, not this one's.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Release Engineering

subtopics.name: Reproducibility six months on, and the changelog the customer reads
subtopics.learn: Test the property directly: pick a run from three months ago and replay it from its fingerprint alone. Enumerate what breaks it - a vendor deprecating a dated snapshot, a dataset edited in place instead of versioned, a judge prompt changed without a version bump, a `@latest` alias in a recorded config, a deleted branch taking the git SHA with it - and mitigate each (retention policy, content hashes, judge versioning, alias bans in serving code, tags not branches). Then render a human-readable prompt changelog straight from the ledger: date, version, one-line intent, who promoted it, the eval delta with its interval, and any rollback. That document is what you hand the customer at the QBR, and generating it from the run history rather than writing it by hand is what guarantees it is true.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Releases and versioning

outcomes: You can stand up a prompt registry with immutable versions and environment labels, and show the same prompt served to staging and production from two different versions with zero code differences between the two deployments.

You can make a pull request fail on an eval regression using langfuse/experiment-action, with the PR comment showing the score, the baseline it was compared against, and the result JSON attached as an artifact.
You can produce, from a run id alone, the prompt version, model snapshot, decoding params, dataset hash, judge version and git SHA that produced any number you have ever reported.
You can slice production traffic by prompt version and show median latency, token counts, cost and score per version, then point at the exact hour a version was promoted.
You can execute a rollback by moving one label, and state a measured convergence time backed by a query showing generations on the old version falling to zero.
You can explain and demonstrate why a fork PR cannot run the eval gate, and show a workflow that handles it without ever exposing the registry keys via pull_request_target.
You can wire a registry UI edit to a CI eval run through a signature-verified webhook and repository_dispatch, so a prompt changed by a non-engineer is scored within minutes.
You can generate a customer-facing prompt changelog directly from the run ledger, with per-change eval deltas and intervals, and defend every line of it.
failureModes: A solutions consultant edits the prompt in the registry UI during a customer workshop and saves it onto the production label; no eval runs, the added examples double the token count, and the change is discovered a week later in the cost report rather than in CI.

The application calls get_prompt once at module import in a long-lived worker, so the fetched version is pinned for the process lifetime and every rollout and rollback silently does nothing until the next restart.

Rollback moves the label and everyone declares the incident over, but stale-while-revalidate plus a 60-second TTL plus warm pods that prefetched at startup means part of the fleet serves the bad version for another cache cycle, and the graph keeps showing failures nobody can explain.

The gate compares each PR against main HEAD instead of the version currently labelled production, so three individually-passing changes drift the score down eight points with no red build anywhere in the history.
A prompt change and a dataset edit land in the same afternoon, the delta is uninterpretable because two things moved, and the team burns a day arguing about a number that no longer means anything.

The eval step silently no-ops on external contributor PRs because forks get no secrets, someone switches the trigger to pull_request_target to fix it, and now arbitrary PR code executes with the customer's registry and model API keys in scope.

Serving code resolves prompts:/finding-summary@latest and the registry sits on the request path with no compiled-in fallback, so an engineer's laptop can ship an unreviewed draft into the customer's tenant and a two-minute SaaS blip becomes a full outage of the customer-facing feature.
interviewQuestions: Your customer wants their compliance analyst to be able to change the wording of a generated summary without waiting for an engineering deploy. Design the whole path: where the text lives, who can promote it, what runs before it reaches production, and what happens when it turns out to be wrong at 4pm on a Friday.

You move the production label back to the previous prompt version and tell the customer the rollback is done. Their dashboard still shows failures for another eight minutes. Explain every mechanism that could cause that, and how you would have known the number in advance.
Walk me through the fingerprint you record for a single eval run, field by field, and for each field tell me the specific bug that field exists to catch.

A team hands you a repo where prompts live in Git and are also editable in a registry UI, and both are 'the source of truth'. Describe the failure this guarantees, and what you would change in what order - given you cannot take the UI away from the customer.

Design the CI gate for prompt changes on a customer-facing extraction pipeline: what triggers it, what it compares against, where the thresholds come from, how much it costs per week, and what specifically stops the team from marking it non-required after the third false failure.

Six months into a deployment the customer asks you to reproduce the accuracy number from your Q2 report. Tell me exactly what you need to have stored to do that, what commonly makes it impossible, and what you would say if you could not reproduce it.

You inherit a system where prompt changes are deployed via a UI, evals exist but run manually and nobody remembers the last result, and the model id in config is a floating alias. Rank the fixes and justify the ordering to a customer who is asking why you are not shipping features this sprint.
63.proofOfWork: A public repository, `prompt-registry-ci`, that demonstrates the full loop against a self-hosted registry brought up by `docker compose up` so a reviewer needs no vendor account and no API key - the model calls run against a recorded-fixture provider by default. It contains a `prompts/` package whose only public surface is `get(name, env)` returning a compiled prompt plus its resolved version, model snapshot and decoding config, with a compiled-in fallback template and a unit test that asserts the process still serves a prompt when the registry is unreachable and that no call site anywhere resolves `@latest`. The CI workflow runs the eval gate on `pull_request` with path filters, third-party actions pinned to release SHAs, `concurrency: cancel-in-progress`, a hard USD ceiling in the harness, and a `repository_dispatch` twin triggered by a signature-verifying webhook receiver (`receiver/`, with tests for HMAC verification, replay dedupe and rate limiting) so a version created in the registry UI is scored without a PR. The repository history is the evidence: one merged PR where the gate passed with the paired delta and interval in the comment, one PR where it failed on a per-class floor with the flipped case ids named and the baseline run id shown, and one commit reverting a promoted version. `RUNBOOK.md` documents the rollback with the real measured convergence time from a rehearsal (stopwatch value, the verification query counting generations by prompt version, and the graph before and after), and `scripts/changelog.py` renders `CHANGELOG.md` - date, version, intent, promoter, eval delta with interval, rollbacks - purely from the append-only run ledger in `runs/`, with a CI check that fails if the committed changelog differs from the regenerated one, so the customer-facing document cannot drift from the runs that produced it.

64.topic: Cost and latency engineering: prompt caching, batching, smaller models
64.why: The moment an AI deployment leaves pilot, the customer's finance team gets an invoice and their users get a spinner, and both land on the FDE. Nobody renews a system that costs $4 per ticket and takes eleven seconds to first token, and 'use a cheaper model' is not an answer you can give without evidence that quality held. This topic is the difference between an FDE who says 'we could try Haiku' and one who walks into the QBR with a table showing 62% lower cost per resolved ticket, p95 first-token down from 4.1s to 900ms, and an eval delta of -0.6 points inside the noise band.
prerequisites: LLM fundamentals (topic 45): tokenisation, context windows, and the fact that output tokens are priced roughly 5x input tokens - the whole cost model collapses if you reason in 'characters' or 'requests'.

Evals as infrastructure (topic 53): a versioned eval set with per-category breakdowns and a CI gate, because every cost reduction in this topic is only shippable if you can prove the quality delta is inside the noise band.

LLM observability (topic 54): per-request spans carrying model id, token counts and latency, so you have the before half of the before/after table without retrofitting instrumentation under time pressure.
Model gateway, routing, fallbacks, canaries (topic 55): the LiteLLM proxy in front of the Kaupex stack is where routing rules and per-tenant budgets actually get enforced, not in application code.

Production Python (topics 25 and 26): asyncio fan-out with bounded concurrency, connection reuse, exponential backoff with jitter, and resumable jobs - batch backfills are a job-scheduling problem before they are an LLM problem.
Basic statistics literacy: paired comparison on the same items, and enough sense of confidence intervals to know that a 1-point move on 80 eval questions is noise while a 9-point move is a result.

subtopics.name: Instrument the ledger before you change one line of prompt
subtopics.learn: Write every request to a `llm_calls` table with request_id, tenant_id, feature, model, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, ttft_ms, total_ms, stop_reason, and a prompt_version hash. Derive cost in a single pure function `cost(model, usage) -> Decimal` fed by a checked-in price table, never by hard-coded constants sprinkled through the code. Reconcile that derived number weekly against the Usage and Cost Admin API (`/v1/organizations/usage_report/messages` and `/v1/organizations/cost_report`, Admin key required, workspace-scoped keys will not work); if your ledger and the invoice disagree by more than a couple of percent you are missing a call path. Optimising without this table means you will 'save 40%' and be unable to prove it.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Usage and Cost Admin API

subtopics.name: Token accounting and pre-flight estimation
subtopics.learn: Use `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with the exact same `model`, `system`, `tools` and `messages` you intend to send, so a large retrieval payload is priced before it is spent and can be rejected at the door rather than blowing a per-request budget. Internalise the asymmetry: output tokens cost about 5x input tokens on every current Claude model, so a 400-token answer can outweigh a 6,000-token context, and 'trim the system prompt' is usually the wrong first move. Know that `usage.input_tokens` in a cached response excludes cached tokens - total input is `cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens` - and that summing only `input_tokens` will silently under-report your spend by an order of magnitude once caching is on.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Token counting

subtopics.name: Decompose latency: TTFT, TPOT, and everything that is not the model
subtopics.learn: Split end-to-end latency into queue/network time, time to first token (dominated by prefill over the whole prompt), inter-token latency multiplied by output length (decode), and your own post-processing. Learn to read the shape: a TTFT that scales with prompt size is a prefill problem (cache it, shrink it), a total time that scales with answer length is a decode problem (cap `max_tokens`, lower effort, shorten the output contract), and flat overhead is your infrastructure (TLS handshakes per call, cold Lambda, a synchronous retrieval hop). Measure at the client with a monotonic clock around the streaming iterator, recording the timestamp of the first `content_block_delta`, not the completed response.

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking - Primer on Latency and Bandwidth

subtopics.name: Percentiles that survive review
subtopics.learn: Report p50/p95/p99 from histogram buckets, never from averaging pre-aggregated percentiles across pods - averaging quantiles is arithmetically meaningless and is the fastest way to lose credibility with a customer's SRE. Choose bucket boundaries that actually straddle your SLO (for TTFT: 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s) because a p95 computed from three coarse buckets is a linear interpolation, not a measurement. Slice by feature and by tenant before you slice by nothing: a single p95 across a fast classifier and a slow summariser hides both. Always publish n alongside the percentile - a p99 over 200 requests is two data points.

resource.label: Prometheus Docs - Histograms and summaries

subtopics.name: Prompt caching mechanics: cache_control, minimums, TTL, usage fields
subtopics.learn: Mark a content block with `"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}` to cache the entire prefix up to and including that block; the default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed for free on every hit, and measured from the start of the request that writes or reads it - a 4-minute streamed response burns 4 of those 5 minutes. Know that the minimum cacheable prefix is model-dependent (512 tokens on Opus 5, 1,024 on Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8, 4,096 on Haiku 4.5) and that a shorter prefix silently does nothing: no error, no cache. Verify every time by asserting on `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` and `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` - if both are 0 the block was never cached, which is the single most common reason a 'caching rollout' produces zero savings.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Prompt layout for hit rate, and the invalidation table
subtopics.learn: The cache key is the literal prefix in the order `tools` -> `system` -> `messages`, matched byte-for-byte, so anything that varies per request (a timestamp, the user's name, a request id, a shuffled retrieval list) must live after your last breakpoint or your hit rate is zero. Memorise the invalidation rules that bite: editing any tool definition (name, description, or schema) invalidates the whole cache; toggling web search or citations invalidates system and messages; changing `tool_choice` or adding/removing an image anywhere invalidates messages; changing thinking config or `output_config.effort` invalidates message blocks. You get at most 4 explicit breakpoints (top-level automatic caching consumes one of the 4, and a 5th returns a 400) - spend them on boundaries between content of genuinely different change frequency: tools, static instructions, retrieved corpus, conversation tail.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Tool use with prompt caching

subtopics.name: Multi-turn incremental caching, 1-hour TTL, and pre-warming
subtopics.learn: For growing conversations, put `cache_control` at the top level of the request body (automatic caching) so the breakpoint tracks the last cacheable block as turns accumulate, or place explicit breakpoints yourself when different sections change at different rates. Reach for `{"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}` when the gap between turns exceeds five minutes - it doubles the write price (2x base input versus 1.25x) so it only pays off when the prefix is large and reuse is certain; when mixing TTLs, the 1-hour entries must appear before any 5-minute entries in the prompt. Pre-warm before a burst with a `max_tokens: 0` request whose breakpoint sits on the last block shared with real traffic (not on the placeholder user message) and with identical thinking and effort settings, otherwise you pay for a cache entry your production traffic never hits.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Prompt caching (automatic caching, TTL, pre-warming)

subtopics.name: Cache break-even arithmetic, and when caching loses money
subtopics.learn: Write the formula down and keep it in the repo: with a prefix of N tokens, a write costs 1.25N (or 2N at 1h) and each hit costs 0.1N against a baseline of N per request, so k requests within the TTL cost `1.25N + 0.1N(k-1)` cached versus `kN` uncached - break-even is just above k = 1.2 for the 5-minute cache and roughly k = 2.2 for the 1-hour cache. Then apply the real-world discount: your actual saving is `hit_rate` times the theoretical maximum, and hit rate is what your prompt layout and traffic shape determine. Compute the two numbers that decide whether to bother: cached prefix as a fraction of total input tokens, and input cost as a fraction of total cost - if 80% of your spend is output tokens, a perfect cache changes almost nothing and you are optimising the wrong half of the bill.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Pricing

subtopics.name: The Message Batches API and what it actually guarantees
subtopics.learn: `POST /v1/messages/batches` takes up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, at 50% of standard prices, with most batches finishing inside an hour but a hard 24-hour expiry - results become available when all requests complete or at 24 hours, whichever is first. Poll `processing_status` until it flips from `in_progress` to `ended`, then stream the `.jsonl` from `results_url` rather than downloading it whole. Each result carries a per-request type of `succeeded`, `errored`, `canceled` or `expired`, and you are not billed for canceled or expired requests - which also means a job that quietly expires produces a silent gap in your output, not an error. Note that `max_tokens: 0` is rejected inside a batch, so cache pre-warming is not a batch trick.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Batch processing

subtopics.name: Designing batch jobs that are resumable and reconcilable
subtopics.learn: Make `custom_id` a deterministic function of your domain key (it must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`), for example `sha1(tenant:doc_id:prompt_version)[:32]`, so the same input never gets processed twice and results join back to your rows without an ordering assumption - batch results are not returned in submission order. Persist the batch id, the submitted key set, and a per-key status the moment you submit, then reconcile submitted-versus-returned after `ended` and requeue `expired` and retryable `errored` entries in the next batch. Triage workloads honestly: evals, backfills, bulk classification, document enrichment and nightly summarisation are batchable; anything a human is waiting on is not, and 'we'll batch the chat endpoint' is how you turn a latency complaint into an outage.

resource.label: Claude API Reference - Create a Message Batch

subtopics.name: Model tiering and cascade routing
subtopics.learn: Stop treating the model as a global constant. Classify each call site by what it actually demands - extraction, classification and routing usually hold on the small model; multi-step reasoning, ambiguous synthesis and code generation usually do not - and set the model per call site behind the gateway, not in scattered application code. Implement a cascade where the small model runs first and escalation is triggered by a machine-checkable signal (schema validation failure, a refusal, a self-reported confidence field, a retrieval-support check), then compute the blended cost: `p_escalate` above roughly 0.35 usually makes the cascade more expensive and slower than just calling the big model once. Measure escalation rate per category, because a cascade with a 70% escalation rate on legal questions is a cascade you should turn off for legal questions only.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Models overview

subtopics.name: Output-token discipline: max_tokens, effort, stop conditions
subtopics.learn: Since output is the expensive half, attack it directly: set `max_tokens` to a real ceiling rather than the model maximum, use `output_config.effort` (low/medium/high on supported models) to cut how many tokens Claude spends before answering, and use `stop_sequences` where the output has a hard terminator. Alarm on `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` - a truncated answer is a paid failure and, if you retry it, you paid twice for one wrong answer. Instruct for brevity in the contract, not in adjectives: 'answer in at most 3 bullets, no preamble, no restatement of the question' reliably outperforms 'be concise'. Critically, changing effort or thinking config invalidates cached message blocks, so an effort experiment and a caching rollout must not ship in the same change or you will not know which one moved the number.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Effort

subtopics.name: Structured output as a cost lever
subtopics.learn: Prose answers pay for connective tissue you then throw away with a regex. Constrain the response to a schema - structured outputs or a tool schema with `tool_choice` forcing a single tool - so the model emits only the fields you consume, which typically removes 30-60% of output tokens on extraction and classification work while simultaneously removing your parsing failure mode. Design the schema for cheapness as well as correctness: enums instead of free text, short field names, no 'explanation' field unless a human actually reads it, and no repetition of input back into the output. Remember the caching interaction from the invalidation table: tool definitions sit at the very front of the cache prefix, so a one-word tweak to a tool description invalidates every cache entry you have.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Structured outputs

subtopics.name: Streaming: fixing perceived latency without fixing latency
subtopics.learn: Set `"stream": true` and consume the SSE event sequence (`message_start`, `content_block_start`, `content_block_delta`, `content_block_stop`, `message_delta`, `message_stop`); read final token counts from the `message_delta` event's `usage`, and note that `message_start` already carries input and cache token counts so you can log cost before generation finishes. Streaming does not reduce total time or cost by a single token - it converts an 8-second blank screen into 700ms to first word, which is the metric users actually complain about. Know where it breaks: buffering proxies and some CDN configurations coalesce the stream and hand you the whole body at the end, so verify TTFT through the real ingress and not against localhost, and know that long non-streaming requests are also the ones most likely to hit gateway idle timeouts.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Streaming Messages

subtopics.name: Context compaction: stop paying to resend history
subtopics.learn: Long agent loops re-send every prior tool result on every turn, so cost grows quadratically in turn count even before quality degrades. Apply, in order: clear or truncate stale tool results (context editing), summarise older turns into a compact state block, cap retrieved chunks by a token budget rather than a fixed k, and drop raw payloads that the model has already extracted from. Every one of these edits rewrites the prompt prefix and therefore invalidates the message cache from the edit point forward - so compact at deliberate checkpoints (say, every N turns) rather than continuously, and measure the combined effect, because naive per-turn pruning can cost more in cache misses than it saves in tokens.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Context editing

subtopics.name: Concurrency, rate limits, and the throughput ceiling
subtopics.learn: Limits are enforced per model class as RPM, ITPM and OTPM using a continuously-replenishing token bucket, so a burst of 200 parallel calls fails differently than the same volume spread over a minute. On a 429, honour the `retry-after` header and back off with jitter; steer proactively off `anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining` and `anthropic-ratelimit-output-tokens-remaining` rather than waiting to be rejected. Two traps worth memorising: the spend-cap 429 carries no `retry-after` and will never succeed on retry until the next billing period, so your SDK's automatic retries will burn your entire timeout budget on a certainty; and a cache entry only becomes available once the first response has begun, so fanning out 50 identical-prefix requests at t=0 pays 50 cache writes instead of 1 write plus 49 reads.

resource.label: Claude API Reference - Rate limits

subtopics.name: The non-regression gate for a model downgrade
subtopics.learn: A downgrade is only shippable with a paired comparison: same eval items, same prompts, same temperature, incumbent versus candidate, reported per category rather than as one mean. Define the acceptance band before you run it (for example: overall within 2 points, no single category down more than 5 points, zero regressions on the safety and refusal subsets) so you cannot rationalise afterwards. Expect prompts to be model-specific - a prompt tuned on the large model often needs more explicit structure and few-shot examples on the small one, and 'Haiku failed' frequently means 'we did not re-tune the prompt'. Wire the comparison into CI as a job that fails the PR and attaches the before/after table, so the cost saving cannot silently decay when someone edits the prompt three weeks later.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Using the Evaluation Tool

subtopics.name: Unit economics and the customer-facing number
subtopics.learn: Customers do not budget in tokens; they budget in units of work. Define the denominator with them - cost per resolved ticket, per compiled task, per document processed, per seat per month - and report cost per unit plus p95 latency as the two headline numbers, with token counts as supporting detail. Set the same shape as an SLO with an error budget (for example: p95 TTFT under 1.5s, cost per compiled task under $0.08) so a regression is an alert rather than a surprise on the invoice, and enforce per-tenant budget caps at the gateway with a graceful degrade path (downgrade the model, disable enrichment) instead of a hard failure. Always attach the quality delta to the cost delta in the same table: a saving reported without an eval number reads as a risk, not a win.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Implementing SLOs

outcomes: You can produce a per-feature cost breakdown for a running system from your own `llm_calls` ledger and reconcile it to within 2% of the Usage and Cost Admin API figures for the same period.

You can raise the prompt cache hit rate on a real workload above 80% and prove it from `cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens)`, not from an assumption that caching is on.

You can state the caching break-even from memory (1.25x write, 0.1x read, so roughly 1.2 reuses within the 5-minute TTL; 2x write, so roughly 2.2 reuses at 1h) and decide whether a given call site should be cached at all.

You can convert an offline workload to the Message Batches API with deterministic `custom_id`s, reconcile submitted against returned keys, requeue `expired` and `errored` entries, and show the 50% price reduction as a line in the ledger.
You can cut Kaupex model spend by at least 30% with the eval delta inside a pre-declared acceptance band, and name which change produced which fraction of the saving.
You can look at a latency histogram and say within five minutes whether the bottleneck is prefill, decode, or your own infrastructure, and name the specific lever for each.

You can debug a caching rollout that produced zero savings by checking, in order: prefix below the model minimum, per-request content ahead of the breakpoint, a tool-definition or effort change invalidating the prefix, and parallel cold-start fan-out.
You can present a one-page before/after table to a customer stakeholder with cost per unit of work, p50/p95 latency, eval score by category, and sample size, and defend every cell.
failureModes: A request id, a `datetime.now()` stamp, or the user's name is interpolated into the system prompt ahead of the cache breakpoint, so every request writes a fresh cache entry and the 'caching optimisation' raises the bill by 25%.

The cached prefix is 700 tokens against a model with a 1,024-token minimum, so caching silently no-ops with no error returned, and nobody notices for a month because the code never asserts on `cache_read_input_tokens`.

Someone fixes a typo in a tool description, which invalidates the entire cache prefix for every tenant at once, and the resulting stampede of cache writes shows up as a cost spike that gets blamed on traffic growth.

A latency experiment toggles `output_config.effort` or thinking config per request, which invalidates message-block caches, so the effort A/B test and the caching rollout silently cancel each other out and the team concludes caching does not work.

A nightly batch backfill hits the 24-hour expiry, the `expired` results are never reconciled against the submitted key set, and a few thousand documents are permanently missing from the index with no error anywhere in the logs.

The service hits its monthly spend cap and returns 429s with no `retry-after`; the SDK's automatic retries hammer a certainty, requests pile up behind the retry budget, and a billing limit presents as a full outage.

The team downgrades to a smaller model on the strength of a 60-question aggregate score, and the regression that only existed in the 8-question refusal subset ships to production as a compliance incident.
interviewQuestions: A customer's monthly bill for your assistant tripled with flat request volume. Walk me through your diagnosis in order, and tell me what data you need in place beforehand for that diagnosis to take minutes instead of a week.
Explain prompt caching to their platform architect: what is the cache key, what invalidates it, what does it cost to write versus read, and at what reuse count does it stop being worth doing?

Design the request path for a support assistant with a 40,000-token policy corpus, 2,000 tenants, and a p95 TTFT budget of 1.5 seconds. Where do your cache breakpoints go, what is cached per tenant versus shared, and what happens at 09:00 when every tenant arrives cold at once?

You want to move from the large model to the small one to save 60%. What exactly do you run before you propose it, what is your acceptance band, and what do you tell the customer if the small model is 3 points worse overall but 9 points worse on multi-hop questions?
When is a cascade (small model first, escalate on failure) more expensive than just calling the large model, and how would you compute the escalation-rate threshold for a specific workload?
You enabled caching and the bill did not move. Give me the five things you check, in the order you check them, and the exact field you look at for each.
Which parts of this pipeline would you move to the Batch API, which would you refuse to move, and what breaks operationally when a batch expires at 24 hours instead of completing?
64.proofOfWork: Build `llm-cost-lab`: a small repository that runs one fixed workload from the Kaupex Task Compiler under six named configurations - baseline, caching only, caching plus structured output, small model only, cascade with escalation, and batch for the offline half - through a single `make bench CONFIG=<name>` entrypoint that writes every call to a SQLite ledger and emits a generated markdown report. The report must contain one row per configuration with columns for cost per unit of work, total input/cache-write/cache-read/output tokens, cache hit rate, p50 and p95 TTFT, p95 end-to-end latency, eval score overall and by category, escalation rate where applicable, and n - every cell traceable to a stored run_id. Include three things that prove you measured rather than assumed: a plot of cost per request against cache hit rate as the inter-request gap sweeps past the 5-minute TTL boundary; a break-even chart for 5-minute versus 1-hour TTL as a function of reuse count for your actual prefix size; and a deliberate negative result documented in the README, such as a configuration where caching or cascading cost more, with the arithmetic explaining why. Add a CI job that fails the build if cost per unit rises more than 10% or any eval category drops more than 5 points, plus a two-page COST-REVIEW.md written for a non-engineer stakeholder that leads with cost per resolved unit and the quality delta, not with tokens.

65.topic: Platform fluency for take-homes: Anthropic and OpenAI APIs side by side
65.why: FDE take-homes and customer POCs are timeboxed, and the person grading you is watching whether your budget went into the problem or into plumbing you should already know. Customers almost never let you pick the vendor either — they are already on Bedrock, or Azure, or have a procurement contract with one provider — so 'can you do this on our stack?' has to be answerable with a running demo rather than a maybe. Being able to write the tool loop, the strict output schema, the streaming consumer and the batch job on either API from memory turns a two-day integration into an afternoon, and turns a vendor-migration question into a one-page diff instead of a project.
prerequisites: Topic 47 (tool use, structured outputs and MCP servers): the concepts of a tool schema, a tool-execution loop and a JSON output contract. This topic is those same ideas executed twice, fast, from memory, under a stopwatch.

Topic 46 (prompt engineering as code): a versioned prompt file, a golden set of inputs, and a one-command regression run — you need these to prove the two implementations actually produce equivalent output rather than merely both returning 200.

Fluent Python (and enough TypeScript to read SDK examples): `httpx`/`requests`, SSE parsing, `asyncio.gather`, Pydantic v2 models, `os.environ` secret handling, and comfort reading a raw `curl -i` response including headers.

JSON Schema literacy: `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`, `$ref`/`$defs`, and specifically the difference between a property that is not in `required` and one whose type is a union with `null`.

Topic 43 (LLM-era system design): retries with exponential backoff and jitter, timeouts, idempotency and latency budgets — without these your client is tutorial-shaped, not production-shaped, and graders notice.
Two funded API keys (Anthropic and OpenAI, roughly $20 each) and a stopwatch. This topic is a drill; without live keys against current models you are reading documentation, not building fluency.

subtopics.name: Auth, base URLs, and a scaffold you can type from memory
subtopics.learn: Both platforms are POST-JSON over HTTPS and the auth differs in exactly one header. Anthropic: `POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` with `x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` (required — omitting it is a 400), and `content-type: application/json`. OpenAI: `POST https://api.openai.com/v1/responses` with `Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY`, plus optional `OpenAI-Organization` and `OpenAI-Project` headers. Both SDK clients read the key from the environment with zero arguments (`anthropic.Anthropic()`, `OpenAI()`). Build yourself a scaffold — pinned SDK versions, `.env.example`, a `smoke.py` that makes one call on each provider, and the equivalent `curl` in the README — and time it: keys to first 200 should be under ten minutes on both.

resource.label: Claude Docs — API getting started

subtopics.name: Request and response shapes, memorised in parallel
subtopics.learn: Anthropic minimal body: `{model, max_tokens (REQUIRED — omitting it 400s), messages: [{role, content}], system (top-level, there is no "system" role)}`, returning `{id, type: "message", role: "assistant", content: [blocks], stop_reason, usage: {input_tokens, output_tokens}}`. OpenAI Responses minimal body: `{model, input (string or item array), instructions, max_output_tokens (optional)}`, returning `{id: "resp_...", status, output: [items], usage: {input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens}}` with `output_text` as an SDK-only convenience. Anthropic `content` is always a list, so `response.content[0].text` breaks the moment a `thinking` or `tool_use` block precedes the text. Know the `stop_reason` enum — `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `tool_use`, `pause_turn`, `refusal`, `model_context_window_exceeded` — and its OpenAI counterpart `status: "incomplete"` plus `incomplete_details.reason`. Know too that `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` are deprecated on Claude models released after Opus 4.6 (non-default values are rejected with a 400) and that OpenAI reasoning models reject `temperature` as well.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Messages API reference (body parameters and returns)

subtopics.name: System prompt placement and who owns conversation state
subtopics.learn: Anthropic has no system role: the system prompt is the top-level `system` parameter, either a string or an array of `TextBlockParam` (the array form exists so you can attach `cache_control` to it). OpenAI Responses uses top-level `instructions`, or a `developer`/`system` role item inside `input` — and `instructions` is not carried forward when you chain with `previous_response_id`, which surprises people mid-conversation. The larger difference is statefulness: Anthropic is always stateless, so you resend the full `messages` array every turn and you own truncation; OpenAI Responses can be stateful via `store: true` plus `previous_response_id`. Decide deliberately and be able to defend it: stateful means fewer tokens on the wire and less code, stateless is what most enterprise customers with data-retention rules will actually approve. Practise forcing stateless on OpenAI with `store: false` and resending the item list yourself.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Conversation state guide

subtopics.name: Content blocks and multimodal input on both
subtopics.learn: Anthropic message `content` is a string or a list of typed blocks: `{"type":"text"}`, `{"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/png","data":...}}` or a `{"type":"url"}` source, `{"type":"document"}` for PDFs, plus `tool_use`, `tool_result` and `thinking`. OpenAI Responses uses input parts `{"type":"input_text"}`, `{"type":"input_image","image_url": <data URI or https URL>}` and `{"type":"input_file"}`, with model text returning as `output_text` parts carrying `annotations`. Drill both directions: base64 a PNG and a five-page PDF and get the same structured extraction out of each API. Respect the ceilings — an Anthropic Messages request caps at 32 MB and returns 413 `request_too_large` above it, so anything larger goes through the Files API rather than inline base64.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Vision (image and document inputs)

subtopics.name: Tool schemas: three envelopes around one JSON Schema
subtopics.learn: The parameter schema is identical JSON Schema on both platforms; only the wrapper differs, and this is the single most-fumbled thing under time pressure. Anthropic: `tools: [{name, description, input_schema: {type: "object", properties, required}}]` — note `input_schema`, not `parameters`. OpenAI Responses: `tools: [{type: "function", name, description, parameters, strict}]`, flat. OpenAI Chat Completions: `tools: [{type: "function", function: {name, description, parameters, strict}}]`, nested one level deeper. Build a `toolspec.py` that holds the raw JSON Schema once plus two adapter functions emitting the two envelopes, and unit-test the adapters. That file is the reusable asset a take-home actually rewards, and it is what you paste into a customer repo on day one.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Function calling guide

subtopics.name: The agent loop: tool_result vs function_call_output
subtopics.learn: Write both loops from memory. Anthropic: the response arrives with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_...","name","input"}` blocks where `input` is already a parsed object; you append the assistant message verbatim with all blocks in original order, then append a **user** message whose content is `[{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"toolu_...","content": <string or blocks>, "is_error": bool}]`, and every `tool_use` in a turn must get a matching `tool_result` in the immediately following message or the API 400s. OpenAI Responses: the model emits a `function_call` item with `call_id` and `arguments` as a **JSON string** you must `json.loads` (and defend against malformed JSON unless `strict: true`); you append that item plus `{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":...,"output":"<string>"}`. Chat Completions instead uses `tool_calls` on the assistant message answered by a `{"role":"tool","tool_call_id":...}` message. Always add a hard `max_iterations` guard.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Implementing tool use (the tool-result round trip)

subtopics.name: tool_choice, forcing, and parallel tool calls
subtopics.learn: Anthropic `tool_choice` takes `{"type":"auto"}`, `{"type":"any"}` (must call some tool), `{"type":"tool","name":"x"}` (must call that one) and `{"type":"none"}`, with `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` capping a turn at one call. OpenAI takes `tool_choice: "auto" | "none" | "required" | {"type":"function","name":"x"}` plus `parallel_tool_calls: false`. Understand what forcing costs before you reach for it: forced tool use is incompatible with some thinking configurations on Claude and returns a 'Forced tool use not supported' 400, and on both platforms forcing removes the model's ability to say 'I don't have enough information to call this' — exactly the behaviour a customer-facing agent needs. Handle the multi-call case properly: one assistant turn can contain N tool calls, you execute all N (concurrently is fine), and you return all N results together in the next turn.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Tool use overview (tool_choice and parallel use)

subtopics.name: Structured output on OpenAI: text.format and the strict subset
subtopics.learn: Responses API: `text: {format: {type: "json_schema", name: "...", schema: {...}, strict: true}}`. Chat Completions: `response_format: {type: "json_schema", json_schema: {name, schema, strict: true}}`. Under `strict: true` every object needs `"additionalProperties": false` and every declared property must appear in `required`; optionality is expressed as a union with null (`"type": ["string", "null"]`), and getting this wrong is the most common 400 in this whole topic. Prefer the SDK helpers over hand-rolled schemas: `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=MyPydanticModel)` then read `.output_parsed`, or `zodTextFormat()` in TypeScript. Handle the two escape hatches that both return HTTP 200 and neither matches your schema: a `refusal`, and `status: "incomplete"` with `incomplete_details.reason == "max_output_tokens"`.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Structured Outputs guide

subtopics.name: Structured output on Anthropic: output_config.format and strict tools
subtopics.learn: Anthropic gives two independent levers you can use together. JSON outputs: top-level `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema: {...}}}` constrains the assistant's text block to schema-valid JSON. Strict tool use: `strict: true` on an individual tool grammar-constrains that tool's name and inputs. Note the migration trap — the older beta field was `output_format` with header `structured-outputs-2025-11-13`, still accepted for a transition period, so old sample code compiles and modern SDKs may raise a `TypeError` on it. Use `client.messages.parse()` with a Pydantic model for the ergonomic path. Keep the portable fallback in muscle memory too: define one tool and force it with `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"emit"}`, then read `block.input` — it works on every model, every gateway, and older Bedrock deployments where constrained decoding is unavailable.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Structured outputs

subtopics.name: The schema subset both engines refuse, and grammar limits
subtopics.learn: Constrained decoding compiles your schema into a grammar, so both platforms support only a subset, and the subsets differ. On Anthropic, supported: `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`, `$ref`/`$defs`, `default`, string formats (`date-time`, `date`, `email`, `uri`, `uuid`, `ipv4`), and array `minItems` of 0 or 1 only. Not supported: recursive schemas, external `$ref`, numeric constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`), `minLength`/`maxLength`, and regex lookahead/lookbehind or backreferences — each returns a 400. Hard limits per request: 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters across all strict schemas, 16 union-typed parameters, plus an internal compiled-grammar ceiling that surfaces as 'Schema is too complex for compilation' and a 180-second compile timeout. Compiled grammars cache for 24 hours from last use, so never benchmark latency on a cold schema. Finally: enum capitalisation is not guaranteed, so compare enum values case-insensitively.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Strict tool use

subtopics.name: Streaming Anthropic: the content-block state machine
subtopics.learn: With `stream: true` you get SSE with typed events: `message_start` (carries `usage.input_tokens`), then per block `content_block_start` → repeated `content_block_delta` → `content_block_stop`, then `message_delta` (carries the final `stop_reason` and cumulative `usage.output_tokens`), then `message_stop`, with `ping` and `error` interleaved. Learn the delta types: `text_delta`; `input_json_delta`, whose `partial_json` fragments you must concatenate before parsing (tool arguments stream as a fragmented JSON string even though the non-streaming field is an object); `thinking_delta`; and `signature_delta`. Use `with client.messages.stream(...) as stream:` and `stream.get_final_message()` (TypeScript `stream.finalMessage()`) rather than reassembling blocks by hand. Know the operational reason this matters: long non-streaming requests hit a server-side time limit, so high-`max_tokens` calls must stream.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Streaming Messages (event types and deltas)

subtopics.name: Streaming OpenAI: semantic events vs raw token deltas
subtopics.learn: The Responses API streams semantic events with a `type` and a monotonic `sequence_number`: `response.created`, `response.output_item.added`, `response.content_part.added`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, `response.output_text.done`, then `response.completed` / `response.failed` / `response.incomplete`. Chat Completions instead streams raw `choices[0].delta` chunks terminated by `data: [DONE]`, and returns no usage numbers at all unless you pass `stream_options: {include_usage: true}` — forgetting that flag is why a cost dashboard goes blank the day someone enables streaming. Write one normaliser that reduces both providers' streams to the same `(event, text_chunk, tool_arg_fragment, usage)` tuple, and instrument it to report time-to-first-text-token separately from total wall-clock, because those two numbers move independently and customers feel the first one.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Streaming responses guide

subtopics.name: Anthropic thinking blocks inside a tool loop
subtopics.learn: Configure with `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` where N >= 1024 and N < `max_tokens`, or `{type: "adaptive"}`. Responses then carry `thinking` blocks before text, each with an encrypted `signature`. The rule that breaks people: in multi-turn and tool-use conversations you must pass thinking blocks back unchanged and in original order — you cannot edit, reorder or partially drop them (including `redacted_thinking` blocks) or you get a 400 saying the thinking block no longer matches the conversation, which typically fires on turn three of a live demo. Use `display: "omitted"` when you are not showing reasoning to users: the thinking text is empty but the signature is preserved for continuity, and time-to-first-text improves because the server skips streaming thinking tokens. Remember thinking tokens count against `max_tokens`, so a 10k budget under an 8k cap is a 400.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Thinking (signatures, preservation, tool use)

subtopics.name: OpenAI reasoning items, effort, and reasoning tokens
subtopics.learn: Set `reasoning: {effort: "low"|"medium"|"high", summary: "auto"}` on reasoning models. You pay for hidden reasoning tokens, reported at `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`; they bill as output and they consume `max_output_tokens`, so a tight cap plus high effort yields `status: "incomplete"`, an empty message, and a full invoice. In a tool loop you must preserve reasoning context across turns: either chain with `previous_response_id`, or when running stateless (`store: false`) pass the reasoning items back in `input` and request `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`. Build the same two-tool agent with reasoning enabled on both platforms and record tokens, latency and answer quality per effort level — that comparison table is precisely the kind of evidence a take-home write-up should lead with.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform — Reasoning models guide

subtopics.name: Prompt caching: explicit breakpoints vs automatic prefix caching
subtopics.learn: Anthropic is explicit: put `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on a content block, or once at the top level of the request to let the breakpoint auto-advance as the conversation grows. The cached prefix spans `tools`, then `system`, then `messages`, in that order, up to and including the marked block; default TTL is 5 minutes, refreshed free on every hit, with a 1-hour option. Writes cost 1.25x base input and reads 0.1x, and you verify a hit by comparing `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` against `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` — if reads stay zero your prefix is not byte-identical, and a timestamp in the system prompt, a reordered tool list, or a changed `output_config.format` will each do that silently. OpenAI caches automatically above roughly 1024 tokens with no breakpoints; you steer routing with `prompt_cache_key` and verify with `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. Same discipline on both: static content first, volatile content last.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Prompt caching

subtopics.name: Batch: inline requests array vs JSONL file upload
subtopics.learn: Both are 50% cheaper with a 24-hour window; the mechanics are entirely different. Anthropic: `POST /v1/messages/batches` with `requests: [{custom_id, params: {<full Messages body>}}]` sent inline, up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, where `custom_id` must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`; poll `processing_status` until it reads `"ended"` (not `"completed"`), read `request_counts.{processing,succeeded,errored,canceled,expired}`, then stream the `.jsonl` at `results_url` — results are unordered, so you join on `custom_id`. `max_tokens: 0` cache pre-warming is rejected inside a batch. OpenAI: first upload a JSONL of `{custom_id, method: "POST", url: "/v1/responses", body: {...}}` with `purpose: "batch"`, then `POST /v1/batches` with `input_file_id`, `endpoint` and `completion_window: "24h"`; poll `status` through `validating → in_progress → finalizing → completed`, then download `output_file_id` and, separately, `error_file_id`. Write one bulk-classification job both ways and record wall-clock and cost.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Batch processing (Message Batches API)

subtopics.name: Errors, retries, timeouts, rate-limit headers, request IDs
subtopics.learn: Memorise the Anthropic taxonomy: 400 `invalid_request_error`, 401 `authentication_error`, 403 `permission_error`, 404 `not_found_error`, 413 `request_too_large` (32 MB on Messages), 429 `rate_limit_error`, 500 `api_error`, 529 `overloaded_error`. Retry 429/500/529 with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `retry-after`, and never retry a 400. Read your remaining budget from `anthropic-ratelimit-{requests,input-tokens,output-tokens}-{limit,remaining,reset}` — `reset` is an RFC 3339 timestamp, not a seconds count — and from OpenAI's `x-ratelimit-remaining-{requests,tokens}` and `x-ratelimit-reset-*`. Both SDKs retry by default: set `max_retries` and a per-request `timeout` explicitly instead of inheriting defaults, and think hard about retrying a stream, since a mid-stream failure has already emitted partial output to the user. Log the `request-id` header (Anthropic) and `x-request-id` (OpenAI) on every call — without it you cannot file a useful support ticket, and filing one is a real FDE deliverable.

resource.label: Claude Docs — Rate limits (response headers and 429 handling)

subtopics.name: The portability layer and the 90-minute timed port
subtopics.learn: Build the thinnest abstraction that survives contact: one `generate(messages, tools, schema) -> Result` interface, two adapters, and a golden-file test asserting both providers parse to the same object across 20 fixed inputs. Resist the urge to add a config DSL — abstract the request envelope and the tool-result plumbing, and deliberately leave caching, thinking and batch leaky per-provider. Know the shortcut and its price: Anthropic exposes an OpenAI-SDK-compatible endpoint (point the OpenAI client at `base_url="https://api.anthropic.com/v1/"` with an Anthropic key), which is fine for a same-day bake-off but drops thinking, prompt caching, PDF support and citations, so it never ships to a customer. Then drill: set a 90-minute timer and rebuild the same feature — tool loop, strict schema, streaming, and a cost/latency report — on the other API without looking at the first repo. Log every stall and turn each one into a snippet in your scaffold.

resource.label: Claude Docs — OpenAI SDK compatibility (and its documented limitations)

outcomes: You can open a blank file with no documentation and write a working multi-turn tool-calling loop on the Anthropic Messages API and on the OpenAI Responses API in under twenty minutes each, including correct `tool_result` and `function_call_output` plumbing and a `max_iterations` guard.

You can recite the field-level diffs on demand — `input_schema` vs `parameters`, top-level `system` vs `instructions`, `max_tokens` required vs `max_output_tokens` optional, parsed `input` object vs `arguments` JSON string — and correct a colleague's code by reading it, without running it.

You can enforce a JSON contract three ways (OpenAI `text.format` with `strict: true`, Anthropic `output_config.format`, and the forced-tool fallback) and justify which one you would deploy on a customer's Bedrock estate and why.

You can consume both streaming protocols, reassemble a complete tool call from `input_json_delta` and `response.function_call_arguments.delta` fragments, and report time-to-first-token separately from total latency on the same prompt.
You can push the same 5,000-item job through both Batch APIs, join unordered results on `custom_id`, account for expired and errored requests, and produce a cost and wall-clock comparison table.

You can demonstrate a prompt-cache hit on both platforms by pointing at `cache_read_input_tokens` and `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, and diagnose in one sentence why a previously-hitting cache stopped hitting.
You can classify any API failure as retryable or not within seconds, name the header that tells you how long to wait, and produce the provider request ID needed to open a support ticket.
You can complete a 90-minute timed port of a feature from one API to the other and hand a grader a README they can run end to end with two commands.
failureModes: Returning only some of a turn's `tool_result` blocks — or dropping the assistant's `tool_use` blocks while trimming history for context — producing an opaque 400 that only appears on the third turn of a live customer demo.

Treating OpenAI's `arguments` as a dict because the Anthropic equivalent is one: the code passes on happy-path fixtures and throws the first time a real customer prompt yields a nested object under load.

Carrying `temperature=0` across from an older repo onto a current Claude or an OpenAI reasoning model, which hard-400s in the customer's environment while continuing to work locally against a pinned older model.

Setting `max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` below the thinking or reasoning budget, so responses come back `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` or `status: "incomplete"` with empty content and a full bill, and the team spends a day blaming the prompt.
Enabling streaming on Chat Completions without `stream_options: {include_usage: true}`, silently zeroing the token counts that feed the customer's cost dashboard and internal chargeback report.
Putting a timestamp, session ID or reordered tool list at the front of the prompt, destroying every prompt-cache hit and roughly tripling input cost with no error surfacing anywhere.

Shipping the OpenAI-compatibility endpoint into a customer POC because it made the demo fast, then discovering during hardening that prompt caching, thinking and PDF support are unavailable on that path and the rewrite lands in the go-live week.
interviewQuestions: Whiteboard the tool-calling loop for the Anthropic Messages API and the OpenAI Responses API in parallel columns. Where does the tool result go in each, what is its identifier called, and what does the API do if you return two results for one call or none for one that was requested?

A customer must run on Bedrock and needs guaranteed schema-valid JSON on every request. Walk me through your options, what each costs in latency and flexibility, and what you do if their pinned model version does not support constrained decoding.

We swapped models and p95 latency doubled while input and output token counts stayed flat. Give me your debugging order across both APIs — what do you check first, and which specific usage field settles the argument?

Design a provider-agnostic LLM client for a team shipping to three customers on three different clouds. What do you abstract, what do you deliberately leave leaky, and how do you test that the abstraction has not started lying to you?

A bulk-extraction job over 200,000 documents must finish overnight at minimum cost. Compare the two Batch APIs concretely — submission, polling, result retrieval — and tell me exactly what you do about the requests that expire at the 24-hour boundary.

Explain prompt caching on both platforms to a customer's finance lead in plain language, then tell me three changes an engineer could ship tomorrow that would silently destroy the savings without raising a single error.
You have ninety minutes and a take-home that says 'build a research agent, any provider.' Which do you pick, what do you cut, what do you instrument, and what goes in the README?
65.proofOfWork: Beyond the two per-API repos, publish a third repo called `llm-api-parity` whose entire purpose is to prove the two are interchangeable and to document precisely where they are not. It contains one provider-neutral scenario file of roughly thirty cases — plain completion, single tool call, parallel tool calls, a tool that raises and must come back as `is_error` / an error string, strict-schema extraction, a deliberately unsupported schema feature, an oversized image, a forced stop at `max_tokens`, a cache-warm then cache-hit pair, and a ten-item batch — plus two thin adapters and a single `pytest` suite that runs every scenario against both providers and asserts the same parsed result object. `PARITY.md` is generated by the run, not hand-written: a table with one row per scenario and columns for both providers showing pass/fail, the exact request field names used, latency p50 and TTFT, input/output/cached/reasoning token counts, and cost, with a footnote for each behavioural divergence you found (for example which schema keywords 400 on which side, and what each returns when a tool result is missing). Add `CHEATSHEET.md`: a one-page side-by-side of endpoint, auth header, required fields, tool envelope, tool-result envelope, structured-output field, streaming event names, batch submission shape, and error taxonomy — short enough to read in ninety seconds before an interview. Add `PORT_LOG.md` recording the timed drill: start time, stop time, every point where you had to look something up, and the snippet you added to your scaffold so it never costs you a lookup again. Finally include `scripts/verify.sh` that runs the whole suite against live keys in under five minutes and prints a spend total, so anyone — a grader, a customer architect, a future you — can reproduce the parity claims rather than take your word for them.

66.why: An FDE is the person sitting in the room when the customer's security team returns a pentest report two weeks before go-live, and the deployment either survives that meeting or slips a quarter. You will be deploying your own code inside someone else's VPC, against their SSO, holding their regulated data, which means you personally own the authorization boundary, the secrets, and the answer to 'can tenant A see tenant B'. Reading the OWASP list is worthless here - you need to have actually exploited broken object-level authorization and a forged JWT with your own hands, because that is the only way you can look at a customer's API and see the bug before their auditor does.
prerequisites: Auth (topic 27): OAuth2 authorization-code flow, OIDC id_token vs access_token, JWT structure and claims (iss, aud, exp, sub), and how RBAC claims get into a request context - you cannot attack what you cannot draw.

Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems (topic 30): tenant_id propagation, Postgres row-level security, PII classification and audit trails, since most real findings in an FDE deployment are authorization findings, not memory-corruption findings.

FastAPI in production (topic 26) and PostgreSQL at depth (topic 29): dependency injection for auth, parameterised queries via bound parameters, and enough SQL to know why string interpolation into a WHERE clause is the whole bug.
Networking (topic 2): TLS handshake and certificate validation, HTTP request/response structure, headers, redirects, and proxies - you will spend ten hours reading raw HTTP in an intercepting proxy.
CI/CD and supply chain (topic 18): a pipeline you can add jobs to, plus SBOM/scanning concepts, because half of A06 is a CI problem rather than a code problem.

A local runnable copy of your own stack - Dokeo (Python/FastAPI/Postgres) and DefenderMate (TypeScript/Next.js) - with seeded data for at least two tenants and three roles, because the deliverable requires finding a real issue in your own code.

subtopics.name: Burp workbench: proxy, CA cert, scope, Repeater loop
subtopics.learn: Install Burp Suite Community, install its CA certificate into the browser trust store, and set target scope so Proxy history is not drowned in telemetry noise. Learn the loop you will run 200 times today: intercept a request, send it to Repeater with Ctrl+R, mutate one parameter, resend, diff status code / Content-Length / response time. Know Intruder's Sniper and Cluster bomb modes and that Community throttles Intruder hard, so scripted requests with Python plus `requests` are often faster for enumeration. Configure match-and-replace rules to swap the session cookie or Authorization header automatically - that is how you test cross-tenant access without re-logging in every request.

resource.label: PortSwigger: Burp Suite desktop documentation

subtopics.name: Map your own attack surface before touching a lab
