Change management: protected main branch, required reviews with CODEOWNERS, required status checks, linear history, and a documented emergency-change path that still creates a record after the fact - the failure is not lacking a process, it is having an undocumented break-glass. Access: joiner-mover-leaver driven by IdP groups rather than manual grants, MFA enforced, no long-lived cloud keys (IRSA / OIDC federation from CI), and a quarterly access review whose output is a dated artifact listing every human and machine principal with prod access and the reviewer's decision. Pull the IAM credential report and the repo's collaborator list today and see how many stale principals you find.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - configuring branches and merges (protection rules)

subtopics.name: Encryption and key management claims you can actually defend
subtopics.learn: 'Encrypted at rest' is the most over-claimed control in enterprise software. Know precisely what RDS/EBS/S3 default encryption buys (protection against physical media and snapshot exfiltration) and what it does not (anything about which application, engineer or query can read the plaintext). Learn the vocabulary you will be asked about: envelope encryption, CMK versus AWS-managed key, key policy versus IAM policy, kms:Decrypt against kms:GenerateDataKey, automatic key rotation, and BYOK/HYOK when a customer demands to hold the key. Understand crypto-shredding - a per-tenant data key whose deletion renders that tenant's data unrecoverable - because it is often the only workable answer to erasure inside immutable backups. For transit, be able to state the TLS version and where termination happens, including in-cluster hops.

resource.label: AWS KMS Developer Guide - concepts and key policies

subtopics.name: Audit trails, log retention and the telemetry leak
subtopics.learn: Three distinct audit layers get conflated: infrastructure (CloudTrail organisation trail with log file validation and digest files, plus the Kubernetes API audit policy), database (pgaudit or logical audit tables), and application (who did what to which tenant's record, immutable, append-only). Decide retention deliberately per layer - one year is the common SOC 2 expectation, HIPAA documentation retention is six years, GDPR storage limitation pushes the other way - and write the number down. Then do the thing that actually matters: grep your logging, tracing and LLM-observability payloads for regulated fields. Prompts, completions, span attributes and error payloads carrying names, emails, PHI or full request bodies into a third-party log SaaS is the single most common real-world violation.

resource.label: AWS CloudTrail User Guide (trails, validation, retention)

subtopics.name: GDPR core: controller vs processor, lawful basis, Art 28 and subprocessors
subtopics.learn: Get the role right first, because everything follows from it: your customer is normally the controller and you are the processor acting on documented instructions, but the moment you use their data to improve your own product you have become a controller and inherited a lawful-basis problem. Know Art 6(1)(a)-(f) well enough to recognise that B2B SaaS usually rests on contract or legitimate interests, and that Art 9 special-category data (health, biometrics) needs a separate condition. Read Art 28(3) and be able to list what the DPA must contain - documented instructions, confidentiality, Art 32 security, subprocessor terms, assistance with data-subject rights and breach notification, deletion or return at end of contract, audit rights. Then produce your subprocessor list: cloud region, model provider, log SaaS, email sender, CRM - and know the notice-and-objection mechanics for adding one.

resource.label: EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR

subtopics.name: RoPA, DSARs and erasure across a real stack
subtopics.learn: Write the Art 30 record of processing for DefenderMate - purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention, security measures - and use it as the inventory that drives everything else. Then design the Art 17 erasure path and confront every store: Postgres rows (and referencing tables, and soft-deleted rows), Redis idempotency keys, S3 exports (versioned buckets need version deletes plus noncurrent-version lifecycle), the search or vector index, Kafka topics (tombstones plus compaction, not deletes), the warehouse, application and third-party logs, the LLM provider's retention window, and downstream systems like HubSpot. Backups are the honest hard case: the accepted answer is a documented rolling retention window plus a rule that restored data is re-processed for deletion, or crypto-shredding - not a claim you surgically edited a snapshot. Also know Art 15 access, Art 20 portability and the one-month response clock.

resource.label: ICO guidance - Right to erasure, including how it applies to backups and third parties

subtopics.name: Art 32 security, the 72-hour breach clock, DPIAs and transfers
subtopics.learn: Art 32 names four things auditors quote back at you: pseudonymisation and encryption, ongoing confidentiality/integrity/availability/resilience, restoration after an incident, and regular testing of measures - so your DR test and your pentest are compliance evidence, not just engineering hygiene. Art 33 gives the controller 72 hours from becoming aware to notify the supervisory authority, which means your job as processor is to notify the customer 'without undue delay' and to be able to answer, fast: what categories of data, how many subjects, what window, what was accessed versus merely exposed. Rehearse that you cannot answer any of it without the audit trail from the previous subtopic. Know when a DPIA is triggered (Art 35: systematic large-scale monitoring, special-category data at scale, automated decisions with legal effect) and the transfer rules in Chapter V: adequacy, SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment, and what a data-residency demand actually costs you architecturally.

resource.label: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR

subtopics.name: HIPAA vocabulary and the BAA boundary
subtopics.learn: Learn the terms precisely because misusing them destroys credibility instantly: PHI and ePHI, covered entity versus business associate (you are almost always a BA, and your model provider and log SaaS become subcontractor BAs), and the Business Associate Agreement that must exist before a single record flows. Know the Security Rule structure at 45 CFR 164.308/310/312 - administrative, physical, technical safeguards - and the required-versus-addressable distinction at 164.306(d): addressable does not mean optional, it means implement it or document why an equivalent measure is reasonable. Memorise the technical safeguards list (access control with unique user identification and emergency access, audit controls, integrity, person or entity authentication, transmission security) and the minimum-necessary principle. Know that breach notification runs to 60 days with a 500-record threshold that changes who gets told when, and that 'HIPAA compliant' is never a property of a cloud service, only of how you configure an eligible service under a BAA.

resource.label: HHS - HIPAA Security Rule (for professionals)

subtopics.name: De-identification: Safe Harbor vs Expert Determination
subtopics.learn: The highest-leverage move in a healthcare engagement is getting the data out of scope. Learn the two lawful routes at 164.514(b): Safe Harbor, which removes 18 enumerated identifiers (names, all geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, all date elements finer than year, ages over 89, phone, email, MRN, device identifiers, full-face photos, any other unique identifying number) with no actual knowledge of residual re-identification risk; and Expert Determination, where a qualified statistician certifies very small risk, which is what you need if you must keep dates or fine-grained geography. Understand that a limited data set under a data use agreement is a third, middle option. Then apply it: decide whether the LLM classifier can operate on de-identified text, and whether tokenising identifiers before the prompt moves the model provider out of BA scope entirely.

resource.label: HHS - Guidance on De-identification of PHI

subtopics.name: PCI DSS: scope reduction is the whole game
subtopics.learn: Learn just enough vocabulary to be useful and dangerous in the right direction: the cardholder data environment, PAN, sensitive authentication data (full track data, CVV2, PIN - never storable after authorisation, even encrypted), truncation and tokenisation, and network segmentation as the mechanism that keeps systems out of scope. Know the assessment ladder - merchant levels, self-assessment questionnaires versus a QSA-led Report on Compliance, and the Attestation of Compliance you will be asked to produce or consume. The FDE-relevant insight is that SAQ A (fully outsourced payment page) versus SAQ A-EP (your page controls the payment form) is a difference of one script tag, and that current PCI DSS requirements on payment-page script integrity and change detection make third-party tags on checkout a live issue. Your default engineering answer is always: do not let the PAN touch your systems.

resource.label: Stripe Docs - Integration security guide: validating PCI compliance, low-risk integrations and out-of-scope card data

subtopics.name: The LLM-specific compliance surface
subtopics.learn: This is where you add value no compliance lead can: articulate the AI-specific data flows. Cover training on customer data (API traffic is normally excluded by default - verify, do not assume), retention and abuse-monitoring windows and how zero-data-retention agreements change them, the model provider as a named subprocessor with notice obligations, and whether a BAA exists for healthcare traffic. Add the ones people miss: prompts and completions captured in your LLM observability tool are a second copy of regulated data in a second vendor; embeddings derived from personal data are still personal data; an LLM-as-judge or fallback model is a third processor nobody disclosed; and automated classification affecting individuals raises GDPR Art 22 and transparency obligations, plus EU AI Act duties depending on use. Write the AI data-flow paragraph for DefenderMate that you would hand a CISO.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform - Your data (retention, training, controls)

subtopics.name: Map once, answer many: crosswalks, questionnaires and machine-readable controls
subtopics.learn: Frameworks overlap by roughly 80 percent, so build one internal control set and crosswalk it outward rather than restarting per customer. Learn the shape of the standard questionnaires - CSA CAIQ against the Cloud Controls Matrix, and the SIG - and keep a maintained answer bank keyed to your control IDs so a 300-question review becomes an hour of review plus a short list of genuine gaps. Know that ISO 27001 is a certified management system while SOC 2 is an attestation report, and that a customer asking for both usually needs one. Look at OSCAL to understand where machine-readable control catalogues and system security plans are heading. Finish with the professional skill: writing a truthful 'not implemented, here is the compensating control and the date' row instead of a hopeful yes - one discovered overstatement costs more than ten honest gaps.

resource.label: Cloud Security Alliance - Cloud Controls Matrix and CAIQ

outcomes: You can produce a control map for DefenderMate with at least 30 rows, each carrying framework references, a named implementation mechanism, a retrievable evidence artifact, an owner and a test frequency, and a written justification for every 'not applicable'.

You can read a vendor SOC 2 Type II report and, in ten minutes, state the audit period, the criteria categories in scope, any exceptions, the carve-outs, and the complementary user entity controls that now belong to you.

You can draw DefenderMate's regulated data flow end to end - browser, webhook, Redis, Postgres, model provider, S3, CRM, email, logs and traces - and name every processor and subprocessor that touches personal data.

You can walk through a GDPR Art 17 erasure request store by store, including what happens in versioned S3, Kafka, the vector index, third-party logs and backups, and defend the backup answer without claiming something you cannot do.
You can answer a CAIQ or SIG questionnaire from your own answer bank, marking honest gaps with compensating controls and dates rather than aspirational yeses.
You can correctly use the terms controller, processor, business associate, BAA, CDE, PAN, Type I/Type II, addressable safeguard, DPIA and SCC in conversation without a compliance lead correcting you.
You can state, for any control you claim, exactly which command or API call produces the evidence, and run it in front of someone.
You can identify in a live conversation which questions you must route to legal, and say so without stalling the meeting.
failureModes: Regulated data leaks into telemetry: full request bodies, prompts and completions land in a third-party log or LLM-tracing SaaS that is not on the subprocessor list and has a 30-day retention nobody disclosed.
Erasure is implemented in Postgres only, and the deleted subject reappears from an S3 export, the analytics warehouse, HubSpot, or a restored backup that nobody re-processed.

The control map claims 'encrypted at rest' pointing at RDS storage encryption, and the auditor's follow-up - who can read the plaintext - reveals that every engineer with prod read access can, so the control fails on effectiveness.

Evidence is gathered as screenshots in the week before the audit, and the request for a complete population of production changes in the period cannot be satisfied because the emergency-change path bypassed the pipeline and left no record.
Sales commits to HIPAA before anyone checks whether a BAA exists with the model provider and the log vendor, and PHI has already been flowing through both for weeks.
A seeded staging or demo environment is loaded from a production dump, sits outside the audited boundary with weaker access controls, and is real customer data nobody counted.

The blocker turns out to be a complementary user entity control in the cloud provider's own SOC 2 - customer-side MFA, key configuration, access review - that was assumed to be inherited and was never implemented.
interviewQuestions: A hospital's compliance lead asks whether patient notes can be sent to a hosted LLM. What do you say in the meeting, what do you need to verify before you commit to anything, and what architecture would you propose if the answer turns out to be no?
Walk me through the difference between SOC 2 Type I and Type II, and give me a concrete reason a customer would reject a Type I report we just paid for.

Design the deletion path for a GDPR Article 17 request in a system with Postgres, Redis, versioned S3 exports, a vector index, Kafka and a third-party CRM. What can you not delete, and how do you defend that to the customer's DPO?

We discover that 20,000 records containing customer personal data have been written to application logs shipped to a third-party SaaS for the last nine months. Take me through the next 72 hours: what you do first, who decides what, and what you need from the system to answer their questions.
A prospect sends a 300-question security questionnaire and wants it back in three days. How do you run that, and how do you decide what to answer yes, no, and compensating control?

A customer says they will only buy if we deploy entirely inside their VPC so no data leaves their account. What does that actually change legally, what does it change operationally for us, and what breaks in the product?

Their payments team currently posts card numbers to their own backend before forwarding to a gateway. How do you reduce their PCI scope, and what do you have to be careful not to promise while doing it?
70.proofOfWork: Ship a public repository, compliance-pack, that turns the control map from theatre into running code for DefenderMate. It contains: (1) controls.yaml, one entry per control with framework crosswalk references (SOC 2 CC-series, GDPR articles, HIPAA 45 CFR 164 citations, PCI requirements), implementation, owner, frequency and status, rendered into the reviewable spreadsheet by a script; (2) an evidence/ collector - a make evidence target that hits the GitHub API for the merge population, dumps pg_policies and pg_roles, pulls the IAM credential report and AWS Config rule compliance, and writes dated JSON per control so evidence is generated, not screenshotted; (3) a data-flow diagram plus a one-page Art 30 record of processing and a subprocessor table listing every vendor that touches personal data, with region and retention; (4) a runnable erasure runbook, erase_subject.py, that deletes a test subject across Postgres, Redis, versioned S3, the search index and the CRM sandbox, and emits a signed proof-of-deletion report naming what was deleted, what was crypto-shredded and what remains in backups until the retention window expires; and (5) a two-page customer-facing security overview written in the register a CISO reads, ending with an honest gaps table carrying owners and dates. The test of the artifact is that a compliance lead can pick any row and you can produce its evidence live in under a minute.

71.why: When something breaks inside a customer's environment, the FDE is the only person in the room who both understands the system and has the customer's trust, which means you become the incident commander and the customer-facing voice at the same time - a conflict you have to resolve deliberately rather than by accident at 2am. The technical fix is rarely the hard part; the hard part is running a call with your customer's VP of Engineering on it, deciding when to say the word 'breach', and starting a regulatory clock you cannot stop. This topic is the rehearsal: you run a real tabletop against your own architecture, and you build the five-minute briefing that a customer's board or CISO will actually sit through, because the deployment survives or dies on whether they believe you had control.
prerequisites: Incident response and postmortems (topic 23) and SRE fundamentals (topic 20): SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, on-call rotation mechanics, and the basic incident lifecycle - this topic is the security-flavoured, customer-facing escalation of that material, not a repeat of it.

Application security hands-on (topic 61) and threat modelling and secrets lifecycle (topic 62): you need a real threat model and a real set of findings to build believable scenarios and injects from, plus a secrets rotation runbook you can actually execute under time pressure.

Compliance (topic 64): the control map, and specifically which of your customers are under GDPR, HIPAA, PCI or a SOC 2 report, because notification obligations are what turn an outage into a legal event.

Observability (topic 21): the ability to answer 'when did this start, who was affected, and what did they access' from traces, structured logs and audit tables - a tabletop where nobody can answer the scoping question is the most common real failure.
Cloud and Kubernetes security (topics 10, 15, 63): IAM roles, IRSA, key revocation, NetworkPolicy and node isolation - the containment actions you will be asked to perform live.
A deployed system you own end to end - Dokeo and DefenderMate, with their architecture diagrams, on-call contacts and runbooks - because a tabletop against a hypothetical system teaches nothing.

subtopics.name: The declaration threshold: when a bug becomes an incident
subtopics.learn: Write down, before the exercise, the exact conditions under which you declare - and internalise that the cost of declaring early is a Slack channel, while the cost of declaring late is a six-week dwell time. Define triggers concretely for your stack: any confirmed cross-tenant data read, any credential found outside a secrets manager, any unexplained IAM principal, any 403-to-200 change on an admin route, any customer report of seeing data they should not. Learn PagerDuty's key move - anyone can declare, and declaring is never punished - and why 'we thought it might be a display bug' is the sentence that appears in every bad post-incident report. Also define what is explicitly not an incident so the channel does not become a triage queue.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: What is an incident?

subtopics.name: A severity scale that a customer will accept
subtopics.learn: Build a SEV1-SEV5 table where each level names the observable condition, the response expectation, who gets woken, and the external communication obligation - not adjectives like 'major'. Add the security dimension explicitly: SEV1 includes confirmed unauthorised access to customer data or production credentials, regardless of whether the service is up, because availability-only scales systematically under-rate breaches. Learn to separate severity (impact now) from priority (what we work on) from CVSS (vulnerability badness, topic 61) - conflating them is why a CVSS 9.8 in a dev-only dependency gets a page. Write the mapping to your contract: which SEV levels trip a customer notification SLA and within how many hours.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: Severity levels

subtopics.name: Roles, and the FDE's dual-hat problem
subtopics.learn: Learn the four roles that make an incident call work: Incident Commander (owns the incident, makes decisions, does not debug), Scribe (timestamps every decision and finding in the channel), Subject Matter Expert (does the actual work, one task at a time), and Customer/Internal Liaison (owns all outbound communication). The FDE-specific trap is that you are the SME, the IC and the Liaison simultaneously, and doing all three means all three are done badly - practise explicitly handing off: 'I am the SME, I need an IC from your side or I will take IC and hand SME to Priya.' Learn the IC's authority rule - the IC's decision stands during the incident and is reviewed after, never debated during - and how to state that out loud to a customer executive who outranks you.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: Different roles

subtopics.name: Running the call: the IC loop and the decision log
subtopics.learn: Drill the loop: state current status, take structured input round-robin ('what do you know, what do you need'), assign one owner and one deadline per action, set a re-sync interval (10 minutes for SEV1), repeat. Practise the verbal patterns that keep a bridge from degenerating - 'hold, one conversation', 'that is a theory, what would prove it', 'we are timeboxing this to five minutes then rolling back', and closed-loop confirmation ('Priya, revoke the key, confirm back when done'). Keep a single source of truth channel with timestamps: every hypothesis, every action taken, every command run, every 'we decided not to'. That log is the artifact your postmortem, your customer's auditor and possibly their lawyers will read, so it must be written during the incident, never reconstructed after.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: During an incident

subtopics.name: Security incidents differ: containment, eradication, evidence
subtopics.learn: Understand why a security incident inverts your reliability instincts. In an outage you restore service as fast as possible; in a suspected compromise, the first restart can destroy the only evidence of what happened, and a premature block tips off an attacker who then burns their other access. Learn the sequence - detect, scope, contain, eradicate, recover - and that scoping ('what else did this principal touch') usually precedes containment. Know the concrete tension points: rotating a credential closes the door but also breaks the customer's integration; isolating a node preserves memory but drops live traffic; a public status page update is also a public disclosure. Learn who must be in the loop that is never in an outage call: the customer's security team, their legal/privacy counsel, and often an external IR retainer.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: Security incident response

subtopics.name: NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle mapped onto your own runbook
subtopics.learn: Read the four phases - Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity - and then do the useful part: map each phase to a named artifact in your own deployment. Preparation is your contact tree, jump-box access and pre-provisioned break-glass role; Detection is the specific alert rule and the log source that fires it; Analysis is the query you would actually run against the audit table; Containment is the exact CLI call. Learn the standard's vocabulary because customer security teams speak it - 'event' vs 'incident', indicator, precursor, chain of custody - and learn why the standard insists that severity is a function of functional impact, information impact and recoverability rather than a single number.

resource.label: NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

subtopics.name: Containment actions you must be able to execute in under five minutes
subtopics.learn: Turn theory into muscle memory by writing and dry-running the actual commands for your stack, with the pre-authorisation you would need. Credential kill: revoke an IAM access key, attach an explicit Deny policy to a role, and know that AWS STS session tokens already issued keep working until they expire unless you add a Deny with an `aws:TokenIssueTime` condition. Identity kill: revoke refresh tokens and force re-auth at the IdP, invalidate sessions server-side (which is why JWT-only sessions with no revocation list is a containment liability, topic 27). Network kill: tighten a security group, apply a deny-all NetworkPolicy to a namespace, cordon and drain a node while taking a snapshot first. Data kill: disable an integration's webhook, and know your object-storage versioning and retention settings before you need them.

resource.label: AWS IAM User Guide: Disabling permissions for temporary security credentials

subtopics.name: The clocks: regulatory and contractual notification windows
subtopics.learn: Know precisely what starts running the moment you say 'confirmed'. GDPR Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours of becoming aware, with Article 34 covering notice to data subjects when risk is high; the clock starts at awareness, not at full understanding, and a phased notification is explicitly allowed. HIPAA's Breach Notification Rule runs on 60 days for affected individuals, with different rules above and below 500 records. Most enterprise MSAs and DPAs impose a tighter contractual clock on you as a processor - commonly 24 or 48 hours to notify the controller - and that is usually the one that bites first. The FDE's job is not to make the legal call; it is to know the clock exists, get counsel engaged immediately, and produce the facts (what data, whose, how many, when) that the call depends on.

resource.label: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 33-34

subtopics.name: Customer communication during the incident
subtopics.learn: Write the update template and practise using it under pressure: what is happening in one sentence, who is affected, what we know, what we do not yet know, what we are doing, when the next update comes - and then actually send the next update on time even when there is no news, because silence is what destroys trust. Learn the language discipline: no speculation, no attribution, no 'breach' or 'data loss' until confirmed, no blaming a vendor, no promises about root cause during the incident. Understand the difference between the internal channel (raw, fast, wrong sometimes) and the external update (slower, checked, quotable) and never let the two merge. Know that anything you write may be forwarded to the customer's legal team and their regulator, and write accordingly.

resource.label: Atlassian Incident Management Handbook

subtopics.name: Designing the tabletop: objectives, injects and evaluation criteria
subtopics.learn: Build the exercise like an engineer, not a workshop facilitator. Write three or four measurable objectives ('the team can scope which tenants were affected within 20 minutes using only real tooling'), a scope statement of what is in play and what is assumed working, and a set of timed injects that escalate the scenario - initial alert at T+0, an ambiguous second signal at T+10, a journalist or customer executive appearing at T+25, evidence of exfiltration at T+35. Every inject should force a decision, not just add detail. Define evaluation criteria in advance and a data-collection plan (who observes, what they record), plus explicit ground rules: no-fault, artificial time compression is allowed, and 'I would look it up' is not an answer - open the runbook and show it.

resource.label: CISA Tabletop Exercise Packages (CTEP)

subtopics.name: Choosing a scenario grounded in your own architecture
subtopics.learn: Reject generic ransomware scenarios and pick something derived from your own threat model (topic 62) so the exercise actually stresses real gaps. Strong candidates for an AI deployment: a support engineer's laptop compromise leading to a stolen long-lived API key with tenant-wide read access; a cross-tenant leak surfacing because one customer sees another's document in a RAG answer; a model-provider outage combined with a fallback route that silently sends regulated data to a second vendor; a compromised CI token pushing a signed image; a prompt-injection payload in an uploaded document causing an agent to call a tool with elevated credentials. Ground each inject in a real artifact - an actual log line format, an actual dashboard, an actual IAM role name - so participants must use real systems rather than imagine them.

resource.label: OWASP GenAI Security Project: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 (risks and attack scenarios)

subtopics.name: Facilitating live: running the tabletop with a client stand-in
subtopics.learn: Run it for real, 45-60 minutes, with a friend playing the customer stakeholder and a written role card telling them their pressure moves - demanding a root cause in the first ten minutes, asking whether to notify regulators, asking whether their competitor's data was touched, threatening to page their CEO. Your facilitation job is to keep time, deliver injects on schedule, never rescue the participants, and take notes on decision latency rather than on correctness. Practise the IC skills that only show up under pressure: declaring severity out loud, refusing to answer an unanswerable question ('I will not speculate; you will have a scoped answer by 14:30'), parking scope creep, and making an explicit, logged decision when the information is incomplete. Record it - the recording is where you will see yourself talking over the customer.

resource.label: PagerDuty Incident Response: Incident commander training

subtopics.name: Hotwash and after-action report
subtopics.learn: Run the hotwash within fifteen minutes of finishing, while it is raw: each participant states one thing that worked and one thing that did not, then the facilitator presents observations against the pre-written objectives. Convert it into an after-action report with a findings table - observation, root cause, recommendation, owner, due date, and whether the gap is a documentation gap, a tooling gap, an access gap or a decision-authority gap. The most valuable output is usually mundane and specific: nobody had standing access to the audit query, the break-glass role required an approval from someone in another timezone, the contact list had a person who left. Track the corrective actions like real work with real tickets, and re-run the same scenario in three months to prove the gaps closed.

resource.label: NIST SP 800-84: Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs

subtopics.name: The blameless postmortem, written so an outsider can learn from it
subtopics.learn: Write the postmortem for the tabletop as if it were real: summary, impact in user and business terms, a timestamped timeline with detection and mitigation times marked, root causes (plural, and never a person's name), what went well, what went poorly, where we got lucky, and action items with owners and priorities. Learn the actual mechanism of blamelessness - you assume every participant acted reasonably given what they knew, so 'the engineer ran the wrong command' becomes 'the command was destructive by default and the runbook did not distinguish it from the safe variant'. Compute and record the metrics that make a trend visible: time to detect, time to declare, time to scope, time to contain, time to communicate externally. Note explicitly that the customer-facing version is a different, shorter document than the internal one, and say what is deliberately omitted.

resource.label: Google SRE Book: Postmortem Culture - Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Debrief facilitation: the questions that surface real causes
subtopics.learn: Learn to run the review meeting itself, because a badly facilitated debrief produces a document full of 'add more monitoring'. Use questions that reconstruct how the situation looked at the time rather than how it looks now: 'what did you expect to see when you ran that', 'what would have had to be true for your action to be correct', 'when did you realise this was different from the usual', 'what else was going on for you that hour'. Actively suppress counterfactuals ('they should have just...') and hindsight framing, and separate the fact-gathering pass from the remediation pass so the group cannot jump to fixes before the story is complete. Practise handling the customer executive who wants a single name and a single cause, and have the reframing ready before you are in the room.

resource.label: Etsy Debriefing Facilitation Guide (official repository)

subtopics.name: The five-minute board briefing: structure, evidence, rehearsal
subtopics.learn: Build the deliverable to a hard five-minute budget with a bottom-line-up-front structure: what happened and whether customer data was affected (15 seconds), current status and whether it is contained (30 seconds), scope and how you know - the evidence, not the assurance (90 seconds), what you changed so it cannot recur (90 seconds), what you still do not know and when you will know it (45 seconds), what you need from the board (30 seconds). Speak in impact, obligation and risk-reduction, not in Kubernetes; anchor to a framework the board already uses, such as the NIST CSF functions, so remediation lands as a control improvement rather than a task list. Rehearse against the four questions that always come: are we still exposed, do we have to notify anyone, has this happened before, and what would have caught it sooner. Record, watch it back, cut every hedge and every filler clause, and re-record until it lands under five minutes without rushing.

resource.label: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1: Integrating Cybersecurity and Enterprise Risk Management (ERM)

outcomes: You can declare an incident against a written threshold, assign a severity from a scale that names observable conditions, and state the customer notification obligation that severity triggers, in under two minutes from first signal.

You can act as incident commander on a live bridge with a customer executive present: assigning single owners with deadlines, enforcing one conversation, maintaining a timestamped decision log, and refusing to speculate about root cause.

You can design a tabletop exercise for a specific customer architecture with written objectives, at least four timed injects that each force a decision, evaluation criteria, and a data-collection plan - and facilitate it for 45-60 minutes without rescuing the participants.

You can execute or precisely describe containment for your own deployment: revoking an IAM key and denying already-issued STS sessions, forcing IdP re-auth and server-side session invalidation, applying a deny-all NetworkPolicy, and isolating a node after snapshotting it.

You can state the GDPR 72-hour Article 33 clock, the HIPAA 60-day rule and the typical 24-48 hour contractual processor obligation, say what starts each clock, and name the facts you must produce for counsel to make the call.
You can write a blameless postmortem with a timestamped timeline, plural root causes, no individual named, and time-to-detect / declare / scope / contain / communicate recorded as metrics.

You can deliver a recorded five-minute executive security briefing in bottom-line-up-front order that a non-technical board member can follow, and answer the four standard follow-ups - still exposed, notification required, happened before, what would have caught it sooner - without notes.

You can produce an after-action report that classifies every finding as a documentation, tooling, access or decision-authority gap, with an owner and a due date, and re-run the scenario to demonstrate the gaps closed.
failureModes: Nobody declares for six hours because the first signal looks like a display bug, so the timeline in the postmortem starts at the moment someone finally believed a customer rather than at the first alert, and the 72-hour clock had already been running.

The FDE runs the bridge as commander, subject-matter expert and customer liaison at once, stops updating the customer while deep in a query, and the customer's VP escalates to your CEO because twenty minutes of silence read as a cover-up.

A well-meaning engineer restarts the suspicious pod to 'clear it', destroying the process memory and the only unrotated copy of the container filesystem, and the incident permanently loses the ability to answer whether data left the environment.

The compromised access key is revoked but already-issued STS session tokens keep working for another eleven hours because no Deny with a token-issue-time condition was attached, and the team believes containment is complete.

The scoping question - which tenants, which records, which time window - cannot be answered because audit logging captured the request but not the resource identifiers, so the customer is forced into an over-broad notification to every account.

A status page update written by an engineer uses the word 'breach' before legal has made a determination, and that sentence is quoted back in a regulator's follow-up and in a customer's contract termination notice.

The tabletop produces a tidy report with fourteen action items, none of them get a ticket or an owner, and the same missing break-glass access blocks the response during the real incident four months later.
interviewQuestions: You are on site with a customer and their analyst says she just saw a document in a search result that belongs to a different business unit. It is 4pm on a Thursday. Walk me through the next sixty minutes - what you declare, who you pull in, what you touch and what you deliberately do not touch, and what you say to her manager.

Design a tabletop exercise for a deployment of our product inside a regulated customer. Tell me the scenario, the injects and their timing, who is in the room, what you are measuring, and how you would know afterwards whether the exercise was worth their time.

Explain the tension between restoring service and preserving evidence in a suspected compromise. Give me two concrete decisions where those goals conflict in a Kubernetes and AWS deployment, and tell me how you would decide and who has the authority to make that call.

You have five minutes with the customer's board the morning after. Give me the briefing. Then I will ask you the questions they will ask, and you will not be allowed to say 'we are still investigating' more than once.

During the incident, the customer's CTO tells you to roll back to last week's release immediately. You believe the rollback will destroy the evidence you need and may not even remove the attacker's access. What do you do?

Your postmortem draft says the root cause was that an engineer disabled a check to unblock a demo. Rewrite that finding blamelessly and tell me what you would actually change - and how you would defend the rewrite to a customer executive who wants accountability.

How do you scope a suspected cross-tenant data exposure? Be specific about which logs, which fields and which queries you would need, and tell me what you would have had to instrument months earlier for that answer to take minutes instead of days.
71.proofOfWork: Publish a public incident-readiness pack for one of your own deployments (Dokeo or DefenderMate) that a customer's security team could adopt as-is. It contains four linked pieces. First, an incident response plan: declaration threshold, a SEV1-SEV5 table where each level names an observable condition and its notification obligation, the role definitions with the explicit rule for how the FDE hands off IC or SME when they cannot hold both, and a contact and escalation tree with the break-glass access path named. Second, an executable containment runbook - a real script or documented command sequence with a dry-run mode that revokes an API key, attaches a deny policy covering already-issued sessions, forces IdP re-authentication, applies a deny-all NetworkPolicy to the workload namespace, and snapshots a node before isolating it - with evidence you actually ran it against a staging environment and the wall-clock time each step took. Third, the tabletop artifacts: the scenario and inject schedule with timestamps, the observer notes, the recording or transcript of the 45-60 minute exercise you ran with someone playing the customer, and an after-action report whose findings are each classified as a documentation, tooling, access or decision-authority gap with an owner, a due date and a link to the ticket that closed it. Fourth, the blameless postmortem written from the exercise with time-to-detect, declare, scope, contain and communicate recorded as numbers, alongside the customer-facing short version and an explicit note on what was omitted from it and why. Then re-run the same scenario six to eight weeks later and add a one-page delta showing which timings improved, which findings recurred, and what you changed in the plan as a result - a second run is the part almost nobody does, and it is the part that proves the pack is real.

72.why: An FDE is handed a signed contract and a stated requirement that is almost always a solution somebody already picked - 'we need a dashboard', 'we need RAG over our SharePoint', 'we need an agent that does triage' - and building exactly that is the most common way an engagement ships on time and still fails. You are the only person on the vendor side who will sit with the analyst who does the work at 09:00 and the VP who signed the cheque at 16:00, so the single problem statement both of them will agree with does not exist until you go and manufacture it. Bad discovery does not fail loudly: you deliver in week six, adoption is zero by week ten, and the renewal conversation becomes about your product instead of their process.
prerequisites: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets from 'SRE fundamentals' (topic 20). A discovery success metric is an SLI with a baseline, a target and a measurement method, not an adjective.

The compliance vocabulary from 'Compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI' (topic 64): BAA, DPA, sub-processor, data residency, right to erasure. You cannot ask constraint questions in a language you do not speak.
Enough Postgres and warehouse fluency (topics 29 and 36) to ask for a schema dump or a CSV export in the interview and have three defensible numbers out of it before the follow-up call.

A running demo you can put on screen in 90 seconds - Kaupex or DefenderMate - because FDE discovery is bidirectional: you probe, they react to something concrete, and you learn from the reaction, not from the compliment.
Five real humans who will give you 45 minutes each: ex-clients, friends running small businesses, an ops manager at a company you once contracted for. Booked before you start reading, not after.
Recording and transcription set up and tested end to end, plus a git repo for the write-ups. Discovering that your recorder was muted after interview three costs you the interview.

subtopics.name: Three different things called 'discovery' and which one you are doing
subtopics.learn: Separate sales discovery (does a deal exist, run pre-signature by an AE), product discovery (what should the product become, run continuously by PM/design), and delivery discovery - the FDE job - which starts after money changed hands and asks: what does this specific customer actually do all day, what will they let us deploy, and what has to be true in ninety days for them to renew. Know why the third is the hardest: the contract has already named a deliverable, your champion has already told their boss what it does, and your job is to find the real problem without making anyone look wrong for having mis-stated it. Write down, for your own engagement, the one sentence you would have to change in the SOW if discovery went badly - that is your risk surface.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - How the discovery phase works

subtopics.name: The Mom Test: three rules and the three signals you are being lied to
subtopics.learn: Internalise the three rules until you can apply them mid-sentence: talk about their life instead of your idea; ask about specifics in the past instead of generics or opinions about the future; talk less and listen more. Learn the three failure signals that mean the conversation produced nothing - compliments ('that's really cool', 'I love it'), fluff (generics, hypotheticals, 'I always/usually/never'), and ideas (their feature requests, which are data about a problem, never a spec). Practise the conversions out loud: 'would you use a tool that does X?' becomes 'walk me through the last time you did X'; 'how much would you pay?' becomes 'what do you spend on this today, and who signs that invoice?'; 'do you think this is a problem?' becomes 'what did you do about it last month?'

resource.label: The Mom Test (Rob Fitzpatrick) - book site

subtopics.name: Question taxonomy and a leading-question audit you can run on your own transcript
subtopics.learn: Classify every question you ask into open ('walk me through', 'what happened next', 'who else was involved'), closed (yes/no - fine for pinning facts, useless for exploring), leading (contains the answer: 'so that's slow, right?'), loaded (assumes a fact not in evidence: 'when the sync breaks, what do you do?'), and hypothetical (worthless: 'would you', 'could you see yourself', 'if we built'). Build a grep-able red-flag list - 'would you', 'do you think', 'wouldn't it be', 'how much would you pay', 'does that make sense', 'right?' - and after each interview run it over the transcript and count hits per hour. Set a target that trends downward across the five interviews and record the number in every write-up; an unmeasured habit does not change.

resource.label: NN/g - Open-Ended vs. Closed Questions in User Research

subtopics.name: Stakeholder map: buyer, champion, operator, gatekeeper, saboteur
subtopics.learn: Build a five-row map before interview one: economic buyer (owns budget, cares about the number in the board deck), champion (staked their reputation on you, will tell you what they want to hear), operator (does the work you are about to change, is the only source of ground truth about the workflow), gatekeeper (security, legal, procurement, platform - can veto and never gets invited), and the person who loses if this works (headcount, a tool they built, a fiefdom). Assign a different question set to each: the buyer gets 'what does this have to move for you to fund phase two', the operator gets 'show me the last five cases you handled', the gatekeeper gets 'what has to be true before you would sign off on a deployment in your VPC'. Explicitly answer 'who has not been in a room with us yet, and why' - the missing name is usually the one who kills the project in month three.

resource.label: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework - Strategy (motivations, outcomes, stakeholders)

subtopics.name: Booking, consent, recording and the 45-minute session shape
subtopics.learn: Get on the operator's calendar directly rather than through the champion, using a framing that costs them nothing: 'I want to understand how the work actually gets done so we don't build the wrong thing - 45 minutes, no prep, no slides.' Open every session with the same 60-second block: who you are, why you are there, that there are no wrong answers, that you will record for accuracy and share the write-up back, and an explicit yes/no on recording that you capture in the transcript. Then run a fixed shape - 5 minutes context, 25 minutes past-behaviour and screen-share walkthrough, 10 minutes constraints and metrics, 5 minutes commitments - and hold to it, because a session that runs long is a session the operator will not grant you twice.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - Getting informed consent for user research

subtopics.name: Laddering: from raw request to decision to business metric
subtopics.learn: Treat every stated request as the top of a ladder and climb down it in the room: 'we need a dashboard' -> what decision does the dashboard support -> who makes that decision, how often, on what data today -> what happens when they get it wrong -> what does that cost per occurrence. Use one-word probes to keep them talking ('and then?', 'because?', 'walk me through that'), and stop laddering at the first number tied to money, time or risk, because that is the level at which the buyer will fund it. Learn Shape Up's distinction between the raw idea and the shaped problem, and the appetite question - 'is this a two-week thing or a two-month thing for you?' - asked of the customer rather than of yourself, so scope gets bounded by their patience, not by your ambition.

resource.label: Shape Up (Basecamp) - Chapter 3: Set Boundaries (appetite, narrowing the problem)

subtopics.name: Workflow archaeology: watch the work, do not ask about the work
subtopics.learn: Get a screen share and make them process a real case in front of you while you stay silent - 'do it exactly as you would if I weren't here, including the bits you'd normally skip'. Count and record the artefacts nobody mentions in a requirements doc: the shadow spreadsheet, the copy-paste between two systems (the swivel chair), the Slack DM that is actually an approval step, the saved email search that is actually a queue, the person they ping when it is ambiguous. Time the case end to end with a stopwatch, note every hand-off and every point where work waits, and ask 'how often is this the easy version?' - the exception path is usually 30 to 60 percent of volume and is where automation dies.

resource.label: NN/g - Contextual Inquiry: observing and interviewing users in their context

subtopics.name: Quantify the pain from their own data, not from their adjectives
subtopics.learn: Convert anecdote to arithmetic before the follow-up call: volume (cases per week), unit cost (minutes per case x loaded hourly rate), error rate, rework rate, and cost of delay (what one day of latency costs). Ask for the smallest real artefact that gets you there - a CSV export of the last 90 days of tickets, a table dump, a query result - and be specific about columns and timeframe so it can be approved as low-risk. Load it in DuckDB (`read_csv_auto`, then `SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at), count(*), median(closed_at - created_at)`), and come back with three numbers, the query that produced them, and one number you are unsure about - inviting the correction is what makes the other two credible.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - CSV Import (read_csv and the CSV sniffer)

subtopics.name: Read the system, not just the people: schemas, APIs and the integration inventory
subtopics.learn: In parallel with the human interviews, ask for the machine-readable truth: an OpenAPI document, a `\d+` schema dump or ERD, five real (redacted) payloads, and a list of every system the process touches. For each system record whether it is the system of record or a system of reference, who owns it internally, whether it has an API or only a CSV export, its auth model, and its rate limits. Then ask the single highest-yield engineering question in discovery - 'what breaks today, and how do you find out?' - because the existing failure modes tell you more about the real architecture than any diagram they will draw for you.

resource.label: OpenAPI Specification (latest)

subtopics.name: Constraint discovery: the questions that kill projects if asked late
subtopics.learn: Run a fixed constraint checklist in every engagement before you design anything: where may data physically live and may it leave their VPC or their country; is there egress to third-party model APIs or is this air-gapped; who owns the deploy and what is the change-freeze calendar; what identity provider and what does 'SSO' mean here concretely (Entra, Okta, Keycloak, SAML vs OIDC); what security review, pen test or vendor questionnaire stands between you and production and how long has that taken for the last vendor; what is the data-retention and deletion obligation. Capture each answer with a named owner and a date, and treat 'I think it's fine' as unanswered. Every one of these is cheap in week one and an architecture rewrite in week ten.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Framework

subtopics.name: Define the success metric and run the pre-mortem before writing code
subtopics.learn: Write the success metric in SLI form - indicator, measurement method, current baseline, target, date, and who reads it - for example 'median analyst time-to-triage on inbound alerts, measured from webhook receipt to analyst disposition in the DefenderMate audit log, currently 22 minutes, target under 5 minutes for 80 percent of alerts by 31 March, reviewed monthly by the SOC lead'. Insist that the baseline is measured, not remembered, and that the instrumentation to measure it is part of phase one rather than an afterthought. Then run a 15-minute pre-mortem with the champion: 'it is six months from now and this was quietly switched off - write down the three most likely reasons' - and turn each reason into either a discovery question you have not asked or a risk with an owner.

resource.label: Google SRE Workbook - Implementing SLOs

subtopics.name: Opportunity mapping: keeping the problem space separate from the solution space
subtopics.learn: Structure what you heard as an opportunity solution tree: one desired outcome at the root (the metric above), opportunities beneath it phrased as the customer's own unmet needs and pain points in their words, and solutions only as leaves attached to a specific opportunity. Enforce the discipline that a solution with no parent opportunity gets deleted, and that an opportunity supported by one loud stakeholder and zero operators is marked as such. Choose the target opportunity explicitly on reach (how many people, how often), impact on the root metric, your confidence given the evidence count, and effort under the customer's constraints - and write the reason down, because in month three someone will ask why you did not build the other thing.

resource.label: Product Talk (Teresa Torres) - Opportunity Solution Trees

subtopics.name: Interviewing the incumbent engineering team without becoming the threat
subtopics.learn: The customer's own platform or data team is simultaneously your best source of ground truth and the group most likely to quietly stall you, because a vendor arriving with a mandate reads as a verdict on their backlog. Interview them first, not last, and lead with the questions that concede status: 'what have you already tried here', 'what did you build that we should reuse rather than replace', 'what would you have done with another two engineers'. Ask directly what they want to own after go-live and what they refuse to be paged for, then make that split explicit in the problem statement - an FDE who hands over a runbook and an on-call boundary gets change windows; one who does not, does not.

resource.label: Atlassian Team Playbook - Roles and Responsibilities play

subtopics.name: Synthesis: from raw transcript to evidence with a count behind it
subtopics.learn: Within 24 hours of each session, cut the transcript into atomic observations, tag each with speaker, role, and type (fact, quote, pain, workaround, constraint, request, metric), and keep verbatim wording for anything you will later quote back. Cluster across interviews and attach a support count to every claim - 'four of five operators maintain a private spreadsheet' is an insight; 'users want better search' is a paraphrase of one person. Deliberately record disconfirming evidence and the claims that only the champion made, and mark every open question with the person who can close it, so synthesis produces a to-do list rather than a mood.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - Analyse a research session

subtopics.name: The one-page problem statement the client will actually sign
subtopics.learn: Write one page, in their vocabulary, with six fixed sections: current state with numbers and the query behind them; who is affected and how often; what it costs today; the constraint set with named owners; the success metric with baseline, target and date; and explicit non-goals ('this does not replace the case management system', 'this does not touch PHI in phase one'), plus open questions with owners. Lead with the customer's own quoted words rather than your framing, keep every number traceable to a source, and cut every adjective that is not attached to a measurement. Then do the read-back: send it, get on a call, read it aloud, and ask 'what did I get wrong?' - written agreement without a spoken correction usually means they skimmed it.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One

subtopics.name: Closing for commitment: advancement versus a polite stall
subtopics.learn: End every session by asking for something that costs the other person real resource - an introduction to the operator or the gatekeeper by name, a data export, read access to a system, a named owner for an open question, or a specific 30-minute slot on a specific day. Learn to distinguish advancement (they did a thing) from a stall dressed as enthusiasm ('this is great, send me something and I'll take it to the team'), and record which you got in the write-up. Treat repeated compliments plus zero commitments as the strongest possible negative signal, and say so in the write-up rather than filing it as validation.

resource.label: The Mom Test - teaching notes on commitment and advancement (chapter 5)

subtopics.name: Build the reusable script and self-scorecard, then run the five
subtopics.learn: Produce a single artefact you will use on real engagements: a 45-minute agenda, the consent line, a 12-question core bank with follow-up probes for each, role-specific branches for buyer / operator / gatekeeper / incumbent engineer, the constraint checklist, the closing-ask menu, and a one-page write-up template. Pair it with a scorecard you fill in after every session - your talk ratio (target under 30 percent), leading questions per hour, number of specific past events obtained, number of numbers obtained, commitments obtained, and one thing you would ask differently. Run all five interviews, score each, and revise the script between sessions so the diffs to the script are themselves the evidence of learning.

resource.label: NN/g - Writing an Effective Guide for a UX Interview

outcomes: You can run a 45-minute discovery session end to end from your own script - consent, context, past-behaviour walkthrough, screen-share observation, constraints, closing ask - and finish on time with the transcript, the scorecard and the write-up committed the same day.
You can show a talk-ratio under 30 percent and a leading-question count that falls measurably from interview one to interview five, evidenced by the tagged transcripts, not by your recollection.

You can take any stated request ('we need a dashboard', 'we need an agent') and ladder it in under ten minutes to the decision it supports, the person who makes that decision, and one number in money, time or risk.
You can turn a customer's raw data export into three defensible baseline numbers with the DuckDB queries attached, and present them with an explicit statement of which one you are least sure about.

You can produce a one-page problem statement that the interviewee confirms verbally with no substantive correction, containing a measured baseline, a dated success metric, named constraint owners and explicit non-goals.

You can name, for any engagement, every stakeholder in the five-role map plus the person who has not yet been in a room with you, and state what each one would have to see to consider the project a success.

You can distinguish, in writing, an advancement from a stall for each of your five sessions, and can point to the specific commitment obtained (intro, export, access, calendar slot) or record its absence as a negative signal.

You can run the constraint checklist cold - data residency, egress, identity provider, change windows, security review, retention - and get every item to either an answer with an owner and date or an explicit 'unknown, blocking'.
failureModes: You interview the champion and the VP, never the analyst who does the work, and ship a workflow whose second step the operations team is contractually forbidden from performing, which nobody discovers until UAT.

You demo Kaupex in the discovery call, get 'wow, that's exactly what we need', log it as validation, and only realise months later that no data export, no system access and no second meeting ever came out of that session.

The stated problem is a solution: they ask for a chatbot over their documentation, you build retrieval, and the real defect is that the documentation is three years stale - so the bot now answers confidently and wrongly at scale, which is worse than the search box it replaced.

Nobody measured the baseline, so at the quarterly review the customer's own analyst produces a number from a different definition that says the system made things slower, and you have no instrumented counter-argument.
Data residency comes up in month three: the customer's legal team will not permit egress to a hosted model API, the entire architecture assumed one, and the replan costs more than the original build.

The customer's platform team was treated as a delivery obstacle rather than interviewed, so they own the deploy, never schedule your change window, and the pilot sits in staging until the sponsor loses interest.
You say 'yes, we can do that' three times in a discovery room, the notes become the SOW, and you spend the engagement delivering scope that was never tied to the success metric or to anyone's budget.
interviewQuestions: A customer signed for 'an AI agent that triages our security alerts'. You get one 45-minute session with the SOC analyst before design starts. Give me your actual first six questions, in order, and tell me what each one is trying to disconfirm.

Your champion tells you the team spends 'hours a day' on manual reconciliation. Walk me through how you convert that into a number you would be willing to put in a board deck, including exactly what artefact you ask for and what you do with it.

How do you tell the difference between a customer who is genuinely enthusiastic and one who is being polite? Give me the concrete signals you look for in the session and the thing you ask for at the end that settles it.

You have finished discovery and concluded that the deliverable named in the signed SOW will not move the metric the buyer cares about. Your champion picked that deliverable and told their VP it would work. What do you do, in what order, and what exactly do you say to the champion?

Design the constraint interview for a healthcare customer who wants patient-intake summarisation. What do you ask, whom do you ask, and which single answer, if it comes back wrong, invalidates your default architecture?

In discovery you find that the customer's own platform team already built half of what you were hired to build, and it mostly works. How does that change your problem statement, your architecture and your relationship with that team?
Give me a time you built the wrong thing because discovery was thin. What was the specific question you failed to ask, how would you have asked it, and what is now in your script because of it?
72.proofOfWork: A public `discovery-kit` repository that a hiring manager can evaluate in fifteen minutes and another engineer can pick up and use on a live engagement. It contains: (1) the versioned discovery script with its git history visible, so the diffs between interview one and interview five are themselves the evidence of learning, plus the consent line, the role-specific question branches, the constraint checklist and the closing-ask menu; (2) five write-ups against a fixed template, each with its filled-in scorecard (talk ratio, leading questions per hour, specific past events obtained, numbers obtained, commitment obtained or explicitly absent) and a summary chart showing those metrics trending across the five; (3) one fully annotated transcript with every question tagged open / closed / leading / loaded / hypothetical and a short written self-critique of the three worst moments; (4) a `baseline/` folder containing one real (anonymised) data export, the DuckDB queries that turn it into three baseline numbers, and a note on which number is weakest and why; (5) a one-page problem statement for the strongest of the five engagements, written in the interviewee's own quoted language, that they confirmed on a read-back call, with the confirmation email or note included; and (6) a `delta.md` comparing the hypothesis you wrote down before interview one with the final problem statement, naming precisely what you were wrong about and which question surfaced it - the last file being the one that actually demonstrates the skill.

73.topic: Engagement documents: site survey, PRD-lite, SOW, ADRs, design docs, runbooks
73.why: An FDE is the only person in the room who sits between a sponsor who wants an outcome, a platform team that owns the environment, and an on-call engineer who will be woken up by whatever you deploy, and the artifact that keeps those three aligned is writing, not code. Every expensive delivery failure - the six-week slip on an IAM role nobody was assigned, the security veto three days before go-live, the 3am incident where the customer cannot restart your service - is traceable to a document that was never written or was written for the wrong reader. Producing a site survey, a PRD-lite, a SOW section set, ADRs, a design doc and runbooks that a customer's lead accepts without rewriting is the difference between a contractor who ships code and a forward-deployed engineer who ships a working system the customer can own.
prerequisites: Discovery (topic 66): stakeholder mapping, the questions that surface the real problem, and a set of discovery notes you can trace every requirement back to.
SRE fundamentals (topic 20) and incident response (topic 23): SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, severity ladders and escalation, because runbooks and go-live criteria are written in that vocabulary.
Observability (topic 21): what a dashboard, an alert rule and a trace actually look like, so a runbook can point at real signals instead of describing them.
Enough of the deployment stack to describe an architecture accurately: Kubernetes core and production ops (topics 7 and 8), Terraform (topic 12), AWS networking and IAM (topics 13 and 15).
Threat modelling and secrets lifecycle (topic 62) plus compliance basics (topic 64): data classification, trust boundaries, and what a customer security review asks for.
Git at depth (topic 4) and comfort with Markdown, PR review and CI, since the whole pack is docs-as-code in the customer's repository.

subtopics.name: Map the pack: six documents, six readers, one index
subtopics.learn: Before writing anything, fix the stack: the site survey answers 'what actually exists and what will block us', the PRD-lite answers 'what are we building, for whom, and how will we know it worked', the SOW answers 'what are we on the hook for, by when, and who signs it off', ADRs answer 'why this and not that', the design doc answers 'how it works and how it fails', and the runbook answers 'what does the on-call engineer do at 3am'. Each has a different reader - platform lead, product sponsor, procurement, customer architect, on-call - and a different failure mode when missing. Use the Diataxis split (tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation) to stop mixing modes inside one file, because a runbook that explains architecture is a runbook nobody follows. Ship a one-page index listing every document with its owner, reviewer, status and last-verified date.

resource.label: Diataxis - a systematic framework for technical documentation

subtopics.name: Site survey I: environment, access and the deploy path
subtopics.learn: Inventory the target the way an installer would, with a value, a source and evidence for every line: cloud accounts and regions, VPC CIDRs and whether they collide with yours, subnet and NAT layout, egress rules (allowlist, TLS-intercepting forward proxy, or no egress at all), Kubernetes distribution and version, CNI, ingress controller and any admission policies already enforced, container registry and whether images must be mirrored internally, identity provider and SSO/SCIM, bastion or VPN access and how many days a laptop grant takes, secrets manager, CI system, and who is allowed to merge to the deploying branch. Then draw the deploy path end to end - repo, build, scan, sign, registry, environment promotion, approval gate - and name the human who approves each gate. Anything you were told rather than verified gets marked as unverified until you have run the command yourself.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected Framework

subtopics.name: Site survey II: data, security and compliance reality
subtopics.learn: Capture the facts that decide whether the architecture is even permissible: data classification for every input and output (public, internal, PII, PHI, regulated), residency and cross-border rules, retention and deletion obligations, whether prompts and completions may leave the tenant boundary or call a third-party model API at all, encryption requirements (KMS or customer-managed keys at rest, mTLS in transit), audit log retention, and the control framework in force (SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA with a BAA, FedRAMP). Get the security review process in writing: who runs it, which artifacts they expect (architecture and data flow diagrams, a questionnaire such as ASVS or SIG, pen test evidence, SBOM), and the lead time in weeks. The highest-value line in this section is 'PII in scope: yes or no, and here is the field-level list', because it changes retrieval design, logging, eval datasets and where the model can run.

resource.label: NIST SP 800-122 - Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally Identifiable Information (PII)

subtopics.name: Site survey III: constraints, blockers and the RAID register
subtopics.learn: Convert findings into a decision-ready register rather than prose, using four buckets: risks (probability, impact, mitigation, owner), assumptions (what you are betting on and what it costs if false), issues (blocking now, with owner and needed-by date) and dependencies (what the customer must provide and when). Every row names a human, not a team, and carries a date. Learn to recognise the constraints that historically kill delivery: no outbound internet, no cluster admin, a change freeze covering your go-live quarter, one overloaded DBA, procurement lead time on a GPU quota increase, or a policy that blocks the model provider entirely. State each item's schedule impact in days, because 'we are blocked on IAM' moves nobody while 'this pushes go-live past the November freeze' moves everyone.

resource.label: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework

subtopics.name: PRD-lite: one page that fixes problem, scope and success
subtopics.learn: Write one page, not ten, with fixed sections: problem with a baseline number, the two or three user journeys expressed as the job to be done, in-scope list, an explicit non-goals list, success metrics with their measurement definition and an instrumentation owner, and an assumptions block. Force every metric to be computable: not 'faster triage' but 'median minutes from ticket creation to first correct routing decision, computed from created_at and routed_at in the ticketing system, baseline 42 minutes over the last 90 days'. Write the non-goals section first when scope is contested - it is the section that saves the engagement. Trace every claim back to a named stakeholder from your discovery notes so the sponsor can see whose words these are.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One

subtopics.name: Requirements language and testable acceptance criteria
subtopics.learn: Adopt RFC 2119 keywords - MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, MAY - and use them deliberately, because an ambiguous 'should' in a SOW is where disputes live. Rewrite every soft requirement as an observable condition: 'the system MUST return a routing decision for 95 percent of tickets within 3 seconds, measured as p95 at the API gateway over a rolling 24 hours' beats 'responses should be fast'. Attach a verification method to each requirement - an automated test id, a load-test scenario, an eval run, or a named manual check - so acceptance becomes a script rather than an argument. Ban seamless, robust, scalable, real-time and AI-powered from requirement text, and treat any requirement you cannot write a failing test for as a discovery gap to take back to the sponsor before signing.

resource.label: RFC 2119 - Key words for use in RFCs to indicate requirement levels

subtopics.name: SOW anatomy: deliverables, obligations, assumptions, exclusions, change control
subtopics.learn: Learn each section and the specific failure it defends against: deliverables (which artifacts are handed over, in what format, to which repository), milestones with dates and acceptance or payment triggers, customer obligations (access, environments, data, named SMEs, decision turnaround) each with a needed-by date, assumptions listed explicitly so that a broken one triggers a change request instead of unpaid work, exclusions and out-of-scope, acceptance criteria with a named signer per deliverable, a change control procedure (who raises, how it is priced, who approves, what happens to the timeline), and post-go-live support terms with an expiry date. Understand where risk sits in fixed-fee versus time-and-materials, and why fixed-fee plus vague assumptions is the standard way delivery teams go negative. Practise writing the exclusion list: it is short, blunt, and the most re-read part of the document.

resource.label: FAR 37.602 - Performance work statement: required scope, results, measurable standards and constraints

subtopics.name: ADRs: what counts as a decision and the canonical shape
subtopics.learn: An ADR records one architecturally significant decision - expensive to reverse, spanning components or teams, or one the customer will question later. Learn the shape: an ordinal title (0007-postgres-pgvector-for-retrieval), status (proposed, accepted, superseded by 0012, deprecated), date, context stating the forces and the customer-specific constraints, the decision in the active voice ('We will...'), consequences split into what improves, what gets worse and what you now have to live with, and alternatives considered with a concrete reason each was rejected. The value is concentrated in Context and Consequences; a record with no rejected alternatives is a preference, not a decision. Keep it to a page that a reviewer can read in ten minutes.

resource.label: Architectural Decision Records - adr.github.io

subtopics.name: Running an ADR log: template, numbering, supersession, review
subtopics.learn: Keep the log in the customer's repo at docs/adr/ as numbered Markdown, pick one template (MADR is the common default) and never edit an accepted ADR - supersede it with a new record that links back, so the history of why the design moved stays readable. Wire ADR review into the pull request that implements the decision so the two cannot diverge, and use a lightweight tool or a template file plus a PR checklist rather than a bespoke process. Learn the practical triggers for writing one: you are about to choose a datastore, a queue, an auth model, a tenancy model, a model provider or a deployment target, or you have just spent an hour of a meeting arguing. Expect five to fifteen ADRs across a typical engagement, and expect the customer to reuse them long after you leave.

resource.label: joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record - templates and examples

subtopics.name: Design doc: Google-style structure and the review it exists for
subtopics.learn: The design doc exists to surface disagreement early and cheaply, not to describe finished code. Structure it as context and scope, goals and explicit non-goals, the design itself (data model, APIs, request flow, storage, tenancy, failure behaviour), alternatives considered, cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, observability, cost, operations), then estimate and rollout. Write it before you build, circulate it with a fixed review window and named reviewers including the customer's architect and security lead, resolve comments in the document rather than in DMs, and mark it as a point-in-time artifact that stops being maintained once shipped - after that the code and the runbook are the living truth. Length is a signal: three to ten pages is right, twenty means the scope is wrong.

resource.label: Design Docs at Google

subtopics.name: Diagrams that survive an architecture review: C4 and diagrams-as-code
subtopics.learn: Use the C4 levels deliberately - System Context (who and which systems, the one diagram a sponsor understands), Container (deployable units, datastores, protocols and ports), Component only where a container is genuinely complex - and never ship a diagram that mixes levels. Add the two diagrams security reviewers ask for by name: a data flow diagram with trust boundaries drawn, and a network or deployment diagram showing VPCs, subnets, ingress, egress and where credentials are issued. Keep diagrams as code (Mermaid or Structurizr) beside the document so they are reviewable in a pull request and regenerable, and label every arrow with the protocol and the direction of initiation, since 'who calls whom' is what determines firewall rules and service accounts.

resource.label: The C4 model for visualising software architecture

subtopics.name: The design doc sections FDEs skip: failure modes, capacity, rollback, cost
subtopics.learn: Add the sections that make an operations team accept the design. Failure modes: for each dependency, what happens when it is slow, down or returns garbage, plus the specific timeout, retry policy with jitter and cap, circuit breaker and degraded mode you chose.
