Drill four fixed phrases until they are automatic: (1) restate the ask and the output shape - 'you want one row per customer per month with revenue and refund rate, I will produce a DataFrame with those four columns'; (2) announce before you type - 'I'm going to check dtypes and null counts before I aggregate, because if amount came in as object the sum will silently concatenate'; (3) name the assumption out loud with its falsifier - 'I'm assuming order_id is unique; if the merge inflates row count I'm wrong and I'll dedupe on the max updated_at'; (4) narrate the failure without apologising - 'that returned 1.2 million rows, more than either input, so this is a fan-out on a non-unique key; I'll check value_counts on the join key'. Practise the hardest case explicitly: keep talking while reading a traceback. Set a rule that any silence over fifteen seconds must be filled with 'let me say what I'm looking at' and then read the error aloud.

resource.label: Exercism - Python track (timed practice exercises)

subtopics.name: Build the drill rig: fixture datasets, timer, one-take recording, grade sheet
subtopics.learn: Assemble the harness once so no drill costs setup time. Curate three real, messy CSV corpora from your own exports (bank or payments transactions, a CRM or email-tool export, and a log or event stream) at 50k-2M rows, each with genuine defects: mixed date formats, thousands separators in numeric columns, trailing whitespace in keys, duplicated rows with different updated_at, and a column that is 40% null. Load the same data into a local Postgres via docker compose so every question can be asked in both pandas and SQL. Set up a visible countdown timer in the recorded frame, a scratch notebook template with the first cell already doing df.info(), df.isna().sum() and df.head(), and a GRADES.md table with one row per drill and columns for the five rubric axes plus longest-silence seconds. Record at 1080p with a large terminal font - unreadable text makes the tape useless for review.

resource.label: OBS Studio (open-source screen recording)

subtopics.name: pandas operation vocabulary you must type cold, no lookup
subtopics.learn: Rehearse the ~15 operations that cover the overwhelming majority of interview data manipulation until muscle memory: groupby().agg() with named aggregations (df.groupby(['a','b']).agg(rev=('amount','sum'), n=('id','nunique')).reset_index()), transform for group-broadcast columns, merge with explicit how and validate='one_to_many', concat with ignore_index, pivot_table with aggfunc and fill_value versus melt for long form, sort_values with ascending as a list, drop_duplicates(subset=..., keep='last') after a sort, assign for chained derivation, query and boolean masks with parentheses around each condition, loc-based assignment to avoid SettingWithCopyWarning, nlargest/rank(method='dense'), cut and qcut for bucketing, and value_counts(dropna=False). Know the two idioms for 'top N per group' - sort_values then groupby().head(n), and rank over a transform - and which one is faster. Drill by writing each from a blank cell against your fixture data and checking the shape of the result before looking at the values.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Group by: split-apply-combine

subtopics.name: Dirty-data reflexes: dtypes, missing-value semantics, and parsing
subtopics.learn: The interview dataset is dirty on purpose, and the score is decided in the first three minutes. Build a fixed opening move: df.info(), df.isna().sum(), df.nunique(), df.describe(include='all'), and df.duplicated().sum(). Then know the specific traps and their fixes - an object-dtype numeric column from thousands separators or currency symbols (pd.to_numeric(s.str.replace(r'[^0-9.\-]','',regex=True), errors='coerce') and count the coerced NaNs, do not hide them); mixed date formats (pd.to_datetime(..., format='mixed', errors='coerce') or explicit format plus a fallback pass, and never trust dayfirst inference); float NaN versus pd.NA versus None and why NaN != NaN breaks equality filters; integer columns that become float64 the moment a null appears, and Int64 nullable dtype as the fix; whitespace and case in join keys (str.strip().str.lower()) which is the single most common silent zero-match cause; and category dtype for memory when a key column has 20 distinct values over 2M rows. Say the null count out loud every time you coerce - interviewers are listening for whether you noticed you destroyed data.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Working with missing data

subtopics.name: SQL window functions under time pressure
subtopics.learn: Window functions are the single highest-yield SQL topic in FDE loops because they are how every 'compare each row to its group' question is answered. Get fluent enough to write without hesitation: ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK with PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY and know exactly how they differ on ties; LAG/LEAD with the offset and default arguments for period-over-period deltas; SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for rolling windows, and the critical distinction between ROWS and RANGE frames when the order key has duplicates; FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE and why LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame to do what you meant; NTILE for bucketing; and named windows via the WINDOW clause when three expressions share a frame. Know the ordering rule that WHERE cannot reference a window result, so top-N-per-group needs a CTE or subquery in Postgres - and that Snowflake and Databricks give you QUALIFY instead. Drill by writing the same 'second-highest order per customer' query three ways.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Window Functions (function reference)

subtopics.name: Join semantics, NULL traps, and aggregation correctness in SQL
subtopics.learn: Most wrong answers in a SQL round are join or NULL bugs, not syntax. Internalise: LEFT JOIN plus a filter on the right table's column in WHERE silently becomes an INNER JOIN (the predicate must move into the ON clause); a join on a non-unique key fans out rows and inflates every downstream SUM, so the reflex is to check counts before and after and use COUNT(DISTINCT id) or pre-aggregate the many-side in a CTE; NOT IN with a subquery containing a single NULL returns zero rows while NOT EXISTS does the right thing; COUNT(col) skips NULLs but COUNT(*) does not; AVG ignores NULLs so a mean over a partially-null column is over a different denominator than you think; and integer division truncates unless you cast. Know COALESCE versus NULLIF, FILTER (WHERE ...) on aggregates as the clean alternative to CASE-inside-SUM, and DISTINCT ON as the Postgres shortcut for per-group latest. Practise stating the invariant before running: 'this should return exactly one row per customer per month; I will assert that with a GROUP BY HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 check.'

resource.label: PostgreSQL - Table Expressions (joins, ON vs WHERE, lateral)

subtopics.name: AI-assisted build: rules of engagement and review discipline
subtopics.learn: In the assistant-allowed round the assistant is not the subject - your control loop is. Fix a protocol before the drills: state the plan and the file layout out loud before prompting; prompt in units small enough to review in under a minute (one function, one endpoint, one test file) rather than 'build the whole thing'; read every generated diff line by line out loud, naming what you accept and what you reject and why; write or at least specify the tests yourself so the assistant cannot grade its own homework; and never paste code you cannot explain. Know the specific things assistants get wrong that you must catch on sight: invented library functions and kwargs, silent except: pass, off-by-one in slicing and date ranges, timezone-naive datetimes mixed with aware ones, no pagination on a list endpoint, secrets or absolute paths hardcoded, and tests that assert the implementation rather than the behaviour. Practise saying 'I'm rejecting this because...' - the sentence the interviewer is waiting for.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform documentation

subtopics.name: Drill 1 (25 min, recorded): messy transaction CSV to a reconciled monthly metric
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill on the payments corpus. Task: produce monthly net revenue per customer segment from a raw export where amount has currency symbols, dates come in two formats, refunds appear as separate negative rows with a matching original_transaction_id, and roughly 3% of rows are exact duplicates from a re-export. Requirements you must hit inside 25 minutes: profile first and say the row count and null counts aloud; dedupe explicitly with a stated key; coerce numerics and report how many values failed to parse; produce one row per (segment, month) with revenue, refund_amount, refund_rate and transaction count; and finish with a reconciliation - the sum of your output must equal the sum of the cleaned input, asserted in code, not eyeballed. Score yourself on whether you had a defensible partial answer by minute 15.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - IO tools (read_csv parsing options, dtypes, parse_dates)

subtopics.name: Drill 2 (25 min, recorded): multi-table join with fan-out you must catch
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill designed so the naive answer is wrong. Given orders, order_items, customers and a customers_history table with one row per attribute change, compute revenue per customer tier as of the order date. The traps: joining customers_history without an as-of condition multiplies every order by the number of history rows; order_items has a many relationship to orders so a naive merge inflates order-level totals; and a few customer_ids exist in orders but not customers. Do it correctly with merge(..., validate='m:1') to make the fan-out raise instead of silently corrupting, an explicit pre-aggregation of order_items before joining up, and pd.merge_asof for the point-in-time tier lookup with by= and direction='backward'. Narrate the row-count check after every merge - 'orders was 84,102 rows, after the merge it is 84,102, good' - because that sentence is what a senior reviewer is listening for.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Merge, join, concatenate and compare

subtopics.name: Drill 3 (25 min, recorded): event stream sessionisation and rolling windows
subtopics.learn: Timed pandas drill on the event corpus. Task: from raw timestamped events, define sessions with a 30-minute inactivity gap per user, then report median session length, events per session, and a 7-day rolling count of active users. The mechanics you must execute cleanly: sort by user and timestamp, compute the gap with groupby('user_id')['ts'].diff(), build session ids with (gap > pd.Timedelta('30min')).groupby(level).cumsum(), aggregate per session, then resample('D') and rolling('7D') on a DatetimeIndex. Handle the real complications out loud: timestamps arriving as UTC strings that must be tz-localised before comparison (mixing naive and aware raises), days with zero events that must appear as zeros rather than be dropped by groupby, and a user whose clock is skewed producing a negative diff. Report medians and p95, not means.

resource.label: pandas User Guide - Time series and date functionality

subtopics.name: Drill 4 (30 min, recorded): SQL window analytics on an undocumented schema
subtopics.learn: Timed SQL drill against your local Postgres with the schema shown but not explained - the realistic customer situation. Answer four escalating questions in one session: monthly revenue with month-over-month percent change using LAG; each customer's second-largest order using ROW_NUMBER in a CTE; a 28-day trailing average of daily orders with an explicit ROWS frame; and each customer's rank within their segment by lifetime value with ties handled by DENSE_RANK. Constraints that make it real: you must first orient yourself out loud by querying the catalog (information_schema.columns, plus a quick COUNT(*) and a five-row sample per table) rather than assuming, and every query must be preceded by a one-sentence statement of the expected grain of the result. Verify each result with an independent check - a spot-check on one customer computed a different way.

resource.label: PostgreSQL Tutorial - Window Functions

subtopics.name: Drill 5 (30 min, recorded): dedupe, point-in-time correctness, gaps and islands
subtopics.learn: Timed SQL drill on the three patterns that separate people who have shipped customer pipelines from people who have not. One: deduplicate a change-data-capture table to the latest row per business key using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) = 1, and explain why the tiebreak column matters when updated_at is not unique. Two: an as-of join - attach the price that was in effect when each order was placed, using a LATERAL subquery or a range-bounded join, and demonstrate the wrong answer you get without it. Three: gaps and islands - find each customer's longest run of consecutive active months using the difference-of-row-numbers trick, and separately find the missing months with generate_series and a LEFT JOIN. Say the grain and the expected row count before executing every one.

resource.label: PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)

subtopics.name: Drill 6 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): CSV to a tested, runnable service
subtopics.learn: Timed build with an assistant in the loop. Deliverable: a small FastAPI service that ingests one of your messy CSVs, normalises it, and exposes GET /metrics with query params for date range and segment, plus a health endpoint, with pytest tests that pass and a one-command run. Sequence it deliberately - contract first (write the response Pydantic model and one failing test before any implementation), then the loader, then the endpoint, then pagination and input validation. Non-negotiables that the interviewer will look for: typed request/response models with explicit field constraints, 422 on bad input rather than a 500, a test that exercises the empty-result case and a test on the parsing of one deliberately dirty row, and no unbounded response. Narrate every accept/reject decision on generated code, and at minute 40 stop building and spend five minutes running the tests and stating what is not done.

resource.label: FastAPI - Tutorial: User Guide

subtopics.name: Drill 7 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): LLM extraction with strict schema and a mini eval
subtopics.learn: Timed build: turn 200 unstructured records (support tickets, invoices or emails from your own corpus) into validated structured rows. Required shape: a Pydantic model with enums and constrained types as the extraction schema, a provider call using structured output or a tool schema so the model cannot return free text, validation on the way out with a rejected-rows path rather than a silent drop, bounded concurrency with a semaphore, retries with jittered backoff on transient errors only, and a per-record cache keyed on content hash so re-runs are free. Then the part most candidates skip and the one that wins the round: hand-label 20 records, score the extractor field-by-field, and report precision on the two fields that matter plus a count of records that failed validation. Say the cost and the p95 latency out loud at the end.

resource.label: Pydantic documentation (models, validation, constrained types)

subtopics.name: Drill 8 (45 min, recorded, AI-assisted): mid-build requirement change
subtopics.learn: The realistic FDE variant: build for 25 minutes, then have a pre-written envelope change the requirement, exactly as a customer does on a Thursday. Sample changes to draw from - the metric must now be computed per timezone-local day instead of UTC; the input arrives as a stream of JSON lines instead of one CSV; the customer needs the last 12 months backfilled and the job must be idempotent on re-run; a second file format must be supported with the same output contract. What is scored is the first ninety seconds after the change: do you restate the new requirement, name what breaks, propose the smallest change that satisfies it, and say explicitly what you are dropping to fit the time - or do you silently start refactoring. Keep the existing tests green through the change, add one test that would have failed before it, and finish with a spoken summary of what shipped, what regressed, and what you would do next.

resource.label: pytest documentation (fixtures, parametrize, tmp_path)

subtopics.name: Watch the tapes: error taxonomy and the second pass
subtopics.learn: The recordings are worthless unless you mine them. For each of the eight, log in GRADES.md: minutes to first correct partial answer, longest silence in seconds, the number of times you ran code before saying what you expected it to return, every correctness bug and its class (dtype, join fan-out, NULL, timezone, off-by-one, assistant-generated), and the one sentence you wish you had said. Build a running error taxonomy and note that the same two classes will account for most of your failures - drill those specifically rather than doing more random exercises. Then do a second pass on the two worst drills under the same clock and confirm the delta with numbers, not feeling. Add assert-based self-checks to your fixture repo (pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal against a saved expected output) so future re-runs are graded automatically instead of by memory.

resource.label: pandas - Testing utilities (assert_frame_equal)

outcomes: You can profile an unfamiliar dirty dataset and state its row count, null profile, duplicate count and the two dtype problems that will bite you, out loud, within the first three minutes of a timed drill.
You can produce a correct grouped, joined and time-bucketed answer in pandas within 25 minutes on a dataset you have never seen, and reconcile the output total against the cleaned input in code.
You can write ROW_NUMBER, LAG, a ROWS-framed rolling aggregate, an as-of join and a gaps-and-islands query in SQL without a reference open, and explain the ROWS-versus-RANGE difference on demand.
You can catch a join fan-out at the moment it happens because you state the expected row count before every merge and check it after - visible on every one of your eight tapes.

You can complete a 45-minute AI-assisted build that ends with passing tests, a typed contract, and a spoken list of what is not done, having narrated an accept/reject decision on every block of generated code.
You can absorb a mid-build requirement change and, within ninety seconds, restate it, name what breaks, propose the minimal change, and say what you are cutting to fit the clock.
You keep your longest silence under fifteen seconds across all eight recordings, including while reading a traceback, measured from the tape rather than estimated.
You can show an error taxonomy across eight drills with your two dominant bug classes named, and a second-pass recording that demonstrates a measured improvement on both.
failureModes: You merge two customer tables without checking cardinality, the many-side fans out, and every revenue number you present to the customer is inflated by a factor nobody notices until finance reconciles the quarter.
A numeric column arrives as object because of thousands separators, the sum silently concatenates strings or coerces to NaN, and the dashboard ships with a metric that is off by orders of magnitude.
A LEFT JOIN with the right table's column filtered in WHERE quietly becomes an INNER JOIN, so customers with no matching rows vanish from the report and the customer's own count never matches yours.
Timestamps are compared across a mix of tz-aware and naive datetimes, so daily aggregates are shifted by hours and month boundaries land in the wrong bucket for every customer outside UTC.
You accept assistant-generated code with a bare except that swallows parse errors, and the pipeline reports success while silently discarding every malformed record for weeks.

You go quiet for four minutes debugging, the interviewer loses the thread, and the write-up says 'strong coder, unclear how they would work with a customer in the room' - which is a no for an FDE role.
You spend twenty of your twenty-five minutes perfecting ingestion and never produce a number, so there is nothing to grade on the axis that actually matters.
interviewQuestions: Here is a 900k-row export and a question about monthly revenue. Talk me through your first three minutes before you write any aggregation - what do you check and what would make you stop and ask me something?
You join orders to a customer attributes table and the row count goes from 84,000 to 310,000. Walk me through how you diagnose it and what the correct query looks like if attributes change over time.
Write, out loud, the query for each customer's second-largest order. Now do it in a dialect without QUALIFY, and tell me what changes if two orders tie exactly.
You used an assistant to generate this loader. Show me a line you rejected and tell me why - and tell me what class of bug you have learned to look for first in generated code.
Your extraction pipeline reports 98% success but the customer says records are missing. The code has no errors in the logs. How do you find out what happened?

Halfway through a build the customer says the metric must be per local business day, not UTC, and they need twelve months backfilled idempotently. What do you change, what do you drop, and what do you tell them by end of day?
You are on a screen share with a customer's data engineer and your first answer turns out to be wrong. What do you actually say, and what do you do next?
85.proofOfWork: Beyond the eight recorded drills, publish a repository called fde-drill-kit that turns your practice into a reusable, evidence-backed system another engineer could run tomorrow. It ships three synthetic-but-realistic corpora (payments, CRM and event-stream) generated by a seeded script so the defects are reproducible and documented - a defects.md naming each planted trap (mixed date formats, currency-symbol numerics, CDC duplicates with non-unique updated_at, whitespace in join keys, a tz-skewed clock, orphan foreign keys) and the query or cell that exposes it. It ships a docker compose that loads the same data into Postgres so every prompt exists in both pandas and SQL form, a prompts/ directory with all eight drill prompts written the way an interviewer would write them (underspecified, with the ambiguity deliberate), and a solutions/ directory with a reference answer plus an assert-based grader using pandas.testing.assert_frame_equal and SQL count assertions, so anyone can self-score without your judgement. The credibility comes from the evidence section: a GRADES.md with one row per drill recording minutes-to-first-partial-answer, longest silence in seconds, bug classes hit, and rubric score across all five axes, plus the second-pass rows for the two worst drills showing the measured delta; an ERRORS.md distilling the taxonomy down to your two dominant failure classes with the specific drill timestamps where each occurred; and an index page linking the eight unedited recordings. Send that one link when a recruiter asks how you prepare, and it answers the coding question and the self-improvement question at once.

86.why: The two rounds that actually decide an FDE loop are the ones with no whiteboard: a role-play where an interviewer plays a customer stakeholder who does not want you there, and a learning round where they hand you an unfamiliar API or internal DSL and expect working output in twenty minutes. Both are direct simulations of the job - week two on site you are in a room with an architect whose system you are replacing, and week three you are reading someone's undocumented internal service at 9pm because the demo is Thursday. What gets you rejected is almost never ignorance; it is talking past a hostile question, and saying 'yes, we can do that by Friday' about something that needs their security team, which is the same behaviour that kills real deployments.
prerequisites: Your narrative and motivation work from topic 72, so the sim does not stall on 'why are you here' and you can spend the whole clock on the customer's problem.

The resume-defence discipline from topic 73: numerator, denominator, window, instrument - because in a client sim you will be asked to back a claim you make about your own past work while the clock runs.
Decomposition drills (topic 75) and LLM system design mocks (topic 76): the sim collapses if you cannot cut a vague ask into a demoable slice in under five minutes.

SLO literacy from the observability/SLO topic - good events over valid events over a window - so 'we need it to be 100% accurate' becomes a negotiable threshold conversation rather than a promise or a fight.

Enough hands-on fluency from topics 25-30 and 45-49 (Python services, Postgres, RAG, evals) that the technical objections in the sim - schema, latency, PII, retrieval quality - land on real knowledge rather than talking points.
Two or three practice partners willing to play adversarial for 45 minutes without rescuing you, plus a recording setup (screen + audio) and a transcription tool you have already tested end to end.

subtopics.name: Reverse-engineer what each round actually scores
subtopics.learn: Write the two rubrics before you practise anything, because you cannot improve against a vibe. Client sim scores roughly: discovery quality (did you find the real constraint, or the one they volunteered), structure (did the conversation have a shape and an ending), pushback handling (did you stay in the room), commitment hygiene (did you promise things you do not control), and closing (is there a dated next step with named owners). Learning interview scores: how fast you get to a first working call, whether your questions are falsifying rather than clarifying, whether you narrate a mental model out loud, and how quickly you notice and correct a wrong assumption. Convert each dimension into a behavioural anchor you can count on tape - 'asked 9 questions before naming a solution' - not a 1-5 gut score.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Structured interview (behavioural anchors and scoring)

subtopics.name: Build four scenario packs from real deployment shapes
subtopics.learn: Write four packs your partner reads and you do not: (1) a mid-size insurer wants LLM triage on claims notes and the ops director thinks it is a headcount cut; (2) a stalled deployment where your champion left and the new VP wants to cancel in 30 days; (3) integration blocked by a security architect who will not allow data to leave the VPC; (4) a customer who was burned by the previous vendor's pilot that never reached production. Each pack gives the persona a goal, a fear, one hidden constraint that only surfaces if you ask the right question (e.g. the 'API' is a nightly SFTP drop of fixed-width files), and three landmines to detonate at minute 10, 25 and 35. Add a success bar per pack: exactly what you must have extracted and committed to for it to count as a pass.

resource.label: CISA Tabletop Exercise Packages - scenario design with objectives, injects and discussion questions

subtopics.name: The ten-minute pre-brief you run before any customer call
subtopics.learn: Standardise a pre-call kit and run it before every sim so it is muscle memory on site: how the company makes money and which line item your work touches; the org around your champion (who signs, who blocks, who gets blamed); the systems of record they already run (Salesforce? SAP? a Snowflake they just migrated to?); public signals - 10-K risk factors, earnings call language, job postings that reveal their stack, status page incident history, engineering blog. Turn it into three written hypotheses about where the pain is, each phrased so a single question in the meeting can kill it. Walking in with hypotheses is what separates discovery from an interrogation.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Form 10-K (risk factors, MD&A, segment reporting)

subtopics.name: The discovery ladder: symptom to workflow to system to metric
subtopics.learn: Drill a fixed four-rung sequence. Symptom: 'what happens today, walk me through the last time it went wrong.' Workflow: who touches it, in what order, in which tool, and what do they do when the tool is wrong. System: what is the system of record, what writes to it, how does data arrive and at what cadence, what is the actual schema. Metric: volume per day, minutes per unit, error rate, cost of a false positive versus a false negative, and who currently owns that number. Ban solution-shaped questions ('would you want a dashboard?') until you are on the fourth rung - the customer will happily design the wrong thing with you. Practise until you can run all four rungs in eight minutes without a script.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Five whys (root-cause questioning and its limits)

subtopics.name: Constraint and authority elicitation in the room
subtopics.learn: Get the boring blockers on the table in the first meeting, because they are what actually slip deployments: where the data physically lives and whether you can get a sample this week, who provisions credentials and how long that has historically taken, whether there is a VPC/air-gap/on-prem requirement, whether a DPA or vendor security review is needed and who runs it, what date is genuinely fixed (board demo, audit, contract renewal) and what happens if it slips. Then map authority explicitly - who is responsible, who approves, who must merely be consulted or informed - and ask out loud 'who else has to say yes after this meeting?' Anyone you fail to name will surface in week four as a surprise veto.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Responsibility assignment matrix (RACI)

subtopics.name: Hostile stakeholder taxonomy and what each one actually wants
subtopics.learn: Learn the five archetypes and the tell for each. The threatened incumbent built the pipeline you are replacing and attacks your design because attacking his own record is unthinkable - he wants credit and continuity, so make him the owner of the interface. The burned buyer opens with 'the last vendor promised this too' and wants a checkable near-term proof, not a roadmap. The gatekeeper architect asks latency and encryption questions as a proxy for control - answer precisely, then ask him to define the acceptance bar. The proxy attends for an absent decision-maker and cannot say yes, only no - your goal is a meeting with the principal. The budget skeptic wants a number tied to their own P&L line. Misreading which one you are facing produces technically correct answers that lose the room.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Chesterton's fence (why the existing system exists)

subtopics.name: De-escalation mechanics: acknowledge, specify, bound
subtopics.learn: Under attack, run a three-beat pattern instead of defending. Acknowledge by restating the objection more precisely than they stated it ('you are saying that if the classifier is wrong on a high-value claim, your adjuster carries the liability, not us'). Specify by separating the factual claim from the fear - which part is measurable, which part is trust. Bound by giving an answer with a number and a condition ('on the 200 notes you gave us, precision at the threshold we would ship is X; below that we route to a human'). Never counter-assert, never 'actually', never speed up. On tape, watch for the physical tells - words per minute jumping, filler stacking, the pronoun switching from 'we' to 'I' - because interviewers score composure from exactly those signals.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Active listening (reflection, paraphrase, clarification)

subtopics.name: Disagreeing on technical substance without losing the room
subtopics.learn: Rehearse the three standard wrong asks and hold the line on each. 'Just fine-tune it on our data' - agree with the goal, name why retrieval and evals come first, offer a cheap test that settles it. 'Put everything in the vector database' - ask what queries must be answered and show which ones need filters, joins or recency that similarity search will not give. 'It has to be 100% accurate' - reframe as an error budget: what is the cost of each error class, what threshold routes to a human, what is the review loop. The move is always: accept the objective, name the constraint that breaks their approach, propose a decisive experiment with a date. Practise saying 'I think that will not work, and here is the test that would prove me wrong' out loud until it sounds calm.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives (error budgets)

subtopics.name: Security, PII and data-residency objections
subtopics.learn: The single most common blocker in an AI deployment conversation is 'our data cannot go to a model provider', and vague answers here read as unserious. Be able to state, without notes: enterprise zero-retention and no-training-by-default terms, in-VPC or cloud-marketplace model hosting as an alternative, what redaction at the boundary can and cannot remove, why prompt injection makes tool permissions the real attack surface rather than the prompt, and what you log for audit (inputs, outputs, retrieved doc ids, user, timestamp). Then invert the question: ask what their existing approved path for a SaaS vendor looks like, and which control they need evidence for. You are trying to convert a blanket objection into a named control with an owner.

resource.label: OWASP LLM02:2025 - Sensitive Information Disclosure (PII exposure, sanitisation limits, controls)

subtopics.name: Commitment hygiene: the four verbs you are allowed to use
subtopics.learn: Every future-tense sentence in a customer meeting is a contract. Restrict yourself to four forms: 'I will X by DATE' only when every dependency is inside your control; 'I will find out and come back to you by DATE' for anything that needs someone else; 'we could X, which would cost roughly Y' for an option that is explicitly not yet a commitment; and 'we will not do X' as a stated boundary. Ban the killers outright - 'that should be easy', 'we can definitely', 'by end of week' about anything crossing a team boundary, 'no problem'. Practise catching yourself mid-sentence and converting: 'we can have that by Friday' becomes 'I can have the pipeline running Friday if I have read access by Tuesday; the SSO piece depends on your identity team, so I will get you a date from them by Wednesday.'

resource.label: Wikipedia - Statement of work (deliverables, acceptance, dependencies)

subtopics.name: Estimating live without lying
subtopics.learn: When asked 'how long', never emit a single number. Decompose out loud into 3-5 chunks (access and data landing, ingest and normalisation, the model/logic slice, evaluation, the integration to their system of record), give a range on each, and name the top two uncertainty drivers plus the assumption that would blow the estimate up ('this assumes the notes are text, not scanned PDFs'). Anchor on a reference class - 'the last three deployments of this shape took 4-7 weeks to first production traffic' - rather than on optimism. The strongest available answer is often a timeboxed spike: 'give me three days and the sample file and I will replace this range with a real number.' Note explicitly that your estimate is conditional on a dated input from them, which makes slippage a shared fact rather than your failure.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Reference class forecasting

subtopics.name: Scope the thin slice and land the close
subtopics.learn: Every sim must end with the same four-part close, delivered in under 90 seconds: one sentence restating the problem in their words and their units; the thinnest demoable slice with a date (one workflow, one data source, one user, one metric); the three things you need from them, each with a named person and a date - access, a sample of real data, and a decision-maker's calendar; and the explicit non-goals for this slice. Choose the slice by what retires the most risk, not what demos best: if the whole deployment dies on data quality, the slice is a profiling report on their actual export, not a chat UI. Rehearse the close on its own until it is automatic, because in a real meeting it always gets squeezed into the last two minutes.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Minimum viable product

subtopics.name: Handling the mid-meeting scope grenade
subtopics.learn: At minute 30 someone asks 'can it also handle the EU entity / French documents / our legacy system?' Wrong answers are 'sure' and 'that is out of scope'. The move: acknowledge it as a real requirement, ask the sizing question ('does the pilot fail if it ships without it, or is it a phase-two must?'), write it in a visible parking lot with the person's name against it, and restate the slice unchanged. If it genuinely invalidates the slice, say so immediately and re-scope in the room rather than absorbing it silently - silent absorption is how a four-week pilot becomes a four-month one with the same original date.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Scope creep

subtopics.name: The two-hour written recap
subtopics.learn: Within two hours of every sim, send the recap you would send a real customer, and have your partner grade it against what they actually said. Fixed sections: decisions made; open questions with an owner and a date each; what I committed to (dated, only things you control); what I did not commit to (explicit, so it cannot be assumed later); risks and the assumption each one rests on. Keep it under 300 words, put the asks in a list not a paragraph, and send it in the existing thread so it is searchable. The purpose is to force the customer to correct you in writing while the meeting is still fresh - a recap nobody disputes is the cheapest contract you will ever get.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing Two - writing for your reader

subtopics.name: Learning interview: the twenty-minute doc triage protocol
subtopics.learn: Fix a protocol so you never freeze on unfamiliar docs. Minutes 0-3: map the shape - quickstart, reference, errors/limits, changelog - and find the smallest complete example. Minutes 3-8: get one end-to-end call working with hardcoded inputs, verifying the environment (auth, versions, endpoint) before writing any logic. Minutes 8-15: expand only along the axis the task requires, reading the reference page for the exact parameters you use rather than reading linearly. Throughout: grep the docs and the repo instead of scrolling, read error messages as specification, check the errors/limits page before assuming a bug is yours, and use --help, man and the tool's own introspection first. Never read a doc site front-to-back on a clock.

resource.label: MIT Missing Semester - Shell tools and scripting (finding help)

subtopics.name: Learning interview: state the model, then apply it, out loud
subtopics.learn: Before you write anything, say the mental model back in 60 seconds: the objects, the verbs, the lifecycle, the units, and the failure states ('so a Workflow is durable and must be deterministic, an Activity is the part allowed to be non-deterministic and gets retried by policy - what happens if an Activity is not idempotent?'). Then ask two falsifying questions, not clarifying ones: questions whose answer changes what you build. While working, narrate hypothesis, test, result, update - 'I expect this to fail on the second call because the token is scoped per session; let us see.' Interviewers cannot score silent competence, and in front of a customer the same narration is what turns confusion into visible progress instead of dead air.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Think aloud protocol

subtopics.name: Learning drill mechanics: timer, artifact, error-first log
subtopics.learn: Structure every learning rep identically: a 20-minute hard timer, a stated goal you did not choose in advance (have your partner pick), a working artifact at the end, and a 'what I got wrong first' note listing every incorrect assumption and how long it cost you. Score three things: time to first working call, number of times you guessed a flag or field name instead of checking it, and whether you verified output or assumed it. Guessing an API parameter and asserting it confidently is the single most damaging habit in this round - in front of a customer it is how you end up debugging your own hallucination on a screen share. Start with jq: build a filter over a real nested JSON export using to_entries, select, --slurp and --raw-output, and explain why the streaming model differs from loading the whole file.

resource.label: jq tutorial - build filters over a real nested JSON API response

subtopics.name: Four unfamiliar-tool reps with concrete targets
subtopics.learn: Run four timed reps on tools you do not know, each producing an artifact. DuckDB: query a Parquet file directly with read_parquet, aggregate with a window function, and COPY the result out - explain columnar versus row scan cost. Temporal: write a workflow plus an activity with a retry policy, and state the determinism constraint and what breaks if you call time.now() inside a workflow. Terraform: plan and apply a trivial resource, then explain state, drift, and why -target is a break-glass rather than a workflow. A model API: make one structured-output/tool-use call and describe how errors and token limits surface. Space the four reps across the month rather than batching them, so you are practising cold starts, which is the actual skill being tested.

resource.label: Temporal docs - Workflows (replay, determinism constraints, why Date.now() breaks)

subtopics.name: Tape review: score your own recordings against the rubric
subtopics.learn: Transcribe all eight recordings and count, do not impressionistically judge. Metrics per sim: questions asked before you first named a solution (target 8+), your share of talk time during discovery (target under 45%), seconds of dead air after the hardest pushback, number of unhedged future-tense statements, number of times you said 'I do not know' followed by a path, and whether the close contained all four parts. Per learning interview: time to first working call, guessed-versus-checked ratio, and the count of wrong assumptions you caught yourself. Chart the six numbers across the four reps - flat lines mean you are performing, not practising, and the fix is usually a harder partner rather than more reps.

resource.label: OpenAI Whisper (speech-to-text, official repo)

subtopics.name: The promises-you-couldn't-keep ledger
subtopics.learn: Mine every transcript for future-tense and capability statements and classify each: (a) in your control and dated - fine; (b) depended on someone else - should have been 'I will get you a date'; (c) technically false or unknowable at the time - the dangerous class; (d) vague enough that the customer and you would remember it differently - the class that actually causes deployment disputes. Compute promises-per-sim and the share in classes (b)-(d), and write the replacement phrasing for each one. Review it like a blameless postmortem: the interesting question is what pressure produced the promise - an uncomfortable silence, a status challenge, wanting to be liked - because that pressure is identical on site with a real customer and a real renewal date.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

outcomes: You can run a 45-minute client simulation that ends with a restated problem, a dated thin slice, three named asks with owners, and explicit non-goals - without ever proposing a solution in the first eight minutes.
You can name which hostile archetype you are facing within five minutes, cite the tell that told you, and adapt the conversation accordingly on tape.
You can take a direct attack on your design and respond with acknowledge-specify-bound in under 20 seconds of dead air, verified by transcript timing across four recordings.
You can convert any 'can you do it by Friday' into a conditional commitment that names the dependency, the owner and the date you will supply the real answer.
You can produce a written recap within two hours that your role-play partner signs off as an accurate record of decisions, commitments and non-commitments.
You can go from zero knowledge of a tool to a working, verified artifact in under 20 minutes while narrating hypotheses, with a written log of every wrong assumption and its cost.
You can state an unfamiliar system's object model, lifecycle and failure states back in 60 seconds and ask two questions whose answers would change your implementation.
You have a promises ledger across eight recordings showing the count of unbacked commitments falling rep over rep, with the replacement phrasing written for each.
failureModes: A date is committed in the room that silently depends on the customer's security review or identity team, and when it slips by three weeks the customer records it as the vendor missing a deadline rather than their own queue.

The pilot is scoped off the workflow the champion described, and in week three the data turns out to arrive as a nightly fixed-width SFTP drop rather than the API everyone referred to, invalidating the ingest design.

The engineer wins the argument with the customer's architect on technical merit, publicly, and the architect - who owns the change-approval process - becomes a permanent silent blocker on every subsequent request.

'It needs to be accurate' is accepted without defining an error budget, a threshold or a human-review route, so a 92%-precision system that saves real money is judged a failure against an unstated 100% bar.

A capability is asserted from memory during a demo - a parameter, a connector, a limit that does not exist - and the customer's engineer finds the doc page contradicting it within the hour, which costs more trust than saying 'I do not know' would have.
Scope added mid-meeting is absorbed silently rather than parked, and the four-week pilot quietly becomes ten weeks of work still owed on the original date.
The meeting ends warm with no owner, no date and no written recap, and by the next call the customer remembers a broader promise than was made, with no artifact that can settle it.
interviewQuestions: You are two weeks into a deployment. The customer's lead architect - who built the rules engine you are replacing - says in front of his VP that your approach will not scale and that they have seen this fail before. What do you say next, word for word, and what do you do after the meeting?

A customer asks in the room whether you can have this live before their board demo in three weeks. You genuinely do not know. Give me your actual answer, and tell me what you would need to say instead if it turns out the answer is no.

Their compliance lead says no customer data may leave their VPC and no third-party model may be used. Walk me through how you keep the project alive - what you ask, what options you put on the table, and what you would refuse to promise.
Run discovery on me: I am a support operations director drowning in tickets and I have already decided I want a chatbot. You have ten minutes to find out whether that is the right thing to build.
Here is the documentation for an internal service you have never seen. In twenty minutes, get a working call through and tell me what the system's failure modes are - narrate as you go.

Tell me about a time you told a customer or a stakeholder something that turned out not to be true. How did you find out, how did you handle it, and what did you change about how you commit to things?
Your champion just left the company and the new VP wants to cancel in 30 days. You get one 30-minute meeting. What is your agenda, and what is the single artifact you bring?
86.proofOfWork: Beyond the eight recordings and the promises ledger, publish a redacted 'deployment call kit' repository that turns this month into a reusable instrument rather than a set of memories. It contains: the four scenario packs, written so any partner can run them cold - persona brief, hidden constraint, three timed landmines, and the explicit pass bar per scenario; the two scoring rubrics with behavioural anchors and a CSV of your own scores across all eight reps, plus a small chart showing the six countable metrics (questions before first solution, discovery talk ratio, dead-air seconds after hardest pushback, unhedged commitments, time-to-first-working-call, guessed-versus-checked ratio) trending across reps, including the ones that did not improve; a de-escalation phrasebook built from your own transcripts, where each entry is the objection as it was actually spoken, the response you actually gave with a timestamp, and the rewritten response, so the improvement is traceable to a specific moment on tape; the promises ledger with every future-tense statement classified as in-control, dependent, false, or ambiguous, with a per-rep rate and replacement phrasing; and one 20-minute unedited screen recording of a learning rep on a tool you had never used, ending in a working artifact and a committed 'what I got wrong first' note listing each wrong assumption and the minutes it cost. The part a hiring manager will actually read is the phrasebook and the ledger - together they show someone who instruments their own behaviour under pressure, which is precisely the trait that keeps a deployment from quietly overcommitting itself to death.

87.topic: STAR stories (ten) and two full-loop simulations
87.why: An FDE is hired to be trusted alone in a customer's building, so the behavioural round is not a personality check - it is the panel's only direct evidence about how you behave when a VP is angry, when you broke their pipeline, when the scope was never written down, and when you had to hand the system to someone less skilled than you and leave. Every other round in the loop tests whether you could build it; this one tests whether the company can put you in front of a paying customer without supervision. Ten pre-built, evidence-backed stories plus two rehearsed full loops is the difference between recalling incidents live under time pressure and executing a bank you already know cold.
prerequisites: The positioning and narrative from topic 72 - why FDE, why this company, travel and comp answers - since every story must ladder back to that same thesis.
The line-by-line resume defence from topic 73: each of the ten stories has to be traceable to a bullet you already committed to in writing.
Real delivered work with real numbers you can defend - the Lumen FDE deployment, the Omnibound GTM systems, the Deepline provider integrations - not hypotheticals.
Postmortem discipline from topic 23 (blameless timeline, contributing factors, action items with owners) so the failure and conflict stories have a defensible structure.
Discovery technique from topic 66 and the engagement document set from topic 67, which supply the vocabulary for the discovery, ambiguity and hand-off stories.
Cost literacy from topics 19 and 59, and security/compliance ground truth from topics 62 and 64, so the cost and security stories survive a follow-up.

The other four month-9 rounds already rehearsed at least once each - take-home (74), decomposition (75), LLM system design (76), coding (77), client sim (78) - because the full-loop simulations chain them back to back.

subtopics.name: What the FDE behavioural round is actually scoring
subtopics.learn: Write the scorecard down before writing any story. The panel is grading five independent axes: customer judgement (did you protect the relationship and the outcome, not your ego), ownership past the boundary of your job description, calibrated honesty about failure, ability to operate with no spec and no authority, and whether you make yourself unnecessary rather than indispensable. Learn the two dominant anti-signals: the hero story where you personally saved everything and nobody else exists, and the failure story where the root cause conveniently turns out to be someone else's team. Note the structural difference from a SWE behavioural loop - here the counterparty in most stories is a customer, not a colleague, and 'I escalated to my manager' is a weaker answer than 'I told the sponsor directly, in writing, the same day'.

resource.label: Exponent - Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: STAR mechanics: the 15/15/50/20 split and why the R loses points
subtopics.learn: Budget a three-minute answer as roughly 25 seconds of Situation, 25 of Task, 90 of Action, 40 of Result - then enforce it with a timer. Situation is who the customer was, what the system did, and one number establishing scale; anything else is stalling. Task is your specific ownership stated in first person singular, plus the constraint that made it hard. Action is a sequence of decisions with the alternatives you rejected and why - not a list of activities. Result is where nearly everyone fails: it needs a number, a comparison to the baseline, a durability claim (is it still true today?), and a 'what I would do differently'. Practise the specific fix for the most common defect - saying 'we' when the interviewer needs 'I' - by rewriting each story once in strict first person and reading it back for the places where the team genuinely deserves credit and you should say so.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Situation, task, action, result

subtopics.name: Incident harvest: 40 raw candidates before you write a single story
subtopics.learn: Do not start from the ten slots - start from raw material, or you will invent stories to fit labels. Spend this block mining sources you can actually cite: git log across your repos filtered to the months that mattered, closed PRs and their review threads, Slack and email archives searched for 'sorry', 'blocked', 'rollback', 'can we talk', incident channels, invoices and cloud bills, and your own calendar for the weeks that were obviously bad. Write 40 one-line candidates in a single file with a date, the counterparty, and the artifact that proves it happened. Only then map candidates onto slots. Kill anything with no artifact behind it; a story you cannot evidence is a story you will hedge on under follow-up, and hedging reads as fabrication.

resource.label: US OPM - Structured Interviews guide (behavioural questioning)

subtopics.name: The ten-slot coverage matrix and the anti-overlap rule
subtopics.learn: Build a grid: rows are the ten slots (discovery, conflict, failure, ambiguity, shipping, security, cost, hand-off, leadership, learning), columns are the attributes a panel probes - customer-facing, technical depth, cross-team influence, money, risk, a decision you regret. Every column needs at least two rows covering it, and no single project may occupy more than three rows or the bank collapses when an interviewer says 'give me a different example'. Explicitly place at least three stories where you were wrong and at least two where the counterparty was a paying customer's executive rather than an engineer. Then map each row onto the values language of your targets - Amazon's Customer Obsession, Ownership, Dive Deep, Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit; Earn Trust - not to parrot it but to check the bank has no blind spot the frame would expose.

resource.label: Amazon Leadership Principles

subtopics.name: The story card: metric spine, counterfactual, and defensible numbers
subtopics.learn: Standardise a one-page card per story: title, slot, 25-word hook, the four STAR blocks in bullets (never prose you will recite), a metric spine, an evidence list, three anticipated follow-ups with answers, and the two other slots this story can be re-cut for. The metric spine is the discipline that separates senior from mid: baseline value, post value, measurement window, the instrument that produced both numbers, and the confounders you are aware of. If your claim is 'cut p95 latency from 4.2s to 900ms', you must be able to say which endpoint, over which window, measured by which exporter, and what else changed that week. Where you genuinely cannot measure, say the counterfactual explicitly ('the alternative was three analysts doing it manually at roughly six minutes a case') rather than inventing precision - a fabricated number that collapses under one follow-up costs more than an honest estimate.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives (how to state a metric honestly)

subtopics.name: Stories 1-2: Discovery, and Ambiguity with no spec and no owner
subtopics.learn: Story 1 (discovery): a time the stated ask was not the real problem. The Action must contain actual questions you asked and the specific moment the picture changed - the ride-along, the exported spreadsheet someone was maintaining by hand, the row count that did not match. The Result must show you redirected the work without telling the sponsor they were stupid, and the number is the thing that actually moved. Story 2 (ambiguity): no requirements doc, contradictory stakeholders, or an unowned decision. Show the mechanism you used to manufacture clarity - a written assumption register circulated for objections, a one-week timeboxed spike with a stated exit question, a decision you made unilaterally and documented as an ADR with a named reversal date. Be ready for the killer follow-up on both: 'what if the sponsor had said no?'

resource.label: Google - Introduction to Machine Learning Problem Framing

subtopics.name: Stories 3-4: Conflict with a customer, and a failure you caused
subtopics.learn: Story 3 (conflict) must be with someone who had power over you - a customer architect who refused your design, a sponsor who wanted a feature you believed was wrong - and must end in either a changed mind with the mechanism shown (a shadow run with diffed outputs, a two-week bake-off, a cost model on one page) or in disagree-and-commit where you name what you did to make their choice succeed anyway. Story 4 (failure) must be one where you were the proximate cause, told in blameless-postmortem shape: timeline with timestamps, detection (who noticed - alert or customer?), time to mitigate, contributing factors plural, and action items that actually shipped with a link. State the blast radius honestly, including whose data or money was affected and how you communicated it. The tell of a rehearsed-but-fake failure story is a failure with no cost; pick one that hurt.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Stories 5-6: Shipping under a hard constraint, and a security or data-handling call
subtopics.learn: Story 5 (shipping): a real deadline with a real consequence, where the interesting content is what you cut and who you told. Name the scope you hammered, the thing you shipped manually or half-automated on purpose, the tech debt you took on knowingly, and whether you ever paid it back - 'we never went back' is an acceptable answer if you say why. Story 6 (security): a moment you handled credentials, PII, tenant isolation or third-party access properly when the fast path was to not. Concrete anchors beat abstractions: rotating a key that had been pasted into a config, moving from a long-lived access key to a role assumption, adding row-level security instead of filtering in application code, refusing to accept a production dump over email and building a sampled synthetic set instead, or catching an IDOR/broken-access-control issue before a customer did. Know the actual control name you applied.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 A01:2021 - Broken Access Control (IDOR, tenant isolation, enforcement in data not app code)

subtopics.name: Stories 7-8: Cost, and a hand-off that survived you leaving
subtopics.learn: Story 7 (cost): you found or prevented real spend. Show the instrumentation before the fix - cost per request, per tenant, per case - and the decision that followed: prompt caching, a smaller model on the cheap path, batching, right-sizing an instance family, killing an idle GPU, or an architectural change that removed the spend entirely. Give the monthly delta and the run-rate, and be honest about engineering time versus savings. Story 8 (hand-off): a system you built that someone else now runs. The Result is not 'they were happy' - it is the artifact set (runbook with the three most likely alerts and their first three commands, dashboard, on-call owner named, an escalation path, a documented process for prompt/model or schema changes) plus evidence it held: an incident they resolved without you, a change they shipped, a month you were not paged. Say what you got wrong about the hand-off, because everyone gets something wrong.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected - Cost Optimization Pillar

subtopics.name: Stories 9-10: Leadership without authority, and learning a domain cold
subtopics.learn: Story 9 (leadership): you changed the behaviour of people who did not report to you and could have ignored you. The mechanism is the story - a written proposal that got adopted, a prototype that ended an argument, a review standard you enforced by doing the first ten yourself, a customer team you trained. Name the person who disagreed and what convinced them, and give the credit outward where it is due; a leadership story where you are the only competent character reads as the opposite of leadership. Story 10 (learning): a domain or technology you were unqualified for on day one and shipped in. Show the method, not the outcome - who you shadowed, the glossary you built, the first thing you got embarrassingly wrong, how long until you were useful, and the calibration you now apply ('I assume week one is worthless and price it in'). This is the story that predicts whether you can be dropped into an unfamiliar vertical next quarter.

resource.label: Will Larson (StaffEng) - To lead, you have to follow (influence over people who don't report to you)

subtopics.name: Three lengths per story: 60 seconds, 3 minutes, 8 minutes
subtopics.learn: Every card gets three rehearsed versions, because interviewers cut you off at different depths. The 60-second version is answer-first in Minto pyramid order - the outcome and your role in the first sentence, then three supporting bullets - used when the interviewer is behind schedule or when the story is a supporting example inside a larger answer. The 3-minute version is the default full STAR. The 8-minute version is the deep-dive the hiring manager pulls you into, with architecture, the two alternatives you rejected, and the specific numbers; it must survive a whiteboard. Rehearse the transitions between them out loud, and rehearse the interrupt: when someone says 'skip ahead to what you did', you drop the Situation mid-sentence and land on Action cleanly rather than finishing your set-up.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle, answer-first structure)

subtopics.name: Follow-up drilling: the four probe types and defending your numbers
subtopics.learn: The story is the setup; the score comes from the follow-ups. Drill four types against every card until you stop flinching. Depth probes ('why that database / that chunk size / that retry policy?') test whether you actually built it - answer with the alternative and its trade-off. Counterfactual probes ('what if the customer had refused?') test judgement, not memory. Attribution probes ('what did you personally write?' / 'who else could have done this?') test honesty - answer them precisely and do not inflate. Credibility probes ('how do you know it was 40%?') test the metric spine - answer with instrument and window. Then run a two-level five-whys on each of your own stories and find the layer where you run out of answer; that layer is your prep list. Rehearse three sentences you can say honestly when you genuinely do not know, ending with what you would check.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Five whys

subtopics.name: Company-specific reframes without sounding coached
subtopics.learn: One bank, three lenses. For a Palantir-style loop, foreground the forward-deployed posture: on-site, unfamiliar data, institutional resistance, shipping something a non-engineer used. For an Anthropic-style loop, foreground judgement under uncertainty, safety and honesty trade-offs, and the times you slowed down or told a customer no. For a Databricks or platform-vendor loop, foreground scale, cost per unit of work, and enabling the customer's own engineers rather than doing the work for them. The reframe is which detail you lead with and which number you quote - never a different set of facts. Read the actual careers and values pages of your target list before the loop and note the specific language they use, then check your stories can answer their frame without you reciting their words back at them, which is the fastest way to sound coached.

resource.label: Anthropic - Core Views on AI Safety (the primary values document an Anthropic-style loop reframes toward)

subtopics.name: Delivery: filler, pacing, and landing the 'so what'
subtopics.learn: Record every story once and watch it with the sound on and once with the transcript only. Count filler ('so', 'basically', 'kind of', 'I guess') per minute and drive it under three by replacing each with a silent pause - a beat reads as thinking, filler reads as hedging. Check three delivery defects specifically: trailing off at the end instead of landing the result, upspeak that turns claims into questions, and burning 60 of your 180 seconds on Situation. Fix the landing with a fixed closing move - one sentence of result with the number, one sentence of what you would do differently, then stop talking and let them ask. On video calls, look at the camera for the first and last sentence of each story. Re-record until three consecutive stories land inside 3:00 +/- 20 seconds without notes.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Filler (linguistics)

subtopics.name: Full-loop simulation #1: four back-to-back rounds, same day, recorded
subtopics.learn: Run a real loop shape in one sitting with only short breaks, because fatigue is the variable no single mock tests: 45 min coding or data manipulation (topic 77), 45 min decomposition or LLM system design (topics 75/76), 45 min client simulation with a hostile or confused stakeholder (topic 78), 45 min behavioural drawn from your bank with the interviewer free to demand a second example for any slot. Use a peer, or book paid sessions on interviewing.io if you want strangers who will not go easy. Rules: camera on, no notes visible, no restarts, record everything. Instruct your interviewer in advance to do the two things friends avoid - interrupt mid-story, and push twice on every number. Note your own energy at rounds three and four; that drop is what you are training against.

resource.label: interviewing.io - Senior engineer's guide to FAANG interview loops (round-by-round onsite structure)

subtopics.name: Full-loop simulation #2, after-action review, and bank revision
subtopics.learn: Run the second loop at least three days after the first, with a different opponent and a shuffled round order so you cannot rely on warm-up. Debrief both with a structured after-action review rather than vibes: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why the gap, what changes - written within an hour while the tape is fresh. Score each behavioural answer on five axes (structure held, first-person ownership, number defended under probe, time budget hit, honest failure content) and diff the two loops. Then do the revision work the debrief demands: retire the two stories that consistently drew weak follow-ups, promote a bench story, and rewrite every Result whose number you could not defend twice. Finish with a one-page cheat card - ten titles, ten numbers, ten 'what I'd do differently' clauses - that you read in the sixty seconds before every real interview.

resource.label: Wikipedia - After-action review

outcomes: You can name any of the ten slots cold and deliver that story in 3:00 +/- 20 seconds, with no notes, on camera, hitting a 15/15/50/20 STAR split.
Every story's Result contains a baseline, a post value, a measurement window and the instrument that produced both - and you can survive two consecutive 'how do you know that number?' probes on each.
You can give a second, non-overlapping example for at least six of the ten slots when the interviewer says 'that one doesn't count, give me another'.

You can tell a failure story in which you were the proximate cause, state the blast radius including whose data or money was affected, and name shipped action items - without shifting blame or minimising cost.
You can compress any story to 60 seconds answer-first and expand it to an 8-minute deep dive with architecture and rejected alternatives, and switch between them when interrupted mid-sentence.
You can re-frame the same story for a Palantir-, Anthropic- and Databricks-style loop by changing which detail leads and which number you quote, without changing any fact.
You have two recorded four-round loops with written after-action reviews, a scored diff between them, and at least two stories retired or rewritten as a direct result.
You can say 'I don't know' about a detail in your own story and follow it with what you would check, in under fifteen seconds, without hedging or filler.
failureModes: The Result is 'the customer was happy' with no number, so the story is unfalsifiable and the interviewer moves on without writing down a single piece of evidence.
You inflate a metric slightly - 40% instead of the 15% you can actually source - and it collapses under one credibility probe, which retroactively discredits the other nine stories.
Every story is 'we' with no separable personal contribution, and the panel cannot tell whether you led the work or sat next to it.
The failure story is a cost-free failure (a flaky test, a missed typo), which reads as either dishonesty or as never having owned anything that could break.
Three of your ten stories come from the same project, so 'give me a different example' takes you to material you have not rehearsed and you improvise a weaker version of a story you already told.
You burn 90 of 180 seconds setting up the situation, get cut off in the middle of the Action, and never reach the result that was the entire point.
You recite the company's values language back at the interviewer, which reads as coached and makes them discount the stories that would otherwise have landed.
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a time you deployed something at a customer site that broke in production. What broke, how did you find out, and what did you say to the customer in the first hour?
Describe a time a customer stakeholder was firmly against your technical recommendation. Walk me through how it resolved - and if they won, what did you do to make their approach succeed?
Give me an example of a project where nobody could tell you what success looked like. How did you decide what to build, and what did you write down?
Tell me about the most expensive mistake you have made - in money, in time, or in a customer relationship. What is different about how you work now because of it?
Describe a system you handed off and left. How do you know it survived? What did the team hit that you had not documented?
Tell me about a time you had to say no to a customer, or tell them the thing they asked for was the wrong thing. What did you say, and what happened next?
Give me a time you had to get people who didn't report to you - possibly at the customer, not your company - to change how they worked. What actually moved them?
87.proofOfWork: Beyond the story bank and the two loop debriefs, assemble a private evidence dossier that turns the bank from claims into an auditable record, and a public sanitised subset of it. For each of the ten stories, the dossier holds the artifact set that proves it: commit SHAs or PR links for the change, the dashboard screenshot or query showing the before and after values with visible axes and dates, the actual postmortem or ADR document, the cost graph with the run-rate delta annotated, the runbook you handed over with its git history showing who edited it after you left, and the message you sent the customer when things broke. Each card carries a one-line provenance note stating how each number was produced and what could confound it, plus a redaction policy line naming what you will not disclose about the client and how you will say so in the room. Add a ten-clip playlist of the 60-second versions recorded in one sitting, a follow-up ledger listing every probe question you were asked across both loops with a self-score and whether you could defend the number, and a short 'retired stories' note explaining which two stories were cut and what pattern of weak follow-ups killed them. The dossier proves the bank is calibrated and sourced rather than rehearsed, and the follow-up ledger - not the stories themselves - is the artifact a hiring manager would find most convincing if you ever chose to show it.

88.topic: Public proof: three case studies and repos
88.why: An FDE is hired on evidence that you have shipped something real inside somebody else's constraints, and almost nobody in the loop will read your code — they will read one page and decide whether to spend an hour on you. More importantly, the artifact you are building here is the same artifact the job produces weekly: the architecture write-up a customer's principal engineer reviews, the post-incident narrative their VP forwards to their CISO, the handover doc that decides whether your work survives after you leave the account. Writing three of them about DefenderMate, Kaupex and Dokeo is not marketing overhead, it is a rehearsal of the deliverable, and the recruiter screen, the referral DM and the 'tell me about something you built' round all get their raw material from the same three pages.
prerequisites: Deep working knowledge of the three systems themselves plus commit access to their repos and read access to whatever metrics, logs or invoices still exist — you cannot reconstruct a p95 or a monthly bill from memory, and unverifiable numbers are worse than no numbers.

Git at depth from topic 4: `git log --stat`, `git bisect` and `git reflog` to reconstruct the real timeline of what broke, and enough comfort with history rewriting (`git filter-repo`, force-push, fork/clone semantics) to publish a repo whose history is clean.

Docker and Compose from topics 5 and 6, because 'clone and run in one command' is the difference between a repo a stranger evaluates and a repo a stranger closes; each case study repo needs a working `docker compose up` path with seeded data.

SLI and SLO vocabulary from topic 20 and the golden signals from topic 21, so the numbers in each case study are stated as measurable claims (p95 of X over window W, measured at point P) rather than adjectives like 'fast' and 'scalable'.

A publishing surface you control: rasul.in deployed from a repo you can edit (Next.js on Vercel), an image/asset path that survives, and a GitHub profile whose public repo list is the second thing a hiring manager clicks.

A written answer, before you start, to what each client or employer permits you to disclose — check contracts and NDAs for Kaupex and any client-owned parts of DefenderMate and Dokeo, and get an explicit yes in writing for anything you are unsure about.

subtopics.name: Pick the reader and write the one-screen thesis
subtopics.learn: Name exactly one reader per case study — an FDE hiring manager with 90 seconds who is asking 'has this person delivered under real constraints, and can they explain it' — and write a four-line thesis block that appears above the fold: the problem in the customer's or user's words, the constraint that made it hard, what you built, and one measured result. Every later section either supports that thesis or gets cut. Distinguish the four documentation modes so you do not accidentally write a tutorial: a case study is explanation (why this shape, what it cost), not a how-to, and never a feature tour. Write the thesis for all three projects before drafting any of them, because the three theses must differ — if DefenderMate and Dokeo both come out as 'built a full-stack app with an LLM in it', you have not found the actual story of either.

resource.label: Diataxis - a systematic framework for technical documentation

subtopics.name: Fix the section template and the order, once
subtopics.learn: Lock a single template used identically by all three pages so a reader who has seen one can skim the next two: Context (who, scale, constraint), Architecture (one diagram plus a five-sentence walk of the primary flow), Key decisions (three, each with the rejected alternative and its cost), What broke (one real incident with timeline, detection, root cause, fix), What I would change (three, ranked, with the trigger that would force each), Numbers (with the measurement method), Run it yourself (the one command). Write in the second-person-free active voice the Google style guide prescribes: present tense, short sentences, no 'we simply', no 'obviously', expand every acronym on first use including your own product names. Cap each page at roughly 1,200-1,600 words and enforce it — length is the most common reason a hiring manager stops reading.

resource.label: Google developer documentation style guide - Highlights

subtopics.name: What you are legally allowed to publish, and the license on each repo
subtopics.learn: Before writing a line, classify every artifact: your own code, client-owned code, employer-owned code, third-party code, and customer data. Anything client- or employer-owned needs written permission or must be abstracted (describe the architecture and the problem shape, publish a reimplementation or a redacted subset, never paste their source). Anonymise the customer if the contract requires it ('a mid-market MSP with 40 analysts') and check that the anonymisation actually holds once your architecture diagram and their public case studies are read together. Put an explicit `LICENSE` file in every public repo — a repo with no license is legally all-rights-reserved and signals carelessness — and choose deliberately: MIT or Apache-2.0 for something you want reused (Apache-2.0 if you care about an explicit patent grant), and if you are publishing a reference implementation rather than a product, say so in the README. Add a `NOTICE`/attribution section for any vendored third-party code and confirm its license permits redistribution.

resource.label: Choose a License - Appendix: license comparison table (permissions, conditions, limitations, patent grant)

subtopics.name: Scrub secrets and customer data out of code and history
subtopics.learn: Assume the repos contain credentials until proven otherwise. Run a full-history scan (`gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts='--all'`, plus `trufflehog git file://.`) and treat every hit as live: rotate first, then scrub, because a rewritten history does not un-leak a key that was pushed. Purge with `git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env` or `--replace-text` rather than `filter-branch`, understand that this rewrites every commit SHA so the remote must be force-pushed and any fork/PR references still hold the old blobs, and remember GitHub keeps unreachable objects visible until garbage collection — for anything sensitive the safe move is a fresh repo seeded from a clean tree.
