Replace real config with `.env.example` holding placeholder values plus a `README` line per variable, add a `.gitignore` that covers `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.tfstate` and local dumps, enable GitHub secret scanning and push protection on each repo, and scrub screenshots too: real tenant names, customer emails, internal hostnames and API keys leak through PNGs more often than through code.

resource.label: gitleaks - secret scanning for git repos (official repository)

subtopics.name: Repo hygiene: the 60 seconds a stranger actually spends
subtopics.learn: Optimise for the strict order in which GitHub is read: repo description and topics, README top third, file tree, last commit date, then maybe one file. Give each repo a one-line description that names the problem not the stack, 5-8 topics, and a README whose first screen is the thesis block, the architecture diagram, and the run command — badges and a table of contents belong below that, if at all. Make the file tree legible: no `test2/`, no `old/`, no committed `node_modules` or build output, a top-level `docs/` with the ADRs and runbooks, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` only if you would genuinely accept a PR. Link the case study page from the README and the README from the case study page, so whichever entry point the reader hits, the other is one click away. Pin the three repos on your GitHub profile and write a profile README that is three lines and three links, not a skills wall.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Repositories

subtopics.name: Make each repo run in one command on a machine that is not yours
subtopics.learn: A case study that cannot be executed is a claim; a repo that boots is proof. Ship a `docker compose up` path per project with everything it needs: pinned image tags (never `latest`), a `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` plus real `healthcheck` blocks so the app does not race Postgres, a named volume for data, and a seed step that loads deterministic synthetic fixtures — invented tenants, invented alerts, invented documents — so nothing real ever ships. Stub external dependencies behind an interface: a fake LLM provider that returns canned classifications when `LLM_PROVIDER=fake`, a webhook generator script instead of a live integration. Then verify honestly: clone into a fresh directory on a machine with nothing warm (or a clean container), time it, and write the real number in the README ('first run pulls ~800 MB and takes about 3 minutes'). Add a `make demo` target that boots the stack, seeds it, fires traffic, and prints the URL to open.

resource.label: Docker Docs - Control startup and shutdown order in Compose (healthcheck, depends_on service_healthy)

subtopics.name: One architecture diagram per project, at the container level
subtopics.learn: Draw at the C4 container level — deployable units and data stores, not classes and not a wall of cloud vendor icons — and hold yourself to a hard limit of roughly 12 boxes. Include a legend (solid arrow = synchronous call, dashed = asynchronous/event, cylinder = persistent store), label every arrow with the protocol and the payload ('HTTPS webhook, alert JSON', 'NOTIFY/LISTEN, job id'), and mark the trust boundary so a reader can see what is exposed to the internet, what is tenant-scoped, and where credentials live. Draw the system as it actually is, including the ugly parts — the cron that exists because the queue was added late, the shared database two services both write to — because a diagram that is too clean is the single fastest way to fail the follow-up question. Number the primary flow 1..n and make the five-sentence walk in the case study follow those numbers exactly.

resource.label: C4 model - software architecture diagrams

subtopics.name: Diagrams as code so they do not rot
subtopics.learn: Commit the diagram source next to the code as Mermaid (`docs/architecture.md` with a ```mermaid flowchart or sequenceDiagram block) so it renders natively in the GitHub README and in your site's markdown pipeline, and can be diffed in a PR when the architecture changes. Learn enough syntax to be fast: `flowchart LR` with `subgraph` for trust boundaries, `-->` versus `-.->` for sync versus async, `[( )]` for datastores, and `sequenceDiagram` with `participant`, `activate` and `Note over` for the one flow worth showing step by step (Kaupex's compile-approve-publish chain is the obvious candidate). Export a PNG or SVG for the case study page and for slides, but treat the exported file as a build artifact, never the source of truth. Add the diagram to the repo's PR checklist so it is updated in the same commit as the change it describes.

resource.label: Mermaid - Flowchart syntax (subgraph, arrow types, node shapes)

subtopics.name: Numbers: measure them again, and state how you measured
subtopics.learn: Every quantitative claim needs a metric, a window, a measurement point and a method, in that order — 'p95 end-to-end classification latency 42 s over 30 days, measured from webhook receipt to row committed, from the Prometheus histogram in the ingestion service' beats 'fast classification' by an order of magnitude in an interview. Re-derive each number from an artifact you still have (Grafana, a Postgres query, a cloud bill, a k6 run) and if you cannot, either re-run the measurement against the Compose stack or delete the claim. Distinguish load-test numbers from production numbers and label them as such. Prefer before/after pairs with the change named ('adding the partial index on `(tenant_id, status)` took the dashboard query from 1.8 s to 90 ms at 2M rows') and include at least one honest cost figure per project (monthly infrastructure spend, or cost per 1,000 classifications) — cost is the number FDE interviewers probe hardest and portfolios almost never contain.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: The 'what broke' section: one real incident, told blamelessly
subtopics.learn: Pick the single most instructive real failure per project and write it as a compressed postmortem: trigger, detection (what alerted, or the honest 'a user told me'), timeline with timestamps, the impact in user terms, the root cause traced past the proximate error to the contributing conditions, the mitigation, and the durable fix with a link to the commit or config change. Use the SRE postmortem discipline — blameless language, 'the deploy pipeline allowed X' rather than 'I forgot X', and separate the fix that stopped the bleeding from the fix that made the class of failure impossible. Include the uncomfortable part: how long detection took and why. This section is the highest-signal thing on the page, because every FDE interviewer is trying to establish whether you operate systems or only build them, and a candidate who volunteers a specific outage with a real time-to-detect reads as someone who has been on call.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: The 'what I would change' section as ADRs, not regrets
subtopics.learn: Convert hindsight into decisions with costs. For each project write three ranked changes in the ADR shape — context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences — and add the trigger that would force it ('move classification from an in-process worker to a durable queue when sustained ingest exceeds ~50 events/s or when a redeploy starts dropping in-flight work'). Backfill 3-5 ADRs per repo under `docs/adr/NNNN-title.md` for the decisions you actually made, marking superseded ones rather than deleting them; a reader who sees ADR 0003 superseded by 0007 learns more about your judgement than any prose. Ban regret language: not 'I should have used Postgres', but 'SQLite was correct until concurrent writers appeared; the migration cost was one afternoon and the trigger was the second worker'. Interviewers use this section to test whether you understand the cost of the alternative you are recommending.

resource.label: Architecture decision record (ADR) - templates and examples

subtopics.name: Draft the DefenderMate case study: multi-tenant, webhook-driven, LLM in the loop
subtopics.learn: Write the full page for DefenderMate with the tenant story as the spine: alerts arrive by webhook, an LLM classifies them, a Next.js dashboard and a weekly digest deliver the value — so the interesting engineering is isolation, asynchrony and trust, not the UI. Be explicit about the tenancy model you chose (shared schema with `tenant_id` on every row, or schema-per-tenant, or database-per-tenant), where isolation is actually enforced (row-level security, a repository layer that refuses an unscoped query, tenant taken from the verified token and never from the request body), and what the noisy-neighbour story is. Cover webhook hardening concretely: HMAC signature verification with a per-tenant secret and a constant-time compare, replay protection via a timestamp window plus a delivery-id dedupe table, fast 2xx acknowledgement with processing deferred, and bounded retries. State the freshness SLI for classification and the fallback when the model provider returns 429 or times out. Name the prompt-injection surface — attacker-controlled alert text reaching a model whose output drives a UI — and what you did or would do about it.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn - Architecting multitenant solutions on Azure

subtopics.name: Draft the Kaupex case study: the compile-approve-publish pipeline
subtopics.learn: Write Kaupex around its hardest property: a multi-step chain (task compile, human approval, publish) running on a single Hetzner VPS with Postgres, where every step can fail, be retried, or wait days for a human. Make the durability story explicit — where state lives between steps, what happens if the box reboots mid-publish, whether a retried publish is idempotent and what the idempotency key is, how the human approval is represented (a row and a signal, not an in-memory promise) — and describe the compensation path when publish half-succeeds, which is a saga whether or not you called it one. Cover the single-box realities honestly: backups (pgbackrest to object storage, and the restore you actually tested), the RPO/RTO you can defend, systemd units and resource limits for the worker, and what a single machine costs per month versus the managed alternative. Close with the ADR for when this must become a real durable execution engine and what that migration looks like — that trigger-and-migration answer is exactly the shape of an FDE design conversation.

resource.label: Temporal Docs - Understanding Temporal: durable execution, retries and long-running workflows

subtopics.name: Draft the Dokeo case study: packaging and deployment as the product
subtopics.learn: Write Dokeo as the delivery-engineering story, because that is what an FDE is hired to do: a Python application turned into something a stranger can deploy. Cover the image (multi-stage build, `uv sync --frozen`, non-root UID, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, the size before and after), the Kubernetes surface (Deployment with all three probes and a `preStop` for graceful drain, Service with a named `targetPort`, Ingress with TLS via cert-manager, ConfigMap and Secret separation, requests and limits derived from measurement rather than guessed), and the Helm chart with `values.schema.json` so a customer cannot mis-configure it silently. Include the migration-on-deploy story (a pre-upgrade Job that fails the release rather than serving a half-migrated schema) and the rollback story with a concrete `helm rollback` or Argo sync. Add the environment matrix — what changes between k3s, EKS and Cloud Run — since 'runs in the customer's cluster, whatever it is' is the whole pitch.

resource.label: Kubernetes Documentation - Concepts

subtopics.name: Screenshots, terminal casts and a 90-second demo per project
subtopics.learn: Produce visual proof that loads fast and cannot be faked-looking: two or three screenshots per project taken at a consistent viewport with seeded synthetic data, cropped to the thing being claimed, annotated with a single arrow or box, exported as WebP or optimised PNG under ~200 KB each and served with explicit width and height so the page does not shift. For anything CLI-shaped — `make demo`, the restore drill, the Helm install — record an asciinema cast rather than a video: it is a few kilobytes, the text is selectable and searchable, and it embeds anywhere. Add one 90-second screen recording per project with a scripted narration (10 s problem, 20 s architecture, 45 s the flow working end to end, 15 s the number), rehearsed once so there is no dead air, and host it where it will still exist in a year. Check every asset for leaked tenant names, emails and hostnames before publishing, and write real `alt` text for each image.

resource.label: asciinema - terminal session recorder (official repository)

subtopics.name: Publish on rasul.in: routes, metadata, performance, accessibility
subtopics.learn: Ship the three pages as real routes (`/work/defendermate`, `/work/kaupex`, `/work/dokeo`) plus an index at `/work` that shows all three theses so a reader can choose. Content lives in markdown/MDX in the repo, not in a CMS you will stop paying for. Set per-page metadata deliberately: a `<title>` that reads well in a browser tab and a search result, a 150-160 character description that is the thesis, canonical URL, and Open Graph plus Twitter card tags with a 1200x630 image — the OG card is what actually renders when someone drops your link in a hiring Slack, and a missing one costs you the click. Hold the page to a real budget: no client-side data fetching for static prose, images lazy-loaded below the fold, fonts subset and preloaded, and a Lighthouse pass on mobile before you call it done. Accessibility is not optional on a page whose job is to be read: one `h1`, ordered heading levels, AA contrast, visible focus rings, alt text on every diagram, and no information conveyed by colour alone.

resource.label: Next.js Docs - generateMetadata: titles, descriptions, canonical URLs and Open Graph tags

subtopics.name: Discoverability, the comprehension test, and the maintenance rule
subtopics.learn: Close the loop so the pages get read and stay true. Make them findable: descriptive URLs, a sitemap and `robots.txt`, internal links from the site index and each repo README, and outbound links from your GitHub profile — but do not chase SEO, the traffic that matters arrives from a link you sent. Then run a comprehension test, which is the only real quality gate: give each page to three people (one senior engineer, one non-engineer, one recruiter), time them for 90 seconds, then ask what the system does, what was hard, and what you would change; anything two of three cannot answer is a rewrite, not a defence. Ask one engineer to try the one-command run on a clean machine and log every step where they had to think. Finally set a maintenance rule you will actually keep: the diagram and the numbers are updated in the same PR as the change they describe, dead links are checked quarterly, and every page carries a visible 'last verified' date — a stale portfolio reads as a stale engineer.

resource.label: Google Search Central - Search documentation

outcomes: You can hand any of the three case study pages to a senior engineer who has 90 seconds and have them correctly state what the system does, what the hard constraint was, and what broke — verified with three readers, not assumed.

You can point a stranger at each repo and have them go from `git clone` to a working, seeded local stack with one documented command, on a machine that has never run your code, in the time your README claims.
You can defend every number on every page by naming the metric, the window, the measurement point and the artifact it came from, and you have deleted every claim that failed that test.

You can tell one real incident per project with timestamps, the actual time to detect, a root cause traced past the proximate error, and the difference between the mitigation and the durable fix, without blaming a person.

You can produce a container-level architecture diagram for each system from its committed Mermaid source, walk the numbered primary flow in five sentences, and point at the trust boundary and the part you are least happy with.
You can state, for each project, three ranked changes you would make with the concrete trigger that would force each one and the cost of the alternative you rejected, in ADR form and in speech.

You can prove the repos are safe to be public: a clean full-history secret scan, rotated credentials, `.env.example` with documented variables, a deliberate LICENSE, and screenshots and casts with no real customer data in them.

You can send one link in a referral DM or an application that answers 'has this person delivered under real constraints' without a call, and you have at least one instance of someone responding to that link specifically.
failureModes: A credential is scrubbed from the working tree but not from history, or scrubbed from history but never rotated, and the key is still live in a customer's Slack integration or LLM provider account weeks after the repo goes public.
The public repo abstracts a client system so thinly that the architecture diagram plus the client's own public marketing identifies them, breaching an NDA that nobody re-read before publishing.

The page claims a latency or throughput number that came from a laptop benchmark in a good mood; an interviewer asks how it was measured and at what percentile, the answer collapses, and every other claim on the page becomes suspect.

`docker compose up` works only on the author's machine because an image is unpinned, a healthcheck is missing so the app races Postgres, or a required environment variable is undocumented — the reviewer hits an unhandled stack trace in the first two minutes and never returns.

The architecture diagram shows the intended design rather than the deployed one, omitting the cron job and the shared database, so the first follow-up question exposes that the author is describing a system they did not actually operate.
A screenshot taken from a live environment ships with real tenant names, an internal hostname and a session token visible in a URL bar, and it is served from a CDN long after the image is swapped.

The case studies are published once and never touched; the architecture changes, the links rot, the numbers refer to an instance size that no longer exists, and a reader in month six is evaluating a version of the system that stopped being true.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through the DefenderMate architecture at the container level, then tell me exactly where tenant isolation is enforced. If I compromise one tenant's API token, what can I reach, and what stops an unscoped query from ever leaving your data layer?

Kaupex has a compile step, a human approval that might take three days, and a publish step. The box reboots after publish has partially succeeded. Walk me through what state exists, what a retry does, and how you know the retry is safe.

Pick the worst outage you had in any of these three systems. Give me the timeline: what triggered it, how you found out, how long detection took, what you did in the first ten minutes, and what you changed so that class of failure cannot recur.

Your case study says classification p95 is under a minute. How is that measured, from which point to which point, over what window, and what happens to that number when the model provider starts returning 429s for twenty minutes?

A customer wants Dokeo running in their own cluster, and their security team forbids the managed pieces you rely on. Take me through the chart and the image: what changes, what you lose, and how you keep one codebase across their environment and yours.

You listed 'move classification to a durable queue' as something you would change. Why did you not do it originally, what specifically would force the change, and what does the migration look like while the system stays up?

If I gave you two weeks on any one of these three systems with the goal of handing it to a customer's own engineers to operate, what would you build, what would you write, and how would you know at the end that the handover actually worked?
88.proofOfWork: A public `case-studies` repository that is the operating system behind the three live pages, so a reader can see not just the output but the standard it was held to. It contains: (1) `TEMPLATE.md`, the locked section order with word budgets and the rules for each section, plus `STYLE.md` with the voice rules and the ban list; (2) `claims.md`, one row per quantitative statement across all three pages with the metric, window, measurement point, source artifact (Grafana panel, SQL query, k6 run, cloud invoice) and the date it was last re-verified, including the claims you deleted and why; (3) `docs/adr/` with the backfilled architecture decision records for all three systems, superseded records kept and marked; (4) `diagrams/` with the committed Mermaid sources and exported SVGs, and a note in each repo's PR checklist requiring the diagram to change in the same commit as the architecture; (5) `incidents/` with the three long-form postmortems the case study sections were compressed from, blameless, with real timestamps and time-to-detect; (6) `review/comprehension-test.md`, the 90-second test results from three readers per page (senior engineer, non-engineer, recruiter) with their verbatim answers to 'what does it do, what was hard, what would they change', the rewrites each failure triggered, and a clean-machine run log from one engineer who tried `make demo` cold, with every step where they had to think; and (7) `security/publication-checklist.md`, the pre-publish gate you ran for each repo — full-history gitleaks output, rotation log, `.env.example` coverage, license decision, screenshot and cast scrub — signed off with a date, so the whole thing doubles as a reusable process another engineer could run on their own portfolio.

89.why: FDE hiring is a trust problem before it is a skills problem: the manager has to believe you can be put in front of someone else's infrastructure, with their credentials and their risk, and not break it. A public write-up of an agent you actually operate - what it is allowed to execute, what stopped it, what it cost, what broke at 03:00 - is the cheapest way to transfer that belief before the loop starts, because it is the same artifact you would hand a customer's platform team during a pilot review. The profile is the index for it: if a recruiter's search never returns you, or the headline says 'full-stack developer', the write-up is a good essay nobody with hiring authority ever reads.
prerequisites: A Hermes agent you actually run on a box you own - container up, gateway responding, at least one cron job that has been firing for a few weeks - not a local demo. The deep operational pass on this system is topic 52 in month 6; this topic publishes the version you have now.
Shell, SSH and Docker fluency (topics 0, 1 and 5): you can read journalctl and docker logs, inspect a running container, and describe the host's firewall rules from memory.
Working knowledge of MCP servers and tool schemas (topic 47), enough to explain your HubSpot server's tool surface and which calls are read-only.

A publishing surface you control - rasul.in building and deploying, with the ability to add a route, dates, an OG image and a feed - plus the case-study template and the site work from topic 80 in month 2.
Secrets hygiene from topic 62: you know the difference between removing a key and rotating it, and you can scan git history rather than only the working tree.
Three to five hard numbers you can substantiate from logs or a provider dashboard: jobs run per day, success rate, per-job token and dollar cost, wall-clock latency, host cost per month.

subtopics.name: Fix the one claim and the one reader before writing a word
subtopics.learn: Write a single sentence of the form 'reader X should believe Y after reading this' and keep it above the draft. Here the reader is a hiring manager or platform lead deciding whether you can be trusted to put an autonomous agent inside someone else's perimeter, and the claim is operational, not architectural - something like 'a self-hosted agent with shell and CRM access can run unattended for weeks if you constrain it exactly this way, and here is the bill.' Reject the two default framings that produce forgettable posts: the tutorial ('how to install Hermes') and the tour ('here is my setup'). Test it by asking whether a competent engineer could disagree with the sentence; if nobody could, it is a description, not a claim.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One - Audience

subtopics.name: Reconstruct ground truth from logs before you write prose
subtopics.learn: Assemble the evidence first into one scratch file of dated facts: git log of the config repo, the current config.yaml and jobs.json, docker logs and journalctl for the last 30 days, hermes doctor output, the model provider's usage page for tokens and dollars, and the date of every incident (container OOM, HubSpot 429s, a cron that stopped firing, a context blowup). Writing first and looking up numbers afterwards is how you end up publishing 'roughly 5x faster'. Mark every fact you cannot substantiate - those become sentences you delete, not sentences you hedge.

resource.label: NousResearch/hermes-agent

subtopics.name: The spine: constraint, options, decision, mechanism, result, regret
subtopics.learn: Use the ADR shape (context / decision / consequences) stretched to narrative length, and outline all six sections as bullets before drafting. For this piece: the constraint (an agent that reaches a live CRM and must run on infrastructure you control), the two or three options actually on the table (a hosted agent platform, an agent framework you assemble yourself, Hermes), what you chose and the trade-off you accepted, how it works at the level of config keys and tool names, what it produced with numbers, and what you would do differently. The regret section is not optional - the honest cost you paid is what makes a reader trust the rest of the document.

resource.label: Architecture Decision Records - adr.github.io

subtopics.name: Write the blast-radius section first - it is the part that gets you hired
subtopics.learn: The section that separates an operator from a demo is the one stating exactly what the agent may execute and what stops it: the terminal backend and the container limits it runs under, the approvals policy and hardline blocklist, the file-write allowlist, the MCP tools.include allowlist that keeps the HubSpot server read-only except for one confirm-gated write path, and what authenticates the gateway. Then state the threat you did not close: text arriving from the CRM is model input, so an instruction planted in a note reaches whatever tools remain enabled. Name concretely what an attacker gets in each case rather than asserting that it is 'sandboxed'.

resource.label: Model Context Protocol - documentation

subtopics.name: Numbers that survive a skeptical staff engineer
subtopics.learn: Every claim states baseline, method, window, sample size and percentile. Concretely: host spec and monthly cost, jobs executed per day over N days, success rate with success explicitly defined, p50/p95 wall clock per job, tokens in and out and dollars per job by model pin, and the cost delta after context compression or model routing. Never a bare average for latency and never 'reliable' without a denominator. Frame delivery against a stated objective - 'the 07:00 digest arrived on 27 of 30 days, the three misses were HubSpot rate limits' - rather than a nine-count, and label any figure that came from a single manual run.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: One diagram, one level, with the trust boundary drawn
subtopics.learn: Draw a single system-context diagram: caller to gateway, gateway to the Hermes container, container to the model provider, container to your HubSpot MCP server, MCP server to the HubSpot API, plus the cron scheduler - with the host you control as an explicit dashed boundary and every arrow labelled with protocol and who initiates. Stay at one C4 level; mixing a container, a Python class and a cloud account in one picture is the most common diagram failure. Author it as Mermaid inside the repo so it cannot drift from the config, caption it with its claim ('everything inside the dashed box runs on hardware you control'), and put the same content in the alt text.

resource.label: The C4 model for visualising software architecture

subtopics.name: The companion repo: make the claim reproducible in one command
subtopics.learn: The write-up is only as credible as the artifact it links to. Ship a public repo with a version-pinned compose file, a redacted and diffable config.yaml, jobs.json, and a bootstrap target that takes a bare instance to a responding gateway. Tag a release and link the tag, never main, so the commands in the post cannot drift under you. Make every command copy-pasteable: no leading dollar sign inside the copy region, placeholders as <HUBSPOT_TOKEN>, long flags rather than short ones, and the expected output shown immediately after. Run the entire sequence on a clean instance before publishing.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Repositories

subtopics.name: Redaction, rotation, and not publishing an attack surface
subtopics.learn: Run a secret scan over the full git history, not just the working tree, before the repo goes public - a clean HEAD means nothing if a token sat in commit 40. Anything that ever appeared (HubSpot private app token, model provider key, gateway bearer) is burned: rotate it, do not blur it or rewrite history and hope. Strip host identifiers from prose and screenshots - public IP, SSH port, gateway hostname, the portal ID inside HubSpot URLs, shell prompts, internal email addresses. Assume that publishing the gateway path means scanners arrive within hours, so verify the firewall exposes only what you intend and that auth is enforced before the post goes live, not after.

resource.label: gitleaks - secret scanning for git repos

subtopics.name: Publishing mechanics: title, slug, canonical, card, dates
subtopics.learn: Ship with a title that states the specific claim rather than the topic, a TL;DR paragraph above the fold carrying the headline numbers, a stable slug you will never change, a canonical link tag, and both published and updated dates. Add og:title, og:description and a real og:image so the link renders as a card in LinkedIn and Slack instead of a bare URL; unfurls are cached aggressively, so get the tags right before the first share and force a refresh with the platform's own post inspector if you change them afterwards. Confirm the page is statically generated or server-rendered so crawlers and unfurlers see the text.

resource.label: The Open Graph protocol

subtopics.name: Headline and About: what a recruiter's boolean search actually matches
subtopics.learn: Recruiters search literal strings across the headline, About and experience fields, so the headline (220 characters) must contain the exact title you are targeting - 'Forward Deployed Engineer' - plus two or three systems words that filter you in (agents, LLM, Kubernetes, Python) and zero adjectives. About allows 2,600 characters but is read through the first two lines before 'see more', so open with the claim, not the origin story, then three short blocks: what you deploy, evidence with numbers, what you are looking for. Ban 'passionate', 'results-driven', emoji bullets and third person. Turn off 'Share profile updates with your network' in settings before you start editing.

resource.label: LinkedIn Help - Use Boolean search on LinkedIn

subtopics.name: Experience entries that read like delivery, not employment
subtopics.learn: Give each role a one-line scope statement, then three to five bullets in the shape: shipped X under Y constraint, by this mechanism, with this measured result. Reuse the exact numbers from the write-up so the two documents corroborate each other rather than contradicting each other in a screening call. The title field drives filters more than the bullets do - keep the legal title and put the functional description in the scope line rather than inventing 'Forward Deployed Engineer' for a role that was not one. Compress anything older than about eight years to a single line, and run the same sentence surgery you would run on a doc: active voice, no nominalisations, no vague quantifiers.

resource.label: Federal Plain Language Guidelines

subtopics.name: Featured, Skills, custom URL, and the open-to-work decision
subtopics.learn: Featured is the only place a profile reader clicks through from, so pin exactly three items in order - the Hermes write-up, the tagged repo, one case study from month 2 - each with a rewritten one-line description rather than the auto-pulled meta text. Skills feed matching, so order them deliberately, lead with the ones you would be filtered on, and delete anything you would not defend under questioning. Set the custom URL, a banner that is not a stock gradient, and a real headshot. Then decide consciously between the recruiter-only open-to-work signal and the public photo frame: the public frame produces more inbound and is visible to everyone you currently work with.

resource.label: LinkedIn Help - Let recruiters know you're Open to Work

subtopics.name: The launch post: 3,000 characters, only the first three lines matter
subtopics.learn: The post is not the write-up. Write roughly 150 words: line one is the surprising number or fact, then three or four short lines on what you built and what broke, then one line inviting a specific disagreement, then the link. Truncation hits after a couple of lines on mobile, so nothing load-bearing goes below the fold. Two or three hashtags maximum, no 'thoughts?' bait, and no asking people to comment for the link. Post once rather than as a series - a second post two weeks later about the thing you got wrong outperforms reposting the same URL.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing Two

subtopics.name: Distribution: five venues, fifteen direct sends, zero flame wars
subtopics.learn: Publishing is not distribution. Choose venues where the reader lives - LinkedIn, the project's own GitHub discussions or community, one relevant subreddit, X, and direct one-to-one sends to ten to fifteen named people (former colleagues, hiring managers, anyone visibly doing agent deployments) with one sentence saying why you thought of them. The direct sends produce nearly all of the useful replies. On community forums use the plain descriptive title, never editorialised bait, read the venue's rules first, and be present for the first few hours to answer substantively. When someone finds a real error, fix the post, add a dated correction note and thank them; when someone is merely hostile, do not reply.

resource.label: Hacker News guidelines

subtopics.name: Instrument the funnel and read signal, not vanity metrics
subtopics.learn: Before publishing, confirm the page is indexed and that your name plus 'forward deployed' surfaces both the profile and the post; add the URL to the sitemap and check coverage in Search Console. Afterwards, the metrics that matter are which companies and titles viewed the profile in the two weeks following the post, how many inbound messages named the write-up specifically, and whether anyone you do not know forwarded it - not impressions and not reactions. Log every inbound with its source and outcome in a sheet, because that is the seed of the target list and pipeline work in the following months.

resource.label: Google Search Central - documentation

subtopics.name: Keep it from rotting: version pins, a verified-against line, a cadence
subtopics.learn: A deployment write-up starts decaying the moment the agent, the MCP spec or the HubSpot API changes. Pin the version everywhere it appears, put a dated 'verified against vX.Y on <date>' line at the top, and hold a 30-minute block each month to re-run the bootstrap on a clean instance and either update the post or add a note. Watch the upstream repo for releases so you learn about breaking changes before a reader does, and run a link checker on a schedule rather than only on push. Add an issue template inviting reproduction reports - an issue from a stranger who actually ran your repo is the strongest hiring signal the artifact can generate.

resource.label: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 specification

outcomes: You can state in one sentence the claim the write-up makes and name the kind of engineer who would plausibly disagree with it.
You can defend every number in the piece - baseline, method, window, sample size, percentile - and point at the log line, command or dashboard each one came from.

You can describe the agent's blast radius in under two minutes: what it may execute, what the approvals policy and tool allowlist block, what authenticates the gateway, and what a prompt injection arriving through a CRM note would still reach.

You can hand someone a tagged repo and have them go from a bare instance to a responding gateway with one command, with a clean secret scan over the full git history and every previously exposed credential rotated.

You can show a profile whose headline contains the exact target title, whose About makes the claim in its first two lines before truncation, and whose Featured section pins the write-up, the repo and one case study in that order.
You can name the ten to fifteen people you sent the piece to directly, the one-line note you used, and what each replied.
You can produce a two-week readout showing profile views by company and title, inbound messages that referenced the write-up by name, and at least one forward from someone you do not know.
You can re-run the published commands on a clean instance and show they still work, or show the dated correction note where they did not.
failureModes: A HubSpot private-app token sat in an early commit of the config repo, the working tree scan passes, the repo goes public, and the key is scraped and used before you notice.

The write-up covers only the happy path, the first serious comment asks what happens when the model decides to run a destructive shell command, and with no answer in the post the whole thing reads as a demo.
The commands link to main instead of a tag, an upstream release renames a config key two weeks later, and every new reader fails at step three while the top comment is a stack trace.

The profile rewrite happens with 'Share profile updates with your network' still enabled, so the entire network - including the current employer - gets notified line by line that you are repositioning.
The headline stays 'Full-Stack Developer | React | Node | Python', so every recruiter search for 'forward deployed' or 'solutions architect' misses the profile no matter how good the write-up is.
A terminal screenshot leaves the host IP, gateway hostname and shell prompt visible, and scanners find the exposed port before the post is 24 hours old.

The post goes out cold with no direct sends, collects a few hundred impressions from people who cannot hire you, and the conclusion drawn is that writing does not work rather than that distribution never happened.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through the deployment in your write-up. What would you refuse to run that way for a customer with a SOC 2 audit next quarter, and what would you put in its place?
Your agent has shell access and a CRM it can write to. Draw the blast radius. If I get an injected instruction into a record the agent reads, what do I actually get, and what stops me?

The scheduled job silently stopped delivering three days ago and nobody noticed. Walk me through detection and diagnosis using only what is on that box, then tell me what you would add so the third day never happens again.

A customer wants exactly this, inside their VPC, with no egress to a hosted model provider and their own SSO in front of it. What in your design survives, what has to be replaced, and what is the first thing you tell them they cannot have?
Your post claims a specific cost and latency per job. I am skeptical. Tell me how you measured it, what the sample was, and what you did not control for.

Your titles have been engineering titles, but your profile and this post position you as a forward deployed engineer. Make the case for the jump - what have you shipped that is FDE work rather than backend work?

You are the first FDE we hire and we want the team publishing deployment write-ups. Design the process: what gets written, who reviews it, what the confidentiality and security gates are, and how you stop it becoming marketing.
89.proofOfWork: Beyond the live write-up and the updated profile, build a dated positioning readout - a single page written to be shown to an interviewer, closing the loop between what you published and what it caused. It contains four parts. First, the before and after of the profile as screenshots plus an explicit diff of headline, About opener, job titles and Skills order, with one line on why each change was made. Second, the exact list of the ten to fifteen people you sent the piece to directly, the one-sentence note used for each, and the reply. Third, a two-week funnel table from profile-view and post analytics: viewers by company and title, inbound messages that named the write-up, forwards from strangers, and the referral conversations that resulted, each row carrying an outcome so it can be pasted straight into next month's target sheet. Fourth, an objection ledger with one row per hard question the piece received - the question, whether it exposed a real gap in the deployment or only in the writing, the paragraph or config change made in response, and the commit or edit link proving it landed. Close it with an eight-minute recorded screen teardown in which you clone the tagged repo onto a clean instance, run the bootstrap, show the health check green, trigger one scheduled job, and narrate the blast radius directly from the config file. That recording is what you send when a hiring manager asks whether you can show them something you actually operate, and it is most of the answer to the design question you will get in the loop.

90.topic: Target list: 40 companies, referrals, warm intros
90.why: Forward-deployed work is portfolio management under scarcity: you cannot deploy into every account, so you qualify hard, rank on a rubric you can defend, find the one human inside each account who can actually unblock you, and keep a live state machine of who owes what to whom by when. Running your own search that way is the identical skill with your career as the account, and the interviewer will read the quality of your list as a direct sample of how you would triage their customers. The mechanics also matter on their own terms - FDE is the least consistently-titled and most location-gated engineering role in the market, so a list built by keyword search alone will be 60-70% roles you are not legally eligible for and reqs that were filled before you found them.
prerequisites: The positioning spine, company dossier format and comp model from 'Narrative: why FDE, why this company, travel, comp' (topic 72) - this topic feeds that one forty targets, and the walk-away number and travel/authorisation limits from topic 72 become gate columns here.
A resume that already survives 'Resume defence: every line' (topic 73), because a referrer forwards the resume, not your intentions.

At least two public artifacts a stranger can read in five minutes - a write-up or repo from 'Technical writing and public write-ups' (topic 69). A referral with nothing to link to is a name, not a referral.

Spreadsheet mechanics beyond typing: named ranges, data validation with a fixed enum list, conditional formatting, filter views, and one of QUERY / FILTER / ARRAYFORMULA. You will be maintaining forty rows weekly for five months.

Enough Python to GET a JSON endpoint, persist a snapshot, and diff two snapshots - the packaging and script hygiene from 'Production Python architecture' (topic 25) is sufficient; you do not need a framework.
A LinkedIn profile already updated to the FDE positioning, since every person you contact will open it within thirty seconds of your message and the profile is what they judge, not the message.

subtopics.name: Build the title taxonomy: what actually counts as an FDE role
subtopics.learn: There is no single title. Collect the real vocabulary and learn which words map to the job you want: Forward Deployed Engineer / FDSE, Deployment Strategist, Applied AI Engineer, Solutions Engineer, Solutions Architect, Resident Solutions Architect, Delivery / Implementation Engineer, Professional Services Engineer, Customer Engineer, Field Engineer, Partner Solutions Architect. Then learn the disqualifiers, because half of these titles are pre-sales with a quota: search the JD text for 'quota', 'attainment', 'territory', 'support the AE', 'pipeline generation' (pre-sales) versus 'post-signature', 'production', 'on-call', 'customer's environment', 'own the deployment' (delivery). Record two fields per row - title_family and pre_or_post_sales - because they change the comp structure (variable component), the interview loop, and whether the job is engineering at all.

resource.label: Exponent - Forward Deployed Engineer interview guide

subtopics.name: Map the sourcing surfaces before writing a single row
subtopics.learn: Enumerate where reqs actually live so you are not repeatedly scraping the same surface: company-hosted ATS boards (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday, SmartRecruiters), the aggregators (LinkedIn Jobs, Wellfound, Naukri for India-entity roles), curated startup directories with filters for stage, batch and location, monthly community hiring threads, and the highest-signal surface of all - the careers page of a company you already have a person inside. Note which surfaces are queryable programmatically and which are not; the ATS boards are, the aggregators are not. Assign each of your forty rows a source column so that six weeks in you can see which surface produced the rows that actually converted, and stop working the ones that produced noise.

resource.label: Hacker News - 'Ask HN: Who is hiring?' monthly thread archive (whoishiring submissions)

subtopics.name: Query craft: boolean and search operators against ATS domains
subtopics.learn: Stop browsing job boards; query them. Learn the operator set and use it against the domains that host reqs: site: restricts to a host (job-boards.greenhouse.io, boards.greenhouse.io, jobs.lever.co, jobs.ashbyhq.com), quotes force an exact phrase, OR groups synonyms, a leading minus excludes, intitle:/inurl: target the slug, and after:YYYY-MM-DD limits to recently indexed pages. Build and save six to ten canonical queries - one per title-family crossed with a location qualifier - rather than improvising each session, e.g. an exact-phrase query for the title, OR'd with two synonyms, minus the words that signal pre-sales. Log which query produced each row so you can retire the ones with a zero hit rate.

resource.label: Google Search Help - Refine Google searches (site:, exact phrase, minus, before:/after:, filetype:)

subtopics.name: Pull reqs from public ATS job-board APIs instead of scraping
subtopics.learn: The major ATS vendors expose a public, unauthenticated job-board API intended for embedding a careers page - use it. Greenhouse serves a board's whole req list as JSON at boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board_token}/jobs, with ?content=true to include the full JD body, and a per-job endpoint for detail; Lever serves api.lever.co/v0/postings/{company}?mode=json. Find a company's board token by opening their careers page and reading the embed URL or the network requests. Write one script that takes a list of (company, ats_vendor, token) and emits a normalised row per req: req_id, title, location, department, absolute_url, updated_at, and the raw JD text. This is the single highest-leverage thirty minutes in the whole topic - it turns list maintenance from an hour a week into a command.

resource.label: Greenhouse Job Board API - board jobs endpoint and ?content=true for full JD bodies

subtopics.name: LinkedIn Jobs as a filter, not a firehose
subtopics.learn: Use the structured filters rather than scrolling: Date posted (past 24 hours / past week - anything older than three weeks on an aggregator is usually stale or reposted), Experience level, Remote / On-site / Hybrid, Company, and Job function. Put boolean in the keyword box with quotes, OR and NOT. Then learn to distrust the 'Remote' facet: it is set by whoever posted the req and routinely means remote-within-one-country. Open the actual req on the company's own ATS board before you create a row, because the aggregator copy is frequently a truncated or out-of-date mirror. Set up saved searches with alerts so new reqs arrive rather than being hunted, and treat the alert email as an inbox to triage into the sheet, not as reading material.

resource.label: LinkedIn Help - Filter and sort job search results (date posted, experience level, company, function)

subtopics.name: The eligibility gate: entity, employer-of-record, contractor, timezone
subtopics.learn: This gate kills more rows than fit does, so evaluate it before you invest in a referral path. For each company answer four booleans with evidence: does it have an Indian legal entity or GCC that hires directly (check the careers-page location filter and the headcount on their LinkedIn people-by-location view); will it hire in India through an employer-of-record or PEO arrangement (common for US startups without an entity, and it determines whether you get RSUs or nothing); will it engage you as an independent contractor (USD invoiced, you carry GST registration, advance tax and FEMA/FIRC paperwork, usually no equity plan eligibility); and is the req's 'remote' actually 'remote, must be authorised to work in the US'. Add a numeric overlap_hours column: IST is UTC+05:30, which gives roughly two to three usable hours with US Eastern and effectively zero with US Pacific during their working day - for a customer-facing role that means evening customer calls, and you should price it, not discover it.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Professional employer organization (PEO / employer-of-record model)

subtopics.name: Attach a comp band to every row before you rank
subtopics.learn: A fit score without a band is a wish list. For each row record comp_low, comp_high, currency, level_assumption and comp_source. Calibrate the level first - senior at a frontier lab, at a public data-infrastructure company, and at a Series B are three different ladders and three different bands - then read the band for that level and location. Critically, tag whether the band is a US band or an India band: for the same title and level these commonly differ by a factor of two to four, and a global-remote role paid on a US band is the rare row worth twenty ordinary rows. Never carry a single number; carry a range with the assumption written beside it, and mark rows where you are extrapolating rather than reading.

resource.label: Levels.fyi - engineering compensation by company, level and location

subtopics.name: Triangulate the band: filed wage data and pay-transparency variants
subtopics.learn: Self-reported aggregators skew high and are thin at senior levels for niche titles, so add two independent reads. First, statutory wage filings for work-visa petitions give real base salaries by employer, title and year - base only, no equity or bonus, so never compare them to a total-comp figure. Second, exploit pay-transparency law: several US jurisdictions require a posted salary range, so when a company posts the same req across multiple locations, open the Colorado, New York City, California or Washington variant of that req on their own ATS board and read the band off it even though you are applying elsewhere. Reconcile the three sources instead of averaging them, and write one sentence per row explaining why they differ - that sentence is what you say when a recruiter asks how you arrived at your number.

resource.label: US DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification - performance and disclosure data (filed H-1B/PERM wages by employer and job title)

subtopics.name: A fit rubric that another person could reproduce
subtopics.learn: Score on named, bounded dimensions rather than gut feel: role authenticity (is this post-signature delivery engineering, 0-3), stack overlap with your actual proof - Kubernetes, Python/FastAPI, Postgres, LLM evals, Temporal - (0-3), domain you can speak to (0-2), company trajectory measured by hiring velocity and funding or revenue stage (0-2), referral reachability (0-3), and comp band versus your target (0-3). Keep the eligibility booleans out of the score - they are gates that zero the row, not weights, otherwise a high-fit ineligible role floats to the top. Implement it as spreadsheet columns with data validation on the 0-3 inputs and a formula for the weighted total normalised to 100; hand the rubric and three JDs to someone else and check they land within ten points of you. If they cannot, your rubric is vibes with arithmetic on top.

resource.label: Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Creating and using rubrics (bounded dimensions, sample rubrics)

subtopics.name: Tracker schema: columns, enums, and an explicit state machine
subtopics.learn: Design the sheet as a table a script can write to, not a document. Minimum columns: company, hq, ats_vendor, board_token, req_id, req_title, req_url, posted_date, first_seen, last_seen, jd_snapshot_path, archetype, gate_eligible, overlap_hours, fit_score, comp_low, comp_high, comp_source, referral_path_type, referral_person, referral_relationship, intro_broker, status, owner, next_step, next_step_due, last_touch, outcome, notes. Constrain status to a real enum with data validation - sourced, qualified, path_identified, intro_requested, intro_made, applied, recruiter_screen, loop, offer, closed_lost, closed_no_path - and define the legal transitions in a comment so 'applied' cannot silently become the terminal state for eleven rows. Every non-closed row must always have a non-empty next_step and a next_step_due date; a row with neither is not in your pipeline, it is a memory.

resource.label: Google Sheets API - guides (values, ranges, batch updates)

subtopics.name: Dedup, freshness decay, and snapshotting the JD
subtopics.learn: Reqs are mutable and mortal. Snapshot the full JD text to a file the moment you create a row, because postings get edited (scope, level, location, and especially the posted salary range) and deleted, and you need the original text later for resume tailoring, for the 'why this company' hypothesis, and to notice when they quietly downgrade the level. Poll the ATS endpoints weekly and diff by req_id: a req_id that disappears is closed, a new req_id with an identical title is a repost - which is a signal, usually meaning the first hire failed or the band was too low. Do the set operations in SQL over the snapshot CSVs rather than by eye - anti-joins for closed, joins on normalised company+title for duplicates across surfaces - and treat any row whose posted_date is older than about eight weeks with no movement as decayed.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - SQL set operations (UNION / EXCEPT / INTERSECT for diffing snapshots)

subtopics.name: Enumerate your referral graph exhaustively, then intersect it with the list
subtopics.learn: Do this as a data exercise, not as remembering. Export every edge you already have into one file: first-degree connections, former colleagues at every employer, university and school alumni, people you worked with as a vendor or client, community members from Slack/Discord/meetups, contributors to repos you contributed to, people who replied to or shared your write-ups, and second-degree connections where you have a strong shared connection who would actually vouch. Then inner-join that person table against your forty companies on current employer - the joins you did not expect are the point. The research on this is old and stable: the ties that produce job outcomes are disproportionately weak ties, people outside your daily circle who sit in different information pools, so do not stop at the ten people you talk to weekly. Target a named human at twenty of the forty rows.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Interpersonal ties (strength of weak ties)

subtopics.name: Find the right human inside the account, not just any human
subtopics.learn: Rank who to reach in this order: a peer FDE at your target level in the same org (their referral carries the most weight, they are usually paid a bonus for it, and they can tell you what the loop actually contains), then the hiring manager named or implied by the req (search titles like Head of / Director of Forward Deployed, Solutions Engineering, Professional Services, Delivery), then anyone in the org who can route you internally, then the recruiter. A recruiter conversation is not a referral - keep them in different columns. Use people search with the current-company facet plus the connection-degree facet, and read the profile before contacting: tenure under three months means they cannot refer you yet at most companies, and someone who joined from a company you also worked at is a warmer edge than a stranger with a shared logo.

resource.label: LinkedIn Help - search, filters and connection degrees

subtopics.name: The forwardable blurb and the double opt-in intro
subtopics.learn: Never ask a broker to compose anything. Send them a self-contained block under 120 words they can forward untouched: one line of who you are with a single verifiable proof, the exact req (title, req id, link) so nobody has to search, one line on why you are credible for that specific req, one explicit ask - a referral submission or a fifteen-minute call, pick one, not both - and a graceful out that makes 'no' cheap. Run it double opt-in: ask the broker for permission before they forward, so the target is never ambushed and the broker is never embarrassed. Attach nothing; put the resume behind a link. Give a soft deadline anchored to the req's posted date rather than to your anxiety, and thank the broker with the outcome afterwards whether or not it worked - that is what makes the second ask possible.

resource.label: Fred Wilson (AVC) - The Double Opt-In Introduction, the post that defined the practice

subtopics.name: Manufacturing a path where none exists
subtopics.learn: For the twenty rows with no edge, build one over four to six weeks instead of cold-applying and hoping. The plays that work, in descending order of yield: make a real contribution to the company's public repos or docs - a reproducible bug report with a minimal repro, a failing test, a docs fix - which puts your name in front of the engineers who review it; publish a technical write-up that uses their product on a real problem and share it where their team already reads; answer questions in their community forum or Discord well enough to be recognised; show up to their meetup, office hours or conference talk and ask one specific question. All of these leave an artifact you can reference in the first line of an outreach message, which converts it from cold to warm. Budget this as real engineering time - a drive-by typo PR fools nobody.

resource.label: Open Source Guides - How to Contribute to Open Source

subtopics.name: Outreach cadence, and not burning the asset
subtopics.learn: Fix the cadence in advance so it is mechanical: initial ask, then one follow-up at about five business days that adds new information rather than repeating the request, then one final gracious close at about two weeks. Three touches, then stop and record closed_no_path - a fourth touch converts almost nothing and costs the relationship. Enforce a per-person budget so no single well-connected contact gets asked for four intros in a month. Read the professional network's user agreement before you automate anything: automated access and scraping are prohibited and enforcement is account-level, so a scraper run from your primary account can cost you the connection graph that is the entire asset of this topic. Use the public ATS APIs for volume and human hands for the network.

resource.label: LinkedIn - User Agreement (automated access and scraping restrictions)

subtopics.name: Pipeline arithmetic: concurrency, cycle time, and batching offers
subtopics.learn: Treat the search as a queueing system. Little's law says average items in the system equals arrival rate times average time in system, so if a loop takes five weeks end to end and you want four loops running concurrently, you need roughly 0.8 new loops entering per week - which, back-propagated through your own conversion rates, tells you how many intros and applications per week the list must sustain. Measure your real conversion at each transition rather than using folklore, but expect referred applications to convert to a recruiter screen roughly an order of magnitude better than cold ones, which is the entire justification for the referral work. Set an explicit WIP limit - about five active loops - because quality collapses past that, and deliberately batch the start dates so that offers land inside a two-week window; sequential offers give you no leverage, concurrent ones give you all of it.

resource.label: Wikipedia - Little's law (L = λW)

subtopics.name: Weekly cadence, automated refresh, and kill criteria
subtopics.learn: Make maintenance a thirty-minute scheduled ritual with a script doing the mechanical half. Automate: re-poll every board, mark reqs that vanished as closed, flag new reqs at existing target companies, and highlight every row whose next_step_due is past or whose last_touch is older than fourteen days - a time-driven trigger on the sheet or a cron'd script writing back through the Sheets API both work. Do by hand only what needs judgement: set next_step and next_step_due for every open row, and apply kill criteria without sentiment - no referral path found after two weeks of trying, or a req older than eight weeks with no movement, or an eligibility gate that flipped false, closes the row and you source a replacement the same session. The invariant is forty live rows, not forty rows ever created.

resource.label: Google Apps Script - installable triggers (time-driven / clock triggers for scheduled refresh)

outcomes: You can produce forty live rows where every row has a req_url, req_id, posted_date, a stored JD snapshot, an explicit eligibility verdict with the evidence behind it, and a comp band tagged as a US band or an India band with two independent sources.

You can refresh the live/closed status of all forty rows in under ten minutes by running one command against the public ATS endpoints, and produce a diff listing closed reqs, reposts and newly opened reqs at existing targets.
You can point at twenty rows that each name a specific human, your actual relationship to them, the exact ask you will make, and the date you last touched them.
You can hand your rubric and three unseen job descriptions to another engineer and their fit scores land within ten points of yours.
You can state, without opening a calculator, your current loop concurrency, your average cycle time in weeks, and how many new intros per week you need to hold four concurrent loops.
You can explain for any given row why 'Remote' on that posting does or does not include you, citing the specific sentence in the JD or the entity/EOR evidence you found.
You can name the five rows you would leave your current role for and defend the ranking on fit, band and eligibility rather than on brand.
You can show a weekly review that finishes in under thirty minutes and ends with every non-closed row carrying a next_step and a next_step_due.
failureModes: The sheet is built in one enthusiastic weekend and never re-verified, so by week four a third of the reqs are closed, you apply into dead requisitions, and you read the resulting silence as rejection instead of as a stale list.

You ask a weak-tie contact for a referral before they have seen any of your work, they submit a lukewarm one-line referral, and the req is now burned - a tepid referral is strictly worse than a cold application and it costs you the contact too.

You filter on the word 'Remote', skip the 'must be authorised to work in the United States' line buried in the requirements, spend five weeks in a loop, and the offer dies at the immigration check with the hiring manager annoyed at both of you.

You anchor your expectation on a US band for a role that will be paid on an India GCC band, and either price yourself out of a screen you would have passed or accept feeling cheated - because you never recorded which band the number came from.
You submit all forty applications in week one, rejections and offers land months apart, and you negotiate the only offer you have with zero concurrency and therefore zero leverage.

You automate against the professional network from your primary account, get restricted or banned, and lose the connection graph that twenty of your forty rows depended on - to save an hour of clicking.

'Applied' becomes a terminal state: a dozen rows sit with no owner and no next_step_due, the pipeline silently drains over six weeks, and you conclude the market is bad when what actually happened is that nobody was assigned the follow-up.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through your search. Which other companies are you talking to, how did you pick them, and what does that list tell me about what you actually want?

You are the first FDE on a new product. Two hundred customers have asked for a deployment and you have capacity for six this quarter. How do you build the shortlist, what do you measure, and what exactly do you say to the other one hundred and ninety-four?
You have been dropped into an account where you know nobody. Map the stakeholders in your first week: who do you need to find, how do you find them, and what is the one question you ask each of them?
Design the tracker for twelve concurrent customer deployments run by three engineers. What are the fields, what are the states and legal transitions, and what single metric would you put on the wall?

How do you decide to stop working an account that is not converting? Give me the actual criteria, not the principle - and tell me about a time you kept pushing past the point where you should have stopped.
Your champion offers to introduce you to their CTO next week. What exactly do you send the champion beforehand, and why that and not more?

You are comparing two engagements - one with a bigger logo and a worse-defined problem, one smaller with a crisp problem and an engaged owner. How do you compare them quantitatively, and what would change your answer?
90.proofOfWork: Build a small private pipeline repo that turns the forty-row sheet into a system rather than a document, and prove the loop ran rather than that the folder exists. It contains a refresh script that reads a config of (company, ats_vendor, board_token), pulls the public job-board JSON for each, writes a dated snapshot to disk, diffs it against the previous snapshot, and emits three things: a machine-written changelog of closed / reposted / newly-opened requisitions with req ids and dates, a write-back into the tracker that flips status and last_seen automatically, and a one-page weekly markdown digest listing every row whose next_step_due has passed or whose last_touch is more than fourteen days old. Alongside it, keep a referral graph file with a node per person (relationship, company, degree, tie strength, last_asked date) and an edge per way you know them, plus a rendered image of the graph with your forty target companies highlighted so the gaps are visible at a glance. Add a redacted outreach log with the exact text of every intro ask you sent, the broker, the date, the response and the time-to-response, and the exact text of any ask that got no reply so you can diff the ones that worked against the ones that did not. Finish with a six-week retro that states your predicted funnel conversion at each transition beside the observed one, names the two sourcing surfaces and the two referral path types that actually produced screens, and lists the rows you killed with the criterion that killed each - including at least one row you kept too long and what that cost you in weeks.

91.topic: Application pipeline: apply in waves, run three or four loops in parallel
91.why: An FDE job search is structurally identical to the job itself: a portfolio of accounts at different stages, each with a different stakeholder, each moving at a speed you do not control, all needing to be sequenced so decisions land when you need them to. Run serially, a search produces one decision every eight weeks and zero leverage; run as an instrumented pipeline with three or four loops converging, it produces two offers in the same fortnight and a real choice. The same instincts a hiring manager is testing - do you keep every thread alive with an owner and a due date, do you force a decision instead of waiting, do you tell the truth when timelines collide - are exactly the ones this topic drills, which is why running your own pipeline badly is itself a signal.
prerequisites: Three public case studies live with a single index link you can paste into any application (topic 80) - the pipeline moves at the speed of your artifacts, and you cannot tailor what does not exist.

The Hermes write-up published and a LinkedIn profile that reads as FDE rather than generic backend (topic 81), because inbound recruiter flow is a channel you will measure and it only exists if the profile does.
A 40-company target list with tiering, named referral paths and warm-intro routes already researched (topic 82). This topic consumes that list; it does not build it.

Enough technical readiness to survive a first-round screen in your two strongest areas today. Requisition cooldowns are 6-12 months at most large companies, so a wave sent before you can pass a screen spends a company you cannot get back.
Working comfort with a spreadsheet or a checked-in CSV as a system of record: formulas or a 60-line script, conditional formatting or a diff, and a scheduled job that emails you a digest.
An interview-ready environment and calendar hygiene - a quiet room, tested screen share and audio, and a calendar where your own blocks are real events rather than intentions.

subtopics.name: Model the search as a pipeline with explicit states and WIP limits
subtopics.learn: Draw the state machine before you open a spreadsheet: sourced, applied, recruiter screen, hiring-manager screen, technical round(s), full loop, team match, offer, decision - plus the terminal states reject, withdrew, ghosted and paused. Every state gets an owner (me or them), an expected dwell time, and a next-action-by date; a company with no next action is not in your pipeline, it is a memory. Set the work-in-progress limit deliberately: 3-4 companies in loop stages (technical onward) at once, because past four your prep time per loop drops below what actually wins rounds, plus 10-14 in the earlier feeding stages. WIP is the control variable you tune every Friday, not something that happens to you.

resource.label: Atlassian Agile Coach - Kanban (boards, work-in-progress limits, flow)

subtopics.name: Funnel math: the six conversion ratios and your own baselines
subtopics.learn: Instrument six ratios and compute each per channel and per wave: application to recruiter response, response to HM screen, screen to technical, technical to full loop, loop to offer, offer to accept. Know the shape of realistic numbers so you can tell a bad process from bad luck - a strong senior profile applying cold sees roughly 5-15% response, a warm referral pushes that first number to 40-60% and moves the loop-to-offer number almost not at all, which is precisely why referrals matter and precisely why they are not a substitute for readiness. Then back-solve: two offers inside one two-week window implies roughly 6-10 loops, which implies 25-40 real applications with a referral mix, not 200 portal submissions. Write the baseline down before wave one so wave two is a comparison rather than a feeling.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives (choosing indicators and targets)

subtopics.name: Wave sizing with Little's Law: how many applications must be in flight
subtopics.learn: L equals lambda times W. Cycle time W from application to decision is 4-8 weeks at most companies and 8-12 at Palantir-class loops with team matching and a hiring committee. If you want L equals 4 concurrent loops and W is 6 weeks, loops must start at 4/6, about 0.67 per week; at a 25% application-to-loop conversion that is roughly 2.7 applications per week sustained - about 11-12 per two-week wave, forever, not once. Do this arithmetic explicitly, because the non-obvious consequence is that the pipeline you can negotiate with in week 10 was determined by what you sent in week 2. You cannot fix a thin pipeline in the week an offer lands, and every week you skip a wave shows up as an empty slot forty days later.

resource.label: Little's Law (queueing relation between WIP, throughput and cycle time)

subtopics.name: Tracker schema: fields, states, and the one-row-per-application invariant
subtopics.learn: Design the schema once, with the fields that make the weekly review mechanical: company, req_url, req_id, tier, wave, channel (referral, recruiter_inbound, hm_direct, portal), referrer_name, date_applied, stage, stage_entered_at, next_action, next_action_due, owner (me or them), last_contact_at, recruiter_name, recruiter_email, interviewers, artifact_sent, level_target, comp_band_published, comp_anchor_given (boolean), expected_decision_date, outcome, reject_stage, reject_reason_code, notes_url. Enforce three invariants: one row per application, never one per company; stage_entered_at is rewritten on every transition so dwell time per stage is computable at the end; and any row where owner is me and next_action_due is in the past is a defect, not a to-do. Add reject_reason_code as a controlled vocabulary now (prep_gap, communication, scope_mismatch, level_mismatch, headcount_frozen, unknown) - free-text reasons are unanalysable in week ten.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Planning and tracking with Projects (custom fields, views, automation)

subtopics.name: Build it and automate the digest so you never have to check the tracker
subtopics.learn: Whatever the substrate, the rule is that the tracker pushes to you. In Sheets: conditional formatting turning next_action_due red when it is less than TODAY(), a stage histogram and the six ratios computed with COUNTIFS or a single QUERY, a weekly snapshot tab appended by a time-driven Apps Script trigger so you can chart stage counts over time, and a daily 08:00 MailApp.sendEmail digest listing overdue actions plus every row where owner is them and last_contact_at is more than seven days old. If you prefer git: a CSV in the repo, a 60-line Python script producing the same digest, and a cron or GitHub Action running it. Build it in one sitting and then stop building it - a tracker you are still improving in week six is a procrastination artifact.

resource.label: Google Apps Script - Extending Google Sheets (triggers, custom functions)

subtopics.name: Tier the 40 companies and assign waves so wave one is calibration
subtopics.learn: Split the target list from topic 82 into A (you would sign inside 48 hours), B (strong, right level and comp required) and C (fine, mainly loop practice and a floor offer). Then invert the instinct everyone has: wave one is roughly 60% C, 30% B, 10% A. Three reasons, all mechanical - your first three loops are objectively your worst, rejections carry a 6-12 month requisition cooldown at most large companies, and a live C-tier offer is the cheapest negotiating leverage that exists. For every row record the target level and the published or market band for that level and location so tier is a decision you can defend, not a vibe; a company whose band tops out below your floor belongs in C or off the list entirely.

resource.label: Levels.fyi - Software Engineer compensation in the United States (bands by level, company and location)

subtopics.name: Channel strategy and the reality of what a recruiter actually sees
subtopics.learn: Rank the channels by conversion and use them in order: internal referral, warm recruiter or inbound, direct hiring-manager contact, cold portal. Understand what the portal really is - your application lands in an ATS list view where a recruiter sees your name, current title, sometimes one screening-question answer, and decides in seconds; the top third of page one of the resume and the screening answers are therefore the entire product. Two sequencing rules that people get backwards: get the referral in flight before or with the portal submission, because a referral attached to an application that is already sitting in the pile is materially weaker than a referral-sourced application; and apply inside 72 hours of a requisition going live, since review is roughly first-in-first-seen and pipelines close early. Never hold two open applications at one company simultaneously - it reads as spraying.

resource.label: Greenhouse Support - Application review stage (what the recruiter sees per application, the referral priority queue, advance or reject)

subtopics.name: Referral engineering: the forwardable blurb and the ask that converts
subtopics.learn: Write a five-to-six-line blurb in the third person that your contact can paste into Slack with zero editing: who you are, the one number that proves the claim, the specific requisition link, and one sentence on why this company. Make the ask binary and cheap - 'would you be comfortable forwarding this to whoever owns the FDE req? Completely fine if not' - because the open-ended 'can you refer me' silently asks them to write the blurb, which is why it fails. For second-degree paths ask for an introduction to a named person, never a general introduction. Then run the follow-through that determines whether wave three still has referrals available: report back within five business days regardless of outcome, and cap yourself at two asks per contact per quarter. Log referrer_name on the row so the thank-you is scheduled, not remembered.

resource.label: Fred Wilson (AVC) - The Double Opt-In Introduction (the forwardable ask and introductions to a named person)

subtopics.name: Sourcing live requisitions beyond LinkedIn, and the seven title variants
subtopics.learn: LinkedIn misses a large fraction of FDE-shaped roles, and the title is not stable. Every wave, search all of: Forward Deployed Engineer, Forward Deployed Software Engineer, Solutions Engineer, Field Engineer, Deployment Strategist, Applied AI Engineer, and Technical Account Manager where the requisition is genuinely technical. Source from the monthly Hacker News Who Is Hiring thread, YC's startup job board, and company career pages directly - many boards expose a public JSON endpoint you can diff weekly with a short script so new requisitions surface the day they post rather than the week you happen to look. Freshness beats volume: a two-day-old requisition converts several times better than the same one at three weeks.
